## Preface

In recent years there has been renewed interest in the calculus of variations, motivated in part by ongoing research in materials science and other disciplines. Often, the study of certain material instabilities such as phase transi tions, formation of defects, the onset of microstructures in ordered materials, fracture and damage, leads to the search for equilibria through a minimization problem of the type 

$$
\min \left\{I (v): v \in \mathcal {V} \right\},
$$

where the class V of admissible functions v is a subset of some Banach space V. 

This is the essence of the calculus of variations: the identification of neces sary and suficient conditions on the functional I that guarantee the existence of minimizers. These rest on certain growth, coercivity, and convexity condi tions, which often fail to be satisfied in the context of interesting applications, thus requiring the relaxation of the energy. New ideas were needed, and the in troduction of innovative techniques has resulted in remarkable developments in the subject over the past twenty years, somewhat scattered in articles, preprints, books, or available only through oral communication, thus making it dificult to educate young researchers in this area. 

This is the first of two books in the calculus of variations and measure theory in which many results, some now classical and others at the forefront of research in the subject, are gathered in a unified, consistent way. A main concern has been to use contemporary arguments throughout the text to revisit and streamline well-known aspects of the theory, while providing novel contributions. 

The core of this book is the analysis of necessary and suficient conditions for sequential lower semicontinuity of functionals on $L ^ { p }$ spaces, followed by relaxation techniques. What sets this book apart from existing introductory texts in the calculus of variations is twofold: Instead of laying down the theory in the one-dimensional setting for integrands $f = f ( x , u , u ^ { \prime } )$ , we work in N dimensions and no derivatives are present. In addition, it is self-contained in the sense that, with the exception of fundamentally basic results in measure theory that may be found in any textbook on the subject (e.g., Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem), all the statements are fully justified and proved. This renders it accessible to beginning graduate students with basic knowledge of measure theory and functional analysis. Moreover, we believe that this text is unique as a reference book for researchers, since it treats both necessary and suficient conditions for well-posedness and lower semicontinuity of functionals, while usually only suficient conditions are addressed. 

The central part of this book is Part III, although Parts I and II contain original contributions. Part I covers background material on measure theory, integration, and $L ^ { p }$ spaces, and it combines basic results with new approaches to the subject. In particular, in contrast to most texts in the subject, we do not restrict the context to σ-finite measures, therefore laying the basis for the treatment of Hausdorf measures, which will be ubiquitous in the setting of the second volume, in which gradients will be present. Moreover, we call attention to Section 1.1.4, on “comparison between measures”, which is com pletely novel: The Radon–Nikodym theorem and the Lebesgue decomposition theorem are proved for positive measures without our having first to introduce signed measures, as is usual in the literature. The new arguments are based on an unpublished theorem due to De Giorgi treating the case in which the two measures in play are not σ-finite. Here, as De Giorgi’s theorem states, a difuse measure must be added to the absolutely continuous and singular parts of the decomposition. Also, we give a detailed proof of the Morse covering theorem, which does not seem to be available in other books on the subject, and we derive as a corollary the Besicovitch covering theorem instead of proving it directly. 

Part II streamlines the study of convex functions, and the treatment of the direct method of the calculus of variations introduces the reader to the close connection between sequential lower semicontinuity properties and existence of minimizers. Again here we present an unpublished theorem of De Giorgi, the approximation theorem for real-valued convex functions, which provides an explicit formula for the afine functions approximating a given convex function f. A major advantage of this characterization is that additional regularity hypotheses on f are reflected immediately on the approximating afine func tions. 

In Part III we treat sequential lower semicontinuity of functionals defined on $L ^ { p } .$ , and we separate the cases of inhomogeneous and homogeneous functionals. The latter are studied in Chapter 5, where 

$$
I (u) := \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x
$$

with E a Lebesgue measurable subset of the Euclidean space $\mathbb { R } ^ { N } , f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m } $ $( - \infty , \infty ]$ and $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ for $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ . This material is intended for an introductory graduate course in the calculus of variations, since it requires only basic knowledge of measure theory and functional analysis. We treat both bounded and unbounded domains E, and we address most types of strong and weak convergence. In particular, the setting in which the underlying convergence is that of $\left( C _ { b } \left( E \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ is new. 

Chapter 6 and Chapter 7 are devoted to integrands $f = f \left( x , v \right)$ and $f =$ $f \left( x , u , v \right)$ , respectively, and are significantly more advanced, since the proofs of the necessity parts are heavily hinged on the concept of multifunctions. An important tool here is selection criteria, and the reader will benefit from a comprehensive and detailed study of this subject. 

Finally, Chapter 8 describes basic properties of Young measures and how they may be used in relaxation theory. 

The bibliography aims at giving the main references relevant to the contents of the book. It is by no means exhaustive, and many important contributions to the subject may have failed to be listed here. 

To conclude, this text is intended as a graduate textbook as well as a ref erence for more-experienced researchers working in the calculus of variations, and is written with the intention that readers with varied backgrounds may access diferent parts of the text. 

This book prepares the ground for a second volume, since it introduces and develops the basic tools in the calculus of variations and in measure the ory needed to address fundamental questions in the treatment of functionals involving derivatives. 

Finally, in a book of this length, typos and errors are almost inevitable. The authors will be very grateful to those readers who will write to either fonseca@andrew.cmu.edu or giovanni@andrew.cmu.edu indicating those that they have found. A list of errors and misprints will be maintained and updated at the web page http://www.math.cmu.edu/˜leoni/book1.

## 1.1 Measures and Integration

This chapter covers a wide range of properties of measures. Those that we consider basic and well known (for example the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem) will only be stated, and the reader is referred to classical textbooks such as [DB02], [EvGa92], [Fol99], [Rao04], [Ru87], [Z67]. The reader should be warned that in some of these books outer measures are called measures. 

Results that are dificult to find in the literature, that are new, or that may be presented in a more contemporary way will be proved in this text. 

## 1.1.1 Measures and Outer Measures

Definition 1.1. Let X be a nonempty set. A collection ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ is an algebra if 

(i) $\varnothing \in { \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mathrm { : } }$ 

(ii) if $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ then $X \setminus E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

(iii) if $E _ { 1 } , E _ { 2 } \in \mathfrak { M }$ then $E _ { 1 } \cup E _ { 2 } \in \mathfrak { M } .$ 

M is said to be a σ-algebra if it satisfies $( i ) { - } ( i i )$ and 

(iii)<sup></sup> $i f \left\{ E _ { n } \right\} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ then $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

To highlight the dependence of the σ-algebra M on X we will sometimes use the notation M (X). If M is a σ-algebra then the pair (X, M) is called a measurable space. For simplicity we will often apply the term measurable space only to $X$ 

Using De Morgan’s laws and (ii) and $( \mathrm { i i i } ) ^ { \prime }$ , it follows that a σ-algebra is closed under countable intersection. In particular, if E, $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ then $E \cap F \in$ M, and this leads to the notion of restriction of M to a set $E \subset X$ (not necessarily measurable), i.e., the induced σ-algebra 

$$
\mathfrak {M} \lfloor E := \{E \cap F: F \in \mathfrak {M} \}.
$$

Example 1.2. (i) In view of (i) and (ii), every algebra contains X. Hence the smallest algebra (respectively σ-algebra) is $\{ \emptyset , X \}$ and the largest is the collection ${ \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ of all subsets of $X$ 

(ii) If $X \ = \ [ 0 , 1 )$ , the family M of all finite unions of intervals of the type $[ a , b ) \subset [ 0 , 1 )$ is an algebra but not a σ-algebra. Indeed, 

$$
E := \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left[ 0, \frac {1}{n}\right) = \{0 \} \notin \mathfrak {M}.
$$

Let X be a nonempty set. Given any subset ${ \mathcal { F } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ the smallest (in the sense of inclusion) σ-algebra that contains $\mathcal { F }$ is given by the intersection of all σ-algebras on $X$ that contain $\mathcal { F }$ 

If X is a topological space, then the Borel σ-algebra $B \left( X \right)$ is the smallest σ-algebra containing all open subsets of X. The elements of $B \left( X \right)$ are called Borel sets. Unless indicated otherwise, in the sequel it is understood that the Euclidean space $\mathbb { R } ^ { N } , N \geq 1$ , and the extended real line $\overline { { \mathbb { R } } } : = [ - \infty , \infty ]$ are endowed with the Borel σ-algebras associated to the respective usual topologies: In $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ we consider the Euclidean norm 

$$
| x | := \sqrt {(x _ {1}) ^ {2} + \ldots + (x _ {N}) ^ {2}}
$$

with ${ \boldsymbol x } = ( x _ { 1 } , \dots , x _ { N } )$ , and we take as basis of open sets in $\overline { { \mathbb { R } } }$ the collection of all intervals of the form $( a , b ) , ( a , \infty ] , [ - \infty , b )$ with $a , b \in \mathbb { R }$ 

Remark 1.3. If X is a topological space and $Y \subset X$ then 

$$
\mathcal {B} (Y) = \mathcal {B} (X) \lfloor Y.\tag{1.1}
$$

Indeed, $B \left( X \right) \lfloor Y$ is a σ-algebra in $Y$ that contains 

$$
\left\{A \cap Y: A \text {   is   open   in   } X \right\} = \left\{A ^ {\prime}: A ^ {\prime} \text {   is   open   in   } Y \right\}.
$$

By definition of $B \left( Y \right)$ we deduce that $B \left( Y \right) \subset B \left( X \right) \lfloor Y$ . Conversely, let 

$$
\mathfrak {N} := \left\{F \subset X: F \cap Y \in \mathcal {B} (Y) \right\}.
$$

Then N is a σ-algebra in X that contains all open sets in X. Hence $B \left( X \right) \subset \mathfrak { N }$ and so $B \left( Y \right) \supset B \left( X \right) \lfloor Y$ 

Definition 1.4. Let X be a nonempty set, let ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be an algebra, and let $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ 

(i) $\mu$ is a (positive) finitely additive measure if 

$$
\mu (\emptyset) = 0, \quad \mu (E _ {1} \cup E _ {2}) = \mu (E _ {1}) + \mu (E _ {2})
$$

for all $E _ { 1 } , E _ { 2 } \in \mathfrak { M }$ with $E _ { 1 } \cap E _ { 2 } = \emptyset$ 

(ii) $\mu$ is a (positive) countably additive measure if 

$$
\mu (\emptyset) = 0, \quad \mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (E _ {n})
$$

for every countable collection $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ of pairwise disjoint sets such that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } \in \mathfrak { M }$ 

Definition 1.5. Let X be a nonempty set, let ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be a σ-algebra. 

(i) A map $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is called a (positive) measure if 

$$
\mu (\emptyset) = 0, \quad \mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (E _ {n})
$$

for every countable collection $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ of pairwise disjoint sets. The triple $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ is said to be a measure space. 

(ii) Given a measure $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ , a set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ has σ-finite µ measure if it can be written as a countable union of measurable sets of finite measure; $\mu$ is said to be σ-finite if X has σ-finite $\mu$ measure; $\mu$ is said to be finite if $\mu \left( X \right) < \infty$ . Analogous definitions can be given for finitely additive measures. 

(iii) A measure $\mu$ is said to be a probability measure if $\mu \left( X \right) = 1$ 

Exercise 1.6. (i) Let X be a nonempty set. Show that the function $\mu :$ ${ \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ defined by 

$$
\mu \left(E\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \text { card   } E \text {   if   } E \text {   is   finite }, \\ \infty \qquad \text { otherwise }, \end{array} \right.
$$

is a measure. Here card is the cardinality. The measure $\mu$ is called the counting measure. Prove that $\mu$ is finite (respectively σ-finite) if and only if X is finite (respectively denumerable). 

(ii) Given a sequence $\{ x _ { n } \}$ of nonnegative numbers we introduce $\mu : \mathcal P ( \mathbb { N } ) $ $[ 0 , \infty ]$ as 

$$
\mu (E) := \sum_ {n \in E} x _ {n}, \quad E \subset \mathbb {N}.
$$

Prove that $\mu$ is a σ-finite measure. 

If $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ is a measure space then the restriction of $\mu$ to a subset $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ is the measure $\mu \lfloor E : \mathfrak { M } \to \lbrack 0 , \infty \rbrack$ defined by 

$$
(\mu \lfloor E) (F) := \mu (F \cap E), \quad F \in \mathfrak {M}.
$$

Often, when there is no possibility of confusion, we use the same notation $\mu \vert E$ to denote the restriction of the measure $\mu$ to the σ-algebra ${ \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor E .$ 

Among properties of measures we single out the following monotone convergence results. 

Proposition 1.7. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. 

(i) $H \left\{ E _ { n } \right\}$ is an increasing sequence of subsets of M then 

$$
\mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu \left(E _ {n}\right).
$$

(ii) $H \left\{ E _ { n } \right\}$ is a decreasing sequence of subsets of M and $\mu \left( E _ { 1 } \right) < \infty$ then 

$$
\mu \left(\bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu \left(E _ {n}\right).
$$

Proof. (i) If $\mu \left( E _ { n } \right) = \infty$ for some $n \in \mathbb N$ then both sides in (i) are $\infty$ and there is nothing to prove. Thus assume that $\mu \left( E _ { n } \right) < \infty$ for all $n \in \mathbb N$ and define 

$$
F _ {n} := E _ {n} \setminus E _ {n - 1},
$$

where $E _ { 0 } : = \varnothing$ . Since $\{ E _ { n } \}$ is an increasing sequence, it follows that the sets $F _ { n }$ are pairwise disjoint with $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } = { \bar { \bigcup } } _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } F _ { n }$ , and so by the properties of measures we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {n}\right) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(F _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {l \to \infty} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \mu \left(F _ {n}\right) \\ = \lim _ {l \to \infty} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \left(\mu \left(E _ {n}\right) - \mu \left(E _ {n - 1}\right)\right) = \lim _ {l \to \infty} \mu \left(E _ {l}\right). \end{array}
$$

(ii) Apply part (i) to the increasing sequence $\{ E _ { 1 } \setminus E _ { n } \}$ 

Example 1.8. Without the hypothesis $\mu \left( E _ { 1 } \right) < \infty$ , property (ii) may be false. Indeed, consider the counting measure defined in Exercise 1.6 with $X : = \mathbb { N }$ and define $E _ { n } : = \{ n , n + 1 , \ldots , \}$ . Then $\{ E _ { n } \}$ is a decreasing sequence, $\mu \left( E _ { n } \right) = \infty$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , but 

$$
\mu \left(\bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \mu (\emptyset) = 0 \neq \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu (E _ {n}) = \infty .
$$

It turns out that for a finitely additive measure, property (i) is equivalent to countable additivity. Indeed, we have the following proposition. 

Proposition 1.9. Let X be a nonempty set, let ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be an algebra, and let $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a finitely additive measure. Then $\mu$ is countably additive if and only if 

$$
\mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu \left(E _ {n}\right)\tag{1.2}
$$

for every increasing sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ such that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

In addition, if $\mu$ is finite then $\mu$ is countably additive if and only if 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu (E _ {n}) = 0\tag{1.3}
$$

for every decreasing sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ such that $\textstyle \bigcap _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } = \varnothing$ 

Proof. If $\mu$ is countably additive, then (1.2) and (1.3) follow as in the proof of Proposition 1.7. Suppose now that (1.2) holds. Let $\{ F _ { n } \} \subset { \mathfrak { M } }$ be a sequence of mutually disjoint sets such that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } F _ { n } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , and define 

$$
E _ {n} := \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {n} F _ {k}.
$$

Then by (1.2) we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu \left(\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {k}\right) = \mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu \left(E _ {n}\right) \\ = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \mu \left(F _ {k}\right) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(F _ {k}\right), \end{array}
$$

and with this we have shown that $\mu$ is countably additive. 

Finally, assume that $\mu$ is finite and that (1.3) holds. We claim that (1.2) is satisfied. Let $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ be an increasing sequence such that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ Then the sequence 

$$
F _ {n} := \left(\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {k}\right) \setminus E _ {n}
$$

is decreasing and $\textstyle \bigcap _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } F _ { n } = \varnothing$ . Hence from (1.3), 

$$
0 = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu (F _ {n}) = \mu \left(\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {k}\right) - \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu (E _ {n}),
$$

and this proves (1.2). 

Exercise 1.10. Let $X : = \mathbb { N }$ and let M be the algebra consisting of all finite subsets of N and their complements. Show that the set function $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to$ $\{ 0 , \infty \}$ given by 

$$
\mu \left(E\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0 & \text {if E is finite,} \\ \infty & \text {otherwise,} \end{array} \right.
$$

is a finitely additive measure satisfying property (ii) of Proposition 1.7 but it is not countably additive. 

Using the previous proposition one may characterize finitely additive measures that are not countably additive. This brings us to the following definition. 

Definition 1.11. Let X be a nonempty set and let ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be an algebra. A finitely additive measure $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is said to be purely finitely additive if there exists no nontrivial countably additive measure $\nu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ with $0 \leq \nu \leq \mu$ 

Theorem 1.12 (Hewitt–Yosida). Let X be a nonempty set, let ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be an algebra and let $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ be a finitely additive measure. Then µ can be uniquely written as a sum of a countably additive measure and a purely finitely additive measure. 

Proof. For $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ define 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu_ {p} \left(E\right) := \sup \Big \{\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu \left(E _ {n}\right): \left\{E _ {n} \right\} \subset \mathfrak {M},   E _ {n + 1} \subset E _ {n} \text { for all } n, \\ E _ {n} \subset E \text { for all } n,   \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n} = \emptyset \Big \}, \\ \mu_ {c} \left(E\right) := \mu \left(E\right) - \mu_ {p} \left(E\right). \end{array}
$$

One can verify that $\mu _ { p }$ and $\mu _ { c }$ are finitely additive measures. We now show that $\mu _ { c }$ is countably additive. Let $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ be a decreasing sequence with $\textstyle \bigcap _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } = \varnothing$ . Then from the definition of $\mu _ { p }$ for each $l \in \mathbb N$ we have 

$$
\infty > \mu (E _ {l}) \geq \mu_ {p} (E _ {l}) \geq \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu (E _ {n}),
$$

and so, letting $l \to \infty$ , we obtain 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {p} (E _ {n}) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu (E _ {n}) <   \infty ,
$$

which implies that li $\scriptstyle 1 _ { n \to \infty } \mu _ { c } \left( E _ { n } \right) = 0$ . The claim now follows from Proposition 1.9. 

Next we show that $\mu _ { p }$ is a purely finitely additive measure. Let $\nu : \mathfrak { M } \to$ $[ 0 , \infty ]$ be a countably additive measure with $0 \leq \nu \leq \mu _ { p }$ . For any $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ set $r : = { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 3 } } } \nu \left( E \right)$ . Then $\mu _ { p } \left( E \right) \geq 3 r$ , and so if $r > 0$ there exists a decreasing sequence $\left\{ E _ { n } \right\} \subset { \mathfrak { M } }$ of subsets of E, with $\textstyle \bigcap _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } = \varnothing$ , such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu \left(E _ {n}\right) > 2 r.
$$

Then $\mu _ { p } \left( E _ { n } \right) > 2 r$ for every $n \in \mathbb { N }$ (since the sequence $\left\{ E _ { k } \right\} _ { k = n } ^ { \infty }$ is admissible in the definition of $\mu _ { p } \left( E _ { n } \right) )$ ), while $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } \nu ( E _ { n } ) = 0 } \end{array}$ . Hence 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \nu \left(E \setminus E _ {n}\right) = 3 r,
$$

and so for all n suficiently large, 

$$
\mu_ {p} (E) = \mu_ {p} (E _ {n}) + \mu_ {p} (E \setminus E _ {n}) > 2 r + \nu (E \setminus E _ {n}) > 4 r.
$$

Inductively we would obtain $\mu _ { p } \left( E \right) > l r$ for every $l \in \mathbb N$ , and this would contradict the fact that $\mu _ { p }$ is finite. Hence $\nu \equiv 0$ and $\mu _ { p }$ is a purely finitely additive measure. 

Exercise 1.13. Prove that $\mu _ { p }$ and $\mu _ { c }$ are finitely additive measures and that the decomposition $\mu = \mu _ { p } + \mu _ { c }$ in the previous theorem is unique. 

Example 1.14. The finitely additive measure $\mu$ defined in Exercise 1.10 is purely finitely additive. Indeed, if $\nu : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a countably additive measure with $0 \leq \nu \leq \mu$ , then since $\mu \left( \{ 1 , \ldots , n \} \right) = 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb N$ , we have that $\nu \left( \{ 1 , \ldots , n \} \right) = 0$ and so from Proposition $1 . 7 ( \mathrm { i } )$ it follows that 

$$
\nu \left(\mathbb {N}\right) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \nu \left(\{1, \dots , n \}\right) = 0.
$$

Hence $\nu \equiv 0$ and $\mu$ is purely finitely additive. 

The next proposition will be particularly useful for the analysis of derivatives of measures and in the application of the blowup method (see Theorem 5.14). 

Proposition 1.15. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with µ finite and let $\{ E _ { j } \} _ { \mathfrak { i } \in J } \subset \mathfrak { M }$ be an arbitrary family of pairwise disjoint subsets of X. Then $\mu \left( E _ { j } \right) = 0$ for all but at most countably many $j \in J$ 

Proof. Fix $k \in \mathbb N$ and let 

$$
J _ {k} := \left\{j \in J: \mu (E _ {j}) > \frac {1}{k} \right\}.
$$

We claim that the set $J _ { k }$ is finite. Indeed, if I is any finite subset of $J _ { k }$ , then 

$$
\infty > \mu (X) \geq \mu \left(\bigcup_ {j \in I} E _ {j}\right) = \sum_ {j \in I} \mu \left(E _ {j}\right) \geq \frac {1}{k} \sum_ {j \in I} 1 = \frac {1}{k} \operatorname{card} I,
$$

which implies that $J _ { k }$ cannot have more than $\lceil k \mu \left( X \right) \rceil$ elements, where $\lceil k \mu \left( X \right) \rceil$ is the integer part of $k \mu \left( X \right)$ . Thus 

$$
\{j \in J: \mu (E _ {j}) > 0 \} = \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} J _ {k}
$$

is at most countable. 

The definition below introduces very important properties of measures that may be perceived as some sort of Darboux continuity. 

Definition 1.16. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. 

(i) The measure $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is said to have the finite subset property or to be semifinite if for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $\mu \left( E \right) > 0$ , there exists $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $F \subset E$ , such that $0 < \mu \left( F \right) < \infty$ 

(ii) A set $E ~ \in ~ \mathfrak { M }$ of positive measure is said to be an atom if for every $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $F \subset E$ , either $\mu \left( F \right) = 0 o r \mu \left( F \right) = \mu \left( E \right)$ . The measure $\mu$ is said to be nonatomic if there are no atoms, that is, if for every set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ of positive measure there exists $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $F \subset E$ , such that $0 < \mu \left( F \right) < \mu \left( E \right)$ 

Example 1.17. (i) We will show in Remark 1.161 that the Lebesgue measure is nonatomic. An important class of non-σ-finite nonatomic measures is given by the Hausdorf measures $\mathcal { H } ^ { s } , s > 0$ (see $[ \mathrm { F o L e 1 0 } ] )$ 

(ii) To construct an example of a measure with the finite subset property that is not σ-finite, let X be an uncountable set, and to every finite set assign a measure equal to its cardinality; to all other sets assign measure ∞. 

Exercise 1.18. Let X be a nonempty set and let $f : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be any function. The set function $\mu : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ defined by 

$$
\mu (E) := \sup \left\{\sum_ {x \in F} f (x): F \subset E, F \text { finite } \right\}, \quad E \subset X,
$$

is a measure. Show that 

(i) $\mu$ has the finite subset property if and only if $f \left( x \right) < \infty$ for all $x \in X$ ; (ii) $\mu$ is σ-finite if and only if $f \left( x \right) ~ < ~ \infty$ for all $x \in \ X$ and the set $\{ x \in X : f \left( x \right) > 0 \}$ is countable. In the special case $f \equiv 1$ we obtain the counting measure, while if 

$$
f \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1 \text {   if   } x = x _ {0}, \\ 0 \text {   otherwise }, \end{array} \right.
$$

for some fixed $x _ { 0 } \in X$ , then for every $E \subset X$ , 

$$
\mu \left(E\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1 \text {   if   } x _ {0} \in E, \\ 0 \text {   otherwise. } \end{array} \right.
$$

Then $\mu$ is called Dirac delta measure with mass concentrated at the point $x _ { 0 }$ and is denoted by $\delta _ { x _ { 0 } }$ . Prove that the set $\{ x _ { 0 } \}$ is an atom. 

Remark 1.19. (i) It follows from the definition that a nonatomic measure has the finite subset property. Another important class of measures with the finite subset property is given by σ-finite measures. Indeed, if $\mu$ is a σ-finite measure, then 

$$
X = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} X _ {n}
$$

with $X _ { n } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\mu \left( X _ { n } \right) < \infty$ . Hence if $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\mu \left( E \right) > 0$ , then there exists n such that $0 < \mu \left( E \cap X _ { n } \right) \leq \mu \left( X _ { n } \right) < \infty$ 

(ii) The reader should be warned that in the literature there are at least two, more restrictive, definitions of atoms. In some papers atoms are defined as above, but they are required to have finite measure, while in others a set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ of positive measure is said to be an atom if for every $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $F \subset E$ , either $\mu \left( F \right) = 0$ or $\mu \left( E \setminus F \right) = 0$ . The main diference consists in the fact that with these two definitions there could be nonatomic measures of the form $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \{ 0 , \infty \}$ , while with the definition that we have adopted, any set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor E \to \{ 0 , \infty \}$ is considered an atom. Note that for measures with the finite subset property (and in particular for finite or σ-finite measures) all these definitions are equivalent, since sets $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor E \to \{ 0 , \infty \}$ are automatically excluded. The main advantage with our approach is that nonatomic nonfinite measures preserve many of the important features of nonatomic finite measures such as the Darboux property given in the following theorem. Readers more familiar with the other definitions of atoms should simply assume in all the theorems on nonatomic measures that the finite subset property holds. 

The next two results play an important role in the study of the well posedness of energy functionals as illustrated in Theorem 5.1. 

Proposition 1.20. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with $\mu$ nonatomic. Then the range of $\mu$ is the closed interval $[ 0 , \mu \left( X \right) ]$ 

Proof. Fix $0 < t < \mu \left( X \right)$ and let 

$$
\mathcal {C} := \left\{E \in \mathfrak {M}: 0 <   \mu (E) \leq t \right\}.
$$

We claim that C is nonempty. Indeed, since $\mu$ is nonatomic, there exists $X _ { 1 } \in$ M with $0 < \mu \left( X _ { 1 } \right) < \mu \left( X \right)$ . Using again the fact that $\mu$ is nonatomic, it is possible to partition 

$$
X _ {1} = F _ {1} \cup F _ {2},
$$

where $F _ { i } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $0 < \mu ( F _ { i } ) < \mu ( X _ { 1 } ) , i = 1 , 2$ . Therefore one of the two sets $F _ { 1 }$ and $F _ { 2 }$ has measure equal to at most ${ \scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \mu \left( X _ { 1 } \right)$ , and we call that set $E _ { 1 }$ . By induction, assuming that $E _ { 1 } , \ldots , E _ { n }$ have been selected with 

$$
0 <   \mu \left(E _ {n}\right) \leq \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}} \mu \left(X _ {1}\right),\tag{1.4}
$$

as before we find $E _ { n + 1 } ~ \subset ~ E _ { n }$ such that $E _ { n + 1 } \ \in \ { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $0 < \mu \left( E _ { n + 1 } \right) \leq$ ${ \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \mu \left( E _ { n } \right)$ . We have constructed a sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ satisfying (1.4), and so for n large enough, $E _ { n } \in \mathcal { C }$ 

Next we claim that there exists a measurable set with measure t. The proof is again by induction. Set $F _ { 0 } : = \varnothing$ , and suppose that $F _ { n }$ has been given. Define 

$$
t _ {n} := \sup \left\{\mu (E): E \supset F _ {n}, E \in \mathfrak {M}, \mu (E) \leq t \right\}
$$

and let $F _ { n + 1 } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ be such that $F _ { n + 1 } \supset F _ { n }$ and 

$$
t _ {n} - \frac {1}{n} \leq \mu (F _ {n + 1}) \leq t _ {n}.\tag{1.5}
$$

Note that $0 \leq t _ { n + 1 } \leq t _ { n } \leq t$ , and so there exists 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} t _ {n} = s \leq t.\tag{1.6}
$$

Set 

$$
F _ {\infty} := \bigcup_ {n} F _ {n}.\tag{1.7}
$$

By Proposition 1.7(ii) and (1.5), 

$$
\mu \left(F _ {\infty}\right) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu \left(F _ {n}\right) = s.
$$

It remains to show that $s = t .$ . If $s < t$ then 

$$
\mu \left(X \setminus F _ {\infty}\right) = \mu \left(X\right) - \mu \left(F _ {\infty}\right) > t - s > 0,
$$

and so reasoning as in the first part of the proof with $X \backslash F _ { \infty }$ in place of X and $t - s$ in place of t there would exist a set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $E \subset X \setminus F _ { \infty }$ and 

$$
0 <   \mu (E) \leq t - s.
$$

Thus 

$$
s = \mu (F _ {\infty}) <   \mu (E \cup F _ {\infty}) \leq t,
$$

and so by (1.6) it would follow that $t _ { n } < \mu ( E \cup F _ { \infty } )$ for all n suficiently large. Since $F _ { n } \subset E \cup F _ { \infty }$ by (1.7), this would contradict the definition of $t _ { n }$ for all n suficiently large. 

A consequence of the previous theorem is the following result, which will be repeatedly used in the second part of the book (see, e.g., the proof of Theorem 5.1). 

Corollary 1.21. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with $\mu$ nonatomic. Let $\{ r _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of positive numbers such that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} r _ {n} \leq \mu (X).
$$

Then there exists a sequence of mutually disjoint measurable sets $\{ E _ { n } \}$ such that $\mu \left( E _ { n } \right) = r _ { n }$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

Proof. By Proposition 1.20 there exists a measurable set $E _ { 1 }$ such that $\mu \left( E _ { 1 } \right) = r _ { 1 }$ . Since $\mu \left( X \setminus E _ { 1 } \right) \geq r _ { 2 }$ , again invoking the previous proposition we may find a measurable set $E _ { 2 } \subset X \setminus E _ { 1 }$ such that $\mu \left( E _ { 2 } \right) = r _ { 2 }$ . A simple induction argument yields a family of measurable sets $E _ { n }$ with 

$$
E _ {n} \subset X \setminus \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {n - 1} E _ {i}, \quad \mu (E _ {n}) = r _ {n}.
$$

This concludes the proof. 

If a measure $\mu$ has atoms, then it is possible to decompose it into the sum of a nonatomic measure and a purely atomic measure, that is, a measure such that every set of positive measure contains an atom. Precisely, we have the following result. 

Proposition 1.22. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Then there exist measures $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that $\mu _ { 1 }$ is purely atomic, $\mu _ { 2 }$ is nonatomic, and $\mu = \mu _ { 1 } + \mu _ { 2 }$ 

We begin with a preliminary result that is of interest in itself. 

Lemma 1.23. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $\Re \subset \mathfrak { M }$ be a family closed under finite unions and such that $\varnothing \in { \mathfrak { N } }$ . Then the set functions $\mu _ { 1 }$ $\mu _ { 2 } : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ defined by 

$$
\mu_ {1} (E) := \sup \left\{\mu (E \cap F): F \in \mathfrak {N} \right\}, \quad E \in \mathfrak {M},\tag{1.8}
$$

$$
\mu_ {2} (E) := \sup \left\{\mu (E \cap F): F \in \mathfrak {M}, \mu_ {1} (F) = 0 \right\}, \quad E \in \mathfrak {M},\tag{1.9}
$$

are measures, $\mu = \mu _ { 1 } + \mu _ { 2 }$ , and $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \right) = \mu \left( E \right)$ for all $E \in { \mathfrak { N } }$ . Moreover, for each $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ the suprema in the definition of $\mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ are actually attained by measurable sets. 

Proof. Step 1: We begin by showing that $\mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ are measures. Observe that if $E \in \mathfrak { N }$ , then the right-hand side of (1.8) coincides with $\mu \left( E \right)$ , and so $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \right) = \mu \left( E \right)$ . In particular, since $\varnothing \in \mathfrak { N }$ we have that $\mu _ { 1 } \left( \varnothing \right) = 0$ . Let $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset$ M be any sequence of pairwise disjoint sets. Then for every $F \in \mathfrak { N }$ 

$$
\mu \left(\left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \cap F\right) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(E _ {n} \cap F\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu_ {1} \left(E _ {n}\right),
$$

and taking the supremum over al $F \in \mathfrak { N }$ , we obtain that 

$$
\mu_ {1} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu_ {1} \left(E _ {n}\right).
$$

To prove the reverse inequality it sufices to assume that $\textstyle \mu _ { 1 } ( \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } ) < \infty$ Since $\mu _ { 1 }$ is monotone with respect to inclusion, it follows that $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E _ { n } \right) < \infty$ for all $n \in \mathbb N$ , and so for very fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ and for each $n \in \mathbb N$ we may find $F _ { n } \in \mathfrak { N }$ such that 

$$
\mu_ {1} \left(E _ {n}\right) \leq \mu \left(E _ {n} \cap F _ {n}\right) + \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n}}.
$$

Hence for every $l \in \mathbb N$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \mu_ {1} (E _ {n}) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \left(\mu (E _ {n} \cap F _ {n}) + \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n}}\right) \leq \mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {l} (E _ {n} \cap F _ {n})\right) + \varepsilon \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n} \cap \left(\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {l} F _ {k}\right)\right) + \varepsilon \leq \mu_ {1} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) + \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { k = 1 } ^ { l } F _ { k }$ belongs to N. By letting first $l \to \infty$ and then $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ we conclude that $\mu _ { 1 }$ is a measure. 

Moreover, since N is closed under finite unions, for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ we may find an increasing sequence of sets $\{ F _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { N }$ such that 

$$
\mu_ {1} (E) = \mu (E \cap F _ {\infty}), \quad \text { where } F _ {\infty} := \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {n}.\tag{1.10}
$$

This shows that the supremum in the definition of $\mu _ { 1 }$ is attained. 

Since $\mu _ { 1 }$ is a measure, the family ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { 1 } : = \{ F \in { \mathfrak { M } } \colon \mu _ { 1 } ( F ) = 0 \}$ is closed under finite unions and contains ∅, and so, applying what we just proved with $\mu _ { 1 }$ and N replaced by $\mu _ { 2 }$ and ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { 1 }$ , respectively, we obtain that also $\mu _ { 2 }$ is a measure and that the supremum in the definition of $\mu _ { 2 }$ is attained. 

Step 2: It remains to show that $\mu = \mu _ { 1 } + \mu _ { 2 }$ . Fix $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . Since $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ $\mu _ { 2 } \left( E \right) \leq \mu \left( E \right)$ , then if $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \right) = \infty \mathrm { o r } \mu _ { 2 } \left( E \right) = \infty$ , there is nothing to prove. Thus assume that $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \right) , \mu _ { 2 } \left( E \right) < \infty$ and let $F _ { \infty }$ be defined as in (1.10). We claim that $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \setminus F _ { \infty } \right) = 0$ . Indeed, if $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \setminus F _ { \infty } \right) > 0$ then we would be able to find $F \in \mathfrak { N }$ such that 

$$
\mu_ {1} \left(E \setminus F _ {\infty}\right) \geq \mu \left(\left(E \setminus F _ {\infty}\right) \cap F\right) > 0.
$$

But then 

$$
\mu_ {1} (E) = \mu (E \cap F _ {\infty}) <   \mu (E \cap (F _ {\infty} \cup F)) = \lim _ {l \rightarrow \infty} \mu \left(E \cap \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {l} F _ {n} \cup F\right)\right),
$$

and since $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { l } F _ { n } \cup F \in \mathfrak { N }$ , if l is suficiently large we would contradict the definition of $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ . Hence $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \setminus F _ { \infty } \right) = 0$ , and so by (1.9) we have $\mu _ { 2 } \left( E \right) \ge \mu \left( E \setminus F _ { \infty } \right)$ . Thus 

$$
\mu_ {1} (E) + \mu_ {2} (E) \geq \mu (E \cap F _ {\infty}) + \mu (E \setminus F _ {\infty}) = \mu (E).
$$

To prove the reverse inequality find an increasing sequence of measurable sets $\{ G _ { k } \}$ , with $\mu _ { 1 } \left( G _ { k } \right) = 0$ , such that 

$$
\mu_ {2} (E) = \mu (E \cap G _ {\infty}), \quad \text { where } G _ {\infty} := \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} G _ {k}.
$$

Note that 

$$
\mu_ {1} (G _ {\infty}) = 0.\tag{1.11}
$$

We claim that 

$$
\mu \left(E \cap F _ {\infty} \cap G _ {\infty}\right) = 0.
$$

Indeed, if not, then for all l suficiently large, 

$$
\mu \left(E \cap \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {l} F _ {n}\right) \cap G _ {\infty}\right) > 0,
$$

and so 

$$
\mu_ {1} \left(E \cap G _ {\infty}\right) \geq \mu \left(E \cap \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {l} F _ {n}\right) \cap G _ {\infty}\right) > 0,
$$

which contradicts (1.11). Hence the claim holds, and in turn, 

$$
\mu_ {1} (E) + \mu_ {2} (E) = \mu (E \cap F _ {\infty}) + \mu (E \cap G _ {\infty}) = \mu (E \cap (F _ {\infty} \cup G _ {\infty})) \leq \mu (E).
$$

This concludes the proof. 

We are now ready to prove Proposition 1.22. 

Proof (Proposition 1.22). Define $\mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ as in (1.8) and (1.9), where N is the family of all countable unions of atoms together with the empty set. By the previous lemma we have that $\mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ are measures, that $\mu = \mu _ { 1 } + \mu _ { 2 }$ and $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \right) = \mu \left( E \right)$ for all $E \in { \mathfrak { N } }$ . We show that $\mu _ { 1 }$ is purely atomic. Suppose that $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \right) > 0$ . By (1.8) we may find a countable family $\{ F _ { n } \}$ of µ-atoms such that 

$$
\mu \left(E \cap \bigcup_ {n} F _ {n}\right) > 0.
$$

Then $\mu \left( E \cap F _ { n } \right) > 0$ for some µ-atom $F _ { n }$ . We claim that $E \cap F _ { n }$ is a $\mu _ { 1 } \mathrm { - a t o m }$ To see this, assume by contradiction that there exists $G \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that 

$$
0 <   \mu_ {1} (E \cap F _ {n} \cap G) <   \mu_ {1} (E \cap F _ {n}).
$$

Then 

$$
0 <   \mu_ {1} (E \cap F _ {n} \cap G) <   \mu_ {1} (E \cap F _ {n}) \leq \mu (E \cap F _ {n}) \leq \mu (F _ {n}),
$$

and by (1.8) applied to $E \cap F _ { n } \cap G$ there exists $F \in \mathfrak { N }$ such that 

$$
0 <   \mu (E \cap F _ {n} \cap G \cap F) \leq \mu_ {1} (E \cap F _ {n} \cap G) <   \mu (F _ {n}),
$$

which contradicts the fact that $F _ { n }$ is a $\mu { \mathrm { - a t o m } }$ . This shows that $E \cap F _ { n }$ is a $\mu _ { 1 } \mathrm { - a t o m }$ and that $\mu _ { 1 }$ is purely atomic. 

Next we prove that $\mu _ { 2 }$ is nonatomic. Suppose that $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\mu _ { 2 } \left( E \right) > 0$ By (1.9) there is $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $\mu _ { 1 } \left( F \right) = 0$ , such that 

$$
\mu_ {2} (E) \geq \mu (E \cap F) > 0.\tag{1.12}
$$

Then $E \cap F$ is not a µ-atom, since otherwise, $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \cap F \right) > 0$ . Since $\mu \left( E \cap F \right) >$ 0 and $E \cap F$ is not a $\mu { \mathrm { - a t o m } }$ , we may find $G \subset E \cap F$ , with $G \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , such that 

$$
0 <   \mu (G) <   \mu (E \cap F).
$$

Since $\mu _ { 1 } \left( F \right) = 0$ and $G \subset E \cap F$ , we have that $\mu _ { 1 } \left( G \right) = 0$ , and so $\mu _ { 2 } \left( G \right) =$ $\mu \left( G \right)$ . Hence also by (1.12), 

$$
0 <   \mu_ {2} (G) <   \mu (E \cap F) \leq \mu_ {2} (E),
$$

which proves that $\mu _ { 2 }$ is nonatomic. 

Remark 1.24. In particular, if $\mu$ is purely atomic, then $\mu _ { 2 } \equiv 0$ and so $\mu = \mu _ { 1 }$ By (1.8), for any $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) > 0$ we may find a countable family $\{ F _ { n } \}$ of µ-atoms such that 

$$
\mu (E) = \mu \left(E \cap \bigcup_ {n} F _ {n}\right).
$$

Letting 

$$
E _ {n} := E \cap \left(F _ {n} \setminus \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {n - 1} F _ {i}\right)
$$

and disregarding those $E _ { n } \mathrm { { ^ { s } } }$ , if any, having measure zero, we have that 

$$
\mu (E) = \mu \left(\bigcup_ {n} E _ {n}\right),
$$

where $\{ E _ { n } \}$ is a countable collection of pairwise disjoint of atoms. 

We call attention to the fact that while the finite subset property may not prevent atoms from occurring, it eliminates very degenerate measures of the form $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \{ 0 , \infty \}$ . Indeed, the following proposition confirms this. 

Proposition 1.25. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Then $\mu$ satisfies the finite subset property $i f$ and only if for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) > 0$ , 

$$
\mu (E) = \sup \left\{\mu (F): F \in \mathfrak {M}, F \subset E, 0 <   \mu (F) <   \infty \right\}.\tag{1.13}
$$

Proof. If (1.13) holds, then the finite subset property follows by the definition of supremum. Conversely, let $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) > 0$ and set 

$$
S := \sup \left\{\mu (F): F \in \mathfrak {M}, F \subset E, 0 <   \mu (F) <   \infty \right\}.
$$

If $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ , then $\mu \left( E \right) = S . { \mathrm { ~ I f ~ } } \mu \left( E \right) = \infty$ , then we may find a sequence of increasing sets $F _ { n } \subset E , F _ { n } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $\mu \left( F _ { n } \right) < \infty$ , and such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu \left(F _ {n}\right) = S.
$$

Define 

$$
F := \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {n}.
$$

Then 

$$
\mu (F) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu (F _ {n}) = S.
$$

We claim that $S = \infty$ . If not, then $\mu \left( E \setminus F \right) = \infty$ , and so by the finite subset property we can find $F ^ { \prime } \subset E \setminus F , F ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , such that $0 < \mu \left( F ^ { \prime } \right) < \infty$ . Hence $F \cup F ^ { \prime } \subset E$ with 

$$
S = \mu (F) <   \mu (F) + \mu (F ^ {\prime}) <   \infty ,
$$

and this contradicts the definition of $S$ 

If a measure $\mu$ does not satisfy the finite subset property, then it is possible to construct another measure that satisfies it and that coincides with $\mu$ on sets of finite measure. Indeed, we have the following proposition. 

Proposition 1.26. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Then there exist measures $\mu _ { 1 } : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ and $\mu _ { 2 } : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \{ 0 , \infty \}$ such that $\mu _ { 1 }$ has the finite subset property and $\mu = \mu _ { 1 } + \mu _ { 2 }$ . In particular, $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \right) = \mu \left( E \right)$ for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ 

Proof. Define $\mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ as in (1.8) and (1.9), where 

$$
\mathfrak {N} := \left\{E \in \mathfrak {M}: \mu (E) <   \infty \right\}.
$$

Since N is closed under finite unions and contains $\varnothing .$ by Lemma 1.23 we have that $\mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ are measures, that $\mu = \mu _ { 1 } + \mu _ { 2 }$ , and $\mu _ { 1 } \left( E \right) = \mu \left( E \right)$ for all $E \in { \mathfrak { N } }$ . In particular, if E, $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\mu \left( F \right) < \infty$ , then $\mu \left( E \cap F \right) < \infty$ , and so $\mu \left( E \cap F \right) = \mu _ { 1 } \left( E \cap F \right)$ . Hence 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mu_ {1} (E) = \sup \left\{\mu (E \cap F): F \in \mathfrak {M}, \mu (F) <   \infty \right\}} \\ & {\qquad = \sup \left\{\mu_ {1} (E \cap F): F \in \mathfrak {M}, \mu_ {1} (F) <   \infty \right\},} \end{array}
$$

and so $\mu _ { 1 }$ has the finite subset property in view of Proposition 1.25. 

It remains to show that $\mu _ { 2 } : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \{ 0 , \infty \}$ . If by contradiction 

$$
0 <   \mu_ {2} (E) <   \infty
$$

for some $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , then by (1.9) we would find $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $\mu _ { 1 } \left( F \right) = 0$ and 

$$
0 <   \mu (E \cap F) <   \infty ;
$$

but then $\mu \left( E \cap F \right) ~ = ~ \mu _ { 1 } \left( E \cap F \right)$ , which would contradict the fact that $\mu _ { 1 } \left( F \right) = 0$ 

In applications, the ability to exclude sets of measure zero and to ensure that subsets of sets of measure zero are still measurable is often of the utmost importance. In what follows, if $\mu$ is a measure we write that a property holds µ a.e. on a measurable set E if there exists a measurable set $F \subset E$ such that $\mu \left( F \right) = 0$ and the property holds everywhere on the set $E \setminus F$ 

Definition 1.27. Given a measure space $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ , the measure $\mu$ is said to be complete if for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ it follows that every $F \subset E$ belongs to M. 

The next proposition shows that it always possible to render a measure complete. 

Proposition 1.28. Given a measure space $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ let M<sup></sup> be the family of all subsets $E \subset X$ for which there exist F, $G \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $\mu \left( G \backslash F \right) = 0$ and $F \subset E \subset G$ . Define $\mu ^ { \prime } \left( E \right) : = \mu \left( G \right)$ . Then M<sup></sup> is a σ-algebra that contains M and $\mu ^ { \prime } : \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a complete measure. 

Example 1.29. Possibly the most important example of completion of a measure is the Lebesgue measure defined on the Borel σ-algebra, as will be detailed at the end of the next subsection. 

We now introduce the notion of outer measure. 

Definition 1.30. Let X be a nonempty set. 

(i) A map $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is an outer measure $i f$ 

a) $\mu ^ { * } \left( \varnothing \right) = 0 ;$ 

b) $\mu ^ { * } \left( E \right) \leq \mu ^ { * } \left( F \right)$ for all $E \subset F \subset X $ ; 

c) $\begin{array} { r } { \mu ^ { * } \left( \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } \right) \leq \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \mu ^ { * } \left( E _ { n } \right) } \end{array}$ for every countable collection $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset$ P (X); 

(ii) given an outer measure $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ , a set $E \subset X$ has σ-finite $\mu ^ { * }$ outer measure if it can be written as a countable union of sets of finite outer measure; $\mu ^ { * }$ is said to be σ-finite if X has σ-finite $\mu ^ { * }$ outer measure; $\mu ^ { * }$ is said to be finite if $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( X \right) < \infty$ 

Remark 1.31. The reader should be warned that in several of books $( \mathrm { e . g . }$ , [DuSc88], [EvGa92], [Fe69]) outer measures are called measures. 

Just as in the case of measures, if $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is an outer measure and if $E \subset X$ , then the restriction of $\mu ^ { * }$ to $E$ is the outer measure $\mu ^ { * } \lfloor E$ ${ \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ defined by 

$$
\left(\mu^ {*} \lfloor E\right) (F) := \mu^ {*} (F \cap E)
$$

for all sets $F \subset X$ 

Often, when there is no possibility of confusion, we use the same notation $\mu ^ { * } \lfloor E$ to denote the restriction of the outer measure $\mu ^ { * }$ to $\mathcal { P } \left( E \right)$ 

Clearly, a measure $\mu$ on a measurable space (X, M) is an outer measure if ${ \mathfrak { M } } = { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ . Note, however, that when ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subsetneq { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ it is always possible to extend $\mu$ to ${ \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ as an outer measure. Indeed, more generally we have the following proposition. 

Proposition 1.32. Let X be a nonempty set and let ${ \mathcal { G } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be such that $\varnothing \in { \mathcal { G } }$ and there exists $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset { \mathcal { G } }$ with $\textstyle X = \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n }$ . Let $\rho : \mathcal { G }  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be such that $\rho \left( \varnothing \right) = 0$ . Then the map $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ defined by 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) := \inf \left\{\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \rho (E _ {n}): \{E _ {n} \} \subset \mathcal {G}, E \subset \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n} \right\}, \quad E \subset X,\tag{1.14}
$$

is an outer measure. 

Proof. Since $\varnothing \in { \mathcal { G } }$ we have that $\mu ^ { * } \left( \varnothing \right) = 0$ . If $E \subset F \subset X$ then any sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset { \mathcal { G } }$ admissible for $F$ in $( 1 . 1 4 )$ is also admissible for $E ,$ and so $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( E \right) \leq$ $\mu ^ { * } \left( F \right)$ . Finally, let $\{ F _ { k } \} \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ . If $\mu ^ { * } \left( F _ { k } \right) = \infty$ for some $k \in \mathbb N$ , then 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {k}\right) \leq \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} \left(F _ {k}\right) = \infty .
$$

Thus assume that $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( F _ { k } \right) < \infty$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$ and for a fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ and for each k find a sequence $\left\{ E _ { n } ^ { ( k ) } \right\} \subset \mathcal { G }$ admissible for $F _ { k }$ in (1.14) and such that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \rho \left(E _ {n} ^ {(k)}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} (F _ {k}) + \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {k}}.
$$

Since the sequence $\left\{ E _ { n } ^ { ( k ) } \right\} _ { k , n \in \mathbb { N } }$ is admissible for $\textstyle \bigcup _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } F _ { k }$ , we have that (see Example 1.82 below) 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {k}\right) \leq \sum_ {k, n = 1} ^ {\infty} \rho \left(E _ {n} ^ {(k)}\right) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \rho \left(E _ {n} ^ {(k)}\right) \leq \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} \left(F _ {k}\right) + \varepsilon .
$$

By letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ we conclude the proof. 

Remark 1.33. Note that if $E \in \mathcal G$ , then taking $E _ { 1 } : = E , E _ { n } : = \varnothing$ for all $n \geq 2$ , it follows from the definition of $\mu ^ { * }$ that $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( E \right) \leq \rho \left( E \right)$ , with the strict inequality possible. However, if $\rho$ is countably subadditive, that is, if 

$$
\rho (E) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \rho (E _ {n})
$$

for all $E \subset \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n }$ with $E \in { \mathcal { G } } , \{ E _ { n } \} \subset { \mathcal { G } }$ , then $\mu ^ { * } = \rho$ on $\mathcal { G } .$ 

The construction of the measure $\mu ^ { * }$ in the previous proposition is commonly used to build an outer measure from a family $\mathcal { G }$ of elementary sets $( \mathrm { e . g . } $ cubes in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N } )$ for which a basic notion of measure $\rho$ is known. 

Exercise 1.34. Let $f : \mathbb { R } \to \mathbb { R }$ be increasing. Let $\mathcal { G }$ be the family of all intervals $( a , b ] \subset \mathbb { R }$ , and define 

$$
\rho ((a, b ]) := f (b) - f (a).
$$

The outer measure $\mu ^ { * }$ given by Proposition 1.32 is called the Lebesgue–Stieltjes outer measure generated by $f .$ Show that 

$$
\mu^ {*} ((a, b ]) = f (b) - \lim _ {t \rightarrow a ^ {+}} f (a) \leq f (b) - f (a) = \rho ((a, b ]),
$$

and therefore strict inequality occurs at points where f is not continuous from the right. 

Definition 1.35. Let X be a nonempty set and let $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be an outer measure. A set $E \subset X$ is said to be $\mu ^ { * } .$ -measurable if 

$$
\mu^ {*} (F) = \mu^ {*} (F \cap E) + \mu^ {*} (F \setminus E)
$$

for all sets $F \subset X$ 

Remark 1.36. Note that if $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( E \right) = 0$ , then by the monotonicity of the outer measure, $\mu ^ { * } \left( F \cap E \right) \mathrm { ~ = ~ } 0$ for all sets $F \subset X$ . Hence E is $\mu ^ { * } { \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l e } } .$ Moreover, if E is an arbitrary subset of X and if $F \subset X$ is a $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable set, then $F \cap E$ is $\mu ^ { * } \lfloor E \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l e }$ 

Theorem 1.37 (Carath´eodory). Let X be a nonempty set and let $\mu ^ { * }$ : ${ \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be an outer measure. Then 

$$
\mathfrak {M} ^ {*} := \{E \subset X: E i s \mu^ {*} - m e a s u r a b l e \}\tag{1.15}
$$

is a σ-algebra and $\mu ^ { * } : \mathfrak { M } ^ { * } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a complete measure. 

From Proposition 1.32 and Remark 1.33 we have the following. 

Corollary 1.38. Let X be a nonempty set, let ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be an algebra, and let $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a finitely additive measure. Let $\mu ^ { * }$ be the outer measure defined in (1.14) (with $\mathcal { G } : = \mathfrak { M }$ and $\rho : = \mu )$ . Then every element of M is µ<sup>∗</sup>-measurable. Moreover, $i f \mu$ is countably additive, then $\mu ^ { * } = \mu$ on M. 

Proof. To show that every element of M is $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable fix $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and let $F$ be any subset of X. By (1.14), for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ find a sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ such that $F \subset \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n }$ and 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(E _ {n}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} (F) + \varepsilon .
$$

Since M is an algebra we have that $\{ E _ { n } \cap E \} , \{ E _ { n } \setminus E \} \subset { \mathfrak { M } }$ are admissible sequences in (1.14) for the sets $F \cap E$ and $F \setminus E$ , and so 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu^ {*} (F \cap E) + \mu^ {*} (F \setminus E) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} (\mu (E _ {n} \cap E) + \mu (E _ {n} \setminus E)) \\ = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (E _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (F) + \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Given the arbitrariness o $\ : \varepsilon > 0 \ :$ , it follows that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (F \cap E) + \mu^ {*} (F \setminus E) \leq \mu^ {*} (F).
$$

Since by Carath´eodory’s theorem $\mu ^ { * }$ is an outer measure, the opposite in equality is immediate. Thus $E$ is µ<sup>∗</sup>-measurable. 

The last part of the statement is a consequence of Remark 1.33. 

Remark 1.39. Note that the previous result implies that every countably ad ditive measure $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ defined on an algebra M may be extended as a measure to a σ-algebra that contains M. It actually turns out that when $\mu$ is finite, this extension is unique. Indeed, let $\nu : { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be any measure such that $\nu = \mu$ on M, where ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ is the σ-algebra of all µ<sup>∗</sup>-measurable sets. Note that ν and $\mu ^ { * }$ are finite, since 

$$
\nu (X) = \mu^ {*} (X) = \mu (X) <   \infty .
$$

Let $E ~ \in ~ \mathfrak { M } ^ { \ast }$ and consider any sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \ \subset \ { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $E \subset$ $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n }$ . Then 

$$
\nu (E) \leq \nu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \nu (E _ {n}) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (E _ {n}).
$$

Taking the infimum over all such covers and using (1.14) yields 

$$
\nu (E) \leq \mu^ {*} (E)
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ . Since $\mu ^ { * }$ and ν are additive on ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ and coincide with $\mu$ on M, for any $E \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ , we have 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) + \mu^ {*} (X \setminus E) = \mu^ {*} (X) = \mu (X) = \nu (X) = \nu (E) + \nu (X \setminus E),
$$

which in view of the previous inequality (for E and $X \setminus E )$ and the fact that ν and $\mu ^ { * }$ are finite implies that $\mu ^ { * } \left( E \right) = \nu \left( E \right)$ 

When X is a metric space then the class of metric outer measures on X is of special interest: 

Definition 1.40. Let X be a metric space and let $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be an outer measure. Then $\mu ^ { * }$ is said to be a metric outer measure $i f$ 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E \cup F) = \mu^ {*} (E) + \mu^ {*} (F)
$$

for all sets $E , F \subset X$ , with 

$$
\operatorname{dist} (E, F) := \inf \left\{d (x, y): x \in E, y \in F \right\} > 0.
$$

Proposition 1.41. Let X be a metric space and let $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a metric outer measure. Then every Borel set is $\mu ^ { * } - m e a s u r a b l e .$ 

## 1.1.2 Radon and Borel Measures and Outer Measures

In this subsection we study regularity properties of measures and outer measures. These will play an important role in the characterization of some dual spaces. 

Definition 1.42. An outer measure $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is said to be regular if for every set $E \subset X$ there exists a µ<sup>∗</sup>-measurable set $F \subset X$ such that $E \subset F$ and $\mu ^ { * } \left( E \right) = \mu ^ { * } \left( F \right)$ 

An important property of regular outer measures is the fact that Propo sition $1 . 7 ( \mathrm { i } )$ continues to hold. 

Proposition 1.43. Let $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a regular outer measure. If $\{ E _ { n } \}$ is an increasing sequence of subsets of X then 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu^ {*} \left(E _ {n}\right).
$$

Proof. Since $\mu ^ { * }$ is regular there exist $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable sets $F _ { n } \supset E _ { n }$ such that $\mu ^ { * } \left( E _ { n } \right) = \mu ^ { * } \left( F _ { n } \right)$ . The sets 

$$
G _ {n} := \bigcap_ {i = n} ^ {\infty} F _ {i}
$$

are $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable, with $E _ { n } \subset G _ { n } \subset F _ { n }$ , and 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (G _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (F _ {n}) = \mu^ {*} (E _ {n}).
$$

Since $G _ { n } \subset G _ { n + 1 }$ , we may apply Proposition 1.7 to $\mu ^ { * } : \mathfrak { M } ^ { * } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ , where ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ is defined in (1.15), to obtain that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} G _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu^ {*} \left(G _ {n}\right) \\ = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu^ {*} \left(E _ {n}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right), \end{array}
$$

from which the result follows. 

Example $1 . 4 4$ . The previous proposition fails if $\mu ^ { * }$ is not regular. Indeed, let $X : = \mathbb { N }$ and for each $E \subset \mathbb { N }$ define 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(E\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0 \text {   if   } E = \emptyset , \\ 1 \text {   if   } E \text {   is   finite }, \\ 2 \text {   if   } E \text {   is   infinite }. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then $\mu ^ { * }$ is an outer measure, and taking $E _ { n } : = \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ we see that 

$$
2 = \mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \neq \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu^ {*} (E _ {n}) = 1.
$$

The next proposition shows that any measure may be extended to a regular outer measure. 

Proposition 1.45. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Let $\mu ^ { * }$ be the outer measure defined in (1.14) (with $\mathcal { G } : = \mathfrak { M }$ and $\rho : = \mu )$ . Then $\mu ^ { * }$ is a regular outer measure, and for every $E \subset X$ 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) = \inf \left\{\mu (F): F \in \mathfrak {M}, F \supset E \right\}.\tag{1.16}
$$

Moreover, every element of M is $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable and $\mu ^ { * } = \mu$ on M. 

Proof. In view of Corollary 1.38 we have only to show that (1.16) holds and that the outer measure $\mu ^ { * }$ is regular. For any fixed $E \subset X$ and for any $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $F \supset E$ , we have 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) \leq \mu^ {*} (F) = \mu (F),
$$

and so 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) \leq \inf \left\{\mu (F): F \in \mathfrak {M}, F \supset E \right\}.
$$

To prove the opposite inequality consider any sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ such that $E \in \textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n }$ . Since $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } \in \mathfrak { M }$ we have 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (E _ {n}) \geq \mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \geq \inf \left\{\mu (F): F \in \mathfrak {M}, F \supset E \right\}.
$$

Taking the infimum over all such sequences $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ yields 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) \geq \inf \left\{\mu (F): F \in \mathfrak {M}, F \supset E \right\},
$$

and so (1.16) holds. 

To prove regularity note that if $\mu ^ { * } \left( E \right) = \infty$ then $X \in { \mathfrak { M } } , X \supset E$ and 

$$
\mu (X) = \mu^ {*} (X) \geq \mu^ {*} (E) = \infty .
$$

If $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( E \right) < \infty$ , then by (1.16), for each $n \in \mathbb N$ we may find measurable sets $F _ { n } \supset E$ such that 

$$
\mu (F _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (E) + \frac {1}{n}.
$$

Then the measurable set 

$$
F := \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {n}
$$

contains $E _ { i }$ , and 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) \leq \mu (F) \leq \mu (F _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (E) + \frac {1}{n} \rightarrow \mu^ {*} (E)
$$

as $n \to \infty$ . Hence $\mu ^ { * } \left( E \right) = \mu \left( F \right)$ 

Remark $1 . 4 6 .$ In view of the previous proposition and Proposition 1.28, given a measure space $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ , the two measures $\mu ^ { * } : \mathfrak { M } ^ { * } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ and $\mu ^ { \prime } : \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime } \to$ $[ 0 , \infty ]$ are complete and extend $\mu .$ . We claim that ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime } \subset { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ and that $\mu ^ { \prime } = \mu ^ { * }$ on $\mathfrak { M } ^ { ' }$ . Indeed, if $E \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ then there exist $F .$ , $G \in { \mathfrak { M } } .$ , with $\mu \left( G \backslash F \right) = 0$ and $F \subset E \subset G$ , such that $\mu ^ { \prime } \left( E \right) : = \mu \left( G \right)$ . Write $E = F \cup ( E \setminus F )$ . Since $E \backslash F \subset G \backslash F $ , by the monotonicity of the outer measure $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ we have that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E \setminus F) \leq \mu^ {*} (G \setminus F) = \mu (G \setminus F) = 0,
$$

and thus, since $\mu ^ { * } : \mathfrak { M } ^ { * } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is complete, it follows that $E \setminus F \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ and in turn 

$$
E = F \cup (E \setminus F) \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {*},
$$

where we have used the fact that $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . In particular 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) = \mu^ {*} (F) + \mu^ {*} (E \setminus F) = \mu (F) + 0 = \mu (G) = \mu^ {\prime} (E).
$$

Hence ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime } \subset { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ and $\mu ^ { \prime } = \mu ^ { * }$ on ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime }$ 

Exercise 1.47. Given an outer measure $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ it is possible to construct a regular outer measure by defining for every $E \subset X$ , 

$$
\nu^ {*} (E) := \inf \left\{\mu^ {*} (F): E \subset F, F \mu^ {*} \text {-measurable} \right\}.
$$

Prove that if $E$ is $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable, then $E$ is $\nu ^ { * }$ -measurable and $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( E \right) =$ $\nu ^ { * } \left( E \right)$ . Conversely, show that if $E$ is $\nu ^ { * }$ -measurable and $\nu ^ { * } \left( E \right) < \infty$ , then $E$ is $\mu ^ { * } { \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l e } }$ 

Definition 1.48. Let X be a topological space and let $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be an outer measure. 

(i) A set $E \subset X$ is said to be inner regular $i f$ 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) = \sup \left\{\mu^ {*} (K): K \subset E, K \text { compact } \right\},
$$

and it is outer regular if 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) = \inf \left\{\mu^ {*} (A): A \supset E, A \text {open} \right\}.
$$

(ii) A set $E \subset X$ is said to be regular if it is both inner and outer regular. 

The previous definition introduces concepts of regularity for subsets of $X$ and next we address regularity properties of outer measures. 

Definition 1.49. Let X be a topological space and let $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be an outer measure. 

(i) $\mu ^ { * }$ is said to be a Borel outer measure $i f$ every Borel set is $\mu ^ { * } - m e a s u r a b l e ;$ (ii) $\mu ^ { * }$ is said to be a Borel regular outer measure if $\mu ^ { * }$ is a Borel outer measure and for every set $E \subset X$ there exists a Borel set $F \subset X$ such that $E \subset F$ and $\mu ^ { * } \left( E \right) = \mu ^ { * } \left( F \right)$ 

There is a class of Borel outer measures that plays a pivotal role in the calculus of variations. These are the Radon outer measures, as introduced next. 

Definition 1.50. Let X be a topological space, and let $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be an outer measure. Then $\mu ^ { * }$ is said to be a Radon outer measure $i f$ 

(i) $\mu ^ { * }$ is a Borel outer measure; 

(ii) $\mu ^ { * } \left( K \right) < \infty$ for every compact set $K \subset X$ 

(iii) every open set $A \subset X$ is inner regular; 

(iv) every set $E \subset X$ is outer regular. 

We investigate the relation between Radon outer measures and Borel regular measures. 

Remark 1.51. Note that a Radon outer measure is always Borel regular. In deed, let $E \subset X$ . If $\mu ^ { * } \left( E \right) = \infty$ then note that X is open, $X \supset E$ , and $\mu ^ { * } \left( X \right) = \mu ^ { * } \left( E \right) = \infty$ . If $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( E \right) < \infty$ , then by outer regularity, for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ we may find open sets $A _ { n } \supset E$ such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (A _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (E) + \frac {1}{n}.
$$

Then the Borel set 

$$
B := \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {n}
$$

contains E, and 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) \leq \mu^ {*} (B) \leq \mu^ {*} (A _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (E) + \frac {1}{n} \rightarrow \mu^ {*} (E)
$$

as $n \to \infty$ 

The converse of the previous remark is false in general (see Exercise 1.59 below), but there are some partial results in that direction. 

Proposition 1.52. Let X be a locally compact Hausdorf space such that every open set $A \subset X$ is σ-compact. Let $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Borel outer measure such that $\mu ^ { * } \left( K \right) < \infty$ for every compact set $K \subset X$ . Then every Borel set is inner regular and outer regular. 

If, in addition, $\mu ^ { * }$ is a Borel regular outer measure, then it is a Radon outer measure. 

Proof. Since X is σ-compact we may write 

$$
X = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} K _ {n},
$$

where $\{ K _ { n } \}$ is an increasing sequence of compact sets. By Theorem A.12 we may find open sets $U _ { n }$ such that $K _ { n } \subset U _ { n } \subset X$ and $\overline { { U _ { n } } }$ is compact. Without loss of generality we may assume that the sequence $\{ U _ { n } \}$ is increasing. 

Step 1: Fix $n \in \mathbb N$ and let $\boldsymbol { \mu } _ { n } ^ { * }$ denote the restriction of $\mu ^ { * }$ to ${ \mathcal { P } } \left( U _ { n } \right)$ . We claim that every Borel subset of $U _ { n }$ is inner and outer regular with respect to the outer measure $\boldsymbol { \mu } _ { n } ^ { * }$ . Note that since $\overline { { U _ { n } } }$ is compact, $\mu _ { n } ^ { * }$ is a finite outer measure. Let 

$$
\mathfrak {M} _ {n} := \left\{E \subset U _ {n}: E \text {   is   } \mu_ {n} ^ {*} \text {   inner   and   outer   regular } \right\}.
$$

If $A \subset U _ { n }$ is open, then it is outer regular. Since A is σ-compact, there exists an increasing sequence $\{ C _ { j } \}$ of compact subsets of A such that 

$$
A = \bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} C _ {j},
$$

and so by Carath´eodory’s theorem and Proposition 1.7, 

$$
\lim _ {j \to \infty} \mu_ {n} ^ {*} (C _ {j}) = \mu_ {n} ^ {*} (A).
$$

This shows that ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { n }$ contains all open subsets of $U _ { n }$ , and therefore the claim is proved provided we prove that ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { n }$ is a σ-algebra. 

The sets $U _ { n }$ and ∅ belong to ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { n } .$ , and ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { n }$ is closed with respect to countable unions. To prove the latter, let $\{ E _ { i } \} \subset { \mathfrak { M } } _ { n }$ and let $\varepsilon > 0$ . For every $i \in \mathbb N$ there exist 

$$
C _ {i} \subset E _ {i} \subset A _ {i} \subset U _ {n}
$$

such that $C _ { i }$ is compact, $A _ { i }$ is open, and 

$$
\mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(A _ {i} \setminus C _ {i}\right) \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {i + 1}},
$$

where we have used the fact that $\boldsymbol { \mu } _ { n } ^ { * }$ restricted to the Borel sets of $U _ { n }$ is a finite measure by Carath´eodory’s theorem. Also, by Proposition 1.7, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {l \to \infty} \mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {i} \setminus \left(\bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {l} C _ {j}\right)\right) = \mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {i} \setminus \left(\bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} C _ {j}\right)\right) \\ \leq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(A _ {i} \setminus C _ {i}\right) \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2}, \end{array}
$$

and therefore we may find l large enough that 

$$
\mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {i} \setminus \left(\bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {l} C _ {j}\right)\right) \leq \mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {i} \setminus \left(\bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {l} C _ {j}\right)\right) \leq \varepsilon .
$$

Hence $\textstyle \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { i }$ is inner regular, and outer regularity follows from 

$$
\mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {i} \setminus \left(\bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {j}\right)\right) \leq \mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {i} \setminus \left(\bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} C _ {j}\right)\right) \leq \varepsilon .
$$

It remains to show that if $E \in \mathfrak { M } _ { n }$ then $U _ { n } \backslash E \in \mathfrak { M } _ { n }$ . Again for a fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ there exist 

$$
C \subset E \subset A \subset U _ {n}
$$

such that C is compact, A is open, and 

$$
\mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(A \setminus C\right) \leq \varepsilon .\tag{1.17}
$$

Then $U _ { n } \backslash C$ is open, $U _ { n } \setminus E \subset U _ { n } \setminus C$ , and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu_ {n} ^ {*} (U _ {n} \setminus C) = \mu_ {n} ^ {*} (U _ {n}) - \mu_ {n} ^ {*} (C) \leq \mu_ {n} ^ {*} (U _ {n}) - \mu_ {n} ^ {*} (A) + \varepsilon \\ = \mu_ {n} ^ {*} (U _ {n} \setminus A) + \varepsilon \leq \mu_ {n} ^ {*} (U _ {n} \setminus E) + \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

and this proves the outer regularity of $U _ { n } \backslash E$ . On the other hand, since $U _ { n }$ is σ-compact, it is possible to find a compact set $K \subset U _ { n }$ such that 

$$
\mu_ {n} ^ {*} (U _ {n}) \leq \mu_ {n} ^ {*} (K) + \varepsilon .
$$

Then $K \setminus A$ is compact, $K \setminus A \subset U _ { n } \setminus E$ , and by (1.17), 

$$
\mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(U _ {n} \setminus E\right) \leq \mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(U _ {n} \setminus A\right) + \varepsilon \leq \mu_ {n} ^ {*} \left(K \setminus A\right) + 2 \varepsilon ,
$$

thus showing that $U _ { n } \setminus E$ is inner regular. 

Step 2: Let $B \subset X$ be any Borel subset and fix $\varepsilon > 0$ . By Step 1 there exists an open set $A _ { 1 } \subset U _ { 1 }$ such that $B \cap U _ { 1 } \subset A _ { 1 }$ and 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(A _ {1}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(B \cap U _ {1}\right) + \frac {\varepsilon}{2}.
$$

Inductively, assume that for $k = 1 , \dots , n$ there exist open sets $A _ { k } \subset U _ { k }$ such that $B \cap U _ { k } \subset A _ { k }$ , 

$$
A _ {1} \subset A _ {2} \subset \ldots \subset A _ {n},
$$

and 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(A _ {k}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(B \cap U _ {k}\right) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {i}}.
$$

To construct $A _ { n + 1 }$ , by Step 1 find an open set $A _ { n + 1 } ^ { \prime } \subset U _ { n + 1 }$ such that 

$$
(B \setminus U _ {n}) \cap U _ {n + 1} \subset A _ {n + 1} ^ {\prime}
$$

and 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(A _ {n + 1} ^ {\prime}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(\left(B \setminus U _ {n}\right) \cap U _ {n + 1}\right) + \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n + 1}}.
$$

Setting $A _ { n + 1 } : = A _ { n } \cup A _ { n + 1 } ^ { \prime }$ , it follows that $B \cap U _ { n + 1 } \subset A _ { n + 1 }$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu^ {*} (A _ {n + 1}) \leq \mu^ {*} (A _ {n}) + \mu^ {*} (A _ {n + 1} ^ {\prime}) \leq \mu^ {*} (B \cap U _ {n}) \\ \qquad + \mu^ {*} ((B \setminus U _ {n}) \cap U _ {n + 1}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {i}} + \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n + 1}} \\ \qquad = \mu^ {*} (B \cap U _ {n + 1}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n + 1} \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {i}}. \end{array}
$$

We observe that $B \subset \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } A _ { n }$ , and by Carath´eodory’s theorem and Proposition 1.7, 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu^ {*} (A _ {n}) \leq \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu^ {*} (B \cap U _ {n}) + \varepsilon = \mu^ {*} (B) + \varepsilon .
$$

We conclude that B is outer regular. 

To prove inner regularity fix $t < \mu ^ { * } \left( B \right)$ and choose n large enough that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (B \cap U _ {n}) > t.
$$

By Step 1 find a compact set $C \subset B \cap U _ { n }$ such that $\mu ^ { * } \left( C \right) > t$ . This shows that $\mu ^ { * } \left( B \right)$ can be approximated by the outer measures of compact subsets of B. 

Step 3: If $\mu ^ { * }$ is a Borel regular outer measure, then for every set $E \subset X$ there exists a Borel set $F \subset X$ such that $E \subset F$ and $\mu ^ { * } \left( E \right) = \mu ^ { * } \left( F \right)$ . Applying the first part of the proof to $F$ , for every $\varepsilon > 0$ we may find an open set 

$$
A \supset F \supset E
$$

such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) = \mu^ {*} (F) \leq \mu^ {*} (A) + \varepsilon .
$$

Hence every set E is outer regular, and so $\mu ^ { * }$ is a Radon outer measure. 

Remark 1.53. It follows from the previous proposition that if X satisfies the properties thus stated and if $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a Borel regular outer measure, then for any µ<sup>∗</sup>-measurable set $E \subset X$ with $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( E \right) < \infty$ the restriction $\mu ^ { * } \lfloor E$ of $\mu ^ { * }$ to E is a Radon outer measure. 

Given an arbitrary Radon outer measure, in general we cannot conclude that every set is inner regular (see Example 1.58). However, the following result holds.
