Proposition 1.54. Let X be a topological space and let $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Radon outer measure. Then every σ-finite µ<sup>∗</sup>-measurable set is inner regular. 

Proof. Let $E \subset X$ be a σ-finite $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable set. 

Step 1: Assume first that $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( E \right) < \infty$ . By outer regularity of $E _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ , for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists an open set $A \supset E$ such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (A) <   \mu^ {*} (E) + \varepsilon ,
$$

while by inner regularity of open sets there exists a compact set $K \subset A$ such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (A) <   \mu^ {*} (K) + \varepsilon .
$$

Since E is $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable, we have that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) + \mu^ {*} (A \setminus E) = \mu^ {*} (A) <   \mu^ {*} (E) + \varepsilon ,
$$

and so 

$$
\mu^ {*} (A \setminus E) <   \varepsilon .
$$

Hence by outer regularity we may choose an open set $U \supset A \setminus E$ such that $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( U \right) < \varepsilon$ . The compact set $C : = K \backslash U$ is contained in E, and using the fact that U is $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu^ {*} (C) = \mu^ {*} (K \setminus U) = \mu^ {*} (K) - \mu^ {*} (K \cap U) \\ > \mu^ {*} (A) - \varepsilon - \mu^ {*} (U) > \mu^ {*} (E) - 3 \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Hence E is inner regular. 

Step 2: If $\mu ^ { * } \left( E \right) = \infty$ , then since E has σ-finite $\mu ^ { * }$ outer measure, we may find a sequence of sets $E _ { n } \subset E$ such that 

$$
E = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}
$$

and $\mu ^ { * } \left( E _ { n } \right) < \infty$ . By Remark 1.51 there exist Borel sets $F _ { n }$ such that $E _ { n } \subset F _ { n }$ and $\mu ^ { * } \left( E _ { n } \right) = \mu ^ { * } \left( F _ { n } \right)$ . Then $F _ { n } \cap E$ is $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable, 

$$
\mu^ {*} (F _ {n} \cap E) \leq \mu^ {*} (F _ {n}) = \mu^ {*} (E _ {n}) <   \infty ,
$$

and 

$$
E = \bigcup_ {n = 1} \left(F _ {n} \cap E\right).
$$

We can now modify $\{ F _ { n } \cap E \}$ to make it increasing. In particular, it follows that 

$$
\infty = \mu^ {*} (E) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu^ {*} (F _ {n} \cap E).
$$

Let $M > 0$ and let n be so large that $\mu ^ { * } \left( F _ { n } \cap E \right) > M$ . By applying Step 1 to $F _ { n } \cap E$ we may find a compact set $K \subset F _ { n } \cap E$ such that $\mu ^ { * } \left( K \right) > M$ Hence 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) = \sup \left\{\mu^ {*} (K): K \subset E, K \text {compact} \right\} = \infty ,
$$

and the proof is complete. 

We now introduce analogous regularity properties for measures. 

Definition 1.55. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. If X is a topological space, then 

(i) µ is a Borel measure if every Borel set is in M; 

(ii) µ is a Borel regular measure $i f \mu$ is a Borel measure and if for every set 

$E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ there exists a Borel set F such that $E \subset F$ and $\mu \left( E \right) = \mu \left( F \right)$ ; 

(iii) a Borel measure $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a Radon measure if 

a) $\mu \left( K \right) < \infty$ for every compact set $K \subset X$ 

b) every open set $A \subset X$ is inner regular; 

c) every set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ is outer regular. 

Hausdorf measures $\mathcal { H } ^ { s } , s > 0$ (see $\mathrm { [ F o L e 1 0 ] ) }$ , represent an important class of regular Borel measures that are not Radon measures. 

For a Borel measure it is possible to define the notion of support. 

Definition 1.56. Let X be a topological space and let $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Borel measure. The support of $\mu$ is the set 

supp $\mu : = \{ x \in X : \ \mu \left( U \right) > 0$ for all (open) neighborhoods U of x} . 

Exercise 1.57. Let X be a topological space and let $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Borel measure. Prove that the support of $\mu$ is closed. Show also that if $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $E \subset X \backslash$ supp $\mu ,$ then $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ . Is the converse true? 

Proposition 1.54, which continues to hold for Radon measures, asserts that any measurable set with σ-finite measure is inner regular. The next example shows that there exist Radon measures for which non σ-finite sets may fail to be inner regular. 

Exercise 1.58. Consider $X = \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ endowed with the following topology: A set $A \subset X$ is open if and only if for every $y \in \mathbb R$ the set 

$$
A _ {y} := \{x \in \mathbb {R}: (x, y) \in A \}
$$

is open in R with respect to the Euclidean topology. Show that $X$ is a locally compact Hausdorf space. For every Borel set $B \subset X$ define 

$$
\mu \left(B\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \infty \qquad \text {if B_{y} \neq\emptyset for uncountably many y\in\mathbb {R} ,} \\ \sum_ {y \in \mathbb {R}} \mathcal {L} ^ {1} \left(B _ {y}\right) \text {otherwise,} \end{array} \right.
$$

where $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 }$ is the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb { R }$ (see the end of the subsection for its definition). Prove that $\mu$ is a Radon measure but the set $\{ 0 \} \times \mathbb { R }$ is not inner regular, since $\mu \left( \left\{ 0 \right\} \times \mathbb { R } \right) = \infty$ , while $\mu \left( K \right) = 0$ for any compact set $K \subset \{ 0 \} \times \mathbb { R }$ 

We have proved in Remark 1.51 that Radon measures are Borel regular. The converse is not true in general, as the next example shows. 

Example 1.59. Let X be an uncountable set with the discrete topology. For every $E \subset X$ define 

$$
\mu \left(E\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0 \text { if } E \text { is   countable }, \\ \infty \text { otherwise }. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then $\mu : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  \{ 0 , \infty \}$ is a measure (and also an outer measure). Since every subset of X is open, $\mu$ is a Borel regular measure and every set is outer regular. Since compact sets are necessarily finite, for every compact set $K \subset X$ we have $\mu \left( K \right) = 0$ , and so uncountable sets cannot be inner regular. Hence $\mu$ is not a Radon measure. 

However, the following holds. 

Proposition 1.60. Let X be a locally compact Hausdorf space such that every open set $A \subseteq X$ is σ-compact. Let $\mu : { \mathcal { B } } \left( X \right) \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a (Borel) measure. 

(i) $I f \mu$ is finite on compact sets, then $\mu$ is a Radon measure and every Borel set E is inner regular. 

(ii) If $B \in B \left( X \right)$ and $\mu \left( B \right) < \infty$ , then B is inner regular. 

Proof. The proof of (i) follows closely that of Proposition 1.52, where now ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { n }$ is defined as 

$$
\mathfrak {M} _ {n} := \left\{E \in \mathcal {B} \left(U _ {n}\right): E \text {   is   } \mu_ {n} \text {   inner   and   outer   regular } \right\}
$$

and where $\mu _ { n }$ denotes the restriction of $\mu$ to $B \left( U _ { n } \right)$ . We omit the details. 

(ii) is a consequence of (i) applied to the finite measure $\mu : B \left( B \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right)$ 

Exercise 1.61. Without the assumption that open sets are σ-compact the previous proposition fails. Indeed, let Y be the set of countable ordinals, let $\omega _ { 1 }$ be the first uncountable ordinal, and define $X : = Y \cup \{ \omega _ { 1 } \}$ . In X consider the smallest topology that contains all sets of the form $\lbrace \alpha \in X : \alpha < \beta \rbrace$ and $\lbrace \alpha \in X : \alpha > \beta \rbrace$ for $\beta \in X$ . Prove that X is a compact Hausdorf space, and that Y is an open set that is not σ-compact. Check that for every Borel set $B \subset X$ either $B \cup \{ \omega _ { 1 } \} { \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } } ( X \setminus B ) \cup \{ \omega _ { 1 } \}$ (but not both) contains an uncountable closed set. Define 

$$
\mu \left(B\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1 \text {   if   } B \cup \{\omega_ {1} \} \text {   contains   an   uncountable   closed   set }, \\ 0 \text {   if   } (X \setminus B) \cup \{\omega_ {1} \} \text {   contains   an   uncountable   closed   set }. \end{array} \right.
$$

Show that $\mu$ is a measure, but $\left\{ \omega _ { 1 } \right\}$ is not outer regular since $\mu \left( \{ \omega _ { 1 } \} \right) = 0$ but $\mu \left( A \right) = 1$ for every open set A containing $\omega _ { 1 }$ . We refer to $\left[ \mathrm { A l i B o 9 9 } \right]$ for more details. 

We study next the relation between regularity properties for outer measures and regularity properties of measures. If $\mu ^ { * }$ is a Borel regular (respectively Radon) outer measure, then its restriction $\mu$ to the σ-algebra of all $\mu ^ { * } -$ measurable sets is a Borel regular (respectively Radon) measure. Conversely, given a Borel regular (respectively Radon) measure $\mu ,$ , it is always possible to extend it to a Borel regular (respectively Radon) outer measure. This is a consequence of the following result. 

Theorem 1.62 (De Giorgi–Letta). Let $( X , \tau )$ be a topological space. $A s -$ sume that $\rho : \tau  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is an increasing set function such that 

(i) $\rho \left( \varnothing \right) = 0 .$ 

(ii) (subadditivity) $\rho \left( A _ { 1 } \cup A _ { 2 } \right) \le \rho \left( A _ { 1 } \right) + \rho \left( A _ { 2 } \right)$ for all $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } \in \tau$ ; 

(iii) (inner regularity) $\rho \left( A \right) = \operatorname* { s u p } \left\{ \rho \left( A _ { 1 } \right) : A _ { 1 } \subset \subset A \right\}$ for every $A \in \tau$ 

Then the extension of ρ to every set $E \subset X$ defined by 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) := \inf \left\{\rho (A): A \in \tau , E \subset A \right\}\tag{1.18}
$$

is an outer measure and every set is outer regular. 

Moreover, if X is a metric space and ρ satisfies the additional hypothesis 

(iv) (superadditivity) $\rho \left( A _ { 1 } \cup A _ { 2 } \right) \ge \rho \left( A _ { 1 } \right) + \rho \left( A _ { 2 } \right)$ for all $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } \in \tau$ , with $A _ { 1 } \cap A _ { 2 } = \varnothing$ ; 

then $\mu ^ { * }$ is a Borel outer measure and every set is outer regular. 

Proof. Step 1: We prove that under hypotheses (i)–(iii) the set function $\mu ^ { * }$ is an outer measure. Note that, in view of the definition (1.18), $\mu ^ { * } = \rho$ on $\tau$ Hence by (i) we have that $\mu ^ { * } \left( \varnothing \right) = 0$ . If $E \subset F \subset X$ , then any open set that contains $F$ also contains $E$ , and so $\mu ^ { * } \left( E \right) \leq \mu ^ { * } \left( F \right)$ 

It remains to prove countable subadditivity for $\mu ^ { * }$ . We prove it first for $\rho .$ Let $\left\{ A _ { n } \right\}$ be a sequence of open sets and consider any open set $A ^ { \prime }$ compactly contained in $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } A _ { n }$ . Since the family $\left\{ A _ { n } \right\}$ is an open cover for the compact set $\overline { { A ^ { \prime } } } .$ , there exists $l \in \mathbb N$ such that the finite family $\left\{ A _ { n } \right\} _ { n = 1 } ^ { l }$ is still an open cover for $\overline { { A ^ { \prime } } }$ , and so, by the fact that $\rho$ is increasing and nonnegative and by (ii), 

$$
\rho \left(A ^ {\prime}\right) \leq \rho \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {l} A _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \rho \left(A _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \rho \left(A _ {n}\right).
$$

Taking the supremum over all open sets $A ^ { \prime }$ compactly contained in $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } A _ { n }$ and using (iii), we obtain 

$$
\rho \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \rho \left(A _ {n}\right).
$$

Hence $\rho$ is countably subadditive, and we now prove that the same holds for $\mu ^ { * }$ . Let $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ . For all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and for a fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ find $A _ { n }$ open, with $E _ { n } \subset A _ { n }$ , such that 

$$
\rho (A _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (E _ {n}) + \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n}}.
$$

Then $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } \subset \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } A _ { n }$ , and so 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \leq \rho \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \rho (A _ {n}) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} (E _ {n}) + \varepsilon .
$$

By letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ we conclude that $\mu ^ { * }$ is an outer measure. Since $\mu ^ { * } = \rho$ on $\tau$ it follows from (1.18) that every set is outer regular by construction. 

Step 2: We now assume that X is a metric space and (i)–(iv) hold. In view of Proposition 1.41 it sufices to prove that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E \cup F) = \mu^ {*} (E) + \mu^ {*} (F)\tag{1.19}
$$

for all sets $E , F \subset X$ , with dist $( E , F ) > 0 . { \mathrm { F i x } } \varepsilon > 0$ and find an open set $A .$ with $E \cup F \subset A$ , such that 

$$
\rho (A) \leq \mu^ {*} (E \cup F) + \varepsilon .
$$

Since $d : = \mathrm { d i s t } \left( E , F \right) > 0$ we may construct open sets $A _ { 1 }$ and $A _ { 2 }$ , with $E \subset A _ { 1 } \subset A$ and $F \subset A _ { 2 } \subset A$ , and such that $A _ { 1 } \cap A _ { 2 } = \varnothing \left( \mathrm { e . g . } \right.$ , take $A _ { 1 }$ to be the union of all balls $B \left( x , r \right) \subset A$ , where $x \in E$ and $\begin{array} { r } { 0 < r < \frac { d } { 2 } } \end{array}$ , and take $A _ { 2 }$ to be the union of all balls $B \left( x , r \right) \subset A$ , where $x \in F$ and $\begin{array} { r } { 0 < r < \frac { d } { 2 } ) } \end{array}$ . Hence by (1.18), (iv), and the fact that $\rho$ is increasing, 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) + \mu^ {*} (F) \leq \rho (A _ {1}) + \rho (A _ {2}) = \rho (A _ {1} \cup A _ {2}) \leq \rho (A) \leq \mu^ {*} (E \cup F) + \varepsilon .
$$

Letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ , and using also the fact that $\mu ^ { * }$ is an outer measure, we conclude that (1.19) holds, and this concludes the proof. 

The De Giorgi–Letta theorem will often be used in [FoLe10] to study relaxation problems in Sobolev spaces, where the integral functionals under consideration are naturally defined on open sets. 

As a corollary we have the following: 

Proposition 1.63. Let $( X , \tau )$ be a locally compact Hausdorf space and let $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Radon measure. For every set $E \subset X$ define 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) = \inf \left\{\mu (A): A \in \tau , E \subset A \right\}.
$$

Then $\mu ^ { * }$ is a Radon outer measure, the σ-algebra ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ of $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable sets contains M, and $\mu ^ { * }$ coincides with $\mu$ on M. 

Proof. Since X is a locally compact Hausdorf space, using the inner regularity of open sets for any open set $A$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu \left(A\right) = \sup \left\{\mu \left(K\right): K \subset A,   K \text { compact} \right\} \\ = \sup \left\{\mu \left(A _ {1}\right): A _ {1} \subset \subset A,   A _ {1} \text { open } \right\}. \end{array}
$$

Hence we may apply the De Giorgi–Letta theorem with $\rho : = \mu$ to obtain that $\mu ^ { * }$ is an outer measure. Using the outer regularity of $\mu ,$ it follows that $\mu ^ { * } = \mu$ on M. 

It remains to show that every set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ is $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable. Let $F$ be any set. Given an open set $A \supset F$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu \left(A\right) = \mu \left(A \cap E\right) + \mu \left(A \setminus E\right) = \mu^ {*} \left(A \cap E\right) + \mu^ {*} \left(A \setminus E\right) \\ \geq \mu^ {*} \left(F \cap E\right) + \mu^ {*} \left(F \setminus E\right). \end{array}
$$

Taking the infimum over all open sets containing $F$ , we obtain 

$$
\mu^ {*} (F) \geq \mu^ {*} (F \cap E) + \mu^ {*} (F \setminus E),
$$

and this implies that E is $\mu ^ { * } { \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l e } }$ . 

Contemporary methods in relaxation theory exploit the structure of Radon measures, together with Radon–Nikodym-type theorems, to obtain characterizations of efective or relaxed energy densities. Therefore it is of the utmost interest to be able to determine whether a set function is (the restriction of) a Radon measure by means of a criterion easier to manipulate than Definition 1.55. 

Theorem 1.64. Let $( X , \tau )$ be a locally compact Hausdorf space. Assume that $\mu : \tau \to [ 0 , \infty )$ is a set function and that ν is a finite Radon measure such that 

(i) $\mu \left( A \right) \leq \mu \left( A \setminus \overline { { C } } \right) + \mu \left( B \right)$ for all A, $B , C \in \tau$ with ${ \overline { { C } } } \subset B \subset A ,$ 

(ii) for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and for every $A \in \tau$ there exists $C \in \tau$ such that $C \subset \joinrel \subset A$ and $\mu \left( A \setminus \overline { { C } } \right) \leq \varepsilon ;$ 

(iii) $\nu \left( X \right) \leq \mu \left( X \right)$ 

(iv) $\nu \left( { \overline { { A } } } \right) \geq \mu \left( A \right)$ for every $A \in \tau$ 

$$
\text {   Then   } \mu (A) = \nu (A) \text {   for   every   } A \in \tau .
$$

Proof. Fix $A \in \tau$ . We first prove that $\mu \left( A \right) \leq \nu \left( A \right)$ . Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and choose $C \in \tau$ as in (ii). Let $B \in \tau$ be such that ${ \overline { { C } } } \subset B \subset { \overline { { B } } } \subset A$ . By (i), (ii), and (iv) we have 

$$
\mu (A) \leq \mu (A \setminus \overline {{C}}) + \mu (B) \leq \varepsilon + \nu (\overline {{B}}) \leq \varepsilon + \nu (A),
$$

and it sufices to let $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ 

To prove the reverse inequality, using the inner regularity of the measure $\nu ,$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$ we may find a compact set $K \subset A$ such that 

$$
\nu (A) \leq \varepsilon + \nu (K).
$$

In turn, by Theorem A.12 there exists $C \in \tau$ , with $\overline { { C } }$ compact, such that $K \subset C \subset { \overline { { C } } } \subset A$ . Since 

$$
\nu (A) \leq \varepsilon + \nu (\overline {{C}}),
$$

by (iii), the first part of this proof, and (i), in this order, we have 

$$
\nu (A) \leq \varepsilon + \nu (X) - \nu (X \setminus \overline {{C}}) \leq \varepsilon + \mu (X) - \mu (X \setminus \overline {{C}}) \leq \varepsilon + \mu (A),
$$

and the conclusion follows by letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ 

We end this subsection by introducing in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ the Lebesgue measure and the σ-algebra of Lebesgue–measurable sets. In the Euclidean space $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ consider the family of elementary sets 

$$
\mathcal {G} := \left\{Q (x, r): x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}, 0 <   r <   \infty \right\} \cup \{\emptyset \}
$$

and define $\rho \left( Q \left( x , r \right) \right) : = r ^ { N }$ and $\rho \left( \varnothing \right) : = 0$ , where 

$$
Q (x, r) := x + \left(- \frac {r}{2}, \frac {r}{2}\right) ^ {N}.
$$

For each set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ define 

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {o} ^ {N} (E) := \inf \left\{\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(r _ {n}\right) ^ {N}: \left\{Q \left(x _ {n}, r _ {n}\right) \right\} \subset \mathcal {G}, E \subset \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} Q \left(x _ {n}, r _ {n}\right) \right\}.
$$

By Proposition 1.32, $\mathcal { L } _ { o } ^ { N }$ is an outer measure, called the N–dimensional Lebesgue outer measure. Using Remark 1.33 it can be shown that 

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {o} ^ {N} (Q (x, r)) = \rho (Q (x, r)) = r ^ {N}\tag{1.20}
$$

and that $\mathcal { L } _ { o } ^ { N }$ is translation-invariant, i.e., $\mathcal { L } _ { o } ^ { N } \left( x + E \right) = \mathcal { L } _ { o } ^ { N } \left( E \right)$ for all $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and all $E \doteq \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

The class of all $\mathcal { L } _ { o } ^ { N }$ -measurable subsets of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is called the σ-algebra of Lebesgue measurable sets, and by Carath´eodory’s theorem, $\mathcal { L } _ { o } ^ { N }$ restricted to this σ-algebra is a complete measure, called the N–dimensional Lebesgue measure and denoted by $\bar { \mathcal { L } } ^ { N }$ . Given a Lebesgue measurable set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , we will write indiferently 

$$
\mathcal {L} ^ {N} (E) \text {or} | E |
$$

for the Lebesgue measure of $E$ . 

Proposition 1.65. The Lebesgue measure $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ has the following properties: 

(i) L<sup>N</sup> ([a<sub>1</sub>, b<sub>1</sub>] × . . . × [a<sub>N</sub>, b<sub>N</sub>]) = (b<sub>1</sub> − a<sub>1</sub>) . . . (b<sub>N</sub> − a<sub>N</sub>); 

(ii) $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ is translation-invariant, $i . e . , \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( x + E \right) = \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( E \right)$ for every Lebesgue measurable set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

(iii) for every linear operator $L : \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and every Lebesgue measurable set $E \subset \overline { { \mathbb { R } ^ { N } } } , \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( L \left( E \right) \right) = \left| \operatorname* { d e t } L \right| \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( E \right)$ 

Using Proposition 1.41 we have the following proposition: 

Proposition 1.66. The outer measure $\mathcal { L } _ { o } ^ { N }$ is a metric outer measure, so that every Borel subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is Lebesgue measurable. 

Moreover, if µ is any positive translation-invariant Borel measure on $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ finite on compact sets, then $\mu \left( B \right) = c \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( B \right)$ for some $c \geq 0$ and for every Borel subset B $o f \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

Remark 1.67. Using the axiom of choice it is possible to construct sets that are not Lebesgue measurable. It may also be proved that there are Lebesgue measurable sets that are not Borel sets. Hence $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } : \mathcal { B } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \longrightarrow \left[ 0 , \infty \right]$ is not a complete measure. 

We observe that the Lebesgue outer measure is a Radon outer measure. Indeed, outer regularity of arbitrary sets follows from (1.20) and the definition of $\mathcal { L } _ { o } ^ { N }$ , while inner regularity of open sets is an immediate consequence of the fact that each open set can be written as a countable union of closed cubes with pairwise disjoint interiors. 

In view of Proposition 1.54 it turns out that every Lebesgue measurable set is the union of a Borel set with a set of Lebesgue measure zero. Hence the σ-algebra of Lebesgue measurable sets is the completion of the Borel σ-algebra for the Lebesgue measure. 

Proposition 1.68. $\mathcal { L } _ { o } ^ { N }$ is a Radon outer measure. Moreover, every Lebesgue measurable set E is the union of a Borel set and a set of Lebesgue measure zero. 

## 1.1.3 Measurable Functions and Lebesgue Integration

In this subsection we introduce the notions of measurable and integrable func tions. 

Definition 1.69. Let X and Y be nonempty sets, and let M and N be algebras on X and $Y$ , respectively. A function u $: X  Y$ is said to be measurable if $u ^ { - 1 } \left( E \right) \in \mathfrak { M }$ for every set $E \in { \mathfrak { N } }$ 

Remark 1.70. If M is a σ-algebra on a set X and N is the smallest σ-algebra that contains a given family $\mathcal { G }$ of subsets of a set Y, then $u : X \to Y$ is measurable if and only if $u ^ { - 1 } \left( E \right) \in \mathfrak { M }$ for every set $E \in { \mathcal { G } }$ . Indeed, the family of sets 

$$
\left\{E \in \mathfrak {N}: u ^ {- 1} (E) \in \mathfrak {M} \right\}
$$

is a σ-algebra that contains ${ \mathcal { G } } _ { : }$ , and so it must coincide with N. Thus, in particular, if Y is a topological space and $\Re = B \left( \boldsymbol { Y } \right)$ , then it sufices to verify that $u ^ { - 1 } \left( A \right) \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ for every open set $A \subset Y$ 

If X and $Y$ are topological spaces, ${ \mathfrak { M } } : = B \left( X \right)$ and $\mathfrak { N } : = B \left( Y \right)$ , then a measurable function $u : X \to Y$ will be called a Borel function. 

If $u \ : \ X \ \to \ Y$ is measurable and if $E ~ \in ~ \mathfrak { M }$ , then the restriction $u : X \backslash E  Y$ is a measurable function between the measurable spaces $( X \setminus E , \mathfrak { M } \lfloor ( X \setminus E ) )$ and $( Y , \mathfrak { N } )$ . Conversely, if X is a measure space with measure $\mu ,$ and the function u is defined only on $X \setminus E$ with $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ , then in general, measurability of u on $X \setminus E$ does not entail the measurability of an arbitrary extension of u to X unless $\mu$ is complete. 

Proposition 1.71. Let (X, M) and $( Y , \mathfrak { N } )$ be two measurable spaces, and let $u : X \to Y$ be a measurable function. Let $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a complete measure. $I f v : X \to Y$ is a function such that $u \left( x \right) = v \left( x \right)$ for $\mu \ a . e . \ x \in X$ , then v is measurable. 

Going back to the setting in which $u : X \setminus E \to Y$ with $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ , since Lebesgue integration does not take into account sets of measure zero, we will see that integration of u depends mostly on its measurability on $X \setminus E$ . For this reason, we extend Definition 1.69 to read as follows. 

Definition 1.72. Let (X, M) and (Y, N) be two measurable spaces, and let $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a measure. Given a function $u : X \backslash E  Y$ where $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ , u is said to be measurable over X if $u ^ { - 1 } \left( F \right) \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ for every set $F \in \mathfrak { N }$ 

We are now in a position to introduce the notion of integral. 

Definition 1.73. Let X be a nonempty set, and let M be an algebra on X. A simple function is a measurable function $s : X \to \mathbb { R }$ whose range consists of finitely many points. 

If $c _ { 1 } , \ldots , c _ { \ell }$ are the distinct values of s, then we write 

$$
s = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\ell} c _ {n} \chi_ {E _ {n}},
$$

where $\chi _ { E _ { n } }$ is the characteristic function of the set $E _ { n } : = \{ x \in X : s ( x ) = c _ { n } \}$ i.e., 

$$
\chi_ {E _ {n}} \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1 \text {   if   } x \in E _ {n}, \\ 0 \text {   otherwise }. \end{array} \right.
$$

If $\mu$ is a finitely additive (positive) measure on X and $s \geq 0$ , then for every measurable set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ we define the Lebesgue integral of s over E as 

$$
\int_ {E} s d \mu := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\ell} c _ {n} \mu (E _ {n} \cap E),\tag{1.21}
$$

where if $c _ { n } = 0$ and $\mu \left( E _ { n } \cap E \right) = \infty$ , then we use the convention 

$$
c _ {n} \mu (E _ {n} \cap E) := 0.
$$

Theorem 1.74. Let X be a nonempty set, let M be an algebra on X, and let $u : X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a measurable function. Then there exists a sequence $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ of simple functions such that 

$$
0 \leq s _ {1} (x) \leq s _ {2} (x) \leq \dots \leq s _ {n} (x) \rightarrow u (x)
$$

for every $x \in X$ . The convergence is uniform on any set on which u is bounded from above. 

Proof. For $n \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ and $0 \leq k \leq 2 ^ { 2 n } - 1$ define 

$$
E _ {n, k} := \left\{x \in X: \frac {k}{2 ^ {n}} \leq u (x) <   \frac {k + 1}{2 ^ {n + 1}} \right\}, \quad E _ {n} := \left\{x \in X: u (x) \geq 2 ^ {n} \right\},
$$

and let 

$$
s _ {n} := \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {2 ^ {2 n} - 1} \frac {k}{2 ^ {n}} \chi_ {E _ {n, k}} + 2 ^ {n} \chi_ {E _ {n}}.
$$

If $u \left( x \right) = 0$ then $x \in E _ { n , 0 }$ , and so $s _ { n } \left( x \right) = 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . If $0 < u \left( x \right) < \infty$ then $x \in E _ { n , \lceil 2 ^ { n } u ( x ) \rceil }$ for all $n \in \mathbb N$ suficiently large, where · is the integer part. Hence 

$$
0 \leq s _ {n} (x) = \frac {\lceil 2 ^ {n} u (x) \rceil}{2 ^ {n}} \leq \frac {\lceil 2 ^ {n + 1} u (x) \rceil}{2 ^ {n + 1}} = s _ {n + 1} (x) \rightarrow u (x)
$$

as $n \to \infty$ . If $u \left( x \right) = \infty$ then $x \in E _ { n }$ for all $n ,$ , and so $s _ { n } \left( x \right) = 2 ^ { n } \nearrow \infty$ 

Note that by the definition of the sets $E _ { n , k }$ we have that $\textstyle 0 \leq u - s _ { n } \leq { \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { n } } }$ on the set where $u < 2 ^ { n }$ . Hence we have uniform convergence on each set on which u is bounded from above. 

In the remainder of this subsection, M is a σ-algebra and $\mu \mathrm { ~ a ~ }$ (countably additive) measure. In view of the previous theorem, if $u : X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a measurable function, then we define its (Lebesgue) integral over a measurable set $E$ as 

$$
\int_ {E} u d \mu := \sup \left\{\int_ {E} s d \mu : s \text {   simple,   } 0 \leq s \leq u \right\}.
$$

In order to extend the notion of integral to functions of arbitrary sign, consider $u : X  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ and set 

$$
u ^ {+} := \max \left\{u, 0 \right\}, \quad u ^ {-} := \max \left\{- u, 0 \right\}.
$$

Note that $u = u ^ { + } - u ^ { - } , | u | = u ^ { + } + u ^ { - }$ , and $u$ is measurable if and only if $u ^ { + }$ and $u ^ { - }$ are measurable. Also, if u is bounded, then so are $u ^ { + }$ and $u ^ { - }$ , and in view of Theorem 1.74, u is then the uniform limit of a sequence of simple functions. 

Definition 1.75. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, and let $u : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a measurable function. Given a measurable set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , if at least one of the two integrals $\int _ { E } u ^ { + } \ : d \mu$ and $\textstyle \int _ { E } u ^ { - }  d \mu$ is finite, then we define the (Lebesgue) integral of u over the measurable set $E$ by 

$$
\int_ {E} u d \mu := \int_ {E} u ^ {+} d \mu - \int_ {E} u ^ {-} d \mu .
$$

If both $\int _ { E } u ^ { + } \ : d \mu$ and $\int _ { E } u ^ { - } \ : d \mu$ are finite, then u is said to be (Lebesgue) integrable over the measurable set $E$ 

In the special case that $\mu$ is the Lebesgue measure, we denote $\int _ { E } u d { \mathcal { L } } ^ { N }$ simply by 

$$
\int_ {E} u d x.
$$

If $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ is a measure space, with X a topological space, and if M contains $B \left( X \right)$ , then $u : X  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is said to be locally integrable if it is Lebesgue integrable over every compact set. 

A measurable function $u : X  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is Lebesgue integrable over the measurable set E if and only if 

$$
\int_ {E} | u | d \mu <   \infty .
$$

Finally, if $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ is such that $\mu \left( F \right) = 0$ and $u : X \setminus F \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is a measurable function in the sense of Definition 1.72, then we define the (Lebesgue) integral of u over the measurable set E as the Lebesgue integral of the function 

$$
v \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} u \left(x\right) \text {if} x \in X \setminus F, \\ 0 \qquad \text {otherwise}, \end{array} \right.
$$

provided $\textstyle \int _ { E } v d \mu$ is well-defined. Note that in this case 

$$
\int_ {E} v d \mu = \int_ {E} \tilde {v} d \mu ,
$$

where 

$$
\tilde {v} \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} u \left(x\right) \text { if } x \in X \setminus F, \\ w \left(x\right) \text { otherwise }, \end{array} \right.
$$

and w is an arbitrary measurable function defined on $F .$ 

Remark 1.76. If M is an algebra on X and $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a finitely additive measure on $X$ , we can still define a notion of integral as follows: we say that a measurable function $u : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is integrable if there exists a sequence $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ of measurable simple functions, each of them bounded and vanishing outside a set of finite measure (depending on n), such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu \left(\{x \in X: | u (x) - s _ {n} (x) | > \varepsilon \}\right) = 0
$$

for each $\varepsilon > 0$ , and 

$$
\lim _ {n, l \to \infty} \int_ {X} | s _ {n} - s _ {l} | d \mu = 0.
$$

It may be shown that for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ the limit li $\scriptstyle \mathrm { n } _ { n \to \infty } \int _ { E } s _ { n }$ dµ exists in R and does not depend on the particular sequence $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ . The integral of u over the measurable set E is defined by 

$$
\int_ {E} u d \mu := \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} s _ {n} d \mu .
$$

The following result follows from Theorem 1.74. 

Corollary 1.77. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, and let $u : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a measurable function. If the set $\left\{ x \in X : \left| u \left( x \right) \right| > 0 \right\}$ has σ-finite measure and u is finite µ a.e., then there exists a sequence $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ of simple functions, each of them bounded and vanishing outside a set of finite measure (depending on n), such that $s _ { n } \left( x \right) \to u \left( x \right)$ as $n \to \infty$ for µ a.e. $x \in X$ and 

$$
\left| s _ {n} (x) \right| \leq \left| u (x) \right|
$$

for µ a.e. $x \in X$ and $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

Proof. Step 1: Assume first that $u \geq 0$ . Since $\{ x \in X : u ( x ) > 0 \}$ has $\sigma -$ finite measure we can find an increasing sequence $\{ X _ { n } \}$ of measurable sets of finite measure such that 

$$
\{x \in X: u (x) > 0 \} = \bigcup_ {n} X _ {n}.
$$

For $n \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ and $0 \leq k \leq 2 ^ { 2 n } - 1$ define 

$$
E _ {n, k} := \left\{x \in X _ {n}: \frac {k}{2 ^ {n}} \leq u (x) <   \frac {k + 1}{2 ^ {n + 1}} \right\},
$$

and let 

$$
s _ {n} := \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {2 ^ {2 n} - 1} \frac {k}{2 ^ {n}} \chi_ {E _ {n, k}}.
$$

Then as in the proof of Theorem 1.74, it is possible to show that at each point x where u is finite, $s _ { n } \left( x \right) \to u \left( x \right)$ as $n \to \infty$ 

Step 2: In the general case it sufices to apply Step 1 to $u ^ { + }$ and $u ^ { - }$ . 

Remark 1.78. Note that if u is Lebesgue integrable, then the hypotheses of the previous corollary hold, since 

$$
\{x \in X: | u (x) | > 0 \} = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left\{x \in X: | u (x) | > \frac {1}{n} \right\}
$$

and 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \mu \left(\left\{x \in X: | u (x) | > \frac {1}{n} \right\}\right) \leq \int_ {X} | u | d \mu <   \infty .
$$

Similarly, $\mu \left( \{ x \in X : | u ( x ) | = \infty \} \right) = 0 .$ 

The next two results are pivotal in the theory of integration of nonnegative functions. 

Theorem 1.79 (Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, and let $u _ { n } : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a sequence of measurable functions such that 

$$
0 \leq u _ {1} (x) \leq u _ {2} (x) \leq \dots \leq u _ {n} (x) \rightarrow u (x)
$$

for every $x \in X$ . Then u is measurable and 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} u _ {n} d \mu = \int_ {X} u d \mu .
$$

Example 1.80. The Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem does not hold in general for decreasing sequences. Indeed, consider $X = \mathbb { R }$ and let $\mu$ be the Lebesgue measure $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 }$ . Define 

$$
u _ {n} := \frac {1}{n} \chi_ {[ n, \infty)}.
$$

Then $u _ { n } \geq u _ { n + 1 }$ and 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} u _ {n} d x = \infty \neq 0 = \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \lim _ {n \to \infty} u _ {n} d x.
$$

Corollary 1.81. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, and let $u _ { n } : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a sequence of measurable functions. Then 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \int_ {X} u _ {n} d \mu = \int_ {X} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} u _ {n} d \mu .
$$

Proof. Apply the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem to the increasing sequence of partial sums and use linearity of the integral. 

Example 1.82. Given a doubly indexed sequence $\left\{ a _ { n k } \right\}$ , with $a _ { n k } \geq 0$ for all $n , k \in \mathbb { N }$ , we have 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} a _ {n k} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} a _ {n k}.
$$

To see this, it sufices to consider $X = \mathbb { N }$ with counting measure and to define $u _ { n } : \mathbb { N } \longrightarrow [ 0 , \infty ]$ by $u _ { n } \left( k \right) : = a _ { n k }$ . Then 

$$
\int_ {X} u _ {n} d \mu = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} a _ {n k},
$$

and the result now follows from the previous corollary. 

Lemma 1.83 (Fatou lemma). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. 

(i) $I f u _ { n } : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a sequence of measurable functions, then 

$$
u := \liminf _ {n \to \infty} u _ {n}
$$

is a measurable function and 

$$
\int_ {X} u   d \mu \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} u _ {n}   d \mu ;
$$

(ii) if $u _ { n } : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is a sequence of measurable functions such that 

$$
u _ {n} \leq v
$$

for some measurable function $v : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ with $\textstyle \int _ { X } v d \mu < \infty$ , then 

$$
u := \limsup _ {n \to \infty} u _ {n}
$$

is a measurable function and 

$$
\int_ {X} u   d \mu \geq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} u _ {n}   d \mu .
$$

Example $\it 1 . 8 4$ . Fatou’s lemma (i) fails for real-valued functions. Indeed, consider $X = \mathbb { R }$ and let $\mu$ be the Lebesgue measure $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 }$ . Define 

$$
u _ {n} := - \frac {1}{n} \chi_ {[ 0, n ]}.
$$

Then 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} u _ {n}   d x = - 1 <   0 = \int_ {\mathbb {R}} \lim _ {n \to \infty} u _ {n}   d x.
$$

For functions of arbitrary sign we have the following convergence result. 

Theorem 1.85 (Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, and let $u _ { n } \ : \ X \ \to \ [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a sequence of measurable functions such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} u _ {n} (x) = u (x)
$$

for $\mu \ a . e . \ x \in X$ . If there exists a Lebesgue integrable function v such that 

$$
\left| u _ {n} (x) \right| \leq v (x)
$$

for $\mu \ a . e . \ x \in X$ and all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , then u is Lebesgue integrable and 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} | u _ {n} - u | d \mu = 0.
$$

In particular, 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} u _ {n} d \mu = \int_ {X} u d \mu .
$$

Example 1.86. If v is not integrable then the theorem fails in general. Indeed, consider $X = [ 0 , 1 ]$ and let $\mu$ be the Lebesgue measure $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 }$ . Define 

$$
u _ {n} := n \chi_ {\left[ 0, \frac {1}{n} \right]}.
$$

Then 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {1} u _ {n} d x = 1 \neq 0 = \int_ {0} ^ {1} \lim _ {n \to \infty} u _ {n} d x.
$$

The results below provide applications of the finite value property and nonatomic measures (see Proposition 1.20) in the case that the measure is given by an integral. They will be used to study well-posedness of functionals of the form $\textstyle \int _ { E } f \left( x , v \left( x \right) \right)$ dx in Chapter 6. 

Proposition 1.87. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, let µ satisfy the finite value property, and let u, $v : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be measurable functions such that 

$$
\int_ {E} u d \mu \leq \int_ {E} v d \mu
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ . Then $u \left( x \right) \leq v \left( x \right)$ for µ a.e. $x \in X$ 

Proof. For $k \in \mathbb N$ define $u _ { k } : = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ u , k \} , v _ { k } : = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ v , k \}$ . It is enough to show that 

$$
u _ {k} (x) \leq v _ {k} (x) \text {   for   } \mu \text {   a.e.   } x \in X.
$$

For $n \in \mathbb { N }$ define 

$$
E _ {n, k} := \left\{x \in X: u _ {k} (x) > v _ {k} (x) + \frac {1}{n} \right\}.
$$

We claim that $\mu \left( E _ { n , k } \right) = 0$ for all $k , n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Indeed, assume by contradiction that $\mu \left( E _ { n , k } \right) > 0$ for some $k , n \in \mathbb { N }$ . By the finite value property there exists a measurable set $F \subset E _ { n , k }$ such that $0 < \mu \left( F \right) < \infty$ . By definition of $E _ { n , k }$ 

$$
k \geq u _ {k} (x) > v _ {k} (x) + \frac {1}{n}
$$

for all $x \in F$ , and so, since $k > v _ { k } \left( x \right) = \operatorname* { i n f } \left\{ v \left( x \right) , k \right\}$ , we have that 

$$
v (x) + \frac {1}{n} = v _ {k} (x) + \frac {1}{n} <   u _ {k} (x) \leq u (x),
$$

and upon integration over $F _ { ; }$ 

$$
\int_ {F} v d \mu + \frac {1}{n} \mu (F) \leq \int_ {F} u d \mu \leq \int_ {F} v d \mu ,
$$

where in the last inequality we have used the hypothesis. Since $\mu \left( F \right) < \infty$ and $v \leq k$ on $F .$ , it follows that the right-hand side of the previous inequality is finite, and thus $\mu \left( F \right) = 0$ , which is a contradiction. 

Remark 1.88. If u is integrable, then we can dispense with the hypothesis that $\mu$ has the finite value property. Indeed, the sets $E _ { n , k }$ constructed in the proof are contained in the set $\{ x \in X : u ( x ) > 0 \}$ , which has σ-finite measure in view of Remark 1.78. 

Proposition 1.89. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, let µ be nonatomic, and let $u : X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a measurable function. Then the measure 

$$
\nu (E) := \int_ {E} u d \mu , \quad E \in \mathfrak {M},\tag{1.22}
$$

is nonatomic if and only if 

$$
\mu \left(\{x \in X: u (x) = \infty \}\right) = 0.
$$

Proof. Assume that ν is nonatomic. If 

$$
\mu \left(\{x \in X: u (x) = \infty \}\right) > 0,
$$

then any subset of this set has either zero or infinite ν measure, and this violates the hypothesis. 

Conversely, suppose that $\mu \left( \{ x \in X : u \left( x \right) = \infty \} \right) = 0 .$ . Let 

$$
E _ {0} := \left\{x \in X: 0 <   u (x) <   \infty \right\}.
$$

If $\mu \left( E _ { 0 } \right) = 0$ , then $\nu \equiv 0$ and there is nothing to prove. Thus assume that $\mu \left( E _ { 0 } \right) > 0$ . Since $\nu \left( X \setminus E _ { 0 } \right) = 0$ , to prove that ν is nonatomic it sufices to show that this holds for $\nu : \mathfrak { M } \lfloor E _ { 0 }  [ 0 , \infty ]$ . Let $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ be a subset of $E _ { 0 }$ with $\nu \left( E \right) > 0$ . Since 

$$
E _ {0} = \bigcup_ {k} E _ {k},
$$

where 

$$
E _ {k} := \left\{x \in X: \frac {1}{k} <   u (x) <   k \right\},
$$

there exists $k _ { 0 }$ such that $\mu \left( E \cap E _ { k _ { 0 } } \right) > 0$ . Since $\mu$ is nonatomic there exists $F \in { \mathfrak { M } } , F \subset E \cap E _ { k _ { 0 } }$ , such that 

$$
0 <   \mu (F) <   \mu (E \cap E _ {k _ {0}}).
$$

If $\nu \left( F \right) = 0$ then $u = 0 ~ \mu ~ \mathrm { a . e }$ . on $F _ { ; }$ , and if $\nu \left( \left( E \cap E _ { k _ { 0 } } \right) \setminus F \right) = 0$ then $u = 0$ $\mu \ \mathrm { a . e . }$ . on $( E \cap E _ { k _ { 0 } } ) \setminus F$ . By the definition of $E _ { k _ { 0 } }$ these would imply that $\mu \left( F \right) = 0 \mathrm { o r } \mu \left( \left( E \cap E _ { k _ { 0 } } \right) \setminus F \right) = 0$ , both contradicting the choice of $F$ . Hence 

$$
\nu (F), \nu ((E \cap E _ {k _ {0}}) \setminus F) > 0.
$$

Since $u \leq k _ { 0 }$ on $F$ and $\mu \left( F \right) < \infty$ , we obtain $\infty > \nu \left( F \right) > 0$ . It follows that 

$$
0 <   \nu (F) <   \nu (F) + \nu ((E \cap E _ {k _ {0}}) \setminus F) \leq \nu (E).
$$

Hence ν is nonatomic. 

Corollary 1.90. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with $\mu$ nonatomic. 

(i) Let $u : X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a measurable function such that 

$$
\int_ {X} u d \mu = \infty .
$$

Then there exists a denumerable partition of X into disjoint sets $X _ { n } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that 

$$
\int_ {X _ {n}} u d \mu = \infty .
$$

(ii) Let $\{ u _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of measurable functions $u _ { n } : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\int_ {X} u _ {n} d \mu = \infty
$$

for every n. Then there exists a partition of X into disjoint sets $X _ { n } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that 

$$
\int_ {X _ {n}} u _ {n} d \mu = \infty .
$$

Proof. Step 1: Let $u : X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a measurable function such that 

$$
\int_ {X} u d \mu = \infty .
$$

We prove that there exists a partition of X into two disjoint sets $E _ { i } \in \mathfrak { M }$ such that 

$$
\int_ {E _ {i}} u d \mu = \infty , i = 1, 2.
$$

Let 

$$
X _ {\infty} := \left\{x \in X: u (x) = \infty \right\}.
$$

If $\mu \left( X _ { \infty } \right) > 0$ , then since $\mu$ is nonatomic we may find $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $F \subset X _ { \infty }$ and 

$$
0 <   \mu (F) <   \mu (X _ {\infty}).
$$

It sufices to define $E _ { 1 } : = F$ and $E _ { 2 } : = X \setminus F \supset X _ { \infty } \setminus F .$ 

If $\mu \left( X _ { \infty } \right) = 0$ , then by Proposition 1.89 the measure ν defined in (1.22) is nonatomic. Therefore by Proposition 1.20 there exists $F _ { 1 } \in \mathfrak { M }$ such that $\textstyle \int _ { F _ { 1 } } u d \mu \ = \ 1$ . Since $\textstyle \int _ { X \setminus F _ { 1 } } u d \mu = \infty$ , the same argument yields $F _ { 2 } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , $F _ { 2 } \subset X \setminus F _ { 1 }$ , such that $\textstyle \int _ { F _ { 2 } } u d \mu = 1$ . Inductively, we construct a sequence of mutually disjoint sets $F _ { n } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $\textstyle \int _ { F _ { n } } u d \mu = 1$ . It sufices to set 

$$
E _ {1} := \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {2 n}, \quad E _ {2} := X \setminus E _ {1} \supset \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {2 n - 1}.
$$

By induction the statement in (i) now follows. 

Step 2: To prove (ii) for every $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and $k \in \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \}$ , define 

$$
D _ {n, k} := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \big \{x \in X: \frac {1}{2 ^ {k + 1}} \leq u _ {n} (x) <   \frac {1}{2 ^ {k}} \big \} & \text { if } k <   \infty , \\ \big \{x \in X: u _ {n} (x) = \infty \big \} & \text { if } k = \infty . \end{array} \right.
$$

For fixed $n \in \mathbb N$ construct a sequence $\{ C _ { n , k } \} _ { k \in \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \} }$ such that $C _ { n , k } \subset D _ { n , k }$ and 

$$
\mu \left(C _ {n, k}\right) = \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}} \mu \left(D _ {n, k}\right).\tag{1.23}
$$

This is undertaken by induction on n. Indeed, assume that $\{ C _ { l , k } \} _ { k \in { \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \} } }$ has been obtained for all $l < n$ . For each $l < n$ set 

$$
\mathcal {F} _ {l} := \left\{C _ {l, k}: k \in \mathbb {Z} \cup \{\infty \} \right\} \cup \left\{X \setminus \bigcup_ {k \in \mathbb {Z} \cup \{\infty \}} C _ {l, k} \right\}.
$$

Then $\mathcal { F } _ { l }$ is a countable partition of $X$ , because the sets $\{ C _ { l , k } : k \in \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \} \}$ are pairwise disjoint. Hence also 

$$
\mathcal {G} _ {n} := \left\{\bigcap_ {i = 1} ^ {n - 1} E _ {i}: E _ {i} \in \mathcal {F} _ {i} \text {   for   all   } i = 1, \dots , n - 1 \right\}
$$

is a countable partition of X. Write $\mathcal { G } _ { n } = \{ G _ { j } \}$ and for $k \in \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \}$ apply Proposition 1.20 to each $G _ { j } \cap D _ { n , k }$ to find a subset $H _ { j , n , k } \subset G _ { j } \cap D _ { n , k }$ such that 

$$
\mu \left(H _ {j, n, k}\right) = \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}} \mu \left(G _ {j} \cap D _ {n, k}\right).
$$

Set 

$$
C _ {n, k} := \bigcup_ {j} H _ {j, n, k},
$$

and observe that $C _ { n , k } \subset D _ { n , k }$ and for every $E \in { \mathcal { G } } _ { n }$ 

$$
\mu \left(C _ {n, k} \cap E\right) = \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}} \mu \left(D _ {n, k} \cap E\right).\tag{1.24}
$$

In particular, (1.23) follows, and this completes the construction of the sequence $\left\{ C _ { n , k } \right\} _ { k \in \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \} }$ 

Note also that if $l \in \mathbb N$ then each $E \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { n } , n = 1 , \dots , l - 1$ , may be written as the disjoint union 

$$
E = \bigcup_ {i \in \{1, \dots , l - 1 \} \backslash \{n \}} \bigcup_ {E _ {i} \in \mathcal {F} _ {i}} E _ {1} \cap \dots \cap E _ {n - 1} \cap E \cap E _ {n + 1} \cap \dots \cap E _ {l - 1}.
$$

Hence for all integers $l > n$ and all $h \in \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \}$ , condition (1.24) (with $C _ { n , k }$ replaced by $C _ { l , h } )$ implies 

$$
\mu \left(C _ {l, h} \cap C _ {n, k}\right) = \frac {1}{2 ^ {l}} \mu \left(D _ {l, h} \cap C _ {n, k}\right).\tag{1.25}
$$

Next we claim that for every $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and $k \in \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \}$ }, 

$$
\mu \left(C _ {n, k} \cap \left(\bigcup_ {l = n + 1} ^ {\infty} \bigcup_ {h \in \mathbb {Z} \cup \{\infty \}} C _ {l, h}\right)\right) \leq \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}} \mu \left(C _ {n, k}\right).\tag{1.26}
$$

By (1.25) and since the collection $\{ D \ i , h \in \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \} \}$ is a partition of $X$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu \left(C _ {n, k} \cap \left(\bigcup_ {l = n + 1} ^ {\infty} \bigcup_ {h \in \mathbb {Z} \cup \{\infty \}} C _ {l, h}\right)\right) \leq \sum_ {l = n + 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {h \in \mathbb {Z} \cup \{\infty \}} \mu \left(C _ {n, k} \cap C _ {l, h}\right) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qend{array}
$$

and so $C _ { n , k }$ satisfies (1.26). 

Step 3: For every $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and $k \in \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \}$ set 

$$
B _ {n, k} := C _ {n, k} \setminus \left(\bigcup_ {l = n + 1} ^ {\infty} \bigcup_ {h \in \overline {{\mathbb {N}}}} C _ {l, h}\right).
$$

Fix $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Since $B _ { n , k } \subset C _ { n , k }$ for all $k \in \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \}$ , it follows that the sets $B _ { n , k }$ for $k \in \mathbb { Z } \cup \{ \infty \}$ , are pairwise disjoint. If $\mu \left( B _ { n , \infty } \right) > 0$ , then by the definition of $D _ { n , \infty }$ 

$$
\int_ {B _ {n, \infty}} u _ {n} d \mu = \infty .
$$

If $\mu \left( B _ { n , \infty } \right) = 0$ , then (1.23) and (1.26) yield 

$$
\mu \left(B _ {n, k}\right) \geq \left(1 - \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}}\right) \mu \left(C _ {n, k}\right) \geq \frac {1}{2 ^ {n + 1}} \mu \left(D _ {n, k}\right),\tag{1.27}
$$

and by the definition of $D _ { n , k }$ , for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {k = - \infty} ^ {\infty} \int_ {B _ {n, k}} u _ {n} d \mu \geq \sum_ {k = - \infty} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {k + 1}} \mu (B _ {n, k}) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \frac {1}{2 ^ {n + 1}} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {k + 1}} \mu (D _ {n, k}) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \frac {1}{2 ^ {n + 1}} \frac {1}{2} \int_ {X} u _ {n} d \mu = \infty , \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that $\mu \left( B _ { n , \infty } \right) \ = \ 0$ and (1.27) imply that $\mu \left( D _ { n , \infty } \right) = 0$ 

Hence we may take 

$$
X _ {n} := \bigcup_ {k \in \mathbb {Z} \cup \{\infty \}} B _ {n, k}.
$$

This completes the proof. 

The next proposition will be used in Chapter 2 to extend the Riemann– Lebesgue lemma to finite nonatomic measures. 

Proposition 1.91. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with µ finite and nonatomic. Then there exists a measurable function $u : X \to [ 0 , 1 )$ such that for any Borel set $B \subset [ 0 , 1 ]$ , 

$$
\mu \left(u ^ {- 1} (B)\right) = \mathcal {L} ^ {1} (B) \mu (X).\tag{1.28}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

for some nonnegative integer $\ell ,$ it follows that $\ell \leq k - 1$ . Moreover, since $x \in X \setminus E _ { * }$ we have that 

$$

and so 

$$

$$

and thus $u \left( x \right) < \theta$ . Hence (1.35) holds. 

We claim that $\left\{ x \in X : \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { l } { \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { n } } } \chi _ { E _ { n } } \left( x \right) < \theta \right\}$ is the union of k pairwise disjoint sets of the form 

$$
E _ {1} ^ {(j _ {1})} \cap \ldots \cap E _ {l} ^ {(j _ {l})},
$$

where $j _ { i } = 0 , 1$ , for all $i = 1 , \dots , l$ . Note that if this is true, then by (1.35) and since $\mu \left( E ^ { * } \right) = 0$ , it follows that 

$$

$$

The extension of the previous formula to values of $\theta$ that are not dyadic rational follows from the countable additivity of $\mu .$ . Indeed, given any $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 ]$ it sufices to construct a sequence of dyadic rational numbers $\theta _ { n } ~ { \nearrow } ~ \theta$ . Then by Proposition 1.7, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mu \left(\{x \in X: u (x) <   \theta \}\right) & = \mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \{x \in X: u (x) <   \theta_ {n} \}\right) \\ & = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu \left(\{x \in X: u (x) <   \theta_ {n} \}\right) \\ & = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \theta_ {n} \mu (X) = \theta \mu (X). \end{array}
$$

To prove the claim for $k = 1 , \dots , 2 ^ { l }$ , set 

$$

$$
\sum_ {n \in \{1, \dots , l \}: j _ {n} = 0} 2 ^ {l - n}

for some $( j _ { 1 } , \dots , j _ { l } ) \in I _ { k , l }$ , it follows that 

$$
\operatorname{card} I _ {k, l} = k.
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu \left(\left\{x \in X: a \leq u (x) <   b \right\}\right) \\ = \mu \left(\left\{x \in X: u (x) <   b \right\}\right) \setminus \mu \left(\left\{x \in X: u (x) <   a \right\}\right) \\ = (b - a) \mu (X). \end{array}
$$

In particular, if $b = a$ then $\mu \left( u ^ { - 1 } \left( \left\{ a \right\} \right) \right) = 0$ , and so since any open set $A \subset [ 0 , 1 ]$ is the disjoint union of open intervals, it follows that 

$$

$$

for any open set $A \subset [ 0 , 1 ]$ . Since the sets of Borel sets $B \subset [ 0 , 1 ]$ for which (1.28) holds is $\mathrm { a \ \sigma \mathrm { - a l g e b r a } }$ and it contains all open sets, it follows that (1.28) holds for every Borel set $B \subset [ 0 , 1 ]$ 

The next proposition will be used to study well-posedness of functionals of the form $\textstyle \int _ { E } f \left( x , v \left( x \right) \right)$ dx in Chapter 6. 

Proposition 1.92. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure with $\mu$ satisfying the finite subset property. If $u : X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a measurable function and if 

$$
\int_ {X} u d \mu > \alpha
$$

for some $\alpha \geq 0$ , then there exists a nonnegative integrable simple function s such that $0 \leq s \leq u$ in X, with $s < u$ on $\{ x \in X : u ( x ) > 0 \}$ , and 

$$
\int_ {X} s d \mu > \alpha .
$$

Proof. By Theorem 1.74 and the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem we can find a nonnegative simple function ˜s such that $0 \leq \tilde { s } \leq u$ in X and 

$$
\int_ {X} \tilde {s} d \mu > \alpha .
$$

Write 

$$
\tilde {s} = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\ell} c _ {n} \chi_ {E _ {n}},
$$

where $c _ { n } > 0$ for $n = 1 , \ldots , \ell .$ . Without loss of generality, we may assume that ˜s is integrable. Indeed, if this were not the case then there would exist $n \in \{ 1 , \ldots , \ell \}$ such that $\mu \left( E _ { n } \right) = \infty$ . By Proposition 1.25 we may find a set 

$F \subset E _ { n } , F \in \mathfrak { M }$ , such that $\textstyle { \frac { \alpha } { c _ { n } } } < \mu ( F ) < \infty$ , and it sufices to observe that the integrable simple function $c _ { n } \chi _ { F }$ is below u and 

$$
\int_ {X} c _ {n} \chi_ {F} d \mu > \alpha .
$$

Suppose now that $\tilde { s }$ is integrable. Define 

$$
s := (1 - \delta) \tilde {s},
$$

where $0 < \delta < 1$ is so small that 

$$
(1 - \delta) \int_ {X} \tilde {s} d \mu > \alpha .
$$

The function s has the desired properties. 

Remark 1.93. In view of Remark 1.19, the previous proposition holds for $\sigma -$ finite measures. 

We conclude this subsection with regularity properties for measurable functions when the underlying measure is Radon. 

Theorem 1.94 (Lusin). Let X be a locally compact Hausdorf space, and let $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Radon outer measure. Let $u : X \to \mathbb { R }$ be a measurable function and let $E \subset X$ be a $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable set such that $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( E \right) < \infty$ . Then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a compact set $K \subset X$ such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(E \setminus K\right) <   \varepsilon
$$

and $u : K \to \mathbb { R }$ is continuous. 

Remark 1.95. If X is a metric space, then Lusin’s theorem continues to hold if $\mu ^ { * }$ is a Borel regular outer measure, although the set K may be only closed and not necessarily compact. 

Corollary 1.96. Let X be a locally compact Hausdorf space, and let $\mu ^ { * }$ : ${ \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a σ-finite Radon outer measure. Let $u : X \to \mathbb { R }$ be a measurable function. Then there exists a Borel function $v : X \to \mathbb { R }$ such that $u = v \ f o r \ \mu ^ { * } \ a . e . \ x \in X$ 

Next we present a regularity result for functions integrable with respect to a Radon measure. 

Theorem 1.97 (Vitali–Carath´eodory). Let X be a locally compact Hausdorf space, and let $\mu : B ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Radon measure. If $u : X \to \mathbb { R }$ is an integrable function and $\varepsilon > 0$ , then there exist $v , w : X \to \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
v (x) \leq u (x) \leq w (x)
$$

for µ a.e. $x \in X$ , v is upper semicontinuous and bounded above, w is lower semicontinuous and bounded below, and 

$$
\int_ {X} (w - v) d \mu \leq \varepsilon .
$$

## 1.1.4 Comparison Between Measures

Given a measure space $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ and a measurable function $u : X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ ], we define 

$$
\nu (E) := \int_ {E} u d \mu , \quad E \in \mathfrak {M}.\tag{1.36}
$$

Then ν is a measure and $\nu \left( E \right) = 0$ whenever $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ . The measure $\nu$ is said to be absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ . More generally, we have the following definition. 

Definition 1.98. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\mu , \nu : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be two measures. 

(i) $\mu ,$ ν are said to be mutually singular, and we write $\nu \perp \mu$ , if there exist two disjoint sets $X _ { \mu } , \ X _ { \nu } \in \mathfrak { M }$ such that $X = X _ { \mu } \cup X _ { \nu }$ and for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ we have 

$$
\mu (E) = \mu (E \cap X _ {\mu}), \quad \nu (E) = \nu (E \cap X _ {\nu}).
$$

(ii) ν is said to be absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu ,$ and we write $\nu \ll \mu$ , if for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ we have $\nu \left( E \right) = 0$ 

(iii) ν is said to be difuse with respect to $\mu$ if for every set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ we have $\nu \left( E \right) = 0$ 

The term absolute continuity comes from the fact that if $\nu$ is finite then $\nu \ll \mu$ if and only if 

$$
\lim _ {\mu (E) \to 0} \nu (E) = 0.
$$

More precisely, we have the following result. 

Proposition 1.99. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\mu , \nu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to$ $[ 0 , \infty ]$ be two measures with ν finite. Then ν is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ if and only if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
\nu (E) \leq \varepsilon\tag{1.37}
$$

for every measurable set $E \subset X$ with $\mu \left( E \right) \leq \delta$ 

Proof. If (1.37) holds and if $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ is such that $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ , then necessarily $\nu \left( E \right) \leq \varepsilon { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ a l l ~ } } \varepsilon > 0$ , so that $\nu \left( E \right) = 0$ . Thus $\nu \ll \mu$ 

Conversely, assume by contradiction that $\nu \ll \mu$ and that (1.37) fails. Then we can find $\varepsilon > 0$ and a sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ such that $\textstyle \mu \left( E _ { n } \right) \leq { \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { n } } }$ and $\nu \left( E _ { n } \right) \geq \varepsilon$ . Define 

$$
F _ {k} := \bigcup_ {n = k} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}, \quad F := \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {k}.
$$

Then 

$$
\mu (F) \leq \mu (F _ {k}) \leq \sum_ {n = k} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}} = \frac {1}{2 ^ {k - 1}} \rightarrow 0
$$

as $k \to \infty$ . On the other hand, since ν is finite, by Proposition 1.7(ii), 

$$
\nu (F) = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \nu (F _ {k}) \geq \varepsilon ,
$$

which contradicts the fact $\nu \ll \mu$ 

Example 1.100. If $\nu$ is not finite then condition (1.37) still implies that $\nu \ll \mu$ , but the converse does not hold in general. To see this, let $X \ = \ ( 0 , 1 )$ , M $\mathbf { \Sigma } = B \left( \left( 0 , 1 \right) \right)$ , take $\mu$ to be the Lebesgue measure, and 

$$
\nu (E) := \int_ {E} \frac {1}{x} d x, E \in \mathfrak {M}.
$$

Then $\nu \ll \mu$ but (1.37) fails. 

It turns out that (1.36) gives a complete characterization of all measures ν absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ if $\mu$ is σ-finite (see the Radon– Nikodym theorem below). 

Theorem 1.101 (Radon–Nikodym, I). Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\mu , \nu : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be two measures, with µ σ-finite and ν absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ . Then there exists a measurable function u : $X $ $[ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\nu (E) = \int_ {E} u d \mu
$$

for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . The function u is unique up to a set of $\mu$ measure zero. 

The function u is called the Radon–Nikodym derivative of $\nu$ with respect to $\mu ,$ and we write $\begin{array} { r } { u = \frac { d \nu } { d \mu } } \end{array}$ 

The proof of this theorem is hinged on the following two lemmas. 

Lemma 1.102. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\mu , \nu : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be two measures. For every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ define 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \nu_ {a c} (E) := \sup \left\{\int_ {E} u   d \mu : u: X \to [ 0, \infty ] m e a s u r a b l e, \right. \\ \qquad \left. \int_ {E ^ {\prime}} u   d \mu \leq \nu (E ^ {\prime}) f o r a l l E ^ {\prime} \subset E, E ^ {\prime} \in \mathfrak {M} \right\}. \end{array}\tag{1.38}
$$

Then $\nu _ { a c }$ is a measure, with $\nu _ { a c } \ll \mu _ { : }$ , and for each $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ the supremum in the definition of $\nu _ { a c }$ is actually attained by a function u admissible for $\nu _ { a c } \left( E \right)$ Moreover, if $\nu _ { a c }$ is σ-finite, then u may be chosen independently of the set E. 

Proof. Step 1: We prove that $\nu _ { a c }$ is a measure, with $\nu _ { a c } \ll \mu$ . It follows from (1.38) that $\nu _ { a c } \left( \emptyset \right) = 0$ . Let $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ be a countable collection of pairwise disjoint sets and let $\textstyle E : = \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n }$ . Let $u : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a measurable function such that $\textstyle \int _ { E ^ { \prime } } u d \mu \leq \nu \left( E ^ { \prime } \right)$ for all $E ^ { \prime } \subset E , E ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ . Then for every $n \in \mathbb { N } .$ , 

$$
\int_ {E ^ {\prime}} u d \mu \leq \nu (E ^ {\prime})
$$

for all $E ^ { \prime } \subset E _ { n } , E ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , and so 

$$
\int_ {E} u d \mu = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \int_ {E _ {n}} u d \mu \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \nu_ {a c} (E _ {n}).
$$

Hence taking the supremum over all such $u ,$ we obtain 

$$
\nu_ {a c} (E) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \nu_ {a c} (E _ {n}).\tag{1.39}
$$

Conversely, for each $\varepsilon > 0$ and $n \in \mathbb N$ let $u _ { n } : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a measurable function such that $\textstyle \int _ { E ^ { \prime } } u _ { n } d \mu \leq \nu ( E ^ { \prime } )$ for all $E ^ { \prime } \subset E _ { n } , E ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , and 

$$
\nu_ {a c} (E _ {n}) \leq \int_ {E _ {n}} u _ {n} d \mu + \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n}}.
$$

Define $\begin{array} { r } { u : = \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \chi _ { E _ { n } } u _ { n } } \end{array}$ . Then for all $E ^ { \prime } \subset E$ , with $E ^ { \prime } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , we have 

$$
\int_ {E ^ {\prime}} u d \mu = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \int_ {E ^ {\prime} \cap E _ {n}} u _ {n} d \mu \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \nu (E ^ {\prime} \cap E _ {n}) = \nu (E ^ {\prime}),
$$

and so for every $l \in \mathbb N$ 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \nu_ {a c} (E _ {n}) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \left(\int_ {E _ {n}} u _ {n} d \mu + \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n}}\right) \leq \int_ {E} u d \mu + \varepsilon \leq \nu_ {a c} (E) + \varepsilon .
$$

Letting $l  \infty$ first and then $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ , and using (1.39), we conclude that $\nu _ { a c }$ is a measure. 

From the definition of $\nu _ { a c }$ it follows that if $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ , then $\nu _ { a c } \left( E \right) = 0$ , which shows that $\nu _ { a c } \ll \mu$ 

Step 2: We claim that for each $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ the supremum in the definition of $\nu _ { a c }$ is actually reached by a measurable function $u .$ . Indeed, note first that if $u ,$ $v : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ are measurable functions such that 

$$
\int_ {E ^ {\prime}} u d \mu \leq \nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right), \quad \int_ {E ^ {\prime}} v d \mu \leq \nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right)
$$

for all $E ^ { \prime } \subset E , E ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , then max $\{ u , v \}$ satisfies the same property, since 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {E ^ {\prime}} \max \left\{u, v \right\} d \mu = \int_ {E ^ {\prime} \cap \left\{u \geq v \right\}} u   d \mu + \int_ {E ^ {\prime} \cap \left\{u <   v \right\}} v   d \mu \\ \qquad \leq \nu \left(E ^ {\prime} \cap \left\{u \geq v \right\}\right) + \nu \left(E ^ {\prime} \cap \left\{u <   v \right\}\right) \\ \qquad = \nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right). \end{array}\tag{1.40}
$$

Hence we can find an increasing sequence of measurable functions $u _ { n } : X \to$ [0, ∞] such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} u _ {n} d \mu = \nu_ {a c} (E)
$$

and $\textstyle \int _ { E ^ { \prime } } u _ { n } d \mu \leq \nu ( E ^ { \prime } )$ for all $E ^ { \prime } \subset E , E ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ . Define $u : = \dim _ { n \to \infty } u _ { n }$ . By the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem we have 

$$
\int_ {E} u d \mu = \nu_ {a c} (E).
$$

Step 3: Suppose first that $\nu _ { a c }$ is finite, and let u be a function obtained in Step 2 for the set X. We claim that 

$$
\nu_ {a c} (E) = \int_ {E} u d \mu\tag{1.41}
$$

for any set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . Since u is admissible for $X$ , we have that $\textstyle \int _ { E ^ { \prime } } u d \mu \leq \nu ( E ^ { \prime } )$ for all $E ^ { \prime } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . Hence 6 

$$
\nu_ {a c} (E) \geq \int_ {E} u d \mu .
$$

If this inequality were strict for some $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , then we could find a function v admissible for $\nu _ { a c } \left( E \right)$ such that 

$$
\int_ {E} v d \mu > \int_ {E} u d \mu .\tag{1.42}
$$

Define 

$$
\overline {{u}} \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} v \left(x\right) \text {   for   } x \in E \cap \left\{v > u \right\}, \\ u \left(x\right) \text {   elsewhere }. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then u is admissible for $\nu _ { a c } \left( X \right)$ , and so 

$$
\nu_ {a c} (X) \geq \int_ {X} \overline {{u}} d \mu = \int_ {X} u d \mu + \int_ {E \cap \{v > u \}} (v - u) d \mu > \int_ {X} u d \mu ,
$$

where we have used (1.42) and the fact that $\textstyle \int _ { X } u d \mu < \infty$ , since $\nu _ { a c }$ is finite. We have reached a contradiction. 

If $\nu _ { a c }$ is σ-finite then we may decompose X as 

$$
X = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} X _ {n},
$$

where $\nu _ { a c } \left( X _ { n } \right)$ and the sets $X _ { n }$ are disjoint. For each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ choose a function $u _ { n }$ admissible for $\nu _ { a c } \left( X _ { n } \right)$ for which (1.41) holds with $u _ { n }$ in place of u and for every measurable subset of $X _ { n }$ . The function 

$$
u := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \chi_ {X _ {n}} u _ {n}
$$

has the desired property. 

Lemma 1.103. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\mu , \nu : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ be two finite measures. For every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ define 

$$
\left(\nu - \mu\right) ^ {+} (E) := \sup \left\{\nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right): E ^ {\prime} \subset E, E ^ {\prime} \in \mathfrak {M} \right\}.\tag{1.43}
$$

Then $( \nu - \mu ) ^ { + }$ is a measure, and for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ we have 

$$
(\nu - \mu) ^ {+} (E) = \sup \left\{\nu (E ^ {\prime}) - \mu (E ^ {\prime}): E ^ {\prime} \subset E, E ^ {\prime} \in \mathfrak {M}, (\mu - \nu) ^ {+} (E ^ {\prime}) = 0 \right\}.
$$

Proof. Step 1: We begin by showing that $( \nu - \mu ) ^ { + }$ is a measure. Since 

$$
(\nu - \mu) ^ {+} (\emptyset) = \nu (\emptyset) - \mu (\emptyset) = 0
$$

we have $( \nu - \mu ) ^ { + } \left( E \right) \geq 0$ for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . Let $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ be a countable collection of pairwise disjoint sets and let $\textstyle E : = \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n }$ . Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and let $E _ { n } ^ { \prime } \subset E , E _ { n } ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , be such that 

$$
\nu (E _ {n} ^ {\prime}) - \mu (E _ {n} ^ {\prime}) \geq (\nu - \mu) ^ {+} (E _ {n}) - \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n}}.
$$

Then by (1.43), 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (\nu - \mu) ^ {+} (E) \geq \nu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n} ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n} ^ {\prime}\right) \\ = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} [ \nu (E _ {n} ^ {\prime}) - \mu (E _ {n} ^ {\prime}) ] \geq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} (\nu - \mu) ^ {+} (E _ {n}) - \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ we conclude that 

$$
(\nu - \mu) ^ {+} (E) \geq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} (\nu - \mu) ^ {+} (E _ {n}).
$$

Conversely, for any $E ^ { \prime } \subset E , \ E ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , let $E _ { n } ^ { \prime } : = E ^ { \prime } \cap E _ { n }$ . Then 

$$
\nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left[ \nu \left(E _ {n} ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E _ {n} ^ {\prime}\right) \right] \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} (\nu - \mu) ^ {+} \left(E _ {n}\right),
$$

and taking the supremum over all such $E ^ { \prime }$ we obtain 

$$
(\nu - \mu) ^ {+} (E) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} (\nu - \mu) ^ {+} (E _ {n}),
$$

and this establishes that $( \nu - \mu ) ^ { + }$ is a measure. 

Step 2: To verify the second part of the statement it sufices to show that for $E ^ { \prime } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\left( \mu - \nu \right) ^ { + } \left( E ^ { \prime } \right) > 0$ there exists $E ^ { \prime \prime } \subset E ^ { \prime } , E ^ { \prime \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , such that $\left( \mu - \nu \right) ^ { + } \left( E ^ { \prime \prime } \right) = 0$ and 

$$
\nu \left(E ^ {\prime \prime}\right) - \mu \left(E ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \geq \nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right).
$$

We proceed by induction. By (1.43) and the fact that $\left( \mu - \nu \right) ^ { + } \left( E ^ { \prime } \right) > 0$ there exists $E _ { 1 } ^ { \prime \prime } \subset E ^ { \prime } , E _ { 1 } ^ { \prime \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , such that 

$$
\mu \left(E _ {1} ^ {\prime \prime}\right) - \nu \left(E _ {1} ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \geq 0, \quad \mu \left(E _ {1} ^ {\prime \prime}\right) - \nu \left(E _ {1} ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \geq (\mu - \nu) ^ {+} \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) - 1.\tag{1.44}
$$

Setting $E _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } : = E ^ { \prime } \setminus E _ { 1 } ^ { \prime \prime }$ , by $( 1 . 4 4 ) _ { 1 }$ we obtain 

$$
\nu \left(E _ {1} ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E _ {1} ^ {\prime}\right) = \nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) + \mu \left(E _ {1} ^ {\prime \prime}\right) - \nu \left(E _ {1} ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \geq \nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right),
$$

and since by Step $1 \ ( \mu - \nu ) ^ { + }$ is a measure, by definition of $\left( \mu - \nu \right) ^ { + }$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {(\mu - \nu) ^ {+} (E _ {1} ^ {\prime}) = (\mu - \nu) ^ {+} (E ^ {\prime}) - (\mu - \nu) ^ {+} (E _ {1} ^ {\prime \prime})} \\ & {\qquad \leq (\mu - \nu) ^ {+} (E ^ {\prime}) - (\mu (E _ {1} ^ {\prime \prime}) - \nu (E _ {1} ^ {\prime \prime})) \leq 1,} \end{array}
$$

where in the last inequality we have used $( 1 . 4 4 ) _ { 2 }$ . Recursively, suppose now that $E _ { n - 1 } ^ { \prime } \subset E ^ { \prime }$ has been selected such that $E _ { n - 1 } ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , and 

$$
\nu \left(E _ {n - 1} ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E _ {n - 1} ^ {\prime}\right) \geq \nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right), \quad (\mu - \nu) ^ {+} \left(E _ {n - 1} ^ {\prime}\right) \leq \frac {1}{n - 1}.
$$

If $\left( \mu - \nu \right) ^ { + } \left( E _ { n - 1 } ^ { \prime } \right) = 0$ , then we may take $E ^ { \prime \prime } : = E _ { n - 1 } ^ { \prime }$ . If $\left( \mu - \nu \right) ^ { + } \left( E _ { n - 1 } ^ { \prime } \right) >$ 0, then by (1.43) there exists $E _ { n } ^ { \prime \prime } \subset E _ { n - 1 } ^ { \prime } , E _ { n } ^ { \prime \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , such that 

$$
\mu \left(E _ {n} ^ {\prime \prime}\right) - \nu \left(E _ {n} ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \geq 0, \quad \mu \left(E _ {n} ^ {\prime \prime}\right) - \nu \left(E _ {n} ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \geq (\mu - \nu) ^ {+} \left(E _ {n - 1} ^ {\prime}\right) - \frac {1}{n}.
$$

Setting $E _ { n } ^ { \prime } : = E _ { n - 1 } ^ { \prime } \setminus E _ { n } ^ { \prime \prime }$ one can show exactly as before that 

$$
\nu \left(E _ {n} ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E _ {n} ^ {\prime}\right) \geq \nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right), \quad (\mu - \nu) ^ {+} \left(E _ {n} ^ {\prime}\right) \leq \frac {1}{n}.
$$

Define $\textstyle E ^ { \prime \prime } : = \bigcap _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ . Since $\mu , \nu ,$ , and $\left( \mu - \nu \right) ^ { + }$ are finite measures, by Proposition 1.7(ii) we may let $n \to \infty$ in the previous inequalities to obtain 

$$
\nu \left(E ^ {\prime \prime}\right) - \mu \left(E ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \geq \nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) - \mu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right), \quad (\mu - \nu) ^ {+} \left(E ^ {\prime \prime}\right) = 0.
$$

This concludes the proof. 

We are now ready to prove the Radon–Nikodym theorem. 

Proof (Radon–Nikodym theorem $I )$ . The proof is divided into several steps. 

Step 1: Assume that $\mu$ and ν are finite measures. In view of Lemma 1.102, let $u$ be a measurable function that realizes $\nu _ { a c } \left( X \right)$ , that is, 

$$
\nu_ {a c} (X) = \int_ {X} u d \mu .
$$

Since ν is finite again by Lemma 1.102, we have that 

$$
\nu_ {a c} (E) = \int_ {E} u d \mu
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

By the definition of $\nu _ { a c } \left( X \right)$ for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ we obtain that 

$$
\nu^ {\prime} (E) := \nu (E) - \int_ {E} u d \mu \geq 0.\tag{1.45}
$$

Then $\nu ^ { \prime }$ is a measure and $\nu ^ { \prime } \ll \mu$ . We claim that $\nu ^ { \prime } \equiv 0$ . Indeed, if this is not the case, then there exists $E _ { 0 } \in \mathfrak { M }$ such that 

$$
\nu^ {\prime} (E _ {0}) = \nu (E _ {0}) - \int_ {E _ {0}} u d \mu > 0.
$$

Since $\nu ^ { \prime } \ll \mu$ it follows that $\mu \left( E _ { 0 } \right) > 0$ , and so we can find $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $\nu ^ { \prime } \left( E _ { 0 } \right) > \varepsilon \mu \left( E _ { 0 } \right)$ . Hence $( \nu ^ { \prime } - \varepsilon \mu ) ^ { + } \left( E _ { 0 } \right) > 0$ , and by Lemma 1.103 there exists $E _ { 0 } ^ { \prime } \subset E _ { 0 } , E _ { 0 } ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , such that 

$$
\nu^ {\prime} \left(E _ {0} ^ {\prime}\right) > \varepsilon \mu \left(E _ {0} ^ {\prime}\right), \quad \left(\varepsilon \mu - \nu^ {\prime}\right) ^ {+} \left(E _ {0} ^ {\prime}\right) = 0.
$$

Using again the fact that $\nu ^ { \prime } \ll \mu ,$ , we have that $\mu \left( E _ { 0 } ^ { \prime } \right) > 0$ . Since 

$$
(\varepsilon \mu - \nu^ {\prime}) ^ {+} (E _ {0} ^ {\prime}) = 0,
$$

it follows that for any $E ^ { \prime \prime } \subset E _ { 0 } ^ { \prime }$ , with $E ^ { \prime \prime } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , we have that 

$$
\varepsilon \mu \left(E ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \leq \nu^ {\prime} \left(E ^ {\prime \prime}\right) = \nu \left(E ^ {\prime \prime}\right) - \int_ {E ^ {\prime \prime}} u d \mu ,
$$

i.e., 

$$
\int_ {E ^ {\prime \prime}} \left(u + \varepsilon \chi_ {E _ {0} ^ {\prime}}\right) d \mu \leq \nu \left(E ^ {\prime \prime}\right).\tag{1.46}
$$

Therefore, by (1.45) and (1.46), for any $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {E} \left(u + \varepsilon \chi_ {E _ {0} ^ {\prime}}\right) d \mu = \int_ {E \setminus E _ {0} ^ {\prime}} u d \mu + \int_ {E \cap E _ {0} ^ {\prime}} \left(u + \varepsilon \chi_ {E _ {0} ^ {\prime}}\right) d \mu \\ \leq \nu \left(E \setminus E _ {0} ^ {\prime}\right) + \nu \left(E \cap E _ {0} ^ {\prime}\right) = \nu (E). \end{array}
$$

This implies that $u + \varepsilon \chi _ { E _ { 0 } ^ { \prime } }$ is an admissible function for $\nu _ { a c } \left( X \right)$ , and thus 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\nu_ {a c} (X) \geq \int_ {X} (u + \varepsilon \chi_ {E _ {0} ^ {\prime}}) d \mu = \int_ {X} u d \mu + \varepsilon \mu (E _ {0} ^ {\prime})} \\ & {\qquad = \nu_ {a c} (X) + \varepsilon \mu (E _ {0} ^ {\prime}).} \end{array}
$$

Since $\nu _ { a c } \left( X \right) < \infty$ and $\mu \left( E _ { 0 } ^ { \prime } \right) > 0$ , we have reached a contradiction, and the claim that $\nu ^ { \prime } \equiv 0$ is proved. 

To prove uniqueness, assume that there exists another measurable function $v : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\nu (E) = \int_ {E} v d \mu
$$

for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . Note that both u and v have finite integrals since $\nu$ is finite. As in (1.40), one can show that 

$$
\nu (E) = \int_ {E} \max \{u, v \} d \mu
$$

for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , and so 

$$
\int_ {X} \left[ \max \left\{u, v \right\} - u \right] d \mu = \int_ {X} \left[ \max \left\{u, v \right\} - v \right] d \mu = 0,
$$
