which implies that max $\left\{ u , v \right\} \left( x \right) = u \left( x \right) = v \left( x \right)$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ 

Step 2: Assume next that $\mu$ is finite and ν σ-finite. Consider a sequence of disjoint measurable sets $X _ { n }$ such that 

$$
X = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} X _ {n}
$$

and $\nu \left( X _ { n } \right) < \infty$ . Applying Step 1 to the measures $\mu \lfloor X _ { n }$ and $\nu \lfloor X _ { n }$ , we can find a unique sequence of measurable functions $u _ { n } : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , 

$$
\nu \left(E \cap X _ {n}\right) = \int_ {E \cap X _ {n}} u _ {n} d \mu .
$$

Let 

$$
u := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \chi_ {X _ {n}} u _ {n}.
$$

Then for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 5 

$$
\nu (E) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \nu (E \cap X _ {n}) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \int_ {E \cap X _ {n}} u _ {n} d \mu = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \int_ {E \cap X _ {n}} u d \mu = \int_ {E} u d \mu .
$$

The uniqueness of u follows from the uniqueness of $u _ { n }$ . 

Step 3: Assume that $\mu$ is finite and ν arbitrary. Without loss of generality we may assume that $\nu \left( X \right) = \infty$ . Let 

$$
T := \sup \left\{\mu (E): E \in \mathfrak {M}, \nu (E) <   \infty \right\}.
$$

Note that $T < \infty$ since $\mu \left( X \right) < \infty$ . Find a sequence of increasing sets $E _ { n }$ $E _ { n } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $\nu \left( E _ { n } \right) < \infty$ , such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu (E _ {n}) = T.
$$

Define 

$$
E _ {\sigma} := \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}.
$$

Then 

$$
\mu \left(E _ {\sigma}\right) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu \left(E _ {n}\right) = T.
$$

Note that $\nu : \mathfrak { M } \lfloor E _ { \sigma } \  \ \lbrack 0 , \infty \rbrack$ is σ-finite by construction, and so by the previous step there exists a unique measurable function $u _ { \sigma } : E _ { \sigma } \ :  \ : [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\nu (E) = \int_ {E} u _ {\sigma} d \mu\tag{1.47}
$$

for every $E \in \mathfrak { M } \lfloor E _ { \sigma }$ . We claim that $\nu : \mathfrak { M } \lfloor X \setminus E _ { \sigma }  [ 0 , \infty ]$ takes values only in $\{ 0 , \infty \}$ (hence it does not have the finite subset property). Indeed, if there exists $F \subset X \setminus E _ { \sigma } , F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , such that 

$$
0 <   \nu (F) <   \infty ,
$$

then $\mu \left( F \right) > 0$ (since $\nu \ll \mu )$ and so 

$$
T = \mu (E _ {\sigma}) <   \mu (E _ {\sigma}) + \mu (F) = \mu (E _ {\sigma} \cup F),\tag{1.48}
$$

and since $E _ { \sigma } \cup F$ is admissible in the definition of $T$ we arrive at a contradiction. Note also that if $\mu \left( F \right) > 0$ for some $F \subset X \setminus E \sigma , F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , then $\nu \left( F \right) = \infty$ . Indeed, if $\nu \left( F \right) < \infty$ , then again $E _ { \sigma } \cup F$ is admissible in the definition of $T ,$ , and the same argument as in (1.48) leads to a contradiction. 

Define 

$$
u \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} u _ {\sigma} \left(x\right) \text {   if   } x \in E _ {\sigma}, \\ \infty \qquad \text {   if   } x \in X \setminus E _ {\sigma}. \end{array} \right.
$$

We claim that the function u has the desired properties. Let $E \in \mathfrak { M }$ . If $\mu \left( E \cap \left( X \setminus E _ { \sigma } \right) \right) > 0$ , then, as we just showed, $\nu \left( E \cap ( X \setminus E _ { \sigma } ) \right) = \infty$ , and so since $u = \infty$ on $E \cap ( X \setminus E _ { \sigma } )$ , we get 

$$
\infty = \nu (E) = \int_ {E} u d \mu .
$$

If $\mu \left( E \cap ( X \setminus E _ { \sigma } ) \right) = 0$ , then $E$ is contained in $E _ { \sigma }$ up to a set of $\mu$ measure zero (and hence of ν measure zero, since $\nu \ll \mu )$ , and so the claim follows from (1.47). 

Finally, to prove uniqueness let $v : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be another measurable function such that 

$$
\nu (E) = \int_ {E} v d \mu
$$

for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . By uniqueness in the set $E _ { \sigma }$ (see Step 2) we have $v \left( x \right) =$ $u _ { \sigma } \left( x \right)$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in E _ { \sigma }$ . Thus it sufices to show that $v \left( x \right) = \infty$ for µ a.e. $x \in X \setminus E _ { \sigma }$ 

Assume that there exists a set $F \subset X \setminus E _ { \sigma } , F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , such that $\mu \left( F \right) > 0$ and $v < \infty$ on $F$ . Then, as shown before, $\nu \left( F \right) = \infty$ . Let 

$$
F _ {n} := \{x \in F: v (x) \leq n \}.
$$

Since $F _ { n } \subset F _ { n + 1 }$ and $F = \textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } F _ { n }$ , we must have 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu (F _ {n}) = \mu (F) > 0,
$$

and so $\mu \left( F _ { n } \right) > 0$ for all n suficiently large, say $n \geq n _ { 0 }$ . But then $\nu \left( F _ { n _ { 0 } } \right) = \infty$ , which is a contradiction since 

$$
\infty = \nu \left(F _ {n _ {0}}\right) = \int_ {F _ {n _ {0}}} v d \mu \leq n _ {0} \mu \left(F _ {n _ {0}}\right) <   \infty .
$$

This completes the proof of this step. 

Step 4: In the general case in which $\mu$ is σ-finite and ν arbitrary, consider a sequence of disjoint measurable sets $X _ { n }$ such that 

$$
X = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} X _ {n}
$$

and $\mu \left( X _ { n } \right) < \infty$ . We now proceed exactly as in Step 2, with the only diference that we apply Step 3 in place of Step 1. 

Remark 1.104. Under the hypotheses of the Radon–Nikodym theorem, it can be shown that $\nu = \nu _ { a c }$ . Indeed, we know that 

$$
\nu (E) = \int_ {E} u d \mu
$$

for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and for some measurable function $u : X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ , and so u is admissible for $\nu _ { a c } \left( E \right)$ . Hence 

$$
\nu (E) \geq \nu_ {a c} (E) \geq \int_ {E} u d \mu = \nu (E),
$$

where the first inequality always holds in view of the definition of $\nu _ { a c }$ 

Exercise 1.105. Note that the Radon–Nikodym theorem fails in general without some hypotheses on $\mu .$ . This is illustrated in the next two exercises. 

(i) Let X be an uncountable set and let M be the family of all sets $E \subset X$ such that either E or its complement is countable. For every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ define 

$$
\mu \left(E\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \text { card   } E \text {   if   } E \text {   is   finite }, \\ \infty \qquad \text { otherwise }, \end{array} \right.
$$

and 

$$
\nu \left(E\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0 \text { if } E \text { is   countable }, \\ \infty \text { otherwise }. \end{array} \right.
$$

Show that $\nu \ll \mu$ but the Radon–Nikodym theorem fails. 

(ii) Let $X = [ 0 , 1 ]$ , let ${ \mathfrak { M } } : = B \left( [ 0 , 1 ] \right)$ , and let $\mu , \nu$ be respectively the counting measure and the Lebesgue measure $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 }$ . Prove that $\nu$ is finite, $\nu \ll \mu$ , but the Radon–Nikodym theorem fails. 

To extend the Radon–Nikodym theorem to non-σ-finite measures we in troduce the concept of supremum of a family of measurable functions: 

Definition 1.106. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let ${ \mathcal { F } } = \left\{ u _ { \alpha } \right\} _ { \alpha \in J }$ be a family of measurable functions $u _ { \alpha } : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ . A measurable function $u _ { 0 } : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is called the essential supremum function of the family $\mathcal { F }$ if 

(i) $u _ { 0 } \left( x \right) \geq u _ { \alpha } \left( x \right)$ for every $\alpha \in J$ and for µ a.e. $x \in X$ ; 

(ii) if $u : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is a measurable function such that $u \left( x \right) \geq u _ { \alpha } \left( x \right)$ for every $\alpha \in J$ and for µ a.e. $x \in X$ , then u $( x ) \geq u _ { 0 } \left( x \right)$ for µ a.e. $x \in X$ 

In an analogous way we can define the essential infimum function of the family $\mathcal { F }$ . 

Remark 1.107. (i) Condition (ii) in Definition 1.106 is actually local in the sense that if $u : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is a measurable function such that 

$$
u (x) \geq u _ {\alpha} (x)
$$

for every $\alpha \in J$ and for $\mu$ a.e. x in a measurable subset $E \subset X$ , then for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in E$ , 

$$
u (x) \geq u _ {0} (x).
$$

To see this, it sufices to apply property (ii) in Definition 1.106 to the function 

$$
v \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} u \left(x\right) \text { if } x \in E, \\ u _ {0} \left(x\right) \text { if } x \in X \setminus E. \end{array} \right.
$$

(ii) In the special case in which the family $\mathcal { F }$ consists of characteristic functions, that is, 

$$
\mathcal {F} = \{\chi_ {E _ {\alpha}} \} _ {\alpha \in J}, E _ {\alpha} \in \mathfrak {M},
$$

then $u _ { 0 } : X \longrightarrow \{ 0 , 1 \} , \mathrm { i . e . , } u _ { 0 } = \chi _ { E _ { 0 } }$ , where 

$$
E _ {0} := \left\{x \in X: u _ {0} (x) = 1 \right\}.
$$

Indeed, by property (i) in Definition 1.106 we have that $u _ { 0 } \left( x \right) \geq 0$ for $\mu$ ${ \mathrm { a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ . Now let 

$$
\overline {{u}} _ {0} := \chi_ {E _ {0}}.
$$

Then $\overline { { u } } _ { 0 } \leq u _ { 0 }$ , and for fixed $\alpha$ let $X _ { \alpha }$ be such that $\mu \left( X \setminus X _ { \alpha } \right) = 0$ and for every $x \in X _ { \alpha }$ 

$$
u _ {0} (x) \geq u _ {\alpha} (x).
$$

Let $x \in X _ { \alpha }$ . If $u _ { \alpha } \left( x \right) = 1$ , then $u _ { 0 } \left( x \right) \geq 1 = \overline { { u } } _ { 0 } \left( x \right)$ , and if $u _ { \alpha } \left( x \right) = 0$ , then obviously $\overline { { u } } _ { 0 } \left( x \right) \geq u _ { \alpha } \left( x \right)$ . Hence $\overline { { u } } _ { 0 } \left( x \right) \geq u _ { \alpha } \left( x \right)$ for all $x \in X _ { \alpha }$ , and so by property (ii) in Definition 1.106 we deduce that $\overline { { u } } _ { 0 } \left( x \right) \geq u _ { 0 } \left( x \right)$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ . This shows that 

$$
u _ {0} (x) = \chi_ {E _ {0}} (x)
$$

for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ 

The set $E _ { 0 }$ is called the essential union of the family of sets $\{ E _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in J }$ 

Next we prove the existence of the essential supremum function of a family $\mathcal { F }$ of measurable functions for σ-finite measures. 

Theorem 1.108. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, with $\mu$ a σ-finite measure, and consider a family ${ \mathcal { F } } = \{ u _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in J }$ of measurable functions $u _ { \alpha } : X \to$ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ . Then there exists a countable set $I _ { 0 } \subset J$ such that the measurable function $u _ { 0 } : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ defined by 

$$
u _ {0} \left(x\right) := \sup _ {\alpha \in I _ {0}} u _ {\alpha} \left(x\right), \quad x \in X,\tag{1.49}
$$

is the essential supremum of $\mathcal { F }$ . 

Proof. If the set of indices J is countable, then it sufices to take $I _ { 0 } : = J$ . The function $u _ { 0 }$ is measurable and satisfies properties (i) and (ii) of Definition 1.106. 

If J is uncountable, then assume, without loss of generality, that $\mu$ is finite. Extend arctan to $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ by setting arctan $\textstyle ( - \infty ) : = - { \frac { \pi } { 2 } }$ and arctan $\infty : = \frac { \pi } { 2 }$ and set 

$$
t := \sup \left\{\int_ {X} \arctan \left(\sup _ {\alpha \in I} u _ {\alpha}\right) d \mu : I \subset J, I \text {   countable } \right\}.\tag{1.50}
$$

Note that $t \leq { \frac { \pi } { 2 } } \mu \left( X \right)$ . For every $n \in \mathbb N$ we may find a countable set $I _ { n } \subset J$ such that 

$$
t \leq \int_ {X} \arctan \left(\sup _ {\alpha \in I _ {n}} u _ {\alpha}\right) d \mu + \frac {1}{n}.\tag{1.51}
$$

Set 

$$
I _ {0} := \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} I _ {n}
$$

and define $u _ { 0 }$ as in (1.49). Property (ii) of Definition 1.106 is satisfied. To prove (i) of Definition 1.106 note that by (1.50) and (1.51), for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , 

$$
t - \frac {1}{n} \leq \int_ {X} \arctan \left(\sup _ {\alpha \in I _ {n}} u _ {\alpha}\right) d \mu \leq \int_ {X} \arctan (u _ {0}) d \mu \leq t,
$$

and therefore 

$$
\int_ {X} \arctan (u _ {0}) d \mu = t.
$$

On the other hand, for every $\beta \in J$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{l} t = \int_ {X} \arctan \left(u _ {0}\right) d \mu \leq \int_ {X} \arctan \left(\max \left\{u _ {0}, u _ {\beta} \right\}\right) d \mu \\ \leq \int_ {X} \arctan \left(\sup _ {\alpha \in I _ {0} \cup \{\beta \}} u _ {\alpha}\right) d \mu \leq t, \end{array}
$$

where we have used again (1.50). Since all inequalities are identities, this implies that for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ 

$$
u _ {0} (x) \geq u _ {\beta} (x).
$$

This concludes the proof. 

Definition 1.109. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. The measure $\mu$ is said to be localizable if any family of measurable sets admits an essential union. 

Next we show that if a measure is localizable, then the existence of the essential supremum holds not only for families of characteristic functions, but for any family of measurable functions. Note that since by the previous theorem a σ-finite measure is localizable, the proposition below generalizes Theorem 1.108. 

Proposition 1.110. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with $\mu$ localizable. Then any family ${ \mathcal F } = \{ u _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in J }$ of measurable functions $u _ { \alpha } : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ admits an essential supremum. 

Proof. Define $E _ { \alpha , r } : = \{ x \in X : u _ { \alpha } \left( x \right) \geq r \}$ with $r \in \mathbb { Q }$ , and let $E _ { r }$ be the essential union of the family $\{ E _ { \alpha , r } \} _ { \alpha \in J }$ . Set 

$$
u _ {0} (x) := \sup \left\{w _ {r} (x): r \in \mathbb {Q} \right\},
$$

where 

$$
w _ {r} \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} r & \text {if} x \in \bigcup_ {t > r} E _ {t}, \\ - \infty & \text {otherwise}. \end{array} \right.
$$

We claim that $u _ { 0 }$ is the essential supremum of $\mathcal { F }$ . Indeed, for every $r \in \mathbb { Q }$ and $\alpha \in J$ there exists $N _ { \alpha , r } \in \mathfrak { M }$ such that $\mu \left( N _ { \alpha , r } \right) = 0$ and $E _ { r } \supset E _ { \alpha , r } \setminus N _ { \alpha , r } .$ Set 

$$
N _ {\alpha} := \bigcup_ {r \in \mathbb {Q}} N _ {\alpha , r}.
$$

Then $N _ { \alpha }$ has measure zero, and we show that $u _ { 0 } \left( x \right) \geq u _ { \alpha } \left( x \right)$ if $x \notin N _ { \alpha }$ . If $u _ { \alpha } \left( x \right) = - \infty$ , then there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, let $r \in \mathbb { Q }$ be such that $u _ { \alpha } \left( x \right) > r$ . Then $x \in E _ { \alpha , t } \setminus N _ { \alpha }$ for some $t > r , t \in \mathbb { Q }$ , and so $x \in E _ { t }$ Hence $u _ { 0 } \left( x \right) \ge w _ { r } \left( x \right) = r$ . Given the arbitrariness of r we conclude that $u _ { 0 } \left( x \right) \geq u _ { \alpha } \left( x \right)$ 

Next let $u : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a measurable function such that 

$$
u (x) \geq u _ {\alpha} (x)
$$

for every $\alpha \in J$ and for all $x \notin M _ { \alpha }$ , for some set of measure zero $M _ { \alpha }$ . We claim that $u \left( x \right) \geq u _ { 0 } \left( x \right)$ for $\mu .$ . a.e. x $\in X$ 

For $r \in \mathbb { Q }$ define 

$$
F _ {r} := \left\{x \in X: u (x) \geq r \right\}.
$$

Since $F _ { r } \supset E _ { \alpha , r } \backslash M _ { \alpha }$ , by definition of essential union there is a set of measure zero $P _ { r }$ such that $F _ { r } \supset E _ { r } \setminus P _ { r }$ 

Let 

$$
P := \bigcup_ {r \in \mathbb {Q}} P _ {r}.
$$

In order to show that 

$$
u (x) \geq u _ {0} (x) = \sup \left\{w _ {r} (x): r \in \mathbb {Q} \right\}
$$

for $x \notin P$ , note that if $u _ { 0 } \left( x \right) = - \infty$ , then there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, let $r \in \mathbb { Q }$ be such that $w _ { r } \left( x \right) = r$ . Then $x \in E _ { t } \setminus P _ { t }$ for some $t > r$ , and therefore $x \in F _ { t }$ , and so 

$$
u (x) \geq t > w _ {r} (x).
$$

Hence $u \left( x \right) \geq u _ { 0 } \left( x \right)$ 

We are now ready to prove an extension of the Radon–Nikodym theorem that will play a fundamental role in the characterization of the dual of $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ in the next chapter. 

Theorem 1.111 (Radon-Nikodym, II). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } )$ be a measurable space and let $\mu , \nu : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be two measures, with $\mu$ localizable and ν absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ and such that 

$$
\nu (E) = \sup \left\{\nu (E \cap F): F \in \mathfrak {M}, \mu (F) <   \infty \right\}\tag{1.52}
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . Then there exists a measurable function u $: X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\nu (E) = \int_ {E} u d \mu
$$

for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . Moreover, if µ has the finite subset property, then u is unique up to a set of µ measure zero. 

Proof. Let 

$$
\mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime} := \left\{E \in \mathfrak {M}: \mu (E) <   \infty \right\}.
$$

For every set $E \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ we apply the Radon–Nikodym theorem I to obtain a unique function $u _ { E } : E \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\nu (F) = \int_ {F} u _ {E} d \mu
$$

for every $F \in { \mathfrak { M } } , F \subset E$ . Extend $u _ { E }$ by zero on $X \backslash E .$ Note that by uniqueness, if $E _ { 1 } , E _ { 2 } \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ , then $u _ { E _ { 1 } } \left( x \right) = u _ { E _ { 2 } } \left( x \right)$ for $\mu \ \mathrm { a . e . }$ $x \in E _ { 1 } \cap E _ { 2 }$ , while if $E _ { 1 } , E _ { 2 } \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ with $E _ { 1 } \subset E _ { 2 }$ then $u _ { E _ { 1 } } \left( x \right) = 0$ for µ a.e. $x \in E _ { 2 } \setminus E _ { 1 }$ , and so $u _ { E _ { 1 } } \left( x \right) \leq u _ { E _ { 2 } } \left( x \right)$ ) for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ 

Let u be the essential supremum of the family $\{ u _ { E } : E \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime } \}$ (the function u exists in view of the previous proposition). We claim that 

$$
\int_ {F} u d \mu = \sup _ {E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}} \int_ {F} u _ {E} d \mu\tag{1.53}
$$

for every $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . Fix $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . By definition of essential supremum we have 

$$
\int_ {F} u d \mu \geq \sup _ {E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}} \int_ {F} u _ {E} d \mu .
$$

To prove the reverse inequality it sufices to consider the case in which 

$$
\alpha := \sup _ {E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}} \int_ {F} u _ {E} d \mu <   \infty .
$$

Consider a sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ such that 

$$
\alpha = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {F} u _ {E _ {n}} d \mu <   \infty .\tag{1.54}
$$

Since 

$$
u _ {E _ {n}} \leq u _ {F _ {n}} \mathrm{for} \mu \mathrm{a.e.} x \in X,
$$

where $\textstyle F _ { n } : = \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } E _ { i } \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime }$ , without loss of generality we may assume that $u _ { E _ { n } } \leq u _ { E _ { n + 1 } }$ for $\mu$ a.e. $x \in X$ and for every $n \in \mathbb N$ . Then by the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem, 

$$
\alpha = \int_ {F} u _ {\infty} d \mu ,
$$

where $u _ { \infty } : = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } u _ { E _ { n } }$ . We show that for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime }$ • 

$$
u _ {\infty} (x) \geq u _ {E} (x) \text {   for   } \mu \text {   a.e.   } x \in F.\tag{1.55}
$$

By Remark 1.107 (i) this will imply that $u _ { \infty } \left( x \right) \geq u \left( x \right)$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in F$ and, in turn, 

$$
\alpha = \int_ {F} u _ {\infty} d \mu \geq \int_ {F} u d \mu .
$$

It remains to prove (1.55). If (1.55) fails, then there exists $F ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M } , F ^ { \prime } \subset F$ , with $\mu \left( F ^ { \prime } \right) > 0$ and such that $u _ { \infty } < u _ { E }$ in $F ^ { \prime }$ for some $E \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime }$ . Let 

$$
\varepsilon := \int_ {F ^ {\prime}} u _ {E} d \mu - \int_ {F ^ {\prime}} u _ {\infty} d \mu > 0.
$$

By (1.54) we may choose n so large that 

$$
\alpha \leq \int_ {F} u _ {E _ {n}} d \mu + \frac {\varepsilon}{2}.
$$

Then, since $u _ { E _ { n } } \leq u _ { \infty }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \alpha \leq \int_ {F} u _ {E _ {n}} d \mu + \frac {\varepsilon}{2} \leq \int_ {F \setminus F ^ {\prime}} u _ {E _ {n}} d \mu + \int_ {F ^ {\prime}} u _ {\infty} d \mu + \frac {\varepsilon}{2} \\ <   \int_ {F \setminus F ^ {\prime}} u _ {E _ {n}} d \mu + \int_ {F ^ {\prime}} u _ {E} d \mu \\ = \int_ {F} u _ {E _ {n} \cup E} d \mu \leq \alpha , \end{array}
$$

and we have reached a contradiction. 

Thus (1.55), and in turn (1.53), holds, and so for every $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {F} u   d \mu = \sup _ {E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}} \int_ {F} u _ {E}   d \mu = \sup _ {E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}} \int_ {F \cap E} u _ {E}   d \mu \\ = \sup _ {E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}} \nu (F \cap E) = \nu (F) \end{array}
$$

by (1.52). 

Finally, to prove uniqueness assume that $\mu$ has the finite subset property and let $v : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be another measurable function such that 

$$
\nu (E) = \int_ {E} v d \mu
$$

for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . By uniqueness in the case that $\mu$ is finite (see the Radon– Nikodym theorem I), for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime }$ we have that $v \left( x \right) = u \left( x \right)$ for $\mu \ \mathrm { a . e . }$ $x \in E$ , and so $v \left( x \right) \geq u _ { E } \left( x \right)$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ (since $u _ { E } = 0 \mathrm { o n } X \backslash E )$ . By the properties of the essential supremum it follows that $v \left( x \right) \geq u \left( x \right)$ for $\mu \ \mathrm { a . e . }$ $x \in X$ . Assume that there exists a set $F \subset X , F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , such that $\mu \left( F \right) > 0$ and $v > u$ on $F$ . Let 

$$
F _ {n} := \{x \in F: u (x) \leq n \}.
$$

Since $u < \infty$ on $F$ we have that $F = \textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } F _ { n }$ , and since $F _ { n } \subset F _ { n + 1 }$ , then 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu \left(F _ {n}\right) = \mu \left(F\right) > 0.
$$

Therefore $\mu \left( F _ { n } \right) > 0$ for all n suficiently large, say $n \geq n _ { 0 }$ . Since $\mu$ has the finite subset property there exists $F ^ { \prime } \subset F _ { n _ { 0 } } , F ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , such that $0 < \mu \left( F ^ { \prime } \right) <$ $\infty$ . But then $F ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ , and so we have a contradiction since on sets of M there is uniqueness. 

Remark 1.112. Note that if $\mu$ is finite or σ-finite, then in view of Proposition 1.110, µ is localizable, it has the finite subset property, and condition (1.52) holds. Thus the previous theorem is a genuine extension of Theorem 1.101. 

The Radon–Nikodym theorem allows us to express ν in terms of $\mu$ when $\nu \ll \mu$ . In the general case, when ν and $\mu$ are not related a priori, De Giorgi’s theorem (see below) allows us to write ν as the sum of three mutually singular measures 

$$
\nu = \nu_ {a c} + \nu_ {s} + \nu_ {d},
$$

where $\nu _ { a c }$ is introduced in Lemma 1.102, and $\nu _ { s }$ and $\nu _ { d }$ are defined in the next lemma. 

Lemma 1.113. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\mu , \nu : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be two measures. For every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ define 

$$
\nu_ {s} (E) := \sup \left\{\nu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right): E ^ {\prime} \subset E, E ^ {\prime} \in \mathfrak {M}, \mu \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) = 0 \right\},\tag{1.56}
$$

$$
\nu_ {d} (E) := \sup \left\{\nu (E ^ {\prime}): E ^ {\prime} \subset E, E ^ {\prime} \in \mathfrak {M} s u c h t h a t \right.\tag{1.57}
$$

$$
\left. \text {   for   all   } E ^ {\prime \prime} \subset E ^ {\prime}, \text {   with   } E ^ {\prime \prime} \in \mathfrak {M} \text {   and   } \nu (E ^ {\prime \prime}) > 0, \mu (E ^ {\prime \prime}) = \infty \right\}.
$$

Then $\nu _ { s }$ and $\nu _ { d }$ are measures, $\nu _ { d }$ is difuse with respect to $\mu _ { : }$ , and for each $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ the suprema in the definition of $\nu _ { s }$ and $\nu _ { d }$ are actually attained by measurable sets. 

Moreover, if $\nu _ { s }$ is σ-finite then there exists a set $X _ { s } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that 

$$
\mu \left(X _ {s}\right) = 0 = \nu_ {d} \left(X _ {s}\right) \quad a n d \quad \nu_ {s} (E) = \nu \left(E \cap X _ {s}\right)
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . In particular, $\nu _ { s } \perp \mu$ and $\nu _ { s } \perp \nu _ { d }$ 

Proof. To see that $\nu _ { s }$ is a measure and that the supremum in the definition of $\nu _ { s }$ is attained, it sufices to observe that for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , 

$$
\nu_ {s} (E) = \sup \left\{\nu (E \cap F): F \in \mathfrak {N} \right\},
$$

where $\mathfrak { N } : = \{ F \in \mathfrak { M } : \mu ( F ) = 0 \}$ . Since N is closed under finite unions and contains $\varnothing$ , we are in a position to apply Lemma 1.23 (with $\nu _ { s }$ in place of $\mu _ { 1 } )$ 

The same reasoning applies to $\nu _ { d }$ , since for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

$$
\nu_ {d} (E) = \sup \left\{\nu (E \cap F): F \in \mathfrak {N} \right\},
$$

where now 

$\mathfrak { N } : = \{ F \in \mathfrak { M }$ : for all G ⊂ F with G ∈ M and $\nu \left( G \right) > 0 , \mu \left( G \right) = \infty \}$ 

which is closed under finite unions and contains $\varnothing .$ . 

It follows from (1.57) that $\nu _ { d }$ is difuse with respect to $\mu .$ 

To address the singularity of $\nu _ { s }$ with respect to $\nu _ { d }$ and $\mu ,$ , we assume first that $\nu _ { s }$ is finite. Choose $X _ { s } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that 

$$
\nu_ {s} (X) = \nu (X _ {s})\tag{1.58}
$$

and $\mu \left( X _ { s } \right) = 0$ . Given a set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , let $E _ { s } \in \mathfrak { M } , E _ { s } \subset E .$ , be such that $\nu _ { s } \left( E \right) = \nu \left( E _ { s } \right)$ and $\mu \left( E _ { s } \right) = 0$ . We observe that $\nu ( E _ { s }  X _ { s } ) = 0$ , or else, since $E _ { s } \cup X _ { s }$ is admissible for $\nu _ { s } \left( X \right)$ and $\nu _ { s }$ is finite, we would have 

$$
\nu_ {s} (X) \geq \nu (E _ {s} \cup X _ {s}) = \nu (X _ {s}) + \nu (E _ {s} \setminus X _ {s}) > \nu (X _ {s}),
$$

and this contradicts (1.58). Therefore using (1.56) and the fact that $\mu \left( X _ { s } \right) = 0$ , we have 

$$
\nu_ {s} (E) = \nu (E _ {s} \cap X _ {s}) \leq \nu (E \cap X _ {s}) \leq \nu_ {s} (E \cap X _ {s}) \leq \nu_ {s} (E).
$$

The fact that $\nu _ { d } \left( X _ { s } \right) = 0$ follows from the fact that $\mu \left( X _ { s } \right) = 0$ 

The case that $\nu _ { s }$ is σ-finite is straightforward. 

Theorem 1.114 (De Giorgi). Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\mu _ { ; }$ , $\nu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be two measures. Then $\nu _ { s } , \nu _ { a c } , \nu _ { d }$ are measures and 

$$
\nu = \nu_ {s} + \nu_ {a c} + \nu_ {d}
$$

with $\nu _ { a c } \ll \mu$ and $\nu _ { d }$ difuse with respect to µ. Moreover, if ν is σ-finite, then these three measures are mutually singular and $\nu _ { s } \perp \mu .$ 

A particular setting of De Giorgi’s theorem addresses the case in which $\mu$ is σ-finite, and thus $\nu _ { d } \equiv 0$ 

Theorem 1.115 (Lebesgue decomposition theorem). Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\mu , \nu : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be two measures, with $\mu \ \sigma { - } f i n i t e$ Then 

$$
\nu = \nu_ {a c} + \nu_ {s}\tag{1.59}
$$

with $\nu _ { a c } \ll \mu$ . Moreover, if ν is $\sigma { - } f i n i t e ,$ , then $\nu _ { s } \perp \mu$ and the decomposition (1.59) is unique, that is, if 

$$
\nu = \overline {{\nu}} _ {a c} + \overline {{\nu}} _ {s},
$$

$$
\nu_ {a c} = \overline {{\nu}} _ {a c} \quad a n d \quad \nu_ {s} = \overline {{\nu}} _ {s}.
$$

for some measures $\overline { { \nu } } _ { a c } , \ : \overline { { \nu } } _ { s }$ , with $\overline { { \nu } } _ { a c } \ll \mu$ and $\overline { { \nu } } _ { s } \perp \mu$ , then 

When it is important to highlight the underlying measure $\mu ,$ , we write (1.59) as 

$$
\nu = \nu_ {a c, \mu} + \nu_ {s, \mu}.\tag{1.60}
$$

Proof. In view of Lemmas 1.102 and 1.113, $\nu _ { a c }$ and $\nu _ { s }$ are measures. 

Step 1: We claim that $\nu = \nu _ { a c } + \nu _ { s }$ . Fix $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and let $E _ { s } \in \mathfrak { M } , E _ { s } \subset E$ , be such that $\mu \left( E _ { s } \right) = 0$ and $\nu _ { s } \left( E \right) = \nu \left( E _ { s } \right)$ (see Lemma 1.113). If $\nu \left( E _ { s } \right) = \infty$ then (1.59) is satisfied when evaluated at E. 

Suppose now that $\nu \left( E _ { s } \right) < \infty$ . We claim that $\nu \lfloor E \setminus E _ { s }$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu {  { \lfloor E \setminus E _ { s } } }$ . Indeed, let $F ~ \in ~ \mathfrak { M }$ be such that $\mu \left( F \cap ( E \setminus E _ { s } ) \right) = 0$ . By replacing F with $F \cap ( E \setminus E _ { s } )$ , without loss of generality, we may assume that $F \subset E \setminus E _ { s } . \mathrm { I f } \nu ( F ) > 0$ , then $E _ { s } \cup F$ is admissible in the definition of $\nu _ { s } \left( E \right)$ , and so 

$$
\infty > \nu_ {s} (E) = \nu (E _ {s}) \geq \nu (E _ {s} \cup F) = \nu (E _ {s}) + \nu (F) > \nu (E _ {s}),
$$

and we have reached a contradiction. Therefore $\nu \left( F \right) = 0$ , and the claim is proved. 

Hence the finite measure $\nu \lfloor ( E \setminus E _ { s } )$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu \lfloor ( E \setminus E _ { s } )$ , and thus by Remark 1.104 we have that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \nu \left(E \setminus E _ {s}\right) = (\nu \lfloor (E \setminus E _ {s})) \left(E \setminus E _ {s}\right) = (\nu \lfloor (E \setminus E _ {s})) _ {a c} \left(E \setminus E _ {s}\right) \\ = \nu_ {a c} \left(E \setminus E _ {s}\right) = \nu_ {a c} \left(E\right), \end{array}
$$

where in the last equality we have used the fact that $\mu \left( E _ { s } \right) = 0$ and $\nu _ { a c } \ll \mu$ Hence 

$$
\nu (E) = \nu (E \setminus E _ {s}) + \nu (E _ {s}) = \nu_ {a c} (E) + \nu_ {s} (E).
$$

Step 2: Suppose that ν is σ-finite. Then by Lemma 1.113 we have $\nu _ { s } \perp \mu$ 

To prove uniqueness of the decomposition, assume that 

$$
\nu = \nu_ {a c} + \nu_ {s} = \overline {{\nu}} _ {a c} + \overline {{\nu}} _ {s},\tag{1.61}
$$

with $\overline { { \nu } } _ { a c } \ll \mu$ and $\overline { { \nu } } _ { s } \perp \mu$ . Let $X _ { \overline { { \nu } } _ { s } } \in \mathfrak { M }$ be such that 

$$
\mu \left(X _ {\overline {{\nu}} _ {s}}\right) = 0 \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \overline {{\nu}} _ {s} \left(E\right) = \overline {{\nu}} _ {s} \left(E \cap X _ {\overline {{\nu}} _ {s}}\right)\tag{1.62}
$$

for every $E \in \mathfrak { M }$ . Then by (1.61), $\nu \lfloor X \setminus X _ { \overline { { \nu } } _ { s } } \ = \ \overline { { \nu } } _ { a c } \lfloor X \setminus X _ { \overline { { \nu } } _ { s } }$ , which is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu ,$ and so by Remark 1.104 and (1.62) , for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \overline {{\nu}} _ {a c} (E) = \overline {{\nu}} _ {a c} (E \setminus X _ {\overline {{\nu}} _ {s}}) = (\overline {{\nu}} _ {a c} \lfloor X \setminus X _ {\overline {{\nu}} _ {s}}) (E) = (\nu \lfloor (X \setminus X _ {\overline {{\nu}} _ {s}})) (E) \\ = (\nu \lfloor (E \setminus X _ {\overline {{\nu}} _ {s}})) _ {a c} (E) = \nu_ {a c} (E \setminus X _ {\overline {{\nu}} _ {s}}) = \nu_ {a c} (E). \end{array}
$$

Hence $\begin{array} { r } { \overline { { \nu } } _ { a c } = \nu _ { a c } . } \end{array}$ , and so in the case that ν is finite, it follows from (1.61) that $\nu _ { s } = \overline { { \nu } } _ { s }$ . If ν is σ-finite, then by restricting ν to $X _ { n }$ , where 

$$
X = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} X _ {n}, \nu (X _ {n}) <   \infty ,
$$

we conclude that $\nu _ { s } \lfloor X _ { n } = \overline { { \nu } } _ { s } \lfloor X _ { n }$ for every n, which implies that $\nu _ { s } = \overline { { \nu } } _ { s }$ 

Final $\mathrm { l y , }$ we consider the case that $\mu$ is not necessarily σ-finite. 

Proof (De Giorgi’s Theorem). Fix $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . We claim that 

$$
\nu (E) = \nu_ {a c} (E) + \nu_ {s} (E) + \nu_ {d} (E).
$$

It sufices to prove this equality in the case that the right-hand side is finite. We are then in a setting in which $\nu _ { a c }$ and $\nu _ { s }$ are finite measures, and so we may apply Lemmas 1.102 and 1.113 to ensure the existence of a measurable function $u : E \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ and $E _ { s } \subset E$ , with $E _ { s } \in \mathfrak { M }$ and $\mu \left( E _ { s } \right) = 0$ , such that 

$$
\nu_ {a c} \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) = \int_ {E ^ {\prime}} u d \mu , \quad \nu_ {s} \left(E ^ {\prime}\right) = \nu \left(E ^ {\prime} \cap E _ {s}\right),\tag{1.63}
$$

for every $E ^ { \prime } \subset E , E ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M }$ . Since $\mu \left( E _ { s } \right) = 0$ it follows from (1.57) that $\nu _ { d } \left( E _ { s } \right) = 0$ . Define 

$$
E _ {a c} := \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}, \quad E _ {n} := \left\{x \in E \setminus E _ {s}: u (x) > \frac {1}{n} \right\}.
$$

Since $E _ { a c } \subset E \setminus E _ { s }$ , by $( 1 . 6 3 ) _ { 2 }$ we have that $\nu _ { s } \left( E _ { a c } \right) = 0$ . By the definition of $E _ { n }$ and (1.63) it follows that 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \mu (E _ {n}) \leq \int_ {E _ {n}} u d \mu = \nu_ {a c} (E _ {n}) \leq \nu_ {a c} (E) <   \infty ,
$$

and thus $\nu _ { d } \left( E _ { a c } \right) = 0$ by (1.57). Moreover, by the Lebesgue decomposition theorem we have that 

$$
\nu (E _ {a c}) = \nu_ {a c} (E _ {a c}),
$$

and in turn, $\nu _ { a c } \left( E _ { a c } \right) = \nu _ { a c } \left( E \right)$ . To conclude, we write 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \nu (E) = \nu (E _ {a c}) + \nu (E _ {s}) + \nu (E \setminus (E _ {a c} \cup E _ {s})) \\ = \nu_ {a c} (E) + \nu_ {s} (E) + \nu (E \setminus (E _ {a c} \cup E _ {s})), \end{array}
$$

and it sufices to prove that 

$$
\nu \left(E \setminus (E _ {a c} \cup E _ {s})\right) = \nu_ {d} \left(E\right).
$$

We have 

$$
\nu_ {d} (E) = \nu_ {d} \left(E \setminus \left(E _ {a c} \cup E _ {s}\right)\right) \leq \nu \left(E \setminus \left(E _ {a c} \cup E _ {s}\right)\right).
$$

If the inequality were strict, then in view of the definition of $\nu _ { d }$ there would exist $F \subset E \setminus ( E _ { a c } \cup E _ { s } ) , F \in \mathfrak { M }$ , with $\nu \left( F \right) > 0$ and $\mu \left( F \right) < \infty$ . Invoking once again the Lebesgue decomposition theorem, this would imply that 

$$
\nu (F) = \nu_ {a c} (F) + \nu_ {s} (F) = 0,
$$

and we have reached a contradiction. 

Corollary 1.116. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\mu , \nu , v : { \mathfrak { M } } \to$ $[ 0 , \infty ]$ be σ-finite measures, with $\mu \perp v$ . Then 

$$
\nu = \nu_ {a c, \mu} + \nu_ {a c, v} + \nu_ {s, \mu + v},
$$

where we are using the notation introduced in (1.60). 

Proof. By the Lebesgue decomposition theorem write 

$$
\nu = \nu_ {a c, \mu + v} + \nu_ {s, \mu + v},\tag{1.64}
$$

and find $X _ { \mu + v } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , 

$$
(\mu + \upsilon) (E) = (\mu + \upsilon) (E \cap X _ {\mu + \upsilon}),\tag{1.65}
$$

$$
\nu_ {s, \mu + v} (E) = \nu_ {s, \mu + v} (E \cap (X \setminus X _ {\mu + v})).\tag{1.66}
$$

Note that by (1.64) and (1.65), 

$$
\nu \lfloor (X \setminus X _ {\mu + v}) = \nu_ {s, \mu + v} \lfloor (X \setminus X _ {\mu + v}).\tag{1.67}
$$

Let $X _ { \mu } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ be such that for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , 

$$
\mu \left(E\right) = \mu \left(E \cap X _ {\mu}\right), \quad v \left(E\right) = v \left(E \cap \left(X \setminus X _ {\mu}\right)\right).\tag{1.68}
$$

Since by (1.65), $\mu \lfloor ( X \setminus X _ { \mu + v } ) = \upsilon \lfloor ( X \setminus X _ { \mu + v } ) = 0$ , we deduce that, also from (1.68), 

$$
\mu \left(E\right) = \mu \left(E \cap X _ {\mu} \cap X _ {\mu + v}\right), \quad v \left(E\right) = v \left(E \cap (X _ {\mu + v} \setminus X _ {\mu})\right)\tag{1.69}
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . We have 

$$
\nu (E) = \nu \left(E \cap X _ {\mu} \cap X _ {\mu + v}\right) + \nu \left(E \cap \left(X _ {\mu + v} \setminus X _ {\mu}\right)\right) + \nu \left(E \cap \left(X \setminus X _ {\mu + v}\right)\right).\tag{1.70}
$$

If $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ for some $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $E \subset X _ { \mu } \cap X _ { \mu + v }$ , then by (1.68) we have $\left( \mu + v \right) \left( E \right) = 0 \mathrm { : }$ ; hence ${ \nu _ { a c , \mu + v } \left( E \right) = 0 . \ \mathrm { O n } }$ the other hand, by (1.66), $\nu _ { s , \mu + v } \left( E \right) = 0$ , and due to (1.64) we conclude that $\nu \left( E \right) = 0$ . With this we have shown that $\nu \lfloor ( X _ { \mu } \cap X _ { \mu + v } ) \ll \mu$ , and so for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , 

$$
\nu \left(E \cap X _ {\mu} \cap X _ {\mu + v}\right) = \nu_ {a c, \mu} \left(E \cap X _ {\mu} \cap X _ {\mu + v}\right).\tag{1.71}
$$

In turn, by (1.69) we get that for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

$$
\nu_ {a c, \mu} (E \cap X _ {\mu} \cap X _ {\mu + v}) = \nu_ {a c, \mu} (E),
$$

and hence by (1.71), for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , 

$$
\nu \left(E \cap X _ {\mu} \cap X _ {\mu + v}\right) = \nu_ {a c, \mu} (E).\tag{1.72}
$$

Similarly, using (1.69) and (1.66), we have that $\nu \lfloor ( X _ { \mu + v } \setminus X _ { \mu } ) \ll v .$ , yielding 

$$
\nu \left(E \cap (X _ {\mu + v} \setminus X _ {\mu})\right) = \nu_ {a c, v} \left(E\right)\tag{1.73}
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , where we have used $( 1 . 6 9 ) _ { 2 }$ . We conclude by observing that by (1.70), (1.72), (1.73), (1.66), and (1.67), 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \nu (E) = \nu (E \cap X _ {\mu} \cap X _ {\mu + v}) + \nu (E \cap (X _ {\mu + v} \setminus X _ {\mu})) + \nu_ {s, \mu + v} (E \setminus X _ {\mu + v}) \\ = \nu_ {a c, \mu} (E) + \nu_ {a c, v} (E) + \nu_ {s, \mu + v} (E) \end{array}
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , which is the desired result. 

We conclude this subsection by discussing the Radon–Nikodym theorem for finitely additive measures. The next example shows that the Radon– Nikodym theorem does not hold in general for finitely additive measures. 

Example 1.117. Let $X = [ 0 , 1 ]$ , let M be the σ-algebra of all Lebesgue measur able sets of [0, 1], and let ν be a nontrivial purely finitely additive measure ν (for the existence of ν we refer to Example 2.45) with ν absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 }$ . Then $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 } \ll ( \mathcal { L } ^ { 1 } + \nu )$ , and so if the Radon–Nikodym theorem were to hold, we could find a measurable function $u : [ 0 , 1 ]  [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {L} ^ {1} (E) = \int_ {E} u d (\mathcal {L} ^ {1} + \nu) = \int_ {E} u d \mathcal {L} ^ {1} + \int_ {E} u d \nu\tag{1.74}
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . Note that $0 \leq u \left( x \right) \leq 1$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 }$ a.e. $x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ and, in turn, for $\nu \ \mathrm { a . e . } \ x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ . Hence 

$$
\upsilon (E) := \int_ {E} u d \nu \leq \nu (E)
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , and since ν is purely finitely additive, then so must be $\upsilon$ From (1.74) and the uniqueness of the decomposition in the Hewitt–Yosida theorem, it follows that $\upsilon \equiv 0$ . Again by (1.74) this implies that u $( x ) = 1$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ and, in turn, for $\nu \ \mathrm { a . e . } \ x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ . Therefore $\nu = v = 0$ , which is a contradiction. 

The next result gives necessary and suficient conditions for the validity of the Radon–Nikodym theorem for finitely additive measures. Since this result will not be used in the remainder of the book we omit its proof, which may be found in [May79]. 

Theorem 1.118. Let X be a nonempty set, let ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be an algebra, and let $\mu , \nu : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ be two finite finitely additive measures. Then there exists an integrable function $u : X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\nu (E) = \int_ {E} u d \mu
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ if and only if 

(i) for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $\nu \left( E \right) < \varepsilon$ for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) < \delta _ { : }$ ; 

(ii) for $a l l \varepsilon > 0$ there exists $E _ { \varepsilon } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $\mu \left( X \setminus E _ { \varepsilon } \right) < \varepsilon$ , such that 

$$
\sup \left\{\frac {\nu (E ^ {\prime})}{\mu (E ^ {\prime})}: E ^ {\prime} \subset E _ {\varepsilon}, E ^ {\prime} \in \mathfrak {M}, \mu (E ^ {\prime}) > 0 \right\} <   \infty ,
$$

and for all $\eta > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that for all $E \subset E _ { \varepsilon } , E \in \mathfrak { M }$ , there exists $F \subset E , F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , such that $\mu \left( F \right) > \delta \mu \left( E \right)$ and 

$$
\sup \left\{\frac {\nu (E ^ {\prime})}{\mu (E ^ {\prime})}: E ^ {\prime} \subset F, E ^ {\prime} \in \mathfrak {M}, \mu (E ^ {\prime}) > 0 \right\} <   \eta .
$$

## 1.1.5 Product Spaces

Given two measurable spaces (X, M) and $( Y , \mathfrak { N } )$ we denote by ${ \mathfrak { M } } \otimes { \mathfrak { N } } \subset$ $\mathcal { P } \left( \boldsymbol { X } \times \boldsymbol { Y } \right)$ the smallest σ-algebra that contains all sets of the form $E \times F$ where $E \in \mathfrak { M } , F \in \mathfrak { N }$ . The σ-algebra $\mathfrak { M } \otimes \mathfrak { N }$ is called the product σ-algebra of M and N. 

Exercise 1.119. Let X and Y be topological spaces and let $B \left( X \right)$ and $B \left( Y \right)$ be their respective Borel σ-algebras. Prove that 

$$
\mathcal {B} (X) \otimes \mathcal {B} (Y) \subset \mathcal {B} (X \times Y).
$$

Show also that if X and $Y$ are separable metric spaces, then 

$$
\mathcal {B} (X) \otimes \mathcal {B} (Y) = \mathcal {B} (X \times Y),
$$

so that in particular, $\begin{array} { r } { B \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) = B \left( \mathbb { R } \right) \otimes \ldots \otimes B \left( \mathbb { R } \right) } \end{array}$ 

Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ and $( Y , \mathfrak { N } , \nu )$ be two measure spaces. For every $E \in X \times Y$ define 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (\mu \times \nu) ^ {*} (E) := \inf \left\{\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(F _ {n}\right) \nu \left(G _ {n}\right): \left\{F _ {n} \right\} \subset \mathfrak {M},   \left\{G _ {n} \right\} \subset \mathfrak {N}, \right. \\ E \subset \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(F _ {n} \times G _ {n}\right) \Bigg \}, \end{array}\tag{1.75}
$$

where we define $\mu ( F _ { n } ) \nu ( G _ { n } ) : = 0$ whenever $\mu ( F _ { n } ) = 0$ or $\nu ( G _ { n } ) = 0$ 

By Proposition 1.32, $( \mu \times \nu ) ^ { * } : \mathcal { P } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is an outer measure, and it is called the product outer measure of $\mu$ and ν. By Carath´eodory’s theorem, the restriction of $\left( \mu \times \nu \right) ^ { * }$ to the σ-algebra $\mathfrak { M } \times \mathfrak { N }$ of $\left( \mu \times \nu \right) ^ { * }$ -measurable sets is a complete measure, denoted by $\mu \times \nu$ and called the product measure of $\mu$ and $\nu .$ 

Note that ${ \mathfrak { M } } \times { \mathfrak { N } }$ is, in general, larger than the product σ-algebra $\mathfrak { M } \otimes \mathfrak { N }$ 

Theorem 1.120. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ and $( Y , \mathfrak { N } , \nu )$ be two measure spaces. 

(i) If $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $G \in { \mathfrak { N } }$ , then $F \times G$ is $\left( \mu \times \nu \right) ^ { * }$ -measurable and 

$$
(\mu \times \nu) (F \times G) = \mu (F) \nu (G);
$$

(ii) $i f \mu$ and ν are complete and E has σ-finite $\mu \times \nu$ measure, then for µ a.e. $x \in X$ the section 

$$
E _ {x} := \{y \in Y: (x, y) \in E \}
$$

belongs to the σ-algebra N, and for $\nu \ a . e . \ y \in Y$ the section 

$$
E _ {y} := \{x \in X: (x, y) \in E \}
$$

belongs to the σ-algebra M. Moreover, 

$$
(\mu \times \nu) (E) = \int_ {Y} \mu (E _ {y}) d \nu (y) = \int_ {X} \nu (E _ {x}) d \mu (x).
$$

The previous result is a particular case of Tonelli’s theorem in the case that $u = \chi _ { E }$ 

Theorem 1.121 (Tonelli). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ and $( Y , \mathfrak { N } , \nu )$ be two measure spaces. Assume that $\mu$ and ν are complete and $\sigma { - } f i n i t e ,$ and let u : $X \times Y \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be an ${ \mathfrak { M } } \times { \mathfrak { N } }$ measurable function. Then for µ a.e. $x \in X$ the function $u \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is measurable and the function $\textstyle \int _ { Y } u \left( \cdot , y \right)$ dν (y) is measurable. Sim-$i l a r l y ,$ for ν a.e. $y \in Y$ the function $u \left( \cdot , y \right)$ is measurable and the function $\textstyle \int _ { X } u \left( x , \cdot \right) \ d \mu \left( x \right)$ is measurable. Moreover, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {X \times Y} u (x, y) d (\mu \times \nu) (x, y) = \int_ {X} \left(\int_ {Y} u (x, y) d \nu (y)\right) d \mu (x) \\ = \int_ {Y} \left(\int_ {X} u (x, y) d \mu (x)\right) d \nu (y). \end{array}
$$

Remark 1.122. In the case that $u : X \times Y  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is $\mathfrak { M } \otimes \mathfrak { N }$ measurable, then Tonelli’s theorem still holds even if the measures $\mu$ and ν are not complete, and the statements are satisfied for every $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$ (as opposed to for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ and for $\nu \ \mathrm { a . e . } \ y \in Y )$ 

A simple consequence of Tonelli’s theorem is the following result. 

Theorem 1.123. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $u : X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a measurable function. Then 

$$
\int_ {X} u d \mu = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \mu (\{x \in X: u (x) > t \}) d t.\tag{1.76}
$$

Proof. If the set $\{ x \in X : u ( x ) > 0 \}$ has non-σ-finite $\mu$ measure, then at least one of the sets 

$$
\left\{x \in X: u (x) > \frac {1}{n} \right\}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N},
$$

has infinite $\mu$ measure. Hence $\mu \left( \{ x \in X : u \left( x \right) > t \} \right) = \infty$ for all $0 \leq t \leq \frac { 1 } { n }$ , which implies that both sides of (1.76) are infinite. 

If the set $\{ x \in X : u ( x ) > 0 \}$ has σ-finite $\mu$ measure, then by replacing $\mu$ with 

$$
\mu \lfloor \{x \in X: u (x) > 0 \},
$$

we may assume that $\mu$ is σ-finite. Applying Tonelli’s theorem we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(\{x \in X: u (x) > t \}\right) d t = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \int_ {X} \chi_ {\{y \in X: u (y) > t \}} (x) d \mu (x) d t \\ \qquad = \int_ {X} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \chi_ {\{y \in X: u (y) > t \}} (x) d t d \mu (x) \\ \qquad = \int_ {X} \int_ {0} ^ {u (x)} d t d \mu (x) = \int_ {X} u (x) d \mu (x), \end{array}
$$

and the proof is complete. 

The version of Tonelli’s theorem for integrable functions of arbitrary sign is the well–known Fubini’s theorem: 

Theorem 1.124 (Fubini). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ and $( Y , \mathfrak { N } , \nu )$ be two measure spaces. Assume that $\mu$ and ν are complete, and let $u : X \times Y  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be $\mu \times \nu -$ integrable. Then for µ a.e. $x \in X$ the function u $( x , \cdot )$ is ν-integrable, and the function $\textstyle \int _ { Y } u \left( \cdot , y \right)$ dν $( y )$ is µ-integrable. 

Similarly, for $\nu \ a . e . \ y \in \ Y$ the function u $( \cdot , y )$ is µ-integrable, and the function $\textstyle \int _ { X } u \left( x , \cdot \right) \ d \mu \left( x \right)$ is ν-integrable. Moreover, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {X \times Y} u (x, y) d (\mu \times \nu) (x, y) = \int_ {X} \left(\int_ {Y} u (x, y) d \nu (y)\right) d \mu (x) \\ = \int_ {Y} \left(\int_ {X} u (x, y) d \mu (x)\right) d \nu (y). \end{array}
$$

Remark 1.125. In the case that $u : X \times Y  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is $\mathfrak { M } \otimes \mathfrak { N }$ measurable, then Fubini’s theorem still holds even if the measures $\mu$ and ν are not complete. 

We present below several examples on the validity of Tonelli’s and Fubini’s theorems. 

Exercise 1.126. (i) This exercise shows that the σ-finiteness of $\mu$ and $\nu$ is not a necessary condition. Let $X =  { \mathbb { N } }$ and let $\mu$ be the counting measure. Let $( Y , \mathfrak { N } , \nu )$ be any measure space with $\nu$ complete but not necessarily σ-finite. Prove that Fubini’s and Tonelli’s theorems continue to hold. 

(ii) This exercise shows that without some condition on the measures $\mu$ and $\nu ,$ Fubini’s and Tonelli’s theorems may fail in general. Let $X = Y = [ 0 , 1 ]$ let ${ \mathfrak { M } } = { \mathfrak { N } } = B \left( [ 0 , 1 ] \right)$ , let $\mu$ be the Lebesgue measure, and let $\nu$ be the counting measure. Note that $\nu$ is not σ-finite. Show that the diagonal 

$$
D := \{(x, x): x \in [ 0, 1 ] \}
$$

belongs to $\mathfrak { M } \otimes \mathfrak { N }$ but 

$$
\int_ {Y} \mu (D _ {y}) d \nu (y) \neq \int_ {X} \nu (D _ {x}) d \mu (x).
$$

(iii) This exercise shows that Fubini’s theorem may fail without integrability. Let $X = Y = \mathbb { N }$ , let ${ \mathfrak { M } } = { \mathfrak { N } } = { \mathcal { P } } \left( \mathbb { N } \right)$ , and let $\mu = \nu$ be the counting measure. Consider the function 

$$
u \left(n, l\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text { if } n = l, \\ - 1 & \text { if } l = n + 1, \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }. \end{array} \right.
$$

Prove that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {X} \left(\int_ {Y} u (x, y) d \nu (y)\right) d \mu (x) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {\infty} u (n, l) = 1 \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \neq 0 = \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} u (n, l) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad = \int_ {Y} \left(\int_ {X} u (x, y) d \mu (x)\right) d \nu (y). \end{array}
$$

(iv) Finally, without the hypothesis that u is an ${ \mathfrak { M } } \times { \mathfrak { N } }$ measurable function, Fubini’s and Tonelli’s theorems fail. Let $X = Y$ be the set of all ordinals less than or equal to the first uncountable ordinal $\omega _ { 1 }$ , let ${ \mathfrak { M } } = { \mathfrak { N } }$ be the σ-algebra consisting of all countable sets and their complements, and for every $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ define 

$$
\mu \left(F\right) = \nu \left(F\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1 \text {   if   } F \text {   is   countable, } \\ 0 \text {   otherwise. } \end{array} \right.
$$

Let $E = \{ ( x , y ) \in X \times Y : x < y \}$ . Prove that the sections $E _ { x }$ and $E _ { y }$ are measurable, but 

$$
\int_ {Y} \mu (E _ {y}) d \nu (y) \neq \int_ {X} \nu (E _ {x}) d \mu (x).
$$

Remark 1.127. Fubini’s theorem fails for finitely additive measures. See The orem 3.3 in [He-Yo52]. 

Next we extend Tonelli’s theorem to the case that $\mu \times \nu$ has the finite subset property. We begin with a preliminary result. 

Proposition 1.128. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ and $( Y , \mathfrak { N } , \nu )$ be two measure spaces, with $\mu _ { ; }$ , ν nonzero. If $\mu \times \nu$ has the finite subset property then µ, ν have the finite subset property. 

Proof. Assume that $\mu \times \nu$ has the finite subset property, and let $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ be such that $\mu \left( F \right) = \infty$ . Since ν is not zero, there exists $G \in \mathfrak { N }$ with $\nu \left( G \right) > 0$ Hence $\left( \mu \times \nu \right) \left( F \times G \right) = \mu \left( F \right) \nu \left( G \right) = \infty$ , and by hypothesis there exists $E ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M } \times \mathfrak { N }$ with $E ^ { \prime } \subset F \times G$ such that $0 < ( \mu \times \nu ) ( E ^ { \prime } ) < \infty$ . Find two sequences $\{ F _ { n } \} \subset { \mathfrak { M } } , \{ G _ { n } \} \subset { \mathfrak { N } }$ admissible in the definition of $\left( \mu \times \nu \right) \left( E ^ { \prime } \right)$ (see (1.75)) such that 

$$
0 <   \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(F _ {n}\right) \nu \left(G _ {n}\right) <   \infty .
$$

Since 

$$
E ^ {\prime} \subset \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(\left(F _ {n} \cap F\right) \times \left(G _ {n} \cap G\right)\right)
$$

we have 

$$
0 <   (\mu \times \nu) (E ^ {\prime}) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (F _ {n} \cap F) \nu (G _ {n} \cap G) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu (F _ {n}) \nu (G _ {n}) <   \infty ,
$$

and so $0 < \mu \left( F _ { n } \cap F \right) < \infty$ for some $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . This shows that $\mu$ has the finite subset property. A similar proof yields the same conclusion for $\nu .$ 

Remark 1.129. Note that if $\mu , \nu$ are σ-finite measures, then $\mu \times \nu$ is also σ-finite (and so in particular it has the finite subset property). Indeed, writing 

$$
X = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} X _ {n}, \quad Y = \bigcup_ {l = 1} ^ {\infty} Y _ {l},
$$

where $\{ X _ { n } \} \subset { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\{ Y _ { l } \} \subset \mathfrak { N }$ are sequences of sets of finite measure, we have that 

$$
X \times Y = \bigcup_ {n, l = 1} ^ {\infty} X _ {n} \times Y _ {l},
$$

where $\left( \mu \times \nu \right) \left( X _ { n } \times Y _ { l } \right) = \mu \left( X _ { n } \right) \nu \left( Y _ { l } \right) < \infty .$ 

In view of the previous remark, the following result extends Tonelli’s the orem. 

Theorem 1.130. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ and $( Y , \mathfrak { N } , \nu )$ be two measure spaces, with µ and ν complete. Assume that $\mu \times \nu$ has the finite subset property. Let $u : X \times Y  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be an ${ \mathfrak { M } } \times { \mathfrak { N } }$ measurable function. If one of the two iterated integrals $\textstyle { \int _ { X } { \bigl ( } \int _ { Y } u ( x , y ) }$ <sub>dν (y)</sub> <sub>dµ (x) and</sub> $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { Y } \left( \int _ { X } u \left( x , y \right) d \mu \left( x \right) \right) d \nu \left( y \right) } \end{array}$ is well-defined and finite, then so is the other, and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {X \times Y} u (x, y) d (\mu \times \nu) (x, y) = \int_ {X} \left(\int_ {Y} u (x, y) d \nu (y)\right) d \mu (x) \\ = \int_ {Y} \left(\int_ {X} u (x, y) d \mu (x)\right) d \nu (y). \end{array}
$$

Proof. Assume that the iterated integral 

$$
L := \int_ {Y} \left(\int_ {X} u (x, y) d \mu (x)\right) d \nu (y)
$$

is well-defined and finite. We claim that the set $\left\{ \left( x , y \right) \in X \times Y : u \left( x , y \right) > 0 \right\}$ has σ-finite $\mu \times \nu$ measure. Indeed, if not, then we can find $n \in \mathbb { N }$ such that the set 

$$
E _ {n} := \left\{(x, y) \in X \times Y: u (x, y) > \frac {1}{n} \right\}
$$

has $\mu \times \nu$ infinite measure. Since $\mu \times \nu$ has the finite subset property, by Proposition 1.25 there exists $E ^ { \prime } \subset E _ { n } , E ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M } \times \mathfrak { N }$ , such that 

$$
2 L n <   (\mu \times \nu) (E ^ {\prime}) <   \infty .
$$

Then, by Fubini’s theorem, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 2 L <   \frac {(\mu \times \nu) (E ^ {\prime})}{n} = \frac {1}{n} \int_ {Y} \left(\int_ {X} \chi_ {E ^ {\prime}} (x, y) d \mu (x)\right) d \nu (y) \\ \leq \int_ {Y} \left(\int_ {X} u (x, y) d \mu (x)\right) d \nu (y) = L, \end{array}
$$

which is a contradiction. Hence the set 

$$
E := \{(x, y) \in X \times Y: u (x, y) > 0 \}
$$

has σ-finite $\mu \times \nu$ measure, and so we may find a sequence $\{ E _ { n } ^ { \prime } \}$ of pairwise disjoint sets with $E _ { n } ^ { \prime } \in \mathfrak { M } \times \mathfrak { N }$ such that $\left( \mu \times \nu \right) \left( E _ { n } ^ { \prime } \right) < \infty$ and 

$$
E = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n} ^ {\prime}.
$$

Fix $n \in \mathbb N$ . In view of (1.75) we may find two sequences $\left\{ F _ { k } ^ { ( n ) } \right\} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ 2 $\left\{ G _ { k } ^ { ( n ) } \right\} \subset \mathfrak { N }$ such that 

$$
E _ {n} ^ {\prime} \subset \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(F _ {k} ^ {(n)} \times G _ {k} ^ {(n)}\right), \quad \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(F _ {k} ^ {(n)}\right) \nu \left(G _ {k} ^ {(n)}\right) \leq (\mu \times \nu) \left(E _ {n} ^ {\prime}\right) + 1.
$$

Note that if $\mu ( F _ { k } ^ { ( n ) } ) = 0$ (respectively $\nu ( G _ { k } ^ { ( n ) } ) = 0 )$ for some $k \in \mathbb N$ , then Tonelli’s theorem holds on measurable subsets of $F _ { k } ^ { ( n ) } \times Y$ (respectively $X \times$ $G _ { k } ^ { ( n ) } )$ , since all three integrals reduce to zero. Thus, we may assume that $0 < \mu ( F _ { k } ^ { ( n ) } ) , \nu ( G _ { k } ^ { ( n ) } ) < \infty$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$ 

In particular, $\mu \lfloor \bigcup _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } F _ { k } ^ { ( n ) }$ and $\textstyle \nu \lfloor \bigcup _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } G _ { k } ^ { ( n ) }$ are $\sigma { \mathrm { - f i n i t e } }$ . Hence we can apply the classical Tonelli’s theorem to the function $u \chi _ { E _ { n } ^ { \prime } }$ restricted to $\left( \bigcup _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } F _ { k } ^ { ( n ) } \right) \times \left( \bigcup _ { k = 1 } ^ { \infty } G _ { k } ^ { ( n ) } \right)$ , and then sum over n. 

Remark 1.131. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $u : X  [ 0 , \infty ]$ . If in place of the standard definition of measurability we assume that $u ^ { - 1 } \left( A \right) \cap F \in$ 

M for every open set $A \subset [ 0 , \infty ]$ and for every $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( F \right) < \infty$ , and define 

$$
\int_ {X} u d \mu := \sup \left\{\int_ {F} u d \mu : F \in \mathfrak {M}, \mu (F) <   \infty \right\}
$$

then, interpreting iterated integrals in this new way, it is possible to prove a converse of the previous theorem, namely that if $\mu$ and $\nu$ are complete and have the finite subset property, and if Tonelli’s theorem holds, then $\mu \times \nu$ has the finite subset property (see [Muk73]). Note that for σ-finite measures these new definitions of measurability and integrability coincide with the classical ones. 

## 1.1.6 Projection of Measurable Sets

The projection of a Borel set $B \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ on the x-axis in general is not a Borel set but it is Lebesgue measurable. To prove this result we need to introduce the notion of Suslin sets. One of the major complications in what follows is the notation. Let 

$$
\mathcal {I} := \left\{\alpha = \left(\alpha_ {1}, \dots , \alpha_ {n}\right) \in \mathbb {N} ^ {n}: n \in \mathbb {N} \right\} = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mathbb {N} ^ {n}.
$$

If $\alpha = ( \alpha _ { 1 } ) \in \mathcal { T }$ and $\alpha _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { N }$ , we write $\alpha _ { 1 }$ for α. Also, if $\alpha = ( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { n } )$ and $\beta = ( \beta _ { 1 } , \ldots , \beta _ { n } )$ , we say that $\alpha \leq \beta$ if $\alpha _ { i } \leq \beta _ { i }$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ . If $\alpha = ( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { n } ) \in \mathbb { N } ^ { n }$ and $k \in \mathbb N$ , we define $( \alpha , k ) : = ( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { n } , k ) \in \mathbb { N } ^ { n + 1 }$ Finally, if $\alpha = ( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { n } ) \in \mathbb { N } ^ { n }$ and $k \in \mathbb N$ , with $k \leq n$ , we set $\alpha | _ { k } : =$ $( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { k } )$ 

Let $\mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } } : = \{ f : \mathbb { N } \} \mathbb { N } \}$ . To simplify the notation for every $f \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ and $n \in \mathbb N$ we write $f | _ { n }$ for $( f \left( 1 \right) , \ldots , f \left( n \right) ) \in { \mathcal { I } }$ . Hence if $f \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ and $\alpha =$ $( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { n } ) \in \mathbb { N } ^ { n }$ , then $\left. f \right| _ { n } \leq \alpha$ means that $f \left( i \right) \leq \alpha _ { i }$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ . If $f , g \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ , then $f \leq g$ means that $g \left( i \right) \leq f \left( i \right)$ for all $i \in \mathbb N$ 

Definition 1.132. A Suslin scheme on a set X is a function 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {E}: \mathcal {I} \to \mathcal {P} (X), \\ \alpha \mapsto E _ {\alpha}. \end{array}
$$

Given a Suslin scheme $\mathcal { E } _ { i }$ , the Suslin set A (E) is defined as 

$$
A \left(\mathcal {E}\right) := \bigcup_ {f \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {f | _ {k}} = \bigcup_ {f \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {(f (1), \dots , f (k))}.
$$

$I f { \mathcal { F } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ , a Suslin-F set is any Suslin set $A \left( \mathcal { E } \right)$ , where $\mathcal { E } : \mathcal { T }  \mathcal { F }$ 

Given a Suslin set A (E), for any $\alpha = ( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { n } ) \in \mathbb { N } ^ { n }$ we define 

$$
S^{\alpha}:= \bigcup_{\substack{f\in \mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}\\ f|_{n}\leq \alpha}}\bigcap_{k = 1}^{\infty}E_{f|_{k}}.
$$

If $n = 1$ , that is, $\alpha = \left( \alpha _ { 1 } \right)$ , we will write $S ^ { \alpha _ { 1 } }$ for $S ^ { \alpha }$ . Note that the sequence $\{ S ^ { n } \} _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ is increasing and 

$$
A \left(\mathcal {E}\right) = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} S ^ {n}.\tag{1.77}
$$

Also, for any $\alpha = ( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { \ell } ) \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \ell }$ the sequence $\left\{ S ^ { ( \alpha , n ) } \right\} _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ is increasing and 

$$
S ^ {\alpha} = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} S ^ {(\alpha , n)}.\tag{1.78}
$$

Finally, for any $g \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ and $n \in \mathbb { N }$ we define 

$$
S_{g|_{n}}:= \bigcup_{\substack{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}^{n}\\ \alpha \leq g|_{n}}}\bigcap_{k = 1}^{n}E_{\alpha |_{k}} = \bigcup_{\substack{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}^{n}\\ \alpha \leq g|_{n}}}E_{(\alpha_{1})}\cap E_{(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})}\cap \ldots \cap E_{(\alpha_{1},\ldots ,\alpha_{n})}.\tag{1.79}
$$

The sequence $\left\{ S _ { g \mid _ { n } } \right\} _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ is decreasing and 

$$
S_{g}:= \bigcap_{n = 1}^{\infty}S_{g|_{n}} = \bigcup_{\substack{f\in \mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}\\ f\leq g}}\bigcap_{k = 1}^{\infty}E_{f|_{k}}.\tag{1.80}
$$

We prove that the class of Suslin sets is closed under countable unions and intersections. 

Theorem 1.133. Let X be a nonempty set and let ${ \mathcal { F } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be such that $X \in { \mathcal { F } }$ . Then the class of $\mathit { S u s l i n - F }$ sets is closed under countable unions and intersections. 

Proof. Let $\{ E ^ { ( n ) } \}$ be a sequence of Suslin-F sets, that is, 

$$
E ^ {(n)} = \bigcup_ {f \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {f | _ {k}} ^ {(n)}.
$$

For every $g \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ and $j \in \mathbb N$ define 

$$
E _ {g | _ {j}} = E _ {(g (1), \ldots , g (j))} := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} X & \text { if } j = 1, \\ E _ {(g (2), \ldots , g (j))} ^ {(g (1))} & \text { if } j \geq 2. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \bigcup_ {g \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {g | _ {j}} = \bigcup_ {g \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {j = 2} ^ {\infty} E _ {g | _ {j}} = \bigcup_ {g \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {j = 2} ^ {\infty} E _ {(g (2), \ldots , g (j))} ^ {(g (1))} \\ = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \bigcup_ {f \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {(f (1), \ldots , f (k))} ^ {(n)} = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E ^ {(n)}, \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that as g varies in $\mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ the value $g \left( 1 \right)$ ranges over all of N and we have made the “change of variables” $f \left( k \right) : = g \left( k - 1 \right)$ , $k : = j - 1$ . Hence $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E ^ { ( n ) }$ is a Suslin ${ } _ { - \mathcal { F } }$ set. 

Next we show that $\textstyle \bigcap _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E ^ { ( n ) }$ is a Suslin- $\mathcal { F }$ set. For every $g \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ and $j \in \mathbb N$ write $j$ in a unique way as 

$$
j = 2 ^ {l} i,\tag{1.81}
$$

where $l \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ and $i \in \mathbb N$ is odd, and define 

$$
E _ {g | _ {j}} := E _ {(g (2 ^ {l} 1), g (2 ^ {l} 3), \dots , g (2 ^ {l} i))} ^ {(l + 1)}.\tag{1.82}
$$

We claim that 

$$
\bigcup_ {g \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {g | _ {j}} = \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E ^ {(n)}.\tag{1.83}
$$

Indeed, if $l \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ and $g \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ , then 

$$
\bigcap_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {g | _ {j}} \subset \bigcap_ {i \text {odd}} E _ {g | _ {2 ^ {l} i}} = \bigcap_ {i \text {odd}} E _ {(g (2 ^ {l} 1), g (2 ^ {l} 3), \dots , g (2 ^ {l} i))} ^ {(l + 1)} = \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {(f _ {l} (1), \dots , f _ {l} (k))} ^ {(l + 1)},
$$

where $f _ { l } \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ is defined as $f _ { l } \left( p \right) : = g \left( 2 ^ { l } \left( 2 p - 1 \right) \right)$ for $p \in \mathbb N$ . Hence 

$$
\bigcup_ {g \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {g | _ {j}} \subset \bigcup_ {f \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {f | _ {k}} ^ {(l + 1)} = E ^ {(l + 1)}
$$

for all $l \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ , which implies that 

$$
\bigcup_ {g \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {g | _ {j}} \subset \bigcap_ {l = 0} ^ {\infty} E ^ {(l + 1)} = \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E ^ {(n)}.\tag{1.84}
$$

Conversely, let 

$$
x \in \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E ^ {(n)} = \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \bigcup_ {f \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {f | _ {k}} ^ {(n)},
$$

and for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ choose $f ^ { ( n ) } \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ such that 

$$
x \in \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {f ^ {(n)} \big | _ {k}} ^ {(n)}.
$$

Using (1.81) we define $g \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ as 

$$
g (j) = g \left(2 ^ {l} i\right) := f ^ {(l + 1)} \left(\frac {i + 1}{2}\right), \quad j \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Then for all $j \in \mathbb N$ , again by (1.81), we have 

$$
x \in E _ {\left(f ^ {(l + 1)} (1), f ^ {(l + 1)} (2), \dots , f ^ {(l + 1)} \left(\frac {i + 1}{2}\right)\right)} ^ {(l + 1)} = E _ {(g (2 ^ {l} 1), g (2 ^ {l} 3), \dots , g (2 ^ {l} i))} ^ {(l + 1)} = E _ {g | _ {j}},
$$

where we have used (1.82). Hence 

$$
\bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E ^ {(n)} \subset \bigcup_ {g \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {g | _ {j}},
$$

which, together with (1.84), gives (1.83). 

We are now ready to study the measurability of Suslin sets. If $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ is a measure space and $\mathcal { E } : \mathcal { T }  \mathfrak { M }$ , then in general, the Suslin-M set $A \left( \mathcal { E } \right)$ does not belong to M. However, the next result shows that $A \left( \mathcal { E } \right)$ belongs to the σ-algebra ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu }$ of all $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable subsets, where $\mu ^ { * }$ is the outer measure given in Corollary 1.38. 

Theorem 1.134. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu }$ be the $\sigma \mathrm { - }$ algebra of all $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable subsets, where $\mu ^ { * } : { \mathcal { P } } ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is the outer measure 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) := \inf \left\{\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(E _ {n}\right): \left\{E _ {n} \right\} \subset \mathfrak {M}, E \subset \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n} \right\}, \quad E \subset X.
$$

Then any $S u s l i n \mathrm { - } \mathfrak { M } _ { \mu }$ set belongs to ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu }$ 

Proof. Let $A \left( \mathcal { E } \right)$ be $\mathrm { a } \ \mathrm { S u s l i n } { - } \mathfrak { M } _ { \mu }$ set, that is, 

$$
A \left(\mathcal {E}\right) = \bigcup_ {f \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {f | _ {k}},
$$

where $\mathcal { E } : \mathcal { T } \longrightarrow \mathfrak { M } _ { \mu }$ . In view of Carath´eodory’s theorem and Proposition 1.45, $\mu ^ { * }$ is a regular outer measure that coincides with $\mu$ on M and such that ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu }$ . Moreover, for every $E \subset X$ , 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) = \inf \left\{\mu (F): F \in \mathfrak {M}, F \supset E \right\}.\tag{1.85}
$$

In view of the subadditivity of $\mu ^ { * }$ , to prove that $A \left( \mathcal { E } \right)$ belongs to ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu }$ it sufices to show that for any set $F \subset X$ 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(F \cap A \left(\mathcal {E}\right)\right) + \mu^ {*} \left(F \setminus A \left(\mathcal {E}\right)\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(F\right).
$$

Without loss of generality we may assume that $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( F \right) < \infty$ . Using (1.85), we may find $G \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $G \supset F$ and $\mu ^ { * } \left( F \right) = \mu \left( G \right)$ . Since the sequence $\{ S ^ { n } \cap G \} _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ is increasing, by Proposition 1.43 and (1.77), 

$$
\mu^ {*} (A (\mathcal {E}) \cap G) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu^ {*} (S ^ {n} \cap G),
$$

and thus for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a positive integer $n _ { 1 }$ such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(S ^ {n _ {1}} \cap G\right) \geq \mu^ {*} \left(A (\mathcal {E}) \cap G\right) - \frac {\varepsilon}{2}.\tag{1.86}
$$

Inductively, if $( n _ { 1 } , n _ { 2 } , \ldots , n _ { k } ) \in \mathbb { N } ^ { k }$ have been defined so that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(S ^ {\left(n _ {1}, n _ {2}, \dots , n _ {k}\right)} \cap G\right) \geq \mu^ {*} \left(S ^ {\left(n _ {1}, n _ {2}, \dots , n _ {k - 1}\right)} \cap G\right) - \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {k}},\tag{1.87}
$$

using the fact that the sequence $\left\{ S ^ { ( n _ { 1 } , n _ { 2 } , \ldots , n _ { k } , n ) } \cap G \right\} _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ is increasing, by Proposition 1.43 and (1.78) we have 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(S ^ {\left(n _ {1}, n _ {2}, \dots , n _ {k}\right)} \cap G\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mu^ {*} \left(S ^ {\left(n _ {1}, n _ {2}, \dots , n _ {k}, n\right)} \cap G\right),
$$

and so there exists $n _ { k + 1 } \in \mathbb { N }$ such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(S ^ {\left(n _ {1}, n _ {2}, \dots , n _ {k + 1}\right)} \cap G\right) \geq \mu^ {*} \left(S ^ {\left(n _ {1}, n _ {2}, \dots , n _ {k}\right)} \cap G\right) - \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {k + 1}}.
$$

In this way we obtain a function $g \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ defined by $g \left( k \right) : = n _ { k }$ for $k \in \mathbb N$ Corresponding to g we have the sequence of sets $\left\{ S _ { g \mid _ { k } } \right\} _ { k \in \mathbb { N } }$ defined in (1.79). Note that since $\mathcal { E } : \mathcal { T }  \mathfrak { M } _ { \mu }$ , the sets $\boldsymbol { S } _ { g \vert _ { k } }$ belong to ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu } ,$ since they are a countable union of finite intersections of measurable sets. Using the fact that $S ^ { g | _ { k } } \subset S _ { g | _ { k } } , ( 1 . 8 6 )$ and (1.87) yield 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu^ {*} \left(S _ {g | _ {k}} \cap G\right) \geq \mu^ {*} \left(S ^ {g | _ {k}} \cap G\right) = \mu^ {*} \left(S ^ {(n _ {1}, n _ {2}, \ldots , n _ {k})} \cap G\right) \\ \geq \mu^ {*} \left(A \left(\mathcal {E}\right) \cap G\right) - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {i}}. \end{array}
$$

Therefore since $S _ { g | _ { k } } \in \mathfrak { M } _ { \mu }$ we obtain 

$$
\mu^ {*} (G) = \mu^ {*} \left(S _ {g | _ {k}} \cap G\right) + \mu^ {*} \left(G \setminus S _ {g | _ {k}}\right) \geq \mu^ {*} (A (\mathcal {E}) \cap G) + \mu^ {*} \left(G \setminus S _ {g | _ {k}}\right) - \varepsilon .
$$

As the sequence $\left\{ S _ { g \mid _ { k } } \right\} _ { k \in \mathbb { N } }$ decreases to $S _ { g } \subset A \left( \mathcal { E } \right) \left( \mathrm { s e e } \left( 1 . 8 0 \right) \right)$ , the sequence $G \backslash S _ { g \vert _ { k } }$ increases to $\ddot { G } \setminus S _ { g } \supset G \setminus A \left( \mathcal { E } \right)$ , and so by Proposition 1.43 (or Proposition 1.7), letting $k \to \infty$ in the previous inequality gives 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mu^ {*} (F) = \mu^ {*} (G) & \geq \mu^ {*} (A (\mathcal {E}) \cap G) + \mu^ {*} (G \setminus S _ {g}) - \varepsilon \\ & \geq \mu^ {*} (A (\mathcal {E}) \cap G) + \mu^ {*} (G \setminus A (\mathcal {E})) - \varepsilon \\ & \geq \mu^ {*} (A (\mathcal {E}) \cap F) + \mu^ {*} (F \setminus A (\mathcal {E})) - \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

where we have used the facts that $G \supset F$ and $\mu ^ { * } \left( F \right) = \mu \left( G \right)$ . Given the arbitrariness of $\varepsilon$ and $F$ it follows that $A \left( \mathcal { E } \right)$ is µ<sup>∗</sup>-measurable. 

We now prove the first projection theorem. 

Theorem 1.135. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let Y be a complete separable metric space. Let R be the class of all rectangles $F \times C _ { : }$ , where $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $C \subset Y$ is closed. Then the projection $\pi _ { X } \left( E \right)$ of every Suslin-R set $E \subset X \times Y$ on X is a Suslin-M set. In particular, $\pi _ { X } \left( E \right)$ belongs to ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu }$ 

Proof. Since Y is a complete separable metric space we may find a countable family $\{ y _ { i } \} \subset Y$ dense in $Y$ . Let $\{ U _ { i } \}$ be the countable family of closed balls centered at $y _ { i }$ and rational diameter less than $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } }$ . 

Since each $U _ { i }$ is a complete separable space we may cover it with a countable family $\{ U _ { i j } \}$ of closed balls of rational diameter less than $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { 2 } } }$ . Continuing this process for each $\alpha = ( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { n } ) \in \mathbb { N } ^ { n }$ we construct a closed ball $U _ { \alpha }$ such that diam $U _ { \alpha } \in \mathbb { Q }$ 

$$
\mathrm{diam} U _ {\alpha} \leq \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}},
$$

and 

$$
U _ {\alpha} \subset \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} U _ {(\alpha , k)}.
$$

Hence we may write 

$$
X \times Y = \bigcup_ {g \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(X \times U _ {g | _ {k}}\right).\tag{1.88}
$$

Let $E \subset X \times Y$ be a Suslin-R set. Then there exists a Suslin scheme $\mathcal { E } : \mathcal { T }  \mathcal { R }$ such that 

$$
E = A \left(\mathcal {E}\right) = \bigcup_ {f \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(F _ {f | _ {k}} \times C _ {f | _ {k}}\right),
$$

where $\boldsymbol { F } _ { f \vert _ { k } } \in \mathfrak { M }$ and $C _ { f \vert _ { k } } \subset Y$ is closed. By (1.88) we have 

$$
E = \bigcup_ {g \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcup_ {f \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(F _ {f | _ {k}} \times \left(C _ {f | _ {k}} \cap U _ {g | _ {k}}\right)\right),
$$

where we have used the fact that for each $k \in \mathbb N$ , 

$$
F _ {f | _ {k}} \times C _ {f | _ {k}} = \bigcup_ {g \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \left(F _ {f | _ {k}} \times \left(C _ {f | _ {k}} \cap U _ {g | _ {k}}\right)\right),
$$

since by construction the family $\big \{ U _ { g \vert _ { k } } \big \} _ { g \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } } }$ covers $Y$ 

With a suitable change of indexing we may write 

$$
E = \bigcup_ {h \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(F _ {h | _ {k}} \times \tilde {C} _ {h | _ {k}}\right),
$$

where $\tilde { C } _ { h \vert _ { k } } \subset Y$ is closed and diam $\boldsymbol { \tilde { C } } _ { h \vert _ { k } } \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$ for every $h \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ . By replacing each $\tilde { C } _ { h \vert _ { k } }$ with the closed se 

$$
\hat {C} _ {h | _ {k}} := \tilde {C} _ {h | _ {1}} \cap \ldots \cap \tilde {C} _ {h | _ {k}},
$$

without loss of generality we may assume that $\tilde { C } _ { h | _ { k + 1 } } \subset \tilde { C } _ { h | _ { k } }$ , so that since $Y$ is complete and diam $\boldsymbol { \tilde { C } } _ { h \vert _ { k } } \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$ , the closed set 

$$
\tilde {C} _ {h} := \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \tilde {C} _ {h | _ {k}}
$$

is nonempty if and only if $\tilde { C } _ { h \vert _ { k } }$ is nonempty for each $k \in \mathbb N$ 

Moreover, again without loss of generality, we may assume that $F _ { h \vert _ { k } }$ is empty whenever $\tilde { C } _ { h \vert _ { k } }$ is empty. Hence if ${ \tilde { C } } _ { h }$ is empty then so is 

$$
F _ {h} := \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {h | _ {k}},
$$

and so we may write 

$$
\pi_ {X} (E) = \bigcup_ {h \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \pi_ {X} \left(F _ {h} \times \tilde {C} _ {h}\right) = \bigcup_ {h \in \mathbb {N} ^ {\mathbb {N}}} \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {h | _ {k}},
$$

where $\pi _ { X } : X \times Y \to X$ is the projection on X. Thus $\pi _ { X } \left( E \right)$ is a Suslin-M set. 

It now follows from Theorem 1.134 that $\pi _ { X } \left( E \right) \in { \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu }$ 

As a corollary of this theorem we can prove the result announced at the beginning of the subsection. 

Theorem 1.136 (Projection). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let Y be a complete separable metric space. Then for every $E \in \mathfrak { M } _ { \mu } \otimes B \left( Y \right)$ the projection of E on X belongs to ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu }$ 

Here ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu }$ is the σ-algebra defined in Theorem 1.134. 

Proof. Let C be the class of all Suslin-R sets whose complement is still a Suslin-R set. We claim that this class is a σ-algebra. Indeed, if $E \in { \mathcal { C } }$ then $( X \times Y ) \setminus E \in { \mathcal { C } }$ by definition of C.
