If $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset { \mathcal { C } }$ then $E _ { n }$ and $( X \times Y ) \setminus E _ { n }$ are Suslin-R sets, and so, by Theorem 1.133, 

$$
\bigcup_ {n = 1} E _ {n} \text {   and   } (X \times Y) \setminus \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} E _ {n}\right) = \bigcap_ {n = 1} ((X \times Y) \setminus E _ {n})
$$

are still Suslin-R sets. Hence $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } E _ { n } \in { \mathcal { C } }$ . Finally, the empty set belongs to C since both $X \times Y$ and $\varnothing$ are Suslin-R sets. 

Since C contains all rectangles of the form $F \times C$ , where $F \in { \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu }$ and C is closed, it must contain ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu } \otimes B \left( Y \right)$ . Hence if $E \in { \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu } \otimes B \left( Y \right)$ then E is a Suslin-R set, and so by the previous theorem $\pi _ { X } \left( E \right)$ is a Suslin-M set. We now use Theorem 1.134 to conclude that $\pi _ { X } \left( E \right)$ belongs to ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { \mu }$ 

As a direct application of the projection theorem, and of the fact that the σ-algebra of Lebesgue measurable sets in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ is the completion of $B \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } \right)$ , it follows that if $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ is a Borel set, then the projection $\pi _ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ on the x-axis is Lebesgue measurable, but not necessarily a Borel set. 

## 1.2 Covering Theorems and Diferentiation of Measures in R<sup>N</sup>

## 1.2.1 Covering Theorems in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$

Throughout this subsection we take as ambient space X the Euclidean space $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , and we present several covering theorems and their applications to the derivatives of measures. 

Definition 1.137. A set $F \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is said to be 

(i) star-shaped with respect to a set $G \subset F$ if F is star-shaped with respect to each point of G, i.e., if $\theta x + \left( 1 - \theta \right) y \in F$ for all $x \in F , y \in G$ , and $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ ; 

(ii) convex if it is star-shaped with respect to itself, i.e., if $\theta x + \left( 1 - \theta \right) y \in F$ for all x, $y \in F$ and $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ ; 

(iii) a γ-Morse set associated with x, with $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and $\gamma \geq 1$ , if there exists $r > 0$ such that 

$$
\overline {{B (x , r)}} \subset F \subset \overline {{B (x , \gamma r)}}\tag{1.89}
$$

and F is star-shaped with respect to $\overline { { B \left( x , r \right) } }$ 

Example 1.138. A regular pentagram is an example of a nonconvex set that is star-shaped with respect to a ball. 

Given a point $\boldsymbol { x } _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and a function $\varphi : S ^ { N - 1 } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ , the set 

$$
E := \left\{x _ {0} + s x: x \in S ^ {N - 1}, 0 \leq s <   \varphi (x) \right\}
$$

is star-shaped with respect to $x _ { 0 }$ 

It turns out that if $\varphi$ is suficiently regular, then E is actually star-shaped with respect to a ball centered at $x _ { 0 }$ 

Proposition 1.139. Let $A \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be an open, bounded set star-shaped with respect to a point $x _ { 0 } \in A$ . If A is star-shaped with respect to a closed ball centered at $x _ { 0 }$ , then the function $\varphi : S ^ { N - 1 } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ , defined by 

1.2 Covering Theorems and Diferentiation of Measures in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

$$
\varphi (x) := \sup \left\{s \geq 0: x _ {0} + s x \in A \right\} \quad x \in S ^ {N - 1},
$$

is a Lipschitz function, $i . e .$ , there exists a constant $L > 0$ such that 

$$
| \varphi (x) - \varphi (y) | \leq L | x - y |
$$

for all x, $y \in S ^ { N - 1 }$ 

The proof follows from Theorem 4.107. 

Exercise 1.140. Prove the converse of the previous proposition, namely that if $A \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is an open, bounded set star-shaped with respect to a point $x _ { 0 } \in A$ and if the function $\varphi$ is Lipschitz, then the set A is star-shaped with respect to a closed ball centered at $x _ { 0 }$ 

Remark 1.141. It follows from the above proposition that an open bounded set star-shaped with respect to a closed ball $\overline { { B \left( x _ { 0 } , r \right) } }$ may be approximated from inside by an increasing uncountable family of closed sets star-shaped with respect to the same ball. Indeed, it sufices to consider 

$$
A _ {\varepsilon} = \left\{x _ {0} + s x: x \in S ^ {N - 1}, 0 \leq s \leq \varphi (x) - \varepsilon \right\},
$$

where $0 < \varepsilon < r$ , and where we have used the fact that $\varphi \geq r$ and is finite in view of the boundedness of the set A. 

Definition 1.142. Given a set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , a family $\mathcal { F }$ of nonempty subsets of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is said to be a 

(i) cover for E if 

$$
E \subset \bigcup_ {F \in \mathcal {F}} F;
$$

(ii) fine cover for E if for every $x \in E$ there exists a subfamily $\mathcal { F } _ { x } \subset \mathcal { F }$ of sets containing x such that 

$$
\inf \left\{\operatorname{diam} F: F \in \mathcal {F} _ {x} \right\} = 0;\tag{1.90}
$$

(iii) Morse cover for E if there exists $\gamma \geq 1$ such that for every $x \in E$ there exists $a \gamma { - } M o r s e$ set F associated with x and such that $F \in { \mathcal { F } } ,$ 

(iv) fine Morse cover for E if there exists $\gamma \geq 1$ such that for every $x \in E$ there exists a subfamily $\mathcal { F } _ { x } ~ \subset ~ \mathcal { F }$ of γ-Morse sets associated with x for which (1.90) holds. 

Example 1.143. Given a set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , the two families 

$$
\left\{B (x, r): 0 <   r <   1, x \in E \right\}, \quad \left\{Q (x, r): 0 <   r <   1, x \in E \right\}
$$

are fine Morse covers for E. More generally, if C is any bounded, convex closed set containing the origin in its interior, then the family 

$$
\{x + r C: 0 <   r <   1, x \in E \}
$$

is a fine Morse cover for $E .$ 

We now present the main covering theorem of this subsection. 

Theorem 1.144 (Morse covering theorem). Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and let $\mathcal { F }$ be a family of subsets of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ such that 

$$
\sup \left\{\operatorname{diam} F: F \in \mathcal {F} \right\} <   \infty .\tag{1.91}
$$

Assume that $\mathcal { F }$ is a Morse cover for E. Then there exist $\ell = \ell \left( \gamma , N \right) \in \mathbb { N }$ and $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \mathcal { F } _ { \ell } \subset \mathcal { F }$ such that each $\mathcal { F } _ { n } , n = 1 , \ldots , \ell .$ , is a countable family of disjoint sets in $\mathcal { F }$ and 

$$
E \subset \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\ell} \bigcup_ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {n}} F.
$$

Lemma 1.145. Let $\gamma \geq 1 , 1 < t \leq 2$ , and consider $x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and $F _ { 1 } , \ldots , F _ { n } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ such that 

(i) $F _ { i }$ is $a \gamma { - } M$ orse set associated with $x _ { i }$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n ,$ 

(ii) $F _ { i } \cap F _ { n } \neq \emptyset$ for all $1 \leq i < n ,$

Proof (Theorem $\it { 1 . 1 4 4 } )$ . For every $x \in E$ select $F \left( x \right) \in { \mathcal { F } }$ such that $F \left( x \right)$ is a γ-Morse set associated with x. We divide the proof into three steps. 

Step 1: Assume first that E is bounded. We construct a countable subfamily of $\mathcal { F }$ that still covers E. By (1.91) we may choose $x _ { 1 } \in E$ such that

By (1.102) it follows that $x \notin E _ { n + 1 }$ , and so, in view of (1.100), we conclude that

x \in \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {n} F (x _ {i}).
$$

In order to prove (1.104), for every $n \in J$ let $F _ { n } : = F \left( x _ { n } \right)$ and let $r _ { n } > 0$ be such that

Moreover, the balls $B \left( x _ { i } , \frac { r _ { i } } { \beta } \right)$ and $B \left( x _ { j } , \frac { r _ { j } } { \beta } \right)$ are disjoint, where $\beta : = \operatorname* { m a x } \left\{ 3 , 2 \gamma \right\}$ . Indeed, since $x _ { j } \notin F _ { i }$ , then

Step 2: Let $\{ F _ { i } \} _ { i \in J }$ be the countable subfamily of $\mathcal { F }$ constructed in Step 1 and that still covers the bounded set E. If $J = \{ 1 \}$ then there is nothing left to prove. Otherwise, for any fixed integer $k > 1$ let

Construct a function $\sigma : J \to \{ 1 , \dots , c ( \gamma , N ) \}$ in the following way. If $j ~ \le ~ c ( \gamma , N )$ set $\sigma \left( j \right) : = j$ . For $j ~ > ~ c ( \gamma , N )$ we define $\sigma \left( j \right)$ recursively: assuming that $\sigma \left( 1 \right) , \ldots , \sigma \left( j - 1 \right)$ have been assigned, set $\sigma \left( j \right) : = l$ , where $l \in \{ 1 , \ldots , c ( \gamma , N ) \}$ satisfies the property

whenever $i \in \{ 1 , \ldots , j - 1 \}$ is such that $\sigma \left( i \right) = l$ . Note that there is at least one such number l. Indeed, if not, then for every $l \in \{ 1 , \ldots , c ( \gamma , N ) \}$ there would exist $i _ { l } \in \{ 1 , \ldots , j - 1 \}$ such that $\sigma \left( i _ { l } \right) = l$ and $F _ { j } \cap F _ { i _ { l } } \neq \emptyset$ . In particular, $i _ { l } \in I _ { j - 1 }$ . Since ${ \mathit { l } } \neq { \mathit { l } } ^ { \prime }$ implies that $i _ { l } \neq i _ { l ^ { \prime } }$ , this would entail that the cardinality of $I _ { j - 1 }$ would be at least $c \left( \gamma , N \right)$ , and this is a contradiction. 

For $n \in \{ 1 , \ldots , c ( \gamma , N ) \}$ let

It remains to show that distinct elements of ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ are mutually disjoint. Step 3: If the set E is unbounded, then for each $k \in \mathbb N$ apply the previous steps to the set

As a corollary of the Morse covering theorem we have the following theorem of Besicovitch: 

Theorem 1.146 (Besicovitch covering theorem). There exists a constant , depending only on the dimension N of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , such that for any collection $\mathcal { F }$ of (nondegenerate) closed balls with 

$$
\sup \left\{\operatorname{diam} B: B \in \mathcal {F} \right\} <   \infty
$$

there exist $\mathcal { F } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \mathcal { F } _ { \ell } \subset \mathcal { F }$ such that each $\mathcal { F } _ { n } , n = 1 , \ldots , \ell ;$ , is a countable family of disjoint balls in F and 

$$
E \subset \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\ell} \bigcup_ {B \in \mathcal {F} _ {n}} B,
$$

where E is the set of centers of balls in $\mathcal { F }$ . 

Proof. It sufices to take $\gamma = 1$ and for each $x \in E$ define ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { x }$ to be the family of all balls in $\mathcal { F }$ that are centered at x. 

An important consequence of the Morse covering theorem is the following result, which will be crucial in the characterization of Radon–Nikodym derivatives in the next subsections. 

Theorem 1.147 (Morse measure covering theorem). Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and let F be a fine Morse cover of closed subsets for E. Let $\mu ^ { * } : \mathcal { P } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Radon outer measure. Then for every open set $A \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ there exists a countable family $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 } \subset \mathcal { F }$ of pairwise disjoint subsets such that 

$$
\bigcup_ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {0}} F \subset A, \quad \mu^ {*} \left((E \cap A) \setminus \bigcup_ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {0}} F\right) = 0.
$$

Step 1: Assume that E is bounded. We show that there exists a finite subfamily $\{ F _ { 1 } , \ldots , F _ { m _ { 1 } } \} \subset \mathcal { F }$ of mutually disjoint subsets of A such that

$$

$$

$$

Set

Just as before, we may find a finite subfamily $\{ F _ { m _ { 1 } + 1 } , \ldots , F _ { m _ { 2 } } \} \subset \mathcal { F } ^ { ( 2 ) }$ of mutually disjoint subsets of A such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu^ {*} \left((E \cap A) \setminus \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {m _ {2}} F _ {i}\right) = \mu^ {*} \left((E \cap A _ {2}) \setminus \bigcup_ {i = m _ {1} + 1} ^ {m _ {2}} F _ {i}\right) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \theta \mu^ {*} (E \cap A _ {2}) \leq \theta^ {2} \mu^ {*} (E \cap A). \end{array}
$$

By induction, we construct a countable family ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { 0 } = \{ F _ { i } \} \subset { \mathcal { F } }$ of pairwise disjoint subsets contained in A such that for every $k \in \mathbb N$ , 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left((E \cap A) \setminus \bigcup_ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {0}} F\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left((E \cap A) \setminus \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {m _ {k}} F _ {i}\right) \leq \theta^ {k} \mu^ {*} (E \cap A).
$$

Since $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( E \right) < \infty$ we conclude the proof in this case by letting $k \to \infty$ 

Step 2: If E is unbounded, then applying Proposition 1.15 to the Radon measure $\mu ^ { * } : \mathcal { B } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right]$ , choose an increasing sequence of radii $\{ r _ { n } \}$ such that $r _ { n } \to \infty$ and 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\partial B \left(0, r _ {n}\right)\right) = 0.\tag{1.110}
$$

Applying Step 1 to 

$$
E _ {n} := E \cap \left(B (0, r _ {n + 1}) \setminus \overline {{B (0 , r _ {n})}}\right)
$$

and 

$$
A _ {n} := A \cap \left(B \left(0, r _ {n + 1}\right) \setminus \overline {{B \left(0 , r _ {n}\right)}}\right),
$$

we find a countable family of mutually disjoint sets $\left\{ F _ { i } ^ { ( n ) } \right\} _ { i \in \mathbb { N } }$ contained in $A _ { n }$ and that cover $E _ { n }$ up to a set of $\mu ^ { * }$ outer measure zero. Therefore the collection of 

$$
\left\{F _ {i} ^ {(n)} \right\} _ {i, n \in \mathbb {N}}
$$

is a family of mutually disjoint sets contained in $A .$ , and in view of (1.110) it covers $E$ up to a set of $\mu ^ { * }$ outer measure zero. 

Remark 1.148. (i) In the special case that E is open and $\mu ^ { * }$ is the Lebesgue measure, the previous theorem still holds for a fine cover $\mathcal { F }$ of closed, not necessarily star-shaped, sets satisfying the inclusion property (1.89). The proof follows closely that of the previous theorem. We note first that since E is open, without loss of generality we may assume that ${ \overline { { B \left( x , \gamma r \right) } } } \subset E$ whenever $x \in E$ and there exists $F \in { \mathcal { F } }$ such that (1.89) holds. Applying the previous theorem to $E$ and to this cover $\left\{ { \overline { { B \left( x , \gamma r \right) } } } \right\}$ we may find a disjoint family $\left\{ { \overline { { B \left( x _ { i } , \gamma r _ { i } \right) } } } \right\}$ such that 

1.2 Covering Theorems and Diferentiation of Measures in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

$$
\left| E \setminus \bigcup_ {i} \overline {{B \left(x _ {i} , \gamma r _ {i}\right)}} \right| = 0.
$$

Choose $m _ { 1 }$ large enough that 

$$
\left| E \setminus \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {m _ {1}} \overline {{B (x _ {i} , \gamma r _ {i})}} \right| \leq \frac {1}{2} | E |.
$$

Then 

$$
\left| \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {m _ {1}} \overline {{B \left(x _ {i} , \gamma r _ {i}\right)}} \right| \geq \frac {1}{2} | E |.
$$

It follows that 

$$
\left| E \setminus \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {m _ {1}} \overline {{B (x _ {i} , r _ {i})}} \right| = | E | - \frac {1}{\gamma^ {N}} \left| \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {m _ {1}} \overline {{B (x _ {i} , \gamma r _ {i})}} \right| \leq \left(1 - \frac {1}{2 \gamma^ {N}}\right) | E |,
$$

and so 

$$
\left| E \setminus \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {m _ {1}} F _ {i} \right| \leq \left(1 - \frac {1}{2 \gamma^ {N}}\right) | E |.
$$

Reasoning as in the previous theorem, for every $k \in \mathbb N$ we may find a finite collection of disjoint sets contained in $E$ such that 

$$
\left| E \setminus \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {m _ {k}} F _ {i} \right| \leq \left(1 - \frac {1}{2 \gamma^ {N}}\right) ^ {k} | E |.
$$

It now sufices to let $k  \infty$ . Note that a similar argument holds, more generally, for Radon measures $\mu : { \mathcal { B } } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ with the doubling property, that is, such that 

$$
\mu (B (x, 2 r)) \leq c \mu (B (x, r))
$$

for all $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and $r > 0$ , and for some $c > 0$ (ii) As a simple application of (i), given any open set $\mathcal { Q } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , a bounded open set $A$ containing the origin with $| \partial A | = 0$ , and $\delta > 0$ , it is possible to find a countable family $\{ x _ { i } + r _ { i } A \}$ of mutually disjoint subsets of $\varOmega .$ with $0 < r _ { i } < \delta$ , such that 

$$
\left| \Omega \setminus \bigcup_ {i} (x _ {i} + r _ {i} A) \right| = 0.\tag{1.111}
$$

Indeed, it sufices to set 

$$
\mathcal {F} := \left\{\overline {{(x + r A)}}: x \in \Omega , 0 <   r <   \min \left\{r _ {x}, \delta \right\} \right\},
$$

where $r _ { x } > 0$ is such that $B \left( x , r _ { x } \gamma R \right) \subset \Omega$ and 

$$
B (0, R) \subset A \subset B (0, \gamma R),
$$

for some $R > 0$ and $\gamma \geq 1$ . This property will be used in the study of quasiconvexity in [FoLe10]. Note that the fact that $| \partial A | = 0$ has been used to replace closed sets with open ones in (1.111). 

By taking as Morse covers the families of cubes or balls as in Example 1.143, we obtain the following immediate corollaries. 

Corollary 1.149. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and let $\mathcal { F }$ be a family of closed cubes satisfying the property that for all $x \in E$ and for all $\delta > 0$ there exists $\overline { { Q \left( z , r \right) } } \in \mathcal { F }$ such that $0 ~ < ~ r ~ \leq ~ \delta$ and $x \in Q \left( z , \frac { r } { 2 } \right)$ . Let $\mu ^ { * } : \mathcal { P } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right]$ be a Radon outer measure. Then there exists a countable family $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 } \subset \mathcal { F }$ of closed cubes with pairwise disjoint interior such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(E \setminus \bigcup_ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {0}} F\right) = 0.
$$

Proof. We observe that $\mathcal { F }$ is a fine Morse cover, and therefore we may apply the Morse covering theorem. 

Theorem 1.150 (Vitali–Besicovitch covering theorem). Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and let $\mathcal { F }$ be a family of closed balls such that each point of E is the center of arbitrarily small balls, that is, 

$$
\inf \left\{r: \overline {{B (x , r)}} \in \mathcal {F} \right\} = 0 \text {   for   every   } x \in E.
$$

Let $\mu ^ { * } : \mathcal { P } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right]$ be a Radon outer measure. Then there exists a countable family ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { 0 } ~ \subset ~ { \mathcal { F } }$ of closed balls with pairwise disjoint interior such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(E \setminus \bigcup_ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {0}} F\right) = 0.
$$

Remark 1.151. In general, one cannot replace closed balls with open ones. This is possible, however, if we assume that for each $x \in E$ and for each $\delta > 0$ the number of closed balls in $\mathcal { F }$ centered at x and with radius less than $\delta$ is uncountable. This is a consequence of Proposition 1.15. 

Remark 1.152. Given $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and $\gamma \geq 1$ , let $F \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be an open γ-Morse set associated with x, and let $r > 0$ be such that 

$$
\overline {{B (x , r)}} \subset F \subset \overline {{B (x , \gamma r)}}
$$

and $F$ is star-shaped with respect to $B \left( x , r \right)$ . If $\mu ^ { * } : \mathcal { P } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a Radon outer measure and $\mu ^ { \ast } \left( F \right) < \infty$ , then reasoning as in Remark 1.141, it is possible to construct an increasing uncountable family $\{ { F } _ { t } \} _ { t > 0 }$ of closed γ-Morse sets associated with x such that $\mu ^ { * } \left( \partial F _ { t } \right) = 0$ , 

$$
\overline {{B (x , r)}} \subset F _ {t} \subset \overline {{B (x , \gamma r)}},
$$

and 

$$
\bigcup_ {t > 0} F _ {t} = F.
$$

## 1.2.2 Diferentiation Between Radon Measures in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$

As it will be explained in Chapter 5, when we study lower semicontinuity and relaxation properties of integral functionals, the blowup method allows us to reduce the problem to the characterization of the Radon–Nikodym derivative $\textstyle { \frac { d \nu } { d \mu } }$ , where $\mu$ is the underlying measure of integration (usually the Lebesgue measure), and ν is a measure generated by a sequence of admissible fields. This is the subject of this subsection. 

Theorem 1.153 (Besicovitch derivation theorem). Let 

$$
\mu , \nu : \mathfrak {M} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {N}\right) \to [ 0, \infty ]
$$

be Radon measures. Then there exists a Borel set $M \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , with $\mu \left( M \right) = 0$ , such that for any $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus M$ , 

$$
\frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) = \lim _ {r \rightarrow 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\nu (x + r C)}{\mu (x + r C)} \in \mathbb {R}\tag{1.112}
$$

and 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\nu_ {s} (x + r C)}{\mu (x + r C)} = 0,
$$

where 

$$
\nu = \nu_ {a c} + \nu_ {s}, \quad \nu_ {a c} \ll \mu , \quad \nu_ {s} \perp \mu ,\tag{1.113}
$$

and $C$ is any bounded, convex closed set containing the origin in its interior. 

Note that (1.113) holds in view of the Lebesgue decomposition theorem, since every Radon measure in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is σ-finite. 

Proof. Let 

$$
M _ {1} := \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \mu (B (x, r)) = 0 \text {   for   some   } r > 0 \right\}.
$$

Note that the set $M _ { 1 }$ is open. Using the density of the rationals in the reals it is possible to cover $M _ { 1 }$ with countably many balls of measure zero. Therefore $\mu \left( M _ { 1 } \right) = 0$ . Moreover, since $\nu _ { s } \perp \mu$ there exist two disjoint sets $E _ { \nu _ { s } } , E _ { \mu } \in \mathfrak { M }$ such that $\mathbb { R } ^ { N } = E _ { \nu _ { s } } \cup E _ { \mu }$ and $\mu \left( E _ { \nu _ { s } } \right) = \nu _ { s } \left( E _ { \mu } \right) = 0$ . It sufices to prove (1.112) for $\mu \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus ( M _ { 1 } \cup E _ { \nu _ { s } } )$ 

Fix $\gamma \geq 1$ and for any $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \backslash ( M _ { 1 } \cup E _ { \nu _ { s } } )$ and $r > 0$ let $\mathcal { F } _ { x , r }$ be the family of all closed sets $F \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ such that 

$$
\overline {{B (x , r)}} \subset F \subset \overline {{B (x , \gamma r)}}\tag{1.114}
$$

and $F$ is star-shaped with respect to $\overline { { B \left( x , r \right) } }$ and define 

$$
u _ {\gamma} ^ {-} \left(x\right) := \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \inf _ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {x, r}} \frac {\nu \left(F\right)}{\mu \left(F\right)}, \quad u _ {\gamma} ^ {+} \left(x\right) := \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \sup _ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {x, r}} \frac {\nu \left(F\right)}{\mu \left(F\right)}.\tag{1.115}
$$

Then $u _ { \gamma } ^ { - } \leq u _ { \gamma } ^ { + }$ . We claim that 

$$
u _ {\gamma} ^ {-} = u _ {\gamma} ^ {+} = \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu}\tag{1.116}
$$

$\mu$ a.e. in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N } \backslash ( M _ { 1 } \cup E _ { \nu _ { s } } )$ . Given $t > 0$ , let $E _ { t }$ be a bounded subset of 

$$
\left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus (M _ {1} \cup E _ {\nu_ {s}}): \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) <   t <   u _ {\gamma} ^ {+} (x) \right\}.
$$

Extend $\mu$ and $\nu$ as Radon outer measures $\mu ^ { * }$ and $\nu ^ { * }$ , respectively (see Proposition 1.63), and let A be any open set that contains $E _ { t }$ . Set 

$$
\mathcal {F} := \left\{F \in \mathcal {F} _ {x, r}: x \in E _ {t}, \overline {{B (x , \gamma r)}} \subset A, t \mu (F) <   \nu (F) \right\}.
$$

We claim that $\mathcal { F }$ is $\mathrm { a }$ fine Morse cover for $E _ { t }$ . Indeed, if $x \in E _ { t }$ , then, since $u _ { \gamma } ^ { + } \left( x \right) > t$ , we may find a sequence $r _ { n } \to 0 ^ { + }$ such that 

$$
\sup _ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {x, r _ {n}}} \frac {\nu (F)}{\mu (F)} > t,
$$

and in turn, there exists a sequence of sets $F _ { n } \in \mathcal { F } _ { x , r _ { n } }$ such that $t \mu \left( F _ { n } \right) <$ $\nu \left( F _ { n } \right)$ . It follows from (1.114) that diam $F _ { n } \to 0$ as $r _ { n } \to 0 ^ { + }$ , and so we can assume that $\overline { { B \left( x , \gamma r _ { n } \right) } } \subset A$ for all n. Thus (1.90) holds, and so $\mathcal { F }$ is a fine Morse cover for $E _ { t }$ 

By the Morse measure covering theorem there exists a countable family $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 } \subset \mathcal { F }$ of pairwise disjoint subsets such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(E _ {t} \setminus \bigcup_ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {0}} F\right) = 0.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of $\mathcal { F }$ , 

$$
t \mu^ {*} (E _ {t}) \leq \sum_ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {0}} t \mu (F) \leq \sum_ {F \in \mathcal {F} _ {0}} \nu (F) \leq \nu (A).
$$

By the outer regularity of $\nu ^ { * }$ it follows that $t \mu ^ { * } \left( E _ { t } \right) \leq \nu ^ { * } \left( E _ { t } \right)$ . We claim that this implies that $\mu ^ { * } \left( E _ { t } \right) = 0$ . Indeed, if this is not the case then let $G _ { t } \supset E _ { t }$ be a Borel set such that (see Proposition 1.63 and Remark 1.51) 

1.2 Covering Theorems and Diferentiation of Measures in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

$$
0 <   \mu^ {*} (E _ {t}) = \mu (G _ {t}) <   \infty .
$$

Since $\frac { d \nu _ { a c } } { d \mu }$ is a measurable function, without loss of generality we may assume that 

$$
E _ {t} \subset G _ {t} \subset \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus (M _ {1} \cup E _ {\nu_ {s}}): \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) <   t \right\}.
$$

Hence, using (1.113) and the fact that $\nu _ { s } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \backslash E _ { \nu _ { s } } \right) = 0$ , we have 

$$
\nu^ {*} (E _ {t}) \leq \nu (G _ {t}) = \int_ {G _ {t}} \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} d \mu <   t \mu (G _ {t}) = t \mu^ {*} (E _ {t}) \leq \nu^ {*} (E _ {t}),
$$

which is a contradiction. Therefore $\mu ^ { * } \left( E _ { t } \right) = \mu \left( G _ { t } \right) = 0$ . Since 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus (M _ {1} \cup E _ {\nu_ {s}}): \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) <   u _ {\gamma} ^ {+} (x) \right\} \\ = \bigcup_ {t \in \mathbb {Q}} \bigcup_ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{x \in B (0, n) \setminus (M _ {1} \cup E _ {\nu_ {s}}): \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) <   t <   u _ {\gamma} ^ {+} (x) \right\}, \end{array}
$$

using the subadditivity of $\mu ^ { * }$ , we conclude that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus (M _ {1} \cup E _ {\nu_ {s}}): \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) <   u _ {\gamma} ^ {+} (x) \right\}\right) = 0.
$$

Similarly, one can show that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus (M _ {1} \cup E _ {\nu_ {s}}): \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) > u _ {\gamma} ^ {-} (x) \right\}\right) = 0.
$$

In view of Proposition 1.63 there exists a Borel set $B _ { \gamma }$ such that 

$$
B _ {\gamma} \supset \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} <   u _ {\gamma} ^ {+} \text {or} \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} > u _ {\gamma} ^ {-} \right\} \cup M _ {1} \cup E _ {\nu_ {s}}
$$

and $\mu \left( B _ { \gamma } \right) = 0$ . Then for all $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus B _ { \gamma }$ we have 

$$
\frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) \leq u _ {\gamma} ^ {-} (x) \leq u _ {\gamma} ^ {+} (x) \leq \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x),
$$

which proves (1.116). 

Next we observe that for any compact set $K$ , 

$$
\infty > \nu (K) \geq \nu_ {a c} (K) = \int_ {K} \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} d \mu ,
$$

and so $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { d \nu _ { a c } } { d \mu } \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } , \mu \right) } \end{array}$ . In particular, $\frac { d \nu _ { a c } } { d \mu } \left( x \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ for $\mu \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ Hence, without loss of generality, we may assume that the set $B _ { \gamma }$ also contains the set 

$$
\left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \left| \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) \right| = \infty \right\}.
$$

Choose a sequence $\gamma _ { k } \nearrow \infty$ and let 

$$
M := \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} B _ {\gamma_ {k}}.
$$

If C is any bounded, convex closed set containing the origin in its interior, choose k so large that 

$$
\overline {{B \left(0 , 1 / \gamma_ {k}\right)}} \subset C \subset \overline {{B \left(x , \gamma_ {k}\right)}}.
$$

By (1.115) and (1.116), for all $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus M$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) = u _ {\gamma_ {k}} ^ {-} (x) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\nu (x + r C)}{\mu (x + r C)} \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\nu (x + r C)}{\mu (x + r C)} \leq u _ {\gamma_ {k}} ^ {+} (x) = \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x), \end{array}
$$

and so (1.112) is satisfied. 

Applying (1.112) also to $\nu _ { a c }$ , we obtain that for $\mu \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , 

$$
\frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) = \lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\nu_ {a c} (x + r C)}{\mu (x + r C)} = \lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\nu (x + r C)}{\mu (x + r C)} \in \mathbb {R},
$$

which yields 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\nu_ {s} (x + r C)}{\mu (x + r C)} = 0.
$$

This concludes the proof. 

Remark 1.154. (i) The set M is independent of the choice of C. Moreover, it follows from the proof that a much stronger statement holds, namely if $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \backslash M$ , then for any sequence $r _ { n } \to 0 ^ { + }$ and for every family of closed sets $F _ { n } \overset { \cdot } { \subset } \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ such that 

$$
\overline {{B (x , r _ {n})}} \subset F _ {n} \subset \overline {{B (x , \gamma r _ {n})}}
$$

and $F _ { n }$ is star-shaped with respect to $\overline { { B \left( x , r _ { n } \right) } }$ we have that 

$$
\frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {\nu (F _ {n})}{\mu (F _ {n})}.
$$

(ii) The Besicovitch derivation theorem holds also for bounded, convex open sets C containing the origin. Indeed, it sufices to replace $\mathcal { F } _ { x , r }$ with the family $\mathcal { G } _ { x , r }$ of all open sets $D \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ such that 

$$
B (x, r) \subset D \subset B (x, \gamma r)
$$

and $D$ is star-shaped with respect to $B \left( x , r \right)$ . By Remark 1.152, for any open set $D \in { \mathcal { G } } _ { x , r }$ such that $t \mu \left( D \right) < \nu \left( D \right)$ one can find a closed set $F \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { x , r }$ such that $F \subset D$ and $t \mu \left( F \right) < \nu \left( F \right)$ . Hence $\mathcal { F }$ is still a fine Morse cover for $E _ { t }$ 

It is possible to obtain the following local version of the Besicovitch derivation theorem. 

Theorem 1.155. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Borel set and let µ, $\nu : B ( E )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be two Radon measures. Then 

$$
\nu = \nu_ {a c} + \nu_ {s}, \quad \nu_ {a c} \ll \mu , \quad \nu_ {s} \perp \mu ,
$$

and there exists $M \in { \mathfrak { B } } ( E )$ , with $\mu \left( M \right) = 0$ , such that for any $x \in E \setminus M$ 2 

$$
\frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x) = \lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\nu ((x + r C) \cap E)}{\mu ((x + r C) \cap E)} \in \mathbb {R}\tag{1.117}
$$

and 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\nu_ {s} ((x + r C) \cap E)}{\mu ((x + r C) \cap E)} = 0,\tag{1.118}
$$

where C is any bounded, convex closed set containing the origin in its interior. 

Proof. Consider the extensions $\overline { { \mu } } , \overline { { \nu } } :  { B } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right]$ defined by $\overline { { \mu } } \left( F \right) : =$ $\mu \left( F \cap E \right)$ and $\overline { { \nu } } \left( F \right) : = \nu \left( F \cap E \right)$ for every $F \in \mathcal { B } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . Note that $\overline { { \mu } } , \ : \overline { { \nu } }$ are well-defined, since by Remark 1.3, 

$$
\left\{F \cap E: F \in \mathcal {B} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {N}\right) \right\} = \mathcal {B} (E).
$$

Moreover, if $K \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is compact then $K \cap E$ is a compact set of E for the induced topology, and so $\overline { { \mu } } \left( K \right)$ and $\overline { { \nu } } \left( K \right)$ are finite. By Proposition 1.60 we deduce that $\overline { { \mu } }$ and $\bar { \nu }$ are Radon measures. 

Applying the Besicovitch derivation theorem to the extensions, we have 

$$
\frac {d \overline {{\nu}} _ {a c}}{d \overline {{\mu}}} (x) = \lim _ {r \rightarrow 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\overline {{\nu}} (x + r C)}{\overline {{\mu}} (x + r C)} = \lim _ {r \rightarrow 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\nu ((x + r C) \cap E)}{\mu ((x + r C) \cap E)}
$$

for all $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus M _ { 0 }$ and for some Borel set $M _ { 0 }$ with $\overline { { \mu } } \left( M _ { 0 } \right) = 0$ . Setting $M : = M _ { 0 } \cap E$ , by (1.1) we have $M \in \mathcal { B } \left( E \right)$ 

In view of the Lebesgue and Radon–Nikodym theorems we may write 

$$
\overline {{\nu}} = \overline {{\nu}} _ {a c} + \overline {{\nu}} _ {s},
$$

where $\overline { { \nu } } _ { a c } , \overline { { \nu } } _ { s } : \mathcal { B } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right]$ , with $\overline { { \nu } } _ { a c } \ll \overline { { \mu } } , \overline { { \nu } } _ { s } \perp \overline { { \mu } }$ , and similarly 

$$
\nu = \nu_ {a c} + \nu_ {s},
$$

where $\nu _ { a c } , \nu _ { s } : \mathcal { B } \left( E \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right]$ , with $\nu _ { a c } \ll \mu , \nu _ { s } \perp \mu$ 

Since $\overline { { \nu } } _ { s } \lfloor E : \mathcal { B } ( E ) \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ and $\mu$ are mutually singular, and $\overline { { \nu } } _ { a c } \vert E$ $B ( E )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu ,$ , due to the uniqueness of the decomposition we conclude that $\overline { { \nu } } _ { s } \lfloor E = \nu _ { s }$ and $\overline { { \nu } } _ { a c } \lfloor E = \nu _ { a c }$ on $B \left( E \right)$ . In particular, 

$$
\nu_ {a c} (F) = \int_ {F} \frac {d (\overline {{\nu}} _ {a c}) \lfloor E}{d \overline {{\mu}}} d \mu = \int_ {F} \frac {d \overline {{\nu}} _ {a c}}{d \overline {{\mu}}} d \mu
$$

for every $F \in B \left( E \right)$ , and so $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { d \nu _ { a c } } { d \mu } \left( x \right) = \frac { d \overline { { \nu } } _ { a c } } { d \overline { { \mu } } } \left( x \right) } \end{array}$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in E$ 

Equality (1.112) motivates the following definition: 

Definition 1.156. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and let $\mu , \nu : \mathcal { B } ( E ) \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be two Radon measures. We define the Radon–Nikodym derivative of µ with respect to ν as 

$$
\frac {d \nu}{d \mu} (x) = \lim _ {r \rightarrow 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\nu ((x + r C) \cap E)}{\mu ((x + r C) \cap E)}
$$

whenever the limit exists, is finite, and is independent of the choice of the bounded, convex closed set containing the origin in its interior C. 

Remark 1.157. In view of Theorem 1.155, if $\nu \ll \mu$ , then the notion introduced in the previous definition coincides µ a.e. with the Radon–Nikodym derivative of $\mu$ with respect to ν as in the Radon–Nikodym theorem. 

Also, by (1.117) and (1.118), $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { d \nu } { d \mu } \left( x \right) , \frac { d \nu _ { a c } } { d \mu } \left( x \right) , \frac { d \nu _ { s } } { d \mu } \left( x \right) } \end{array}$ exist and 

$$
\frac {d \nu}{d \mu} (x) = \frac {d \nu_ {a c}}{d \mu} (x), \quad \frac {d \nu_ {s}}{d \mu} (x) = 0
$$

for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in E$ . In particular, 

$$
\nu = \frac {d \nu}{d \mu} \mu + \nu_ {s}.
$$

The next theorem leads to the definition of Lebesgue points, which are a central concept for the study of $L ^ { p }$ spaces in the next chapter. 

Theorem 1.158 (Lebesgue diferentiation theorem). Let 

$$
\mu : \mathfrak {M} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N}) \to [ 0, \infty ]
$$

be a Radon measure, and let $u : \mathbb { R } ^ { N }  \lceil - \infty , \infty \rceil$ be a locally integrable function. Then there exists a Borel set $M \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , with $\mu \left( M \right) = 0$ , such that 

$$
\mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus M \subset \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: u (x) \in \mathbb {R} \right\}
$$

and for any $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus M$ 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\mu (B (x , r))} \int_ {B (x, r)} u (y) d \mu (y) = u (x).
$$

Proof. Define 

$$
\nu (E) := \int_ {E} u ^ {+} d \mu , \quad E \in \mathfrak {M} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N}).
$$

Since u is locally integrable it follows that ν is a Radon measure absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu .$ . Since every Radon measure in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is σ-finite, we can apply the Radon–Nikodym theorem to conclude that 

$$
\frac {d \nu}{d \mu} (x) = u ^ {+} (x) \in \mathbb {R}
$$

for µ a.e. $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ . In turn, by the Besicovitch diferentiation theorem, 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\mu (B (x , r))} \int_ {B (x, r)} u ^ {+} (y) d \mu (y) = u ^ {+} (x) \in \mathbb {R}
$$

for $\mu \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , and similarly 

$$
\lim _ {r \rightarrow 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\mu (B (x , r))} \int_ {B (x, r)} u ^ {-} (y) d \mu (y) = u ^ {-} (x) \in \mathbb {R}
$$

for $\mu \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ . The conclusion now follows. 

By enlarging the “bad” set M we can strengthen the conclusion of the previous theorem. 

Corollary 1.159. Let $\mu : \mathfrak { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \ \to \ [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Radon measure and let $u : \mathbb { R } ^ { N }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a locally integrable function. Then there exists a Borel set $M \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , with $\mu \left( M \right) = 0$ , such that 

$$
\mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus M \subset \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: u (x) \in \mathbb {R} \right\},
$$

and for any $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus M$ 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\mu (B (x , r))} \int_ {B (x, r)} | u (y) - u (x) | d \mu (y) = 0.\tag{1.119}
$$

Proof. Write $\mathbb { Q } ~ = ~ \{ r _ { n } \}$ . Applying the previous theorem to the function $v _ { n } \left( x \right) : = \left| u \left( x \right) - r _ { n } \right|$ , we may find a Borel set $M _ { n } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , with $\mu \left( M _ { n } \right) = 0$ , such that 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\mu (B (x , r))} \int_ {B (x, r)} | u (y) - r _ {n} | d \mu (y) = | u (x) - r _ {n} |\tag{1.120}
$$

for all $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus M _ { n }$ . Since u is locally integrable and $\mu$ is σ-finite, the mea surable set 

$$
M _ {0} := \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: | u (x) | = \infty \right\}
$$

has zero $\mu$ measure. Set 

$$
M := \bigcup_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} M _ {n}.
$$

If $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus M$ then for every $n \in \mathbb { N }$ • 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {r \to 0 ^ {+}} {\limsup} \frac {1}{\mu (B (x , r))} \int_ {B (x, r)} | u (y) - u (x) | d \mu (y) \\ = \underset {r \to 0 ^ {+}} {\limsup} \frac {1}{\mu (B (x , r))} \int_ {B (x, r)} | u (y) + r _ {n} - r _ {n} - u (x) | d \mu (y) \\ \leq \underset {r \to 0 ^ {+}} {\limsup} \frac {1}{\mu (B (x , r))} \int_ {B (x, r)} | u (y) - r _ {n} | d \mu (y) + | u (x) - r _ {n} | \\ = 2 | u (x) - r _ {n} |, \end{array}
$$

where we have used (1.120). Since $u \left( x \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ , it now sufices to select a subse quence of $\{ r _ { n } \}$ converging to $u \left( x \right)$ 

Remark 1.160. It actually follows from Remark 1.154 that if $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \backslash M$ , then for any sequence $r _ { n } \to 0 ^ { + }$ and for every family of closed sets $F _ { n } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ such that 

$$
\overline {{B (x , r _ {n})}} \subset F _ {n} \subset \overline {{B (x , \gamma r _ {n})}}
$$

and $F _ { n }$ is star-shaped with respect to $\overline { { B \left( x , r _ { n } \right) } }$ , we have that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\mu (F _ {n})} \int_ {F _ {n}} | u (y) - u (x) | d \mu (y) = 0.
$$

Moreover, if $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus M$ , then for any family of Borel subsets $\{ E _ { r } \} _ { r > 0 }$ such that $E _ { r } \subset B \left( x , r \right)$ and 

$$
\mu \left(E _ {r}\right) > \alpha \mu \left(B (x, r)\right)
$$

for some constant $\alpha > 0$ independent of $r > 0$ , we have that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {r \to 0 ^ {+}} {\limsup} \frac {1}{\mu (E _ {r})} \int_ {E _ {r}} | u (y) - u (x) | d y \\ \qquad \leq \underset {r \to 0 ^ {+}} {\limsup} \frac {1}{\mu (E _ {r})} \int_ {B (x, r)} | u (y) - u (x) | d y \\ \qquad \leq \frac {1}{\alpha} \underset {r \to 0 ^ {+}} {\lim} \frac {1}{\mu (B (x , r))} \int_ {B (x, r)} | u (y) - u (x) | d \mu (y) = 0. \end{array}
$$

Note that the sets $E _ { r }$ need not contain x. 

Any point $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ for which (1.119) holds is called a Lebesgue point of u. Given a Radon measure $\mu : \mathfrak { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right]$ and a measurable set $E \subset$ $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , by applying the Lebesgue diferentiation theorem to $\chi _ { E }$ we obtain that 

$$
\lim _ {r \rightarrow 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\mu (B (x , r) \cap E)}{\mu (B (x , r))} = \chi_ {E} (x)
$$

for $\mu$ a.e. $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ . A point $x \in E$ for which the previous limit is one is called a point of density one for E. More generally, for any $t \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ a point $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\mu (B (x , r) \cap E)}{\mu (B (x , r))} = t
$$

is called a point of density t for E. 

Remark 1.161. If $\mu : \mathfrak { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right]$ is a Radon measure such that for $\mu$ a.e. $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , 

$$
\mu \left(\{x \}\right) = 0,\tag{1.121}
$$

then $\mu$ is nonatomic. In particular, the Lebesgue measure $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ is nonatomic. Indeed, if $E \in \mathfrak { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ has positive measure, then let $x _ { 0 }$ be a point of density one of E for which (1.121) holds. By Proposition $1 . 7 ( \mathrm { i } )$ , 

$$
\mu \left(B \left(x _ {0}, r\right)\right)\rightarrow \mu \left(\left\{x _ {0} \right\}\right) = 0
$$

as $r \to 0 ^ { + }$ , and so $\mu \left( B \left( x _ { 0 } , r \right) \right) < \mu \left( E \right)$ for all $r > 0$ suficiently small. On the other hand, by (1.121), taking $r > 0$ even smaller if necessary, we have 

$$
0 <   \frac {1}{2} \mu (B (x _ {0}, r)) \leq \mu (B (x _ {0}, r) \cap E) \leq \mu (B (x _ {0}, r)),
$$

where we have used the fact that $x _ { 0 }$ is a point of density one of E. Hence for all $r > 0$ suficiently small the set $F : = B \left( x _ { 0 } , r \right) \cap E$ satisfies the condition 

$$
0 <   \mu (F) <   \mu (E).
$$

For measurable functions that are not necessarily integrable, the analogous concept of Lebesgue points is given by points of approximate continuity. 

Definition 1.162. Let $\mu : \mathfrak { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \ \to \ [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Radon measure, and let $u : \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a measurable function. The function u is said to be approximately continuous at $\boldsymbol { x } _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ if 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\mu (B (x _ {0} , r) \cap u ^ {- 1} (A))}{\mu (B (x _ {0} , r))} = 1\tag{1.122}
$$

for every open set A in the extended real line $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ that contains $u \left( x _ { 0 } \right)$ The point $x _ { 0 }$ is called a point of approximate continuity for u. 

Note that if $u \left( x _ { 0 } \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ then (1.122) is equivalent to requiring that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ , 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\mu \left(B \left(x _ {0} , r\right) \cap \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N} : | u (x) - u (x _ {0}) | \geq \varepsilon \right\}\right)}{\mu \left(B \left(x _ {0} , r\right)\right)} = 0.
$$

We now study the relation between Lebesgue points and points of approximate continuity. 

Proposition 1.163. Let $\mu : \mathfrak { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \ \to \ [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Radon measure, and let $u : \mathbb { R } ^ { N }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a locally integrable function. If $x _ { 0 } ~ \in ~ \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is a Lebesgue point for u, then u is approximately continuous at x . Conversely, $i f u : \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \xrightarrow { } \mathbb { R }$ is bounded on compact sets, measurable, and is approximately continuous at $x _ { 0 }$ , then $x _ { 0 }$ is a Lebesgue point for u. 

Proof. Assume that $\boldsymbol { x } _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is a Lebesgue point for u. Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mu \left(\left\{x \in B \left(x _ {0} , r\right) : | u (x) - u (x _ {0}) | \geq \varepsilon \right\}\right)}{\mu \left(B \left(x _ {0} , r\right)\right)} \\ \leq \frac {1}{\varepsilon} \frac {1}{\mu \left(B \left(x _ {0} , r\right)\right)} \int_ {B (x _ {0}, r)} | u (x) - u (x _ {0}) | d \mu \to 0 \end{array}
$$

as $r \to 0 ^ { + }$ . Hence u is approximately continuous at $x _ { 0 }$ . 

Conversely assume that u : $\mathbb { R } ^ { N } \to \mathbb { R }$ is locally bounded and is approxi mately continuous at $x _ { 0 }$ . Then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{\mu (B (x _ {0} , r))} \int_ {B (x _ {0}, r)} | u (x) - u (x _ {0}) | d \mu \\ \qquad \leq \frac {1}{\mu (B (x _ {0} , r))} \int_ {B (x _ {0}, r) \cap \{| u (y) - u (x _ {0}) | \geq \varepsilon \}} | u (x) - u (x _ {0}) | d \mu \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{\mu (B (x _ {0} , r))} \int_ {B (x _ {0}, r) \cap \{| u (y) - u (x _ {0}) | \leq \varepsilon \}} | u (x) - u (x _ {0}) | d \mu \\ \qquad \leq 2 \left(\sup _ {B (x _ {0}, 1)} | u |\right) \frac {\mu (\{x \in B (x _ {0} , r) : | u (x) - u (x _ {0}) | \geq \varepsilon \})}{\mu (B (x _ {0} , r))} + \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Letting $r \to 0 ^ { + }$ we have 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\mu \left(B \left(x _ {0} , r\right)\right)} \int_ {B (x _ {0}, r)} \left| u \left(x\right) - u \left(x _ {0}\right) \right| d \mu \leq \varepsilon ,
$$

which, in view of the arbitrariness of $\varepsilon > 0$ , shows that $x _ { 0 }$ is a Lebesgue point for $u .$ . 

Exercise 1.164. The converse of the previous proposition does not hold in general without the assumption of local boundedness of u. Indeed, let $\mu$ be the Lebesgue measure $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 }$ and consider the function 

$$
u (x) := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} 2 ^ {n} \chi_ {\left(\frac {1}{2 ^ {n}}, \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}} \left(1 + \frac {1}{n ^ {2}}\right)\right)} (x), \quad x \in \mathbb {R}.
$$

Prove that u is integrable, approximately continuous at $x = 0$ , but 0 is not a Lebesgue point for u. 

Using Lusin’s theorem it is possible to give the following characterization of approximate continuity. 

Theorem 1.165. Let $\mu : \mathfrak { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right]$ be a Radon measure. A function $u : \mathbb { R } ^ { N }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is measurable in the sense of Definition 1.72 if and only $i f u$ is approximately continuous at µ a.e. $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

## 1.3 Spaces of Measures

In this section we introduce the notion of signed measures and we study severa spaces of signed measures that arise as duals of various spaces of bounded and continuous functions. 

## 1.3.1 Signed Measures

Definition 1.166. Let (X, M) be a measurable space. A signed measure is a function $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ such that 

(i) $\lambda \left( \varnothing \right) = 0 ;$ 

(ii) λ takes at most one of the two values ∞ and $- \infty$ , that is, either $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to$ $( - \infty , \infty ] \ o r \ \lambda : \mathfrak { M } \to [ - \infty , \infty )$ ; 

(iii) for every countable collection $\{ E _ { i } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ of pairwise disjoint sets we have 

$$
\lambda \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \lambda \left(E _ {n}\right).
$$

Remark 1.167. We call the attention to the fact that in this text signed measures are not necessarily finite, as is often considered in the literature. Indeed, the way to read (iii) is that whenever $\{ E _ { i } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ is a countable collection of pairwise disjoint sets, then the sequence of partial sums $\left\{ \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { l } \lambda \left( E _ { n } \right) \right\} _ { l }$ is convergent in $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ to $\textstyle \lambda ( \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } )$ 

The following result is the analogue of Proposition 1.9 for signed measures. 

Proposition 1.168. Let (X, M) be a measurable space. A set function $\lambda :$ ${ \mathfrak { M } } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is a signed measure if and only it satisfies (ii) of Definition 1.166, is finitely additive, and for every increasing sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ , 

$$
\lambda \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \lambda \left(E _ {n}\right).\tag{1.123}
$$

Proof. One implication follows from the previous remark and (iii). Suppose now that λ is finitely additive and that (1.123) holds. Let $\{ F _ { n } \} \subset$ M be a sequence of mutually disjoint measurable sets, and define 

$$
E _ {n} := \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {n} F _ {k}.
$$

Then by (1.123) we have 

$$
\lambda \left(\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {k}\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \lambda \left(E _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \lambda \left(F _ {k}\right) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \lambda \left(F _ {k}\right),
$$

and with this we have shown that λ is a signed measure. 

As we will see below, in order to study signed measures it is convenient to write them as diferences of (positive) measures. 

Definition 1.169. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to$ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a signed measure. A set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ is said to be positive (respectively negative) $i f \lambda ( F ) \geq 0$ (respectively $\lambda \left( F \right) \leq 0 )$ for all $F \subset E$ with $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

Note that we may have sets with positive measure that are not positive. 

Example 1.170. Let $X = \mathbb { R }$ , and let $u : \mathbb { R }  \mathbb { R }$ be an odd function, integrable with respect to the Lebesgue measure, and such that $u \left( x \right) > 0$ for $x > 0$ Then 

$$
\lambda (E) := \int_ {E} u (x) d x, \quad E \in \mathcal {B} (\mathbb {R}),
$$

is a signed measure and any set of the form $[ - a , b ] , 0 < a < b .$ , has positive λ measure without being a positive set. 

However, it is possible to prove the following result. 

Proposition 1.171. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\lambda : \mathfrak { M } \to$ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a signed measure. Let $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ be such that $0 < \lambda ( E ) < \infty$ . Then there exists a positive measurable subset $F \subset E$ with $\lambda \left( F \right) > 0$ 

Proof. Step 1: We begin by showing that if $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ is such that $| \lambda \left( E \right) | < \infty$ then for any $F \subset E$ , with $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , we have $| \lambda ( F ) | < \infty$ . Without loss of generality we may assume that $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ - \infty , \infty )$ (the case $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to ( - \infty , \infty ]$ being analogous). Let $F \subset E$ , with $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . If $\lambda \left( F \right) \geq 0$ then there is nothing to prove. Thus assume that $\lambda \left( F \right) < 0$ . Then 

$$
0 <   - \lambda (F) = \lambda (E \setminus F) - \lambda (E) <   \infty ,
$$

where we have used that facts that $| \lambda \left( E \right) | < \infty$ and that $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ - \infty , \infty )$ Step 2: Let $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ be such that $0 < \lambda ( E ) < \infty$ . By the previous step, $\lambda : \mathfrak { M } \lfloor E  \mathbb { R }$ is finite. For every $F \in { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor E$ define 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lambda_ {+} (F) := \sup \left\{\lambda \left(F ^ {\prime}\right): F ^ {\prime} \subset F, F ^ {\prime} \in \mathfrak {M} \right\}, \\ \lambda_ {-} (F) := - \inf \left\{\lambda \left(F ^ {\prime}\right): F ^ {\prime} \subset F, F ^ {\prime} \in \mathfrak {M} \right\}. \end{array}\tag{1.124}
$$

Then, exactly as in the proof of Lemma 1.103 (with $\nu - \mu$ replaced by λ), we have that $\lambda _ { + } : { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor E \to [ 0 , \infty )$ and $\lambda _ { - } : { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor E \to [ 0 , \infty )$ are finite measures, and for every $F \in { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor E$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lambda_ {+} \left(F\right) = \sup \left\{\lambda \left(F ^ {\prime}\right): F ^ {\prime} \subset F, F ^ {\prime} \in \mathfrak {M}, \lambda_ {-} \left(F ^ {\prime}\right) = 0 \right\} \\ = \sup \left\{\lambda \left(F ^ {\prime}\right): F ^ {\prime} \subset F, F ^ {\prime} \in \mathfrak {M}, F ^ {\prime} \text {positive} \right\}. \end{array}\tag{1.125}
$$

Since $0 < \lambda ( E ) < \infty$ it follows that $\lambda _ { + } \left( E \right) > 0$ , and so we may find a positive measurable subset $F \subset E$ with $\lambda \left( F \right) > 0$ 

As a consequence of the previous proposition we have the following important theorem. 

Theorem 1.172 (Hahn decomposition theorem). Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\lambda : \mathfrak { M } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a signed measure. Then X can be decomposed as $X = X ^ { + } \cup X ^ { - }$ , where $X ^ { + }$ is positive and $X ^ { - }$ is negative. 

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ - \infty , \infty )$ (the case $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to ( - \infty , \infty ]$ being analogous). Let 

$$
\lambda_ {+} (X) = \sup \left\{\lambda (E): E \in \mathfrak {M}, E \text { positive } \right\}.
$$

Find a sequence of increasing positive sets $E _ { n } , E _ { n } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \lambda (E _ {n}) = \lambda_ {+} (X).
$$

Define 

$$
X ^ {+} := \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}.
$$

Then $X ^ { + }$ is positive and 

$$
\lambda \left(X ^ {+}\right) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \lambda \left(E _ {n}\right) = \lambda_ {+} (X).
$$

We claim that $X ^ { - } : = X \backslash X ^ { + }$ is negative. Indeed, if not, then there exists $F \subset X ^ { - } , F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , such that 

$$
0 <   \lambda (F) <   \infty .
$$

By the previous proposition there exists a positive measurable subset $F ^ { \prime } \subset F$ with $\lambda \left( F ^ { \prime } \right) > 0$ . But then 

$$
\lambda_ {+} (X) = \lambda (X ^ {+}) <   \lambda (X ^ {+}) + \lambda (X ^ {+}) = \lambda (X ^ {+} \cup F ^ {\prime}) <   \infty ,
$$

and since $X ^ { - } \cup F ^ { \prime }$ is admissible in the definition of $\lambda _ { + } \left( X \right)$ we arrive at a contradiction. 

Example 1.173. Note that the Hahn decomposition may not be unique. As an example let $X = [ - 1 , 1 ]$ , let ${ \mathfrak { M } } = B \left( [ - 1 , 1 ] \right)$ , and let 

$$
\lambda (E) := \int_ {E} x d x, \quad E \in \mathcal {B} ([ - 1, 1 ]).
$$

Then the pairs $( [ 0 , 1 ] , [ - 1 , 0 ) )$ and $( ( 0 , 1 ] , [ - 1 , 0 ] )$ are both Hahn decomposi tions of λ. 

Remark 1. $1 7 4 .$ In general, if $( X ^ { + } , X ^ { - } )$ and $\left( X _ { 1 } ^ { + } , X _ { 1 } ^ { - } \right)$ are Hahn decompositions of a signed measure $\lambda : \mathfrak { M } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ , then $\lambda \left( \dot { E } \right) = 0$ for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with 

$$
E \subset \left(X ^ {+} \Delta X _ {1} ^ {+}\right) \cup \left(X ^ {-} \Delta X _ {1} ^ {-}\right).
$$

Here $\varDelta$ stands for the symmetric diference between two sets, i.e., 

$$
F \Delta G := (F \setminus G) \cup (G \setminus F).
$$

Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\lambda : \mathfrak { M } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a signed measure. By the Hahn decomposition theorem we may uniquely (in the sense of Remark 1.174) decompose X as $X = X ^ { + } \cup X ^ { - }$ , where $X ^ { + }$ is positive and $X ^ { - }$ is negative. For $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ define 

$$
\lambda^ {+} (E) := \lambda (E \cap X ^ {+}), \quad \lambda^ {-} (E) := - \lambda (E \cap X ^ {-}).
$$

Then $\lambda ^ { + } , \lambda ^ { - } : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ are measures, with at least one of them finite, and by construction, they are mutually singular. Moreover, for any $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ we have 

$$
\lambda (E) = \lambda^ {+} (E) - \lambda^ {-} (E).\tag{1.126}
$$

The measures $\lambda ^ { + } , \lambda ^ { - }$ are called, respectively, the upper and lower variation of $\lambda ,$ , while the measure 

$$
\| \lambda \| := \lambda^ {+} + \lambda^ {-}
$$

is called the total variation of λ . Note that both $\lambda ^ { + } , \lambda ^ { - }$ are absolutely continuous with respect to $\| \lambda \|$ 

Remark 1.175. Note that for any $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lambda^ {+} (E) = \sup \left\{\lambda (F): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M}, F \text {positive} \right\} \\ = \sup \left\{\lambda (F): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M} \right\} \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lambda^ {-} (E) = - \inf \left\{\lambda (F): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M}, F \text { negative} \right\} \\ = - \inf \left\{\lambda (F): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M} \right\}. \end{array}
$$

To see this, assume, without loss of generality, that $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ - \infty , \infty )$ . Then, since $X ^ { + }$ is positive, it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lambda^ {+} (E) = \lambda \left(E \cap X ^ {+}\right) \\ \qquad = \sup \{\lambda (F): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M}, F \text {positive} \} \\ \qquad = \lambda_ {+} (E), \end{array}
$$

where $\lambda _ { + }$ has been defined in (1.124) and we have used (1.125) (which holds, since $\lambda$ does not take the value $\infty )$ . Similarly, since $X ^ { - }$ is negative, it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lambda^ {-} (E) = \lambda \left(E \cap X ^ {-}\right) \\ \qquad = - \inf \left\{\lambda (F): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M}, F \text {negative} \right\}. \end{array}
$$

I $: | \lambda ( E ) | < \infty$ then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lambda^ {-} (E) = \lambda^ {+} (E) - \lambda (E) = \lambda_ {-} (E) - \lambda (E) \\ \qquad = \sup \left\{\lambda (F) - \lambda (E): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M} \right\} \\ \qquad = \sup \left\{- \lambda (E \setminus F): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M} \right\} \\ \qquad = - \inf \left\{\lambda (G): G \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M} \right\}. \end{array}
$$

If $\lambda \left( E \right) = - \infty$ then, since $\lambda ^ { + } \left( E \right) < \infty$ , it follows that 

$$
\lambda^ {-} (E) = \lambda^ {+} (E) - \lambda (E) = \infty ,
$$

and so 

$$
\lambda^ {-} (E) = - \inf \left\{\lambda (F): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M} \right\} = - \lambda (F) = \infty .
$$

This completes the proof. 

Definition 1.176. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to$ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a signed measure. A set $E \in \mathfrak { M }$ has σ-finite measure λ if it has σ-finite measure $\| \lambda \| ; \lambda$ is said to be σ-finite if X has σ-finite measure λ. 

Proposition 1.177. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\lambda : \mathfrak { M } \to$ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a signed measure. Then for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ we have that 

$$
\| \lambda \| (E) = \sup \left\{\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} | \lambda (E _ {n}) |: \{E _ {n} \} \subset \mathfrak {M} \text { partition   of } E \right\}.
$$

It turns out that the decomposition (1.126) is unique. 

Theorem 1.178 (Jordan decomposition theorem). Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\lambda : \mathfrak { M } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a signed measure. Then there exists a unique pair $( \lambda ^ { + } , \lambda ^ { - } )$ of mutually singular (nonnegative) measures, one of which is finite, such that $\lambda = \lambda ^ { + } - \lambda ^ { - }$ 

Proof. It remains only to prove the uniqueness of the decomposition. We leave this as an exercise. 

In view of the previous theorem, given a measurable space (X, M), a signed measure $\lambda : \mathfrak { M } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ , a measurable function $u : X  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ , and a measurable set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , if at least one of the two integrals $\int _ { E } u d \lambda ^ { + }$ and $\int _ { E } u d \lambda ^ { - }$ is finite then we define the Lebesgue integral of u over the measurable set E as 

$$
\int_ {E} u d \lambda := \int_ {E} u d \lambda^ {+} - \int_ {E} u d \lambda^ {-}.
$$

If both $\textstyle \int _ { E } u d \lambda ^ { + }$ and $\int _ { E } u d \lambda ^ { - }$ are finite, then u is said to be Lebesgue integrable over the measurable set E. 

We now extend The Lebesgue decomposition theorem to signed measures. 

Definition 1.179. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\lambda , \varsigma : \mathfrak { M } \to$ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ be two signed measures. 

(i) λ, ς are said to be mutually singular, and we write $\lambda \perp \varsigma , i f \| \lambda \|$ and $\| \varsigma \|$ are mutually singular. 

(ii) λ is said to be absolutely continuous with respect to $\varsigma ,$ and we write $\lambda \ll \varsigma , \ i f \ \| \lambda \|$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\| \varsigma \|$ 

If (X, M) is a measurable space, $\lambda : \mathfrak { M } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is a signed measure, and $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a σ-finite (positive) measure, then by applying the Lebesgue decomposition theorem to $\lambda ^ { + }$ and $\mu$ (respectively to $\lambda ^ { - }$ and $\mu )$ we can write 

$$
\lambda^ {+} = \left(\lambda^ {+}\right) _ {a c} + \left(\lambda^ {+}\right) _ {s}, \quad \lambda^ {-} = \left(\lambda^ {-}\right) _ {a c} + \left(\lambda^ {-}\right) _ {s},
$$

where the measures $\left( \lambda ^ { + } \right) _ { a c }$ and $\left( \lambda ^ { + } \right) _ { s }$ are defined in (1.38) and (1.56), and $( \lambda ^ { + } ) _ { a c } , ( \lambda ^ { - } ) _ { a c } \ll \mu$ . Hence we can apply the Radon–Nikodym theorem to find two measurable functions $u ^ { + } , u ^ { - } : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\left(\lambda^ {+}\right) _ {a c} (E) = \int_ {E} u ^ {+} d \mu , \quad \left(\lambda^ {-}\right) _ {a c} (E) = \int_ {E} u ^ {-} d \mu
$$

for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . The functions $u ^ { + }$ and $u ^ { - }$ are unique up to a set of $\mu$ measure zero 

Since either $\lambda ^ { + }$ or $\lambda ^ { - }$ is finite we may define 

$$
\lambda_ {a c} := \left(\lambda^ {+}\right) _ {a c} - \left(\lambda^ {-}\right) _ {a c}, \quad \lambda_ {s} := \left(\lambda^ {+}\right) _ {s} - \left(\lambda^ {-}\right) _ {s}, \quad u := u ^ {+} - u ^ {-}.
$$

Then $\lambda _ { a c }$ is a signed measure with $\lambda _ { a c } \ll \mu$ . Note that if λ is positive then so are $\lambda _ { a c }$ and $\lambda _ { s }$ . 

By the Radon–Nikodym theorem, the Lebesgue decomposition theorem, and the Jordan decomposition theorem we have proved the following result. 

Theorem 1.180 (Lebesgue decomposition theorem). Let (X, M) be a measurable space, let $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a signed measure, and let $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to$ $[ 0 , \infty ]$ be a σ-finite (positive) measure. Then 

$$
\lambda = \lambda_ {a c} + \lambda_ {s}
$$

with $\lambda _ { a c } \ll \mu _ { : }$ , and 

$$
\lambda_ {a c} (E) = \int_ {E} u d \mu
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . Moreover, if λ is σ-finite then $\lambda _ { s } \perp \mu$ and the decomposition is unique, that is, if 

$$
\lambda = \overline {{\lambda}} _ {a c} + \overline {{\lambda}} _ {s},
$$

for some signed measures $\overline { { \lambda } } _ { a c } , \ \overline { { \lambda } } _ { s }$ , with $\overline { { \lambda } } _ { a c } \ll \mu$ and $\overline { { \lambda } } _ { s } \perp \boldsymbol { \mu }$ , then 

$$
\lambda_ {a c} = \overline {{\lambda}} _ {a c} a n d \lambda_ {s} = \overline {{\lambda}} _ {s}.
$$

We call $\lambda _ { a c }$ and $\lambda _ { s }$ , respectively, the absolutely continuous part and the singular part of λ with respect to $\mu _ { ; }$ , and often we write 

$$
u = \frac {d \lambda_ {a c}}{d \mu}.
$$

A particular case of the Lebesgue decomposition theorem is that in which $\mu = \| \boldsymbol { \lambda } \|$ , and here $\lambda = \lambda _ { a c } , \lambda _ { s } = 0$ 

Corollary 1.181. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to$ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a σ-finite signed measure. Then there exists a measurable function $u : X  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ such that $\left| u \left( x \right) \right| = 1$ for $\| \lambda \|$ a.e. $x \in X$ and 

$$
u = \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda \|}.
$$

The previous equation is called the polar decomposition of λ. 

Definition 1.182. Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to$ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a signed measure. If X is a topological space then λ is a signed Radon measure $i f \parallel \lambda \parallel : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a Radon measure. 

If X is a topological space then $\mathcal { M } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ is the space of all signed finite Radon measures $\lambda : B ( X ) $ R endowed with the total variation norm. It can be verified that M (X; R) is a Banach space. 

In applications we will also consider vector-valued measures. 

Definition 1.183. Let (X, M) be a measurable space. A set function $\lambda \ : =$ $\left( \lambda _ { 1 } , \ldots , \lambda _ { m } \right) : { \mathfrak { M } } \longrightarrow \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is a vectorial measure $i f$ each component $\lambda _ { i } : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \mathbb { R }$ is a signed measure, $i = 1 , \ldots , m$ . The total variation of λ is defined by 

$$
\left\| \lambda \right\| := \left\| \lambda_ {1} \right\| + \ldots + \left\| \lambda_ {m} \right\|.
$$

If X is a topological space, then $\lambda : \mathfrak { M } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is a vectorial Radon measure if each component $\lambda _ { i } : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \mathbb { R }$ is a signed Radon measure, $i = 1 , \ldots , m$ and $\mathcal { M } \left( \boldsymbol { X } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ is the space of all vectorial Radon measures $\lambda : B ( X )  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ endowed with the total variation norm. 

Exercise 1.184. In some applications it is more convenient to define the total variation of $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ as 

$$
\left\| \lambda \right\| _ {1} (E) := \sup \left\{\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left| \lambda \left(E _ {n}\right) \right|: \left\{E _ {n} \right\} \subset \mathfrak {M} \text {   partition   of   } E \right\}, \quad E \in \mathfrak {M}.\tag{1.127}
$$

Prove that $\| \lambda \| _ { 1 } : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ is a (positive) measure. Note that in view of Proposition $1 . 1 7 7$ , the definition of $\| \lambda \| _ { 1 }$ is consistent with the case $m = 1$ 

## 1.3.2 Signed Finitely Additive Measures

In this subsection we introduce some important spaces of finitely additive signed measures. Let X be a nonempty set and let ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be an algebra. Let $B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ denote the space of all bounded measurable functions $u : X \to \mathbb { R }$ 

Exercise 1.185. Prove that $B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ is a Banach space endowed with the norm 

$$
\left\| u \right\| _ {\infty} := \sup _ {x \in X} | u (x) |.
$$

By Theorem 1.74 it turns out that $B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ consists of all uniform limits of finite linear combinations of characteristic functions of sets in M. 

Definition 1.186. Let X be a nonempty set and let ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be an algebra. The space ba (X, M) of bounded finitely additive signed measures is composed of all set functions $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \mathbb { R }$ such that 

(i) $\lambda \left( \varnothing \right) = 0 ;$ 

(ii) λ is finitely additive, that is, 

$$
\lambda \left(E _ {1} \cup E _ {2}\right) = \lambda \left(E _ {1}\right) + \lambda \left(E _ {2}\right)
$$

for all $E _ { 1 } , E _ { 2 } \in \mathfrak { M }$ with $E _ { 1 } \cap E _ { 2 } = \varnothing ;$ 

(iii) λ is bounded, that is, its total variation norm 

$$
\| \lambda \| (X) := \sup \left\{\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} | \lambda (E _ {n}) |: \{E _ {n} \} \subset \mathfrak {M} \text {   finite   partition   of   } X \right\}
$$

is finite. 

Exercise 1.187. Prove that ba (X, M) is a Banach space endowed with the total variation norm $\left\| \cdot \right\| \left( X \right)$ 

Analogously to the Hahn decomposition theorem for signed measures, it is possible to prove that if $\lambda \in \mathrm { b a } \left( X , \mathfrak { M } \right)$ , then it may be decomposed as 

$$
\lambda = \lambda^ {+} - \lambda^ {-},
$$

where $\lambda ^ { + } , \lambda ^ { - }$ are (positive) finitely additive measures. Indeed, we have the following result. 

Theorem 1.188. Let X be a nonempty set, let ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be an algebra, and let $\lambda \in$ ba (X, M). Then 

$$
\lambda^ {+} (E) := \sup \left\{\lambda (F): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M} \right\}, \quad E \in \mathfrak {M},
$$

$$
\lambda^ {-} (E) := - \inf \left\{\lambda (F): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M} \right\}, \quad E \in \mathfrak {M},
$$

are (positive) finitely additive measures and $\lambda = \lambda ^ { + } - \lambda ^ { - }$ 

Proof. Let $E _ { 1 } , E _ { 2 } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , with $E _ { 1 } \cap E _ { 2 } = \emptyset$ . Since λ is bounded, for $\varepsilon > 0$ there exist $F _ { i } \subset E _ { i } , F _ { i } \in \mathfrak { M }$ , such that 

$$
\lambda^ {+} (E _ {i}) \leq \lambda (F _ {i}) + \varepsilon ,
$$

i = 1, 2. Hence 

$$
\lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {1} \cup E _ {2}\right) \geq \lambda \left(F _ {1} \cup F _ {2}\right) = \lambda \left(F _ {1}\right) + \lambda \left(F _ {2}\right) \geq \lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {1}\right) + \lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {2}\right) - 2 \varepsilon ,
$$

and by the arbitrariness of ε we deduce that 

$$
\lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {1} \cup E _ {2}\right) \geq \lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {1}\right) + \lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {2}\right).
$$

To prove the reverse inequality, for $\varepsilon > 0$ we may find a set $F \subset E _ { 1 } \cup E _ { 2 }$ , with $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , such that 

$$
\lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {1} \cup E _ {2}\right) \leq \lambda (F) + \varepsilon .
$$

Since $E _ { 1 } \cap E _ { 2 } = \emptyset$ it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {1} \cup E _ {2}\right) \leq \lambda \left(F\right) + \varepsilon = \lambda \left(F \cap E _ {1}\right) + \lambda \left(F \cap E _ {2}\right) + \varepsilon \\ \leq \lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {1}\right) + \lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {2}\right) + \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

and by the arbitrariness of $\varepsilon$ we conclude that $\lambda ^ { + }$ is finitely additive. Since $\lambda ^ { - } = \stackrel { \cdot } { ( } - \lambda ) ^ { + }$ , we obtain that $\lambda ^ { - }$ is finitely additive. 

Since $\lambda ^ { + } \geq \lambda$ and $- \lambda ^ { - } \leq \lambda$ for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 \leq \lambda^ {+} (E) - \lambda (E) = \sup \{\lambda (F) - \lambda (E): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M} \} \\ \quad = \sup \{- \lambda (E \setminus F): F \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M} \} \\ \quad = - \inf \{\lambda (G): G \subset E, F \in \mathfrak {M} \} = \lambda^ {-} (E). \end{array}
$$

This concludes the proof. 

The previous theorem, together with (1.21), Theorem 1.74, and Remark 1.76, leads to the definition of the Lebesgue integral of $u \in B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ , namely 

$$
\int_ {E} u d \lambda := \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} s _ {n} d \lambda\tag{1.128}
$$

for any sequence $\{ s _ { n } \} \subset B \left( X , \mathfrak { M } \right)$ of simple functions that converges uniformly to $u .$ It may be verified that the integral does not depend on the particular approximating sequence $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ 

We consider next the case that X is a normal space. 

Definition 1.189. Let X be a normal space and let M be the smallest algebra that contains all open sets of X. The space rba (X, M) of all regular bounded finitely additive signed measures consists of all set functions $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \mathbb { R }$ such that 

(i) $\lambda \in \mathrm { b a } \left( X , \mathfrak { M } \right)$ ; 

(ii) for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

$$
\lambda^ {+} (E) = \inf \left\{\lambda^ {+} (A): A \text { open }, A \supset E \right\}\tag{1.129}
$$

$$
= \sup \left\{\lambda^ {+} (C): C \text { closed }, C \subset E \right\}\tag{1.130}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lambda^ {-} (E) = \inf \left\{\lambda^ {-} (A): A \text {open} A \supset E \right\} \\ = \sup \left\{\lambda^ {-} (C): C \text {closed} C \subset E \right\}, \end{array}
$$

where $\lambda ^ { + }$ and $\lambda ^ { - }$ are defined in Theorem 1.188. 

Exercise 1.190. Show that the space rba (X, M) is a closed subspace of ba (X, M) and hence a Banach space with the total variation norm · (X). 

In the special case that X is compact, then regular finitely additive measures are measures. Indeed, we have the following: 

Theorem 1.191 (Alexandrof). Let X be a compact topological space and let M be an algebra that contains all open sets. If $\lambda \in$ rba (X, M) then λ is countably additive. 

Proof. In view of Theorem 1.188 it sufices to show that the finitely additive measures $\lambda ^ { + }$ and $\lambda ^ { - }$ defined are countably additive. Let $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ be a sequence of mutually disjoint sets such that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } \in \mathfrak { M }$ . Then 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \lambda^ {+} (E _ {n}) = \lambda^ {+} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {l} E _ {n}\right) \leq \lambda^ {+} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right)
$$

and letting $l \to \infty$ , we get 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \lambda^ {+} (E _ {n}) \leq \lambda^ {+} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right).
$$

To prove the reverse inequality, let C be any closed set contained in $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n }$ For $n \in \mathbb N$ and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ , by (1.129) there exists an open set $A _ { n } \supset E _ { n }$ such that 

$$
\lambda^ {+} (A _ {n}) \leq \lambda^ {+} (E _ {n}) + \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n}}.
$$

Since $C$ is a closed subset of the compact space X we have that C is also compact, and since $\left\{ A _ { n } \right\}$ is an open cover for $C ,$ , there exist $A _ { 1 } , \ldots , A _ { l }$ whose union still covers C. Hence 

$$
\lambda^ {+} (C) \leq \lambda^ {+} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {l} A _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \lambda^ {+} (A _ {n}) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \lambda^ {+} (E _ {n}) + \varepsilon \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \lambda^ {+} (E _ {n}) + \varepsilon .
$$

Taking the supremum over all closed sets $C \subset \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n }$ and using (1.130), we obtain 

$$
\lambda^ {+} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {n}\right) + \varepsilon ,
$$

and letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ gives the desired inequality. 

With exactly the same proof it may be shown that $\lambda ^ { - }$ is countably additive. 

Corollary 1.192. If in addition to the hypotheses of the previous theorem, we assume also that X is a Hausdorf space, then λ can be extended in a unique way as a signed Radon measure to the smallest σ-algebra that contains M. 

Proof. Since $\lambda ^ { + } : \mathfrak { M } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ is a finite countably additive measure, in view of Remark 1.39, the finite measure $( \lambda ^ { + } ) ^ { * } : \mathfrak { M } ^ { * }  [ 0 , \infty )$ defined in (1.14) (with $\mathcal { G } : = \mathfrak { M }$ and $\rho : = \lambda ^ { + } )$ is the unique extension of $\lambda ^ { + }$ to the σ-algebra ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ of all $\left( \lambda ^ { + } \right) ^ { * }$ <sup>∗</sup>-measurable sets. Note that since M contains all open sets, then necessarily $B \left( X \right) \subset { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ . Thus it remains to show that the Borel measure $\left( \lambda ^ { + } \right) ^ { * } : \mathfrak { M } ^ { * } \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right)$ is a Radon measure. In view of Remark A.10 in the appendix, the class of closed sets of X coincides with the class of compact sets. Hence for any open set $A \subset X$ , by (1.130), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left(\lambda^ {+}\right) ^ {*} (A) = \left(\lambda^ {+}\right) (A) = \sup \left\{\lambda^ {+} (C): C \text {closed} C \subset A \right\} \\ \qquad = \sup \left\{\lambda^ {+} (K): K \text {compact} K \subset A \right\} \\ \qquad = \sup \left\{\left(\lambda^ {+}\right) ^ {*} (K): K \text {compact} K \subset A \right\}, \end{array}
$$

and so every open set is inner regular. 

We now show that any $E \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { * }$ is outer regular. By (1.14), for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ we may find a sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ such that $E \subset \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n }$ and 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \lambda^ {+} (E _ {n}) \leq (\lambda^ {+}) ^ {*} (E) + \varepsilon .\tag{1.131}
$$

By (1.129), for every $n \in \mathbb { N }$ we may find an open set $A _ { n } \supset E _ { n }$ such that 

$$
\lambda^ {+} \left(A _ {n}\right) \leq \lambda^ {+} \left(E _ {n}\right) + \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n}}.\tag{1.132}
$$

Since $E \subset \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } A _ { n }$ by (1.131) and (1.132), we have that 

$$
\lambda^ {+} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} A _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \lambda^ {+} (A _ {n}) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \lambda^ {+} (E _ {n}) + \varepsilon \leq (\lambda^ {+}) ^ {*} (E) + 2 \varepsilon .
$$

In turn, 

$$
