\left(\lambda^ {+}\right) ^ {*} (E) \leq \inf \left\{\lambda^ {+} (A): A \text {open} A \supset E \right\} \leq \left(\lambda^ {+}\right) ^ {*} (E) + 2 \varepsilon ,
$$

and given the arbitrariness of $\varepsilon > 0$ we deduce that E is outer regular. This concludes the proof. 

## 1.3.3 Spaces of Measures as Dual Spaces

Let X be a nonempty set and let M be an algebra. In this subsection we identify the dual of certain subspaces of $B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ with ba (X, M), rba (X, M) and ${ \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ 

It turns out that the dual of B (X, M) may be identified with ba (X, M): 

Theorem 1.193 (Riesz representation theorem in B). Let X be a nonempty set and let ${ \mathfrak { M } } \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ be an algebra. Then every bounded linear functional $L : B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right) \to \mathbb { R }$ is represented by a unique $\lambda \in \mathrm { ~ b a } \left( X , \mathfrak { M } \right)$ , in the sense that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \lambda \quad f o r e v e r y u \in B (X, \mathfrak {M}).\tag{1.133}
$$

Moreover, the norm of L coincides with $\| \lambda \| \left( X \right)$ . Conversely, every functional of the form (1.133), where $\lambda \in$ ba (X, M), is a bounded linear functional on $B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ 

Proof. Step 1: Let $L \in ( B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right) ) ^ { \prime }$ and for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ define 

$$
\lambda (E) := L (\chi_ {E}).
$$

Since L is linear and $L \left( 0 \right) = 0$ it follows that $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \mathbb { R }$ is a finitely additive signed measure. To prove that λ is bounded, let $\{ E _ { n } \} _ { n = 1 } ^ { l } \subset \mathfrak { M }$ be a finite partition of X and define 

$$
s := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} c _ {n} \chi_ {E _ {n}},
$$

where $c _ { n } : = \mathrm { s g n } \left( L \left( \chi _ { E _ { n } } \right) \right)$ . Then $s \in B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} | \lambda (E _ {n}) | = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \operatorname{sgn} \left(L (\chi_ {E _ {n}})\right) L (\chi_ {E _ {n}}) \\ \qquad = \left| \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} c _ {n} L (\chi_ {E _ {n}}) \right| = | L (s) | \\ \qquad \leq \| L \| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}} \| s \| _ {\infty} \leq \| L \| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}}, \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that $\| s \| _ { \infty } \leq 1$ . Hence 

$$
\left\| \lambda \right\| (X) \leq \left\| L \right\| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}},\tag{1.134}
$$

which shows that $\lambda \in$ ba (X, M). 

We now show that (1.133) holds. Fix $u \in B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ , and partition the interval $[ - \left\| u \right\| _ { \infty } , \left\| u \right\| _ { \infty } ]$ into l intervals $I _ { n } , n = 1 , \ldots , l$ , of length less than or equal to ε. For each $n = 1 , \ldots , l$ , define 

$$
E _ {n} := u ^ {- 1} \left(I _ {n}\right) \in \mathfrak {M}
$$

and let 

$$
s := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} c _ {n} \chi_ {E _ {n}},
$$

where $c _ { n }$ is any fixed number in $I _ { n }$ . Note that for $x \ \in \ E _ { n }$ we have that u $( x ) \in I _ { n }$ , and so 

$$
\left| u (x) - s (x) \right| \leq \varepsilon .
$$

Hence $\| u - s \| _ { \infty } \leq \varepsilon$ , while by the linearity of $L$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| L (u) - \int_ {X} s   d \lambda \right| = \left| L (u) - \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} c _ {n} \lambda (E _ {n}) \right| \\ \qquad = \left| L (u) - \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} c _ {n} L (\chi_ {E _ {n}}) \right| \\ \qquad = | L (u - s) | \leq \| L \| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}} \| u - s \| _ {\infty} \\ \qquad \leq \| L \| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}} \varepsilon . \end{array}\tag{1.135}
$$

By taking $\textstyle \varepsilon : = { \frac { 1 } { k } }$ we can construct a sequence $\left\{ s _ { k } \right\}$ of simple functions con verging uniformly to u such that 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {X} s _ {k} d \lambda = L (u).
$$

By (1.128) this implies that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \lambda .
$$

Moreover, from (1.135) and the fact that $\| u - s \| _ { \infty } \leq \varepsilon$ we have that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | L (u) | \leq \left| \int_ {X} s d \lambda \right| + \| L \| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}} \varepsilon \\ \qquad \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} | c _ {n} |   | \lambda (E _ {n}) | + \| L \| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}} \varepsilon \\ \qquad \leq (\| u \| _ {\infty} + \varepsilon) \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} | \lambda (E _ {n}) | + \| L \| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}} \varepsilon \\ \qquad \leq (\| u \| _ {\infty} + \varepsilon)   \| \lambda \| (X) + \| L \| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}} \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

and so, by the arbitrariness of $\varepsilon _ { i }$ , we get 

$$
| L (u) | \leq \| u \| _ {\infty} \| \lambda \| (X),
$$

which, together with (1.134), implies that $\left\| \lambda \right\| ( X ) = \left\| L \right\| _ { ( B ( X , \mathfrak { M } ) ) ^ { \prime } } .$ 

Step 2: Conversely, given $\lambda \in$ ba (X, M), for $u \in B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ define 

$$
L (u) := \int_ {X} u d \lambda .
$$

Then $L \in ( B ( X , { \mathfrak { M } } ) ) ^ { \prime }$ and $\| \lambda \| ( X ) = \| L \| _ { ( B ( X , { \mathfrak { M } } ) ) ^ { \prime } }$ . We leave the details as an exercise. 

We consider next the case that X is a normal Hausdorf space. Let $C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ denote the space of all continuous bounded functions $u : X \to \mathbb { R }$ . It is well known that $C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ is a Banach space with the norm $\left\| \cdot \right\| _ { \infty }$ 

Theorem 1.194. Let X be a normal space. Then $C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ is separable if and only if X is a compact metrizable space. 

It turns out that the dual of $C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ may be identified with rba (X, M): 

Theorem 1.195 (Riesz representation theorem in $C _ { b } )$ . Let X be a normal Hausdorf space and let M be the smallest algebra that contains all open sets of X. Then every bounded linear functional $L : C _ { b } ( X )  \mathbb { R }$ is represented by a unique $\lambda \in \operatorname { r b a } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ in the sense that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \lambda \quad f o r e v e r y u \in C _ {b} (X).\tag{1.136}
$$

Moreover, the norm of L coincides with the total variation norm $\| \lambda \| \left( X \right)$ Conversely, every functional of the form (1.136), where $\lambda \in \mathrm { r b a } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ , is a bounded linear functional on $C _ { b } \left( \boldsymbol { X } \right)$ 

The proof of this theorem is rather lengthy, and so we omit it. We refer the reader to [AliBur99]. 

Let X be a compact Hausdorf space and let $C \left( X \right) = C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ be the space of all continuous functions. In view of Corollary 1.192 and the Riesz representation theorem in $C _ { b }$ , we have that the dual of $C \left( X \right)$ may be identified with ${ \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ : 

Theorem 1.196 (Riesz representation theorem in C). Let X be a compact Hausdorf space. Then every bounded linear functiona $L : C ( X )  \mathbb { R }$ is represented by a unique finite signed Radon measure $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ in the sense that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \lambda \quad f o r e v e r y u \in C (X).\tag{1.137}
$$

Moreover, the norm of L coincides with the total variation norm $\| \lambda \|$ . Conversely, every functional of the form (1.137), where $\lambda \ \in \ { \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ , is a bounded linear functional on $C \left( X \right)$ 

Finally, we consider the dual space of the space of continuous functions “that vanish at infinity”. Let X be a topological space, let $C _ { c } \left( X \right)$ be the collection of all continuous functions $u : X \to \mathbb { R }$ whose support is compact, and let $C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ be the completion of $C _ { c } \left( X \right)$ relative by the supremum norm $\left\| \cdot \right\| _ { \infty }$ 

Theorem 1.197. Let X be a normal space. Then $C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ is separable if and only if X is a σ-compact metrizable space. 

Remark 1.198. It can be shown that a normal, separable, locally compact metrizable space is σ-compact. 

If X is compact then 

$$
C _ {0} (X) = C _ {c} (X) = C (X).
$$

If X is a locally compact Hausdorf space, then it can be shown that $u \in$ $C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ if and only if $u \in C \left( X \right)$ and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a compact set $K \subset X$ such that 

$$
| u \left(x\right) | <   \varepsilon \text { for   all } x \in X \setminus K.
$$

Note that the duals of $C _ { c } \left( X \right)$ and $C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ “coincide” in the sense that if $L \in ( C _ { 0 } \left( X \right) ) ^ { \prime }$ then $L \vert C _ { c } \left( X \right) \in \left( C _ { c } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ , and conversely, if $L \in ( C _ { c } \left( X \right) ) ^ { \prime }$ then there exists a unique $\overline { { L } } \in ( C _ { 0 } \left( X \right) ) ^ { \prime }$ such that 

$$
\overline {{{L}}} \lfloor C _ {c} (X) = L, \quad \| \overline {{{L}}} \| = \| L \|.
$$

Exercise 1.199 (Alexandrof compactification). Let X be a locally compact Hausdorf space. Let ∞ denote a point not in X and consider $X ^ { \infty } : =$ $X \cup \{ \infty \}$ . Let $\tau \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X ^ { \infty } \right)$ be the collection of all subsets $A \subset X ^ { \infty }$ such that either A is an open set of $X$ or $\infty \in A$ and $X ^ { \infty } \setminus A$ is a compact set of $X$ Prove that $( X ^ { \infty } , \tau )$ is a compact Hausdorf space, and that $v \in C \left( X ^ { \infty } \right)$ if and only if 

$$
v = u \chi_ {X} + c \chi_ {\{\infty \}}
$$

for some $u \in C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ and $c \in \mathbb { R }$ . Show also that the decomposition of v is unique, and 

$$
\left\| v \right\| _ {C (X ^ {\infty})} = \max \left\{\left\| u \right\| _ {C _ {0} (X)}, | c | \right\}.\tag{1.138}
$$

We now show that the dual of $C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ may be identified with $\mathcal { M } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ 

Theorem 1.200 (Riesz representation theorem in $C _ { 0 } )$ . Let X be a locally compact Hausdorf space. Then every bounded linear functional $L :$ $C _ { 0 } ( \boldsymbol { X } ) \  \ \mathbb { R }$ is represented by a unique finite signed Radon measure $\lambda \ \in$ ${ \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ in the sense that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \lambda \quad f o r e v e r y u \in C _ {0} (X).\tag{1.139}
$$

Moreover, the norm of L coincides with the total variation norm $\| \lambda \| \left( X \right)$ Conversely, every functional of the form (1.139), where $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ , is a bounded linear functional on $C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ 

Proof. It is immediate to verify that given $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ , then (1.139) determines L as an element of $\left( C _ { 0 } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ 

Conversely, given $L \in ( C _ { 0 } \left( X \right) ) ^ { \prime }$ , we use the one-point compactification or Alexandrof compactification defined in the previous exercise to find $\lambda \in$ ${ \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ satisfying (1.139). In $C \left( X ^ { \infty } \right)$ consider the norm 

$$
p \left(v\right) := \left\| L \right\| _ {\left(C _ {0} (X)\right) ^ {\prime}} \left\| v \right\| _ {C \left(X ^ {\infty}\right)}.
$$

In view of (1.138) we have 

$$
| L (u) | \leq p (u)
$$

for all $u \in C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ , and thus by the Hahn–Banach theorem we may extend L to a bounded linear functional $L _ { 1 }$ on $C \left( X ^ { \infty } \right)$ in such a way that $\| L \| _ { ( C _ { 0 } ( X ) ) ^ { \prime } } = \| L _ { 1 } \| _ { ( C ( X ^ { \infty } ) ) ^ { \prime } }$ . By the Riesz representation theorem in $C \left( X ^ { \infty } \right)$ there is a unique finite signed Radon measure $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( X ^ { \infty } ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ with 

$$
\left\| \lambda \right\| \left(X ^ {\infty}\right) = \left\| L _ {1} \right\| _ {(C (X ^ {\infty})) ^ {\prime}},
$$

and such that for every $v \in C \left( X ^ { \infty } \right)$ 

$$
L _ {1} (v) = \int_ {X ^ {\infty}} v d \lambda = \int_ {X} v d \lambda + v (\infty) \lambda (\{\infty \}).
$$

In particular, it follows that for every $u \in C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ we have that 

$$
L _ {1} (u) = L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \lambda .\tag{1.140}
$$

Moreover, $\lambda : B ( X )  \mathbb { R }$ is in $\mathcal { M } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ , and we have 

$$
\left\| \lambda \right\| (X) \leq \left\| \lambda \right\| \left(X ^ {\infty}\right) = \left\| L _ {1} \right\| _ {(C (X ^ {\infty})) ^ {\prime}} = \left\| L \right\| _ {(C _ {0} (X)) ^ {\prime}} \leq \left\| \lambda \right\| (X),
$$

where the last inequality follows from (1.140). This proves tha $\| L \| _ { ( C _ { 0 } ( X ) ) ^ { \prime } } =$ $\| \lambda \| \left( X \right)$ . Note that this implies that $\lambda \left( \left\{ \infty \right\} \right) = 0$ 

Finally, to prove the uniqueness of the representation (1.140) assume that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \lambda = \int_ {X} u d \varsigma
$$

for all $u \in C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ and for some $\varsigma \in { \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ . Extend ς to $\varsigma _ { 1 } \in \mathcal { M } \left( X ^ { \infty } ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ by setting $\varsigma _ { 1 } \left( \{ \infty \} \right) : = 0$ . Then 

$$
L _ {1} (v) = \int_ {X} v d \lambda = \int_ {X} v d \varsigma_ {1}
$$

for all $v \in C \left( X ^ { \infty } \right)$ , and so by the Riesz representation theorem in C it follows that $\varsigma _ { 1 } = \lambda$ , in particular $\varsigma _ { 1 } \lfloor X = \varsigma = \lambda \lfloor X$ 

In the study of distributions in [FoLe10] we will also need the following variants of the previous theorem. 

Theorem 1.201 (Riesz representation theorem in $C _ { c } )$ . Let X be a locally compact Hausdorf space and let $L : C _ { c } ( X )  \mathbb { R }$ be a linear functional. Then 

(i) if L is positive, that is, $L \left( v \right) \geq 0$ for all $v \in C _ { c } \left( X \right)$ with $v \geq 0$ , then there exists a unique (positive) Radon measure $\mu : B ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \mu \quad f o r e v e r y u \in C _ {c} (X);
$$

(ii) if L is locally bounded, that is, for every compact set $K \subset X$ there exists a constant $C _ { K } > 0$ such that 

$$
| L (u) | \leq C _ {K} \| v \| _ {C _ {c} (X)}
$$

for all $v \in C _ { c } \left( X \right)$ with supp $v \subset K$ , then there exist two (positive) Radon measures $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } : { \mathcal { B } } \left( X \right) \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \mu_ {1} - \int_ {X} u d \mu_ {2} \quad f o r e v e r y u \in C _ {c} (X).
$$

Note that since both $\mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ could have infinite measure, their diference is not defined in general, although on every compact set it is a well-defined finite signed measure. The proof of part (i) of the previous theorem is classical (see, e.g., [Ru87]), while (ii) follows from (i) by writing L as the diference of two positive functionals (see Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 2.37 below for an entirely similar argument). 

## 1.3.4 Weak Star Convergence of Measures

Let X be a normal space and let M be an algebra that contains all open sets of X. If $C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ is separable, i.e., if X is a compact metrizable space (see Theorem 1.194), then in view of Theorem A.55 and the Riesz representation theorem, any bounded sequence of measures $\{ \lambda _ { n } \} \subset$ rba (X, M) is sequentially weakly star precompact. In particular, if $u \in C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ then 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {X} u d \lambda_ {n _ {k}} = \int_ {X} u d \lambda\tag{1.141}
$$

for a subsequence $\{ \lambda _ { n _ { k } } \}$ and for some $\lambda \in \operatorname { r b a } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ 

Similarly, invoking now Theorem 1.197 and the Riesz representation the orem in $C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ , we have the following result. 

Proposition 1.202. Let X be a σ-compact metric space, and let $\{ \lambda _ { n } \} \subset$ ${ \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ be a sequence of signed Radon measures such that 

$$
\sup _ {n} \| \lambda_ {n} \| <   \infty .
$$

Then there exist a subsequence $\{ \lambda _ { n _ { k } } \}$ and a signed Radon measure λ such that 

$$
\lambda_ {n _ {k}} \stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} \lambda i n \mathcal {M} (X; \mathbb {R}),
$$

i.e., 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} u d \lambda_ {n} = \int_ {X} u d \lambda
$$

for every $u \in C _ { 0 } \left( X \right)$ 

The following properties will be frequently used in the sequel. 

Proposition 1.203. Let X be a locally compact Hausdorf space and let $\{ \mu _ { n } \} \subset \mathcal { M } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ be a sequence of (positive) Radon measures such that $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { * } { \to } \mu$ in $\mathcal { M } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ . Then 

(i) if $A \subset X$ is open then 

$$
\mu \left(A\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(A\right);
$$

(ii) if $K \subset X$ is compact then 

$$
\mu \left(K\right) \geq \limsup _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(K\right);
$$

(iii) if $A \subset X$ is open, $\overline { { A } }$ is compact, and $\mu \left( \partial A \right) = 0$ , then 

$$
\mu (A) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} (A).
$$

Proof. (i) Let $K \subset A$ be a compact subset. By Corollary A.13 there exists a cutof function $\varphi \in C _ { c } \left( X \right)$ such that $0 \leq \varphi \leq 1 , \varphi \equiv 1$ on $K .$ , and $\varphi \equiv 0$ on $X \setminus A$ . Then 

$$
\mu \left(K\right) \leq \int_ {A} \varphi   d \mu = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {A} \varphi   d \mu_ {n} \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(A\right).
$$

Since $\mu$ is a Radon measure it is inner regular, and so taking the supremum over all compact subsets of A, we have 

$$
\mu \left(A\right) = \sup \left\{\mu \left(K\right): K \subset A \right\} \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(A\right).
$$

(ii) Let $A \supset K$ be an open set and consider a cutof function $\varphi \in C _ { c } \left( X \right)$ such that $0 \leq \varphi \leq 1 , \varphi \equiv 1$ on K, and $\varphi \equiv 0$ on $X \setminus A$ . Then 

$$
\limsup _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(K\right) \leq \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {A} \varphi d \mu_ {n} = \int_ {A} \varphi d \mu \leq \mu \left(A\right).
$$

Since $\mu$ is a Radon measure, taking the supremum over all open supersets of K and using outer regularity, we have 

$$
\limsup _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} (K) \leq \mu (K) = \inf \left\{\mu (A): K \subset A \right\}.
$$

(iii) If $\mu \left( \partial A \right) = 0$ then from (i) and (ii), 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(A\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(\overline {{A}}\right) \leq \mu \left(\overline {{A}}\right) = \mu \left(A\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(A\right).
$$

This concludes the proof. 

As a corollary of the previous proposition we obtain the following result. 

Corollary 1.204. Let X be a locally compact Hausdorf space, and let $\{ \lambda _ { n } \} \subset$ ${ \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ be a sequence of signed Radon measures such that $\lambda _ { n } \stackrel { * } {  } \lambda$ in ${ \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ and $\| \lambda _ { n } \| \overset { * } { \mathop {  } } \nu$ in ${ \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ . If $A \subset X$ is open, $\overline { { A } }$ is compact, and $\nu \left( \partial A \right) = 0$ , then 

$$
\int_ {A} u d \lambda_ {n} \rightarrow \int_ {A} u d \lambda
$$

for all $u \in C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ . In particular, 

$$
\lambda_ {n} (A) \to \lambda (A).
$$

Proof. Fix $u \in C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ . Since $\nu$ is outer regular and $\nu \left( \partial A \right) = 0$ for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists an open set $U \supset \partial A$ such that 

$$
\nu (U) \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2 \left(1 + \| u \| _ {C _ {b} (X)}\right)}.\tag{1.142}
$$

Since $U \cup A$ is an open set containing the compact set ${ \overline { { A } } } .$ , by Corollary A.13 there exists a cutof function $\varphi \in C _ { c } \left( X \right)$ such that $0 \leq \varphi \leq 1 , \varphi \equiv 1$ on ${ \overline { { A } } } .$ and $\varphi \equiv 0$ on $X \setminus ( U \cup A )$ . For any $u \in C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ we have that $\varphi u \in C _ { c } \left( X \right)$ , and so 

$$
\int_ {A} u d \lambda_ {n} - \int_ {A} u d \lambda = \int_ {X} \varphi u d \lambda_ {n} - \int_ {X} \varphi u d \lambda + \int_ {U \setminus A} \varphi u d \lambda_ {n} - \int_ {U \setminus A} \varphi u d \lambda .
$$

In turn, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \int_ {A} u   d \lambda_ {n} - \int_ {A} u   d \lambda \right| \leq \left| \int_ {X} \varphi u   d \lambda_ {n} - \int_ {X} \varphi u   d \lambda \right| \\ \qquad + \| u \| _ {C _ {b} (X)} \left(\| \lambda_ {n} \| (\operatorname{supp} \varphi \setminus A) + \| \lambda \| (\operatorname{supp} \varphi \setminus A)\right). \end{array}
$$

Letting $n \to \infty$ and using part (ii) of the previous proposition, the facts that $\lambda _ { n } \overset { * } {  } \lambda$ in ${ \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ and $\| \lambda \| \leq \nu ,$ and (1.142) yield 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \bigg | \int_ {A} u   d \lambda_ {n} - \int_ {A} u   d \lambda \bigg | & \leq 2   \| u \| _ {C _ {b} (X)}   \nu \left(\text { supp }   \varphi \setminus A\right) \\ & \leq 2   \| u \| _ {C _ {b} (X)}   \nu \left(U\right) \leq \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

The last part of the theorem follows by taking $u \equiv 1$ 

Remark 1.205. The previous corollary continues to hold with the obvious changes for a sequence $\{ \lambda _ { n } \} \subset \mathcal { M } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ of vector-valued Radon measures. 

If X is a topological space, then $C _ { 0 } \left( X \right) \subset C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ , with the strict inclusion possible. Hence, if a sequence of (positive) Radon measures $\{ \mu _ { n } \}$ converges weakly star to some Radon measure µ in M $\left( \boldsymbol { X } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \ : = \ : \left( \boldsymbol { C _ { 0 } } \left( \boldsymbol { X } \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ , then in general we cannot conclude that $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { * } { \to } \mu$ in $\left( C _ { b } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ . The next results provide two suficient conditions for this to happen. 

Proposition 1.206. Let X be a topological space and let $\mu , \mu _ { n } : B ( X ) $ $[ 0 , \infty ) , n \in \mathbb { N }$ , be finite Borel measures such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} (X) = \mu (X)\tag{1.143}
$$

and 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(A\right) \geq \mu \left(A\right)\tag{1.144}
$$

for every open set $A \subset X$ . Then $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { * } { \to } \mu$ in $\left( C _ { b } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ 

In particular, if X is a locally compact Hausdorf space, $\mu , \mu _ { n } , n \in \mathbb { N }$ , are (positive) finite Radon measures, and $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { * } { \to } \mu$ in M (X; R), then $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { * } { \to } \mu$ in $\left( C _ { b } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ if and only if (1.143) holds. 

The proof of the proposition makes use of the following exercise. 

Exercise 1.207. Let $\{ x _ { n } \}$ and $\left\{ y _ { n } \right\}$ be two sequences of real numbers such that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} x _ {n} \geq x, \quad \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} y _ {n} \geq y, \\ \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} (x _ {n} + y _ {n}) \leq x + y, \end{array}
$$

for some x, $y \in \mathbb R$ . Prove that lim $x _ { n } = x$ and $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } y _ { n } = y$ n→∞ 

Proof (Proposition 1.206). Let $u \in C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ . Assume first that $0 \leq u \leq 1$ . Then by Theorem 1.123 and Fatou’s lemma 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} u   d \mu_ {n} = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {1} \mu_ {n} \left(\{x \in X: u (x) > t \}\right)   d t \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \int_ {0} ^ {1} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(\{x \in X: u (x) > t \}\right)   d t \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \int_ {0} ^ {1} \mu \left(\{x \in X: u (x) > t \}\right)   d t \\ \qquad = \int_ {X} u   d \mu , \end{array}
$$

where we have used (1.144) and that fact that the sets $\{ x \in X : u \left( x \right) > t \}$ are open, since u is continuous. 

Similarly, 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} \left(1 - u\right) d \mu_ {n} \geq \int_ {X} \left(1 - u\right) d \mu .
$$

Let 

$$
\begin{array}{l} x _ {n} := \int_ {X} u   d \mu_ {n}, \quad y _ {n} := \int_ {X} (1 - u)   u   d \mu_ {n}, \\ x := \int_ {X} u   d \mu , \quad y := \int_ {X} (1 - u)   d \mu . \end{array}
$$

By (1.143) and the previous exercise we conclude that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} u d \mu_ {n} = \int_ {X} u d \mu
$$

for all $u \in C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ , with $0 \leq u \leq 1$ 

For a general function $u \in C _ { b } \left( X \right) \backslash \{ 0 \}$ it sufices to apply the first part of the proof to the function 

$$
v := \frac {u - \inf _ {X} u}{\sup _ {X} u - \inf _ {X} u}
$$

and use (1.143). 

Finally, if X is a locally compact Hausdorf space and $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { * } { \to } \mu$ in ${ \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ then property (1.144) holds in view of Proposition 1.203(i). Since $1 \in C _ { b } \left( \boldsymbol { X } \right)$ , by the first part of the proposition we have that $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { * } { \to } \mu$ in $\left( C _ { b } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ if and only if (1.143) holds. 

Using the previous proposition we may prove an important theorem, usually stated for probability measures. 

Theorem 1.208 (Prohorov). Let X be a metric space and let $\{ \mu _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of Borel measures, $\mu _ { n } : B ( X )  [ 0 , \infty )$ , such that 

$$
\sup _ {n} \mu_ {n} (X) <   \infty .\tag{1.145}
$$

Assume that for all $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a compact set $K \subset X$ such that 

$$
\sup _ {n} \mu_ {n} \left(X \setminus K\right) \leq \varepsilon .\tag{1.146}
$$

Then there exist a subsequence $\{ \mu _ { n _ { k } } \} ~ o f ~ \{ \mu _ { n } \}$ and a Borel measure $\mu :$ $B ( X )  [ 0 , \infty )$ such that $\mu _ { n _ { k } } \stackrel { * } { \to } \mu$ in $\left( C _ { b } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ 

In particular, if X is a locally compact metric space, $\mu , \mu _ { n } , n \in \mathbb { N }$ , are (positive) finite Radon measures, and $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { * } { \to } \mu$ in ${ \mathcal { M } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ , then $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { * } { \to } \mu$ in $\left( C _ { b } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ if and only if (1.146) holds. 

The proof makes use of the following exercise. 

Exercise 1.209. Let X be a metric space and let $\{ K ^ { ( j ) } \} \subset X$ be an increasing sequence of compact sets. Prove that the set $\textstyle \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } K ^ { ( j ) }$ is separable and construct a countable family A of open sets with the property that for every open set $U \subset X$ and for every $x \in U \cap \left( \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } K ^ { ( j ) } \right)$ there exists $A \in { \mathcal { A } }$ such that $x \in A$ and ${ \overline { { A } } } \subset U$ 

Proof (Prohorov’s theorem). By extracting a subsequence (not relabeled) we may assume that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} (X) = M <   \infty .
$$

If $M = 0$ then $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { * } {  } 0$ in $\left( C _ { b } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ and there is nothing to prove. If $M > 0$ • then without loss of generality we may assume that $\mu _ { n } \left( X \right) = 1$ for all $n \in \mathbb N$ Indeed, if we can prove that a subsequence $\left\{ { \frac { \mu _ { n _ { k } } } { \mu _ { n _ { k } } ( X ) } } \right\}$ of $\left\{ { \frac { \mu _ { n } } { \mu _ { n } ( X ) } } \right\}$ converges weakly star to some Borel measure ν in $\left( C _ { b } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ , then $\{ \mu _ { n _ { k } } \}$ converges weakly star to the Borel measure $M \nu$ in $\left( C _ { b } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ 

By (1.146) we may construct an increasing sequence of compact sets $\{ K ^ { ( j ) } \} \subset X$ such that 

$$
\mu_ {n} \left(K ^ {(j)}\right) > 1 - \frac {1}{j}\tag{1.147}
$$

for all $j , n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Let $\mathcal { A }$ be the countable family of open sets given in the previous exercise and let K be the countable family of compact sets formed by ∅ and finite unions of sets of the form $\overline { { A } } \cap K ^ { ( j ) } , A \in \mathcal { A } , j \in \mathbb { N }$ 

Using a diagonal procedure, we may extract a subsequence of $\{ \mu _ { n } \}$ (not relabeled) such that the limit $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \mu _ { n } \left( K \right)$ exists for all $K \in \mathcal { K }$ . Set 

$$
\mu^ {*} (K) := \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} (K), \quad K \in \mathcal {K},\tag{1.148}
$$

and observe that $0 \leq \mu ^ { * } \leq 1 , \mu ^ { * } \left( \varnothing \right) = 0$ , and for all $K _ { 1 } , K _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { K }$ 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(K _ {1}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(K _ {2}\right) \text {   if   } K _ {1} \subset K _ {2};\tag{1.149}
$$

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(K _ {1} \cup K _ {2}\right) = \mu^ {*} \left(K _ {1}\right) + \mu^ {*} \left(K _ {2}\right) \text {   if   } K _ {1} \cap K _ {2} = \emptyset ;\tag{1.150}
$$

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(K _ {1} \cup K _ {2}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(K _ {1}\right) + \mu^ {*} \left(K _ {2}\right).\tag{1.151}
$$

For every open set $U \subset X$ define 

$$
\mu^ {*} (U) := \sup \left\{\mu^ {*} (K): K \subset U, K \in \mathcal {K} \right\},\tag{1.152}
$$

while for an arbitrary set $E \subset X$ define 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) := \inf \left\{\mu^ {*} (U): E \subset U, U \text { open } \right\}.\tag{1.153}
$$

Step 1: We prove that $\mu ^ { * }$ is an outer measure. 

Substep 1a: We claim that if $C \subset U \subset X$ , where C is closed and U is open, and $C \subset K$ for some $K \in \kappa$ , then there exists $K _ { 0 } \in \kappa$ such that $C \subset K _ { 0 } \subset U$ To see this, for every $x \in C$ choose $A _ { x } \in { \mathcal { A } }$ such that $x \in A _ { x }$ and ${ \overline { { A _ { x } } } } \subset U$ Since C is a closed subset of the compact set K and the family $\{ A _ { x } \} _ { x \in C }$ is an open cover of $C ,$ , we may find a finite subcover $A _ { x _ { 1 } } \ldots , A _ { x _ { \ell } }$ of $C .$ . Using the definition of K and fact that $\{ K ^ { ( j ) } \}$ is an increasing sequence of compact sets, there exists $j \in \mathbb N$ so large that $\overset { \cdot } { C } \subset K ^ { ( j ) }$ . Then the set 

$$
K _ {0} := \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\ell} \left(\overline {{A _ {x _ {n}}}} \cap K ^ {(j)}\right)
$$

belongs to K and $C \subset K _ { 0 } \subset U$ 

Substep 1b: We prove that if $U _ { 1 } , U _ { 2 } \subset X$ are open, then 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(U _ {1} \cup U _ {2}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(U _ {1}\right) + \mu^ {*} \left(U _ {2}\right).
$$

Fix any $K \in \mathcal { K }$ , with $K \subset U _ { 1 } \cup U _ { 2 }$ , and define the closed sets 

$$
\begin{array}{l} C _ {1} := \left\{x \in K: \operatorname{dist} \left(x, X \setminus U _ {1}\right) \geq \operatorname{dist} \left(x, X \setminus U _ {2}\right) \right\}, \\ C _ {2} := \left\{x \in K: \operatorname{dist} \left(x, X \setminus U _ {2}\right) \geq \operatorname{dist} \left(x, X \setminus U _ {1}\right) \right\}. \end{array}
$$

Note that $C _ { 1 } \subset U _ { 1 }$ . Indeed, if by contradiction there existed $x _ { 1 } \in C _ { 1 }$ such that $x \notin U _ { 1 }$ , then $x \in U _ { 2 }$ and, since $X \backslash U _ { 2 }$ is closed, 

$$
0 = \operatorname{dist} \left(x, X \setminus U _ {1}\right) <   \operatorname{dist} \left(x, X \setminus U _ {2}\right),
$$

which contradicts the definition of $C _ { 1 }$ . Hence $C _ { 1 } \subset U _ { 1 }$ , and similarly $C _ { 2 } \subset U _ { 2 }$ 

Since $C _ { i } \subset U _ { i }$ and $C _ { i } \subset K \in \mathcal { K } , i = 1 , 2$ , we may apply Substep 1a to find $K _ { i } \in \mathcal { K }$ such that $C _ { i } \subset K _ { i } \subset U _ { i } , i = 1 , 2$ . Thus by (1.149), (1.151), and (1.152) 

$$
\mu^ {*} (K) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(K _ {1} \cup K _ {2}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(K _ {1}\right) + \mu^ {*} \left(K _ {2}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(U _ {1}\right) + \mu^ {*} \left(U _ {2}\right).
$$

Taking the supremum over all admissible $K \subset U _ { 1 } \cup U _ { 2 }$ and using (1.152) yields the desired inequality. 

Substep 1c: We claim that if $\{ U _ { n } \} \subset X$ is a sequence of open sets, then 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} U _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} \left(U _ {n}\right).
$$

To see this, fix any $K \in \kappa .$ , with $K \subset \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } U _ { n }$ . Since K is compact, we may find $\ell \in \mathbb { N }$ such that $K \subset \textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \ell } U _ { n }$ . By (1.152) and the previous substep we have that 

$$
\mu^ {*} (K) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\ell} U _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\ell} \mu^ {*} (U _ {n}) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} (U _ {n}).
$$

Taking the supremum over all admissible $K \subset \cup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } U _ { n }$ and using (1.152) proves the claim. 

Substep 1d: Finally, we prove that $\mu ^ { * }$ is an outer measure. By (1.149), (1.152), and (1.153), $\mu ^ { * }$ is a monotone set function. Since $\mu ^ { * } \left( \varnothing \right) = 0$ , it remains to prove that $\mu ^ { * }$ is countably subadditive. Let $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset X$ be a sequence of arbitrary sets. Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ , and by (1.153) for each $n \in \mathbb N$ find an open set $U _ { n } \subset X$ such that $E _ { n } \subset U _ { n }$ and 

$$
\mu^ {*} (U _ {n}) \leq \mu^ {*} (E _ {n}) + \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n}}.\tag{1.154}
$$

Then $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } E _ { n } \subset \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } U _ { n }$ , and so by (1.153) and the previous substep 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} U _ {n}\right) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} (U _ {n}) \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu^ {*} (E _ {n}) + \varepsilon ,
$$

where in the last inequality we have used (1.154). Letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ gives the desired result. 

Step 2: We prove that every closed set $C \subset X$ is $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable. Fix a closed set $C \subset X$ . We begin by showing that for any open set $U \subset X$ , 

$$
\mu^ {*} (U) \geq \mu^ {*} (U \cap C) + \mu^ {*} (U \cap (X \setminus C)).\tag{1.155}
$$

Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ . Since $U \cap ( X \setminus C )$ is open, by (1.152) we may find $K _ { 1 } \in \mathcal { K }$ , with $K _ { 1 } \subset U \cap ( X \setminus C )$ , such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(U \cap (X \setminus C)\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(K _ {1}\right) + \varepsilon .\tag{1.156}
$$

Using (1.152) once more, find $K _ { 2 } \in \mathcal { K }$ , with $K _ { 2 } \subset U \cap ( X \setminus K _ { 1 } )$ , such that 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(U \cap (X \setminus K _ {1})\right) \leq \mu^ {*} \left(K _ {2}\right) + \varepsilon .\tag{1.157}
$$

Since the sets $K _ { 1 }$ and $K _ { 2 }$ are disjoint and are contained in $U$ , by (1.152), (1.150), (1.156), and (1.157), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu^ {*} (U) \geq \mu^ {*} (K _ {1} \cup K _ {2}) = \mu^ {*} (K _ {1}) + \mu^ {*} (K _ {2}) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qend{array}
$$

where in the last inequality we have used the fact that $C \subset X \setminus K _ { 1 }$ and the monotonicity of $\mu ^ { * }$ . Letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ yields (1.155). 

Now consider an arbitrary set $E \subset X$ and let $U \subset X$ be any open set that contains it. By (1.155) and the monotonicity of $\mu ^ { * }$ we have that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu^ {*} (U) \geq \mu^ {*} (U \cap C) + \mu^ {*} (U \cap (X \setminus C)) \\ \geq \mu^ {*} (E \cap C) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap (X \setminus C)). \end{array}
$$

Taking the infimum over all open sets that contain E and using (1.153) gives 

$$
\mu^ {*} (E) \geq \mu^ {*} (E \cap C) + \mu^ {*} (E \cap (X \setminus C)),
$$

and so C is $\mu ^ { * } { \mathrm { - m e a s u r a b l { \epsilon } } }$ e. 

Step 3: By the previous step the σ-algebra of all $\mu ^ { * }$ -measurable sets contains $B \left( X \right)$ . Hence, by the Carath´eodory theorem $\mu ^ { * } : \mathcal { B } ( X )  [ 0 , 1 ]$ is a measure. In view of the previous proposition and that fact that $\mu _ { n } \left( X \right) = 1$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , it remains to prove that $\mu ^ { * } \left( X \right) = 1$ and that 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(U\right) \geq \mu^ {*} \left(U\right)\tag{1.158}
$$

for every open set $U \subset X$ . Fix $j \in \mathbb N$ . Reasoning as in Substep 1a, with $C : = K ^ { ( j ) }$ , we have that $K ^ { ( j ) } \in \mathcal { K }$ . Moreover, by (1.147) and (1.148) 

$$
\mu^ {*} (K ^ {(j)}) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} (K ^ {(j)}) \geq 1 - \frac {1}{j},
$$

and so, by (1.152) 

$$
1 \geq \mu^ {*} (X) \geq \mu^ {*} (K ^ {(j)}) \geq 1 - \frac {1}{j} \rightarrow 1
$$

as $j \to \infty$ 

Finally, to prove (1.158), fix an open set $U \subset X$ . For any $K \in \mathcal { K }$ , with $K \subset U$ , by (1.148) and the monotonicity of each $\mu _ { n }$ , we have 

$$
\mu^ {*} \left(K\right) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(K\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \left(U\right).
$$

Taking the supremum over all admissible $K \subset U$ and using (1.152) yields (1.158) and completes the proof. 

If the metric space X has additional properties, then the converse of the previous theorem holds. 

Exercise 1.210. Let X be a complete, separable metric space and let $\mu ,$ $\mu _ { n } : { \mathcal { B } } ( X ) \to [ 0 , \infty ) , n \in \mathbb { N }$ , be finite Borel measures such that $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { * } {  } \mu$ in $\left( C _ { b } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ 

(i) Assume that $\mu _ { n } \left( X \right) = 1$ for all $n \in \mathbb N$ and prove that if $\{ U _ { j } \}$ is an increasing sequence of open sets such that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } U _ { j } = X$ , then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $j \in \mathbb N$ such that 

$$
\mu_ {n} (U _ {j}) \geq 1 - \varepsilon
$$

for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Construct a sequence of open balls $\left\{ B \left( x _ { i } ^ { ( k ) } , \frac { 1 } { k } \right) \right\} _ { i \in \mathbb { N } }$ that covers X and prove that there exists $i _ { k } \in \mathbb { N }$ such that 

$$
\mu_ {n} \left(\bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {i _ {k}} B \left(x _ {i} ^ {(k)}, \frac {1}{k}\right)\right) \geq 1 - \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {k}}
$$

for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Prove that (1.146) holds. 

(ii) Prove that (1.146) holds without the additional hypothesis that $\mu _ { n } \left( X \right) =$ 1 for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

The next exercise provides a simpler proof of Prohorov’s theorem in the case $X = \mathbb { R }$ . For every finite Borel measure $\mu : \mathcal { B } \left( \mathbb { R } \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right)$ define the function $f _ { \mu } : \mathbb { R } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ 

$$
f _ {\mu} (x) := \mu ((- \infty , x ]), \quad x \in \mathbb {R}.
$$

Exercise 1.211. Let $\{ \mu _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of finite Borel measures, $\mu _ { n } :$ ${ \cal B } ( \mathbb { R } )  [ 0 , \infty )$

$L ^ { p }$ Spaces 

This new integral of Lebesgue is proving itself a wonderful tool. I might compare it with a modern Krupp gun, so easily does it penetrate barriers which were impregnable. 

E. B. van Vleck, 1916 

## 2.1 Abstract Setting

In this section we introduce the $L ^ { p }$ spaces and study their properties. Proofs of standard results, such as H¨older’s and Minkowski’s inequalities, will be omitted, and we refer the reader to [Bar95], [DB02], [DuSc88], [EvGa92], [Fol99], [Rao04], [Ru87]. 

## 2.1.1 Definition and Main Properties

Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Given two measurable functions $u , v : X \to$ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ , we say that u is equivalent to v, and we write 

$$
u \sim v \text {   if   } u (x) = v (x) \text {   for   } \mu \text {   a.e.   } x \in X.\tag{2.1}
$$

Note that ∼ is an equivalence relation in the class of measurable functions. With an abuse of notation, from now on we identify a measurable function $u : X  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ with its equivalence class [u]. 

Definition 2.1. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $1 \leq p < \infty$ . Then $L ^ { p } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) : = { \Bigl \{ } u : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ] : u$ measurable and $\| u \| _ { L ^ { p } ( X , \mathfrak { M } , \mu ) } < \infty \}$ 

where 

$$
\left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (X, \mathfrak {M}, \mu)} := \left(\int_ {X} | u | ^ {p} d \mu\right) ^ {1 / p}.
$$

If p = ∞ then 

$L ^ { \infty } ( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu ) : = { \Bigl \{ } u : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ : u measurable and $\| u \| _ { L ^ { \infty } ( X , \mathfrak { M } , \mu ) } < \infty \}$ 

where $\| u \| _ { L ^ { \infty } ( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu ) }$ is the essential supremum esssup $| u |$ of the function $| u |$ that $i s _ { ; }$ , 

$$
\| u \| _ {L ^ {\infty} (X, \mathfrak {M}, \mu)} = \operatorname{esssup} | u | := \inf \left\{\alpha \in \mathbb {R}: | u (x) | <   \alpha \text {   for   } \mu \text {   a.e.   } x \in X \right\}.
$$

For simplicity, and when there is no possibility of confusion, we denote the spaces $L ^ { p } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ simply by $L ^ { p } \left( X , \mu \right)$ or $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ and the norms $\| u \| _ { L ^ { p } ( X , \mathfrak { M } , \mu ) }$ by $\left\| u \right\| _ { L ^ { p } ( X ) } , \left\| u \right\| _ { L ^ { p } } \mathrm { o r } \left\| u \right\| _ { p } .$ 

We denote by $L ^ { p } \left( X , \mathfrak { M } , \mu ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ (or more simply by $L ^ { p } ( X ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ) )$ the space of all functions $u : X  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ whose components are in $L ^ { p } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ . We will endow $L ^ { p } \left( X , \mathfrak { M } , \mu ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ with the norm 

$$
\left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (X, \mathfrak {M}, \mu ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m})} := \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m} \left\| u _ {i} \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (X, \mathfrak {M}, \mu)}.
$$

For $1 \leq p < \infty$ sometimes it will be more convenient to use the equivalent norm 

$$
\left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (X, \mathfrak {M}, \mu ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m})} := \left(\int_ {X} | u | ^ {p} d \mu\right) ^ {1 / p}.
$$

Remark ${ \it 2 . 2 . }$ . In the special case that $X = \mathbb { N }$ and $\mu$ is the counting measure, the spaces $L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { N } \right)$ are also denoted by $\ell ^ { p \ }$ , and we have 

$$
\ell^ {p} = \left\{\left\{x _ {n} \right\} _ {n \in \mathbb {N}}: \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} | x _ {n} | ^ {p} <   \infty \right\}
$$

for $1 \leq p < \infty$ , while 

$$
\ell^ {\infty} = \left\{\{x _ {n} \} _ {n \in \mathbb {N}}: \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} | x _ {n} | <   \infty \right\}.
$$

Let $q$ be the H¨older conjugate exponent of $p , { \mathrm { i . e . } }$ , 

$$
q := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {p}{p - 1} & \text { if } 1 <   p <   \infty , \\ \infty & \text { if } p = 1, \\ 1 & \text { if } p = \infty . \end{array} \right.
$$

Note that, with an abuse of notation, we have 

$$
\frac {1}{p} + \frac {1}{q} = 1.
$$

In the sequel, the H¨older conjugate exponent of $p$ will often be denoted by $p ^ { \prime } .$ 

Theorem 2.3 (H¨older’s inequality). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, let $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , and let q be its H¨older conjugate exponent. If u, $v : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ are measurable functions then 

$$
\left\| u v \right\| _ {L ^ {1}} \leq \left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} \left\| v \right\| _ {L ^ {q}}.\tag{2.2}
$$

In particular, if $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ and $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ then uv $\in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ 

Remark $\it 4 . 4 . \left( \mathrm { i } \right)$ If $1 < p _ { 1 } , \ldots , p _ { n } < \infty$ , with $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { p _ { 1 } } + \ldots + \frac { 1 } { p _ { n } } = 1 } \end{array}$ , and $u _ { i } \in$ $L ^ { p _ { i } } ( X ) , i = 1 , \dots , n .$ , then 

$$
\left\| \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} u _ {i} \right\| _ {L ^ {1}} \leq \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left\| u _ {i} \right\| _ {L ^ {p _ {i}}}.
$$

This inequality follows by applying H¨older’s inequality with $u : = u _ { 1 } , v : =$ $\textstyle \prod _ { i = 2 } ^ { n } u _ { i }$ , and then using an induction argument. 

(ii) Another consequence of H¨older’s inequality is 

$$
\left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {q}} \leq \left(\left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {p}}\right) ^ {\theta} \left(\left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {r}}\right) ^ {1 - \theta},
$$

which holds for $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ , and where $\ : 1 < p < q < r < \infty \ :$ , with $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { q } = \frac { \theta } { p } + \frac { ( 1 - \theta ) } { r } } \end{array}$ . To prove it, apply H¨older’s inequality, with $\textstyle { \frac { p } { \theta q } } , \left| u \right| ^ { \theta q }$ , and ${ \left| u \right| } ^ { \left( 1 - \theta \right) q }$ in place of $p , u$ , and v, respectively, to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {X} | u | ^ {q} d \mu = \int_ {X} | u | ^ {\theta q} | u | ^ {(1 - \theta) q} d \mu \\ \qquad \leq \left(\int_ {X} | u | ^ {\theta q \left(\frac {p}{\theta q}\right)} d \mu\right) ^ {1 / \left(\frac {p}{\theta q}\right)} \left(\int_ {X} | u | ^ {(1 - \theta) q \left(\frac {p}{\theta q}\right) ^ {\prime}} d \mu\right) ^ {1 / \left(\frac {p}{\theta q}\right) ^ {\prime}} \\ \qquad = \left(\int_ {X} | u | ^ {p} d \mu\right) ^ {\theta q / p} \left(\int_ {X} | u | ^ {r} d \mu\right) ^ {(1 - \theta) q / r}. \end{array}
$$

(iii) If $u \ne 0$ and the right-hand side of (2.2) is finite, then the equality in (2.2) holds if and only if there exists $c \geq 0$ such that 

a) $| v | = c | u | ^ { p - 1 } { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } 1 < p < \infty ;$ 

b) $| v | \leq c$ and $\left| v \left( x \right) \right| = c$ whenever u $( x ) \neq 0 { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } p = 1$ ; 

c) $| u | \leq c$ and $| u \left( x \right) | = c$ whenever $v \left( x \right) \neq 0 \mathrm { i f } p = \infty$ 

We now turn to the relation between diferent $L ^ { p }$ spaces. 

Theorem 2.5. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Suppose that $1 \leq p < q <$ ∞. Then 

(i) $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ is not contained in $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ if and only if X contains measurable sets of arbitrarily small positive measure; 

(ii) $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ is not contained in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ if and only if X contains measurable sets of arbitrarily large finite measure. 

Proof. (i) Assume that $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ is not contained in $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ . Then there exists $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ such that 

$$
\int_ {X} | u | ^ {q} d \mu = \infty .\tag{2.3}
$$

For each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ let 

$$
E _ {n} := \left\{x \in X: | u (x) | > n \right\}.
$$

Then 

$$
\mu \left(E _ {n}\right) \leq \frac {1}{n ^ {p}} \int_ {X} | u | ^ {p} d \mu \rightarrow 0
$$

as $n \to \infty$ . Thus, it sufices to show that $\mu \left( E _ { n } \right) > 0$ for all n suficiently large. If to the contrary, $\mu \left( E _ { n } \right) = 0$ for infinitely many n, we have that 

$$
\int_ {X} | u | ^ {q} d \mu = \int_ {\{| u | \leq n \}} | u | ^ {q} d \mu \leq n ^ {q - p} \int_ {\{| u | \leq n \}} | u | ^ {p} d \mu <   \infty ,
$$

which is a contradiction with (2.3). Hence, X contains measurable sets of arbitrarily small positive measure. 

Conversely, assume that X contains measurable sets of arbitrarily small positive measure. Then it is possible to construct a sequence of pairwise disjoint sets $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ such that $\mu \left( E _ { n } \right) > 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and 

$$
\mu \left(E _ {n}\right) \searrow 0.
$$

Let 

$$
u := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} c _ {n} \chi_ {E _ {n}},
$$

where $c _ { n } \nearrow \infty$ are chosen such that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} c _ {n} ^ {q} \mu (E _ {n}) = \infty , \quad \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} c _ {n} ^ {p} \mu (E _ {n}) <   \infty .\tag{2.4}
$$

Then $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right) \backslash L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ 

(ii) Assume that $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ is not contained in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ . Then there exists $u \in$ $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ such that 

$$
\int_ {X} | u | ^ {p} d \mu = \infty .\tag{2.5}
$$

For each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ let 

$$
F _ {n} := \left\{x \in X: \frac {1}{n + 1} <   | u (x) | \leq \frac {1}{n} \right\}
$$

and let 

$$
F _ {\infty} := \{x \in X: 0 <   | u (x) | \leq 1 \} = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {n}.
$$

If $\mu \left( F _ { \infty } \right) < \infty$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {X} | u | ^ {p} d \mu = \int_ {\{| u | \leq 1 \}} | u | ^ {p} d \mu + \int_ {\{| u | > 1 \}} | u | ^ {p} d \mu \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \mu (F _ {\infty}) + \int_ {\{| u | > 1 \}} | u | ^ {q} d \mu <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

which contradicts (2.5). Hence, $\mu \left( F _ { \infty } \right) = \infty$ . On the other hand, since for every $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , 

$$
\infty > \int_ {X} | u | ^ {q} d \mu \geq \int_ {\left\{\frac {1}{n + 1} <   | u | \leq \frac {1}{n} \right\}} | u | ^ {q} d \mu \geq \frac {1}{(n + 1) ^ {q}} \mu \left(F _ {n}\right),
$$

it follows that $X$ contains measurable sets of arbitrarily large finite measure. Indeed, setting 

$$
G _ {n} := \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {n} F _ {k},
$$

we have that $\mu \left( G _ { n } \right) < \infty$ , while by Proposition $1 . 7 ( \mathrm { i } )$ ， 

$$
\mu \left(G _ {n}\right)\rightarrow \mu \left(F _ {\infty}\right) = \infty .
$$

Conversely, assume that $X$ contains measurable sets of arbitrarily large finite measure. Then it is possible to construct a sequence of pairwise disjoint sets $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ of finite measure such that 

$$
\mu \left(E _ {n}\right) \nearrow \infty .
$$

Let 

$$
u := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} c _ {n} \chi_ {E _ {n}},
$$

where $c _ { n } \searrow 0$ are chosen such that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} c _ {n} ^ {q} \mu (E _ {n}) <   \infty , \quad \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} c _ {n} ^ {p} \mu (E _ {n}) = \infty .\tag{2.6}
$$

Then $u \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right) \backslash L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ 

Exercise 2.6. (i) Let $X = [ 0 , 1 ]$ and let $\mu$ be the Lebesgue measure. Show that for every $1 \leq p < \infty$ the function 

$$
u (x) = \frac {1}{x ^ {1 / p} \log^ {2 / p} \left(\frac {2}{x}\right)}
$$

is in $L ^ { p } \left( \left[ 0 , 1 \right] \right)$ but not in $L ^ { q } \left( \left[ 0 , 1 \right] \right)$ for all $q > p .$ 

(ii) Construct sequences $c _ { n } \nearrow \infty$ and $c _ { n } \searrow 0$ for which conditions (2.4) and (2.6) hold, respectively. 

Theorem 2.7 (Minkowski’s inequality). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, let $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , and let u, $v \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ . Then $u + v \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ and 

$$
\left\| u + v \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} \leq \left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} + \left\| v \right\| _ {L ^ {p}}.
$$

By identifying functions with their equivalence classes $[ u ]$ , it follows from Minkowski’s inequality that $\| \cdot \| _ { L ^ { p } }$ is a norm on $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ 

Theorem 2.8. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Then 

(i) $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ is a Banach space for $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ ; 

(ii) $L ^ { 2 } \left( X \right)$ is a Hilbert space. 

Exercise 2.9. When $0 < p < 1$ we can still define the space 

$L ^ { p } ( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu ) : = { \bigg \{ } u : X  [ - \infty , \infty ] :$ u measurable and $\int _ { X } | u | ^ { p } \ d \mu < \infty \}$ 

This is no longer a normed space. Using the elementary inequality 

$$
(a + b) ^ {p} \leq a ^ {p} + b ^ {p},
$$

where $a , b \geq 0$ , show that 

$$
d _ {p} (u, v) := \int_ {X} | u - v | ^ {p} d \mu
$$

is a metric (provided we identify measurable functions that coincide $\mu \ \mathrm { a . e . } )$ and that $\left( L ^ { p } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) , d _ { p } \right)$ is a complete metric space. Prove also that the family of balls is a base for a topology that renders $L ^ { p } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ a topological vector space. 

Next we study some density results for $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ spaces. 

Theorem 2.10. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Then the family of all simple functions in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ is dense in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ for $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ 

Proof. Assume first that $1 \leq p < \infty$ . Since ${ ( u ^ { + } ) ^ { p } , ( u ^ { - } ) ^ { p } \in L ^ { 1 } ( X ) }$ , by Theorem 1.74 there exist increasing sequences $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ and $\{ t _ { n } \}$ of simple functions, each of which is bounded in $X$ and vanishes except on a set of finite measure $\mu ,$ such that $\{ ( s _ { n } ( x ) ) ^ { p } \}$ converges monotonically to $\left( u ^ { + } \right) ^ { p } \left( x \right)$ for µ a.e. $x \in X$ and $\{ ( t _ { n } ( x ) ) ^ { \bar { p } } \}$ converges monotonically to $\left( u ^ { - } \right) ^ { p } \left( x \right)$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ . Then for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ the function $S _ { n } : = s _ { n } - t _ { n }$ is still simple, belongs to $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ ， and 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\left| u \left(x\right) - S _ {n} \left(x\right) \right| ^ {p} = \left| u ^ {+} \left(x\right) - s _ {n} \left(x\right) - \left(u ^ {-} \left(x\right) - t _ {n} \left(x\right)\right) \right| ^ {p}} \\ & {\qquad \leq 2 ^ {p - 1} \left(u ^ {+} \left(x\right) - s _ {n} \left(x\right)\right) ^ {p} + 2 ^ {p - 1} \left(u ^ {-} \left(x\right) - t _ {n} \left(x\right)\right) ^ {p}} \\ & {\qquad \leq 2 ^ {p - 1} \left(u ^ {+} \left(x\right)\right) ^ {p} + 2 ^ {p - 1} \left(u ^ {-} \left(x\right)\right) ^ {p}} \end{array}
$$

for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ . Since $u ( x ) - S _ { n } ( x )  0$ as $n \to \infty$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ , we may apply the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem to conclude that $S _ { n } \to u$ in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ 

For $p = \infty$ the result follows by the second part of Theorem 1.74 applied to the bounded functions $u ^ { + } , u ^ { - }$ 

The next result gives conditions on X and $\mu$ that ensure the density of continuous functions in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ 

Theorem 2.11. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, with X a normal space and $\mu \textit { a }$ Borel measure such that 

$$
\mu (E) = \sup \left\{\mu (C): C \text {closed}, C \subset E \right\} = \inf \left\{\mu (A): A \text {open}, A \supset E \right\}
$$

for every set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with finite measure. Then $L ^ { p } \left( X \right) \cap C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ is dense in $L ^ { { \boldsymbol { p } } } \left( X \right) f o r { \boldsymbol { 1 } } \leq { \boldsymbol { p } } < \infty$ 

Proof. Since by Theorem 2.10 simple functions in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ are dense in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ it sufices to approximate in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ functions $\chi _ { E }$ , with $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ , by functions in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right) \cap C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ . Thus, fix $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ , and for any $\varepsilon > 0$ find an open set $A \supset E$ and a closed set $C \subset E$ such that 

$$
\mu \left(A \setminus C\right) \leq \varepsilon^ {p}.
$$

By Urysohn’s lemma there exists a continuous function $u : X  [ 0 , 1 ]$ such that $u \equiv 1$ in C and $u \equiv 0$ in $X \setminus A$ . Since supp $u \subset A$ and $\mu \left( A \right) < \infty$ , it follows that $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right) \cap C _ { b } \left( X \right)$ . Moreover, 

$$
\int_ {X} | \chi_ {E} - u | ^ {p} d \mu = \int_ {A \backslash C} | \chi_ {E} - u | ^ {p} d \mu \leq \mu (A \setminus C) \leq \varepsilon^ {p},
$$

and the result follows. 

Definition 2.12. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, with X a topological space, $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ a Borel measure, and $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ . A measurable function $u : X  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is said to belong to $L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { p } \left( X \right) \ i f \ u \in \ L ^ { p } \left( K \right)$ for every compact set $K \subset X$ . A sequence $\{ u _ { n } \} \subset L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { p } \tilde { ( X ) }$ is said to converge to u in $L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { p } ( X ) \ i f u _ { n }  u$ in $L ^ { p } \left( K \right)$ for every compact set $K \subset X$ 

Definition 2.13. A measurable space (X, M) is called separable if there exists a sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ such that the smallest σ-algebra that contains all the sets $E _ { n }$ is M. In this case M is said to be generated by the sequence $\{ E _ { n } \}$ 

Example 2.14. The σ-algebra of all Lebesgue measurable sets in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is gener ated by the countable family of cubes with centers in $\mathbb { Q } ^ { N }$ and rational side length. 

Exercise 2.15. Prove that if X is a separable metric space and M is the Borel σ-algebra, then X is a separable measurable space. 

Theorem 2.16. Let (X, M) be a separable measurable space with M generated by a sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ , and assume that µ is σ-finite. Let N be the smallest algebra containing $\{ E _ { n } \}$ . Then simple functions of the form 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} c _ {i} \chi_ {F _ {i}},
$$

where $n \in \mathbb { N } , c _ { i } \in \mathbb { Q }$ , and $F _ { i } \in \mathfrak { N } , \mu \left( F _ { i } \right) < \infty , i = 1 , \ldots , n$ , form a countable dense subset of $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ for $1 \leq p < \infty$ . In particular, $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ is separable for $1 \leq p < \infty$ 

Proof. ## 2.1.2 Strong Convergence in ${ \pmb { L } } ^ { p }$

In this subsection we study diferent modes of convergence and their relation to one another. 

Definition 2.18. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $u _ { n } , u : X \to \mathbb { R }$ be measurable functions. 

(i) $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is said to converge to u almost uniformly if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $\mu \left( E \right) < \varepsilon \ a n d \left\{ u _ { n } \right\}$ converges to u uniformly in $X \setminus E ;$ 

(ii) $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is said to converge to u in measure if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mu \left(\{x \in X: | u _ {n} (x) - u (x) | > \varepsilon \}\right) = 0.
$$

Definition 2.19. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with $\mu { \boldsymbol { \sigma } } { - } f i n i t e ,$ , and let $u _ { n } , u \in L ^ { \infty } ( X ) , n \in \mathbb { N }$ . The sequence $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is said to converge to u with respect to the Mackey topology $i f \left\{ u _ { n } \right\}$ converges to u in measure and 

$$
\sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \| u _ {n} \| _ {L ^ {\infty}} <   \infty .
$$

The next theorem relates the types of convergence introduced in Definition 2.18 with convergence in $L ^ { p }$ 

Theorem 2.20. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $u _ { n } , u : X \to \mathbb { R }$ be measurable functions. 

(i) $H \left\{ u _ { n } \right\}$ converges to u almost uniformly, then it converges to u in measure and pointwise $\mu$ almost everywhere; 

(ii) if $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges to u in measure, then there exists a subsequence $\{ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ such that $\{ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ converges to u almost uniformly (and hence pointwise $\mu$ almost everywhere); 

(iii) if $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges to u in $L ^ { p } , \ 1 \ \leq \ p \ \leq \ \infty$ , then it converges to u in measure and there exist a subsequence $\{ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ and a function $v \in L ^ { p }$ such that $\{ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ converges to u almost uniformly (and hence pointwise $\mu$ almost everywhere) and $\left| u _ { n _ { k } } \left( x \right) \right| \le v \left( x \right)$ for µ a.e. $x \in X$ and for all $k \in \mathbb N$ 

All the other implications fail in general. 

Exercise 2.21. (i) Pointwise convergence $\mu$ almost everywhere does not imply convergence in measure or in $L ^ { p } , 1 \leq p < \infty$ . To see this, let $X = \mathbb { N }$ , ${ \mathfrak { M } } = { \mathcal { P } } \left( \mathbb { N } \right)$ , and let $\mu$ be the counting measure. Define $u _ { n } : = \chi _ { \{ n \} }$ . Show that $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges to zero pointwise but neither in measure nor in $L ^ { p }$ , $1 \leq p < \infty$ 

(ii) Convergence in measure or in $L ^ { p } , 1 \leq p < \infty$ , does not imply pointwise convergence $\mu$ almost everywhere. Let $X = [ 0 , 1 ) , \mathfrak { M } = \mathcal { B } ( [ 0 , 1 ) )$ , and let $\mu$ be the Lebesgue measure. Consider the sequence of intervals $[ 0 , \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } )$ , $[ \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } , 1 ) , ( 0 , \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 3 } } ) , ( \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 3 } } , \frac { \bar { 2 } } { 3 } ) , ( \textstyle { \frac { 2 } { 3 } } , 1 ) , ( 0 , \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 4 } } ) , ( \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 4 } } , \frac { 2 } { 4 } ) , [ \textstyle { \frac { 2 } { 4 } } , \frac { 3 } { 4 } ) , ( \textstyle { \frac { 3 } { 4 } } , 1 ) , . . . .$ Let $u _ { n }$ be the characteristic function of the nth interval of this sequence. Show that $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges to zero in measure and in $L ^ { p } , 1 \leq p < \infty$ , but the limit 

$$
