$$

does not exist for every $x \in [ 0 , 1 )$ 

(iii) Pointwise convergence $\mu$ almost everywhere does not imply almost uniform convergence. Let $\begin{array} { r } { X = \mathbb { N } , \mathfrak { M } = \mathcal { P } \left( \mathbb { N } \right) } \end{array}$ , and let $\mu$ be the counting measure. Define $u _ { n } : = \chi _ { \{ 1 , \ldots , n \} }$ . Show that $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges to one point wise but not almost uniformly. 

Concerning (iii) in the example above, we remark that when the measure is finite, then convergence $\mu$ almost everywhere implies almost uniform convergence. This follows from the next theorem. 

Theorem 2.22 (Egorof). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with $\mu$ finite and let $u _ { n } : X \to \mathbb { R }$ be measurable functions converging pointwise $\mu$ almost everywhere. Then $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges almost uniformly (and hence in measure). 

In order to characterize convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ for $1 \leq p < \infty$ we need to introduce the notion of equi-integrability. 

Definition 2.23. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. A family $\mathcal { F }$ of measurable functions $u : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is said to be 

(i) equi-integrable if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
\int_ {E} | u | d \mu \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all $u \in { \mathcal { F } }$ and for every measurable set $E \subset X$ with $\mu \left( E \right) \leq \delta$ 

(ii) p-equi-integrable, $p > 0$ , if the family of functions $\{ | u | ^ { p } : u \in { \mathcal { F } } \}$ is equiintegrable. 

Theorem 2.24 (Vitali convergence theorem). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, let $1 \leq p < \infty ,$ , and let $u _ { n } , u : X \to \mathbb { R }$ be measurable functions. Then $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges to u in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ if and only if 

(i) $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges to u in measure; 

(ii) $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is p-equi-integrable; 

(iii) for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $E \subset X$ with $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ and 

$$
\int_ {X \setminus E} | u _ {n} | ^ {p} d \mu \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all $n .$ . 

Remark 2.25. Note that condition (iii) is automatically satisfied when X has finite measure. 

Example 2.26. Let $X = \mathbb { R } , \mathfrak { M } = B ( \mathbb { R } )$ , and let $\mu$ be the Lebesgue measure. The sequence $u _ { n } = n \chi _ { \left[ 0 , \frac { 1 } { n } \right] }$ converges in measure to zero, satisfies (iii), but is not equi-integrable, while the sequence $\begin{array} { r } { u _ { n } = \frac { 1 } { n } \chi _ { [ n , 2 n ] } } \end{array}$ converges in measure to zero, is equi-integrable, but does not satisfy (iii). 

Conditions (ii) and (iii) hold if the sequence is dominated by a function $v \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ . Precisely, we have the following result, which will be used to prove the decomposition lemma below. 

Proposition 2.27. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $u _ { n } \ : \ X \ \to$ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ be measurable functions. If there exists $v \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ such that 

$$
\left| u _ {n} (x) \right| \leq v (x)\tag{2.7}
$$

for all n and for µ a.e. $x \in X$ , then $\{ u _ { n } \}$ satisfies conditions $( i i )$ and (iii) of Vitali’s theorem. 

Proof. Define 

$$
\nu (E) := \int_ {E} | v | ^ {p} d \mu , \quad E \in \mathfrak {M}.
$$

Then ν is a finite measure absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu ,$ and so by Proposition 1.99, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
\int_ {E} | v | ^ {p} d \mu \leq \varepsilon\tag{2.8}
$$

for every measurable set $E \subset X$ with $\mu \left( E \right) \leq \delta$ , while by Proposition 1.7(i), 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {t \to \infty} \int_ {\left\{x \in X: \frac {1}{t} <   | v | <   t \right\}} | v | ^ {p} d \mu = \int_ {\left\{x \in X: 0 <   | v | <   \infty \right\}} | v | ^ {p} d \mu \\ = \int_ {X} | v | ^ {p} d \mu , \end{array}\tag{2.9}
$$

where we have used the fact that the set $\{ x \in X : | v ( x ) | = \infty \}$ has $\mu$ measure zero (see Remark 1.78). 

Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and let $\delta > 0$ be such that (2.8) is satisfied. 

Then for every measurable set $E \subset X$ with $\mu \left( E \right) \leq \delta$ , by (2.7) and (2.8) for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ we have 

$$
\int_ {E} | u _ {n} | ^ {p} d \mu \leq \int_ {E} | v | ^ {p} d \mu \leq \varepsilon .
$$

Hence $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is p-equi-integrable. 

Next, by (2.9) there exists $t > 0$ so large that 

$$
\int_ {X} | v | ^ {p} d \mu - \int_ {\left\{x \in X: \frac {1}{t} <   | v | <   t \right\}} | v | ^ {p} d \mu = \int_ {X \setminus \left\{x \in X: \frac {1}{t} <   | v | <   t \right\}} | v | ^ {p} d \mu \leq \varepsilon .
$$

Set 

$$
E _ {\varepsilon} := \left\{x \in X: \frac {1}{t} <   | v (x) | <   t \right\}.
$$

Then $\mu \left( E _ { \varepsilon } \right) < \infty$ by Remark 1.78 and by (2.7), 

$$
\int_ {X \setminus E _ {\varepsilon}} | u _ {n} | ^ {p} d \mu \leq \int_ {X \setminus E _ {\varepsilon}} | v | ^ {p} d \mu \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all $n .$ 

Remark 2.28. Note that any finite family $\{ u _ { 1 } , \ldots , u _ { l } \}$ of functions in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ satisfies the hypothesis of the previous proposition. Indeed, it sufices to define $v : = \operatorname* { m a x } \left\{ \left| u _ { 1 } \right| , \ldots , \left| u _ { l } \right| \right\}$ 

In view of Vitali’s theorem it becomes important to understand equiintegrability. 

Theorem 2.29. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, let $1 \leq p < \infty$ , and let ${ \mathcal { F } } \subset L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ be a bounded set. Then the following conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\mathcal { F }$ is p-equi-integrable; 

(ii) 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \sup _ {u \in \mathcal {F}} \int_ {\{x \in X: | u | > t \}} | u | ^ {p} d \mu = 0;\tag{2.10}
$$

(iii) (De la Vall´ee Poussin) there exists an increasing function $\gamma : [ 0 , \infty ) $ $[ 0 , \infty ]$ , with 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \frac {\gamma (t)}{t} = \infty\tag{2.11}
$$

such that 

$$
\sup _ {u \in \mathcal {F}} \int_ {X} \gamma (| u | ^ {p}) d \mu <   \infty .\tag{2.12}
$$

Proof. By replacing the family $\mathcal { F }$ with $\{ | u | ^ { p } : u \in { \mathcal { F } } \}$ , without loss of generality, we may assume that $p = 1$ . Let 

$$
C := \sup _ {u \in \mathcal {F}} \| u \| _ {L ^ {1} (X)} <   \infty .\tag{2.13}
$$

Step 1: Assume that $\mathcal { F }$ is equi-integrable and, given $\varepsilon > 0$ let $\delta > 0$ be such that 

$$
\sup _ {u \in \mathcal {F}} \int_ {F} | u | d \mu \leq \varepsilon
$$

for every measurable set $F \subset X$ with $\mu \left( F \right) \leq \delta$ . Choose $t _ { \varepsilon } > 0$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { C } { t _ { \varepsilon } } \leq \delta . } \end{array}$ . Then, also by (2.13), for every $u \in { \mathcal { F } }$ and for all $t \geq t _ { \varepsilon }$ we have 

$$
\mu \left(\{x \in X: | u | > t \}\right) \leq \frac {1}{t} \| u \| _ {L ^ {1} (X)} \leq \frac {C}{t} \leq \delta ,
$$

and so 

$$
\sup _ {u \in \mathcal {F}} \int_ {\{x \in X: | u | > t \}} | u | d \mu \leq \varepsilon ,
$$

and this validates (ii). 

Conversely, suppose that (ii) holds, fix $\varepsilon > 0$ , and choose $t _ { \varepsilon } > 0$ such that 

$$
\sup _ {u \in \mathcal {F}} \int_ {\{x \in X: | u | > t _ {\varepsilon} \}} | u | d \mu \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2}.
$$

Then for every measurable set $F \subset X$ with $\textstyle \mu \left( F \right) \leq { \frac { \varepsilon } { 2 t _ { \varepsilon } } }$ and for all $u \in { \mathcal { F } }$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {F} | u | d \mu = \int_ {\{x \in F: | u | > t _ {\varepsilon} \}} | u | d \mu + \int_ {\{x \in F: | u | \leq t _ {\varepsilon} \}} | u | d \mu \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2} + t _ {\varepsilon} \mu (F) \leq \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Step 2: Assume that (ii) holds and construct an increasing sequence of nonnegative integers $\{ k _ { i } \}$ such that 

$$
\sup _ {u \in \mathcal {F}} \int_ {\{x \in X: | u | > k _ {i} \}} | u | d \mu \leq \frac {1}{2 ^ {i + 1}}.
$$

For each $l \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ let $b _ { l }$ be the number of nonnegative integers $i$ such that $k _ { i } < l$ Note that $b _ { l } \nearrow \infty$ as $l  \infty$ . Define 

$$
\gamma (t) := t b _ {l} \quad \text { if } t \in [ l, l + 1).
$$

Then 

$$
\frac {\gamma (t)}{t} \geq b _ {\lceil t \rceil} \rightarrow \infty
$$

as $t  \infty$ , where $\lceil t \rceil$ is the integer part of $t .$ Moreover, for all $u \in \mathcal { F }$ , by Example 1.82, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {X} \gamma (| u |) d \mu = \sum_ {l = 0} ^ {\infty} \int_ {\{l \leq | u | <   l + 1 \}} \gamma (| u |) d \mu \\ \qquad = \sum_ {l = 0} ^ {\infty} b _ {l} \int_ {\{l \leq | u | <   l + 1 \}} | u | d \mu = \sum_ {l = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {i: k _ {i} <   l} \int_ {\{l \leq | u | <   l + 1 \}} | u | d \mu \\ \qquad = \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {l > k _ {i}} \int_ {\{l \leq | u | <   l + 1 \}} | u | d \mu \leq \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \int_ {\{| u | > k _ {i} \}} | u | d \mu \leq \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {i + 1}}. \end{array}
$$

Conversely, assume that (iii) holds and let 

$$
M := \sup _ {u \in \mathcal {F}} \int_ {X} \gamma (| u |) d \mu <   \infty .
$$

By (2.11), for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $t _ { \varepsilon } > 0$ such that 

$$
\gamma (t) \geq \frac {2 t M}{\varepsilon} \quad \mathrm{forall} t \geq t _ {\varepsilon}.
$$

Then for every measurable set $F \subset X$ with $\textstyle \mu \left( F \right) \leq { \frac { \varepsilon } { 2 t _ { \varepsilon } } }$ and for all $u \in { \mathcal { F } }$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {F} | u | d \mu = \int_ {\{x \in F: | u | > t _ {\varepsilon} \}} | u | d \mu + \int_ {\{x \in F: | u | \leq t _ {\varepsilon} \}} | u | d \mu \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2 M} \int_ {X} \gamma (| u |) d \mu + t _ {\varepsilon} \mu (F) \leq \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Hence $\mathcal { F }$ is equi-integrable. 

Remark 2.30. Often the suficient condition (2.12) for equi-integrability is stated for $\mathrm { a }$ continuous, finite, increasing function $\gamma .$ Note that if $\gamma$ takes the value $\infty$ at some $t _ { 0 } \geq 0 ,$ , then $\gamma \equiv \infty$ on $[ t _ { 0 } , \infty )$ . Therefore condition (2.12) implies that the set $\mathcal { F }$ is bounded in $L ^ { \infty }$ . Moreover, $\operatorname { i f } \gamma$ is finite, then it is possible to construct a finite, nonnegative, increasing, continuous, convex function $\widetilde { \gamma }$ below $\gamma$ that still satisfies (2.11) (see Remark 4.99 below), and therefore it sufices to apply the previous theorem with $\widetilde { \gamma }$ in place of $\gamma .$ 

An important consequence of Theorem 2.29 is the following result. 

Lemma 2.31 (Decomposition lemma, I). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, and let $u _ { n } : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be measurable functions such that 

$$
\sup _ {n} \left\| u _ {n} \right\| _ {L ^ {1}} <   \infty .
$$

For $r > 0$ consider the truncation $\tau _ { r } : \mathbb { R } \to \mathbb { R }$ defined by 

$$
\tau_ {r} (z) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} z & \quad i f \quad | z | \leq r, \\ \frac {z}{| z |} r & \quad i f \quad | z | > r. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then there exist a subsequence $\{ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ u _ { n } \}$ and an increasing sequence of positive integers $j _ { k } \to \infty$ such that the truncated sequence $\{ \tau _ { j _ { k } } \circ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ is equi-integrable and 

$$
\mu \left(\{x \in X: u _ {n _ {k}} (x) \neq (\tau_ {j _ {k}} \circ u _ {n _ {k}}) (x) \}\right)\rightarrow 0
$$

as $k \to \infty$ 

We first state and prove a simple auxiliary criterion for equi-integrability. Lemma 2.32. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, and let $u _ { n } : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be measurable functions such that $\mathrm { s u p } _ { n } \| u _ { n } \| _ { L ^ { 1 } } < \infty$ . Then $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is equiintegrable if and only if 

$$
\lim_{\substack{j\to \infty \\ j\in \mathbb{N}}}\sup_{n}\int_{\{x\in X:|u_{n}| > j\}}\left(|u_{n}| - j\right)  d\mu = 0.
$$

Proof. If $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is equi-integrable, then 

$$
\sup _ {n} \int_ {\{x \in X: | u _ {n} | > j \}} (| u _ {n} | - j) d \mu \leq \sup _ {n} \int_ {\{x \in X: | u _ {n} | > j \}} | u _ {n} | d \mu \rightarrow 0
$$

as $j \to \infty$ , where we have used (2.10). 

Conversely, fix $\varepsilon > 0$ , let 

$$
c := \sup _ {n} \left\| u _ {n} \right\| _ {L ^ {1}},
$$

and choose $j \in \mathbb N$ so large that 

$$
\sup _ {n} \int_ {\{x \in X: | u _ {n} | > j \}} (| u _ {n} | - j) d \mu \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2}.
$$

If $\textstyle t \geq { \frac { 2 c j } { \varepsilon } }$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {\{x \in X: | u _ {n} | > t \}} | u _ {n} | d \mu = \int_ {\{x \in X: | u _ {n} | > t \}} (| u _ {n} | - j) d \mu + j \mu (\{x \in X: | u _ {n} | > t \}) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2} + \frac {j}{t} \int_ {X} | u _ {n} | d \mu \leq \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

In view of Theorem 2.29 we conclude that the sequence is equi-integrable. 

Proof (Lemma 2.31). Without loss of generality we may assume that 

$$
\sup _ {n} \int_ {X} | u _ {n} | d \mu \leq 1.
$$

For $j \in \mathbb N$ define 

$$
\varphi \left(j\right) := \sup _ {n} \int_ {\left\{\left| u _ {n} \right| \geq j \right\}} \left(\left| u _ {n} \right| - j\right) d \mu , \quad \varphi_ {\infty} := \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {j \rightarrow \infty} \varphi \left(j\right).\tag{2.14}
$$

If $\varphi _ { \infty } = 0$ , then by the previous lemma we deduce that $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is equi-integrable and the statement of the decomposition lemma is verified with $n _ { k } : = k$ and $j _ { k } : = k$ . If $\varphi _ { \infty } > 0$ , then find $j _ { 1 } , n _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { N }$ so large that 

$$
\int_ {\left\{\left| u _ {n _ {1}} \right| \geq j _ {1} \right\}} \left(\left| u _ {n _ {1}} \right| - j _ {1}\right) d \mu \geq \frac {\varphi_ {\infty}}{2}.
$$

By induction, assume that positive integers $n _ { 1 } < . . . < n _ { k - 1 }$ and $j _ { 1 } < \ldots <$ $j _ { k - 1 }$ have been chosen, and we claim that there exist $j _ { k } > j _ { k - 1 }$ and $n _ { k } > n _ { k - 1 }$ $j _ { k } , n _ { k } \in \mathbb { N }$ , such that 

$$
\int_ {\left\{\left| u _ {n _ {k}} \right| \geq j _ {k} \right\}} \left(\left| u _ {n _ {k}} \right| - j _ {k}\right) d \mu \geq \left(1 - \frac {1}{2 ^ {k}}\right) \varphi_ {\infty}.\tag{2.15}
$$

Indeed, if this were false, then 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {j \to \infty} \sup _ {n > n _ {k - 1}} \int_ {\{| u _ {n} | \geq j \}} \left(| u _ {n} | - j\right) d \mu \leq \left(1 - \frac {1}{2 ^ {k}}\right) \varphi_ {\infty},
$$

and in turn, 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {j \to \infty} \sup _ {n \leq n _ {k - 1}} \int_ {\{| u _ {n} | \geq j \}} (| u _ {n} | - j) d \mu = \varphi_ {\infty} > 0,
$$

and this, in view of the previous lemma, implies that the finite family $\left\{ u _ { 1 } , \ldots , u _ { n _ { k - 1 } } \right\}$ is not equi-integrable. In view of Remark 2.28 we have reached a contradiction, and hence the claim is established. 

Next we show that the sequence $\{ \tau _ { j _ { k } } \circ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ satisfies the properties requested. Note first that 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\mu \left(\left\{x \in X: u _ {n _ {k}} (x) \neq \left(\tau_ {j _ {k}} \circ u _ {n _ {k}}\right) (x) \right\}\right)\\\leq \mu \left(\left\{x \in X: | u _ {n _ {k}} (x) | \geq j _ {k} \right\}\right) \leq \frac {1}{j _ {k}} \int_ {X} | u _ {n} | d \mu \leq \frac {1}{j _ {k}} \rightarrow 0\end{array}
$$

as $k \to \infty$ 

In order to prove equi-integrability of the sequence $\{ \tau _ { j _ { k } } \circ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ , fix $l \in \mathbb N$ and let 

$$
k _ {l} := \min \left\{k \in \mathbb {N}: j _ {k} \geq l \right\}.
$$

Then $k _ { l }  \infty$ as $l \to \infty$ . Note that if $k < k _ { l }$ , then $\{ x \in X : | \tau _ { j _ { k } } \circ u _ { n _ { k } } | \geq l \}$ is empty, while if $k \geq k _ { l }$ , then $j _ { k } \geq l$ , and so 

$$
\min \left\{\left| \tau_ {j _ {k}} \circ u _ {n _ {k}} \right|, l \right\} = \min \left\{\left| u _ {n _ {k}} \right|, l \right\}.
$$

Therefore 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {\left\{\left| \tau_ {j _ {k}} \circ u _ {n _ {k}} \right| \geq l \right\}} \left(\left| \tau_ {j _ {k}} \circ u _ {n _ {k}} \right| - l\right) d \mu \\ = \int_ {X} \left(\left| \tau_ {j _ {k}} \circ u _ {n _ {k}} \right| - \min \left\{\left| \tau_ {j _ {k}} \circ u _ {n _ {k}} \right|, l \right\}\right) d \mu \\ = \int_ {X} \left(\left| u _ {n _ {k}} \right| - \min \left\{\left| u _ {n _ {k}} \right|, l \right\}\right) d \mu - \int_ {X} \left(\left| u _ {n _ {k}} \right| - \left| \tau_ {j _ {k}} \circ u _ {n _ {k}} \right|\right) d \mu \\ = \int_ {\left\{\left| u _ {n _ {k}} \right| \geq l \right\}} \left(\left| u _ {n _ {k}} \right| - l\right) d \mu - \int_ {\left\{\left| u _ {n _ {k}} \right| \geq j _ {k} \right\}} \left(\left| u _ {n _ {k}} \right| - j _ {k}\right) d \mu \\ \leq \varphi (l) - \left(1 - \frac {1}{2 ^ {k}}\right) \varphi_ {\infty} \leq \varphi (l) - \left(1 - \frac {1}{2 ^ {k l}}\right) \varphi_ {\infty}, \end{array}
$$

where we have used (2.15) and the fact that $k \geq k _ { l }$ . We conclude that 

$$
\sup _ {k \in \mathbb {N}} \int_ {\left\{\left| \tau_ {j _ {k}} \circ u _ {n _ {k}} \right| \geq l \right\}} \left(\left| \tau_ {j _ {k}} \circ u _ {n _ {k}} \right| - l\right) d \mu \leq \varphi (l) - \left(1 - \frac {1}{2 ^ {k _ {l}}}\right) \varphi_ {\infty}.\tag{2.16}
$$

Note that the right-hand side of the previous inequality converges to zero as $l  \infty$ , and we invoke the previous lemma to conclude the equi-integrability of the sequence $\{ \tau _ { j _ { k } } \circ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ 

Remark 2.33. (i) In Chapter 8, using Young measures techniques we give an alternative proof of this result in the particular case that X is a bounded Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

(ii) Note that taking the limit inferior in the inequality (2.16) and using the fact that the left-hand side is nonnegative yields 

$$
0 \leq \liminf _ {l \to \infty} \varphi \left(l\right) - \varphi_ {\infty},
$$

which, in view of the definition of $\varphi _ { \infty }$ in (2.14), implies that $\varphi _ { \infty }$ is actually a limit. 

## 2.1.3 Dual Spaces

In view of H¨older’s inequality, if $1 \leq p < \infty$ and q is its H¨older conjugate exponent, then for every $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ the functional 

$$
u \in L ^ {p} (X) \mapsto \int_ {X} u v d \mu
$$

is linear and continuous and thus belongs to $\left( L ^ { p } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ 

Under appropriate hypotheses on the measure $\mu$ it is possible to identify the dual of $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ with $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ for $1 \leq p < \infty$ . We begin with some prelimi nary results, which give the converse of H¨older’s inequality. 

Theorem 2.34. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, let $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , and let q be its H¨older conjugate exponent. Let $u : X  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be measurable and assume that uv is integrable for every $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ . If the set $\{ x \in X : u ( x ) \neq 0 \}$ has $\sigma { - } f i n i t e$ measure, then $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ 

Proof. We begin by showing that 

$$
\mu \left(\{x \in X: | u (x) | = \infty \}\right) = 0.
$$

Indeed, if not, then since $\{ x \in X : u ( x ) \neq 0 \}$ has σ-finite measure we would be able to find a measurable set 

$$
E \subset \{x \in X: | u (x) | = \infty \}
$$

with $0 < \mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ . Since $v : = \chi _ { E } \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ , we would have that 

$$
\infty > \int_ {X} | u v | d \mu = \int_ {E} | u | d \mu = \infty ,
$$

which is a contradiction. Hence we are in a position to apply Corollary 1.77 to construct a sequence of simple functions $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ , each of which is bounded and vanishes except on a set of finite measure, such that $\{ | s _ { n } \left( x \right) | \}$ converges monotonically to $\left| u \left( x \right) \right|$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ . The functionals 

$$
L _ {n} (v) := \int_ {X} s _ {n} v d \mu , \quad v \in L ^ {q} (X),
$$

are linear and continuous with (see the proof of (2.19) below) 

$$
\left\| L _ {n} \right\| _ {(L ^ {q} (X)) ^ {\prime}} = \left\| s _ {n} \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (X)}.
$$

Moreover, since $\left| s _ { n } \left( x \right) \right| \leq \left| u \left( x \right) \right|$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ , for any $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ we have that 

$$
\sup _ {n} | L _ {n} (v) | \leq \sup _ {n} \int_ {X} | s _ {n} v | d \mu \leq \int_ {X} | u v | d \mu <   \infty
$$

by the hypothesis on u. It now follows from the Banach–Steinhaus theorem that there exists $M > 0$ such that 

$$
\sup _ {n} \left\| L _ {n} \right\| _ {(L ^ {q} (X)) ^ {\prime}} = \sup _ {n} \left\| s _ {n} \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (X)} \leq M.
$$

If $1 \leq p < \infty$ , then by the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem we now have 

$$
M ^ {p} \geq \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} | s _ {n} | ^ {p} d \mu = \int_ {X} | u | ^ {p} d \mu ,
$$

so that $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ , while if $p = \infty$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ , we have 

$$
M \geq \lim _ {n \to \infty} | s _ {n} (x) | = | u (x) |,
$$

which implies that $\| u \| _ { L ^ { \infty } ( X ) } \leq M$ 

As a consequence of the previous result we may now prove the converse of H¨older’s inequality. 

Theorem 2.35 (Converse H¨older’s inequality). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, let $1 < p < \infty$ , and let q be its H¨older conjugate exponent. Then the following are equivalent: 

(i) for every measurable function $u : X  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ such that uv $\in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ for all $v \in L ^ { q } ( X ) , u \in L ^ { p } ( X )$ ; 

(ii) µ has the finite subset property. 

Proof. Step 1: Assume that (i) holds. If (ii) fails, then we can find a set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $\mu \left( E \right) = \infty$ , such that $\mu \left( F \right) \in \{ 0 , \infty \}$ for all $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $F \subset E$ . Then the function $u = \chi _ { E }$ is not in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ . On the other hand, if $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ , then 

$$
\{x \in X: v (x) \neq 0 \} = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left\{x \in X: | v (x) | \geq \frac {1}{n} \right\}
$$

and 

$$
\frac {1}{n ^ {q}} \mu \left(\left\{x \in X: | v (x) | \geq \frac {1}{n} \right\}\right) \leq \int_ {X} | v | ^ {q} d \mu <   \infty ,
$$

and so $\textstyle \mu \left( \left\{ x \in E : | v \left( x \right) | \geq { \frac { 1 } { n } } \right\} \right) = 0$ , which implies that $u v = 0$ for $\mu \ \mathrm { a . e }$ . in X. Hence $\overset { \cdot } { u } v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ for all ${ \dot { v } } \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ and u $\not \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ , which contradicts (i). 

Step 2: Assume that $\mu$ has the finite subset property and let $u : X \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be such that $u v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ for all $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ . We claim that $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ . In view of Theorem 2.34 it sufices to show that the set $\{ x \in X : u ( x ) \neq 0 \}$ has σ-finite measure. Let 

$$
E _ {n} := \left\{x \in X: | u (x) | \geq \frac {1}{n} \right\}.
$$

Since 

$$
\{x \in X: u (x) \neq 0 \} = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n},
$$

it remains to show that $\mu \left( E _ { n } \right) < \infty$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Assume by contradiction that $\mu \left( E _ { l } \right) = \infty$ for some $l \in \mathbb N$ . Then, as in the proof of Proposition 1.25, it is possible to show that the set $E _ { l }$ contains a set $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with σ-finite measure such that $\mu \left( F \right) = \infty$ . The function $w : = u \chi _ { F }$ is such that $w v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ for all $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ and the set $\{ x \in X : w \left( x \right) \neq 0 \}$ has $\sigma { \mathrm { - f i n i t e } }$ measure. Hence by Theorem $2 . 3 4 , w \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ , which is in contradiction with the fact that $\begin{array} { r } { | \dot { w } \left( x \right) | \geq \frac { 1 } { n } } \end{array}$ on the set F of infinite measure. 

Remark 2.36. Note that the nonzero function $f = \chi _ { E }$ constructed in Step 1 belongs to $L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ , while $u v = 0$ for $\mu \ { \mathrm { a . e . } }$ . in X and for all $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ 

Using the previous results one can show that the dual of $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ may be identified with $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ for $1 < p < \infty$ 

Theorem 2.37 (Riesz representation theorem in $L ^ { p } )$ . Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, let $1 < p < \infty$ , and let q be its H¨older conjugate exponent. Then every bounded linear functional $L : L ^ { p } ( X )  \mathbb { R }$ is represented by a unique $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ in the sense that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u v d \mu \quad f o r e v e r y u \in L ^ {p} (X).\tag{2.17}
$$

Moreover, the norm of L coincides with $\Vert v \Vert _ { L ^ { q } }$ . Conversely, every functional of the form (2.17), where $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ , is a bounded linear functional on $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ In particular, $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ is reflexive. 

Proof. Step 1: Assume first that µ is finite and that $L : L ^ { p } \left( X \right) \to \mathbb { R }$ is linear, bounded, and $L \geq 0$ , that is, $L \left( u \right) \geq 0$ whenever $u \geq 0$ . Then for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ the function $\chi _ { E }$ is in $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ , and so the set function 

$$
\nu (E) := L \left(\chi_ {E}\right), \quad E \in \mathfrak {M},
$$

is well-defined. We claim that ν is countably additive. By the linearity of L it follows that $\mu$ is finitely additive. Let $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ be a sequence of pairwise disjoint sets and denote by $E$ their union. Then 

$$
\chi_ {\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {l} E _ {n}} \to \chi_ {E} \quad \text { in } L ^ {p} (X),
$$

and hence, by the continuity of $L$ , 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \nu \left(E _ {n}\right) = \nu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {l} E _ {n}\right) = L \left(\chi_ {\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {l} E _ {n}}\right)\rightarrow L \left(\chi_ {E}\right) = \nu \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right)
$$

as $l \to \infty$ . Since ν is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ we may apply the Radon–Nikodym theorem to find a unique nonnegative function $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ such that 2 

$$
L \left(\chi_ {E}\right) = \nu (E) = \int_ {X} \chi_ {E} v d \mu \quad \text { for every } E \in \mathfrak {M}.
$$

By the linearity of $L$ we conclude that 

$$
L (s) = \int_ {X} s v d \mu
$$

for every nonnegative simple function s. 

If $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ is a nonnegative function, then by Theorem 1.74 we may find an increasing sequence $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ of nonnegative simple functions converging to u µ a.e. 

Since $0 \ \leq \ s _ { n } ^ { p } \ \leq \ u ^ { p }$ , by the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem $s _ { n } \to u$ in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ , and so $L \left( s _ { n } \right) \to L \left( u \right)$ . On the other hand, by the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem 

$$
L \left(s _ {n}\right) = \int_ {X} s _ {n} v d \mu \rightarrow \int_ {X} u v d \mu ,
$$

and so 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u v d \mu\tag{2.18}
$$

for all nonnegative $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ 

For a general $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ it sufices to write $u = u ^ { + } - u ^ { - }$ and apply (2.18) to conclude that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u v d \mu
$$

for all $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ . Moreover, since $u v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ for all $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ , it follows from the converse H¨older’s inequality that $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ . Next we show that the norm of $L$ coincides with $\| v \| _ { L ^ { q } ( X ) }$ . By H¨older’s inequality, 

$$
| L (u) | \leq \| u \| _ {L ^ {p} (X)} \| v \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)}
$$

for all $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ , and so 

$$
\left\| L \right\| _ {(L ^ {p} (X)) ^ {\prime}} \leq \left\| v \right\| _ {L ^ {q} (X)}.
$$

To prove the reverse inequality, take $u : = v ^ { q - 1 }$ . Then 

$$
\int_ {X} u ^ {p} d \mu = \int_ {X} v ^ {p (q - 1)} d \mu = \int_ {X} v ^ {q} d \mu <   \infty ,
$$

while 

$$
| L (u) | = \int_ {X} u v d \mu = \int_ {X} v ^ {q} d \mu ,
$$

and so 

$$
\left\| L \right\| _ {(L ^ {p} (X)) ^ {\prime}} = \left\| v \right\| _ {L ^ {q} (X)}.\tag{2.19}
$$

Step 2: We now remove the extra assumption that $\mu$ is finite. Let 

$$
\mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime} := \left\{E \in \mathfrak {M}: \mu (E) <   \infty \right\}.
$$

Note that ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime }$ is not an algebra. For $E \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ define 

$$
M _ {E} := \left\{u \in L ^ {p} (X): u = 0 \text {   outside   } E \right\}.
$$

By identifying $M _ { E }$ with $L ^ { p } \left( E \right)$ we can apply Step 1 to the positive linear continuous functional $L : { \mathit { M } } _ { E } \to \mathbb { R }$ to find a unique function $v _ { E } \in L ^ { q } \left( E \right)$ such that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u v _ {E} d \mu \quad \mathrm{forevery} u \in M _ {E}\tag{2.20}
$$

and 

$$
\left\| v _ {E} \right\| _ {L ^ {q} (E)} = \sup _ {u \in M _ {E} \backslash \{0 \}} \frac {| L (u) |}{\| u \| _ {L ^ {p} (E)}} = \sup _ {u \in M _ {E} \backslash \{0 \}} \frac {| L (u) |}{\| u \| _ {L ^ {p} (X)}} \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X)) ^ {\prime}}.\tag{2.21}
$$

Extend $v _ { E }$ to be zero outside $E .$ 

Note that in view of the uniqueness of $v _ { E }$ , if E, $F \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ then for $\mu \ { \mathrm { { a . e . } } }$ $x \in E \cap F .$ , 

$$
v _ {E} (x) = v _ {E \cap F} (x) = v _ {F} (x).
$$

In particular, 

$$
v _ {E \cup F} = \max \left\{v _ {E}, v _ {F} \right\},\tag{2.22}
$$

while if $E \subset F$ , then 

$$
0 \leq v _ {E} \leq v _ {F}.
$$

By (2.21), 

$$
\sup _ {E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}} \| v _ {E} \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X)) ^ {\prime}} <   \infty ,
$$

and so we may find a sequence of sets $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \| v _ {E _ {n}} \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} = \sup _ {E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}} \| v _ {E} \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)}.
$$

Replacing $v _ { E _ { n } }$ with $\textstyle v _ { \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } E _ { i } }$ , by (2.22) we may assume without loss of generality that the sequence $\left\{ E _ { n } \right\}$ is increasing (and the same holds for $\{ v _ { E _ { n } } \} )$ ). Hence for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ there exists 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} v _ {E _ {n}} (x) =: v (x),
$$

and by the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem, 

$$
\| v \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \| v _ {E _ {n}} \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} = \sup _ {E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}} \| v _ {E} \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X)) ^ {\prime}} <   \infty .
$$

Next we claim that if $E \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime }$ then 

$$
v _ {E} (x) = v (x)\tag{2.23}
$$

for µ a.e. $x \in X$ . Indeed, by (2.22), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sup _ {E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}} \| v _ {E} \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} = \| v \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \| v _ {E _ {n}} \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} \\ \qquad \leq \lim _ {n \to \infty} \| v _ {E _ {n} \cup E} \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \| \max \left\{v _ {E _ {n}}, v _ {E} \right\} \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} \\ \qquad \leq \sup _ {E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}} \| v _ {E} \| _ {L ^ {q} (X)}. \end{array}
$$

Hence 

$$
\left\| v \right\| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \left\| \max \left\{v _ {E _ {n}}, v _ {E} \right\} \right\| _ {L ^ {q} (X)} = \left\| \max \left\{v, v _ {E} \right\} \right\| _ {L ^ {q} (X)},
$$

and so the claim holds. 

By (2.20) and (2.23), for every simple function s vanishing outside a set of finite measure we have 

$$
L (s) = \int_ {X} s v _ {\{s \neq 0 \}} d \mu = \int_ {X} s v d \mu ,
$$

and by Corollary 1.77, the continuity of $L ,$ and the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem, we conclude that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u v d \mu
$$

for all $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ . The fact that $\| L \| _ { ( L ^ { p } ( X ) ) ^ { \prime } } = \| v \| _ { L ^ { q } ( X ) }$ follows exactly as in Step 1. 

Step 3: Finally, to remove the assumption that L is positive, for any linear, bounded functional $L : L ^ { p } ( X )  \mathbb { R }$ , for $u \in L ^ { p } ( X ) , u \geq 0$ , define 

$$
L ^ {+} (u) := \sup \left\{L (v): 0 \leq v \leq u \right\}, \quad L ^ {-} (u) := - \inf \left\{L (v): 0 \leq v \leq u \right\}.
$$

We claim that $L ^ { + }$ is additive. Indeed, let $u _ { 1 } , u _ { 2 } \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ be nonnegative. For any $v _ { i } \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ , with $0 \leq v _ { i } \leq u _ { i } , i = 1 , 2$ , we have 

$$
L \left(v _ {1}\right) + L \left(v _ {2}\right) = L \left(v _ {1} + v _ {2}\right) \leq L ^ {+} \left(u _ {1} + u _ {2}\right),
$$

and by the arbitrariness of $v _ { 1 }$ and $v _ { 2 }$ we get 

$$
L ^ {+} \left(u _ {1}\right) + L ^ {+} \left(u _ {2}\right) \leq L ^ {+} \left(u _ {1} + u _ {2}\right).
$$

To prove the opposite inequality, let $v \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ , with $0 \leq v \leq u _ { 1 } + u _ { 2 }$ , and define 

$$
v _ {1} := \min \left\{v, u _ {1} \right\}, \quad v _ {2} := v - v _ {1}.
$$

Then $0 \leq v _ { i } \leq u _ { i } , i = 1 , 2 .$ , and so 

$$
L (v) = L \left(v _ {1}\right) + L \left(v _ {2}\right) \leq L ^ {+} \left(u _ {1}\right) + L ^ {+} \left(u _ {2}\right).
$$

By the arbitrariness of v we obtain 

$$
L ^ {+} \left(u _ {1} + u _ {2}\right) \leq L ^ {+} \left(u _ {1}\right) + L ^ {+} \left(u _ {2}\right),
$$

and so the claim follows. 

Next observe that by the linearity of L, for $t \geq 0$ and $u \in L ^ { p } ( X ) , u \geq 0$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} L ^ {+} \left(t u\right) := \sup \left\{L \left(v\right): 0 \leq v \leq t u \right\} = \sup \left\{L \left(t w\right): 0 \leq w \leq u \right\} \\ = t \sup \left\{L \left(w\right): 0 \leq w \leq u \right\} = t L ^ {+} \left(u\right), \end{array}
$$

while for any $v \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ , with $0 \leq v \leq u$ , we have 

$$
L (v) \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X)) ^ {\prime}} \| v \| _ {L ^ {p} (X)} \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X)) ^ {\prime}} \| u \| _ {L ^ {p} (X)},
$$

and so 

$$
L ^ {+} (u) \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X)) ^ {\prime}} \| u \| _ {L ^ {p} (X)}.
$$

Similar properties hold for $L ^ { - }$ 

Finally, for all $u \in L ^ { p } ( X ) , u \geq 0$ 4 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} L ^ {+} (u) - L (u) & = \sup \left\{L (v) - L (u): 0 \leq v \leq u \right\} \\ & = \sup \left\{- L (u - v): 0 \leq v \leq u \right\} \\ & = - \inf \left\{L (u - v): 0 \leq u - v \leq u \right\} = L ^ {-} (u). \end{array}
$$

Hence the functionals 

$$
L ^ {+} (u) := L ^ {+} \left(u ^ {+}\right) - L ^ {+} \left(u ^ {-}\right), \quad L ^ {-} (u) := L ^ {-} \left(u ^ {+}\right) - L ^ {-} \left(u ^ {-}\right), \quad u \in L ^ {p} (X),
$$

are linear, continuous, positive, and 

$$
L = L ^ {+} - L ^ {-}.
$$

Applying Step 2 to $L ^ { + } , L ^ { - }$ , we may find unique functions $v _ { 1 } , v _ { 2 } \in L ^ { q } ( X )$ such that 

$$
L ^ {+} (u) = \int_ {X} u v _ {1} d \mu \quad L ^ {-} (u) = \int_ {X} u v _ {2} d \mu \quad \text { for   every } u \in L ^ {p} (X).
$$

The function $v : = v _ { 1 } - v _ { 2 }$ satisfies 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u v d \mu \quad \text { for   every } u \in L ^ {p} (X),
$$

and once again the fact that $\| L \| _ { ( L ^ { p } ( X ) ) ^ { \prime } } = \| v \| _ { L ^ { q } ( X ) }$ follows as in Step 1 with the only change that one should take now $u : = | v | ^ { q - 2 } v$ 

The previous theorem fails if $p = 1$ , as the following exercise shows: 

Exercise 2.38. Let $X = ( 0 , 1 )$ , let M be the σ-algebra consisting of all countable subsets of $( 0 , 1 )$ and their complements, and for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ define $\mu \left( E \right)$ as the cardinality of $E .$ Prove that $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ consists of all functions that vanish outside a denumerable set, and whose remaining values form an absolutely convergent series. Show that if $u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ , then the function $v \left( x \right) : = x u \left( x \right)$ is also in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ and the functional 

$$
L (u) := \int_ {X} x u (x) d \mu (x) \quad u \in L ^ {1} (X)
$$

is linear and continuous. Since this functional takes on an uncountable set of distinct values on the family of characteristic functions of singletons, prove that it cannot be of the form 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u v d \mu \quad \text { for   every } u \in L ^ {1} (X)
$$

for some measurable function $v .$ . Indeed, any measurable function must be constant except for a countable set. 

Theorem 2.39 (Riesz representation theorem in $L ^ { 1 } )$ . Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let 

$$
\mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime} := \left\{E \in \mathfrak {M}: \mu (E) <   \infty \right\}.
$$

Then for every bounded linear functional $L : L ^ { 1 } ( X )  \mathbb { R }$ there exists a unique signed measure $\lambda : \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime } \to \mathbb { R }$ absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ such that 

$$
\| \lambda \| := \sup \left\{\frac {| \lambda (E) |}{\mu (E)}: E \in \mathfrak {M}, 0 <   \mu (E) <   \infty \right\} <   \infty\tag{2.24}
$$

and 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \lambda \quad f o r e v e r y u \in L ^ {1} (X).\tag{2.25}
$$

Moreover, the norm of L coincides with $\| \lambda \|$ . Conversely, every functional of the form (2.25), where λ is as above, is a bounded linear functional on $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right) ^ { 1 }$ 

Proof. Step 1: Assume that $L : L ^ { 1 } ( X )  \mathbb { R }$ is linear, bounded and $L \geq 0$ • that is, $L \left( u \right) \geq 0$ whenever $u \geq 0$ . As in the previous theorem, the set function 

$$
\nu (E) := L \left(\chi_ {E}\right), \quad E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime},
$$

is countably additive, absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu ,$ , with 

$$
\left\| L \right\| _ {\left(L ^ {1} (X)\right) ^ {\prime}} \geq \frac {L (\chi_ {E})}{\left\| \chi_ {E} \right\| _ {L ^ {1} (X)}} = \frac {\nu (E)}{\mu (E)} \quad \text { for   all } E \in \mathfrak {M}, 0 <   \mu (E) <   \infty .
$$

Hence 

$$
\left\| L \right\| _ {(L ^ {1} (X)) ^ {\prime}} \geq \left\| \nu \right\|.\tag{2.26}
$$

To extend ν to the σ-algebra M define 

$$
\tilde {\nu} (E) := \sup \left\{\nu (E \cap F): F \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime} \right\}, \quad E \in \mathfrak {M}.\tag{2.27}
$$

As in the proof of Lemma 1.23, one can verify that $\tilde { \nu }$ is a measure, absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu .$ . Moreover, ${ \tilde { \nu } } = \nu$ on ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime }$ 

For any simple function s of the form 

$$
s = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} c _ {i} \chi_ {E _ {i}},\tag{2.28}
$$

where $c _ { i } \in \mathbb { R }$ and $E _ { i } \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ , we have 

$$
L (s) = \int_ {X} s d \nu .
$$

Given a nonnegative function $u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right) = L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ , in view of Theorem 1.74 one can construct a sequence of nonnegative simple functions $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ , each of which is bounded and vanishes except on a set of finite measure $\mu ,$ , such that $\{ s _ { n } \left( x \right) \}$ converges monotonically to u (x) for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ . Write 

$$
s _ {n} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell_ {n}} c _ {i} ^ {(n)} \chi_ {E _ {i} ^ {(n)}},
$$

where $c _ { i } ^ { ( n ) } \geq 0$ and $E _ { i } ^ { ( n ) } \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ . Then 

$$
\int_ {X} s _ {n} d \nu = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell_ {n}} c _ {i} ^ {(n)} \nu (E _ {i} ^ {(n)}) \leq \| \nu \| \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell_ {n}} c _ {i} ^ {(n)} \mu (E _ {i} ^ {(n)}) = \| \nu \| \int_ {X} s _ {n} d \mu ,
$$

and so by the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem, 

$$
\int_ {X} u d \tilde {\nu} \leq \| \nu \| \int_ {X} u d \mu ,\tag{2.29}
$$

which implies that $u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , { \tilde { \nu } } \right)$ . Using Corollary $1 . 7 7$ and the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem, it follows that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \tilde {\nu}
$$

for every nonnegative $u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ 

If now $u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right) = L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ , we can apply the previous part to $u ^ { + }$ and $u ^ { - }$ to conclude that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \tilde {\nu} \quad \text { for   every } u \in L ^ {1} (X),\tag{2.30}
$$

with (see (2.29)) 

$$
\int_ {X} | u | d \tilde {\nu} \leq \| \nu \| \int_ {X} | u | d \mu ,\tag{2.31}
$$

which implies that $u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , { \tilde { \nu } } \right)$ . By (2.30) and (2.31) we obtain 

$$
\left\| L \right\| _ {(L ^ {1} (X)) ^ {\prime}} \leq \left\| \nu \right\|,
$$

which, together with (2.26), yields $\| L \| _ { ( L ^ { 1 } ( X ) ) ^ { \prime } } = \| \nu \|$ 

Step 2: If $L : L ^ { 1 } ( X )  \mathbb { R }$ is linear, bounded as in the previous theorem, we write 

$$
L = L ^ {+} - L ^ {-},
$$

where for $u \in L ^ { 1 } ( X ) , u \geq 0$ 2 

$$
L ^ {+} (u) := \sup \left\{L (v): 0 \leq v \leq u \right\}, \quad L ^ {-} (u) := - \inf \left\{L (v): 0 \leq v \leq u \right\},
$$

while for $u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ 

$$
L ^ {+} (u) := L ^ {+} \left(u ^ {+}\right) - L ^ {+} \left(u ^ {-}\right), \quad L ^ {-} (u) := L ^ {-} \left(u ^ {+}\right) - L ^ {-} \left(u ^ {-}\right).
$$

One can verify that $L ^ { + }$ and $L ^ { - }$ are linear, continuous, and nonnegative with 

$$
\left\| L \right\| _ {(L ^ {1} (X)) ^ {\prime}} = \left\| L ^ {+} \right\| _ {(L ^ {1} (X)) ^ {\prime}} + \left\| L ^ {-} \right\| _ {(L ^ {1} (X)) ^ {\prime}}.
$$

Hence by the previous step we can find two measures $\lambda ^ { + } , \lambda ^ { - } : \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ such that 

$$
L ^ {\pm} (u) = \int_ {X} u d \lambda^ {\pm} \quad \text { for   every } u \in L ^ {1} (X)
$$

and 

$$
\left\| \lambda^ {\pm} \right\| = \sup \left\{\frac {| \lambda^ {\pm} (E) |}{\mu (E)}: E \in \mathfrak {M}, 0 <   \mu (E) <   \infty \right\} = \left\| L ^ {\pm} \right\| _ {(L ^ {1} (X)) ^ {\prime}}.
$$

It sufices to define $\lambda : = \lambda ^ { + } - \lambda ^ { - }$ 

Exercise 2.40. Prove that the integral $\textstyle \int _ { X }$ u dν˜ constructed in Step 1 of the proof of the previous theorem does not depend on the particular extension $\tilde { \nu }$ of $\nu .$ . Using (2.24) show that 

$$
\left\| \lambda \right\| = \left\| \lambda^ {+} \right\| + \left\| \lambda^ {-} \right\|,
$$

where $\lambda ^ { + } , \lambda ^ { - }$ , and λ are defined in Step 2 of the proof of the previous theorem. 

Using the Radon–Nikodym theorem II we can deduce from the previous theorem the following result. 

Corollary 2.41. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Then the dual of $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ may be identified with $L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ if and only if the measure $\mu$ is localizable and has the finite subset property. 

Proof. In the remainder of the book we will use only the fact if the measure $\mu$ is localizable and has the finite subset property, then the dual of $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ may be identified with $L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ . Thus we prove here only this implication, and we refer to [Rao04] and [Z67] for the converse one. 

Hence assume that $\mu$ is localizable and has the finite subset property and let $L : L ^ { 1 } ( X )  \mathbb { R }$ be linear, bounded, and positive. Let ν and $\tilde { \nu }$ be defined as in the proof of step 1 of the previous theorem. Since $\tilde { \nu }$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ and satisfies (1.52) (see (2.27)), we are in a position to apply the Radon–Nikodym theorem II to obtain a unique measurable function $v : X \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\tilde {\nu} (E) = \int_ {E} v d \mu
$$

for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . We claim that $v \in L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ with 

$$
\left\| \nu \right\| = \left\| v \right\| _ {L ^ {\infty} (X)},
$$

where $\| \nu \|$ is defined in (2.24). Indeed, let 

$$
E _ {0} := \left\{x \in X: v (x) > \| \nu \| \right\}.
$$

Assume by contradiction that $\mu \left( E _ { 0 } \right) ~ > ~ 0$ . Since $\mu$ has the finite subset property, if $\mu \left( E _ { 0 } \right) \ = \ \infty$ we may find a measurable subset $F ~ \subset ~ E _ { 0 }$ with $0 < \mu \left( F \right) < \infty \mathrm { ( i f } \mu \left( E _ { 0 } \right) < \infty$ take $F : = E _ { 0 } )$ . Then $F$ is admissible in the definition of (2.24), and so 

$$
\| \nu \| = \| \nu \| \frac {\mu (F)}{\mu (F)} <   \frac {1}{\mu (F)} \int_ {F} v d \mu = \frac {\nu (F)}{\mu (F)} \leq \| \nu \|,
$$

which is a contradiction. Hence $\mu \left( E _ { 0 } \right) ~ = ~ 0$ , and so $v ~ \in ~ L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ and $\| v \| _ { L ^ { \infty } ( X ) } \leq \| \nu \|$ . In turn, for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $0 < \mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ , we have 

$$
\frac {\nu (E)}{\mu (E)} = \frac {1}{\mu (E)} \int_ {E} v d \mu \leq \| v \| _ {L ^ {\infty} (X)},
$$

and so, taking the supremum over all such $E$ we get $\| \nu \| \leq \| v \| _ { L ^ { \infty } ( X ) }$ . This proves the claim. 

Since 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \tilde {\nu} \quad \text { for   every } u \in L ^ {1} (X),
$$

by taking u to be a simple function s as in (2.28) we get 

$$
L (s) = \int_ {X} s d \nu = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} c _ {i} \nu (E _ {i}) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} c _ {i} \int_ {E _ {i}} v d \mu = \int_ {X} s v d \mu .
$$

The continuity of $L _ { ; }$ , Corollary 1.77, and the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem yield 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u v d \mu \quad \text { for   every } u \in L ^ {1} (X).
$$

This concludes the proof in the case that L is positive. The general case may be treated by the usual decomposition $L = L ^ { + } - L ^ { - }$ . We omit the details. 

Remark $2 . 4 2 .$ Note that if $\mu$ is σ-finite, then, in view of Proposition 1.110, $\mu$ is localizable, and it has the finite subset property. Hence for σ-finite measures the identification $\left( L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime } = L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ is valid. 

The next exercise shows that the dual of $L ^ { p } \left( X \right) , 0 < p < 1$ , is nontrivial if and only if $\mu$ has no atoms of finite measure. 

Exercise 2.43 (The dual of $L ^ { p } ( X ) , 0 < p < 1 )$ . Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $0 < p < 1$ 

(i) Assume that $\mu$ has no atoms of finite measure, that is, if for every set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ of positive finite measure there exists $F \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $F \subset E$ , such that $0 < \mu \left( F \right) < \mu \left( E \right)$ , and let $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right) \backslash \{ 0 \}$ . Prove that the measure 

$$
\nu (E) := \int_ {E} | u | ^ {p} d \mu , \quad E \in \mathfrak {M},
$$

has no atoms, so that the range of $\nu$ is $\left[ 0 , \int _ { X } | u | ^ { p } \ d \mu \right]$ (ii) Under the same hypothesis on $\mu$ prove that if $U \subset L ^ { p } { \mathsf { \bar { ( } } } X )$ is open, convex, and $0 \in U$ , then $U = L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ . Conclude that $\left( L ^ { p } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime } = \left\{ 0 \right\}$ 

(iii) Conversely, let $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ be an atom with positive finite measure. Prove that the set 

$$
U := \{u \in L ^ {p} (X): | u (x) | <   1 \text {   for   } \mu \text {   a.e.   } x \in E \}
$$

is open, convex, and $0 \in U$ , but $U \neq L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ . Hence $\left( L ^ { p } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ is nontrivial. 

Finally, we study the dual of $L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ . Note that in general, 

$$
\left(L ^ {\infty} \left(X\right)\right) ^ {\prime} \supsetneqq L ^ {1} \left(X\right).
$$

Indeed, the dual of $L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ may be identified with ba $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ , which is the space of all bounded finitely additive signed measures absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu ,$ that is, all maps $\lambda : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \mathbb { R }$ such that 

(i) $\lambda \in \mathrm { b a } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ ; 

(ii) $\lambda \left( E \right) = 0$ whenever $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ 

Theorem 2.44 (Riesz representation theorem in $L ^ { \infty } )$ . Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Then every bounded linear functional $L : L ^ { \infty } ( X )  \mathbb { R }$ is represented by a unique $\lambda \in$ ba $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ in the sense that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} u d \lambda \quad f o r e v e r y u \in L ^ {\infty} (X).\tag{2.32}
$$

Moreover, the norm of L coincides with $\| \lambda \|$ . Conversely, every functional of the form (2.32), where $\lambda \in \mathrm { ~ b a } ( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ , is a bounded linear functional on $L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ 

Proof. Let $L \in \mathsf { \Gamma } ( L ^ { \infty } ( X ) ) ^ { \prime }$ . The elements of $L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ are equivalence classes $[ u ] \ ( \mathrm { s e e \ ( 2 . 1 ) } )$ of measurable functions bounded $\mu$ almost everywhere. Given a function $u \in B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ we have that $[ u ] \in L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ and 

$$
\sup _ {x \in X} | u | \geq \| [ u ] \| _ {L ^ {\infty}}.
$$

Define the linear functional 

$$
L _ {1} (u) := L ([ u ]), \quad u \in B (X, \mathfrak {M}).
$$

Then 

$$
| L _ {1} (u) | = | L ([ u ]) | \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {\infty} (X)) ^ {\prime}} \| [ u ] \| _ {L ^ {\infty}} \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {\infty} (X)) ^ {\prime}} \sup _ {x \in X} | u |,
$$

and so 

$$
\left\| L _ {1} \right\| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}} \leq \left\| L \right\| _ {(L ^ {\infty} (X)) ^ {\prime}}.
$$

On the other hand, by the definition of essential supremum, from each equivalence class $[ u ] \in L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ we can select a measurable representative $\tilde { u } : X \to \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
\sup _ {x \in X} | \tilde {u} | = \| [ u ] \| _ {L ^ {\infty} (X)}.
$$

Hence 

$$
\frac {| L ([ u ]) |}{\| [ u ] \| _ {L ^ {\infty} (X)}} = \frac {| L _ {1} (\tilde {u}) |}{\sup _ {x \in X} | \tilde {u} |} \leq \| L _ {1} \| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}},
$$

which shows that $\| L _ { 1 } \| _ { ( B ( X , \mathfrak { M } ) ) ^ { \prime } } = \| L \| _ { ( L ^ { \infty } ( X ) ) ^ { \prime } }$ . It follows, in particular, that $L _ { 1 } \in ( B \left( X , \mathfrak { M } \right) ) ^ { \prime }$ , and so by the Riesz representation theorem in $B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ there exists a unique $\lambda \in \mathrm { b a } \left( X , \mathfrak { M } \right)$ such that 

$$
L _ {1} (u) = \int_ {X} u d \lambda \quad \text { for   every } u \in B (X, \mathfrak {M})
$$

and 

$$
\left\| L \right\| _ {(L ^ {\infty} (X)) ^ {\prime}} = \left\| L _ {1} \right\| _ {(B (X, \mathfrak {M})) ^ {\prime}} = \left\| \lambda \right\|.
$$

Note that if u, $v \in B \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } \right)$ and $u = v \ \mu \mathrm { { a . e } }$ . everywhere, then 

$$
\int_ {X} u d \lambda = L _ {1} (u) = L ([ u ]) = L ([ v ]) = L _ {1} (v) = \int_ {X} v d \lambda .
$$

In particular, if $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ is such that $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ , then $\chi _ { E } \in [ 0 ]$ , and so 

$$
\lambda (E) = \int_ {X} \chi_ {E} d \lambda = L ([ 0 ]) = 0.
$$

This shows that $\lambda \in \mathrm { b a } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ 

Conversely given any $\lambda \in \mathrm { ~ b a } ( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ , since λ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu _ { ; }$ , the functional 

$$
L ([ u ]) := \int_ {X} u d \lambda \quad \text { for   every } [ u ] \in L ^ {\infty} (X)
$$

is well-defined, linear, and bounded. 

The next example shows that ba $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ strictly contains the subspace of finite signed Radon measures absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu .$

## 2.1.4 Weak Convergence in ${ \pmb { L } } ^ { p }$

Let $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ and let $q$ be the H¨older conjugate exponent of $p .$ If $p = 1$ or $p = \infty$ then assume in addition that $\mu$ is $\sigma { \mathrm { - f i n i t e } }$ . for every $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$
