The next result will play a crucial role in the characterization of weakly compact sets in $L ^ { 1 }$ . It gives a property of uniform absolute continuity of a particular sequence of signed measures (see Proposition 1.99). 

Theorem 2.53 (Vitali–Hahn–Saks). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $\{ \lambda _ { n } \}$ be a sequence offinite signed measures such that l $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { i m } _ { n \to \infty } \lambda _ { n } ( E )$ exists in R for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ . If each $\lambda _ { n }$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu _ { ; }$ , then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
| \lambda_ {n} (E) | \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and for every measurable set $E \subset X$ with $\mu \left( E \right) \leq \delta$ 

Proof. Let 

$$
\mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime} := \left\{E \in \mathfrak {M}: \mu (E) <   \infty \right\}.
$$

By identifying sets that difer by a set of $\mu$ measure zero we can regard ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime }$ as a closed subset $\mathcal { F }$ of $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ through the mapping 

$$
E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime} \mapsto \chi_ {E}.
$$

Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and for $k \in \mathbb N$ define the sets 

$$
\mathcal {F} _ {k} := \left\{\chi_ {E}: E \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}, \sup _ {n, l \geq k} | \lambda_ {n} (E) - \lambda_ {l} (E) | \leq \varepsilon \right\}.
$$

We claim that the sets $\mathcal { F } _ { k }$ are closed in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ . Indeed, if $\left\{ \chi _ { E _ { j } } \right\} \subset \mathcal { F } _ { k }$ converges in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ , then, since $\mathcal { F }$ is closed, $\chi _ { E _ { j } }  \chi _ { E _ { \infty } }$ as $j \to \infty$ for some $E _ { \infty } \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ . By extracting a subsequence (not relabeled), if necessary, we may assume that $\chi _ { E _ { j } } \left( x \right) \longrightarrow \chi _ { E _ { \infty } } \left( x \right)$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ (see Theorem 2.20). Let 

$$
Y := E _ {\infty} \cup \bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {j}.
$$

Then $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor Y \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is $\sigma { \mathrm { - f i n i t e } }$ , and so for any $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and by the Radon– Nikodym theorem applied to $\left( \lambda _ { n } \right) ^ { + }$ and $\left( \lambda _ { n } \right) ^ { - }$ restricted to ${ \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor Y$ , there exists $v _ { n } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( Y , { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor Y , \mu \right)$ such that 

$$
\lambda_ {n} (E) = \int_ {E} v _ {n} d \mu , E \in \mathfrak {M} \lfloor Y.
$$

By the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem, for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , 

$$
\lim _ {j \to \infty} \lambda_ {n} (E _ {j}) = \lambda_ {n} (E _ {\infty}).
$$

Since $\left\{ \chi _ { E _ { j } } \right\} \subset \mathcal { F } _ { k }$ for any fixed $n , l \geq k$ and for all $j \in \mathbb N$ , we have 

$$
\left| \lambda_ {n} \left(E _ {j}\right) - \lambda_ {l} \left(E _ {j}\right) \right| \leq \varepsilon ,
$$

and so letting $j \to \infty$ we obtain that 

$$
\left| \lambda_ {n} \left(E _ {\infty}\right) - \lambda_ {l} \left(E _ {\infty}\right) \right| \leq \varepsilon ,
$$

which shows that $\mathcal { F } _ { k }$ is closed in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ 

By hypothesis, $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \lambda _ { n } \left( E \right)$ exists in R for all $E \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ , and so 

$$
\mathcal {F} = \bigcup_ {k = 1} \mathcal {F} _ {k}.
$$

Applying the Baire category theorem to the complete metric space ${ \mathcal F } .$ , at least one of the sets $\mathcal { F } _ { k }$ has nonempty interior. Hence there exist $\delta _ { 1 } > 0 , k \in \mathbb { N }$ , and $\chi _ { E _ { 0 } } \in \mathcal { F } _ { k }$ such that if $\chi _ { E } \in \mathcal { F }$ and if 

$$
\int_ {X} \left| \chi_ {E} - \chi_ {E _ {0}} \right| d \mu <   \delta_ {1},\tag{2.33}
$$

then $\chi _ { E } \in \mathcal { F } _ { k }$ , that is, 

$$
\sup _ {n, l \geq k} | \lambda_ {n} (E) - \lambda_ {l} (E) | \leq \varepsilon .\tag{2.34}
$$

By Proposition 1.99 applied to $\left( \lambda _ { n } \right) ^ { + }$ and $\left( \lambda _ { n } \right) ^ { - }$ , we may find $0 < \delta < \delta _ { 1 }$ such that 

$$
| \lambda_ {n} (E) | \leq \varepsilon\tag{2.35}
$$

for all $1 \leq n \leq k$ and for every measurable set $E \subset X$ with $\mu \left( E \right) \leq \delta$ 

Fix $E \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) \leq \delta$ . Then 

$$
E = \left(E \cup E _ {0}\right) \setminus \left(E _ {0} \setminus E\right),
$$

with 

$$
\int_ {X} \left| \chi_ {E \cup E _ {0}} - \chi_ {E _ {0}} \right| d \mu , \int_ {X} \left| \chi_ {E _ {0} \setminus E} - \chi_ {E _ {0}} \right| d \mu <   \delta_ {1},
$$

and so by (2.33) and (2.34), 

$$
\sup _ {n, l \geq k} | \lambda_ {n} (E \cup E _ {0}) - \lambda_ {l} (E \cup E _ {0}) | \leq \varepsilon ,
$$

$$
\sup _ {n, l \geq k} | \lambda_ {n} (E _ {0} \setminus E) - \lambda_ {l} (E _ {0} \setminus E) | \leq \varepsilon .
$$

It follows that for any $n \geq k$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | \lambda_ {n} (E) | \leq | \lambda_ {k} (E) | + | \lambda_ {k} (E) - \lambda_ {n} (E) | \\ \quad \leq \varepsilon + | \lambda_ {k} (E \cup E _ {0}) - \lambda_ {n} (E \cup E _ {0}) | \\ \quad \quad + | \lambda_ {k} (E _ {0} \setminus E) - \lambda_ {n} (E _ {0} \setminus E) | \\ \quad \leq 3 \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

where we have also used (2.35). This completes the proof. 

In view of Remark 2.51, $L ^ { 1 }$ weak compactness of $L ^ { 1 }$ bounded sequences requires additional conditions, and this brings us to the following result. 

Theorem 2.54 (Dunford–Pettis). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let ${ \mathcal { F } } \subset L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . Then $\mathcal { F }$ is weakly sequentially precompact if and only if 

(i) $\mathcal { F }$ is bounded in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ ; 

(ii) $\mathcal { F }$ is equi-integrable and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $E \subset X$ with $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ such that $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ and 

$$
\sup _ {u \in \mathcal {F}} \int_ {X \setminus E} | u | d \mu \leq \varepsilon .\tag{2.36}
$$

Proof. Step 1: Assume that $\mathcal { F }$ is weakly sequentially precompact. 

Substep 1a: If $\mathcal { F }$ is not bounded in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ , then it contains a sequence $\{ u _ { n } \} \subset \mathcal { F }$ such that $\| u _ { n } \| _ { L ^ { 1 } ( X ) } \to \infty$ . But since $\mathcal { F }$ is weakly sequentially precompact, a subsequence is weakly convergent in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ , and this contradicts Proposition A.68. 

Substep 1b: Assume by contradiction that $\mathcal { F }$ is not equi-integrable. Then we may find a sequence $\{ u _ { n } \} \subset \mathcal { F }$ and sets $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ , with $\mu ( E _ { n } )  0$ , such that for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , 

$$
\int_ {E _ {n}} | u _ {n} | d \mu \geq \varepsilon_ {0}\tag{2.37}
$$

for some $\varepsilon _ { 0 } > 0$ . Since $\mathcal { F }$ is weakly sequentially precompact, there exists a subsequence of $\{ u _ { n } \}$ (not relabeled) such that $u _ { n } \to u$ in $L ^ { \bar { 1 } } \left( X \right)$ . In particular, for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ , we have that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} u _ {n} d \mu = \int_ {E} u d \mu ,
$$

and so the signed measures 

$$
\lambda_ {n} (E) := \int_ {E} u _ {n} d \mu , \quad E \in \mathfrak {M},
$$

satisfy the hypotheses of the Vitali-Hahn-Saks theorem. Hence there is $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
\left| \int_ {E} u _ {n} d \mu \right| \leq \frac {\varepsilon_ {0}}{3}
$$

for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and for every measurable set $E \subset X$ with $\mu \left( E \right) \leq \delta$ . By taking $E _ { n } \cap \left\{ u _ { n } \geq 0 \right\}$ and $E _ { n } \cap \{ u _ { n } < 0 \}$ for all n so large that $\mu \left( E _ { n } \right) \leq \delta$ , we conclude that 

$$
\int_ {E _ {n}} | u _ {n} | d \mu \leq \frac {2 \varepsilon_ {0}}{3},
$$

which contradicts (2.37). 

Substep 1c: Assume by contradiction that (2.36) is violated. Then we may find $\varepsilon _ { 0 } ~ > ~ 0$ with the property that for any measurable set $E \subset X$ , with $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ , there exists $u \in { \mathcal { F } }$ such that 

$$
\int_ {X \setminus E} | u | d \mu \geq \varepsilon_ {0}.
$$

Fix any $E _ { 1 } \in \mathfrak { M }$ with $\mu \left( E _ { 1 } \right) < \infty$ and let $u _ { 1 } \in { \mathcal { F } }$ be such that 

$$
\int_ {X \setminus E _ {1}} | u _ {1} | d \mu \geq \varepsilon_ {0}.
$$

By Remark 2.28 there exists a measurable set $E _ { 2 } \supset E _ { 1 }$ , with $\mu \left( E _ { 2 } \right) < \infty$ , such that 

$$
\int_ {X \setminus E _ {2}} | u _ {1} | d \mu <   \frac {\varepsilon_ {0}}{2}.
$$

By an induction argument we may find an increasing sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ with $\mu \left( E _ { n } \right) < \infty$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , and $\{ u _ { n } \} \subset \mathcal { F }$ such that for al $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

$$
\int_ {E _ {n + 1} \backslash E _ {n}} | u _ {n} | d \mu \geq \frac {\varepsilon_ {0}}{2}.\tag{2.38}
$$

Since $\mathcal { F }$ is weakly sequentially precompact there exists a subsequence of $\{ u _ { n } \}$ (not relabeled) such that $u _ { n } \to u$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . Let 

$$
Y := \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}.
$$

Then $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor Y \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is $\sigma { \mathrm { - f i n i t e } }$ . Hence we may find a sequence $\{ F _ { j } \} \subset$ M	 Y of pairwise disjoint sets of positive finite measure such that $Y =$ $\textstyle \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { \infty } F _ { j }$ . Construct a sequence of positive numbers $\{ a _ { j } \}$ such that 

$$
\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} a _ {j} \mu (F _ {j}) <   \infty
$$

and define $v : Y \to ( 0 , \infty )$ as 

$$
v := \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} a _ {j} \chi_ {F _ {j}}.
$$

Then $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( Y , \mathfrak { M } \vert Y , \mu \right)$ . Set 

$$
\nu (E) := \int_ {E} v d \mu , \quad E \in \mathfrak {M} \lfloor Y.
$$

Since $v > 0$ in Y it follows that the measures $\lambda _ { n } : { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor Y $ R, 

$$
\lambda_ {n} (E) := \int_ {E} u _ {n} d \mu , \quad E \in \mathfrak {M} \lfloor Y,
$$

are absolutely continuous with respect to ν. Moreover, 

$$
\lambda_ {n} (E) \rightarrow \int_ {E} u d \mu
$$

as $n \to \infty$ for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor Y$ . By the Vitali–Hahn–Saks theorem there exists $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
\left| \int_ {E} u _ {n} d \mu \right| \leq \frac {\varepsilon_ {0}}{8}
$$

for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and for every measurable set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } } \lfloor Y$ with $\nu \left( E \right) \leq \delta$ . Since ν is finite, we may apply Proposition 1.7 to conclude that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \nu \left(Y \setminus E _ {n}\right) = 0,
$$

and so for n suficiently large, 

$$
\nu \left(Y \setminus E _ {n}\right) \leq \delta ,
$$

and in turn, 

$$
\left| \int_ {E} u _ {n} d \mu \right| \leq \frac {\varepsilon_ {0}}{8}
$$

for all measurable subsets $E \subset Y \setminus E _ { n }$ . As in the previous step we conclude that 

$$
\int_ {Y \setminus E _ {n}} | u _ {n} | d \mu \leq \frac {\varepsilon_ {0}}{4},
$$

which contradicts (2.38). 

Step 2: Assume that $\{ u _ { n } \} \subset { \mathcal { F } }$ satisfies (i) and (ii). Since $u _ { n } ^ { + } + u _ { n } ^ { - } = | u _ { n } |$ it follows that also $\{ u _ { n } ^ { + } \}$ and $\{ u _ { n } ^ { - } \}$ satisfy (i) and (ii), and so without loss of generality it sufices to assume that $u _ { n } \geq 0$ 

Substep 2a: Assume that the space $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ is separable for some $1 < q < \infty$ and let p be its H¨older conjugate exponent. Let 

$$
C := \sup _ {n} \| u _ {n} \| _ {L ^ {1}} <   \infty ,\tag{2.39}
$$

and for each $k \in \mathbb N$ consider the truncation $T _ { k } \left( s \right) : = \operatorname* { m i n } \left\{ s , k \right\} , s \geq 0$ . Then 

$$
\int_ {X} \left(T _ {k} \left(u _ {n}\right)\right) ^ {p} d \mu \leq k ^ {p - 1} \int_ {X} u _ {n} d \mu \leq k ^ {p - 1} C.
$$

Hence for every fixed $k \in \mathbb N$ the sequence $\{ T _ { k } \left( u _ { n } \right) \} _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ is bounded in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ Let $\{ h _ { j } \}$ be a dense sequence in $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ . Since the sequence $\{ T _ { 1 } \left( u _ { n } \right) \} _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ is bounded in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ by Corollary A.66, we can extract a subsequence $\{ u _ { n ^ { ( 1 ) } } \} \subset$ $\{ u _ { n } \}$ such that the truncated sequence $\left\{ T _ { 1 } \left( u _ { n ^ { ( 1 ) } } \right) \right\}$ is weakly convergent in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ to some function $g _ { 1 }$ . In particular, 

$$
\lim _ {n ^ {(1)} \to \infty} \int_ {X} T _ {1} (u _ {n ^ {(1)}}) h _ {j} d \mu = \int_ {X} g _ {1} h _ {j} d \mu
$$

for all $j \in \mathbb N$ . Similarly, since the sequence $\left\{ T _ { 2 } \left( u _ { n ^ { ( 1 ) } } \right) \right\}$ is bounded in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ we can extract a subsequence $\left\{ u _ { n ^ { ( 2 ) } } \right\} \subset \left\{ u _ { n ^ { ( 1 ) } } \right\}$ such that the truncated sequence $\left\{ T _ { 2 } \left( u _ { n ^ { ( 2 ) } } \right) \right\}$ is weakly convergent in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ to some function $g _ { 2 }$ . In particular, 

$$
\lim _ {n ^ {(2)} \to \infty} \int_ {X} T _ {k} (u _ {n ^ {(2)}}) h _ {j} d \mu = \int_ {X} g _ {k} h _ {j} d \mu
$$

for all $j \in \mathbb N$ and $k = 1 , 2$ 

Recursively, for each $i \in \mathbb N$ we can find a subsequence $\left\{ u _ { n ^ { ( i ) } } \right\} \subset \left\{ u _ { n ^ { ( i - 1 ) } } \right\}$ such that the truncated sequence $\{ T _ { i } \left( u _ { n ^ { ( i ) } } \right) \}$ is weakly convergent in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ to some function $g _ { i }$ . In particular, 

$$
\lim _ {n ^ {(i)} \to \infty} \int_ {X} T _ {k} (u _ {n ^ {(i)}}) h _ {j} d \mu = \int_ {X} g _ {k} h _ {j} d \mu
$$

for all $j \in \mathbb N$ and $k = 1 , \dots , i .$ 

Hence for each $i \in \mathbb N$ there exists an integer $m _ { i }$ such that 

$$
\left| \int_ {X} T _ {k} \left(u _ {n ^ {(i)}}\right) h _ {j} d \mu - \int_ {X} g _ {k} h _ {j} d \mu \right| \leq \frac {1}{i}\tag{2.40}
$$

for all $j , k = 1 , \ldots , i$ and for all $n ^ { ( i ) } \geq m _ { i }$ 

Let $n _ { i }$ be the first natural number $\boldsymbol { n } ^ { ( i ) }$ greater than or equal to $m _ { i }$ . We claim that the subsequence $\{ u _ { n _ { i } } \}$ has the property that 

$$
T _ {k} \left(u _ {n _ {i}}\right)\rightharpoonup g _ {k} \text { in } L ^ {p} (X)\tag{2.41}
$$

as $i \to \infty$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$ . Fix $k \in \mathbb N$ . Since $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ is separable and the sequence $\{ T _ { k } \left( u _ { n _ { i } } \right) \} _ { i \in \mathbb { N } }$ is bounded in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ , it sufices to show that 

$$
\lim _ {i \to \infty} \int_ {X} T _ {k} (u _ {n _ {i}}) h _ {j} d \mu = \int_ {X} g _ {k} h _ {j} d \mu
$$

for all $j \in \mathbb N$ . Fix $\varepsilon > 0 , j \in \mathbb { N }$ , and let $i _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { N }$ be so large that 

$$
i _ {0} \geq \max \left\{\frac {1}{\varepsilon}, k, j \right\}.
$$

Then by (2.40), for all $i \geq i _ { 0 }$ ， 

$$
\left| \int_ {X} T _ {k} \left(u _ {n _ {i}}\right) h _ {j} d \mu - \int_ {X} g _ {k} h _ {j} d \mu \right| \leq \frac {1}{i} \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all $i \geq i _ { 0 }$ . This proves the claim. 

For every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ with $\mu \left( E \right) < \infty$ we have that $\chi _ { E } \in L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ , and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 \leq \int_ {E} g _ {k} d \mu = \lim _ {i \to \infty} \int_ {E} T _ {k} (u _ {n _ {i}}) d \mu \leq \lim _ {i \to \infty} \int_ {E} T _ {k + 1} (u _ {n _ {i}}) d \mu \\ = \int_ {E} g _ {k + 1} d \mu \leq C, \end{array}
$$

where in the last inequality we have used (2.39) and the fact that $T _ { k + 1 } \left( u _ { n _ { i } } \right) \leq$ $u _ { n _ { i } }$ . Since $g _ { k } \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ , the set $\{ x \in X : g _ { k } \left( x \right) \neq 0 \}$ is $\sigma { \mathrm { - f i n i t e } }$ . Hence the inequalities 

$$
0 \leq \int_ {E} g _ {k} d \mu \leq \int_ {E} g _ {k + 1} d \mu \leq C
$$

hold for all $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . We conclude that 

$$
\int_ {X} g _ {k} d \mu \leq C\tag{2.42}
$$

and that $0 \leq g _ { k } \left( x \right) \leq g _ { k + 1 } \left( x \right)$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ . Thus we may find a measurable function g such that $g _ { k } \nearrow ^ { n } g$ . By the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem it follows from (2.42) that $g \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ 

We claim that $u _ { n _ { i } } \ \to \ g$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . Indeed, fix $\varepsilon > 0 , \lambda \in \left( L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ , and by hypothesis, find $E _ { \varepsilon } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\delta > 0$ such that $\mu \left( E _ { \varepsilon } \right) < \infty$ 

$$
\int_ {X \setminus E _ {\varepsilon}} (g + u _ {n _ {i}}) d \mu \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{1 + \| \lambda \|}\tag{2.43}
$$

for all $i \in \mathbb N$ , and 

$$
\int_ {E} u _ {n _ {i}} d \mu \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{1 + \| \lambda \|}\tag{2.44}
$$

for all $i \in \mathbb N$ and for every Lebesgue measurable set $E \subset X$ with $\mu \left( E \right) \leq \delta$ Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {X} (u _ {n _ {i}} - g) d \lambda = \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon}} (T _ {k} (u _ {n _ {i}}) - g _ {k}) d \lambda + \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon}} (g _ {k} - g) d \lambda \\ \qquad + \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon} \cap \{u _ {n _ {i}} > k \}} (u _ {n _ {i}} - k) d \lambda + \int_ {X \setminus E _ {\varepsilon}} (u _ {n _ {i}} - g) d \lambda , \end{array}\tag{2.45}
$$

where $k \in \mathbb N$ is chosen so large that 

$$
\int_ {E _ {\varepsilon}} | g - g _ {k} | d \mu \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{1 + \| \lambda \|}, \quad \mu (\{u _ {n _ {i}} > k \}) \leq \frac {1}{k} \int_ {X} u _ {n _ {i}} d \mu \leq \delta .\tag{2.46}
$$

Hence by (2.44), 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \left| \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon} \cap \left\{u _ {n _ {i}} > k \right\}} (u _ {n _ {i}} - k) d \lambda \right| \leq \| \lambda \| \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon} \cap \left\{u _ {n _ {i}} > k \right\}} (u _ {n _ {i}} - k) d \mu \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qend{array}
$$

and so, also from (2.45), (2.46) , (2.43), we get that 

$$
\left| \int_ {X} \left(u _ {n _ {i}} - g\right) d \lambda \right| \leq \left| \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon}} \left(T _ {k} \left(u _ {n _ {i}}\right) - g _ {k}\right) d \lambda \right| + 3 \varepsilon .
$$

Since $\mu \left( E _ { \varepsilon } \right) < \infty$ by (2.41), it follows that 

$$
\lim _ {i \to \infty} \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon}} \left(T _ {k} (u _ {n _ {i}}) - g _ {k}\right) d \lambda = 0,
$$

and so we conclude that 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {i \to \infty} \left| \int_ {X} \left(u _ {n _ {i}} - g\right) d \lambda \right| \leq 3 \varepsilon .
$$

Given the arbitrariness of ε the proof is concluded in this case. 

Substep 2b: We now remove the additional hypothesis on the separabil ity of $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ . Let ${ \mathfrak { M } } _ { 1 }$ be the smallest σ-algebra containing all the sets $\{ x \in X : u _ { n } \left( x \right) > t \}$ for $t \in \mathbb { Q }$ and $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and let 

$$
Y := \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left\{x \in X: u _ {n} (x) \neq 0 \right\}.
$$

Then $( Y , \mathfrak { M } _ { 1 } \lfloor Y )$ is a separable measurable space and $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } _ { 1 } \lfloor Y \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is σ-finite. Hence $L ^ { q } \left( Y , \mathfrak { M } _ { 1 } \vert Y , \mu \right)$ is separable for all $1 \leq q < \infty$ by Theorem 2.16. Moreover, the restriction of $u _ { n }$ to $Y$ belongs to $L ^ { 1 } \left( Y , \mathfrak { M } _ { 1 } \vert Y , \mu \right)$ and still satisfies the equi-integrability condition as well as hypothesis (ii) in Vitali’s theorem. Hence by Substep 2a there exists a subsequence $\{ u _ { n _ { i } } \}$ of $\{ u _ { n } \}$ and a function $g \in L ^ { 1 } \left( Y , \mathfrak { M } _ { 1 } \vert Y , \mu \right)$ such that $u _ { n _ { i } }$ restricted to Y converges to g in $L ^ { 1 } \left( Y , \mathfrak { M } _ { 1 } \vert Y , \mu \right)$ . Extend g by zero outside Y. Since $\mathfrak { M } _ { 1 } \subset \mathfrak { M }$ we have that $g \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . We claim that $u _ { n _ { i } } \ \to \ g$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . Indeed, $\lambda \in \mathsf { \Gamma } \bigl ( L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right) \bigr ) ^ { \prime }$ , and using again the fact that $\mathfrak { M } _ { 1 } \subset \mathfrak { M }$ , we have that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sup \left\{\frac {| \lambda (E) |}{\mu (E)}: E \in \mathfrak {M} _ {1}, 0 <   \mu (E) <   \infty \right\} \\ \leq \sup \left\{\frac {| \lambda (E) |}{\mu (E)}: E \in \mathfrak {M}, 0 <   \mu (E) <   \infty \right\} <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

and so $\lambda \in \left( L ^ { 1 } \left( Y , \mathfrak { M } _ { 1 } \lfloor Y , \mu \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ . Hence, since $u _ { n _ { i } } = g = 0$ outside $Y$ , we have 

$$
\lim _ {i \to \infty} \int_ {X} u _ {n _ {i}} d \lambda = \lim _ {i \to \infty} \int_ {Y} u _ {n _ {i}} d \lambda = \int_ {Y} g d \lambda = \int_ {X} g d \lambda .
$$

This concludes the proof. 

Exercise 2.55. Prove that if the measure µ is finite and nonatomic in the Dunford–Pettis theorem, then condition (i) is implied by (ii). 

Remark 2.56. By comparing the previous theorem with Vitali’s convergence theorem, it follows that if a sequence $\{ u _ { n } \}$ weakly converges to some function u in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ , then it converges strongly to u if and only if it converges in measure to u. Thus typical examples of sequences converging weakly but not strongly in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ are given by oscillating sequences. 

Exercise 2.57. Let $X = [ 0 , 2 \pi ]$ with the Lebesgue measure. Prove that the sequence $u _ { n } \left( x \right) : = \sin n x$ converges weakly to zero in $L ^ { 1 } \left( \left[ 0 , 2 \pi \right] \right)$ but for all x irrational the limit 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \sin n x
$$

does not exist and the sequence $\{ u _ { n } \}$ does not converge in measure. 

Corollary 2.58. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space, and let $u _ { n } , u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Then $u _ { n } \to u$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ if and only if 

(i) $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } \left\| u _ { n } \right\| _ { L ^ { 1 } } < \infty ; } \end{array}$ 

(ii) $\textstyle \int _ { E } u _ { n } d \mu \to \int _ { E }$ u dµ for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

Proof. Assume that (i) and (ii) hold. Let $\{ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ be a subsequence of $\{ u _ { n } \}$ Reasoning as in the proof of Substeps 1b and 1c of the Dunford–Pettis theorem, we can conclude that $\{ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ is equi-integrable and satisfies (2.36). Hence $\{ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ is weakly sequentially precompact, and so up to a further subsequence (not relabeled) we may assume that $u _ { n _ { k } } \ \to \ v$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . In view of (ii) we have that 

$$
\int_ {E} (u - v) d \mu = 0
$$

for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , which implies that $u \left( x \right) = v \left( x \right)$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ . Thus we have shown that $u _ { n _ { k } }  u$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . Hence the whole sequence converges weakly to u in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ 

The converse implication follows from Proposition 2.46 and the fact that $\chi _ { E } \in \left( L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

The following result allows us to identify the weak limit. 

Theorem 2.59. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with µ finite and let $\{ u _ { n } \}$ be a sequentially weakly compact sequence in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . Then $u _ { n } \to u$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ if and only if 

$$
\int_ {X} \left| u + v \right| d \mu \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \int_ {X} \left| u _ {n} + v \right| d \mu
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . 

Proof. If $u _ { n } \ \to \ u$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ then $u _ { n } + v \implies u + v$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ , and $\mathrm { s o } ,$ , by Proposition 2.46 (i), 

$$
\int_ {X} \left| u + v \right| d \mu \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \int_ {X} \left| u _ {n} + v \right| d \mu .
$$

Conversely, assume that a subsequence of $\{ u _ { n } \}$ (not relabeled) converges weakly in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ to some function w, and let 

$$
X ^ {+} := \left\{x \in X: w (x) > u (x) \right\}, \quad X ^ {-} := \left\{x \in X: w (x) \leq u (x) \right\}.
$$

Since $\{ u _ { n } - u \}$ is equi-integrable, by Theorem 2.29, given $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $t > 0$ such that 

$$
\int_ {\{x \in X: | u _ {n} - u | > t \}} | u _ {n} - u | d \mu \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Set 

$$
v := - u - t \chi_ {X ^ {+}} + t \chi_ {X ^ {-}}.
$$

Since $\mu$ is finite, it follows that $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ , and 

$$
\left| u _ {n} + v \right| \leq t - \left(u _ {n} - u\right) \chi_ {X ^ {+}} + \left(u _ {n} - u\right) \chi_ {X ^ {-}} + 2 \left| u _ {n} - u \right| \chi_ {\{| u _ {n} - u | > t \}}.
$$

Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} t \mu \left(X\right) = \int_ {X} \left| u + v \right| d \mu \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} \left| u _ {n} + v \right| d \mu \\ \quad \leq t \mu \left(X\right) - \int_ {X ^ {+}} \left(w - u\right) d \mu + \int_ {X ^ {-}} \left(w - u\right) d \mu + 2 \varepsilon \\ = t \mu \left(X\right) - \int_ {X} \left| w - u \right| d \mu + 2 \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

and so 

$$
\int_ {X} | w - u | d \mu \leq 2 \varepsilon .
$$

It sufices to let $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ 

Exercise 2.60. Can you extend the previous theorem to the case in which $\mu$ is not finite? 

If $u _ { n } \to u$ in $L ^ { \boldsymbol { p } } ( \boldsymbol { X } ) ( \stackrel { * } {  } \mathrm { i f } \ p = \infty )$ and $v _ { n } \to v$ strongly in $L ^ { q } \left( X \right)$ , where p and q are conjugate exponents, then 

$$
u _ {n} v _ {n} \rightharpoonup u v \text {   in   } L ^ {1} (X).\tag{2.47}
$$

In the case $p = 1$ , using the equi-integrability we may improve this result in the sense that we may replace strong convergence in $L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ with convergence with respect to the Mackey topology. 

Proposition 2.61. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with µ finite. $I f u _ { n }  u$ in $L ^ { 1 } ( X ) , v _ { n }  v$ pointwise for µ a.e. $x \in X$ , and $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } \| v _ { n } \| _ { L ^ { \infty } } < \infty$ , then $u _ { n } v _ { n }  u v$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ 

Proof. In view of Corollary 2.58, it sufices to show that 

$$
\int_ {E} u _ {n} v _ {n} d \mu \rightarrow \int_ {E} u v d \mu
$$

for every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ . Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ . Since $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is equi-integrable, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
\int_ {F} | u _ {n} | d \mu \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{6 \left(1 + \sup _ {k} \| v _ {k} \| _ {L ^ {\infty}}\right)}\tag{2.48}
$$

for all n and for every measurable set $F ~ \subset ~ X$ with $\mu \left( F \right) ~ \leq ~ \delta$ . On the other hand, by $\mathrm { E g o r o f f s }$ theorem there exists a measurable set $X _ { \varepsilon } \subset X$ with $\mu \left( X _ { \varepsilon } \right) \leq \delta$ such that 

$$
v _ {n} \to v \text {   strongly   in   } L ^ {\infty} \left(X \setminus X _ {\varepsilon}\right).
$$

Let $n _ { 0 }$ be large enough so that for all $n \geq n _ { 0 }$ 

$$
\left\| v _ {n} - v \right\| _ {L ^ {\infty} (X \backslash X _ {\varepsilon})} \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{3 \left(1 + \sup _ {k} \left\| u _ {k} \right\| _ {L ^ {1}}\right)}\tag{2.49}
$$

and 

$$
\left| \int_ {E \backslash X _ {\varepsilon}} (u _ {n} - u) v d \mu \right| \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{3},\tag{2.50}
$$

where in the last inequality we have used the fact that $u _ { n } \to u$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ Writing 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {E} u _ {n} v _ {n}   d \mu - \int_ {E} u v   d \mu = \int_ {E \setminus X _ {\varepsilon}} (u _ {n} - u)   v   d \mu + \int_ {E \setminus X _ {\varepsilon}} u _ {n}   (v _ {n} - v)   d \mu \\ + \int_ {E \cap X _ {\varepsilon}} u _ {n} v _ {n}   d \mu - \int_ {E \cap X _ {\varepsilon}} u v   d \mu , \end{array}
$$

we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \int_ {E} u _ {n} v _ {n} d \mu - \int_ {E} u v d \mu \right| \\ \qquad \leq \left| \int_ {E \setminus X _ {\varepsilon}} (u _ {n} - u) v d \mu \right| + \| v _ {n} - v \| _ {L ^ {\infty} (E \setminus X _ {\varepsilon})} \sup _ {k} \int_ {X} | u _ {k} | d \mu \\ \qquad + \sup _ {k} \| v _ {k} \| _ {L ^ {\infty} (X)} \int_ {X _ {\varepsilon}} | u _ {n} | d \mu + \| v \| _ {L ^ {\infty} (X)} \int_ {X _ {\varepsilon}} | u | d \mu \leq \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

where we have used (2.50), (2.49), and (2.48) twice, in this order. Note that to estimate the last term we also used the facts that $\| v \| _ { L ^ { \infty } ( X ) } ~ \le$ lim in $\stackrel { \cdot } { \tau } _ { n  \infty } \| v _ { n } \| _ { L ^ { \infty } ( X ) }$ and, by Proposition 2.46(ii), 

$$
\int_ {X _ {\varepsilon}} | u | d \mu \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X _ {\varepsilon}} | u _ {n} | d \mu .
$$

The proof is complete.

## 2.1.5 Biting Convergence

As we observed already in Remark 2.51, if $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is a bounded sequence in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ there is no guarantee that it admits a weakly convergent subsequence. However, this is possible, provided we exclude a decreasing sequence of measurable sets $\{ E _ { j } \}$ with $\mu ( E _ { j } )  0$ 

Lemma 2.63 (Biting lemma). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with $\mu$ finite and let $\{ u _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of functions bounded in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . Then there exist a function ${ \dot { u } } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ , a subsequence $\left\{ u _ { n _ { k } } \right\} ~ o f \left\{ u _ { n } \right\}$ , and a decreasing sequence of measurable sets $\{ E _ { j } \} \subset X$ , with $\mu ( E _ { j } )  0$ , such that 

$$
u _ {n _ {k}} \rightharpoonup u i n L ^ {1} (X \setminus E _ {j}) f o r e v e r y j \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Proof. By the decomposition lemma there exist a subsequence of $\{ u _ { n } \}$ (not relabeled) and an increasing sequence of numbers $r _ { n }  \infty$ such that the truncated sequence $\{ \tau _ { r _ { n } } \circ u _ { n } \}$ is equi-integrable and 

$$

$$

as $n \to \infty$ . By selecting a further subsequence if necessary, we may assume that 

$$
\mu \left(\{x \in X: u _ {n} (x) \neq (\tau_ {r _ {n}} \circ u _ {n}) (x) \}\right) \leq \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}}
$$

for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . For $j \in \mathbb N$ set 

$$
E _ {j} := \bigcup_ {n = j} ^ {\infty} \left\{x \in X: u _ {n} (x) \neq \left(\tau_ {r _ {n}} \circ u _ {n}\right) (x) \right\}.
$$

Since $u _ { n } ~ = ~ \tau _ { r _ { n } } \circ u _ { n }$ on $X \ \backslash \ E _ { j }$ for all $n \geq j$ , it follows that $\{ u _ { n } \} _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ is equi-integrable on $X \setminus E _ { j }$ 

Since $\mu$ is finite, by the Dunford–Pettis theorem, the sequence $\{ u _ { n } \}$ admits a subsequence $\{ u _ { n , 1 } \}$ converging weakly in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \backslash E _ { 1 } \right)$ to a function $v _ { 1 }$ . By induction, assuming that $\{ u _ { n , k } \}$ has been selected, we extract a subsequence $\{ u _ { n , k + 1 } \} \subset \{ u _ { n , k } \}$ converging weakly in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \backslash E _ { k + 1 } \right)$ to a function $v _ { k + 1 }$ Using a diagonal argument we may select a subsequence $\{ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ u _ { n , k } \}$ such that $\boldsymbol { u } _ { n _ { k } }$ converges weakly to $v _ { j }$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \backslash E _ { j } \right)$ for each fixed $j$ . $$
u \left(x\right) = v _ {j} \left(x\right) \quad \text { if } x \in X \setminus E _ {j} \text { for   some } j \in \mathbb {N}.

for every $j \in \mathbb N$ 

Note that in general we cannot conclude that the entire sequence $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges in the sense of the biting lemma. 

Exercise 2.64. Let $X : = ( 0 , 1 )$ with the Lebesgue measure and for $n , k \in \mathbb { N }$ 2 $n \neq k$ , define

The biting lemma suggests the following definition. 

Definition 2.65. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space. Given $\{ u _ { n } \}$ a bounded sequence in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right) , u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ , we say that $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges weakly to u in the biting sense, and we write $u _ { n } \ \overset { b } {  } \ u _ { : }$ , if there exists a decreasing sequence of Lebesgue measurable sets $\{ E _ { j } \} \subset X$ , with $\mu ( E _ { j } )  0$ , such that

$$

Proposition 2.67. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $\{ u _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of nonnegative functions in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ such that $u _ { n } \stackrel { b } {  } u$ . $$

$$

Proof. Assume that a subsequence $\{ u _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges weakly to u in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . Then

$$

By definition of biting convergence there exists a decreasing sequence $\{ E _ { j } \} \subset$ X of measurable sets with $\mu ( E _ { j } )  0$ such that 

u<sub>n</sub>  u in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \backslash E _ { j } \right)$ for every $j \in \mathbb N$ 

In view of Corollary 2.49, it sufices to prove that for every measurable set $F \subset X$ we have 

$$

Indeed, since $u _ { n _ { k } } \geq 0$ we have 

$$

Similarly, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {X} u   d \mu - \int_ {F} u   d \mu = \int_ {X \setminus F} u   d \mu \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {X \setminus F} u _ {n _ {k}}   d \mu \\ \qquad = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {X} u _ {n _ {k}}   d \mu - \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {F} u _ {n _ {k}}   d \mu \\ \qquad \leq \int_ {X} u   d \mu - \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {F} u _ {n _ {k}}   d \mu , \end{array}
$$

i.e., 

$$

$$

and (2.51) is proved. 

To prove the second statement of the proposition, assume that $u _ { n } \to u$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ . Since $1 \in \left( L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ we have that

Proposition 2.71. Let X be a locally compact Hausdorf space, let $\mu \ :$ $B ( X )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a Borel measure, and let $\{ u _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } \left( X \right)$ be a sequence $o f$ nonnegative functions such that

## 2.2 Euclidean Setting

Throughout this section the ambient space is the euclidean space $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , and we consider the Lebesgue measure $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ . Also, $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ will denote a Lebesgue measurable set, not necessarily bounded. For a multi-index $\alpha = ( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { N } ) \in$ $\left( \mathbb { N } _ { 0 } \right) ^ { N }$ we set 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {\alpha}}{\partial x ^ {\alpha}} := \frac {\partial^ {| \alpha |}}{\partial x _ {1} ^ {\alpha_ {1}} \dots \partial x _ {N} ^ {\alpha_ {N}}}, \quad | \alpha | := \alpha_ {1} + \ldots + \alpha_ {N},
$$

where ${ \boldsymbol x } = ( x _ { 1 } , \dots , x _ { N } )$ . If $\varOmega \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is any open set (not necessarily bounded), for any nonnegative integer $l \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ we denote by $C ^ { l } \left( \varOmega \right)$ the vector space of all functions that are continuous together with their partial derivatives up to order l. We set $C ^ { \infty } \left( \varOmega \right) : = \bigcap _ { l = 0 } ^ { \infty } C ^ { l } \left( \varOmega \right)$ and we define $C _ { c } ^ { l } \left( \varOmega \right)$ and $C _ { c } ^ { \infty } \left( \varOmega \right)$ as the subspaces of $C ^ { l } \left( \varOmega \right)$ and $C ^ { \infty } \left( \varOmega \right)$ , respectively, consisting of all functions that have compact support. 

## 2.2.1 Approximation by Regular Functions

Given a nonnegative bounded function $\varphi : \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ with 

$$
\operatorname{supp} \varphi \subset \overline {{B (0 , 1)}}, \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi (x) d x = 1,\tag{2.54}
$$

for $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ and $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ , define the mollification 

$$
u _ {\varepsilon} (x) := \left(u * \varphi_ {\varepsilon}\right) (x) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y) u (y) d y, \quad x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N},
$$

where 

$$
\varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x) := \frac {1}{\varepsilon^ {N}} \varphi \left(\frac {x}{\varepsilon}\right), x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}.
$$

The functions $\varphi _ { \varepsilon }$ are called mollifiers. Note that supp $\varphi _ { \varepsilon } \subset \overline { { B \left( 0 , \varepsilon \right) } }$ 

Remark 2.72. In the applications we will consider two special cases: 

(i) $\varphi$ is the (renormalized) characteristic function of the unit ball, that is, 

$$
\varphi (x) := \frac {1}{\alpha_ {N}} \chi_ {B (0, 1)} (x), \quad x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N};
$$

(ii) $\varphi$ is the $C _ { c } ^ { \infty }$ function 

$$
\varphi \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} c   \exp \left(\frac {1}{| x | ^ {2} - 1}\right) & \text { if }    | x | <   1, \\ 0 & \text { if }    | x | \geq 1, \end{array} \right.\tag{2.55}
$$

where we choose $c > 0$ such that (2.54) is satisfied. In this case, the functions $\varphi _ { \varepsilon }$ are called standard mollifiers. 

The first main result of this subsection is the following theorem. 

Theorem 2.73. Let $\varphi : \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ be a nonnegative bounded function satisfying (2.54), and let $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$

(ii) $u _ { \varepsilon } ( x )  u ( x )$ as $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ for every Lebesgue point $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ of u (and so for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } )$ 

(iii) If $u \in L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) , 1 \leq p < \infty$ , then 

$$
\left\| u _ {\varepsilon} \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} \leq \left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})}\tag{2.56}
$$

$$
u _ {\varepsilon} \rightarrow u \quad i n L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N}) a s \varepsilon \rightarrow 0 ^ {+}.
$$

$$
K _ {\eta} := \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \operatorname{dist} (x, K) \leq \eta \right\}.
$$

Then $K _ { \eta }$ is compact and since u is uniformly continuous on $K _ { \eta }$ , for any $\rho > 0$ there exists $\delta = \delta \left( \eta , K , \rho \right) > 0$ such that 

$$
| u (x) - u (y) | \leq \frac {\rho}{1 + \| \varphi \| _ {\infty}}\tag{2.57}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} | u _ {\varepsilon} (x) - u (x) | = \left| \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y) u (y) d y - u (x) \right| \\ \qquad = \frac {1}{\varepsilon^ {N}} \left| \int_ {B (x, \varepsilon)} \varphi \left(\frac {x - y}{\varepsilon}\right) [ u (y) - u (x) ] d y \right| \\ \qquad \leq \| \varphi \| _ {\infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon^ {N}} \int_ {B (x, \varepsilon)} | u (y) - u (x) | d y, \end{array}\tag{2.58}
$$

where we have used (2.54) and the fact that supp $\varphi _ { \varepsilon } \subset \overline { { B \left( 0 , \varepsilon \right) } }$ . It follows by (2.57) that 

$$
\left| u _ {\varepsilon} (x) - u (x) \right| \leq \rho
$$

for all $x \in K$ , and so $\| u _ { \varepsilon } - u \| _ { C ( K ) } \leq \rho .$ 

(ii) Let $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue point of u, that is, 

$$
\lim _ {\varepsilon \rightarrow 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\varepsilon^ {N}} \int_ {B (x, \varepsilon)} | u (y) - u (x) | d y = 0.
$$

Then from (2.58) it follows that $u _ { \varepsilon } ( x )  u ( x ) \mathrm { a s } \varepsilon  0 ^ { + }$ 

(iii) Let $u \in L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) , 1 \leq p < \infty$ . We prove (2.56). By H¨older’s inequality and (2.54), for all $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | u _ {\varepsilon} (x) | = \left| \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} (\varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y)) ^ {1 / p ^ {\prime}} (\varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y)) ^ {1 / p} u (y) d y \right| \\ \leq \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y) d y\right) ^ {1 / p ^ {\prime}} \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y) | u (y) | ^ {p} d y\right) ^ {1 / p} \\ = \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y) | u (y) | ^ {p} d y\right) ^ {1 / p}, \end{array}
$$

and so by Fubini’s theorem and (2.54) once more, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {\varepsilon} (x) | ^ {p} d x \leq \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y) | u (y) | ^ {p} d y d x \\ \qquad = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (y) | ^ {p} \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y) d x\right) d y \\ \qquad = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (y) | ^ {p} d y. \end{array}
$$

It remains to show that $u _ { \varepsilon }  u$ in $L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . Fix $\rho > 0$ and find a function $v \in C _ { c } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ such that 

$$
\left\| u - v \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} \leq \rho .
$$

Since $K : = \operatorname { s u p p } v$ is compact, it follows from part (i) that for every $\eta > 0$ the mollification $v _ { \varepsilon }$ of v converges to v uniformly in the compact set 

$$
K _ {\eta} := \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \operatorname{dist} (x, K) \leq \eta \right\}.
$$

Since $v _ { \varepsilon } = v = 0$ in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N } \backslash K _ { \eta }$ for $0 < \varepsilon < \eta$ , we have that 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | v _ {\varepsilon} - v | ^ {p} d x = \int_ {K _ {\eta}} | v _ {\varepsilon} - v | ^ {p} d x \leq \left(\| v _ {\varepsilon} - v \| _ {C (K _ {\eta})}\right) ^ {p} | K _ {\eta} | \leq \rho ,
$$

provided $\varepsilon > 0$ is suficiently small. By Minkowski’s inequality, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\| u _ {\varepsilon} - u \| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} \leq \| u _ {\varepsilon} - v _ {\varepsilon} \| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} + \| v _ {\varepsilon} - v \| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} + \| v - u \| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})}} \\ & {\qquad \leq 2 \| u - v \| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} + \| v _ {\varepsilon} - v \| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} \leq 3 \rho ,} \end{array}
$$

where we have used (2.56) for the function $u - v$ 

More can be said about the regularity of $u _ { \varepsilon }$ if we restrict our attention to standard mollifiers. 

Theorem 2.74. Let $\varphi$ be defined as in (2.55), and let $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . Then $u _ { \varepsilon } \in C ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ for all $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ , and for any multi-index $\alpha _ { i }$ 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {\alpha} u _ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x ^ {\alpha}} (x) = \left(u * \frac {\partial^ {\alpha} \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x ^ {\alpha}}\right) (x) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \frac {\partial^ {\alpha} \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x ^ {\alpha}} (x - y) u (y) d y\tag{2.59}
$$

for all $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

Proof. Fix $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } , \eta > 0$ , and $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ . Let $e _ { i } , i = 1 , \ldots , N$ , be an element of the canonical basis of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , and for any $h \in \mathbb { R }$ , with $0 < | h | \leq \eta$ , consider 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {u _ {\varepsilon} (x + h e _ {i}) - u _ {\varepsilon} (x)}{h} - \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \frac {\partial \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x _ {i}} (x - y) u (y) d y \\ = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \left[ \frac {\varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x + h e _ {i} - y) - \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y)}{h} - \frac {\partial \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x _ {i}} (x - y) \right] u (y) d y \\ = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \left(\frac {1}{h} \int_ {0} ^ {h} \frac {\partial \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x _ {i}} (x - y + t e _ {i}) d t - \frac {\partial \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x _ {i}} (x - y)\right) u (y) d y \\ = \frac {1}{h} \int_ {0} ^ {h} \left(\int_ {B (x, \varepsilon + \eta)} \left[ \frac {\partial \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x _ {i}} (x - y + t e _ {i}) - \frac {\partial \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x _ {i}} (x - y) \right] u (y) d y\right) d t, \end{array}
$$

where we have used Fubini’s theorem and the fact that supp $\varphi _ { \varepsilon } \subset \overline { { B \left( 0 , \varepsilon \right) } }$ 

Since $\varphi _ { \varepsilon } \in C _ { c } ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ , its partial derivatives are uniformly continuous. 

Hence for any for any $\rho > 0$ there exists $\delta = \delta \left( \eta , x , \rho , \varepsilon \right) > 0$ such that 

$$
\left| \frac {\partial \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x _ {i}} (z) - \frac {\partial \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x _ {i}} (w) \right| \leq \frac {\rho}{1 + \| u \| _ {L ^ {1} (B (x , \varepsilon + \eta))}}
$$

for all $z , w \in B \left( x , \varepsilon + \eta \right)$ , with $| z - w | \leq \delta$ . Then for $0 < | h | \leq \operatorname* { m i n } \left\{ \eta , \delta \right\}$ we have 

$$
\left| \frac {u _ {\varepsilon} (x + h e _ {i}) - u _ {\varepsilon} (x)}{h} - \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \frac {\partial \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x _ {i}} (x - y) u (y) d y \right| \leq \rho ,
$$

which shows that 

$$
\frac {\partial u _ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x _ {i}} (x) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \frac {\partial \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x _ {i}} (x - y) u (y) d y.
$$

Note that the only properties that we have used about the function $\varphi _ { \varepsilon }$ are that $\varphi _ { \varepsilon } \in C _ { c } ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { \tilde { N } } \right)$ with supp $\varphi _ { \varepsilon } \subset \overline { { B \left( 0 , \varepsilon \right) } }$ . Hence the same proof carries over if we replace $\varphi _ { \varepsilon }$ with $\begin{array} { r } { \psi _ { \varepsilon } : = \frac { \partial \varphi _ { \varepsilon } } { \partial x _ { i } } } \end{array}$ . Thus by induction we may prove that for any multi-index α, 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {\alpha} u _ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x ^ {\alpha}} (x) = \left(u * \frac {\partial^ {\alpha} \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x ^ {\alpha}}\right) (x) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \frac {\partial^ {\alpha} \varphi_ {\varepsilon}}{\partial x ^ {\alpha}} (x - y) u (y) d y.
$$

This completes the proof. 

If the function u is defined only in an open set $\varOmega \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , with $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ then since supp $\varphi _ { \varepsilon } \subset \overline { { B \left( 0 , \varepsilon \right) } }$ , we may still define 

$$
u _ {\varepsilon} (x) := (u * \varphi_ {\varepsilon}) (x) = \int_ {\Omega} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y) u (y) d y
$$

for $x \in \varOmega _ { \varepsilon }$ , where the open set $\varOmega _ { \varepsilon }$ is given by 

$$
\Omega_ {\varepsilon} := \left\{x \in \Omega : \operatorname{dist} (x, \partial \Omega) > \varepsilon \right\}.
$$

In this case an analogous version of Theorem 2.73 holds. 

Theorem 2.75. Let $\mathcal { Q } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be an open set, let $\varphi : \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ be a nonnegative bounded function satisfying (2.54), and let $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ 

(i) If $u \in C \left( \varOmega \right)$ , then $u _ { \varepsilon } \to u a s \varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ uniformly on compact subsets $o f \varOmega .$ 

(ii) $u _ { \varepsilon } ( x )  u ( x )$ as $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ for every Lebesgue point $x \in \varOmega$ of u. 

(iii) $I f u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { p } ( \varOmega ) , 1 \leq p < \infty$ , then 

$$
\left\| u _ {\varepsilon} \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (\Omega_ {\varepsilon})} \leq \left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (\Omega)}
$$

and for every compact set $K \subset \varOmega$ 

$$
u _ {\varepsilon} \rightarrow u \quad i n L ^ {p} (K) a s \varepsilon \rightarrow 0 ^ {+}.
$$

Proof. The proof is very similar to that of Theorem 2.73. In the proof of (i), for any compact $K \subset \varOmega$ one should take 

$$
0 <   \eta <   \operatorname{dist} (K, \partial \Omega),
$$

so that $K _ { \eta } \subset \varOmega$ . Moreover, for $\varepsilon > 0$ suficiently small we have that $K _ { \eta } \subset \mathcal { \Omega } _ { \varepsilon }$ A similar change can be made in the proof of (iii). We omit the details. 

The analogue of Theorem 2.74 is the following. 

Theorem 2.76. Let $\varOmega \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be an open set, let $\varphi$ be defined as in (2.55), and let $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ . Then $u _ { \varepsilon } \in C ^ { \infty } \left( \varOmega _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ for all $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ , and for any multi-index α the formula (2.59) holds for all $\boldsymbol { x } \in \varOmega _ { \varepsilon }$ 

Proof. The proof is very similar to that of Theorem 2.74. Since now $x \in \varOmega _ { \varepsilon }$ , we have that dist $( x , \partial \varOmega ) > \varepsilon$ , and so one should take 

$$
0 <   \eta <   \mathrm{dist} (x, \partial \Omega) - \varepsilon .
$$

We omit the details. 

An important application of the theory of mollifiers is the existence of smooth partitions of unity. 

Theorem 2.77 (Smooth partition of unity). Let $\mathcal { Q } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be an open set and let $\{ U _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ be an open cover of Ω. Then there exists a sequence $\{ \psi _ { n } \} \subset C _ { c } ^ { \infty } \left( \Omega \right) o \ddot { f }$ nonnegative functions such that 

(i) each $\psi _ { n }$ has support in some $U _ { \alpha }$ ; 

(ii) $\textstyle \sum _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \psi _ { n } \left( x \right) = 1$ for all $x \in \varOmega$ ; 

(iii) for every compact set $K \subset \varOmega$ there exist an integer $\ell \in \mathbb { N }$ and an open set U, with $K \subset U \subset \varOmega$ , such that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\ell} \psi_ {n} (x) = 1
$$

for all $x \in U$ 

Proof. Let $S$ be a countable dense set in $\Omega , \mathrm { e . g . } , S : = \left\{ x \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { N } \cap \Omega \right\}$ , and consider the countable family $\mathcal { F }$ of closed balls 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {F} := \Big \{\overline {{B (x , r)}}: r \in \mathbb {Q}, 0 <   r <   1, x \in S, \\ \overline {{B (x , r)}} \subset U _ {\alpha} \cap \Omega \text {   for   some   } \alpha \in I \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Since $\mathcal { F }$ is countable we may write ${ \mathcal { F } } = \left\{ { \overline { { B \left( x _ { n } , r _ { n } \right) } } } \right\}$ . Since $\{ U _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ is an open cover of $\varOmega ,$ , by the density of S and of the rational numbers we have that 

$$
\Omega = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} B \left(x _ {n}, \frac {r _ {n}}{2}\right).\tag{2.60}
$$

For each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ consider 

$$
\phi_ {n} := \varphi_ {\frac {r _ {n}}{4}} * \chi_ {B \left(x _ {n}, \frac {3}{4} r _ {n}\right)},
$$

where $\varphi \frac { r _ { n } } { 4 }$ are standard mollifiers (with $\begin{array} { r } { \varepsilon : = { \frac { r _ { n } } { 4 } } ) } \end{array}$ . By Theorem $2 . 7 4 , \phi _ { n } \in$ $C ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . Moreover, if $x \in B \left( x _ { n } , { \frac { r _ { n } } { 2 } } \right)$ then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \phi_ {n} (x) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\frac {r _ {n}}{4}} (x - y) \chi_ {B \left(x _ {n}, \frac {3}{4} r _ {n}\right)} (y) d y \\ \qquad = \int_ {B \left(x, \frac {r _ {n}}{4}\right)} \varphi_ {\frac {r _ {n}}{4}} (x - y) \chi_ {B \left(x _ {n}, \frac {3}{4} r _ {n}\right)} (y) d y \\ \qquad = \int_ {B \left(x, \frac {r _ {n}}{4}\right)} \varphi_ {\frac {r _ {n}}{4}} (x - y) d y = 1, \end{array}
$$

where we have used (2.54) and the fact that if $x \in B \left( x _ { n } , { \frac { r _ { n } } { 2 } } \right)$ then 

$$
B \left(x, \frac {r _ {n}}{4}\right) \subset B \left(x _ {n}, \frac {3}{4} r _ {n}\right).
$$

Since $0 \leq \chi _ { B \left( x _ { n } , { \frac { 3 } { 4 } } r _ { n } \right) } \leq 1$ , a similar calculation shows that $0 \leq \phi _ { n } \leq 1$ . On the other hand, if x $\notin \overline { { B \left( x _ { n } , r _ { n } \right) } }$ then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \phi_ {n} (x) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\frac {r _ {n}}{4}} (x - y) \chi_ {B \left(x _ {n}, \frac {3}{4} r _ {n}\right)} (y) d y \\ = \int_ {B \left(x, \frac {r _ {n}}{4}\right)} \varphi_ {\frac {r _ {n}}{4}} (x - y) \chi_ {B \left(x _ {n}, \frac {3}{4} r _ {n}\right)} (y) d y = 0, \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that if $x \notin \overline { { B \left( x _ { n } , r _ { n } \right) } }$ then 

$$
B \left(x, \frac {r _ {n}}{4}\right) \cap B \left(x _ {n}, \frac {3}{4} r _ {n}\right) = \emptyset .
$$

In particular, $\phi _ { n } \in C _ { c } ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ and supp $\phi _ { n } \subset \overline { { B \left( x _ { n } , r _ { n } \right) } }$ . Note that in view of the definition of ${ \mathcal F } ,$ supp $\phi _ { n } \mathrm { ~ C ~ } U _ { \alpha } \cap \varOmega$ for some $\alpha \in I$ 

Define $\psi _ { 1 } : = \phi _ { 1 }$ and 

$$
\psi_ {n} := (1 - \phi_ {1}) \dots (1 - \phi_ {n - 1}) \phi_ {n}\tag{2.61}
$$

for $n \geq 2 , n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Since $0 \leq \phi _ { k } \leq 1$ and supp $\phi _ { k } \subset \overline { { B \left( x _ { k } , r _ { k } \right) } }$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$ , we have that $0 \leq \psi _ { n } \leq 1$ and supp $\psi _ { n } \subset { \overline { { B \left( x _ { n } , r _ { n } \right) } } }$ . This gives (i). To prove (ii) we prove by induction that 

$$
\psi_ {1} + \dots + \psi_ {n} = 1 - (1 - \phi_ {1}) \dots (1 - \phi_ {n})\tag{2.62}
$$

for all $n \in \mathbb N$ . The relation (2.62) is true for $n = 1$ , since $\psi _ { 1 } : = \phi _ { 1 }$ . Assume that (2.62) holds for n. Then by (2.61), 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \psi_ {1} + \ldots + \psi_ {n} + \psi_ {n + 1} = 1 - (1 - \phi_ {1}) \ldots (1 - \phi_ {n}) + \psi_ {n + 1} \\ = 1 - (1 - \phi_ {1}) \ldots (1 - \phi_ {n}) + (1 - \phi_ {1}) \ldots (1 - \phi_ {n})   \phi_ {n + 1} \\ = 1 - (1 - \phi_ {1}) \ldots (1 - \phi_ {n + 1}). \end{array}
$$

Hence (2.62) holds for all $n \in \mathbb { N } .$ 

Since $\phi _ { k } = 1$ in $\begin{array} { r } { B \left( { x } _ { k } , \frac { r _ { k } } { 2 } \right) } \end{array}$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$ , by (2.62), for all n, $m \in \mathbb { N }$ with $m \geq n$ we have that 

$$
\psi_ {1} (x) + \dots + \psi_ {m} (x) = 1 \quad \text { for   all } x \in \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {n} B \left(x _ {k}, \frac {r _ {k}}{2}\right).\tag{2.63}
$$

Thus, in view of (2.60), property (ii) holds. 

Finally, if $K \subset \varOmega$ is compact, again by (2.60), we may find $\ell \in \mathbb N$ so large that 

$$
\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\ell} B \left(x _ {k}, \frac {r _ {k}}{2}\right) \supset K,
$$

and so (iii) follows by (2.63). 

Using mollifiers it is possible to improve the density result of Theorem 2.99: 

Theorem 2.78. Let $\varOmega \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be an open set. Then the space $C _ { c } ^ { \infty } \left( \varOmega \right)$ is dense in $L ^ { p } \left( \varOmega \right) f o r 1 \leq p < \infty$ 

Proof. Let $u \in L ^ { p } \left( \varOmega \right)$ and extend it to be zero outside Ω. Define 

$$
K _ {n} := \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: | x | \leq n, \operatorname{dist} (x, \mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus \Omega) \geq \frac {2}{n} \right\}.
$$

Then $K _ { n }$ is compact, $K _ { n } \subset K _ { n + 1 }$ , and 

$$
\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} K _ {n} = \Omega .
$$

Define $v _ { n } : = u \chi _ { K _ { n } }$ and $u _ { n } : = \varphi _ { \frac { 1 } { n } } * v _ { n }$ n , where ϕ 1 are standard mollifiers (with $\varphi _ { \frac { 1 } { n } }$ $\textstyle \varepsilon : = { \frac { 1 } { n } } )$ . Since supp $\varphi _ { \frac { 1 } { n } } \subset \overline { { B \left( 0 , \frac { 1 } { n } \right) } }$ it follows that 

$$
\operatorname{supp} u _ {n} \subset \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \operatorname{dist} (x, K _ {n}) \leq \frac {1}{n} \right\} \subset \Omega .
$$

Hence by Theorem 2.76, $u _ { n } \in C _ { c } ^ { \infty } \left( \varOmega \right)$ . Moreover, by Minkowski’s inequality, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\| u _ {n} - u \| _ {L ^ {p} (\varOmega)} = \| u _ {n} - u \| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})}} \\ & {\qquad \leq \left\| \varphi_ {\frac {1}{n}} * v _ {n} - \varphi_ {\frac {1}{n}} * u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} + \left\| \varphi_ {\frac {1}{n}} * u - u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})}} \\ & {\qquad \leq \| v _ {n} - u \| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} + \left\| \varphi_ {\frac {1}{n}} * u - u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})}} \\ & {\qquad = \| u \chi_ {K _ {n}} - u \| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} + \left\| \varphi_ {\frac {1}{n}} * u - u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})},} \end{array}
$$

where we have used (2.56). It now follows from the Lebesgue dominated con vergence theorem that 

$$
\left\| u \chi_ {K _ {n}} - u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} \to 0
$$

as $n \to \infty$ , while 

$$
\left\| \varphi_ {\frac {1}{n}} * u - u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (\mathbb {R} ^ {N})} \to 0
$$

by Theorem 2.73. This completes the proof. 

Given a (positive) Radon measure $\mu : B \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \to \left[ 0 , \infty \right]$ and a standard mollifier $\varphi _ { \varepsilon } , \varepsilon > 0$ , we define 

$$
\left(\varphi_ {\varepsilon} * \mu\right) (x) := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y) d \mu (y), \quad x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}.
$$

Theorem 2.79. Let $\mu : { \mathcal { B } } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a (positive) Radon measure. Then for all $u \in C _ { c } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} u (x) (\varphi_ {\varepsilon} * \mu) (x) d x \rightarrow \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} u (x) d \mu (x)\tag{2.64}
$$

as $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ . If, in addition, $\mu \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) < \infty$ , then (2.64) holds for all uniformly continuous bounded functions u. 

Proof. Let $u \in C _ { c } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . Using Fubini’s theorem and (2.54) we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} u (x) (\varphi_ {\varepsilon} * \mu) (x) d x - \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} u (y) d \mu (y) \\ \qquad = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} u (x) \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y) d \mu (y) d x - \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} u (y) d \mu (y) \\ \qquad = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} u (x) \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x - y) d x - \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} u (y) \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x) d x\right) d \mu (y) \\ \qquad = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} u (x + y) \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x) d x - \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} u (y) \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x) d x\right) d \mu (y) \\ \qquad = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \left(\int_ {B (0, \varepsilon)} (u (x + y) - u (y)) \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (x) d x\right) d \mu (y). \end{array}
$$

Since $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { N } } \varphi _ { \varepsilon } \left( x \right) d x = 1 } \end{array}$ , and since u is uniformly continuous and bounded, if either u has compact support or $\mu \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) < \infty$ , by the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem we conclude (2.64). 

Remark 2.80. By considering separately the positive and negative parts of each component, it follows that the previous theorem still applies to vectorvalued Radon measures. 

## 2.2.2 Weak Convergence in ${ \pmb L } ^ { p }$

In this subsection we exploit properties of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and the Lebesgue measure in order to give deeper insight into the notion of weak convergence. The next two results relate to Corollary 2.49 and the Dunford–Pettis theorem, where now the arbitrariness of the measurable set of integration is reduced to testing on cubes. 

Proposition 2.81. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set. $I f 1 < p \leq \infty$ then $u _ { n } \to u$ in $L ^ { p } ( E ) ( \stackrel { * } {  } i f p = \infty )$ if and only if 

(i) $\textstyle \int _ { Q \cap E } u _ { n } d x \to \int _ { Q \cap E }$ u dx for every cube $Q \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

(ii) $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } \left\| u _ { n } \right\| _ { L ^ { p } } < \infty$ 

When $p = 1$ conditions (i) and (ii) of the previous proposition are still necessary but no longer suficient. 

Theorem 2.82 (Dunford–Pettis). Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set. A sequence $u _ { n }$ converges weakly to u in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ if and only if 

(i) $\textstyle \int _ { Q \cap E } u _ { n } d x \to \int _ { Q \cap E }$ u dx for every cube $Q \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ ; 

(ii) $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is equi-integrable; 

(iii) for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $F \subset E$ with $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( F \right) < \infty$ such that 

$$
\int_ {E \setminus F} | u _ {n} | d x \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all n. 

Remark 2.83. Conditions (ii) and (iii) imply (but they are not implied by) $\mathrm { s u p } _ { n } \| u _ { n } \| _ { L ^ { 1 } } < \infty$ (see Exercise 2.55). 

Definition 2.84. A function $u : \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \xrightarrow [ ] { } \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is said to be Q-periodic if $u ( x +$ $e _ { i } ) = u ( x )$ for all $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and every $i = 1 , \ldots , N$ , where $( e _ { 1 } , \dots , e _ { N } )$ is the canonical basis of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ . More generally, u is said to be kQ-periodic, $k \in \mathbb N$ , if $u ( k \cdot )$ is $Q { - } p e r i o d i c$ 

Lemma 2.85 (Riemann–Lebesgue lemma). Let $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { p } \big ( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \big ) , 1 \leq p \leq$ $\infty$ , be kQ-periodic. For every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ set 

$$
u _ {\varepsilon} (x) := u \left(\frac {x}{\varepsilon}\right).
$$

Then $u _ { \varepsilon } \ \to \ \overline { { u } }$ in $L ^ { \boldsymbol { p } } ( E ) \ ( \stackrel { * } {  } \ i f \ p \ = \ \infty )$ for every bounded measurable set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , where 

$$
\overline {{u}} (x) \equiv c o n s t := \frac {1}{k ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (0, k)} u (y) d y.
$$

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that $k = 1$ 

Step 1: Suppose first that $u \in L ^ { \infty } \left( Q \left( 0 , 1 \right) \right)$ . Then $\{ u _ { \varepsilon } \}$ is a bounded sequence in $L ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ , and so there exists a subsequence (not relabeled) such that $u _ { \varepsilon } \stackrel { * } { \to }$ $U$ in $L ^ { \infty } \left( { \dot { \mathbb { R } } } ^ { N } \right)$ . We claim that 

$$
U (x) = \overline {{{u}}} (x) = \int_ {Q (0, 1)} u (y) d y
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in Q \left( 0 , 1 \right)$ . Indeed, let $x _ { 0 }$ be a Lebesgue point for $U . \ { \mathrm { F i x } } \ \delta > 0$ and let $k _ { \varepsilon }$ be the integer part of $\delta / \varepsilon \ ( 0 < \varepsilon < < \delta )$ , so that $\delta / \varepsilon - 1 < k _ { \varepsilon } \leq \delta / \varepsilon$ Decompose 

$$
\frac {1}{\varepsilon} Q \left(x _ {0}, \delta\right) = \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {k _ {\varepsilon} ^ {N}} Q \left(a _ {i} ^ {(\varepsilon)}, 1\right) \cup E _ {\varepsilon},
$$

where 

$$
\mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left(E _ {\varepsilon}\right) = \left(\frac {\delta}{\varepsilon}\right) ^ {N} - k _ {\varepsilon} ^ {N} \leq \left(\frac {\delta}{\varepsilon}\right) ^ {N} - \left(\frac {\delta}{\varepsilon} - 1\right) ^ {N} = \mathrm{O} _ {\delta} \left(\frac {1}{\varepsilon^ {N - 1}}\right).
$$

Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \delta)} (U (x) - \overline {{u}}) d x \right| \\ = \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \left| \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \delta)} \left(u \left(\frac {x}{\varepsilon}\right) - \overline {{u}}\right) d x \right| \\ = \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \left| \varepsilon^ {N} \int_ {\frac {Q (x _ {0} , \delta)}{\varepsilon}} (u (y) - \overline {{u}}) d y \right| \\ = \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \left| \varepsilon^ {N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k _ {\varepsilon} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (a _ {i} ^ {(\varepsilon)}, 1)} (u (y) - \overline {{u}}) d y + \varepsilon^ {N} \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon}} (u (y) - \overline {{u}}) d y \right| \\ \leq 2 \| u \| _ {L ^ {\infty} (Q (0, 1))} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \varepsilon^ {N} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} (E _ {\varepsilon}) = 0, \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { Q \left( a _ { i } ^ { \left( \varepsilon \right) } , 1 \right) } \left( u \left( y \right) - \overline { { u } } \right) d y = 0 } \end{array}$ , due to the Q-periodicity of u. Hence 

$$
0 = \lim _ {\delta \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\delta^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \delta)} \left(U (x) - \overline {{u}}\right) d x = U (x _ {0}) - \overline {{u}}.
$$

Step 2: In the general case let $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { p } \big ( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \big ) , 1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , and consider standard mollifiers of the form 

$$
\varphi_ {n} (x) := n ^ {N} \varphi (n x), \quad x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N},
$$

where $\varphi$ is defined in (2.55). For $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ set 

$$
u _ {n} (x) := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {n} (x - y) u (y) d y \quad \text { and } \quad u _ {n, \varepsilon} (x) := u _ {n} \left(\frac {x}{\varepsilon}\right).
$$

Note that $u _ { n }$ is Q-periodic because for all $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and $i = 1 , \ldots , N$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} u _ {n} \left(x + e _ {i}\right) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {n} \left(x + e _ {i} - y\right) u \left(y\right) d y = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {n} \left(y\right) u \left(x + e _ {i} - y\right) d y \\ = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {n} \left(y\right) u \left(x - y\right) d y = u _ {n} \left(x\right). \end{array}
$$

Hence, since $u _ { n }$ is continuous and Q-periodic, we have that $u _ { n } \in L ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ with $\| u _ { n } \| _ { L ^ { \infty } (  { \mathbb { R } } ^ { N } ) } = \| u _ { n } \| _ { L ^ { \infty } ( Q ( 0 , 1 ) ) }$ and $u _ { n } \to u$ in $L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ 

Now if $Q ^ { \prime }$ is a cube in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and $v \in L ^ { p ^ { \prime } } \left( Q ^ { \prime } \right)$ , where $p ^ { \prime }$ is the conjugate exponent of $p _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ then by H¨older’s inequality, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \int_ {Q ^ {\prime}} (u _ {\varepsilon} v - \overline {{u}} v) d x \right| \leq \int_ {Q ^ {\prime}} | u _ {\varepsilon} - u _ {n, \varepsilon} | | v | d x + \left| \int_ {Q ^ {\prime}} (u _ {n, \varepsilon} - \overline {{u}} _ {n}) v d x \right| \\ \quad + \int_ {Q ^ {\prime}} | \overline {{u}} _ {n} - \overline {{u}} | | v | d x \\ \leq \left| \int_ {Q ^ {\prime}} (u _ {n, \varepsilon} - \overline {{u}} _ {n}) v d x \right| \\ \quad + \| v \| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (Q ^ {\prime})} \left\{\| u _ {\varepsilon} - u _ {n, \varepsilon} \| _ {L ^ {p} (Q ^ {\prime})} + \| \overline {{u}} _ {n} - \overline {{u}} \| _ {L ^ {p} (Q ^ {\prime})} \right\}. \end{array} \tag {2.65}
$$

We may decompose 

$$
\frac {1}{\varepsilon} Q ^ {\prime} \subset \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {L} \overline {{Q \left(a _ {i} ^ {(\varepsilon)} , 1\right)}},
$$

where the cubes $Q \left( a _ { i } ^ { ( \varepsilon ) } , 1 \right)$ are disjoint and $\scriptstyle { \cal L } = \mathrm { O } \left( \frac { 1 } { \varepsilon ^ { N } } \right)$ , and so by periodicity, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| u _ {\varepsilon} - u _ {n, \varepsilon} \| _ {L ^ {p} (Q ^ {\prime})} ^ {p} = \varepsilon^ {N} \int_ {\frac {1}{\varepsilon} Q ^ {\prime}} | u (x) - u _ {n} (x) | ^ {p} d x \\ \leq \varepsilon^ {N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {L} \int_ {Q \left(a _ {i} ^ {(\varepsilon)}, 1\right)} | u (x) - u _ {n} (x) | ^ {p} d x \\ = \varepsilon^ {N} L \| u - u _ {n} \| _ {L ^ {p} (Q (0, 1))} ^ {p} \leq C \| u - u _ {n} \| _ {L ^ {p} (Q (0, 1))} ^ {p}, \end{array}\tag{2.66}
$$

for some $C > 1$ 

Fix $\eta > 0$ and let $n _ { 0 }$ be such that 

$$
\left\| u _ {n _ {0}} - u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} (Q (0, 1))} \leq \frac {\eta}{3 \left(1 + \left\| v \right\| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (Q ^ {\prime})}\right) \left(C ^ {1 / p} + | Q ^ {\prime} | ^ {1 / p}\right)}.\tag{2.67}
$$

Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| \overline {{u}} _ {n _ {0}} - \overline {{u}} \| _ {L ^ {p} (Q ^ {\prime})} = \left| \int_ {Q (0, 1)} (u _ {n _ {0}} - u) d x \right| | Q ^ {\prime} | ^ {1 / p} \\ \leq \| u _ {n _ {0}} - u \| _ {L ^ {p} (Q (0, 1))} | Q ^ {\prime} | ^ {1 / p} \leq \frac {\eta}{3 \left[ 1 + \| v \| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (Q ^ {\prime})} \right]}. \end{array}\tag{2.68}
$$

Finally, by Step 1 we may choose $\varepsilon _ { 0 } = \varepsilon _ { 0 } \left( n _ { 0 } \right) = \varepsilon _ { 0 } \left( \eta \right)$ such that for all $0 < \varepsilon < \varepsilon _ { 0 }$ , 

$$
\left| \int_ {Q ^ {\prime}} (u _ {n _ {0}, \varepsilon} - \overline {{u}} _ {n _ {0}})   v   d x \right| \leq \frac {\eta}{3}.
$$

This together with (2.65)–(2.68) yields 

$$
\left| \int_ {Q ^ {\prime}} \left(u _ {\varepsilon} v - \overline {{u}} v\right) d x \right| \leq \eta
$$

for all $0 ~ < ~ \varepsilon ~ < ~ \varepsilon _ { 0 }$ . Hence we have shown that $u _ { \varepsilon } \ \to \ \overline { { u } }$ in $L ^ { p } ( Q ^ { \prime } ) \ ( \stackrel { * } {  } )$ if $p = \infty )$ and in turn (given the arbitrariness of $Q ^ { \prime } )$ in $L ^ { p } \left( E \right)$ for every bounded measurable set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

Example 2.86. A typical application of this lemma is to u the characteristic function of the interval $( 0 , \theta )$ extended periodically to all of R with period 1. Then $u _ { \varepsilon } \stackrel { * } {  } \overline { { u } }$ in $L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } \right)$ , where 

$$
\overline {{{u}}} (x) \equiv \int_ {0} ^ {1} \chi_ {(0, \theta)} (y) d y = \theta .
$$

As a consequence, if $z \in S ^ { N - 1 } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ then 

$$
\int_ {E} \chi_ {(0, \theta)} \left(\frac {x \cdot z}{\varepsilon}\right) v (x) d x \rightarrow \theta \int_ {E} v (x) d x\tag{2.69}
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and for every bounded measurable set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ . Said diferently, (2.69) may be written as 

$$
\chi_ {E _ {\varepsilon}} \stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} \theta \text {in} L ^ {\infty} (E),\tag{2.70}
$$

where 

$$
E _ {\varepsilon} := \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \frac {x \cdot z}{\varepsilon} \in \bigcup_ {k \in \mathbb {Z}} (k, k + \theta) \right\}.
$$

Property (2.70) may be extended to measures other than the Lebesgue measure. 

Proposition 2.87. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with $\mu$ finite. Then $\mu$ is nonatomic if and only iffor every $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\theta \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ there exists a sequence $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ with $E _ { n } \subset E$ such that $\chi _ { E _ { n } } \stackrel { * } {  } \theta \chi _ { E }$ in $L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ 

Proof. To prove that $\mu$ is nonatomic, let $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ be such that $\mu \left( E \right) > 0$ . With $\textstyle \theta = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } }$ find $\{ E _ { n } \} \subset \mathfrak { M }$ , with $E _ { n } \subset E$ , such that $\chi _ { E _ { n } } \stackrel { * } {  } \frac { 1 } { 2 } \chi _ { E }$ in $L ^ { \infty } \left( X \right)$ ). In particular, 

$$
\mu \left(E _ {n}\right)\rightarrow \frac {1}{2} \mu (E),
$$

and so for n suficiently large we have 

$$
0 <   \mu (E _ {n}) <   \mu (E).
$$

Conversely, assume that $\mu$ is nonatomic and let $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ and $\theta \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ 

Without loss of generality we may assume that $E = X$ 

Step 1: Assume first that M is generated by a countable family of sets $\{ F _ { j } \}$ Let N be the algebra generated by $\{ F _ { j } \}$ . By Theorem 2.16, N is countable, and so we may write $\mathfrak { N } = \{ G _ { j } \}$ . Fix $l \in \mathbb N$ and let $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { T } ^ { ( l ) } }$ be the family of sets I of the form 

$$
I = \{i _ {1}, \dots , i _ {j} \} \subset \mathbb {N} ^ {j},
$$

where $1 \le j \le l$ and $1 \leq i _ { 1 } < . . . < i _ { j } \leq l$ . For every $I \in \mathcal { I } ^ { ( l ) }$ let 

$$
G _ {I} ^ {(l)} := \left(\bigcap_ {j \in I} G _ {j}\right) \setminus \left(\bigcup_ {j \notin I} G _ {j}\right).
$$

The sets $G _ { I } ^ { ( l ) } , I \in \mathcal { T } ^ { ( l ) }$ , belong to N, are pairwise disjoint, and for every $1 \leq j \leq l _ { \cdot }$ , 

$$
G _ {j} = \bigcup_ {I \in \mathcal {I} ^ {(l)}, j \in I} G _ {I} ^ {(l)}.\tag{2.71}
$$

For simplicity in the notation we write 

$$
\left\{G _ {I} ^ {(l)}: I \in \mathcal {I} ^ {(l)} \right\} = \left\{H _ {j} ^ {(l)}: j = 1, \dots , \ell_ {l} \right\}.
$$

By Proposition 1.91 there exist measurable functions $u _ { j } ^ { ( l ) } : H _ { j } ^ { ( l ) } \to [ 0 , 1 )$ such that for any Borel set $B \subset [ 0 , 1 ]$ , 

$$
\mu \left(\left(u _ {j} ^ {(l)}\right) ^ {- 1} (B)\right) = \mathcal {L} ^ {1} (B) \mu \left(H _ {j} ^ {(l)}\right).\tag{2.72}
$$

Define 

$$
u _ {l} := \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\ell_ {l}} \chi_ {H _ {j} ^ {(l)}} u _ {j} ^ {(l)}.
$$

As in the previous example we may construct a sequence of Borel sets $\{ B _ { n } \} \subset$ [0, 1] such that $\chi _ { B _ { n } } \stackrel { * } {  } \theta$ in $L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } , \mathcal { L } ^ { 1 } \right)$ . Set 

$$
E _ {n, l} := u _ {l} ^ {- 1} \left(B _ {n}\right).
$$

For every $l \in \mathbb N$ and $1 \le j \le l _ { - }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {H _ {j} ^ {(l)}} \chi_ {E _ {n, l}}   d \mu = \mu \left(E _ {n, l} \cap H _ {j} ^ {(l)}\right) = \mu \left(u _ {l} ^ {- 1} \left(B _ {n}\right) \cap H _ {j} ^ {(l)}\right) \\ \qquad = \mu \left(\left(u _ {j} ^ {(l)}\right) ^ {- 1} \left(B _ {n}\right) \cap H _ {j} ^ {(l)}\right) = \mu \left(\left(u _ {j} ^ {(l)}\right) ^ {- 1} \left(B _ {n}\right)\right) \\ \qquad = \mathcal {L} ^ {1} \left(B _ {n}\right) \mu \left(H _ {j} ^ {(l)}\right) \to \theta \mu \left(H _ {j} ^ {(l)}\right) \end{array}
$$

as $n \to \infty$ , where we have used (2.72). 

In turn, by (2.71) for every $l \in \mathbb N$ and $1 \le j \le l$ 

$$
\int_ {G _ {j}} \chi_ {E _ {n, l}} d \mu \rightarrow \theta \mu (G _ {j})
$$

as $n \to \infty$ 

Hence for every $l \in \mathbb N$ we may find $n _ { l }$ so large that 

$$
\left| \int_ {G _ {j}} \chi_ {E _ {n _ {l}, l}} d \mu - \theta \mu (G _ {j}) \right| \leq \frac {1}{l}
$$

for all $1 \leq j \leq l .$ 

We claim that the sets $E _ { l } : = E _ { n _ { l } , l }$ have the desired property. Indeed, for any $\varepsilon > 0$ and for every $j \in \mathbb N$ choose $l _ { 0 } \geq j$ so large that $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { l _ { 0 } } \le \varepsilon } \end{array}$ . Then for all $l \geq l _ { 0 }$ 

$$
\left| \int_ {G _ {j}} \chi_ {E _ {l}} d \mu - \theta \mu (G _ {j}) \right| \leq \varepsilon .
$$

The result now follows from Remark 2.17. 

Step 2: We now remove the additional separability assumption. For every $l \in \mathbb N$ , by Corollary 1.21 we partition X into l disjoint subsets $H _ { n } ^ { ( l ) } \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 2 $n = 1 , \ldots , l ,$ such that 

$$
\mu \left(H _ {n} ^ {(l)}\right) = \frac {1}{l} \mu (X)
$$

for all $n = 1 , \ldots , l$ . Let ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime } \subset { \mathfrak { M } }$ be the σ-algebra generated by the collection 

$$
\left\{H _ {n} ^ {(l)}: l \in \mathbb {N}, 1 \leq n \leq l \right\}.
$$

Then $\mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ is generated by a countable family of sets, and we claim that $\mu :$ ${ \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ is nonatomic. Indeed, let $F \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime }$ with $\mu \left( F \right) > 0$ . We show that there exists $G \in { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime } , G \subset F$ , with $0 < \mu \left( G \right) < \mu \left( F \right)$ . Choose l so large that 

$$
\frac {1}{l} \mu (X) <   \mu (F).
$$

Since 

$$
F = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {l} F \cap H _ {n} ^ {(l)},
$$

there exists $n \in \{ 1 , \ldots , l \}$ such that 

$$
\mu \left(F \cap H _ {n} ^ {(l)}\right) > 0.
$$

Set $G : = F \cap H _ { n } ^ { ( l ) } \subset F$ . Then 

$$
0 <   \mu (G) \leq \mu \left(H _ {n} ^ {(l)}\right) \leq \frac {1}{l} \mu (X) <   \mu (F),
$$

and so the claim holds. 

In view of Step 1 there exist $E _ { n } \in \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime }$ such that $\chi _ { E _ { n } } \stackrel { * } { \to } \theta$ in $L ^ { \infty } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime } , \mu \right)$ We show that $\chi _ { E _ { n } } \stackrel { * } { \to } \theta$ in $L ^ { \infty } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ . Let $u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ and define the signed measure 

$$
\lambda_ {u} (F) := \int_ {F} u d \mu , \quad F \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}.
$$
