Then $\lambda _ { u }$ is a finite signed measure absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } ^ { \prime } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ , and so by the Radon–Nikodym theorem there exists $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X , \mathfrak { M } ^ { \prime } , \mu \right)$ such that 

$$
\lambda_ {u} (F) = \int_ {F} v d \mu , \quad F \in \mathfrak {M} ^ {\prime}.
$$

Therefore 

$$
\int_ {E _ {n}} u d \mu = \lambda_ {u} (E _ {n}) = \int_ {E _ {n}} v d \mu \rightarrow \theta \int_ {X} v d \mu = \theta \lambda_ {u} (X) = \theta \int_ {X} u d \mu .
$$

This concludes the proof. 

We conclude this section with a well-known compactness condition that will be used to prove the Rellich-Kondrachov theorem in [FoLe10]. 

Theorem 2.88. Let $1 \leq p < \infty$ and let $\{ u _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of functions converging weakly in $L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . Then $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges strongly in $\dot { L ^ { p } } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ if and only if 

$$
\lim _ {h \to 0} \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {n} (x + h) - u _ {n} (x) | ^ {p} d x = 0,\tag{2.73}
$$

$$
\lim _ {R \to \infty} \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus B (0, R)} | u _ {n} (x) | ^ {p} d x = 0.\tag{2.74}
$$

Proof. Step 1: Assume that (2.73) and (2.74) hold and consider standard mollifiers of the form 

$$
\varphi_ {k} (x) := k ^ {N} \varphi (k x), \quad x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}, \quad k \in \mathbb {N},
$$

where $\varphi$ is defined in (2.55). For $u \in L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ and $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ set 

$$
u ^ {(k)} (x) := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {k} (x - y) u (y) d y.
$$

By H¨older’s inequality and (2.54) we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Big | u ^ {(k)} (x) - u (x) \Big | ^ {p} \leq \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {k} (x - y)   | u (y) - u (x) | ^ {p} d y \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qend{array}\tag{2.75}
$$

Hence by Fubini’s theorem, 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \left| u ^ {(k)} (x) - u (x) \right| ^ {p} d x \leq c k ^ {N} \int_ {B \left(0, \frac {1}{k}\right)} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (x + h) - u (x) | ^ {p} d x d h.\tag{2.76}
$$

Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ . Taking into account (2.73) we have that 

$$
\sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {n} (x + h) - u _ {n} (x) | ^ {p} d x \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all h suficiently small. Hence, by applying (2.76) to $u _ { n }$ we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \left| (u _ {n}) ^ {(k)} (x) - u _ {n} (x) \right| ^ {p} d x \\ \qquad \leq c k ^ {N} \int_ {B \left(0, \frac {1}{k}\right)} \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {n} (x + h) - u _ {n} (x) | ^ {p} d x d h \leq c \varepsilon \end{array}
$$

for all k suficiently large, and so 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \left| (u _ {n}) ^ {(k)} (x) - u _ {n} (x) \right| ^ {p} d x = 0.\tag{2.77}
$$

Let $u _ { 0 }$ be the weak limit of $\{ u _ { n } \}$ . Then we have 

$$
\left\| u _ {n} - u _ {0} \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} \leq \left\| (u _ {n}) ^ {(k)} - u _ {n} \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} + \left\| (u _ {n}) ^ {(k)} - (u _ {0}) ^ {(k)} \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} + \left\| (u _ {0}) ^ {(k)} - u _ {0} \right\| _ {L ^ {p}}.
$$

Fix $\epsilon > 0$ . By $( 2 . 7 7 )$ and Theorem 2.73(iii) there exists $\bar { k }$ depending only on  such that for all $k \geq \bar { k }$ and all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ the first and last terms in the previous inequality are both bounded by , and so 

$$
\left\| u _ {n} - u _ {0} \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} \leq \left\| (u _ {n}) ^ {(k)} - (u _ {0}) ^ {(k)} \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} + 2 \epsilon
$$

for all $k \geq \bar { k }$ and all $n \in \mathbb N$ . Hence to complete the proof it sufices to show that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \left\| (u _ {n}) ^ {(\bar {k})} - (u _ {0}) ^ {(\bar {k})} \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} = 0.\tag{2.78}
$$

By (2.74) and the fact that $u _ { 0 } \in L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ , there exists $R > 1$ such that 

$$
\sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus B (0, R - 1)} | u _ {n} (x) | ^ {p} d x + \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus B (0, R - 1)} | u _ {0} (x) | ^ {p} d x \leq \epsilon ,
$$

and so reasoning as in (2.75) and (2.76), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N} \backslash B (0, R)} \left| (u _ {n}) ^ {(\bar {k})} - (u _ {0}) ^ {(\bar {k})} \right| ^ {p} d x \\ \leq c \bar {k} ^ {N} \int_ {B \left(0, \frac {1}{k}\right)} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N} \backslash B (0, R)} | u _ {n} (x + h) - u _ {0} (x + h) | ^ {p} d x d h \\ \leq c \bar {k} ^ {N} \int_ {B \left(0, \frac {1}{k}\right)} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N} \backslash B (0, R - 1)} | u _ {n} (y) - u _ {0} (y) | ^ {p} d y d h \leq c \epsilon , \end{array} \tag {2}\tag{2.79}
$$

where we have used the change of variables $y = x + h$ . Since $u _ { n }  u _ { 0 }$ in $L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ it follows that for all $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l}(u _ {n}) ^ {\left(\bar {k}\right)} \left(x\right) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\bar {k}} \left(x - y\right) u _ {n} \left(y\right) d y\\\rightarrow \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} \varphi_ {\bar {k}} \left(x - y\right) u _ {0} \left(y\right) d y = (u _ {0}) ^ {\left(\bar {k}\right)} \left(x\right)\end{array}
$$

as $n  \infty$ . Moreover, reasoning as in (2.75) and since $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is bounded in $L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| (u _ {n}) ^ {\left(\bar {k}\right)} (x) - (u _ {0}) ^ {\left(\bar {k}\right)} (x) \right| ^ {p} \leq c \bar {k} ^ {N} \int_ {B \left(0, \frac {1}{k}\right)} | u _ {n} (x + h) - u _ {0} (x + h) | ^ {p} d h \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qend{array}
$$

for all $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Therefore, by the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem we have 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {B (0, R)} \left| (u _ {n}) ^ {(\bar {k})} - (u _ {0}) ^ {(\bar {k})} \right| ^ {p} d x = 0,
$$

which, combined with (2.79), yields (2.78). 

Step 2: Conversely, assume that $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges strongly in $L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . We begin by showing that (2.73) holds for a single function $u \in L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ , that is, 

$$
\lim _ {h \to 0} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (x + h) - u (x) | ^ {p} d x = 0.\tag{2.80}
$$

Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ . By Theorem 2.78 there exists a function $v \in C _ { c } ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ such that 

$$
\left\| v - u \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} \leq \varepsilon .
$$

Hence, by Minkowski’s inequality, and the change of variable $y = x + h$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Big (\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (x + h) - u (x) | ^ {p} d x \Big) ^ {1 / p} \\ \leq \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (x + h) - v (x + h) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \\ + \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | v (x + h) - v (x) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \\ + \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (x) - v (x) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \\ = 2 \| u - v \| _ {L ^ {p}} + \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | v (x + h) - v (x) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \\ \leq 2 \varepsilon + \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | v (x + h) - v (x) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p}. \end{array}
$$

Since v is uniformly continuous and has compact support, we may find $\delta =$ $\delta \left( \varepsilon \right) > 0$ such that 

$$
\left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | v (x + h) - v (x) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all $| h | \leq \delta$ . Hence (2.80) holds. 

Since $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges to $u _ { 0 }$ in $L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ , there exists an integer ¯n such that 

$$
\left\| u _ {n} - u _ {0} \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all $n \geq \bar { n }$ . Hence by Minkowski’s inequality and the change of variable $y = x + h$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {n} (x + h) - u _ {n} (x) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \\ \leq \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {n} (x + h) - u _ {0} (x + h) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \\ \quad + \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {0} (x + h) - u _ {0} (x) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \\ \quad + \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {n} (x) - u _ {0} (x) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \\ = 2 \| u _ {n} - u _ {0} \| _ {L ^ {p}} + \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {0} (x + h) - u _ {0} (x) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \\ \leq 4 \varepsilon + \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {0} (x + h) - u _ {0} (x) | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \end{array}
$$

for all $n \geq \bar { n }$ . Using (2.80) with $u _ { 0 } , \ldots , u _ { \bar { n } - 1 }$ in place of u we conclude that (2.73) holds. 

The proof of (2.74) follows a similar argument (see also Vitali’s convergence theorem) and therefore we omit it. 

## 2.2.3 Maximal Functions

In this subsection we introduce the notion of maximal function and study its properties. Maximal functions will play an important role in the Sobolev space setting in [FoLe10] but they will not be used in the remainder of this volume. 

Throughout this subsection we consider $L ^ { p }$ spaces in the case that the underlying measure is the Lebesgue measure. 

Definition 2.89. Let $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . The (Hardy–Littlewood) maximal function of u is defined by 

$$
\mathrm{M} (u) (x) := \sup _ {r > 0} \frac {1}{| B (x , r) |} \int_ {B (x, r)} | u (y) | d y
$$

for all $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ . For $0 < R \leq \infty$ we also define 

$$
\mathrm{M} _ {R} (u) (x) := \sup _ {0 <   r <   R} \frac {1}{| B (x , r) |} \int_ {B (x, r)} | u (y) | d y.
$$

Note that $\mathrm { M } = \mathrm { M } _ { \infty }$ 

Exercise 2.90. Prove that the sets 

$$
\left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \mathrm{M} (u) (x) > t \right\}, \quad \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \mathrm{M} _ {R} (u) (x) > t \right\}
$$

are open (and so Lebesgue measurable). 

Theorem 2.91. Let $u \in L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right) , 1 \leq p \leq \infty$ . Then 

(i) $u \left( x \right) \leq \mathrm { M } \left( u \right) \left( x \right) < \infty f o r \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } .$ ; 

(ii) $i f p = 1$ then for any $t > 0$ 

$$
\left| \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \mathrm{M} (u) (x) > t \right\} \right| \leq \frac {3 ^ {N}}{t} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (x) | d x;\tag{2.81}
$$

(iii) if $1 < p \leq \infty$ then $\mathrm { ~ M ~ } ( u ) \in L ^ { p } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ and 

$$
\left\| \mathrm{M} (u) \right\| _ {L ^ {p}} \leq C (N, p) \| u \| _ {L ^ {p}}.
$$

The proof of the theorem is hinged on the following covering result. 

Lemma 2.92 (Vitali). Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be the union of a finite number of balls $B \left( x _ { i } , r _ { i } \right) , i = 1 , \ldots , \ell .$ Then there exists a subset $I \subset \{ 1 , \ldots , \ell \}$ such that the balls $\boldsymbol { B } \left( \boldsymbol { x } _ { i } , \boldsymbol { r } _ { i } \right)$ with $i \in I$ are pairwise disjoint and 

$$
E \subset \bigcup_ {i \in I} B \left(x _ {i}, 3 r _ {i}\right).
$$

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that 

$$
r _ {1} \geq r _ {2} \geq \ldots \geq r _ {\ell}.
$$

Put $i _ { 1 } : = 1$ and discard all the balls that intersect $B \left( x _ { 1 } , r _ { 1 } \right)$ . Let $i _ { 2 }$ be the first integer, if it exists, such that $B \left( x _ { i _ { 2 } } , r _ { i _ { 2 } } \right)$ does not intersect $B \left( x _ { 1 } , r _ { 1 } \right)$ . If $i _ { 2 }$ does not exist then set $I : = \{ i _ { 1 } \}$ , while if $i _ { 2 }$ exists discard all the balls $\boldsymbol { B } \left( \boldsymbol { x } _ { i } , \boldsymbol { r } _ { i } \right)$ , with $i ~ > ~ i _ { 2 }$ , that intersect $B \left( x _ { i _ { 2 } } , r _ { i _ { 2 } } \right)$ . Let $i _ { 3 } ~ > ~ i _ { 2 }$ be the first integer, if it exists, such that $B \left( x _ { i _ { 3 } } , r _ { i _ { 3 } } \right)$ does not intersect $B \left( x _ { i _ { 2 } } , r _ { i _ { 2 } } \right)$ . If $i _ { 3 }$ does not exist then set $I : = \{ i _ { 1 } , i _ { 2 } \} ; \mathrm { i f } \ i _ { 3 }$ exists continue the process. Since there is only a finite number of balls the process stops after a finite number of steps and we obtain the desired set $I \subset \{ 1 , \ldots , \ell \}$ 

By construction, the balls $\boldsymbol { B } \left( \boldsymbol { x } _ { i } , \boldsymbol { r } _ { i } \right)$ with $i \in I$ are pairwise disjoint. To prove the last statement let $x \in E$ . Then there exists $i = 1 , \ldots , \ell$ such that $x \in B \left( x _ { i } , r _ { i } \right)$ $\operatorname { I f } i \in I$ then there is nothing to prove. $\operatorname { I f } i \notin I$ then $\boldsymbol { B } \left( \boldsymbol { x } _ { i } , \boldsymbol { r } _ { i } \right)$ is one of the balls that has been discarded and thus there exists $j \in I$ such that $r _ { j } \geq r _ { i }$ and $B \left( x _ { j } , r _ { j } \right) \cap B \left( x _ { i } , r _ { i } \right) \neq \varnothing$ . Let $z \in B \left( x _ { j } , r _ { j } \right) \cap B \left( x _ { i } , r _ { i } \right)$ . Then 

$$
\left| x - x _ {j} \right| \leq \left| x - x _ {i} \right| + \left| x _ {i} - z \right| + \left| z - x _ {j} \right| <   r _ {i} + r _ {i} + r _ {j} \leq 3 r _ {j},
$$

and so $x \in B \left( x _ { j } , 3 r _ { j } \right)$ and the proof is complete. 

We now turn to the proof of Theorem 2.91: 

Proof (Theorem 2.91). We begin by proving (ii). Let 

$$
A _ {t} := \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \mathrm{M} (u) (x) > t \right\}.
$$

By the definition of M (u), for every $x \in A _ { t }$ we can find a ball $\boldsymbol { B } \left( \boldsymbol { x } , \boldsymbol { r } _ { x } \right)$ , with $r _ { x } > 0$ , such that 

$$
\frac {1}{| B (x , r _ {x}) |} \int_ {B (x, r _ {x})} | u (y) | d y > t.\tag{2.82}
$$

Let $K \subset A _ { t }$ be a compact set. Since $\left\{ B \left( x , r _ { x } \right) \right\} _ { x \in A _ { t } }$ is an open cover for K, we may find a finite subcover. By the previous lemma there exists a disjoint finite subfamily $\left\{ B \left( x _ { i } , r _ { i } \right) \right\} _ { i = 1 } ^ { n }$ , such that 

$$
K \subset \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {n} B \left(x _ {i}, 3 r _ {i}\right).
$$

Hence, by (2.82), 

$$
| K | \leq 3 ^ {N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} | B (x _ {i}, r _ {i}) | \leq \frac {3 ^ {N}}{t} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \int_ {B (x _ {i}, r _ {i})} | u | d y \leq \frac {3 ^ {N}}{t} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u | d y.
$$

Using the inner regularity of the Lebesgue measure, together with Exercise 2.90, we obtain that 

$$
\left| \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: M (u) (x) > t \right\} \right| \leq \frac {3 ^ {N}}{t} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u | d y.
$$

Note that this implies, in particular, that M $( u ) \left( x \right) < \infty$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ Thus (i) is proved for $p = 1$ 

In order to prove (iii) it sufices to consider $1 < p < \infty$ , since the case $p = \infty$ is immediate from the definition of M (u). For $t > 0$ define 

$$
u _ {t} \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} u \left(x\right) \text {   if   } | u \left(x\right) | > \frac {t}{2}, \\ 0 \qquad \text {   otherwise.   } \end{array} \right.
$$

We claim that $u _ { t } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . Indeed, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {t} | d y = \int_ {\left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: | u (x) | > \frac {t}{2} \right\}} | u | d y \\ \qquad \leq \left(\frac {2}{t}\right) ^ {p - 1} \int_ {\left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: | u (x) | > \frac {t}{2} \right\}} | u | ^ {p} d y <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

Moreover, since $\begin{array} { r } { | u | \le | u _ { t } | + \frac { t } { 2 } } \end{array}$ we have that $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { M } \left( u \right) \le \mathrm { M } \left( u _ { t } \right) + \frac { t } { 2 } } \end{array}$ , and so 

$$
\left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \mathrm{M} (u) (x) > t \right\} \subset \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \mathrm{M} (u _ {t}) (x) > \frac {t}{2} \right\}.
$$

Part (ii) applied to $u _ { t } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ now yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \big | \big \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \mathrm{M} (u) (x) > t \big \} \big | \leq \frac {3 ^ {N} 2}{t} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u _ {t} | d y \\ = \frac {3 ^ {N} 2}{t} \int_ {\big \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: | u (x) | > \frac {t}{2} \big \}} | u | d y. \end{array}\tag{2.83}
$$

Hence, using Theorem 1.123 and Fubini’s theorem we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} (\mathrm{M} (u) (x)) ^ {p} d x = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \big | \big \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: (\mathrm{M} (u) (x)) ^ {p} > s \big \} \big | d s \\ \qquad = p \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} t ^ {p - 1} \big | \big \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \mathrm{M} (u) (x) > t \big \} \big | d t \\ \qquad \leq p 3 ^ {N} 2 \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} t ^ {p - 2} \int_ {\big \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: | u (x) | > \frac {t}{2} \big \}} | u (y) | d y d t \\ \qquad = p 3 ^ {N} 2 \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (y) | \left(\int_ {0} ^ {2 | u (y) |} t ^ {p - 2} d t\right) d y \\ \qquad = \frac {p 3 ^ {N} 2 ^ {p}}{p - 1} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (x) | ^ {p} d x. \end{array}
$$

This proves (iii) and in turn (i) for $p > 1$ 

Property (ii) in the previous theorem is usually called the weak $L ^ { 1 }$ inequality because, as opposed to the case $p > 1$ (see (iii)), for $p = 1$ the operator 

$$
u \in L ^ {1} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {N}\right) \mapsto \mathrm{M} (u)
$$

is not bounded in $L ^ { 1 }$ . Actually, if u is not identically zero then $\mathrm { ~ M ~ } ( u ) \ \notin$ $L ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . To see this, it sufices to assume, without loss of generality, that 

$$
\int_ {B (0, 1)} | u | d x > 0.
$$

Then if $| x | \geq 1$ it follows that $B \left( 0 , 1 \right) \subset B \left( x , 2 \left| x \right| \right)$ , and thus for some $c > 0$ 

$$
\mathrm{M} (u) (x) \geq \frac {1}{| B (x , 2 | x |) |} \int_ {B (x, 2 | x |)} | u (y) | d y \geq \frac {c}{| x | ^ {N}} \int_ {B (0, 1)} | u | d x,
$$

with $\left| x \right| ^ { - N } \notin L ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus B \left( 0 , 1 \right) \right)$ . Moreover, even local integrability of M (u) does not hold in general. However, it can be shown that M $( u ) \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ ， provided u belongs to the space L log $L \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ 

Definition 2.93. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set. We say that a measurable function $u : E \to \mathbb { R }$ belongs to the space L log L (E) if 

$$
\int_ {E} | u (x) | \log (2 + | u (x) |) d x <   \infty .
$$

Note that 

$$
L \log L \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {N}\right) \subsetneqq L ^ {1} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {N}\right).
$$

Proposition 2.94. Assume that $u \in L \log L \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . Then M (u) is integrable over measurable sets of finite measure. 

Proof. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be any measurable set of finite measure. By Theorem 1.123, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {E} \mathrm{M} (u) (x) d x = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} | \{x \in E: \mathrm{M} (u) > t \} | d t \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq | E | + \int_ {1} ^ {\infty} | \{x \in E: \mathrm{M} (u) > t \} | d t. \end{array}
$$

Now (2.83) and Fubini’s theorem yield 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {E} \mathrm{M} (u) (x) d x \leq | E | + C \int_ {1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{t} \left(\int_ {\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: | u (x) | > t / 2 \}} | u (y) | d y\right) d t \\ \qquad = | E | + C \int_ {\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: | u (x) | > \frac {1}{2} \}} | u (y) | \left(\int_ {1} ^ {2 | u (y) |} \frac {1}{t} d t\right) d y \\ \qquad = | E | + C \int_ {\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: | u (x) | > \frac {1}{2} \}} | u (y) | \log (2 | u (y) |) d y, \end{array}
$$

and so the proof is complete. 

The previous proposition admits a partial converse, which relies on the following decomposition theorem: 

Theorem 2.95 (Calder´on–Zygmund). Let $u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ be a nonnegative function, and let $t > 0$ . Then there exists a countable family $\left\{ Q _ { n } \right\}$ of open mutually disjoint cubes such that 

$$
u (x) \leq t \quad f o r \mathcal {L} ^ {N} a. e. x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \overline {{Q _ {n}}},\tag{2.84}
$$

and for every $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

$$
t <   \frac {1}{| Q _ {n} |} \int_ {Q _ {n}} u (x) d x \leq 2 ^ {N} t.\tag{2.85}
$$

Proof. Fix $t > 0$ and choose $L > 0$ large enough that 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} u (x) d x \leq t L ^ {N}.
$$

Decompose $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ into a rectangular grid such that each cube $Q$ of the partition has side length $L _ { ; }$ , and thus 

$$
\frac {1}{| Q |} \int_ {Q} u (x) d x \leq t.\tag{2.86}
$$

Fix one such cube $Q$ and subdivide it into $2 ^ { N }$ congruent subcubes. Let $Q ^ { \prime }$ be one of these subcubes. If 

$$
\frac {1}{| Q ^ {\prime} |} \int_ {Q ^ {\prime}} u (x) d x > t,
$$

and in view of the fact that 

$$
\frac {1}{| Q ^ {\prime} |} \int_ {Q ^ {\prime}} u (x) d x \leq \frac {2 ^ {N}}{| Q |} \int_ {Q} u (x) d x \leq 2 ^ {N} t,
$$

then (2.85) is satisfied and therefore $Q ^ { \prime }$ will be selected as one of the $Q _ { n }$ . On the other hand, if 

$$
\frac {1}{| Q ^ {\prime} |} \int_ {Q ^ {\prime}} u (x) d x \leq t
$$

(note that by (2.86) there is at least one), then we subdivide $Q ^ { \prime }$ into $2 ^ { N }$ congruent subcubes and we repeat the process. 

In this way we construct a family of cubes $\left\{ Q _ { n } \right\}$ for which (2.85) is satisfied, and it remains to prove (2.84). It can be seen from the construction that the cubes that were not selected to belong to the family $\left\{ Q _ { n } \right\}$ form a fine covering $\mathcal { F }$ of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \overline { { Q _ { n } } }$ . Therefore if $x \ { \overset { \vartriangle } { \in } } \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } { \widehat { Q _ { n } } }$ is a Lebesgue point for u, then by Remark 1.160(ii) we have 

$$
u \left(x\right) = \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\mathrm{diam} F \to 0,   F \in \mathcal {F}, x \in F} \frac {1}{| F |} \int_ {F} u \left(y\right) d y \leq t
$$

and the proof is completed. 

Remark 2.96. A local version of the previous theorem holds. Precisely, if $Q$ is a cube, $u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( Q \right)$ is nonnegative, and if 

$$
t \geq \frac {1}{| Q |} \int_ {Q} u (x) d x,
$$

then it follows from the above proof that there exists a countable family $\{ Q _ { n } \} \subset Q$ of open mutually disjoint cubes such that 

$$
u \left(x\right) \leq t \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text { a.e.   in } Q \setminus \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \overline {{Q _ {n}}},
$$

and for every $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

$$
t <   \frac {1}{| Q _ {n} |} \int_ {Q _ {n}} u (x) d x \leq 2 ^ {N} t.
$$

As a consequence of the Calder´on–Zygmund theorem we obtain a partial reverse of the weak $L ^ { 1 }$ inequality (2.81). 

Corollary 2.97. Let $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . Then there exists a constant C depending on N such that for every cube Q in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and for every $t > 0$ such that 

$$
t > \frac {1}{| Q |} \int_ {Q} | u (x) | d x,\tag{2.87}
$$

we have 

$$
\left| \left\{x \in Q: \mathrm{M} (u) (x) > C t \right\} \right| \geq \frac {C}{t} \int_ {\left\{y \in Q: | u (y) | > t \right\}} | u (x) | d x,\tag{2.88}
$$

where 

$$
C := \min \left\{\frac {1}{\alpha_ {N} N ^ {\frac {N}{2}}}, \frac {1}{2 ^ {N}} \right\}.
$$

Proof. Fix t as in (2.87) and apply the Calder´on–Zygmund theorem together with Remark 2.96 to |u| and t to find a family $\left\{ { \overline { { Q _ { n } } } } \right\} \subset Q$ of closed cubes with mutually disjoint interiors such that 

$$
| u (x) | \leq t \text {   for   } \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {   a.e.   } x \in Q \setminus \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \overline {{Q _ {n}}},\tag{2.89}
$$

and for every $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

$$
t <   \frac {1}{| Q _ {n} |} \int_ {Q _ {n}} | u (y) | d y \leq 2 ^ {N} t.\tag{2.90}
$$

If $x \in Q _ { n }$ then the ball centered at x with radius $R _ { n } : = \sqrt { N } \left| Q _ { n } \right| ^ { \frac { 1 } { N } }$ contains $Q _ { n }$ , and so it follows from (2.90) that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \text {M} (u) (x) \geq \frac {1}{| B (x , R _ {n}) |} \int_ {B (x, R _ {n})} | u (y) | d y \\ \geq \frac {1}{| B (x , R _ {n}) |} \int_ {Q _ {n}} | u (y) | d y \geq \frac {1}{\alpha_ {N} N ^ {\frac {N}{2}}} t. \end{array}
$$

Therefore, in view of (2.89) and (2.90), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \left\{x \in Q: \mathrm{M} (u) (x) > \frac {1}{\alpha_ {N} N ^ {\frac {N}{2}}} t \right\} \right| \geq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} | Q _ {n} | \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \frac {1}{2 ^ {N} t} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \int_ {Q _ {n}} | u (x) | d x = \frac {1}{2 ^ {N} t} \int_ {\{y \in Q: | u (y) | > t \}} | u (x) | d x. \end{array}
$$

It sufices to set 

$$
C := \min \left\{\frac {1}{\alpha_ {N} N ^ {\frac {N}{2}}}, \frac {1}{2 ^ {N}} \right\}.
$$

This concludes the proof. 

We are now ready to prove a partial converse of Proposition 2.94. 

Proposition 2.98. If $Q$ is a cube in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ is such that $\mathrm { ~ M ~ } ( u ) \in L ^ { 1 } \left( Q \right)$ , then $u \in L$ log $L \left( Q \right)$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {Q} | u (x) | \log (2 + | u (x) |) d x \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq C (N, | Q |) \| \mathrm{M} (u) \| _ {L ^ {1} (Q)} \log \left(2 + \| \mathrm{M} (u) \| _ {L ^ {1} (Q)}\right). \end{array}
$$

Proof. Fix 

$$
t := 1 + \frac {1}{| Q |} \int_ {Q} | u (y) | d y.
$$

We have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {Q} | u | \log (2 + | u |) d x \\ \leq \log (2 + t) \int_ {\{x \in Q: | u | \leq t \}} | u | d x + \int_ {\{x \in Q: | u | > t \}} | u | \log (2 + | u |) d x \\ \leq \log (2 + t) \int_ {\{x \in Q: | u | \leq t \}} M (u) d x + \int_ {\{x \in Q: | u | > t \}} | u | \log (3 | u |) d x \\ \leq (\log (2 + t) + \log 3) \int_ {Q} M (u) d x + \int_ {\{x \in Q: | u | > t \}} | u | \log | u | d x, \end{array} \tag {2.}\tag{2.91}
$$

where we have used the fact that $| u | \leq \mathrm { M } \left( u \right) \mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. in $Q$ . 

Using Fubini’s theorem and Theorem 1.123, together with (2.88), we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\int_ {\{x \in Q: | u | > t \}} | u | \log | u | d x = \int_ {\{x \in Q: | u | > t \}} | u | \left(\int_ {1} ^ {| u (y) |} \frac {1}{s} d s\right) d x} \\ & {\qquad = \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{s} \left(\int_ {\{x \in Q: | u | > s \}} | u (x) | d x\right) d s} \\ & {\qquad \leq \frac {1}{C} \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} | \{x \in Q: \mathrm{M} (u) (x) > C s \} | d s} \\ & {\qquad = \frac {1}{C ^ {2}} \int_ {\{x \in Q: \mathrm{M} (u) > C t \}} \mathrm{M} (u) d x \leq \frac {1}{C ^ {2}} \int_ {Q} \mathrm{M} (u) d x.} \end{array}
$$

Hence by (2.91), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {Q} | u | \log (2 + | u |) d x \leq \left(\log (2 + t) + \log 3 + \frac {1}{C ^ {2}}\right) \int_ {Q} \mathrm{M} (u) d x \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq C (N, | Q |) \| \mathrm{M} (u) \| _ {L ^ {1} (Q)} \log \left(2 + \| \mathrm{M} (u) \| _ {L ^ {1} (Q)}\right), \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that 

$$
t \leq 1 + \frac {1}{| Q |} \int_ {Q} \mathrm{M} (u) d x.
$$

The proof is now complete. 

Remark 2.99. A simple covering argument yields an analogue to Proposition 2.98 for arbitrary compact sets. Precisely, if $\mathcal { Q } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is an open set and $\varOmega ^ { \prime } \subset \joinrel \subset \varOmega$ then there exists a constant $C = C \left( N , \varOmega ^ { \prime } , \varOmega \right) > 0$ such that 

$$
\int_ {\Omega^ {\prime}} | u | \log (2 + | u |) d x \leq C \| \mathrm{M} (u) \| _ {L ^ {1} (\varOmega)} \log \left(2 + \| \mathrm{M} (u) \| _ {L ^ {1} (\varOmega)}\right).
$$

We conclude this subsection with an alternative proof of the Lebesgue diferentiation theorem for the Lebesgue measure using maximal functions. 

Theorem 2.100 (Lebesgue diferentiation theorem). Let $u \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ Then there exists a Borel set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , with $| E | = 0 \phantom { . }$ , such that 

$$
\mathbb {R} ^ {N} \setminus E \subset \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: u (x) \in \mathbb {R} \right\}
$$

and for any $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus E$ 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{| B (x , r) |} \int_ {B (x, r)} u (y) d y = u (x).\tag{2.92}
$$

Proof. Since the result is local, we may assume, without loss of generality, that $u \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ . Since for every $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{| B (x , r) |} \int_ {B (x, r)} u (y) d y \right| \leq \mathrm{M} (u) (x), \\ \left| \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{| B (x , r) |} \int_ {B (x, r)} u (y) d y \right| \leq \mathrm{M} (u) (x), \end{array}\tag{2.93}
$$

it follows from Theorem 2.91(i)–(ii) that the function 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \widetilde {u} \left(x\right) := \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\left| B \left(x , r\right) \right|} \int_ {B (x, r)} u \left(y\right) d y \\ \quad - \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\left| B \left(x , r\right) \right|} \int_ {B (x, r)} u \left(y\right) d y \end{array}
$$

is well-defined (and in turn finite) for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , and for every $t > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \big | \big \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \widetilde {u} (x) > 2 t \big \} \big | \leq \big | \big \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \mathrm{M} (u) (x) > t \big \} \big | \\ \leq \frac {\mathbf {3} ^ {N}}{t} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (x) | d x. \end{array}
$$

If we now replace in the previous inequality u with $u - v$ , where $v \in C _ { c } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ , and observe that $\widetilde { u } \left( x \right) = \widetilde { \left( u - v \right) } \left( x \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , then we obtain that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \big | \big \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \widetilde {u} (x) > 2 t \big \} \big | \leq \big | \big \{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \mathrm{M} (u - v) (x) > t \big \} \big | \\ \leq \frac {3 ^ {N}}{t} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {N}} | u (x) - v (x) | d x. \end{array}
$$

Since $C _ { c } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ is dense in $L ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ , the right-hand side of the previous inequality can be made arbitrarily small, and so 

$$
\left| \left\{x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {N}: \widetilde {u} (x) > 2 t \right\} \right| = 0
$$

for all $t > 0$ . Hence $\widetilde { u } \left( x \right) = 0 \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , and in turn, by (2.93) we have that there exists 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{| B (x , r) |} \int_ {B (x, r)} u (y) d y \in \mathbb {R}\tag{2.94}
$$

for all $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \setminus E _ { 1 }$ , where $E _ { 1 }$ is a set of Lebesgue measure zero. 

Take $\textstyle r = { \frac { 1 } { n } }$ , and apply Theorem 2.73 (see also Remark 2.72) to conclude that the sequence of functions 

$$
v _ {n} (x) := \frac {1}{\left| B \left(x , \frac {1}{n}\right) \right|} \int_ {B \left(x, \frac {1}{n}\right)} u (y) d y
$$

converges in $L ^ { 1 }$ to $u .$ . In view of Theorem 2.20(iii), we may extract a subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ converging pointwise to u except on a set $E _ { 2 }$ of Lebesgue measure zero. Therefore if x /∈ $E : = E _ { 1 } \cup E _ { 2 }$ then (2.92) follows from (2.94). 

## 2.3 L<sup>p</sup> Spaces on Banach Spaces

In this section we briefly introduce $L ^ { p }$ spaces on Banach spaces. These will play an important role in the study of Young measures in the last chapter. We will omit most of the proofs, since the only results that will be used in the sequel are Theorem 2.108 and part (i) of the Riesz representation theorem in $L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ , which we will prove. We refer to [DuSc88], [DieU77], [Ed95], and [SY05] for more information on the subject and for the proofs omitted here. 

Definition 2.101. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let Y be a Banach space. A (measurable) simple function s is a function $s : X \to Y$ of the form 

$$
s = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} c _ {i} \chi_ {E _ {i}},
$$

where $\ell \in \mathbb { N } , c _ { 1 } , \ldots , c _ { \ell } \in Y$ are distinct and the sets $E _ { i } \subset X$ are measurable and mutually disjoint. 

(i) A function u $: X  Y$ is said to be strongly measurable if there exists a sequence $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ of (measurable) simple functions $s _ { n } : X \to Y$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \| s _ {n} (x) - u (x) \| _ {Y} = 0 \quad f o r \mu a. e. x \in X.
$$

(ii) A function $u : X \to Y$ is said to be weakly measurable if for any $L \in Y ^ { \prime }$ the function 

$$
x \in X \mapsto L (u (x)) \text {   is   measurable. }
$$

(iii) A function $u : X \to Y ^ { \prime }$ is said to be weakly star measurable if for any $y \in Y$ the map 

$$
x \in X \mapsto \langle u (x), y \rangle_ {Y ^ {\prime}, Y} = u (x) (y) \text {   is   measurable, }
$$

where $\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle _ { Y ^ { \prime } , Y } : Y ^ { \prime } \times Y \to \mathbb { R }$ is the duality pairing. 

Exercise 2.102. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $Y$ be a Banach space. Prove that if a function u $: X  Y$ is strongly measurable then the function $x \in X \mapsto \| u ( x ) \| _ { Y }$ is measurable. 

Exercise 2.103 (Egorof). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with $\mu$ finite, let Y be a Banach space, and let $u , u _ { n } : X \to Y , n \in \mathbb { N }$ , be strongly measurable functions such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \| u _ {n} (x) - u (x) \| _ {Y} = 0
$$

for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ . Prove that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a measurable set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $\mu \left( X \setminus E \right) \leq \varepsilon$ , such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \| u _ {n} (x) - u (x) \| _ {Y} = 0
$$

uniformly on E: (Hint: For every n, $k \in \mathbb N$ define 

$$
E _ {n, k} := \bigcap_ {i, j > n} \left\{x \in X: \| u _ {i} (x) - u _ {j} (x) \| _ {Y} <   \frac {1}{k} \right\}
$$

and prove that there exists an increasing sequence $\{ n _ { k } \} _ { k \in \mathbb { N } }$ such that the set 

$$
E := \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n _ {k}, k}
$$

has the desired properties.) 

The relation between weak and strong measurability is given by the following theorem. 

Theorem 2.104 (Pettis). Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with µ finite and let Y be a Banach space. A function $u : X \to Y$ is strongly measurable if and only if it is weakly measurable and there exists $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ such that the set $u \left( X \backslash E \right)$ is a separable set of Y (in the norm sense). 

Proof. We prove only the easy direction of the theorem, because it will be needed in Theorem 2.108. Thus assume that $u : X \to Y$ is strongly measurable. Then there exists a sequence $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ of simple functions $s _ { n } : X \to Y$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \| s _ {n} (x) - u (x) \| _ {Y} = 0 \quad \text { for } \mu \text { a.e. } x \in X.
$$

Hence for any $L \in Y ^ { \prime }$ we have that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} L \left(s _ {n} (x)\right) = L \left(u (x)\right) \quad \text { for } \mu \text { a.e. } x \in X.
$$

Since the function $L \circ s _ { n } : X \to \mathbb { R }$ is a simple function it follows that the real-valued function 

$$
x \in X \mapsto L (u (x))
$$

is measurable as the pointwise limit of measurable functions. 

By Egorof’s theorem, for every $k \in \mathbb N$ there exists a measurable set $E _ { k } \in$ M, with $\begin{array} { r } { \mu \left( E _ { k } \right) \leq \frac { 1 } { k } } \end{array}$ , such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \| s _ {n} (x) - u (x) \| _ {Y} = 0
$$

uniformly on $X \setminus E _ { k }$ . Since the range of each $s _ { n }$ is finite, the set $\textstyle \bigcup _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } s _ { n } \left( X \right)$ is countable. Hence for every $k \in \mathbb N$ the set $u \left( X \backslash E _ { k } \right)$ is separable, and so is the set 

$$
u \left(X \setminus \left(\bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {k}\right)\right) = u \left(\bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(X \setminus E _ {k}\right)\right) = \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} u \left(\left(X \setminus E _ {k}\right)\right).
$$

To conclude this part of the proof we observe that for every $j \in \mathbb N$ , 

$$
0 \leq \mu \left(\bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {k}\right) \leq \mu (E _ {j}) \leq \frac {1}{j} \rightarrow 0
$$

as $j \to \infty$ 

Example 2.105. Let $\mu$ be the Lebesgue measure on $[ 0 , 1 ]$ and define the function $u : [ 0 , 1 ] \to \ell ^ { \infty }$ by 

$$
u \left(x\right) := \left\{\frac {\operatorname{sgn} \left(\sin \left(2 ^ {n} \pi x\right)\right) + 1}{2} \right\} _ {n \in \mathbb {N}}, \quad x \in [ 0, 1 ].
$$

By Remark 2.42 we may identify $\ell ^ { \infty }$ with the dual $\left( \ell ^ { 1 } \right) ^ { \prime }$ , so for every $y =$ $\{ y _ { n } \} _ { n \in \mathbb { N } } \in \ell ^ { 1 }$ we have that 

$$
x \in [ 0, 1 ] \mapsto (u (x)) (y) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} y _ {n} \frac {\operatorname{sgn} (\sin (2 ^ {n} \pi x)) + 1}{2}
$$

is well-defined. This is a measurable function; hence u is weakly star measurable. It may be verified that there is no set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , with $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ , such that the set u $( X \backslash E )$ is a separable set of $\ell ^ { \infty }$ and, even more, that there exists $L \in ( \ell ^ { \infty } ) ^ { \prime }$ such that the function 

$$
x \in [ 0, 1 ] \mapsto L (u (x)) \text {   is   not   measurable. }
$$

Hence u is not weakly measurable (and so, by the Pettis theorem, it is not strongly measurable). We refer to $\mathrm { [ D i e U 7 7 ] }$ for more details. 

Definition 2.106. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let Y be a Banach space. A (measurable) simple function $s : X \to Y$ is (Bochner) integrable if it has the form 

$$
s = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} c _ {i} \chi_ {E _ {i}},
$$

where $c _ { 1 } , \dotsc , c _ { \ell } \in Y , \ell \in \mathbb { N }$ , are distinct, the sets $E _ { i } ~ \subset ~ X$ are mutually disjoint, and $c _ { i } = 0$ whenever $\mu \left( E _ { i } \right) = \infty$ . For any measurable set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ the Bochner integral of s over E is defined by 

$$
\int_ {E} s d \mu := \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} c _ {i} \mu (E _ {i} \cap E),
$$

where $c _ { i } \mu \left( E _ { i } \cap E \right)$ is set to be zero whenever $c _ { i } = 0$ and $\mu \left( E _ { i } \cap E \right) = \infty$ 

Definition 2.107. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let $Y$ be a Banach space. A strongly measurable function $u : X \to Y$ is (Bochner) integrable if there exists a sequence $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ of simple integrable functions such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \| s _ {n} (x) - u (x) \| _ {Y} = 0 \quad f o r \mu a. e. x \in X
$$

and 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} \| s _ {n} - u \| _ {Y} d \mu = 0.
$$

For any measurable set $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ the Bochner integral of u over E is defined by 

$$
\int_ {E} u d \mu := \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} s _ {n} d \mu .
$$

It may be verified that this limit exists and that is independent of the particular sequence $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ 

Theorem 2.108. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with µ finite and let Y be a Banach space. A strongly measurable function $u : X \to Y$ is (Bochner) integrable if and only $i f \parallel u \parallel _ { Y }$ is Lebesgue integrable over X. 

Proof. Assume that the real-valued function $x \in X \mapsto \| u ( x ) \| _ { Y }$ is integrable. Since u is strongly measurable, by the Pettis theorem there exists $E \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 2 with $\mu \left( E \right) = 0$ , such that the set u $( X \backslash E )$ is a separable subset of Y. Let $\{ y _ { n } \} \subset Y$ be a dense set in $u \left( X \backslash E \right)$ . By Exercise 2.102, for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ the function $x \in X \mapsto \| u \left( x \right) - y _ { n } \| _ { Y }$ is measurable, and so for each $k \in \mathbb N$ the set 

$$
E _ {n, k} := \left\{x \in X \setminus E: \| u (x) - y _ {n} \| _ {Y} <   \frac {1}{k} \right\}
$$

is measurable. By the density of $\left\{ y _ { n } \right\}$ in $u \left( X \backslash E \right)$ we have that 

$$
\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n, k} = X \setminus E
$$

for every $k \in \mathbb N$ . For every $n , k \in \mathbb { N }$ define 

$$
F _ {n, k} := E _ {n, k} \setminus \bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {n - 1} E _ {j, k}.
$$

Then for each fixed $k \in \mathbb N$ , the measurable sets $\{ F _ { n , k } \} _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ are pairwise disjoint with 

$$
\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {n, k} = X \setminus E.
$$

Since $x \in X \mapsto \| u \left( x \right) \| _ { Y }$ is integrable and 

$$
\mu \left(X\right) = \mu \left(X \setminus E\right) = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(F _ {n, k}\right),
$$

we may find an integer $n _ { k } \in \mathbb { N }$ so large that 

$$
\int_ {\bigcup_ {n = n _ {k} + 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {n, k}} \| u \| _ {Y} d \mu \leq \frac {1}{k}, \quad \sum_ {n = n _ {k} + 1} ^ {\infty} \mu \left(F _ {n, k}\right) \leq \frac {1}{k}.\tag{2.95}
$$

Define the simple function 

$$
s _ {k} \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} y _ {n} & \text { if } x \in F _ {n, k}, n = 1, \ldots , n _ {k}, \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then 

$$
\left\| s _ {k} (x) - u (x) \right\| _ {Y} \leq \frac {1}{k} \text {   for   all   } x \in \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {n _ {k}} F _ {n, k},
$$

and so by (2.95)<sub>2</sub>, 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \| s _ {k} (x) - u (x) \| _ {Y} = 0 \quad \text { for } \mu \text { a.e. } x \in X,
$$

while by (2.95)<sub>1</sub>, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {X} \| s _ {k} - u \| _ {Y} d \mu = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {n _ {k}} \int_ {F _ {n, k}} \| s _ {k} - u \| _ {Y} d \mu + \int_ {\bigcup_ {n = n _ {k} + 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {n, k}} \| u \| _ {Y} d \mu \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \frac {1}{k} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {n _ {k}} \mu (F _ {n, k}) + \frac {1}{k} \leq \frac {1}{k} (\mu (X) + 1) \to 0 \end{array}
$$

as $k \to \infty$ . Thus $u : X \to Y$ is Bochner integrable. 

Conversely, assume that $u : X \to Y$ is Bochner integrable and consider a sequence $\left\{ s _ { n } \right\}$ of simple integrable functions such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \| s _ {n} (x) - u (x) \| _ {Y} = 0 \quad \text { for } \mu \text { a.e. } x \in X
$$

and 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {X} \| s _ {n} - u \| _ {Y} d \mu = 0.
$$

Then for $x \in X$ and for $\ell , n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 \leq | | s _ {n} (x) | | _ {Y} - | | s _ {\ell} (x) | | _ {Y} | \leq | | s _ {n} (x) - s _ {\ell} (x) | | _ {Y} \\ \quad \leq | | s _ {n} (x) - u (x) | | _ {Y} + | | s _ {\ell} (x) - u (x) | | _ {Y}, \end{array}
$$

and so 

$$
\int_ {X} | | | s _ {n} | | _ {Y} - | | s _ {\ell} | | _ {Y} | d \mu \leq \int_ {X} | | s _ {n} - u | | _ {Y} d \mu + \int_ {X} | | s _ {\ell} - u | | _ {Y} d \mu \rightarrow 0
$$

as $\ell , n  \infty$ . Thus $\{ \Vert { s } _ { n } \Vert _ { Y } \}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ , and so it converges in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ (and up to a subsequence also pointwise $\mu \ \mathrm { a . e }$ . in $X )$ to a function $v : X \to$ R. On the other hand, for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ 

$$
0 \leq | | s _ {n} (x) | | _ {Y} - | | u (x) | | _ {Y} | \leq | | s _ {n} (x) - u (x) | | _ {Y} \rightarrow 0
$$

as $n \to \infty$ . Hence $v \left( x \right) = \| u \left( x \right) \| _ { Y }$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ , which shows that $\Vert u \Vert _ { Y }$ is integrable. 

Definition 2.109. $L e t \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ be a measure space, let Y be a Banach space, and let $1 \leq p < \infty$ . Then 

$L ^ { p } \left( \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) ; Y \right) : = { \Bigl \{ } u : X \to Y : $ u strongly measurable, 

$$
\left. \left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {p} ((X, \mathfrak {M}, \mu); Y)} <   \infty \right\},
$$

where 

$$
\| u \| _ {L ^ {p} ((X, \mathfrak {M}, \mu); Y)} := \left(\int_ {X} \| u \| _ {Y} ^ {p} d \mu\right) ^ {1 / p}.
$$

If $p = \infty$ then 

$L ^ { \infty } \left( \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) ; Y \right) : = { \Bigl \{ } u : X \to Y : $ u strongly measurable, 

$$
\left\| u \right\| _ {L ^ {\infty} ((X, \mathfrak {M}, \mu); Y)} <   \infty \Big \},
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \| u \| _ {L ^ {\infty} ((X, \mathfrak {M}, \mu); Y)} = \underset {x \in X} {\text { esssup }} \| u (x) \| _ {Y} \\ := \inf \left\{\alpha \in \mathbb {R}: \| u (x) \| _ {Y} <   \alpha \mu a. e. x \in X \right\}. \end{array}
$$

When there is no possibility of confusion we abbreviate $L ^ { p } \left( \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) ; Y \right)$ as $L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ . As in the case $Y = \mathbb { R }$ we identify functions with their equivalence classes. 

Theorem 2.110. Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space and let Y be a Banach space. 

(i) $L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ is a Banach space for $1 \leq p \leq \infty ;$ 

(ii) the family of all integrable simple functions is dense in $L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ for $1 \leq p < \infty ,$ 

(iii) $i f X$ is a separable metric space, µ is a σ-finite Radon measure, and if Y is separable, then $L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ is separable for $1 \leq p < \infty$ 

A major problem in the theory of $L ^ { p }$ spaces on Banach spaces is the identification of the dual of $L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ . Here we will consider only the two important special cases in which Y is either separable or reflexive. 

Definition 2.111. $L e t \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ be a measure space, let Y be a Banach space, and let $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ . Then the space $L _ { w } ^ { p } \left( X ; Y ^ { \prime } \right)$ is the space of all (equivalence classes $o f )$ weakly star measurable functions $u : X \to Y ^ { \prime }$ such that $\Vert u \Vert _ { Y ^ { \prime } } \in$ $L ^ { p } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ . The space $L _ { w } ^ { p } \left( X ; Y ^ { \prime } \right)$ is endowed with the norm 

$$
\| u \| _ {L _ {w} ^ {p} (X; Y ^ {\prime})} := \left(\int_ {X} \| u \| _ {Y ^ {\prime}} ^ {p} d \mu\right) ^ {1 / p}
$$

for $1 \leq p < \infty$ , and 

$$
\| u \| _ {L _ {w} ^ {\infty} (X; Y ^ {\prime})} := \operatorname * {e s s s u p} _ {x \in X} \| u (x) \| _ {Y ^ {\prime}}
$$

for $p = \infty$ 

Theorem 2.112 (Riesz representation theorem in $L ^ { p } )$ . Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be a measure space with $\mu ~ { \boldsymbol { \sigma } } { - } f i n i t e ,$ , let $Y$ be a Banach space, let $1 \leq p < \infty$ and let q be its H¨older conjugate exponent. 

(i) Assume that Y is separable. If $L \in ( L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right) ) ^ { \prime }$ then there exists a unique $v \in L _ { w } ^ { q } \left( X ; Y ^ { \prime } \right)$ such that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} \langle v, u \rangle_ {Y ^ {\prime}, Y} d \mu\tag{2.96}
$$

forevery $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ . Moreover, the normofL coincides with $\Vert v \Vert _ { L _ { w } ^ { q } ( X ; Y ^ { \prime } ) }$ Conversely, every functional of the form (2.96), where $v \in L _ { w } ^ { q } \left( X ; \dot { Y } ^ { \prime } \right)$ , is a bounded linear functional on $L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ 

(ii) Assume that Y is reflexive. Then for $L \in \mathsf { \Gamma } ( L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right) ) ^ { \prime }$ there exists a unique $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X ; Y ^ { \prime } \right)$ such that 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} \langle v, u \rangle_ {Y ^ {\prime}, Y} d \mu\tag{2.97}
$$

foreveryu $: \in L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ . Moreover, the norm ofL coincides with $\Vert { v } \Vert _ { L ^ { q } ( X ; Y ^ { \prime } ) }$ Conversely, every functional of the form (2.97), where $v \in L ^ { q } \left( X ; Y ^ { \prime } \right)$ , is a bounded linear functional on $L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ 

Proof. We prove only (i). Let $L \in \mathsf { \Gamma } ( L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right) ) ^ { \prime }$ . Since Y is separable there exists $\{ y _ { n } \} \subset Y$ such that ${ \overline { { \{ y _ { n } \} } } } = Y$ . For each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ the functional 

$$
L _ {n} (u) := L \left(u y _ {n}\right) \quad u \in L ^ {p} (X) = L ^ {p} (X; \mathbb {R})
$$

is linear and 

$$
\| L _ {n} \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X)) ^ {\prime}} = \sup _ {u \in L ^ {p} (X) \setminus \{0 \}} \frac {| L (u y _ {n}) |}{\| u \| _ {L ^ {p} (X)}} \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}} \| y _ {n} \| _ {Y} <   \infty ,\tag{2.98}
$$

and so by the Riesz representation theorem in $L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ there exists $v _ { y _ { n } } \in$ $L ^ { p ^ { \prime } } \left( X \right)$ such that 

$$
L \left(u y _ {n}\right) = \int_ {X} u v _ {y _ {n}} d \mu \quad \text { for   all } u \in L ^ {p} (X)\tag{2.99}
$$

and (see (2.98)) 

$$
\left\| L _ {n} \right\| _ {(L ^ {p} (X)) ^ {\prime}} = \left\| v _ {y _ {n}} \right\| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (X)} \leq \left\| L \right\| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}} \left\| y _ {n} \right\| _ {Y}.\tag{2.100}
$$

We claim that 

$$
\left\| \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \frac {\left| v _ {y _ {n}} \right|}{\left\| y _ {n} \right\| _ {Y}} \right\| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (X)} \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}}.\tag{2.101}
$$

If $p = 1$ then from (2.100), 

$$
\left| v _ {y _ {n}} (x) \right| \leq \| L \| _ {\left(L ^ {p} (X; Y)\right) ^ {\prime}} \| y _ {n} \| _ {Y} \quad \text { for } \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text { a.e. } x \in X \text { and   for   all } n \in \mathbb {N},
$$

and so the claim follows. 

If $p > 1$ fix $l \in \mathbb N$ and write 

$$
\sup _ {1 \leq n \leq l} \frac {\left| v _ {y _ {n}} (x) \right|}{\left\| y _ {n} \right\| _ {Y}} = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \chi_ {E _ {n}} (x) \frac {\left| v _ {y _ {n}} (x) \right|}{\left\| y _ {n} \right\| _ {Y}}, x \in X,
$$

where the sets $E _ { 1 } , \ldots , E _ { l }$ are measurable and pairwise disjoint. Note that the function 

$$
u := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \chi_ {E _ {n}} \frac {| v _ {y _ {n}} | ^ {p ^ {\prime} - 2}}{\| y _ {n} \| _ {Y} ^ {p ^ {\prime}}} v _ {y _ {n}} y _ {n}
$$

belongs to $L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ . Indeed, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| u \| _ {L ^ {p} (X; Y)} ^ {p} = \int_ {X} \left\| \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \chi_ {E _ {n}} \frac {| v _ {y _ {n}} | ^ {p ^ {\prime} - 2}}{\| y _ {n} \| _ {Y} ^ {p ^ {\prime}}} v _ {y _ {n}} y _ {n} \right\| _ {Y} ^ {p} d \mu \\ = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \int_ {E _ {n}} \frac {| v _ {y _ {n}} | ^ {p ^ {\prime}}}{\| y _ {n} \| _ {Y} ^ {p ^ {\prime}}} d \mu = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \int_ {E _ {n}} \left(\sup _ {1 \leq k \leq l} \frac {| v _ {y _ {k}} |}{\| y _ {k} \| _ {Y}}\right) ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d \mu \\ = \int_ {X} \left(\sup _ {1 \leq k \leq l} \frac {| v _ {y _ {k}} |}{\| y _ {k} \| _ {Y}}\right) ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d \mu . \end{array}\tag{2.102}
$$

Then, by the linearity of L and (2.99), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | L (u) | = \left| \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} L \left(\chi_ {E _ {n}} \frac {| v _ {y _ {n}} | ^ {p ^ {\prime} - 2}}{\| y _ {n} \| _ {Y} ^ {p ^ {\prime}}} v _ {y _ {n}} y _ {n}\right) \right| = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {l} \int_ {E _ {n}} \frac {| v _ {y _ {n}} | ^ {p ^ {\prime}}}{\| y _ {n} \| _ {Y} ^ {p ^ {\prime}}} d \mu \\ = \int_ {X} \left(\sup _ {1 \leq k \leq l} \frac {| v _ {y _ {k}} |}{\| y _ {k} \| _ {Y}}\right) ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d \mu \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}} \| u \| _ {L ^ {p} (X; Y)} \\ = \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}} \left(\int_ {X} \left(\sup _ {1 \leq k \leq l} \frac {| v _ {y _ {k}} |}{\| y _ {k} \| _ {Y}}\right) ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d \mu\right) ^ {1 / p}, \end{array}
$$

where we used (2.102), and so 

$$
\left(\int_ {X} \left(\sup _ {1 \leq k \leq l} \frac {\left| v _ {y _ {k}} \right|}{\left\| y _ {k} \right\| _ {Y}}\right) ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d \mu\right) ^ {1 / p ^ {\prime}} \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}},
$$

and by letting $l \to \infty$ the claim follows from the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem. 

We are now ready to construct the function $v \in L _ { w } ^ { q } ( X ; Y ^ { \prime } )$ in the statement. Since $\left\{ y _ { n } \right\}$ is dense in $Y$ , for every $y \in Y$ we may find a subsequence $\left\{ y _ { n _ { j } } \right\}$ converging to $y .$ . For all $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X \right)$ and $k > j$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \int_ {X} u \left(v _ {y _ {n _ {k}}} - v _ {y _ {n _ {j}}}\right) d \mu \right| = \left| L \left(u y _ {n _ {k}} - u y _ {n _ {j}}\right) \right| \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}} \left\| y _ {n _ {k}} - y _ {n _ {j}} \right\| _ {Y} \| u \| _ {L ^ {p} (X)}, \end{array}
$$

and so by Corollary A.42, 

$$
\left\| v _ {y _ {n _ {k}}} - v _ {y _ {n _ {j}}} \right\| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (X)} \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}} \left\| y _ {n _ {k}} - y _ {n _ {j}} \right\| _ {Y} \rightarrow 0
$$

as $j \to \infty$ . Hence $\left\{ v _ { y _ { n _ { j } } } \right\}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L ^ { p ^ { \prime } } \left( X \right)$ ; thus there exists $v _ { y } \in L ^ { p ^ { \prime } } \left( X \right)$ such that $v _ { y _ { n _ { i } } }  v _ { y }$ in $L ^ { p ^ { \prime } } \left( X \right)$ . Similar reasoning also shows that $v _ { y }$ does not depend on the particular approximating subsequence. From (2.99) and (2.100), taking $n _ { j }$ in place of n and letting $j \to \infty$ , we obtain 

$$
L (u y) = \int_ {X} u v _ {y} d \mu \quad \text { for   all } u \in L ^ {p} (X)\tag{2.103}
$$

and 

$$
\left\| v _ {y} \right\| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (X)} \leq \left\| L \right\| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}} \left\| y \right\| _ {Y}.\tag{2.104}
$$

Define $v : X \to Y ^ { \prime }$ as 

$$
\begin{array}{c} v \left(x\right): Y \to \mathbb {R}, \\ y \mapsto v _ {y} \left(x\right). \end{array}
$$

Note that $v \left( x \right)$ is linear in view of the linearity of $L$ and (2.103). Using once more the fact that $\left\{ y _ { n } \right\}$ is dense in $Y .$ , we have that 

$$
\| v (x) \| _ {Y ^ {\prime}} = \sup _ {n} \frac {| v (x) (y _ {n}) |}{\| y _ {n} \| _ {Y}} = \sup _ {n} \frac {| v _ {y _ {n}} (x) |}{\| y _ {n} \| _ {Y}},
$$

which is finite for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ by (2.101). 

Moreover, for any $y \in Y$ the map $x \in X \mapsto v \left( x \right) ( y ) = v _ { y } \left( x \right)$ is measurable, and so v is weakly star measurable, and by (2.101), 

$$
\| v \| _ {L _ {w} ^ {p} (X; Y ^ {\prime})} = \left\| \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \left(\frac {| v _ {y _ {n}} |}{\| y _ {n} \| _ {Y}}\right) \right\| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (X)} \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}}.
$$

To prove the reverse inequality we observe that the class $s$ of simple functions of the form 

$$
s = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \chi_ {F _ {i}} c _ {i} y _ {i},\tag{2.105}
$$

where $c _ { i } \in \mathbb { R }$ and $F _ { i } \in \mathfrak { M }$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ , is dense in $L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ , and so 

$$
\| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}} = \sup _ {s \in \mathcal {S} \backslash \{0 \}} \frac {| L (s) |}{\| s \| _ {L ^ {p} (X ; Y)}}.
$$

For any $s \in S$ of the form (2.105), by (2.99) and H¨older’s inequality we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | L (s) | = \left| \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \int_ {F _ {i}} c _ {i} v _ {y _ {i}} d \mu \right| \leq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \int_ {F _ {i}} | c _ {i} | \| y _ {i} \| _ {Y} \frac {| v _ {y _ {i}} |}{\| y _ {i} \| _ {Y}} d \mu \\ \quad \leq \int_ {X} \left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \chi_ {F _ {i}} | c _ {i} | \| y _ {i} \| _ {Y}\right) \sup _ {k} \frac {| v _ {y _ {k}} |}{\| y _ {k} \| _ {Y}} d \mu \\ \quad \leq \left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} | c _ {i} | ^ {p} \| y _ {i} \| _ {Y} ^ {p} \mu (F _ {i})\right) ^ {1 / p} \left\| \sup _ {k \in \mathbb {N}} \left(\frac {| v _ {y _ {k}} |}{\| y _ {k} \| _ {Y}}\right) \right\| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (X)} \\ = \| s \| _ {L ^ {p} (X; Y)} \left\| \sup _ {k \in \mathbb {N}} \left(\frac {| v _ {y _ {k}} |}{\| y _ {k} \| _ {Y}}\right) \right\| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (X)}. \end{array}
$$

Hence 

$$
\| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}} = \sup _ {s \in \mathcal {S} \backslash \{0 \}} \frac {| L (s) |}{\| s \| _ {L ^ {p} (X ; Y)}} \leq \left\| \sup _ {k \in \mathbb {N}} \left(\frac {| v _ {y _ {k}} |}{\| y _ {k} \| _ {Y}}\right) \right\| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (X)} = \| v \| _ {L _ {w} ^ {p} (X; Y ^ {\prime})},
$$

and so 

$$
\left\| L \right\| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}} = \left\| v \right\| _ {L _ {w} ^ {p} (X; Y ^ {\prime})}.
$$

Finally, for $s \in S$ of the form (2.105), by the linearity of $y \mapsto v _ { y } \left( x \right)$ for every $x \in X$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} L (s) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \int_ {F _ {i}} c _ {i} v _ {y _ {i}} (x) d \mu (x) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \int_ {F _ {i}} v _ {c _ {i} y _ {i}} (x) d \mu (x) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \int_ {F _ {i}} v _ {s (x)} d \mu (x) \\ = \int_ {X} v _ {s (x)} d \mu (x) = \int_ {X} v (x) (s (x)) d \mu (x) = \int_ {X} \langle v (x), s (x) \rangle_ {Y ^ {\prime}, Y} d \mu (x). \end{array}
$$

For any $u \in L ^ { p } \left( X ; Y \right)$ find a sequence $\{ s _ { j } \} \subset S$ of simple functions such that 

$$
\lim _ {j \rightarrow \infty} \| s _ {j} (x) - u (x) \| _ {Y} = 0 \quad \text { for } \mu \text { a.e. } x \in X.
$$

Then 

$$
L (u) = \lim _ {j \to \infty} L (s _ {j}) = \lim _ {j \to \infty} \int_ {X} v _ {s _ {j} (x)} d \mu (x).
$$

From (2.104), and again using the linearity of $y \mapsto v _ { y } \left( x \right)$ for $\mu { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } x \in X$ , we deduce that 

$$
\left\| v _ {s _ {j} (x)} - v _ {u (x)} \right\| _ {L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (X)} \leq \| L \| _ {(L ^ {p} (X; Y)) ^ {\prime}} \left\| s _ {j} (x) - u (x) \right\| _ {Y} \to 0,
$$

and so 

$$
L (u) = \int_ {X} v _ {u (x)} d \mu (x) = \int_ {X} \langle v (x), u (x) \rangle_ {Y ^ {\prime}, Y} d \mu (x),
$$

and this concludes the proof. 

The Direct Method and Lower Semicontinuity 

# The Direct Method and Lower Semicontinuity

Although this may seem a paradox, all exact science is dominated by the idea of approximation. 

Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) 

The direct method in the calculus of variations is an important tool in relaxation theory and it relies heavily on the notion of lower semicontinuity, which is the subject of the next section. 

## 3.1 Lower Semicontinuity

Definition 3.1. Let V be a topological space and let $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ 

(i) I is lower semicontinuous if the set $\{ v \in V : I ( v ) \leq t \}$ is closed for every $t \in \mathbb { R }$ 

(ii) I is sequentially lower semicontinuous $i f$ the set $\{ v \in V : I ( v ) \leq t \}$ is sequentially closed for every $t \in \mathbb { R }$ 

(iii) I is upper semicontinuous (respectively sequentially upper semicontinuous) $i f - I$ is lower semicontinuous (respectively sequentially lower semicontinuous). 

Remark 3.2. Note that (i) implies (ii). To see this, assume that I is lower semicontinuous, fix $t \in \mathbb { R }$ , and let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset V$ be any sequence converging to $v _ { 0 }$ and such that $I \left( v _ { n } \right) \leq t$ . We claim that $I \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \leq t$ . Indeed, if $t < I \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ then the set $I ^ { - 1 } \left( \left( t , \infty \right] \right)$ is an open set containing $v _ { 0 }$ , and thus $v _ { n } \in I ^ { - 1 } \left( ( t , \infty ] \right)$ for all n suficiently large, which is a contradiction. Hence $I \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \leq t$ , and so the set $\{ v \in V : I ( v ) \leq t \}$ is sequentially closed. 

In general, the converse is not true (see Exercise A.34 below). However, it can be shown that (ii) implies (i) if V satisfies the first axiom of countability (see Proposition 3.12 below). 

The following characterizations of lower semicontinuity will be of use in the sequel. We recall the definition of epigraph and of limit inferior. 

Definition 3.3. Let $( V , \tau )$ be a topological space and let $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ 

(i) The epigraph of I is the set 

$$
\operatorname{epi} I := \left\{(v, t) \in V \times \mathbb {R}: I (v) \leq t \right\}.
$$

(ii) For any $v _ { 0 } \in V$ the limit inferior of I as v tends to $v _ { 0 }$ is defined as 

$$
\liminf _ {v \to v _ {0}} I \left(v\right) := \sup _ {A \in \tau (v _ {0})} \inf _ {v \in A \setminus \{v _ {0} \}} I \left(v\right),
$$

where $\tau \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ stands for the collection of all open sets in τ that contain ${ v _ { 0 } } . ^ { 1 }$ 

Proposition 3.4. Let V be a topological space and let $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ Then the following are equivalent: 

(i) I is lower semicontinuous; 

(ii) epi I is closed; 

(iii) for every $v _ { 0 } \in V$ 

$$
I \left(v _ {0}\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {v \to v _ {0}} I \left(v\right).
$$

Similarly, the following are equivalent: 

(i)<sup></sup> I is sequentially lower semicontinuous; 

$( i i ) ^ { \prime }$ epi I is sequentially closed; 

(iii)<sup></sup> for every $v _ { 0 } \in V$ 

$$
I \left(v _ {0}\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right)
$$

for every sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ converging to $v _ { 0 }$ . 

Proof. Step 1: We prove that (i) is equivalent to (ii). Assume that I is lower semicontinuous and let 

$$
D := (V \times \mathbb {R}) \setminus \operatorname{epi} I = \left\{(v, t) \in V \times \mathbb {R}: I (v) > t \right\}.\tag{3.1}
$$

Fix $( v _ { 0 } , t _ { 0 } ) \in D$ and let $0 < \varepsilon < I \left( v _ { 0 } \right) - t _ { 0 }$ . Then the set 

$$
U := I ^ {- 1} \left(\left(t _ {0} + \varepsilon , \infty \right]\right)
$$

is open and contains $v _ { 0 }$ , and so $U \times ( t _ { 0 } - \varepsilon , t _ { 0 } + \varepsilon )$ is a neighborhood of $( v _ { 0 } , t _ { 0 } )$ If $( v , t ) \in U \times ( t _ { 0 } - \varepsilon , t _ { 0 } + \varepsilon )$ then $I \left( v \right) > t _ { 0 } + \varepsilon > t$ , which implies that $( v , t ) \in D$ . Hence D is open and its complement, epi I, is closed. 

Conversely, assume that epi I is closed (and so the set D defined in (3.1) is open), and for $t _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R }$ consider the set 

$$
U := \left\{v \in V: I (v) > t _ {0} \right\}.
$$

If $v _ { 0 } \in U$ then for any fixed $0 < \varepsilon _ { 0 } < I \left( v _ { 0 } \right) - t _ { 0 }$ the pair $( v _ { 0 } , t _ { 0 } + \varepsilon _ { 0 } )$ belongs to the open set $D ,$ and so we may find a neighborhood $U _ { 0 } ~ \subset ~ V$ of $v _ { 0 }$ and $0 < \varepsilon \le \varepsilon _ { 0 }$ such that 

$$
U _ {0} \times (t _ {0} + \varepsilon_ {0} - \varepsilon , t _ {0} + \varepsilon_ {0} + \varepsilon) \subset D.
$$

In particular, if $v \in U _ { 0 }$ then $I \left( v \right) > t _ { 0 } + \varepsilon _ { 0 } - \varepsilon > t _ { 0 }$ , and so $U _ { 0 } \subset U$ , which shows that $U$ is open and in turn proves the lower semicontinuity of I. 

Step 2: We show that (i) is equivalent to (iii). Let I be lower semicontinuous and assume by contradiction that there exists $v _ { 0 } \in V$ such that 

$$
I \left(v _ {0}\right) > \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {v \to v _ {0}} I \left(v\right).
$$

Fix $I \left( v _ { 0 } \right) > t >$ lim in $\mathrm { f } _ { v  v _ { 0 } } I ( v )$ . Then the open set 

$$
A _ {t} := \{v \in V: I (v) > t \}\tag{3.2}
$$

belongs to $\tau \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ , and so 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {v \to v _ {0}} I (v) = \sup _ {A \in \tau (v _ {0})} \inf _ {v \in A \setminus \{v _ {0} \}} I (v) \geq \inf _ {v \in A _ {t} \setminus \{v _ {0} \}} I (v) \geq t,
$$

which is a contradiction. 

Conversely, assume that (iii) holds and fix $t \in \mathbb { R }$ . If the set $A _ { t }$ defined in (3.2) is nonempty, fix any $v _ { 0 }$ that belongs to it. Since 

$$
\liminf _ {v \to v _ {0}} I \left(v\right) \geq I \left(v _ {0}\right) > t,
$$

by the definition of limit inferior there exists $A \in \tau \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ such that 

$$
\inf _ {v \in A \setminus \{v _ {0} \}} I (v) > t,
$$

which, together with the fact that $I \left( v _ { 0 } \right) > t$ , implies that $A \subset A _ { t }$ . Hence (i) holds. 

Step 3: We prove that $( \mathrm { i } ) ^ { \prime }$ and $( \mathrm { i i i } ) ^ { \prime }$ are equivalent. Let I be sequentially lower semicontinuous and assume by contradiction that there exist $v _ { 0 } \in V$ and a sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ converging to $v _ { 0 }$ such that 

$$
I \left(v _ {0}\right) > \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right).
$$

Fix $I \left( v _ { 0 } \right) > t >$ lim in $\scriptstyle { \mathrm { f } } _ { n \to \infty } I \left( v _ { n } \right)$ and select a subsequence (not relabeled) such that $I \left( v _ { n } \right) \leq t$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Since the set 

$$
C _ {t} := \{v \in V: I (v) \leq t \}\tag{3.3}
$$

is sequentially closed, it follows that $v _ { 0 } \in C _ { t }$ , which is a contradiction. 

Conversely, assume that (iii)<sup></sup> holds and fix $t \in \mathbb { R }$ . If the set $C _ { t }$ defined in (3.3) is nonempty, consider any sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset C _ { t }$ converging to some $v _ { 0 }$ Then 

$$
I \left(v _ {0}\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right) \leq t,
$$

which implies that $v _ { 0 } \in C _ { t }$ . Thus $C _ { t }$ is sequentially closed. 

Step 4: Finally, we show that (ii)<sup></sup> and $( \mathrm { i i i } ) ^ { \prime }$ are equivalent. Suppose that epi I is sequentially closed, fix $v _ { 0 } \in V$ , and let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset V$ be any sequence converging to $v _ { 0 }$ . If 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right) = \infty ,
$$

then there is nothing to show. Hence assume that the limit inferior is finite and find a subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ v _ { n } \}$ such that 

$$
s := \liminf _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {k \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n _ {k}}\right).
$$

Then $\{ ( v _ { n _ { k } } , I \left( v _ { n _ { k } } \right) ) \} \subset$ epi I and $( v _ { n _ { k } } , I \left( v _ { n _ { k } } \right) ) \to ( v _ { 0 } , s )$ , and so $( v _ { 0 } , s ) \in \mathrm { e p i } I$ by hypothesis. This implies that 

$$
I \left(v _ {0}\right) \leq s = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {k \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n _ {k}}\right),
$$

and so $( \mathrm { i i i } ) ^ { \prime }$ is satisfied. 

Finally, assume that (iii)<sup></sup> holds and let $\{ ( v _ { n } , t _ { n } ) \} \subset \mathrm { e p i } I$ be such that $v _ { n } \implies v$ and $t _ { n } \to t$ for some $v \in V$ and $t \in \mathbb R$ . Since $I \left( v _ { n } \right) \leq t _ { n }$ , letting $n \to \infty$ and using the sequential lower semicontinuity of I yields 

$$
I \left(v\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \rightarrow \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right) \leq \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} t _ {n} = t.
$$

Hence $( v , t ) \in \mathrm { e p i } I _ { : }$ , and so epi I is sequentially closed. 

An important property of lower semicontinuous functions is presented in the next proposition. 

Proposition 3.5. Let V be a topological space and let $\{ I _ { \alpha } \}$ be a (possibly uncountable) family of lower semicontinuous (respectively sequentially lower semicontinuous) functions, $I _ { \alpha } : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ . Then the function 

$$
I _ {+} := \sup _ {\alpha} I _ {\alpha}
$$

is still lower semicontinuous (respectively sequentially lower semicontinuous). In addition, if the family $\{ I _ { \alpha } \}$ is finite, then the function 

$$
I _ {-} := \min _ {\alpha} I _ {\alpha}
$$

is still lower semicontinuous (respectively sequentially lower semicontinuous). 

Proof. Step 1: Assume that all the functions $I _ { \alpha }$ are lower semicontinuous. Using the definition of supremum, it follows that for every $t \in \mathbb { R }$ , 

$$
\left\{v \in V: I _ {+} (v) > t \right\} = \bigcup_ {\alpha} \left\{v \in V: I _ {\alpha} (v) > t \right\},
$$

and thus the set $\{ v \in V : I _ { + } ( v ) > t \}$ is open, since it is a union of open sets. Suppose next that all the functions $I _ { \alpha }$ are sequentially lower semicontinuous, fix $v _ { 0 } \in V$ , and let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset V$ be any sequence converging to $v _ { 0 }$ . Then for every α, 

$$
I _ {\alpha} \left(v _ {0}\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I _ {\alpha} \left(v _ {n}\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I _ {+} \left(v _ {n}\right),
$$

and it now sufices to take the supremum over all $\alpha .$ . 

Step 2: Assume that the family $\{ I _ { \alpha } \}$ is finite, say $\{ I _ { \alpha } \} = \{ I _ { 1 } , \ldots , I _ { l } \}$ , and that each $I _ { j } , j = 1 , \ldots , l ,$ is lower semicontinuous. For any $t \in \mathbb { R }$ 

$$
\left\{v \in V: I _ {-} (v) > t \right\} = \bigcap_ {j = 1} ^ {l} \left\{v \in V: I _ {j} (v) > t \right\},
$$

and so the set $\left\{ v \in V : I _ { - } ( v ) > t \right\}$ is open, since it is the finite intersection of open sets. 

If instead, the functions $I _ { 1 } , \ldots , I _ { l }$ are sequentially lower semicontinuous, fix $v _ { 0 } \in \ V$ , let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset V$ be any sequence converging to $v _ { 0 }$ , and find a subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ v _ { n } \}$ such that 

$$
s := \liminf _ {n \to \infty} I _ {-} \left(v _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {k \to \infty} I _ {-} \left(v _ {n _ {k}}\right).
$$

Then there exists an integer $j _ { 0 } \in \{ 1 , \ldots , l \}$ such that 

$$
\min _ {1 \leq j \leq l} I _ {j} \left(v _ {n _ {k}}\right) = I _ {j _ {0}} \left(v _ {n _ {k}}\right)
$$

for infinitely many k. Hence, selecting a further subsequence (not relabeled), we may assume that 

$$
s = \liminf _ {n \to \infty} I _ {-} \left(v _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {k \to \infty} I _ {j _ {0}} \left(v _ {n _ {k}}\right) \geq I _ {j _ {0}} \left(v _ {0}\right) \geq I _ {-} \left(v _ {0}\right),
$$

and this concludes the proof. 

We now show that Weierstrass’s theorem continues to hold for lower semi continuous functions. This fact alone explains the importance of this class of functions in minimization problems. 

Theorem 3.6 (Weierstrass). Let V be a topological space, let $K \subset V$ be compact (respectively sequentially compact), and let I : $V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a lower semicontinuous (respectively sequentially lower semicontinuous) function. Then there exists $v _ { 0 } \in K$ such that 

$$
I \left(v _ {0}\right) = \min _ {v \in K} I (v).
$$

Proof. Assume first that K is compact and I lower semicontinuous and let 

$$
t := \inf _ {v \in K} I (v).
$$

If the infimum is not attained, then for every $v \in K$ we may find $t < t _ { v } < I \left( v \right)$ Then the family of open sets 

$$
U _ {v} := \left\{w \in V: I (w) > t _ {v} \right\}, \quad v \in K,
$$

is an open cover for the compact set $K ,$ , and so we may find a finite cover $U _ { v _ { 1 } } , \ldots , U _ { v _ { l } }$ of the set K. But then for all $v \in K$ 

$$
I (v) \geq \min _ {i = 1, \dots , l} t _ {v _ {i}} > t = \inf _ {w \in K} I (w),
$$

which contradicts the definition of t. 

Suppose instead that $K \subset V$ is sequentially compact and $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is a sequentially lower semicontinuous function. Let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset K$ be such that 

$$
\inf _ {w \in K} I (w) \leq I (v _ {n}) \leq \inf _ {w \in K} I (w) + \frac {1}{n}
$$

for all n. By the sequential compactness of K there exists a subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ v _ { n } \}$ that converges to some $v _ { 0 } \in K$ , and so 

$$
\inf _ {w \in K} I \left(w\right) \leq I \left(v _ {0}\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n _ {k}}\right) \leq \inf _ {w \in K} I \left(w\right),
$$

which implies that $v _ { 0 }$ is the desired minimizer. 

The next result will be used in the proof of Theorem 6.49. Note that for metric spaces, lower semicontinuity is equivalent to sequential lower semicon tinuity; see also Proposition 3.12 below. 

Proposition 3.7. Let V be a separable metric space and let I : $V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a lower semicontinuous function. Then there exists a countable set $Y \subset V$ such that for each $v \in V$ • 

$$
I \left(v\right) = \inf \left\{\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right): \left\{v _ {n} \right\} \subset Y, v _ {n} \to v \right\}.
$$

Proof. In view of the lower semicontinuity of I, it is enough to find a countable set $Y \subset V$ such that for each $v \in V$ , 

$$
I \left(v\right) \geq \inf \left\{\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \rightarrow \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right): \left\{v _ {n} \right\} \subset Y, v _ {n} \rightarrow v \right\}.
$$

For each rational number q let $V _ { q } : = \{ v \in V : I ( v ) \leq q \}$ . Since V is separable, then so is $V _ { q }$ , and thus if $V _ { q } \neq \emptyset$ , then there exists a countable set $Y _ { q } \subset V _ { q }$ that is dense in $V _ { q }$ . Set 

$$
Y := \left(\bigcup_ {q \in \mathbb {Q}} Y _ {q}\right) \cup Y _ {\infty},
$$

where $Y _ { \infty }$ is a countable dense subset of V. Fix $v \in V . { \mathrm { I f } } \ I \left( v \right) = \infty$ , then in view of the lower semicontinuity of I it follows that 

$$
I (v) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} I (v _ {n})
$$

for any sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset Y _ { \infty }$ converging to v. If $I \left( v \right) < \infty$ , then for any rational number $q > I \left( v \right)$ we have that $v \in V _ { q }$ , and so, since $Y _ { q }$ is dense in $V _ { q } ,$ , for any $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $w \in Y _ { q }$ such that $I \left( w \right) \leq q$ and d $( v , w ) \leq \varepsilon$ Hence 

$$
\liminf _ {w \in Y, w \to v} I (w) \leq q,
$$

and it now sufices to let $q \searrow _ { \mathrm { { s } } } I ( v )$ 

When I is not lower semicontinuous often in applications it is of interest to study the greatest lower semicontinuous function below I. 

Definition 3.8. Let V be a topological space and let $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ 

(i) The lower semicontinuous envelope lsc $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ of I is defined by 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{lsc} I (v) := \sup \left\{H (v): H: V \to [ - \infty , \infty ] \right. \\ \text {is lower semicontinuous,} H \leq I \}. \end{array}
$$

(ii) The sequentially lower semicontinuous envelope slsc $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ of I is defined by 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{slsc} I (v) := \sup \left\{H (v): H: V \to [ - \infty , \infty ] \text {is sequentially} \right. \\ \text {lower semicontinuous,} H \leq I \}. \end{array}
$$

In view of Proposition 3.5, lsc I is lower semicontinuous and slsc I is sequen tially lower semicontinuous. When it is important to highlight the underlying topology τ, we write $\mathrm { l s c } _ { \tau } I$ and $\mathrm { s l s c } _ { \tau } I$ 

Exercise 3.9. Let $( V , \tau )$ be a topological space and let $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ Prove that for all $v \in V$ , 

$$
\operatorname{lsc} I \left(v\right) = \sup _ {A \in \tau (v)} \inf _ {w \in A} I \left(w\right) = \min \left\{I \left(v _ {0}\right), \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {v \to v _ {0}} I \left(v\right) \right\},
$$

where, we recall, $\tau \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ stands for the collection of all open sets in $\tau$ that contain $v _ { 0 }$ 

In view of Proposition 3.4 the following proposition is not surprising. 

Proposition 3.10. Let V be a topological space and let $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ Then 

$$
\operatorname{epi} \left(\operatorname{lsc} I\right) = \overline {{\operatorname{epi} I}}.
$$

Proof. Since lsc $I \leq I$ we have 

$$
\operatorname{epi} I \subset \operatorname{epi} (\operatorname{lsc} I),
$$

and therefore ${ \overline { { \operatorname { e p i } I } } } \subset { \overline { { \operatorname { e p i } \left( \operatorname { l s c } I \right) } } } = \operatorname { e p i } \left( \operatorname { l s c } I \right)$ , where in the last equality we used Proposition 3.4. 

Conversely, define 

$$
g (v) := \inf \left\{t: (v, t) \in \overline {{\operatorname{epi} I}} \right\}, \quad v \in V.
$$

We show that $g \leq I$ . Let $v \in V$ be such that $I \left( v \right) < \infty$ . Then for any $t > I \left( v \right)$ we have $( v , t ) \in \mathrm { e p i } I$ , and therefore $g \left( v \right) \leq t .$ . Consequently, $g \left( v \right) \leq I \left( v \right)$ 

Note also that by the definition of g it follows that epi ${ \overline { { I } } } \subset \ \operatorname { e p i } g .$ .
