We prove equality, i.e., that epi $\overline { { { I } } } = \operatorname { e p i } g$ . Let $( v , t ) \in \operatorname { e p i } g$ and let $\varepsilon > 0$ . By the definition of $g$ we may find $t ^ { \prime } < t + \varepsilon$ such that $( v , t ^ { \prime } ) \in \overline { { \mathrm { e p i } I } }$ . The arbitrariness of ε implies that $( v , t ) \in \overline { { \mathrm { e p i } I } }$ 

Since epi g is a closed set, we conclude that g is lower semicontinuous by Proposition 3.4, and thus lsc $I \geq g$ 

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\operatorname{epi} \left(\operatorname{lsc} I\right) \subset \operatorname{epi} g = \overline {{\operatorname{epi} I}},
$$

and this completes the proof. 

Remark 3.11. Note that lsc I is lower semicontinuous and slsc I is sequentially lower semicontinuous. By Remark 3.2 the function lsc I is also sequentiall lower semicontinuous, and so 

$$
\operatorname{lsc} I \leq \operatorname{slsc} I \leq \inf _ {\left\{v _ {n} \right\}} \left\{\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right): \left\{v _ {n} \right\} \subset V,   v _ {n} \to v \right\}.\tag{3.4}
$$

Equality holds if $V$ satisfies the first axiom of countability, as shown in the next proposition. 

Proposition 3.12. Let V be a topological space satisfying the first axiom of countability and let $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ . Then 

$$
\operatorname{lsc} I \left(v\right) = \operatorname{slsc} I \left(v\right) = \inf _ {\left\{v _ {n} \right\}} \left\{\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \rightarrow \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right): \left\{v _ {n} \right\} \subset V, v _ {n} \rightarrow v \right\}
$$

for every $v \in V$ . Moreover, the infimum is attained, that is, for every $v \in V$ there exists a sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ converging to v such that 

$$
\operatorname{lsc} I (v) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} I (v _ {n}).
$$

Proof. Step 1: Fix $v \in V$ . Define 

$$
\varPhi \left(v\right) := \inf \left\{\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right): \left\{v _ {n} \right\} \subset V,   v _ {n} \to v \right\}.
$$

We prove that 

$$
\varPhi (v) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} I (w _ {n})
$$

for some $\{ w _ { n } \} \subset V , w _ { n } \to v$ . Let $\{ U _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { N } }$ be a countable basis of open neighborhoods of v. Find a sequence $\left\{ v _ { n } ^ { ( 1 ) } \right\}$ such that $v _ { n } ^ { ( 1 ) }  v$ and 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n} ^ {(1)}\right) \leq \varPhi \left(v\right) + \frac {1}{2}.
$$

Choose $w _ { 1 } : = v _ { n _ { 1 } } ^ { ( 1 ) } \in U _ { 1 }$ such that 

$$
I \left(w _ {1}\right) \leq \Phi (v) + 1.
$$

Recursively, with $\left\{ v _ { n } ^ { ( k ) } \right\}$ converging to v and 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n} ^ {(k)}\right) \leq \varPhi \left(v\right) + \frac {1}{k + 1},
$$

choose $\begin{array} { r } { w _ { k } : = v _ { n _ { k } } ^ { ( k ) } \in \bigcap _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } U _ { i } } \end{array}$ such that 

$$
I \left(w _ {k}\right) \leq \Phi (v) + \frac {1}{k}.\tag{3.5}
$$

Then $w _ { k } \to v .$ , and so 

$$
\varPhi \left(v\right) \leq \liminf _ {k \to \infty} I \left(w _ {k}\right).
$$

This, together with (3.5), entails 

$$
\varPhi (v) = \lim _ {k \to \infty} I (w _ {k}).
$$

Step 2: In view of (3.4), all that remains to be proved is that $\varPhi \leq$ lsc I, or, equivalently, that epi $\operatorname { ( l s c } I ) \subset \operatorname { e p i } \varPhi$ . By Proposition 3.10 we have that epi $( \ker I ) = { \overline { { \operatorname { e p i } I } } }$ , and so it sufices to prove that epi $\overline { { I } } \subset \operatorname { e p i } \phi$ . Choose $( v , t ) \in$ epi I and, due to the first axiom of countability, find $( v _ { n } , t _ { n } ) \in$ epi I such that $( v _ { n } , t _ { n } ) \to ( v , t )$ . Then $t _ { n } \geq I \left( v _ { n } \right)$ , and so 

$$
t = \lim _ {n \to \infty} t _ {n} \geq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right) \geq \varPhi \left(v\right).
$$

We conclude that $( v , t ) \in \mathrm { e p i } \varPhi$

(3.8) 

Remark 3.13. (i) An important application of this theory concerns the situation in which $V = L ^ { p } ( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu ) , 1 \leq p \leq \infty$ . When $1 < p < \infty$ and V is endowed with the weak topology, then condition (3.7) is always satisfied, and if in addition, $\mu$ is σ-finite and X a separable measurable space (see the Riesz representation theorem and Theorem 2.16), then we are also under condition (3.6).

If $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ is a mea sure space and $\mu$ is σ-finite with X a separable measurable space (see the Riesz representation theorem and Theorem 2.16), then (3.8) applies to $L ^ { \infty } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) = \left( L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ , endowed with the weak star topology.

Let $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ and for all $v \in V$ define 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{lsc} _ {\tau} I (v) := \sup \left\{\varPhi (v): \varPhi \leq I, \varPhi \text {lower} \right. \\ \text {semicontinuous with respect to} \tau \big \} \end{array}

$$

Note that by Remark 3.11 we have 

$$

Definition 3.14. Let V be a normed space and let $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ . The map I is said to be coercive if 

$$
I (v) \rightarrow \infty a s \| v \| \rightarrow \infty .

Proof. The sequential lower semicontinuity of $\mathrm { s l s c } _ { \tau } I$ follows from the fact that $\mathrm { s l s c } _ { \tau } I$ is the supremum of sequentially lower semicontinuous functions. Assume that I is coercive. We divide the proof of the coercivity of $\mathrm { s l s c } _ { \tau } I$ into three steps.

By Step 1 we conclude that $C _ { s } \subset \overline { { B \left( 0 , R \right) } }$

Proof. In view of (3.9) it sufices to show that lsc $I \geq \mathcal { I }$ . Fix $v _ { 0 } \in V$ . If $\mathrm { l s c } _ { \tau } I \left( v _ { 0 } \right) = \infty$ there is nothing to prove. Thus assume that lsc $I \left( v _ { 0 } \right) < \infty$ and let lsc $I \left( v _ { 0 } \right) < t < \infty$ . By the coercivity of I there exists $R > 0$ such that 

$$

Finally, we observe that when $p = 1$ and we consider the weak topology in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ , we are unable to use Proposition 3.16 because the dual of $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ is $L ^ { \infty } \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right)$ (under suitable hypotheses on $\left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) )$ ), which is not separable in general. However, as it turns out, we can still assert that sls $\mathbf { c } _ { \tau } I = \mathcal { T }$ , provided we have a condition stronger than coercivity: 

Proposition 3.18. Let X be a separable, locally compact metric space, and let $\mu$ be a finite Radon measure defined on $B \left( X \right)$ . Let 

$$
I: L ^ {1} (X, \mathcal {B} (X), \mu) \to [ - \infty , \infty ]
$$

satisfy 

$$
I (v) \geq \int_ {X} \gamma (| v (x) |) d \mu
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( X , B \left( X \right) , \mu \right)$ and for some increasing function $\gamma : [ 0 , \infty ) $ $[ 0 , \infty ]$ with 

$$

$$

Then slsc $I = \mathcal T$ , where τ is the $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , B \left( X \right) , \mu \right)$ weak topology. 

Proof. Since $\mathrm { s l s c } _ { \tau } I$ is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to the weak topology in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , B \left( X \right) , \mu \right)$ and $\operatorname { s l s c } _ { \tau } I \leq I .$ we have slsc $I \leq \mathcal { T }$ . To prove the opposite inequality, since $\mathcal { T } \leq I$ (take $v _ { n } \equiv v )$ , it sufices to show that I is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak convergence in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , B \left( X \right) , \mu \right)$ . Let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } \left( X , B \left( X \right) , \mu \right)$ be such that $\textstyle v _ { n } \ \to \ v$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , B \left( X \right) , \mu \right)$ . Without loss of generality we may assume that 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} \mathcal {I} \left(v _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \mathcal {I} \left(v _ {n}\right) <   \infty .
$$

Let 

$$
M := \sup _ {n} \mathcal {I} (v _ {n}) <   \infty ,
$$

fix $0 < \varepsilon < 1$ , and for every n find a sequence $\left\{ v _ { n , k } \right\} _ { k } \subset L ^ { 1 } \left( X , B \left( X \right) , \mu \right)$ such that $v _ { n , k } \to v _ { n }$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( X , B \left( X \right) , \mu \right)$ as $k \to \infty$ and 

$$
\mathcal {I} \left(v _ {n}\right) \geq \lim _ {k \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n, k}\right) - \varepsilon .
$$

Without loss of generality we may assume that 

$$
v _ {n, k} \in \left\{w \in L ^ {1} (X, \mathcal {B} (X), \mu): I (w) \leq M + 1 \right\}
$$

for every n, k. Hence 

$$
\sup _ {n, k} \int_ {X} \gamma \left(\left| v _ {n, k} (x) \right|\right) d \mu \leq M + 1.\tag{3.11}
$$

By (3.10) we have 

$$
\sup _ {n, k} \int_ {X} | v _ {n, k} (x) | d \mu <   \infty ,
$$

and so, identifying $L ^ { 1 }$ functions with measures in $\left( C _ { 0 } \left( X \right) \right) ^ { \prime }$ , we are back to the setting (3.8). By Theorem A.54 we may find a metric d compatible with weak star convergence in a large ball of $( C _ { 0 } \left( X \right) ) ^ { \prime }$ 

In particular, we have 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \lim _ {k \to \infty} d (v _ {n, k}, v) = 0.
$$

Let 

$$
\ell := \liminf _ {n \to \infty} \lim _ {k \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n, k}\right).
$$

We now use a diagonalization argument as follows. Choose $n _ { 1 }$ such that 

$$
\left| \ell - \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} I \left(v _ {n _ {1}, k}\right)\right| + \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} d \left(v _ {n _ {1}, k}, v\right) \leq 1,
$$

and let $k _ { 1 }$ be such that 

$$
\left| I \left(v _ {n _ {1}, k _ {1}}\right) - \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} I \left(v _ {n _ {1}, k}\right)\right| + \left| d \left(v _ {n _ {1}, k _ {1}}, v\right) - \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} d \left(v _ {n _ {1}, k}, v\right)\right| \leq 1.
$$

Then 

$$
\left| \ell - I \left(v _ {n _ {1}, k _ {1}}\right) \right| + d \left(v _ {n _ {1}, k _ {1}}, v\right) \leq 2.
$$

Choose $n _ { 2 } > n _ { 1 }$ such that 

$$
\left| \ell - \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} I (v _ {n _ {2}, k}) \right| + \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} d (v _ {n _ {2}, k}, v) \leq \frac {1}{2},
$$

and let $k _ { 2 } > k _ { 1 }$ be such that 

$$
\left| I \left(v _ {n _ {2}, k _ {2}}\right) - \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} I \left(v _ {n _ {2}, k}\right)\right| + \left| d \left(v _ {n _ {2}, k _ {2}}, v\right) - \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} d \left(v _ {n _ {2}, k}, v\right)\right| \leq \frac {1}{2}.
$$

Note that 

$$
\left| \ell - I \left(v _ {n _ {2}, k _ {2}}\right) \right| + d \left(v _ {n _ {2}, k _ {2}}, v\right) \leq 1.
$$

Continuing in this way we construct a diagonalized sequence $\left\{ v _ { n _ { j } , k _ { j } } \right\}$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {j \to \infty} I (v _ {n _ {j}, k _ {j}}) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \lim _ {k \to \infty} I (v _ {n, k}), \quad \lim _ {j \to \infty} d (v _ {n _ {j}, k _ {j}}, v) = 0.
$$

In view of (3.11) and by Theorem 2.29 and the Dunford–Pettis theorem, we deduce $v _ { n _ { j } , k _ { j } } \to v$ in $L ^ { 1 }$ , and so by the definition of I we conclude that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \mathcal {I} \left(v _ {n}\right) + \varepsilon \geq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \lim _ {k \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n, k}\right) = \lim _ {j \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n _ {j}, k _ {j}}\right) \geq \mathcal {I} \left(v\right).
$$

It now sufices to let $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ to conclude the proof. 

## 3.2 The Direct Method

Let V be a normed space and let $I : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be not identically equa to ∞. Tonelli’s direct method provides conditions on V and I that ensure the existence of a minimum point for I. The procedure may be reduced to four steps: 

Step 1 Consider a minimizing sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset V$ , that is, a sequence such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} I (v _ {n}) = \inf _ {v \in V} I.
$$

Step 2 Prove that $\{ v _ { n } \}$ admits a subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ that converges with respect to some (possibly weaker) topology τ to some point $v _ { 0 } \in V$ Step 3 Establish the sequential lower semicontinuity of I with respect to $\tau .$ Step 4 In view of Steps 1–3, conclude that $v _ { 0 }$ is a minimum of I because 

$$
\inf _ {v \in V} I = \lim _ {n \to \infty} I (v _ {n}) = \lim _ {k \to \infty} I (v _ {n _ {k}}) \geq I (v _ {0}) \geq \inf _ {v \in V} I.
$$

In the above program the challenge usually resides in guaranteeing that Step 3 is satisfied, while, as we will see below, Step 2 usually can be easily proved through natural growth and coercivity conditions of I. Indeed, if I is coercive and if $\{ v _ { n } \}$ is a minimizing sequence, then $\{ v _ { n } \}$ must be bounded, and under condition (3.7) or (3.8) of the previous subsection, this sufices to ensure sequential compactness with respect to $\tau .$ 

In most applications Step 3 fails for I, and this leads us to an important topic at the core of the calculus of variations, namely the introduction of a relaxed function $\mathcal { E } ^ { \prime }$ that is related to I as follows: 

(a) $\mathcal { E } ^ { \prime }$ is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to $\tau _ { \pm }$ ; 

(b) $\mathcal { E } ^ { \prime }$ inherits coercivity from I; 

(c) m $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname { i n } _ { v \in V } \mathcal { E } ^ { \prime } = \operatorname* { i n f } _ { v \in V } I } \end{array}$ 

Note that in (c) the existence of a minimum $v _ { 0 } \in V$ of $\mathcal { E } ^ { \prime }$ is guaranteed by (a), (b), and the direct method. In view of Proposition 3.15 (see also Proposition 3.16), a natural candidate for $\mathcal { E } ^ { \prime }$ is the function slsc I introduced in the previous subsection. Indeed, under the hypotheses of Proposition 3.16 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \inf _ {v \in V} I \geq \min _ {v \in V} \operatorname{slsc} _ {\tau} I = \operatorname{slsc} _ {\tau} I (v _ {0}) \\ = \inf _ {\{v _ {n} \}} \left\{\liminf _ {n \to \infty} I (v _ {n}): \{v _ {n} \} \subset V, v _ {n} \xrightarrow {\tau} v _ {0} \right\} \geq \inf _ {v \in V} I, \end{array}
$$

where in the second equality we have used Proposition 3.16. 

The next task is then to study under what conditions 

$$
I \left(v _ {0}\right) = \mathrm{slsc} _ {\tau} I \left(v _ {0}\right),
$$

i.e., 

$$
I \left(v _ {0}\right) = \min _ {v \in V} I.
$$

We will not address this topic in this text (see, however, Section 5.5).

## 4.1 Convex Sets

We recall that a subset E of a vector space V is convex if for all $v _ { 1 } , v _ { 2 } \in E$ and $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ we have 

$$
\theta v _ {1} + (1 - \theta) v _ {2} \in E.
$$

An induction argument shows that if $v _ { i } ~ \in ~ E , ~ i ~ = ~ 1 , \dots , n $ , then $z : =$ $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \theta _ { i } v _ { i } \in E$ , whenever $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \theta _ { i } = 1 , \theta _ { i } \geq 0$ z convex combination of $v _ { 1 } , \ldots , v _ { n }$ 

The entire space V and the empty set are two examples of convex sets. The arbitrary intersection of convex sets is still convex, but in general the union is not (the simplest example is the union of two disjoint closed segments on the real line). 

Similarly, E is said to be afine if for all $v _ { 1 } , v _ { 2 } \in E$ and $\theta \in \mathbb { R }$ we have 

$$
\theta v _ {1} + (1 - \theta) v _ {2} \in E.
$$

Remark $4 . 1 .$ . Every afine set $E \subset V$ can be written as $v _ { 0 } + W$ , where $v _ { 0 } \in E$ and $W$ is a vector subspace of V. 

Given any set $E \subset V .$ , the convex hull co (E) is the intersection of all convex sets that contain E. 

Proposition 4.2. Let V be a vector space and let $E \subset V$ . Then 

$$
\operatorname{co} (E) = \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \theta_ {i} v _ {i}: n \in \mathbb {N}, \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \theta_ {i} = 1, \theta_ {i} \geq 0, v _ {i} \in E, i = 1, \dots , n \right\}.\tag{4.1}
$$

Proof. If $F$ is any convex set that contains $E _ { : }$ , then it must contain all convex combinations of elements of $E .$ , and so 

$$
F \supset \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \theta_ {i} v _ {i}: n \in \mathbb {N}, \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \theta_ {i} = 1, \theta_ {i} \geq 0, v _ {i} \in E, i = 1, \dots , n \right\} =: G.
$$

Since this holds for all convex sets containing E, it follows that 

$$
\operatorname{co} (E) \supset G.
$$

To prove the opposite inclusion it sufices to show that G is convex and contains E. The latter assertion follows from the fact that if $u \in E$ , then we can take $n = 1$ and $\theta _ { 1 } = 1$ . To show that $G$ is convex, let $0 \leq \theta \leq 1$ and let $u ,$ $v \in V$ be of the form 

$$
u = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \theta_ {i} v _ {i}, \quad v = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {l} s _ {j} w _ {j},
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \theta _ { i } = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { l } s _ { j } = 1 , \theta _ { i } , s _ { j } \geq 0 , v _ { i } , w _ { j } \in E , i = 1 , \dots , n , j = 1 , \dots , l . } \end{array}$ Note that without loss of generality, we may always assume that $n = l .$ . Indeed, $n \neq l$ , say $n > l$ , then it sufices to set $s _ { l + 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n } : = 0$ and $w _ { l + 1 } , \ldots , w _ { n } : =$ $w _ { 1 }$ . Then 

$$
\theta u + (1 - \theta) v = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \theta \theta_ {i} v _ {i} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (1 - \theta) s _ {i} w _ {i},
$$

which is still a convex combination of elements of $E _ { : }$ , and so it belongs to $G .$ 

Note that without loss of generality, in (4.1) one may consider only positive coeficients $\theta _ { i }$ 

Remark 4.3. If the space V is a topological vector space, then the convex hull of an open set $U \subset V$ is open. To see this, for any $n \in \mathbb { N }$ fix $\varLambda : = \{ \theta _ { 1 } , \ldots , \theta _ { n } \}$ with $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \theta _ { i } = 1$ and $\theta _ { i } > 0$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ and consider the set 

$$
U _ {\Lambda} := \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \theta_ {i} v _ {i}: v _ {i} \in U, i = 1, \dots , n \right\}.
$$

Since addition and positive scalar multiplication are both open maps, it follows that $U _ { A }$ is an open set. By the previous proposition, 

$$
\operatorname{co} (U) = \bigcup_ {\Lambda} U _ {\Lambda},
$$

and so $\operatorname { c o } ( U )$ is open. 

Analogously, the afine hull af $( E )$ is the intersection of all afine sets that contain E. Reasoning as in the proof of Proposition 4.2, it can be shown that 

$$
\operatorname{aff} (E) = \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \theta_ {i} v _ {i}: n \in \mathbb {N}, \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \theta_ {i} = 1, \theta_ {i} \in \mathbb {R}, v _ {i} \in E, i = 1, \dots , n \right\}.
$$

Exercise 4.4. Prove that if V is a topological vector space, then the interior and the closure of a convex set are also convex sets. 

Given any set E of a topological vector space V, the intersection of all closed convex sets that contain E coincides with the closure of the convex hull co (E), and is denoted by co (E). The relative interior of E with respect to af (E), denoted by $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( E \right)$ , is the set of points $v \in E$ such that A∩af $( E ) \subset E$ for some open set $A \subset V$ with $v \in A$ . The relative boundary of E with respect to af (E), denoted by $\mathrm { r b } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( E \right)$ , is the set $\overline { { E } } \setminus \operatorname { r i _ { a f f } } \left( E \right)$

(i) Prove that $z _ { 0 } + t \left( z _ { 0 } - z \right) \in$ af (C) for all $t \in \mathbb { R }$ (ii) Prove that the function $g : \mathbb { R } \to$ af (C), defined by $g \left( t \right) : = z _ { 0 } + t \left( z _ { 0 } - z \right)$ $t \in \mathbb { R }$ , is continuous.

Proposition 4.7. Let $C \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a nonempty convex set. Then $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ is convex and nonempty. Moreover, $i f z \in \overline { { C } }$ and $z _ { 0 } \in \operatorname { r i _ { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ , then 

$$
\theta z + (1 - \theta) z _ {0} \in \mathrm{ri} _ {\text { aff }} (C)
$$

for all $0 \leq \theta < 1$ 

Proof. Step 1: If C is a singleton, then ${ \mathrm { r i } } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right) = C$ , and so there is nothing to prove. Thus assume that C has at least two elements. By Exercise 4.6, without loss of generality, we may assume that $0 \in C .$ , so that af (C) is a subspace of $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . In particular, $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ is relatively open in af (C). Since $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is finite-dimensional, there is a finite maximal (with respect to inclusion) set of linearly independent vectors $z _ { 1 } , \dots , z _ { k } \in \operatorname { r i _ { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ . The vectors $z _ { 1 } , \ldots , z _ { k }$ are a basis in af (C), and thus we can define on af (C) the norm 

$$
\left\| w \right\| _ {\mathrm{aff} (C)} := \max _ {1 \leq i \leq k} \left| s _ {i} \right|,
$$

where 

$$
w = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} s _ {i} z _ {i} \in \mathrm{aff} (C).
$$

Since $0 \in C$ , any point of the form 

$$
w = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \theta_ {i} z _ {i} = 0 \left(1 - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \theta_ {i}\right) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \theta_ {i} z _ {i},
$$

where $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \theta _ { i } \leq 1$ and $\theta _ { i } \geq 0$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ , belongs to C. In particular, the point 

$$
w _ {0} := \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \frac {1}{2 k} z _ {i}
$$

belongs to C. We claim that $w _ { 0 } \in \operatorname { r i _ { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ . To see this, consider the open ball 

$$
B _ {\text { aff } (C)} \left(w _ {0}, \frac {1}{2 k}\right) := \left\{w \in \text { aff } (C): \| w - w _ {0} \| _ {\text { aff } (C)} <   \frac {1}{2 k} \right\}.
$$

If $w \in B _ { \mathrm { a f f } ( C ) } \left( w _ { 0 } , \frac { 1 } { 2 k } \right)$ , then we may write $\begin{array} { r } { w = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } s _ { i } z _ { i } } \end{array}$ , where 

$$
\max _ {1 \leq i \leq k} \left| s _ {i} - \frac {1}{2 k} \right| <   \frac {1}{2 k}.
$$

Then $s _ { i } \geq 0$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ and 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} s _ {i} <   \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \frac {1}{k} = 1,
$$

which shows that $w \in C$ . Thus $B _ { \mathrm { a f f } ( C ) } \left( w _ { 0 } , { \frac { 1 } { 2 k } } \right) \subset C$ , and so $w _ { 0 }$ belongs to the interior of C relative to af (C), or equivalently, $w _ { 0 } \in \operatorname { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ 

Step 2: To prove the second part, let $z \in \overline { { C } }$ and $z _ { 0 } \in \operatorname { r i _ { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ . Fix $0 < \theta < 1$ If C is a singleton, then $\operatorname { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right) = C = { \overline { { C } } } .$ , and so there is nothing to prove. Thus assume that $C$ has at least two elements. Hence, as in the previous step there is no loss of generality in assuming that $0 \in C$ . Let $z _ { 1 } , \dots , z _ { k } \in \operatorname { r i _ { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ and $\left\| \cdot \right\| _ { \mathrm { a f f } ( C ) }$ be defined as in the previous step. Since $z _ { 0 } \in \operatorname { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ , there exists an open ball $B _ { \mathrm { a f f } ( C ) } \left( z _ { 0 } , r \right) \subset C$ . Note that since the afine hull of $C$ is a closed set, it must contain $\overline { { C } }$ , and consequently it coincides with the afine hull of $\overline { { C } } .$ . Thus $z \in$ af $( C )$ , and we may find a sequence $\{ w _ { n } \} \subset C$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { \left. z - w _ { n } \right. _ { \mathrm { a f f } ( C ) } \longrightarrow 0 } \end{array}$ . We claim that 

$$
B _ {\mathrm{aff} (C)} \left(\theta z _ {0} + (1 - \theta) z, \theta r\right) \subset C.
$$

To see this, note that if $w \in B _ { \mathrm { a f f } ( C ) } \left( \theta z _ { 0 } + \left( 1 - \theta \right) z , \theta r \right)$ , then 

$$
\left\| w - \left(\theta z _ {0} + (1 - \theta) z\right) \right\| _ {\mathrm{aff} (C)} <   \theta r,
$$

or equivalently, 

$$
\left\| \frac {w}{\theta} - \frac {(1 - \theta)}{\theta} z - z _ {0} \right\| _ {\mathrm{aff} (C)} <   r.
$$

Since $\begin{array} { r } { \left. z - w _ { n } \right. _ { \mathrm { a f f } ( C ) } \to 0 } \end{array}$ we may find $n \in \mathbb { N }$ so large that 

$$
\left\| \frac {w}{\theta} - \frac {(1 - \theta)}{\theta} w _ {n} - z _ {0} \right\| _ {\mathrm{aff} (C)} <   r.
$$

Thus $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { w } { \theta } - \frac { \left( 1 - \theta \right) } { \theta } w _ { n } \in B _ { \mathrm { a f f } ( C ) } \left( z _ { 0 } , r \right) \subset C } \end{array}$ , which implies that 

$$
\frac {w}{\theta} - \frac {(1 - \theta)}{\theta} w _ {n} = \xi \in C.
$$

In turn, $w = ( 1 - \theta ) w _ { n } + \theta \xi \in C$ , and the proof is complete. 

Example $4 . 8 .$ Note that if $C _ { 1 } \subset C _ { 2 }$ are two nonempty convex sets, then in general one cannot conclude that 

$$
\mathrm{ri} _ {\text {aff}} \left(C _ {1}\right) \subset \mathrm{ri} _ {\text {aff}} \left(C _ {2}\right).
$$

Indeed, let $C _ { 2 }$ be the closed unit cube in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ and let $C _ { 1 }$ be one of its faces. Then $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C _ { 2 } \right)$ is the open unit cube, while $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C _ { 1 } \right)$ is the face without its four edges. Hence $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C _ { 1 } \right)$ and $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C _ { 2 } \right)$ are disjoint and nonempty. 

Proposition 4.9. Let $C _ { 1 } , C _ { 2 }$ be two nonempty convex sets of $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Then the following three conditions are equivalent: 

(i) ${ \overline { { C _ { 1 } } } } = { \overline { { C _ { 2 } } } } ,$ 

(ii) $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C _ { 1 } \right) = \mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C _ { 2 } \right)$ ; 

(iii) $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C _ { 1 } \right) \subset C _ { 2 } \subset \overline { { C _ { 1 } } }$ 

Proof. Step 1: We show that for any nonempty convex set $C \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , 

$$
\overline {{C}} = \overline {{\operatorname{ri} _ {\text { aff }} (C)}}, \quad \operatorname{ri} _ {\text { aff }} (\overline {{C}}) = \operatorname{ri} _ {\text { aff }} (C).
$$

Since ${ \mathrm { r i } } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right) \subset C$ , we have that ${ \overline { { \operatorname { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right) } } } \subset { \overline { { C } } }$ . To prove the converse inclu sion, let $z \in { \overline { { C } } }$ and let $z _ { 0 } \in \operatorname { r i _ { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ . Note that in view of Proposition 4.7 such $z _ { 0 }$ exists and 

$$
\theta z + (1 - \theta) z _ {0} \in \mathrm{ri} _ {\mathrm{aff}} (C)
$$

for all $0 \leq \theta < 1$ . This implies that $z \in \operatorname { r i _ { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ . Hence the first identity is established. 

Since the afine hull of $C$ is a closed set, it must contain $\overline { { C } }$ , and consequently, it coincides with the afine hull of $\overline { { C } }$ . Therefore 

$$
\operatorname{ri} _ {\text { aff }} (C) \subset \operatorname{ri} _ {\text { aff }} (\overline {{C}}).
$$

To prove the converse inclusion, let $z \in \mathrm { { r i } _ { a f f } } \left( \overline { { C } } \right)$ and let $z _ { 0 } \in \operatorname { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ . If $z = z _ { 0 }$ then $z \in \operatorname { r i _ { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ , and there is nothing to prove. Thus assume that $z \neq z _ { 0 }$ and let 

$$
w _ {t} := t z + (1 - t)   z _ {0}, \quad t > 1.
$$

Since $z \in { \mathrm { r i } } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( \overline { { C } } \right)$ , if $t - 1$ is suficiently small, then $w _ { t } \in \operatorname { r i _ { a f f } } { \overline { { C } } } \subset { \overline { { C } } }$ . Hence 

$$
z = \frac {1}{t} w _ {t} + \left(1 - \frac {1}{t}\right) z _ {0},
$$

and so $z \in { \mathrm { r i } } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ , again by Proposition 4.7. 

Step 2: If (i) holds, then by Step 1, 

$$
\mathrm{ri} _ {\mathrm{aff}} \left(C _ {1}\right) = \mathrm{ri} _ {\mathrm{aff}} \left(\overline {{C _ {1}}}\right) = \mathrm{ri} _ {\mathrm{aff}} \left(\overline {{C _ {2}}}\right) = \mathrm{ri} _ {\mathrm{aff}} \left(C _ {2}\right),
$$

that is, (ii) is true. 

Similarly, if (ii) holds, then again by Step 1, 

$$
\overline {{C _ {1}}} = \overline {{\mathrm{ri} _ {\mathrm{aff}} (C _ {1})}} = \overline {{\mathrm{ri} _ {\mathrm{aff}} (C _ {2})}} = \overline {{C _ {2}}},
$$

which is (i). 

If (iii) holds, then by Step 1, 

$$
\overline {{\mathrm{ri} _ {\mathrm{aff}} (C _ {1})}} \subset \overline {{C _ {2}}} \subset \overline {{C _ {1}}} = \overline {{\mathrm{ri} _ {\mathrm{aff}} (C _ {1})}},
$$

and (i) is satisfied. 

Finally, if (i) holds, then so does (ii), and we deduce that 

$$
\mathrm{ri} _ {\mathrm{aff}} \left(C _ {1}\right) = \mathrm{ri} _ {\mathrm{aff}} \left(C _ {2}\right) \subset C _ {2} \subset \overline {{C _ {2}}} = \overline {{C _ {1}}},
$$

which is (iii). 

Exercise 4.10. Let $C _ { 1 } , C _ { 2 }$ be two nonempty convex sets of $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and let $t \in \mathbb { R }$ Prove that 

(i) r $\cdot \mathrm { i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( t C _ { 1 } \right) = t \mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C _ { 1 } \right)$ ;

In the remainder of this section we discuss some properties of convex cones that will be used to prove Lemma 7.7 in Chapter 7. 

Definition 4.11. A subset K of $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is a convex cone if it is closed under addition and positive scalar multiplication. The polar $K ^ { * }$ of a convex cone is the set 

$$
K ^ {*} := \left\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \cdot \xi \leq 0 f o r a l l \xi \in K \right\}.
$$

Note that in general there is no guarantee that a convex cone contains the origin. 

Remark 4.12. Given a set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , the smallest convex cone K containing E is given by 

$$
K ^ {\prime} := \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} t _ {i} z _ {i}: n \in \mathbb {N}, t _ {i} > 0, z _ {i} \in E, i = 1, \dots , n \right\}.
$$

Indeed, since K is closed under addition and positive scalar multiplication, it must contain $K ^ { \prime }$ . On the other hand, it follows from its definition that $K ^ { \prime }$ is a convex cone containing $E .$ 

Proposition 4.13. If $K \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is a convex cone, then 

$$
\left(K ^ {*}\right) ^ {*} = \overline {{{K}}}.
$$

Proof. If $\xi \in K ^ { * }$ then 

$$
K \subset \left\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \cdot \xi \leq 0 \right\},
$$

and thus 

$$
K \subset \bigcap_ {\xi \in K ^ {*}} \left\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \cdot \xi \leq 0 \right\} = (K ^ {*}) ^ {*}.
$$

Since the polar set is always closed, we conclude that 

$$
\overline {{K}} \subset (K ^ {*}) ^ {*}.
$$

Conversely, suppose that $z _ { 0 } \not \in { \overline { { K } } }$ . By the second geometric form of the Hahn– Banach theorem there exist $z ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m } , \alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ , and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that 

$$
z ^ {\prime} \cdot z \leq \alpha - \varepsilon \quad \text { for   all } z \in \overline {{K}} \text { and } z ^ {\prime} \cdot z _ {0} \geq \alpha + \varepsilon .
$$

Since K is a cone, ${ \\\mathrm { i f ~ } } z \in K$ and $t > 0$ , then $t z \in K$ , and so 

$$
z ^ {\prime} \cdot t z \leq \alpha - \varepsilon .\tag{4.2}
$$

Hence 

$$
z ^ {\prime} \cdot z \leq \frac {\alpha - \varepsilon}{t},
$$

and letting $t \to \infty$ we conclude that $z ^ { \prime } \cdot z \leq 0$ for all $z \in K$ , and so $z ^ { \prime } \in K ^ { * }$ Also, letting $t \to 0 ^ { + }$ in (4.2), it follows that $\alpha \geq \varepsilon$ , and therefore $z ^ { \prime } \cdot z _ { 0 } \geq$ $2 \varepsilon > 0$ . We conclude that $z _ { 0 } \notin \left( K ^ { * } \right) ^ { * }$ 

Definition 4.14. Given a set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , the convex cone generated by E is the convex cone obtained by adjoining the origin to the smallest convex cone containing E. 

Theorem 4.15. Let $C \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be a nonempty closed convex set not containing the origin, and let K be the convex cone generated by C. Then 

$$
\overline {{K}} = \left\{t z: t > 0,   z \in C \right\} \cup \left\{z: t z + C \subset C \text { for   all } t \geq 0 \right\}.
$$

Proof. Step 1: We claim that 

$$
K = \{t z: t > 0, z \in C \} \cup \{0 \}.
$$

By Remark 4.12, 

$$
K = \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} t _ {i} z _ {i}: n \in \mathbb {N}, t _ {i} \geq 0, z _ {i} \in C, i = 1, \dots , n \right\}.
$$

$\mathrm { I f ~ } z \in K \ \backslash$ {0} then 

$$
z = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} t _ {i} z _ {i}
$$

with $t _ { i } > 0 , z _ { i } \in C , i = 1 , . . . , n$ , for some $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Setting $\textstyle t : = \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { n } t _ { k }$ , then $t > 0$ , and with 

$$
\theta_ {i} := \frac {t _ {i}}{t} \quad i = 1, \dots , n, \quad z _ {0} := \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \theta_ {i} z _ {i},
$$

it follows that $z _ { 0 } \in C$ and $z = t z _ { 0 }$ . This proves the claim. 

Step 2: We show first that 

$$
\overline {{{K}}} \supset \left\{z: t z + C \subset C \text {   for   all   } t \geq 0 \right\}.\tag{4.3}
$$

Indeed, fix $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for which $t z + C \subset C$ for all $t \geq 0$ and let $w \in C$ . Then $n z + w \in C$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , and so 

$$
z + \frac {1}{n} w \in K
$$

for all n. By letting $n \to \infty$ we obtain that z must belong to $\overline { { K } }$ . Thus (4.3) holds, and so, also by Step 1, we have 

$$
\overline {{K}} \supset \{t z: t > 0,   z \in C \} \cup \{z: t z + C \subset C \text {   for   all   } t \geq 0 \} =: D.\tag{4.4}
$$

To prove the converse inclusion, consider $z \in { \overline { { K } } }$ . If z = 0 then $t z + C \subset C$ for all $t \geq 0$ 

$\mathrm { I f } ~ z \neq 0$ , then by Step 1 there exist sequences $\{ t _ { n } \} \subset ( 0 , \infty )$ and $\{ z _ { n } \} \subset C$ such that $t _ { n } z _ { n }  z . \mathrm { I f } \{ t _ { n } \}$ were unbounded, then (up to the extraction of a subsequence) $z _ { n }  0$ , and since C is closed we would get $0 \in C$ , which is in contradiction with the hypotheses. Therefore, up to a subsequence, $t _ { n }  t _ { 0 }$ for some $t _ { 0 } \geq 0$ . Consider first the case $t _ { 0 } > 0$ . Since $\textstyle z _ { n } \to { \frac { z } { t _ { 0 } } }$ we deduce that $\frac { z } { t _ { 0 } } \in C$ , and $\mathrm { s o } ~ z = t _ { 0 } \frac { z } { t _ { 0 } }$ belongs to the set D defined in $( 4 . \ddot { 4 } )$ . If $t _ { 0 } = 0$ , then we claim that given $t > 0$ and $w \in C$ we have $t z + w \in C$ . Indeed, 

$$
t z + w = \lim _ {n \to \infty} t t _ {n} z _ {n} + w = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \left(t t _ {n} z _ {n} + (1 - t t _ {n}) w\right),
$$

which, together with the fact that $t t _ { n } z _ { n } + \left( 1 - t t _ { n } \right) w \in C$ for all n so large that $t t _ { n } \in [ 0 , 1 )$ , and because C is closed, entails $t z + w \in C$ 

## 4.2 Separating Theorems

In this section we prove some separation theorems for convex sets in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ Their counterparts in the infinite-dimensional setting are the Hahn–Banach theorems, which are stated in the appendix. 

Theorem 4.16. Let C, $K \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be nonempty disjoint convex sets, with C closed and K compact. Then there exist a vector $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \backslash \{ 0 \}$ and two numbers $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that 

b · z ≤ α − ε for all z ∈ C and $b \cdot z \geq \alpha + \varepsilon$ for all $z \in K$ 

Proof. The distance function 

$$
z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \mapsto \operatorname{dist} (z, C)
$$

is a continuous function (it is actually Lipschitz), and so by the Weierstrass theorem it admits a minimum on $K$ at some point $z _ { 0 } \in K$ . Moreover, since C is closed, there exists a point $w _ { 0 } \in C$ such that 

$$
\left| z _ {0} - w _ {0} \right| = \operatorname{dist} \left(z _ {0}, C\right).
$$

Define $b = z _ { 0 } - w _ { 0 }$ and observe that $b \neq 0$ , since C and K are disjoint sets. Then 

$$
0 <   | b | ^ {2} = b \cdot (z _ {0} - w _ {0}),
$$

so that $b \cdot w _ { 0 } < b \cdot z _ { 0 }$ . We claim that 

b · w ≤ b · w for all w ∈ C and $b \cdot z _ { 0 } \leq b \cdot z$ for all $z \in K$ 

To see this, fix $w _ { 1 } \in C$ . Since $w _ { 0 }$ minimizes the distance (and so also the square of the distance) to $z _ { \mathrm { 0 } }$ over C, we have that 

$$
(z _ {0} - w) \cdot (z _ {0} - w) \geq (z _ {0} - w _ {0}) \cdot (z _ {0} - w _ {0})
$$

for all $w \in C$ . In particular, taking $w : = w _ { 0 } + \theta \left( w _ { 1 } - w _ { 0 } \right) \in C , 0 < \theta \le 1$ , in the previous inequality yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & 0 \geq (z _ {0} - w _ {0}) \cdot (z _ {0} - w _ {0}) - (z _ {0} - w) \cdot (z _ {0} - w) \\ & \quad = 2 \theta (z _ {0} - w _ {0}) \cdot (w _ {1} - w _ {0}) - \theta^ {2} (w _ {1} - w _ {0}) \cdot (w _ {1} - w _ {0}). \end{array}
$$

Dividing by $\theta > 0$ and letting $\theta \to 0 ^ { + }$ gives 

$$
0 \geq 2 (z _ {0} - w _ {0}) \cdot (w _ {1} - w _ {0}) = 2 b \cdot (w _ {1} - w _ {0}),
$$

which shows that $b \cdot w _ { 1 } \leq b \cdot w _ { 0 }$ 

A similar argument, which is left as an exercise, gives the analogous inequality for K and completes the proof. 

Remark 4.17. The previous proof continues to hold for Hilbert spaces. 

Exercise 4.18. Let $z _ { 1 } , \ldots , z _ { k } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be linearly independent vectors and let $s _ { i } , s _ { i } ^ { ( n ) } \in \mathbb { R } , i = 1 , \dots , k , n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Prove that if

then $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } s _ { i } ^ { ( n ) } = s _ { i } } \end{array}$ for every $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ 

Theorem 4.19. Let $C _ { 1 } , C _ { 2 } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be nonempty convex sets. Then there exist a vector $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \setminus \{ 0 \}$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ such that

Proof. Step 1: Assume that $C _ { 1 } , C _ { 2 } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ are nonempty convex sets with $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C _ { 1 } \right) \cap \mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C _ { 2 } \right) = \emptyset$ . Define

and so by hypothesis 0 $\not \in \mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } ( C )$ . To complete the proof in this case it sufices to prove that there exists $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \setminus \{ 0 \}$ such that $b \cdot z \geq 0$ for all $z \in C$ with strict inequality for at least one element of $C .$ . There are two cases. If $0 \not \in { \overline { { C } } }$ then it sufices to apply Theorem 4.16 to the closed set $\overline { { C } }$ and the compact set {0}. Thus assume that $0 \in \overline { { C } }$ . Define the set

Then $E$ is convex, $\operatorname { r i } _ { \operatorname { a f f } } \left( C \right) \subset E \subset \operatorname { a f f } \left( E \right)$ , and $0 ~ \notin ~ E$ . Since $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ is nonempty by Proposition 4.7 and R<sup>N</sup> is finite-dimensional, there is a finite maximal (with respect to inclusion) set of linearly independent vectors $z _ { 1 } , \dots , z _ { k } \in \operatorname { r i _ { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ . Again by Proposition 4.7 we have that $\operatorname { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ is convex, and so the vector

z _ {0} := \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \frac {1}{k} z _ {i}

Indeed, assume by contradiction that $- z \in { \overline { { E } } }$ and find a sequence $\{ w _ { n } \} \subset E$ converging to $- z _ { 0 }$ . Then by definition of E we may write each $w _ { n }$ as $w _ { n } ~ = ~ t _ { n } \xi _ { n } .$ , where $t _ { n } ~ > ~ 0$ and $\xi _ { n } \in \mathrm { r i _ { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ . Since $z _ { 1 } , \ldots , z _ { k }$ form a maximal set of linearly independent vectors in $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( C \right)$ , each $\xi _ { n }$ can be written as their linear combination (and so can $w _ { n } = t _ { n } \xi _ { n } )$ . Thus we may write

w _ {n} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} s _ {i} ^ {(n)} z _ {i}
$$

for some $s _ { i } ^ { ( n ) } \in \mathbb { R } , i = 1 , \dots , k$ . Hence

\lim _ {n \to \infty} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} s _ {i} ^ {(n)} z _ {i} = \lim _ {n \to \infty} w _ {n} = - z _ {0} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \left(- \frac {1}{k}\right) z _ {i}.

By Exercise 4.18 this implies that lim $\begin{array} { r } { \mathfrak { l } _ { n  \infty } s _ { i } ^ { ( n ) } = - \frac { 1 } { k } } \end{array}$ for every $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ Fix $n \in \mathbb { N }$ so large that $s _ { i } ^ { ( n ) } < 0$ for every $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ and set

Step 2: To prove the converse implication assume that there exist a vector $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \setminus \{ 0 \}$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ such that

By Exercise 4.10,

\mathrm{ri} _ {\text {aff}} (C) = \mathrm{ri} _ {\text {aff}} (C _ {1}) - \mathrm{ri} _ {\text {aff}} (C _ {2}).

b · z = α for all $z \in C _ { 1 }$ and $b \cdot z \geq \alpha$ for all $z \in C _ { 2 }$

## 4.3 Convex Functions

We now turn to the study of convex functions. 

Definition 4.21. A function $f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is said to be 

(i) convex if 

$$
f \left(\theta v _ {1} + (1 - \theta) v _ {2}\right) \leq \theta f \left(v _ {1}\right) + (1 - \theta) f \left(v _ {2}\right)\tag{4.6}
$$

for all $v _ { 1 } , \ v _ { 2 } \ \in \ V$ and $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ for which the right-hand side is welldefined; 

(ii) strictly convex if 

$$
f \left(\theta v _ {1} + (1 - \theta) v _ {2}\right) <   \theta f \left(v _ {1}\right) + (1 - \theta) f \left(v _ {2}\right)
$$

for all $v _ { 1 } , v _ { 2 } \in V , v _ { 1 } \neq v _ { 2 }$ , and $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ for which the right-hand side is well-defined; 

(iii) proper if it is convex, does not take the value $- \infty$ , and is not identically ∞; 

(iv) concave (respectively strictly concave) $i f - f$ is convex (respectively strictly convex). 

In (i) and (ii) the right-hand side is not defined only when $f \left( v _ { 1 } \right) = \pm \infty$ and $f \left( v _ { 2 } \right) = \mp \infty$ 

If E is a subset of the vector space V, then a function $f : E \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is said to be convex if the extension 

$$
\bar {f} (v) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} f (v) & \text {if} v \in E, \\ \infty & \text {if} v \notin E, \end{array} \right.
$$

is a convex function in V. Analogous definitions apply to the concept of strict convexity, concavity, and strict concavity. 

Proposition 4.22. Let V be a vector space. A function $f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is convex if and only if epi f is a convex set. 

Proof. Assume that f is convex and let $( v _ { 1 } , s ) , ( v _ { 2 } , t ) \in \mathrm { e p i } f$ and $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ We claim that 

$$
\theta \left(v _ {1}, s\right) + (1 - \theta) \left(v _ {2}, t\right) \in \operatorname{epi} f.
$$

Indeed, since $s \geq f \left( v _ { 1 } \right) , t \geq f \left( z \right)$ , it follows that 

$$
\theta s + (1 - \theta) t \geq \theta f (v _ {1}) + (1 - \theta) f (v _ {2}) \geq f (\theta v _ {1} + (1 - \theta) v _ {2}),
$$

where we have used the convexity of $f .$ . Hence the claim is proved. 

Conversely, let epi f be a convex set, let $v _ { 1 } , v _ { 2 } \in V$ , and let $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ If $f \left( v _ { 1 } \right) = \pm \infty$ and $f \left( v _ { 2 } \right) = \mp \infty$ , then the right-hand side of (4.6) is not well-defined. 

If $f \left( v _ { 1 } \right) = \infty$ and $f \left( v _ { 2 } \right) > - \infty$ or $f \left( v _ { 1 } \right) > - \infty$ and $f \left( v _ { 2 } \right) = \infty$ , then (4.6) holds. Thus assume that $f \left( v _ { 1 } \right) , f \left( v _ { 2 } \right) < \infty$ and let $s \geq f ( v _ { 1 } ) , t \geq$ $f \left( v _ { 2 } \right)$ . Since $( v _ { 1 } , s ) , ( v _ { 2 } , t ) \in \mathrm { e p i } f$ it follows from the convexity of epi f that $\theta \left( v _ { 1 } , s \right) + \left( 1 - \theta \right) \left( v _ { 2 } , t \right) \in \mathrm { e p i } f$ , that is, 

$$
f \left(\theta v _ {1} + (1 - \theta) v _ {2}\right) \leq \theta s + (1 - \theta) t.
$$

The convexity of f follows by letting $s \searrow f ( v _ { 1 } )$ and $t \setminus f \left( v _ { 2 } \right)$ 

Let V be a vector space. The efective domain of a function $f : V $ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ is the set 

$$
\operatorname{dom} _ {e} f := \left\{v \in V: f (v) <   \infty \right\}.
$$

We observe that if f is convex, then the efective domain of f is a convex set. 

Remark $4 . 2 3 .$ Note that if V is a topological vector space and if $f : V $ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ is a convex function, finite at some point in the interior of $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f .$ then f is proper. Indeed, suppose that $f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ for some $v _ { 0 }$ in the interior of $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ , and that $f \left( v \right) = - \infty$ for some $v \in V$ . Let U be an open neighborhood of $v _ { 0 }$ with $U \subset \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ and set $W : = - v _ { 0 } + U$ . Since $W$ is a neighborhood of zero, it is absorbing, and so there exists $r > 0$ such that $r \left( v _ { 0 } - v \right) \in W , { \mathrm { i . e . } }$ $v _ { 0 } + r \left( v _ { 0 } - v \right) \in U$ . Set $\textstyle \theta : = { \frac { r } { 1 + r } }$ . Note that 

$$
v _ {0} = \theta v + (1 - \theta) (v _ {0} + r (v _ {0} - v)),
$$

and due to the convexity of f we conclude that $f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) = - \infty$ , which is a contradiction. 

## Exercise 4.24. Prove that:

(i) The function $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ 0 , \infty )$ defined by $f \left( z \right) : = | z | ^ { p } , p > 0$ , is convex if and only if $p \geq 1$ , and is strictly convex if and only if $p > 1$ . In particular, if $m = 1 , a , b \geq 0$ , and $p \geq 1$ , then by the convexity of $f$ , 

$$

\log (a b) = \frac {1}{p} \log a ^ {p} + \frac {1}{q} \log b ^ {q} \leq \log \left(\frac {1}{p} a ^ {p} + \frac {1}{q} b ^ {q}\right),

(v) If V is a vector space, the indicator function of a set $E \subset V$ defined by

is a convex function if and only if the set E is convex. 

Note that if f is convex and $c > 0$ , then $c f$ is still convex, the sum of two convex functions $f$ and g is convex (we set $\left( f + g \right) \left( v \right) : = + \infty$ whenever $f \left( v \right) = \pm \infty$ and $g \left( v \right) = \mp \infty )$ , and the pointwise supremum of an arbitrary family of convex functions is again a convex function. If f is convex and if $g : [ - \infty , \infty ]  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is convex and nondecreasing, then $g \circ f$ is convex. 

Proposition 4.25. Let V be a topological vector space and let $f : V $ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ be convex. Then lsc f is convex, and 

$$
\operatorname{epi} \left(\operatorname{lsc} f\right) = \overline {{\operatorname{epi} f}}.
$$

Proof. Since $f$ is convex, then epi f is convex by Proposition 4.22, and by Proposition 3.10 we have 

$$
\operatorname{epi} \left(\operatorname{lsc} f\right) = \overline {{\operatorname{epi} f}};
$$

hence epi $( \ker f )$ is convex because it is the closure of a convex set, i.e., lsc f is convex. 

Proposition 4.26. Let V be a locally convex topological vector space and let $f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a lower semicontinuous convex function. Then 

(i) f is weakly lower semicontinuous; 

(ii) if f assumes the value −∞ at some point, then $f : V  \{ - \infty , \infty \}$ 

Proof. (i) By Propositions 3.4 and 4.22 the set epi f is closed and convex, and so by Theorem $\mathrm { A . 4 7 }$ it is weakly closed. Using once more Proposition 3.4 but now with the weak topology, we conclude that f is weakly lower semicontinuous.

$$
\langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} + \alpha_ {0} t \geq \alpha + \varepsilon \text {   for   all   } (v, t) \in \operatorname{epi} f \text {   and   } \langle v ^ {\prime}, v _ {0} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} + \alpha_ {0} t _ {0} \leq \alpha - \varepsilon .
$$

In particular, since $( v _ { 0 } , f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) ) \in \mathrm { e p i } f$ , we have that 

$$
\langle v ^ {\prime}, v _ {0} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} + \alpha_ {0} f (v _ {0}) \geq \alpha + \varepsilon > \alpha - \varepsilon \geq \langle v ^ {\prime}, v _ {0} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} + \alpha_ {0} t _ {0},
$$

\alpha_ {0} \left(f \left(v _ {0}\right) - t _ {0}\right) > 0.
$$

Since $t _ { 0 } < f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ , we conclude that $\alpha _ { 0 } > 0$ , and so

t \geq \frac {\alpha + \varepsilon}{\alpha_ {0}} - \frac {1}{\alpha_ {0}} \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \text {   for   all   } (v, t) \in \operatorname{epi} f.

In turn, 

$$
f (v) \geq \frac {\alpha + \varepsilon}{\alpha_ {0}} - \frac {1}{\alpha_ {0}} \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \text {   for   all   } v \in \operatorname{dom} _ {e} f,
$$

which contradicts the fact that f assumes the value $- \infty$ at some point. 

Definition 4.27. Let $V _ { 1 } , \ldots , V _ { m }$ be vector spaces. A function 

$$
f: V _ {1} \times \ldots \times V _ {m} \to [ - \infty , \infty ]
$$

is separately convex if it is convex in each variable, i.e., if for every $i \ =$ $1 , \ldots , m$ , and for all $v _ { j } \in V _ { j } , j = 1 , \dotsc , m , j \neq i$ , the function 

$$
f \left(v _ {1}, \dots , v _ {i - 1}, \cdot , v _ {i + 1}, \dots , v _ {m}\right): V _ {i} \rightarrow [ - \infty , \infty ]
$$

is convex. 

If $E \subset V _ { 1 } \times . . . \times V _ { m }$ , we say that a function $f : E \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is separately convex if the function obtained by extending f as ∞ outside E is separately convex. 

Note that a convex function defined on a Cartesian product of vector spaces is separately convex but the converse is not true in general. 

Example 4.28. (i) Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } \to \mathbb { R }$ be defined as 

$$
f (z) = f (z _ {1}, z _ {2}) := z _ {1} z _ {2}.
$$

Then f is convex (actually linear) in each variable but not convex. (ii) Let $E : = \left\{ ( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } : z _ { 1 } z _ { 2 } \geq 0 \right\}$ and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } \to \mathbb { R }$ be defined as 

$$
f \left(z _ {1}, z _ {2}\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0 \text { if } (z _ {1}, z _ {2}) \in E, \\ \infty \text { otherwise }. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then the restriction of f to each line through the origin is convex, but f is not convex. 

## 4.4 Lipschitz Continuity in Normed Spaces

In order to study the regularity of convex functions we need to introduce the notion of Lipschitz and H¨older continuity. 

Definition 4.29. Let V be a normed space and let $E \subset V$ . A function f : $E \to \mathbb { R }$ is said to be 

(i) Lipschitz continuous if 

$$
\operatorname{Lip} (f; E) := \sup \left\{\frac {| f (v) - f (w) |}{\| v - w \|}: v, w \in E, v \neq w \right\} <   \infty ;
$$

(ii) locally Lipschitz continuous $i f$ for every compact set $K \subset E$ 

$$
\sup \left\{\frac {| f (v) - f (w) |}{\| v - w \|}: v, w \in K, v \neq w \right\} <   \infty ;
$$

(iii) H¨older continuous with exponent $0 < \alpha < 1$ if 

$$
\left| f \right| _ {C ^ {0, \alpha} (E)} := \sup \left\{\frac {\left| f (v) - f (w) \right|}{\left\| v - w \right\| ^ {\alpha}}: v, w \in E, v \neq w \right\} <   \infty .
$$

Exercise 4.30. The Weierstrass function 

$$
f (s) := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}} \sin 2 ^ {n} s, \quad s \in \mathbb {R},
$$

satisfies the estimate 

$$
| f (s) - f (t) | \leq C | s - t | \log \frac {1}{| s - t |}
$$

for all $s , t \in \mathbb { R }$ , with $0 < | s - t | < 1$ , and hence provides an example of a function that is H¨older continuous of any order $\alpha < 1$ . Prove that f is not Lipschitz continuous, and actually it is nowhere diferentiable (see [Ha16]). 

Given a subset E of a normed space V and a function $f : E \to \mathbb { R }$ , we define its modulus of continuity by 

$$
\omega (s) := \sup \left\{\left| f (v) - f (w) \right|: v, w \in E, \| v - w \| <   s \right\}, \quad s > 0.
$$

Note that $f$ is uniformly continuous if and only if $\omega ( s )  0$ as $s \to 0 ^ { + }$ . The concave modulus of continuity $\varpi : [ 0 , \infty ]  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is defined as the smallest concave function above $\omega .$ 

Remark 4.31. If $E = V$ and $f$ is uniformly continuous, then it is always possible to replace $\omega$ with $\varpi$ . Indeed, we claim that 

$$
\omega (s) \leq \varpi (s) \leq 2 \omega (s)\tag{4.7}
$$

for all $s \geq 0$ . To see this, note that if $s _ { 0 } ~ > ~ 0$ , then for all $n \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ and $n s _ { 0 } \leq s \leq ( n + 1 ) s _ { 0 }$ we have 

$$
\omega (s) \leq \omega ((n + 1) s _ {0}) \leq (n + 1) \omega (s _ {0}) \leq \omega (s _ {0}) + s \frac {\omega (s _ {0})}{s _ {0}},
$$

where we have used the fact that $\omega$ is subadditive (this is a consequence of the definition of $\omega$ and the fact that $E = V )$ . Since the function 

$$
s \mapsto \omega (s _ {0}) + s \frac {\omega (s _ {0})}{s _ {0}}
$$

is concave and above $\omega ,$ , it follows from the definition of $\varpi$ that 

$$
\varpi (s) \leq \omega (s _ {0}) + s \frac {\omega (s _ {0})}{s _ {0}}
$$

for all $s \geq 0$ , and taking $s = s _ { 0 }$ we deduce (4.7) for all $s > 0$ . For $s = 0$ it sufices to observe that ω is continuous and $\omega \left( 0 \right) = 0$ , and so letting $s \to 0 ^ { + }$ in (4.7) we obtain that $\varpi ( 0 ) = 0$ 

The next result shows that any uniformly continuous function may be extended to all of V with the same concave modulus of continuity. 

Theorem 4.32. Let E be a subset of a normed space V and let $f : E \to \mathbb { R }$ be a uniformly continuous function such that 

$$
\omega (s) \leq a + b s f o r a l l s \geq 0,\tag{4.8}
$$

for some a, $b \geq 0$ . Then there exists a uniformly continuous function $g : V $ R with the same concave modulus of continuity  and such that 

$$
g (v) = f (v) \quad \text {   for   all   } v \in E,\tag{4.9}
$$

and 

$$
\inf _ {V} g = \inf _ {E} f, \sup _ {V} g = \sup _ {E} f.\tag{4.10}
$$

Proof. Step 1: We claim that $\varpi$ is nondecreasing, $\varpi ( 0 ) = 0$ , and $\varpi$ is subadditive, that is, 

$$
\varpi \left(s _ {1} + s _ {2}\right) \leq \varpi \left(s _ {1}\right) + \varpi \left(s _ {2}\right)\tag{4.11}
$$

for all $s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 } \geq 0$ . Since $\varpi$ is concave, if $\varpi$ were decreasing in some interval, then it would be unbounded from below, and this would contradict the fact that it is nonnegative. 

To prove that $\varpi ( 0 ) = 0 .$ , note first that if $a = 0$ , then this follows from the fact that, by $( 4 . 8 ) , \varpi \left( s \right) \le$ bs for all $s \geq 0$ . If $a > 0$ , then fix $0 < \varepsilon < a$ and since $\omega ( s )  0$ as $s \to 0 ^ { + }$ , there exists $\delta _ { \varepsilon } > 0$ such that 

$$
\omega (s) \leq \varepsilon \quad \text { for   all } 0 \leq s \leq \delta_ {\varepsilon}.
$$

The function $\phi : [ 0 , \infty ]  \mathbb { R }$ , defined by 

$$
\phi \left(s\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} a + b s & \text {if} s > \delta_ {\varepsilon}, \\ \varepsilon + \frac {a + b \delta_ {\varepsilon} - \varepsilon}{\delta_ {\varepsilon}} s & \text {if} 0 \leq s \leq \delta_ {\varepsilon}, \end{array} \right.
$$

is concave and above $\omega .$ . Therefore $\varpi \left( 0 \right) \leq \phi \left( 0 \right) = \varepsilon$ , and given the arbitrariness of ε we conclude that $\varpi ( 0 ) = 0$ 

It remains to show that $\varpi$ is subadditive. Let $s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 } > 0$ . Then by concavity, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \varpi (s _ {1}) \geq \frac {s _ {1}}{s _ {1} + s _ {2}} \varpi (s _ {1} + s _ {2}) + \frac {s _ {2}}{s _ {1} + s _ {2}} \varpi (0) = \frac {s _ {1}}{s _ {1} + s _ {2}} \varpi (s _ {1} + s _ {2}), \\ \varpi (s _ {2}) \geq \frac {s _ {2}}{s _ {1} + s _ {2}} \varpi (s _ {1} + s _ {2}) + \frac {s _ {1}}{s _ {1} + s _ {2}} \varpi (0) = \frac {s _ {2}}{s _ {1} + s _ {2}} \varpi (s _ {1} + s _ {2}), \end{array}
$$

and summing the two inequalities, we obtain (4.11). 

Step 2: Since $\varpi$ is nondecreasing and subadditive, for all $v _ { 1 } , v _ { 2 } , w \in V$ , 

$$
\varpi \left(| v _ {2} - w |\right) \leq \varpi \left(| v _ {1} - w | + | v _ {1} - v _ {2} |\right) \leq \varpi \left(| v _ {1} - w |\right) + \varpi \left(| v _ {1} - v _ {2} |\right).\tag{4.12}
$$

Moreover, from the definition of $\omega$ and $\varpi$ it follows that 

$$
\varpi \left(\left| w _ {1} - w _ {2} \right|\right) \geq \left| f \left(w _ {1}\right) - f \left(w _ {2}\right) \right| \text {   for   all   } w _ {1}, w _ {2} \in E.\tag{4.13}
$$

Define 

$$
h (v) := \inf \left\{f (w) + \varpi \left(| v - w |\right): w \in E \right\}, \quad v \in V.\tag{4.14}
$$

We first claim that $h ( v )$ is finite for every $v \in V$ . Fix $w _ { 0 } \in E$ . By (4.12) and (4.13), if $w \in E$ then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f (w) + \varpi \left(| v - w |\right) - f (w _ {0}) \geq \varpi \left(| v - w |\right) - \varpi \left(| w - w _ {0} |\right) \\ \geq - \varpi \left(| v - w _ {0} |\right), \end{array}
$$

and so 

$$
\begin{array}{c} h (v) = \inf \left\{f (w) + \varpi \left(| v - w |\right): w \in E \right\} \\ \geq f (w _ {0}) - \varpi \left(| v - w _ {0} |\right) > - \infty . \end{array}
$$

Note that if $v \in E$ , then we can choose $w _ { 0 } : = v$ in the previous inequality to obtain $h ( v ) \geq f ( v )$ , since $\varpi ( 0 ) = 0$ . On the other hand, taking $w = v$ in (4.14) yields $h ( v ) \leq f \left( v \right)$ , and so (4.9) holds for $h$ (in place of $g )$ . In particular, 

$$
\inf _ {V} h \leq \inf _ {E} f,
$$

and since $\varpi \ge 0$ , we have that 

$$
h \geq \inf _ {E} f,
$$

and thus we conclude that 

$$
\inf _ {V} h = \inf _ {E} f.
$$

Next we claim that 

$$
\left| h (v _ {1}) - h (v _ {2}) \right| \leq \varpi \left(\left| v _ {1} - v _ {2} \right|\right)\tag{4.15}
$$

for all $v _ { 1 } , v _ { 2 } \in V$ . Indeed, let $v _ { 1 } , v _ { 2 } \in V , \varepsilon > 0$ . By (4.14) there exists $w _ { 1 } \in E$ such that 

$$
h (v _ {1}) \geq f (w _ {1}) + \varpi \left(| v _ {1} - w _ {1} |\right) - \varepsilon .
$$

Since $h \left( v _ { 2 } \right) \leq f ( w _ { 1 } ) + \varpi \left( | v _ { 2 } - w _ { 1 } | \right)$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} h (v _ {1}) - h \left(v _ {2}\right) \geq \varpi \left(| v _ {1} - w _ {1} |\right) - \varpi \left(| v _ {2} - w _ {1} |\right) - \varepsilon \\ \geq - \varpi \left(| v _ {1} - v _ {2} |\right) - \varepsilon \end{array}
$$

by (4.12). Given the arbitrariness of $\varepsilon > 0$ and interchanging the roles of $v _ { 1 }$ and $v _ { 2 }$ , we have proved the claim. 

Finally, define 

$$
g (v) := \inf \left\{h (v), \sup _ {E} f \right\}.
$$

Then (4.9) and (4.10) hold for $g .$ . We now show that (4.15) continues to hold for $g .$ Indeed, this is immediate if either $g ( v _ { i } ) = h ( v _ { i } )$ for $i = 1 , 2$ , or if $g ( v _ { i } ) =$ $\operatorname { s u p } _ { E } f$ for $i = 1$ , 2. Thus the only remaining case is $g ( v _ { 1 } ) = h \left( v _ { 1 } \right) < \operatorname* { s u p } _ { E } f$ and $g ( v _ { 2 } ) = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { E } f \leq h \left( v _ { 2 } \right)$ . From (4.15) we obtain 

$$
0 \leq g (v _ {2}) - g (v _ {1}) = \sup _ {E} f - h (v _ {1}) \leq h (v _ {2}) - h (v _ {1}) \leq \varpi (| v _ {1} - v _ {2} |),
$$

which establishes that the concave modulus of continuity of $^ { g , }$ denoted by $\varpi _ { g } .$ , is below $\varpi .$ . Conversely, since $g$ extends $f ,$ it follows that the modulus of continuity of $f$ is less than or equal to that of $^ { g , }$ , and so $\varpi _ { g } = \varpi$ 

Remark 4.33. (i) The previous result may be extended to metric spaces with the obvious adaptations. 

(ii) In the special case that $\omega ( s ) \leq L s ^ { \alpha } , 0 < \alpha \leq 1 , L > 0$ , we have that $\varpi \left( s \right) \ : \leq \ : L s ^ { \alpha }$ . Hence if $0 \textless \alpha \textless 1$ , then we can extend f to a H¨older continuous function g on $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ such that

## 4.5 Regularity of Convex Functions

In this section we address continuity and diferentiability properties of convex functions. 

In the first result we prove that real-valued separately convex functions on finite-dimensional spaces are locally Lipschitz. This is hinged on the following characterization of convex functions on the real line. 

Proposition 4.34. Let $J \subset \mathbb { R }$ be an interval and let $g : J  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ . If g is convex, then for every $t _ { 0 } \in J$ such that $g \left( t _ { 0 } \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ , the diference quotient 

$$
t \mapsto \frac {g (t) - g (t _ {0})}{t - t _ {0}}
$$

is nondecreasing in $J \setminus \{ t _ { 0 } \}$ . The converse is true if $g : J  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ 

Exercise 4.35. Prove the previous proposition. 

If E is a subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and $f : E \to \mathbb { R }$ , then the oscillation of $f$ on E is defined by 

$$
\operatorname{osc} (f; E) := \sup \left\{\left| f \left(z _ {1}\right) - f \left(z _ {2}\right) \right|: z _ {1}, z _ {2} \in E \right\}.
$$

The proof of the next theorem is particularly simple for convex functions (see Remark 4.37 below), but in view of applications to rank one convex functions in [FoLe10], we need a version for separately convex functions. 

Theorem 4.36. If $f : B ( z _ { 0 } , 2 r ) \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  \mathbb { R }$ is separately convex, then

\operatorname{Lip} \left(f; B \left(z _ {0}, r\right)\right) \leq \sqrt {m} \frac {\operatorname{osc} \left(f ; B \left(z _ {0} , 2 r\right)\right)}{r}.
$$

Proof. Step 1: Without loss of generality we may assume that $z _ { 0 } = 0 . { } ^ { 1 }$ Let $L : = \sec \left( f ; B \left( 0 , 2 r \right) \right) / r$ . Assume first that $w , \ z \ \in \ B \left( 0 , r \right)$ are such that $\left( z - w \right) / \left| z - w \right| = \pm e ^ { ( i ) }$ for some element $e ^ { ( i ) }$ of the canonical basis of $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ For simplicity we consider the case $\left( z - w \right) / \left| z - w \right| = e ^ { \left( i \right) }$ . Fix $0 < \varepsilon < r$ . Since $f$ is separately convex, then g is convex, and so by the previous proposition and the fact that $| \xi - w | \geq | z - w |$ we have

where we have used the fact that $| w - \xi | \geq r - \varepsilon$ . Letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ yields 

$$

Next we show that any $w = ( w _ { 1 } , \ldots , w _ { m } ) , z = ( z _ { 1 } , \ldots , z _ { m } ) \in B ( 0 , r )$ can be joined by a chain $\xi ^ { ( 0 ) } : = w , \xi ^ { ( 1 ) } , \ldots , \xi ^ { ( m ) } : = z$ of points in $\boldsymbol { B } \left( 0 , \boldsymbol { r } \right)$ such that $\xi ^ { ( i ) } - \dot { \xi } ^ { ( i - 1 ) } = \left( w _ { \sigma ( i ) } - z _ { \sigma ( i ) } \right) e ^ { ( \sigma ( i ) ) } , i = 1 , \dots , m$ , for a suitable bijection $\sigma : \{ 1 , \dots , m \}  \{ 1 , \dots , m \}$ 

$\begin{array} { r l r } { \mathrm { L e t } J _ { + } } & { : = } & { \{ i \in \{ 1 , \dots , m \} : | w _ { i } | \geq | z _ { i } | \} } \end{array}$ . Construct a bijection $\sigma$ of $\{ 1 , \ldots , m \}$ onto itself in such a way that $\sigma \left( i \right) \in J _ { + }$ if and only i $\mathrm { ~ f ~ } i \le \mathrm { c a r d } \left( J _ { + } \right)$ Define

Then $\xi ^ { ( i ) } - \xi ^ { ( i - 1 ) } = \left( w _ { \sigma ( i ) } - z _ { \sigma ( i ) } \right) e ^ { ( \sigma ( i ) ) }$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , m$ and

Since $\xi ^ { ( i ) } \in B \left( 0 , r \right)$ and $\xi ^ { ( i ) } - \xi ^ { ( i - 1 ) } = \left( w _ { \sigma ( i ) } - z _ { \sigma ( i ) } \right) e ^ { ( \sigma ( i ) ) }$ we can apply (4.16) to obtain

$$

Step 2: Here we prove that if $z _ { \mathrm { 0 } }$ belongs to the interior of $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ , then there exists a neighborhood of $z _ { 0 }$ on which f is bounded and thus its oscillation is finite. 

Without loss of generality we may assume that $z _ { 0 } = 0$ , and consider in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ the equivalent norm 

$$

$$

Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be such that $B _ { \infty } \left( 0 , 2 \varepsilon \right) \subset \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ and set 

$$
a := \max \left\{f (z): z _ {i} \in \{- \varepsilon , 0, \varepsilon \}, i = 1, \dots , m \right\}.

Next we show that

Remark 4.37. (i) It follows from the previous proof (see (4.18)) that if $f$ : $B _ { \infty } ( z _ { 0 } , 2 r ) \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  \mathbb { R }$ is separately convex with $f \left( z _ { 0 } \right) = 0$ , then

Corollary 4.38. Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a proper convex function. Then the restriction off to $\operatorname { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f \right)$ is locally Lipschitz. In particular, if $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ is afine, then the restriction of f to $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ is locally Lipschitz. 

Proof. If $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ consists of a point, then there is nothing to prove. If $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ has more than one point, by Remark 4.1, 

$$
\operatorname{aff} \left(\operatorname{dom} _ {e} f\right) = z _ {0} + W,
$$

where $z _ { 0 } ~ \in ~ \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ and $W$ is a subspace of $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ of dimension $1 \leq \ell \leq m$ By a change of coordinates, without loss of generality we may assume that af $( \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } \bar { f } ) = \mathbb { R } ^ { \ell } \times \{ 0 \}$ . Define 

$$

Then $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g \right)$ reduces simply to the interior of $\mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g$ . The result now follows from Theorem 4.36 applied to $g$ . 

Exercise 4.39. The previous corollary cannot be improved in general. Indeed, let $m = 2$ and consider the function
