The proof of the next result follows from Theorem 4.43 and adapting Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 4.36. We omit the details. 

Theorem 4.47. Let V be a normed space and let $f : V  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a convex function. Then there exists a nonempty open set over which f is bounded from above if and only if f is locally Lipschitz in the interior of $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ , which is nonempty. 

Next we study diferentiability properties of convex functions. We begin by introducing the notion of subdiferential. 

Definition 4.48. Let V be a locally convex topological vector space, let $f :$ $V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ , and let $v _ { 0 } \in V$ be such that $f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ . The function $f$ is said to be subdiferentiable at $v _ { 0 }$ if there exists $v ^ { \prime } \in V ^ { \prime }$ such that 

$$
f (v) \geq f (v _ {0}) + \langle v ^ {\prime}, v - v _ {0} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \quad \text { for   all } v \in V.
$$

The element $v ^ { \prime }$ is called a subgradient of f at $v _ { 0 }$ , and the set of all subgradients at $v _ { 0 }$ is called the subdiferential off at v and is denoted by $\partial f \left( \boldsymbol { v } _ { 0 } \right)$ . Precisely, 

$$
\partial f \left(v _ {0}\right) = \left\{v ^ {\prime} \in V: f (v) \geq f \left(v _ {0}\right) + \langle v ^ {\prime}, v - v _ {0} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \quad \text { for   all } v \in V \right\}
$$

$_ { I f f }$ is not subdiferentiable at $v _ { 0 }$ , then $\partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) : = \varnothing$ 

The one-sided directional derivative of f at $v _ { 0 }$ in the direction $v \in V$ is defined by 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) := \lim _ {t \rightarrow 0 ^ {+}} \frac {f \left(v _ {0} + t v\right) - f \left(v _ {0}\right)}{t}
$$

whenever the limit exists. 

Note that 

$$
f \left(v _ {0}\right) = \min _ {v \in V} f (v) \quad \text { if   and   only   if } 0 \in \partial f \left(v _ {0}\right).\tag{4.22}
$$

Remark $4 . 4 9 .$ If V is a locally convex topological vector space, $f : V $ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ is convex, and $v _ { 0 } \in V$ is such that $f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ , then for every $v \in V$ the one-sided directional derivatives $\frac { \partial ^ { + } f } { \partial v } \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ always exist in view of Proposi tion 4.34. It may be verified that 

$$
v \in V \mapsto \frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} (v _ {0})
$$

is positively homogeneous of degree one, convex, and so subadditive. Moreover, 

$$
- \frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial (- v)} (v _ {0}) \leq \frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} (v _ {0}).
$$

In addition, if f is subdiferentiable at $v _ { 0 }$ , then 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) \geq \sup _ {v ^ {\prime} \in \partial f (v _ {0})} \left\langle v ^ {\prime}, v \right\rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} > - \infty
$$

for all $v \in V$ . Indeed, let $v \in V$ and let $v ^ { \prime } \in \partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ . Then by definition of subdiferential for all $t > 0$ we have 

$$
\frac {f \left(v _ {0} + t v\right) - f \left(v _ {0}\right)}{t} \geq \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}.\tag{4.23}
$$

Dividing by t and letting $t \to 0 ^ { + }$ yields 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) \geq \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V},
$$

and given the arbitrariness of $v ^ { \prime } \in \partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ we get 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) \geq \sup _ {v ^ {\prime} \in \partial f (v _ {0})} \left\langle v ^ {\prime}, v \right\rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}.
$$

Exercise 4.50. Show that the convex function $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ defined by 

$$
f \left(z\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} - \left(1 - | z | ^ {2}\right) ^ {\frac {1}{2}} & \text { if } | z | \leq 1, \\ \infty & \text { otherwise }, \end{array} \right.
$$

is diferentiable, and so subdiferentiable (see Theorem 4.61 below) in the open unit ball $\{ z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m } : | z | < 1 \}$ but it is not subdiferentiable at points z with $| z | = 1$ 

We now study the existence of the subdiferential. 

Theorem 4.51. Let V be a locally convex topological vector space and let $f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a convex function. If there exists $v _ { 0 } \in \ V$ such that $f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ and f is continuous at $v _ { 0 }$ , then $\partial f ( \boldsymbol { v } ) \neq \emptyset$ for all v in the interior $o f \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ . In particular, $\partial f ( { \boldsymbol { v } } _ { 0 } ) \neq \emptyset$ 

We begin with a preliminary result. 

Lemma 4.52. Let V be a locally convex topological vector space, let $f : V $ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ be convex, and let $v _ { 0 } \in V$ be such that $f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ and f is continuous at $v _ { 0 } . \ I f C \subset V \times \mathbb { R }$ is a convex set that does not intersect the interior of epi f and such that $( v _ { 0 } , s _ { 0 } ) \in C$ for some $s _ { 0 } ~ \in ~ \mathbb { R }$ , then there exist $\boldsymbol { v } ^ { \prime } \in \boldsymbol { V } ^ { \prime }$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} f (v) \geq \alpha + \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} & \text {   for   all   } v \in V, \\ t \leq \alpha + \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} & \text {   for   all   } (v, t) \in C. \end{array}
$$

Proof. Since $f$ is convex, by Proposition 4.22 epi f is a convex set of $V \times \mathbb { R }$ and we claim that its interior is nonempty. Indeed, fix $t > f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ . Since $f$ is continuous at $v _ { 0 }$ there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $v _ { 0 }$ such that 

$$
f (v) <   t \quad \text { for   all } v \in U.
$$

Hence the open set $U \times ( t , \infty )$ is a subset of epi f, which shows that the interior of epi f is nonempty. By the first geometric form of the Hahn–Banach theorem, with A being the interior of epi g and $E : = C$ , we may find a continuous linear functional $L : V \times \mathbb { R } \to \mathbb { R } , L \neq 0$ , and a number $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
L (v, t) \geq \alpha \quad \text { for   all } (v, t) \in A \text { and } L (v, t) \leq \alpha \quad \text { for   all } (v, t) \in C.
$$

Note that by the continuity of L it follows that the first inequality actually holds for all $( v , t ) \in$ epi f. The functional L has the form $L \left( v , t \right) = \langle v ^ { \prime } , v \rangle _ { V ^ { \prime } , V } +$ $\alpha _ { 0 } t$ for some $\boldsymbol { v } ^ { \prime } \in V ^ { \prime }$ and $\alpha _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R }$ . Hence 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} + \alpha_ {0} t \geq \alpha & \text { for   all } (v, t) \in \operatorname{epi} f, \\ \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} + \alpha_ {0} t \leq \alpha & \text { for   all } (v, t) \in C. \end{array}\tag{4.24}
$$

Let $v \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ . Then for any $t \geq f \left( v \right)$ , 

$$
\langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} + \alpha_ {0} t \geq \alpha ,
$$

and so letting $t ~  ~ \infty$ , we obtain that $\alpha _ { 0 } ~ \geq ~ 0$ . If $\alpha _ { 0 } ~ = ~ 0$ , then since $( v _ { 0 } , f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) ) \in$ epi f and $( v _ { 0 } , s _ { 0 } ) ~ \in ~ C$ , taking $ { \boldsymbol { v } } \ = \  { \boldsymbol { v } } _ { 0 }$ in (4.24) we get $\langle v ^ { \prime } , v _ { 0 } \rangle _ { V ^ { \prime } , V } = \alpha$ . Again by (4.24), 

$$
\langle v ^ {\prime}, v - v _ {0} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \geq 0 \quad \text { for   all } v \in \operatorname{dom} _ {e} f.
$$

But since f is continuous at $v _ { 0 }$ we may find a neighborhood of zero $U _ { 1 } \subset V$ such that $v _ { 0 } + U _ { 1 } \subset \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ . This implies that 

$$
\langle v ^ {\prime}, u \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \geq 0 \quad \text { for   all } u \in U _ {1},
$$

and since $U _ { 1 }$ is absorbing, we have that 

$$
\langle v ^ {\prime}, u \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \geq 0 \quad \text { for   all } u \in V,
$$

which is a contradiction unless $v ^ { \prime } = 0$ . But since $L \neq 0$ , this is not possible, and so $\alpha _ { 0 } > 0$ , so that by (4.24), 

$$
f (v) \geq \frac {\alpha}{\alpha_ {0}} - \frac {1}{\alpha_ {0}} \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \quad \mathrm{forall} v \in V,
$$

$$
t \leq \frac {\alpha}{\alpha_ {0}} - \frac {1}{\alpha_ {0}} \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \quad \mathrm{forall} (v, t) \in C,
$$

which gives the desired conclusion. 

We are now ready to prove Theorem 4.51. 

Proof (Theorem $4 . 5 1 )$ . By Theorem 4.43 the function $f$ is proper and continuous in the interior of $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ . Hence it sufices to show that $\partial f \left( { { v } _ { 0 } } \right) \ne \emptyset$ . By the previous lemma with $C : = \{ ( v _ { 0 } , f ( v _ { 0 } ) ) \}$ , there exist $\boldsymbol { v } ^ { \prime } \in V ^ { \prime }$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
f (v) \geq \alpha + \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \quad \text { for   all } v \in V, \quad f (v _ {0}) \leq \alpha + \langle v ^ {\prime}, v _ {0} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}.
$$

Taking $v = v _ { 0 }$ it follows that $f \left( \boldsymbol { v } _ { 0 } \right) = \alpha + \langle \boldsymbol { v } ^ { \prime } , \boldsymbol { v } _ { 0 } \rangle _ { V ^ { \prime } , V }$ , and so 

$$
f (v) \geq f (v _ {0}) + \langle v ^ {\prime}, v - v _ {0} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \quad \text { for   all } v \in V.
$$

Hence $\partial f \left( { { v } _ { 0 } } \right) \ne \emptyset$ 

As a corollary of the previous theorem we have the following. 

Corollary 4.53. Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a proper convex function. If $z \in \mathrm { \Gamma } \mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } ( \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f )$ , then $\partial f \left( z \right) \neq \emptyset$ . In particular, if f is real-valued, then $\partial f \left( z \right) \neq \emptyset$ for every $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Proof. Fix a point $z _ { 0 } \in \mathop { \Gamma ^ { \mathrm { i } } } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( \mathop { \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } } f \right)$ . If $\mathrm { d o m } _ { e }$ f consists only of $z _ { \mathrm { 0 } }$ , then 

$$
f \left(z _ {0}\right) = \min _ {z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (z),
$$

and so $0 \in \partial f \left( z _ { 0 } \right)$ by (4.22). 

If dom f has more than one point, by Remark 4.1 the afine hull of its efective domain af $( \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f )$ is, up to a translation, a subspace $W$ of $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ of dimension $1 \leq \ell \leq m$ . Since linear changes of variables preserve convexity, without loss of generality we may assume that af $( \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f ) = \mathbb { R } ^ { \ell } \times \{ 0 \}$ . Define 

$$
g (w) := f ((w, 0)), \quad w \in \mathbb {R} ^ {\ell}.\tag{4.25}
$$

Then the relative interior of $\mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g$ reduces simply to the interior of $\mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g$ , and so, writing $z _ { 0 } = ( w _ { 0 } , 0 )$ , then $w _ { 0 }$ belongs to the interior of $\mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g$ . By Theorem 4.36 the function g is continuous in the interior of $\mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g .$ , and so by Theorem 4.51 we have that $\partial g \left( w _ { 0 } \right)$ is nonempty. Hence there exists $\xi _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { \ell }$ such that 

$$
g (w) \geq g \left(w _ {0}\right) + \xi_ {0} \cdot \left(w - w _ {0}\right) \quad \text { for   all } w \in \operatorname{dom} _ {e} g.
$$

Since af $( \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f ) = \mathbb { R } ^ { \ell } \times \{ 0 \}$ , by (4.25) the previous inequality may be written as 

$$
f (z) \geq f \left(z _ {0}\right) + \left(\xi_ {0}, 0\right) \cdot \left(z - z _ {0}\right) \quad \text { for   all } z \in \operatorname{aff} \left(\operatorname{dom} _ {e} f\right).
$$

On the other hand, if $z \not \in$ af $( \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f )$ , then $f \left( z \right) = \infty$ , and so $( \xi _ { 0 } , 0 ) \ \in$ $\partial f \left( z _ { 0 } \right)$ 

Remark $4 . 5 4$ . It is actually possible to show that if $f \left( z _ { 0 } \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ and $f$ is not subdiferentiable at $z _ { \mathrm { 0 } }$ , then 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} (z _ {0}) = - \infty
$$

for all $v \in - z _ { 0 } + \operatorname { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f \right)$ . See Theorem 4.56 below. 

Exercise 4.55. The set of points at which a convex function is subdiferentiable may be larger than $\operatorname { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f \right)$ . Indeed, let $m = 2$ and consider the function 

$$
f \left(z\right) = f \left(z _ {1}, z _ {2}\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \max \left\{1 - z _ {1} ^ {\frac {1}{2}}, | z _ {1} | \right\} & \text { if } z _ {1} \geq 0, \\ \infty & \text { otherwise }. \end{array} \right.
$$

Prove that $f$ is subdiferentiable everywhere in the half-plane $\{ z _ { 1 } \geq 0 \}$ except in the relative interior of the segment joining $( 0 , 1 )$ and $( 0 , - 1 )$ . Note that the set on which $f$ is subdiferentiable is not convex. 

The following theorem relates the subdiferential to one-sided directional derivatives. 

Theorem 4.56. Let V be a Banach space and let $f : V  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a proper lower semicontinuous convex function. Assume that the interior of $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ is nonempty. If $v _ { 0 } ~ \in ~ \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ , then one of the following two alternatives holds: 

(i) $\partial f \left( { { v } _ { 0 } } \right) = \varnothing$ and 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) = - \infty
$$

for all $v \in - v _ { 0 } + \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } ^ { \circ } f ;$ 

(ii) $\partial f \left( \boldsymbol { v } _ { 0 } \right) \neq \emptyset$ , the function $\begin{array} { r } { v \mapsto \frac { \partial ^ { + } f } { \partial v } \left( v _ { 0 } \right) } \end{array}$ is continuous on $- v _ { 0 } + \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f .$ and 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) = \max _ {v ^ {\prime} \in \partial f (v _ {0})} \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}
$$

for all v in $- v _ { 0 } + \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f .$ 

Proof. Let A denote the interior of $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f .$ 

Step 1: We claim that if $v _ { 0 } \in A$ then 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) = \max _ {v ^ {\prime} \in \partial f (v _ {0})} \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}
$$

for all $v \in V$ . By Corollary 4.45 and Theorem 4.51, f is continuous and subdiferentiable in A, and so by Remark 4.49, 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) \geq \sup _ {v ^ {\prime} \in \partial f (v _ {0})} \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} > - \infty
$$

for all $v \in V$ 

To prove the reverse inequality we show that 

$$
p (v) := \frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} (v _ {0}), \quad v \in V,
$$

is continuous. Since $v _ { 0 } \in A$ , by Corollary 4.45 and Theorem 4.47 there exist $r , M > 0$ such that 

$$
f (w) - f (v _ {0}) \leq M \| w - v _ {0} \|
$$

for all $w \in B \left( v _ { 0 } , r \right)$ . Hence if $v \in V \setminus \{ 0 \}$ , then for $0 < t < r / \| v \|$ we have 

$$
\frac {f (v _ {0} + t v) - f (v _ {0})}{t} \leq M \| v \|,
$$

and letting $t \to 0 ^ { + }$ we conclude that 

$$
p (v) \leq M \| v \|.
$$

Since $p : V \to \mathbb { R }$ is convex by Remark 4.49, it follows from Theorem 4.43 that it is actually continuous. Fix $v _ { 1 } \in V \setminus \{ 0 \}$ . By Lemma 4.52, with $p$ and $v _ { 1 }$ in place of $f$ and $v _ { 0 }$ and with $C : = \{ ( v _ { 1 } , p ( v _ { 1 } ) ) \}$ , we may find $v ^ { \prime } \in V ^ { \prime }$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
p (v) \geq \alpha + \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \quad \text { for   all } v \in V, \quad p (v _ {1}) \leq \alpha + \langle v ^ {\prime}, v _ {1} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}.\tag{4.26}
$$

Replacing v with tv, $t > 0$ , in the first inequality and using the fact that $p$ is positively homogeneous (see Remark 4.49), we obtain that 

$$
t \left(p (v) - \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}\right) \geq \alpha \quad \text { for   all } v \in V \text { and } t > 0.
$$

Letting $t \to 0 ^ { + }$ we conclude that $\alpha \leq 0$ , while if we divide by $t > 0$ and then let $t \to \infty$ we obtain 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) = p \left(v\right) \geq \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \quad \text { for   all } v \in V,
$$

which implies in particular that $v ^ { \prime } \in \partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ . It now follows from the second inequality in (4.26) that $\alpha = 0$ and 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v _ {1}} \left(v _ {0}\right) = p \left(v _ {1}\right) = \langle v ^ {\prime}, v _ {1} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V},
$$

and so the claim holds. 

Step 2: Assume that $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { \partial ^ { + } f } { \partial v } \left( v _ { 0 } \right) = - \infty } \end{array}$ for all $v \in - v _ { 0 } + A$ . We claim that $\partial f \left( \boldsymbol { v } _ { 0 } \right) = \emptyset$ . Indeed, if not, fix $v \in - v _ { 0 } + A$ and let $v ^ { \prime } \in \partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ . By letting $t \to 0 ^ { + }$ in (4.23) we obtain a contradiction. 

Step 3: Assume that $\frac { \partial ^ { + } f } { \partial v _ { 1 } } \left( v _ { 0 } \right) > - \infty$ for some $v _ { 1 } \in - v _ { 0 } + A$ . Consider the sequence of functions 

$$
g _ {n} (v) := \frac {1}{n} \left[ f \left(v _ {0} + \frac {1}{n} v\right) - f (v _ {0}) \right], \quad v \in V.
$$

Each $g _ { n }$ is convex, proper, lower semicontinuous, and continuous on $- v _ { 0 } + A$ by Corollary 4.45. By Remark 4.49 the function 

$$
g \left(v\right) := \inf _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} g _ {n} \left(v\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} g _ {n} \left(v\right) = \frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right), \quad v \in V,
$$

is convex, and since $\mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g \supset \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g _ { 1 }$ , we deduce that $- v _ { 0 } + A \subset \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g$ Also $g \left( v _ { 1 } \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ . Since $g$ is finite at some point in the interior of its domain, g is proper and in particular finite on $- v _ { 0 } + A$ (see Remark 4.23). 

Since $- v _ { 0 } + A$ is a Baire space and $g$ is the limit of a sequence of continuous functions on $- v _ { 0 } + A$ , the set of points at which $g$ is continuous is dense. By Corollary 4.45, g is continuous on $- v _ { 0 } + A$ . Hence by Step 1, for every $v _ { 1 } \in - v _ { 0 } + A$ and $v \in V$ , 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} g}{\partial v} \left(v _ {1}\right) = \max _ {v ^ {\prime} \in \partial g (v _ {1})} \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}.\tag{4.27}
$$

Fix $v ^ { \prime } \in \partial g \left( v _ { 1 } \right)$ and $v \in V$ . Since $g$ is subadditive by Remark 4.49, we have 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) = g (v) \geq g \left(v _ {1} + v\right) - g \left(v _ {1}\right) \geq \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V},
$$

and given the arbitrariness of $v \in V$ it follows that $v ^ { \prime } \in \partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ , and in turn, $\partial g \left( v _ { 1 } \right) \subset \partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ . This implies in particular that $\partial f \left( \boldsymbol { v } _ { 0 } \right)$ is nonempty, and so by Remark 4.49, 

$$
\sup _ {v ^ {\prime} \in \partial f (v _ {0})} \left\langle v ^ {\prime}, v _ {1} \right\rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \leq \frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v _ {1}} \left(v _ {0}\right).
$$

By (4.27) there is $v _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } \in \partial g \left( v _ { 1 } \right)$ such that 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} g}{\partial v _ {1}} \left(v _ {1}\right) = \langle v _ {1} ^ {\prime}, v _ {1} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}.
$$

Then $v _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } \in \partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \langle v _ {1} ^ {\prime}, v _ {1} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} = \frac {\partial^ {+} g}{\partial v _ {1}} (v _ {1}) = \lim _ {t \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {g (v _ {1} + t v _ {1}) - g (v _ {1})}{t} \\ = g (v _ {1}) \lim _ {t \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {(1 + t) - 1}{t} = g (v _ {1}) = \frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v _ {1}} (v _ {0}), \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that g is positively homogeneous. Hence 

$$
\max _ {v ^ {\prime} \in \partial f (v _ {0})} \left\langle v ^ {\prime}, v _ {1} \right\rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} = \frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v _ {1}} \left(v _ {0}\right)
$$

for all $v _ { 1 } \in - v _ { 0 } + A$ 

Remark 4.57. If V is a Banach space and $f : V  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ is a proper lower semicontinuous convex function, then considering the restriction $f$ : af $( \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f )  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ , the previous theorem still holds provided the interior of the effective domain in aff $( \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f )$ is nonempty, i.e., $\mathrm { r i } _ { \mathrm { a f f } } \left( \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f \right) \neq \emptyset$ 

When V is only a locally convex topological vector space we can still prove a weaker form of the previous theorem: 

Proposition 4.58. Let V be a locally convex topological vector space and let $f : V  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a proper convex function. If $v _ { 0 } \in V$ is such that $f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \in$ R and $f$ is continuous at $v _ { 0 }$ , then 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) = \max _ {v ^ {\prime} \in \partial f (v _ {0})} \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}
$$

for all $v \in V$ 

Proof. By Theorem 4.51, f is subdiferentiable at $v _ { 0 }$ , and so by Remark 4.49, 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) \geq \sup _ {v ^ {\prime} \in \partial f (v _ {0})} \left\langle v ^ {\prime}, v \right\rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} > - \infty
$$

for all $v \in V$ . To prove the reverse inequality, as in Step 1 of the previous theorem it sufices to show that the seminorm 

$$
p (v) := \frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} (v _ {0}), v \in V,
$$

is continuous. Since 

$$
p (v) = \inf _ {t > 0} \frac {f (v _ {0} + t v) - f (v _ {0})}{t} \leq f (v _ {0} + v) - f (v _ {0})
$$

and $f$ is continuous at $v _ { 0 }$ , it follows that $p$ is bounded from above in a neigh borhood of $v _ { 0 }$ , and so it is continuous by Theorem 4.43. 

Next we study the subdiferentiability of the sum of two convex functions. 

Proposition 4.59. Let V be a locally convex topological vector space and let $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } : V \to ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be two proper convex, lower semicontinuous functions. $A$ ssume that there exists 

$$
v _ {0} \in \mathrm{dom} _ {e} f _ {1} \cap \mathrm{dom} _ {e} f _ {2}
$$

such that $f _ { 1 }$ is continuous at $v _ { 0 }$ . Then for every $v \in V$ 

$$
\partial \left(f _ {1} + f _ {2}\right) (v) = \partial f _ {1} (v) + \partial f _ {2} (v).
$$

Proof. Step 1: Let $v \in V$ . If $v _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } \in \partial f _ { 1 } \left( v \right)$ and $v _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } \in \partial f _ { 2 } \left( v \right)$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} f _ {1} \left(w\right) \geq f _ {1} \left(v\right) + \langle v _ {1} ^ {\prime}, w - v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} & \text { for   all } w \in V, \\ f _ {2} \left(w\right) \geq f _ {2} \left(v\right) + \langle v _ {2} ^ {\prime}, w - v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} & \text { for   all } w \in V, \end{array}
$$

and $\mathrm { s o } ,$ , adding the two inequalities, we conclude that $v _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } + v _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } \in \partial \left( f _ { 1 } + f _ { 2 } \right) ( v )$ Hence if $\partial f _ { 1 } \left( v \right)$ and $\partial f _ { 2 } \left( \boldsymbol { v } \right)$ are nonempty, then $\partial \left( f _ { 1 } + f _ { 2 } \right) ( v )$ is nonempty and 

$$
\partial \left(f _ {1} + f _ {2}\right) (v) \supset \partial f _ {1} (v) + \partial f _ {2} (v).
$$

Step 2: Conversely, if $\partial \left( f _ { 1 } + f _ { 2 } \right) ( v )$ is nonempty, let $v ^ { \prime } \in \partial \left( f _ { 1 } + f _ { 2 } \right) ( v )$ Then 

$$
\left(f _ {1} + f _ {2}\right) (w) \geq \left(f _ {1} + f _ {2}\right) (v) + \langle v ^ {\prime}, w - v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \quad \text { for   all } w \in V.\tag{4.28}
$$

In particular, $f _ { 1 } ( v ) , f _ { 2 } ( v ) \in \mathbb { R }$ . Define 

$$
g (w) := f _ {1} (w) - f _ {1} (v) + \langle v ^ {\prime}, w - v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}, \quad w \in V,
$$

and 

$$
C := \left\{(w, t) \in V \times \mathbb {R}: t \leq f _ {2} (v) - f _ {2} (w) \right\}.
$$

Then $g$ is a convex function and $C$ a convex set. We claim that g and $C$ satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma 4.52. Indeed, since $f _ { 1 }$ is proper and continuous at $v _ { 0 }$ then so is $g .$ . Moreover, in view of (4.28), if $( w , t ) \in \mathrm { e p i } g \cap C$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} g \left(w\right) = f _ {1} \left(w\right) - f _ {1} \left(v\right) + \langle v ^ {\prime}, w - v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \leq t \leq f _ {2} \left(v\right) - f _ {2} \left(w\right) \\ \quad \leq f _ {1} \left(w\right) - f _ {1} \left(v\right) + \langle v ^ {\prime}, w - v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}, \end{array}
$$

which implies that $g \left( w \right) = t$ and $f _ { 2 } \left( v \right) - f _ { 2 } \left( w \right) = t$ , that is, $( w , t ) \in \partial ( \mathrm { e p i } g ) \cap$ $\partial C$ . Finally, $( v _ { 0 } , f _ { 2 } ( v ) - f _ { 2 } ( v _ { 0 } ) ) \in C$ . Hence we may apply Lemma 4.52 to find $w ^ { \prime } \in V ^ { \prime }$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
g (w) = f _ {1} (w) - f _ {1} (v) + \langle v ^ {\prime}, w - v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \geq \alpha + \langle w ^ {\prime}, w \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \geq f _ {2} (v) - f _ {2} (w)
$$

for all $w \in V$ . Taking $w = v$ yields $\langle w ^ { \prime } , v \rangle _ { V ^ { \prime } , V } = - \alpha$ , so that 

$$
f _ {1} (w) - f _ {1} (v) + \langle v ^ {\prime}, w - v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \geq \langle w ^ {\prime}, w - v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \geq f _ {2} (v) - f _ {2} (w)
$$

for all $w \in V$ , and so $v ^ { \prime } - w ^ { \prime } \in \partial f _ { 1 } \left( v \right)$ and $w ^ { \prime } \in \partial f _ { 2 } \left( v \right)$ . Hence 

$$
v ^ {\prime} = \left(v ^ {\prime} - w ^ {\prime}\right) + w ^ {\prime} \in \partial f _ {1} (v) + \partial f _ {2} (v),
$$

which proves that if $\partial \left( f _ { 1 } + f _ { 2 } \right) ( v )$ is nonempty, then 

$$
\partial \left(f _ {1} + f _ {2}\right) (v) \subset \partial f _ {1} (v) + \partial f _ {2} (v).
$$

Step 3: To conclude the proof we observe that if either $\partial f _ { 1 } \left( v \right)$ or $\partial f _ { 2 } \left( \boldsymbol { v } \right)$ is empty, then by Step 2 so must be $\partial \left( f _ { 1 } + f _ { 2 } \right) ( v )$ . If both $\partial f _ { 1 } \left( v \right)$ and $\partial f _ { 2 } \left( \boldsymbol { v } \right)$ are nonempty, then by Steps 1 and 2, $\partial \left( f _ { 1 } + f _ { 2 } \right) ( v )$ is also nonempty and 

$$
\partial \left(f _ {1} + f _ {2}\right) (v) = \partial f _ {1} (v) + \partial f _ {2} (v).
$$

This completes the proof. 

We now turn to the relation between subdiferentiability and (Gˆateaux) diferentiability. 

Definition 4.60. Let V be a locally convex topological vector space. A function $f : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is Gˆateaux diferentiable at $v _ { 0 } \in V \mathrm { ~ } i f \ f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \in \mathbb { R }$ and there exists $v ^ { \prime } \in V ^ { \prime }$ such that for every $v \in V$ , 

$$
\lim _ {t \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {f (v _ {0} + t v) - f (v _ {0})}{t} = \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}.
$$

The element $v ^ { \prime }$ is called the Gˆateaux diferential of f at $v _ { 0 }$ and is denoted $b y$ $f ^ { \prime } \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ 

Theorem 4.61. Let V be a locally convex topological vector space and let $f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a convex function. If f is Gˆateaux diferentiable at $v _ { 0 } \in V$ , then it is subdiferentiable at v and ∂f $\left( v _ { 0 } \right) = \left\{ f ^ { \prime } \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \right\}$ . Conversely, if f is continuous and finite at $v _ { 0 } \in V$ and the subdiferential of f at $v _ { 0 }$ is a singleton, then f is Gˆateaux diferentiable at v . 

Proof. Assume that f is Gˆateaux diferentiable at $v _ { 0 } \in V$ , let $v \in V$ , and define $g \left( t \right) : = f \left( v _ { 0 } + t v \right)$ . By Proposition 4.34 the diference quotient 

$$
t \mapsto \frac {g (t) - g (0)}{t - 0}
$$

is nondecreasing in $\mathbb { R } \backslash \{ t _ { 0 } \}$ . Hence 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f \left(v _ {0} + v\right) - f \left(v _ {0}\right) = \frac {g \left(1\right) - g \left(0\right)}{1 - 0} \geq \lim _ {t \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {g \left(t\right) - g \left(0\right)}{t - 0} \\ = \lim _ {t \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {f \left(v _ {0} + t v\right) - f \left(v _ {0}\right)}{t} = \langle f ^ {\prime} \left(v _ {0}\right), v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}, \end{array}
$$

which implies that $f ^ { \prime } \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \in \partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ . We claim that $\partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) = \left\{ f ^ { \prime } \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \right\}$ . Indeed, if $v ^ { \prime } \in \partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ , then for any $v \in V$ and $t > 0$ , 

$$
\frac {f (v _ {0} + t v) - f (v _ {0})}{t} \geq \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}.
$$

By letting $t \to 0 ^ { + }$ we obtain that 

$$
\langle f ^ {\prime} (v _ {0}), v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \geq \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \text {   for   all   } v \in V,
$$

which implies that $v ^ { \prime } = f ^ { \prime } \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ 

Conversely, assume that f is continuous and finite at $v _ { 0 } \in V$ and the subdiferential of $f$ at $v _ { 0 }$ is a singleton $\{ v ^ { \prime } \}$ . Then $f > - \infty$ by Remark 4.23, and so by Proposition 4.58 and the fact that $\partial f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) = \{ v ^ { \prime } \}$ we deduce that 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {+} f}{\partial v} \left(v _ {0}\right) = \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}
$$

for all $v \in V$ , which shows that f is Gˆateaux diferentiable at $v _ { 0 }$ . 

The next result shows that for smooth functions convexity is equivalent to the monotonicity of the Gˆateaux diferential. 

Theorem 4.62. Let E be a convex subset of a locally convex topological vector space V and let $f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be Gˆateaux diferentiable in $E$ . Then the following three conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $f : E \to \mathbb { R }$ is convex; 

(ii) for all $v , w \in E$ , 

$$
f (v) \geq f (w) + \langle f ^ {\prime} (w), v - w \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V};
$$

(iii) for all $v , w \in E$ 2 

$$
\langle f ^ {\prime} (v) - f ^ {\prime} (w), v - w \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \geq 0.
$$

Proof. Assume that (i) holds. Since f is Gˆateaux diferentiable in $E _ { i }$ , by the previous theorem f is subdiferentiable at every $w \in E$ and $\partial f \left( w \right) = \left\{ f ^ { \prime } \left( w \right) \right\}$ Hence (ii) holds. 

Assume next that (ii) holds. Then for all $v , w \in E $ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (v) \geq f (w) + \langle f ^ {\prime} (w), v - w \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}, \\ f (w) \geq f (v) - \langle f ^ {\prime} (v), v - w \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}, \end{array}
$$

and by adding these inequalities we obtain that 

$$
0 \geq \langle f ^ {\prime} (w) - f ^ {\prime} (v), v - w \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V},
$$

which gives (iii). 

Finally, assume that (iii) holds and fix $v , w \in E$ . Since $f$ is Gˆateaux diferentiable in $E _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ , the function $g : [ 0 , 1 ]  \mathbb { R }$ , defined by 

$$
g (t) := f (t v + (1 - t) w), \quad t \in [ 0, 1 ],
$$

is diferentiable and 

$$
g ^ {\prime} (t) = \left\langle f ^ {\prime} (t v + (1 - t) w), v - w \right\rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V}.
$$

$s > t$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} g ^ {\prime} (s) - g ^ {\prime} (t) = \langle f ^ {\prime} (s v + (1 - s) w) - f ^ {\prime} (t v + (1 - t) w), v - w \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \\ = \frac {1}{s - t} \langle f ^ {\prime} (s v + (1 - s) w) - f ^ {\prime} (t v + (1 - t) w), \\ (s v + (1 - s) w) - (t v + (1 - t) w) \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \geq 0. \end{array}
$$

Hence $g ^ { \prime }$ is nondecreasing, and so g is convex. In particular, 

$$
f (t v + (1 - t) w) = g (t) \leq (1 - t) g (0) + t g (1) = (1 - t) f (w) + t f (v),
$$

which implies the convexity of $f .$ 

Remark 4.63. A similar result holds for strictly convex functions provided we require the inequalities (i) and (ii) to be strict when $v \neq w$ 

As a consequence of the previous theorem we now specialize the result of Theorem 4.36 to obtain a p-Lipschitz condition for separately convex functions with algebraic growth. 

Proposition 4.64. Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  \mathbb { R }$ be a separately convex function such that 

$$
| f (z) | \leq C (1 + | z | ^ {p})
$$

for some $C > 0 , p \geq 1$ , and $a l l z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Then 

$$
\left| f (z) - f (w) \right| \leq C \left(1 + | z | ^ {p - 1} + | w | ^ {p - 1}\right) | z - w |
$$

for all $z , w \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Proof. Step 1: We first assume that $f \in C ^ { \infty } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ . Let $z : = ( z _ { 1 } , \dots , z _ { m } ) \in$ $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be fixed and consider 

$$
g (t) := f \left(z _ {1}, \ldots , z _ {i - 1}, t, z _ {i + 1}, \ldots , z _ {m}\right), \quad t \in \mathbb {R}.
$$

Since $g$ is convex and smooth by Theorem 4.62 (see also Proposition 4.34), for all s and $t \in \mathbb { R }$ we have 

$$
g (t + s) - g (t) \geq g ^ {\prime} (t) s.
$$

Thus, with $s : = 1 + | z | , t : = z _ { i }$ 

$$
g ^ {\prime} (t) = \frac {\partial f}{\partial z _ {i}} (z) \leq \frac {g (t + s) - g (t)}{s} \leq C \frac {(1 + | z | ^ {p})}{1 + | z |} \leq C \left(1 + | z | ^ {p - 1}\right).
$$

Also, $g \left( t - s \right) - g \left( t \right) \geq - g ^ { \prime } \left( t \right) s ,$ , and so 

$$
- g ^ {\prime} (t) \leq \frac {g (t - s) - g (t)}{s} \leq C \frac {(1 + | z | ^ {p})}{1 + | z |} \leq C \left(1 + | z | ^ {p - 1}\right).
$$

Hence 

$$
\left| \frac {\partial f}{\partial z _ {i}} (z) \right| \leq C \left(1 + | z | ^ {p - 1}\right)
$$

for every $i = 1 , \ldots , m$ 

Let z, $w \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . By the mean value theorem there is $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | f (z) - f (w) | = | \nabla f (\theta z + (1 - \theta) w) \cdot (z - w) | \\ \qquad \leq C \left(1 + | \theta z + (1 - \theta) w | ^ {p - 1}\right) | (z - w) | \\ \qquad \leq C \left(1 + | z | ^ {p - 1} + | w | ^ {p - 1}\right) | z - w |, \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that if $0 < q < \infty$ and $a , b \geq 0$ , then 

$$
(a + b) ^ {q} \leq \max \left\{1, 2 ^ {q - 1} \right\} (a ^ {q} + b ^ {q}).
$$

Step 2: To remove the smoothness hypothesis consider a standard mollifier $\varphi _ { \varepsilon }$ and let 

$$
f _ {\varepsilon} (z) := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (w) f (z - w) d w, \quad \varepsilon > 0.
$$

The function $f _ { \varepsilon }$ is still separately convex and, in addition, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | f _ {\varepsilon} (z) | \leq \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (w) | f (z - w) | d w \leq C \int_ {B (0, \varepsilon)} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (w) (1 + | z - w | ^ {p}) d w \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq C (1 + | z | ^ {p}) \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {\varepsilon} (w) d w = C (1 + | z | ^ {p}), \end{array}
$$

where the constants are independent of ε. By the previous step, 

$$
\left| f _ {\varepsilon} (z) - f _ {\varepsilon} (w) \right| \leq C \left(1 + | z | ^ {p - 1} + | w | ^ {p - 1}\right) | z - w |,
$$

and since $f _ { \varepsilon } \left( z \right) \to f \left( z \right)$ pointwise as $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ (see Theorem 2.75) we obtain the desired result for $f .$ 

We conclude this subsection by proving that diferentiable separately con vex functions are of class $C ^ { 1 }$ 

Theorem 4.65. Let $B \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be an open ball. If $f : B \to \mathbb { R }$ is separately convex and E is the set $o f$ points in B at which f is diferentiable, then $\nabla f : E  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is continuous. 

Proof. Let $z _ { 0 } \in E$ and define 

$$
h (z) := f (z) - f \left(z _ {0}\right) - \nabla f \left(z _ {0}\right) \cdot \left(z - z _ {0}\right), \quad z \in B.
$$

Then the function $h$ is separately convex and diferentiable in E. By Theorem 4.36, 

$$
| \nabla f (z) - \nabla f (z _ {0}) | = | \nabla h (z) | \leq \operatorname{Lip} (h; B (z _ {0}, r)) \leq \sqrt {m} \frac {\mathrm{osc} (h ; B (z _ {0} , 2 r))}{r}
$$

for any $z \in E$ with $| z - z _ { 0 } | < r$ and with $B \left( z _ { 0 } , 2 r \right) \subset B$ . Since f is diferentiable at $z _ { \mathrm { 0 } }$ we have that 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \sup _ {z \in E, | z - z _ {0} | <   r} | \nabla f (z) - \nabla f (z _ {0}) | \leq \lim _ {r \to 0 ^ {+}} \sqrt {m} \frac {\mathrm{osc} (h ; B (z _ {0} , 2 r))}{r} = 0,
$$

and thus $\nabla f ( z )  \nabla f ( z _ { 0 } ) { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } z  z _ { 0 } , z \in E .$ 

## 4.6 Recession Function

In this section we introduce and study some properties of the recession func tion of a convex function. This material will be used in Section 5.2.3 

Definition 4.66. If $C \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is a nonempty convex set, then its recession cone is defined by 

$$
C ^ {\infty} := \left\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: t z + w \in C \text {   for   all   } w \in C \text {   and   } t \geq 0 \right\}.
$$

Proposition 4.67. $I f C \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is nonempty and convex, then 

(i) $C ^ { \infty }$ is convex and $C ^ { \infty } = \{ z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m } : z + w \in C$ for all $w \in C \} , \ i . e . , \ z +$ $C \subset C$ if and only if $t z + C \subset C$ for all $t \geq 0$ 

$H ,$ in addition, C is closed, then 

(ii) $C ^ { \infty }$ is closed; 

$( i i i ) ~ z \in C ^ { \infty }$ if and only $\begin{array} { r } { i f z = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n  \infty } \theta _ { n } w _ { n } } \end{array}$ with $w _ { n } \in C$ and $\theta _ { n } \to 0 ^ { + }$ 

Proof. In part (i) the convexity of $C ^ { \infty }$ and the inclusion 

$$
C ^ {\infty} \subset \{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z + w \in C \text {   for   all   } w \in C \} =: D
$$

are immediate. To prove the converse inclusion let $z \in D$ . Then $z + w \in C$ for all $w \in C$ . By induction, it follows that $w + n z \in C$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Therefore, if $t \in [ n - 1 , n ]$ , then writing $t = \theta \left( n - 1 \right) + \left( 1 - \theta \right)$ n for some $\theta \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , we have 

$$
w + t z = \theta (w + (n - 1) z) + (1 - \theta) (w + n z) \in C
$$

by convexity of $C ,$ and so $z \in C ^ { \infty }$ 

To prove (ii) let $z = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } z _ { n } , z _ { n } \in C ^ { \infty }$ . In view of part (i) it sufices to prove that $w + z \in C$ for all $w \in C$ . Suppose that $w + z \not \in C$ for some $w \in C .$ Since C is closed, there would exist $r > 0$ such that $B \left( w + z , r \right) \cap C = \varnothing$ However, $w + z _ { n } \in C$ for every n and thus 

$$
0 <   r \leq \operatorname{dist} (w + z, C) \leq | (w + z) - (w + z _ {n}) | \rightarrow 0,
$$

and this is a contradiction. 

Similarly, in part (iii), ${ \mathrm { i f ~ } } z = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \theta _ { n } w _ { n }$ , with $w _ { n } \in C$ and $\theta _ { n } \to 0 ^ { + }$ ， and z were not in $C ^ { \infty }$ , then there would exist w $\in { \cal C }$ and $r > 0$ such that $B \left( w + z , r \right) \cap C = \varnothing$ . If n is suficiently large we may assume that $\theta _ { n } \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ and so 

$$
\left(1 - \theta_ {n}\right) w + \theta_ {n} w _ {n} \in C
$$

by convexity of C, with 

$$
w + z = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \left\{\left(1 - \theta_ {n}\right) w + \theta_ {n} w _ {n} + \theta_ {n} w \right\}.
$$

Once again we would reach a contradiction because 

$$
0 <   r \leq \mathrm{dist} (w + z, C) \leq | \theta_ {n} w | \to 0.
$$

Conversely, if $z \in C ^ { \infty }$ and $w _ { 0 } \in C$ , then $n z + w _ { 0 } = w _ { n } \in C$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and so $\theta _ { n } w _ { n }  z$ with $\textstyle \theta _ { n } : = { \frac { 1 } { n } }$ 

Remark 4.68. It can be shown that the notion of recession cone of an arbitrary set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ introduced as 

$$
E ^ {\infty} := \left\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: \text {   there   exist   } w _ {n} \in E, \theta_ {n} \to 0 ^ {+} \text {   such   that   } \theta_ {n} w _ {n} \to z \right\}
$$

inherits several properties of the recession cone of a convex set (see [RocWe98]). Note, however, that $E ^ { \infty }$ defined in this way is always closed, which is in contrast to Definition 4.66 (see Theorem 4.67 (iii)). 

We now introduce the concept of recession function. 

Definition 4.69. Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a proper convex function. The recession function of f is the function $f ^ { \infty } : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ defined by 

$$
f ^ {\infty} (z) := \sup \left\{f (w + z) - f (w): w \in \operatorname{dom} _ {e} f \right\}, \quad z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}.
$$

The next result relates the recession function of a convex function to the recession cone of its epigraph. 

Theorem 4.70. Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a proper convex function. The recession function $f ^ { \infty }$ of f is a positively homogeneous proper convex function and 

$$
\operatorname{epi} f ^ {\infty} = (\operatorname{epi} f) ^ {\infty}.\tag{4.29}
$$

Moreover, if f is lower semicontinuous, then so is $f ^ { \infty }$ , and for every $w \in$ $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ we have 

$$
f ^ {\infty} (z) = \sup _ {t > 0} \frac {f (w + t z) - f (w)}{t} = \lim _ {t \to \infty} \frac {f (w + t z) - f (w)}{t}.\tag{4.30}
$$

Proof. We begin by showing that 

$$
\operatorname{epi} f ^ {\infty} = (\operatorname{epi} f) ^ {\infty}.\tag{4.31}
$$

Note that in view of Propositions 4.22 and $4 . 6 7 ( \mathrm { i } )$ this entails that epi $f ^ { \infty }$ is convex, and so $f ^ { \infty }$ is convex. Convexity of $f ^ { \infty }$ also follows from the fact that $f ^ { \infty }$ is the supremum of a family of convex functions. 

By Proposition 4.67(i) we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\operatorname{epi} f) ^ {\infty} = \{(z, t) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R}: (w, s) + (z, t) \in \operatorname{epi} f \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \text {for all} (w, s) \in \operatorname{epi} f \} \\ \qquad = \{(z, t) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R}: f (w + z) \leq s + t \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \text {for all} w \in \operatorname{dom} _ {e} f \text {and all} s \in \mathbb {R} \text {such that} s \geq f (w) \} \\ \qquad = \{(z, t) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R}: f (w + z) \leq f (w) + t \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \text {for all} w \in \operatorname{dom} _ {e} f \} \\ \qquad = \{(z, t) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R}: f ^ {\infty} (z) \leq t \} = \operatorname{epi} f ^ {\infty}. \end{array}
$$

Since for a fixed $w \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ 8 

$$
f ^ {\infty} (z) \geq f (w + z) - f (w)
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , we have that $f ^ { \infty }$ never takes the value −∞. On the other hand, $f ^ { \infty }$ is not identically $\infty$ because $f ^ { \infty } \left( 0 \right) = 0$ . Hence $f ^ { \infty }$ is proper. 

To prove that $f ^ { \infty }$ is positively homogeneous let $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and $t > 0$ . We first claim that 

$$
t f ^ {\infty} (z) \geq f ^ {\infty} (t z).\tag{4.32}
$$

If $f ^ { \infty } ( z ) = \infty$ there is nothing to prove. Thus assume that $f ^ { \infty } ( z ) < \infty$ . Then $( z , f ^ { \infty } ( z ) ) \in \mathrm { e p i } f ^ { \infty }$ , and so by (4.29) and the definition of recession cone, 

$$
t \left(z, f ^ {\infty} (z)\right) + \operatorname{epi} f \subset \operatorname{epi} f.
$$

In particular, $t \left( z , f ^ { \infty } ( z ) \right) + \left( w , f \left( w \right) \right) \in \mathrm { { e p i } }$ f for all $w \in \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ , and thus 

$$
f (w + t z) \leq f (w) + t f ^ {\infty} (z),\tag{4.33}
$$

or equivalently, 

$$
f (w + t z) - f (w) \leq t f ^ {\infty} (z)
$$

for all $w \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ . Taking the supremum on the left-hand side over all $w \in$ $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f .$ , it follows that 

$$
f ^ {\infty} (t z) \leq t f ^ {\infty} (z)
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and $t > 0$ . To prove the reverse inequality it sufices to replace z and t in the previous inequality with $t z$ and $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { t } }$ . 

Assume next that $f$ is lower semicontinuous. Note that by (4.31) and Proposition $4 . 6 7 ( \mathrm { i i } )$ , epi $f ^ { \infty }$ is closed, and thus by Proposition 3.10, $f ^ { \infty }$ is lower semicontinuous. 

To prove (4.30), in view of Proposition 4.34 it sufices to establish the equality 

$$
f ^ {\infty} (z) = \sup _ {t > 0} \frac {f (w + t z) - f (w)}{t}
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and for any fixed $w \in \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ . Fix $w _ { 0 } \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ . We show first that 

$$
f ^ {\infty} (z) \geq \frac {f (w _ {0} + t z) - f (w _ {0})}{t}
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Reasoning as in the proof of (4.32) we have that (4.33) holds for all $w \in \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ and for every $t \geq 0$ . In particular, 

$$
f \left(w _ {0} + t z\right) \leq f \left(w _ {0}\right) + t f ^ {\infty} (z)
$$

for all $t \geq 0$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , which gives 

$$
\sup _ {t > 0} \frac {f (w _ {0} + t z) - f (w _ {0})}{t} \leq f ^ {\infty} (z)\tag{4.34}
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Conversely, if for $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , 

$$
\sup _ {t > 0} \frac {f (w _ {0} + t z) - f (w _ {0})}{t} = \infty ,
$$

then there is nothing to prove; otherwise, let 

$$
s \geq \frac {f (w _ {0} + t z) - f (w _ {0})}{t}
$$

for all $t > 0$ . Then $s t + f \left( w _ { 0 } \right) \geq f ( w _ { 0 } + t z )$ for all $t > 0$ , and so 

$$
\left(w _ {0} + t z, s t + f \left(w _ {0}\right)\right) \in \operatorname{epi} f\tag{4.35}
$$

for all $t > 0$ . Write 

$$
(z, s) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{n} \left((w _ {0}, f (w _ {0})) + n (z, s)\right).
$$

By (4.35) and Proposition 4.67(iii), it follows that $( z , s ) \in ( \mathrm { e p i } f ) ^ { \infty }$ , and now invoking (4.31), we conclude that $f ^ { \infty } \left( z \right) \leq s$ . Given the arbitrariness of s, we deduce that f(. 

$$
f ^ {\infty} (z) \leq \sup _ {t > 0} \frac {f (w _ {0} + t z) - f (w _ {0})}{t}.
$$

This, together with (4.34), yields (4.30). 

Remark $4 . 7 1$ . For nonconvex functions it is also possible to define the recession function using formula (4.29), and where $( \mathrm { e p i } f ) ^ { \infty }$ is given as in Remark 4.68 (see [RocWe98]). We call attention, however, to the fact that the recession function introduced in this way is always lower semicontinuous, in contrast to the case of a convex function (see Theorem 4.70). 

Exercise 4.72. Prove that: 

(i) If $1 \leq p < \infty$ , then the recession function of $f \left( z \right) : = | z | ^ { p }$ is 

$$
f ^ {\infty} \left(z\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \infty & \text { if } z \neq 0, \\ 0 & \text { if } z = 0, \end{array} \right.
$$

for $p > 1$ , while $f ^ { \infty } \left( z \right) = f \left( z \right) = \left| z \right| { \mathrm { i f } } \ p = 1$ ; 

(ii) the recession function of $f \left( z \right) : = \sqrt { \left| z \right| ^ { 2 } + 1 } \mathrm { \ i s \ } f ^ { \infty } \left( z \right) = \left| z \right| ;$ 

(iii) the recession function of 

$$
f (z) := A z \cdot z,
$$

where A is a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m \times m }$ , is 

$$
f ^ {\infty} \left(z\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \infty & \text { if } A z \neq 0, \\ 0 & \text { if } A z = 0. \end{array} \right.
$$

The next result shows that the recession function is of interest only for convex functions that are not superlinear at infinity. 

Theorem 4.73. Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a proper convex lower semicontinuous function. Then 

$$
\liminf _ {| z | \to \infty} \frac {f \left(z\right)}{| z |} = \inf _ {| z | = 1} f ^ {\infty} \left(z\right).
$$

Proof. By (4.29), 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \inf _ {| z | = 1} f ^ {\infty} (z) = \inf _ {| z | = 1} \inf \left\{t \in \mathbb {R}: (z, t) \in \operatorname{epi} f ^ {\infty} \right\} \\ = \inf _ {| z | = 1} \inf \left\{t \in \mathbb {R}: (z, t) \in (\operatorname{epi} f) ^ {\infty} \right\}. \end{array}
$$

Since f is convex and lower semicontinuous, by Propositions 3.10 and 4.22, epi f is closed and convex, and by Theorem 4.67 (iii) we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \inf _ {| z | = 1} f ^ {\infty} (z) = \inf _ {| z | = 1} \inf \left\{t \in \mathbb {R}: (z, t) \in (\operatorname{epi} f) ^ {\infty} \right\} \\ \quad = \inf _ {| z | = 1} \inf \left\{t \in \mathbb {R}: \text {there are} (w _ {n}, t _ {n}) \in \operatorname{epi} f, \theta_ {n} \to 0 ^ {+}, \right. \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \text {such that} \theta_ {n} (w _ {n}, t _ {n}) \to (z, t) \} \\ \quad = \inf \left\{t \in \mathbb {R}: \text {there are} (w _ {n}, t _ {n}) \in \operatorname{epi} f, \theta_ {n} \to 0 ^ {+}, \right. \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \text {such that} | \theta_ {n} w _ {n} | \to 1, \theta_ {n} t _ {n} \to t \} \\ \quad = \inf \left\{t \in \mathbb {R}: \text {there are} w _ {n} \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}, \theta_ {n} \to 0 ^ {+}, \right. \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \text {such that} | \theta_ {n} w _ {n} | \to 1, \theta_ {n} f (w _ {n}) \to t \} \\ \quad = \inf \left\{t \in \mathbb {R}: \text {there is} w _ {n} \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}, \text {such that} | w _ {n} | \to \infty , \frac {f (w _ {n})}{| w _ {n} |} \to t \right\} \\ \quad = \liminf _ {| z | \to \infty} \frac {f (z)}{| z |}. \end{array}
$$

This concludes the proof. 

Remark $4 . 7 4$ . The previous theorem continues to hold for nonconvex functions provided $f ^ { \infty }$ is defined as in Remark 4.71. 

## 4.7 Approximation of Convex Functions

In this section we show that every convex lower semicontinuous function f may be written as the supremum of a sequence of afine functions. 

If V is a topological vector space, an afine continuous function $g : V \to { \mathbb { R } }$ is a function of the form 

$$
g (v) = \alpha + \langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V},
$$

where $v ^ { \prime } \in V ^ { \prime }$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ 

Proposition 4.75. Let V be a locally convex topological vector space and let $f : V  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a convex and lower semicontinuous function. Then 

(i) there exists an afine continuous function g such that $g \leq f$ ; 

(ii) $f ( v ) = \operatorname* { s u p } \{ g ( v ) : g$ afine continuous, $g \leq f \}$ 

Proof. (i) If $f \equiv \infty$ , then the result is immediate. So assume that there exists $v _ { 0 } \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f ,$ , and fix $t _ { 0 } < f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ . By the second geometric form of the Hahn– Banach theorem, with $C : = \mathrm { e p i } f , K : = \{ ( v _ { 0 } , t _ { 0 } ) \}$ , there exist a continuous linear functional $L : V \times \mathbb { R } \to \mathbb { R }$ and two numbers $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that 

$$
L (v, f (v)) \geq \alpha + \varepsilon \quad \text { for   all } v \in \operatorname{dom} _ {e} f \text { and } L (v _ {0}, t _ {0}) \leq \alpha - \varepsilon .
$$

The functional L has the form $L \left( v , t \right) = \langle v ^ { \prime } , v \rangle _ { V ^ { \prime } , V } + \alpha _ { 0 } t$ for some $\boldsymbol { v } ^ { \prime } \in V ^ { \prime }$ and $\alpha _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R }$ . Hence 

$$
\langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} + \alpha_ {0} f (v) \geq \alpha + \varepsilon \quad \text { for   all } v \in \operatorname{dom} _ {e} f \text { and } \langle v ^ {\prime}, v _ {0} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} + \alpha_ {0} t _ {0} \leq \alpha - \varepsilon .
$$

Taking $v = v _ { 0 }$ we get $\langle v ^ { \prime } , v _ { 0 } \rangle _ { V ^ { \prime } , V } + \alpha _ { 0 } f \left( v _ { 0 } \right) \geq \alpha + \varepsilon > \alpha - \varepsilon \geq \langle v ^ { \prime } , v _ { 0 } \rangle _ { V ^ { \prime } , V } +$ $\alpha _ { 0 } t _ { 0 }$ , and since $t _ { 0 } < f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ it follows that $\alpha _ { 0 } > 0$ and thus 

$$
f (v) \geq g (v) := - \left\langle \alpha_ {0} ^ {- 1} v ^ {\prime}, v \right\rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} + \alpha_ {0} ^ {- 1} (\alpha + \varepsilon) \quad \text { for   all } v \in \operatorname{dom} _ {e} f.
$$

Hence $f \geq g$ in V. 

(ii) If $f \equiv \infty$ , then the result is immediate, so assume as before that there exists $v _ { 0 } \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ . For any fixed $t _ { 0 } < f \left( v _ { 0 } \right)$ , we claim that there exists an afine function g below f with $g ( v _ { 0 } ) \geq t _ { 0 }$ . Indeed, it sufices to observe that in the construction in part (i), 

$$
g (v _ {0}) = - \langle \alpha_ {0} ^ {- 1} v ^ {\prime}, v _ {0} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} + \alpha_ {0} ^ {- 1} (\alpha + \varepsilon) \geq t _ {0}.
$$

This completes the proof. 

Remark 4.76. If f takes the value −∞, then (i) fails, and thus the right-hand side in (ii) is identically $- \infty$ , while there exist functions $f : V  \{ - \infty , \infty \}$ that are convex and lower semicontinuous with $f \not \equiv - \infty$ . As an example let $V = \mathbb { R }$ and define 

$$
f (z) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \infty & \mathrm{if} z > 0, \\ - \infty & \mathrm{if} z \leq 0. \end{array} \right.
$$

When more is known about the space V it may be possible to restrict the supremum in part (ii) of the previous proposition to a countable family of afine functions. For simplicity, here we address the case $V = \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Proposition 4.77. Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be convex and lower semicontinuous. Then 

$$
f (z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot z \right\}\tag{4.36}
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and for some $a _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } , b _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Moreover, 

$$
f ^ {\infty} (z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{b _ {i} \cdot z \right\}\tag{4.37}
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

We begin with a preliminary result based on Lindel¨of’s theorem. 

Proposition 4.78. Let $A \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be an open set, let ${ \mathcal { G } } \subset C \left( A \right)$ , and let 

$$
f = \sup _ {g \in \mathcal {G}} g.\tag{4.38}
$$

Then there exists a countable subfamily $\mathcal { G } _ { 1 } \subset \mathcal { G }$ such that 

$$
f = \sup _ {g \in \mathcal {G} _ {1}} g.
$$

Proof. The space $C \left( A \right)$ has a countable base of open sets when it is endowed with the topology compatible with the metric 

$$
d \left(g, h\right) := \max _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}} \frac {\left\| g - h \right\| _ {C (K _ {n})}}{1 + \left\| g - h \right\| _ {C (K _ {n})}},
$$

where 

$$
A = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} K _ {n},
$$

$K _ { n }$ is compact, nonempty, and $K _ { n }$ is contained in the interior of $K _ { n + 1 }$ . Let 

$$
\mathcal {A} _ {1} := \left\{B (g, r): g \in \mathcal {G}, 0 <   r \leq 1 \right\}.
$$

By Lindel¨of’s theorem, $\mathcal { A } _ { 1 }$ admits a countable subfamily $\mathcal { D } _ { 1 }$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {G} \subset \bigcup_ {B (g, r) \in \mathcal {A} _ {1}} B (g, r) = \bigcup_ {B (g, r) \in \mathcal {D} _ {1}} B (g, r).
$$

Inductively, for every $k \in \mathbb N$ let 

$$
\mathcal {A} _ {k} := \left\{B (g, r): g \in \mathcal {G}, 0 <   r \leq \frac {1}{k} \right\},
$$

and again by Lindel¨of’s theorem we may find a countable subfamily $\mathcal { D } _ { k } \subset \mathcal { A } _ { k }$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {G} \subset \bigcup_ {B (g, r) \in \mathcal {A} _ {k}} B (g, r) = \bigcup_ {B (g, r) \in \mathcal {D} _ {k}} B (g, r).\tag{4.39}
$$

Write 

$$
\mathcal {D} _ {k} = \left\{B \left(g _ {j} ^ {(k)}, r _ {j} ^ {(k)}\right): j \in \mathbb {N} \right\}.
$$

We claim that 

$$
f = \sup _ {j, k \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{g _ {j} ^ {(k)} \right\}.\tag{4.40}
$$

Indeed, by (4.38), 

$$
f \geq \sup _ {j, k \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{g _ {j} ^ {(k)} \right\}.
$$

Conversely, fix $z \in A$ and let $t < f \left( z \right)$ . By (4.38) we may find $g \in { \mathcal { G } }$ such that 

$$
t <   g (z).\tag{4.41}
$$

Let $\begin{array} { r } { 0 < \varepsilon < \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left( g \left( z \right) - t \right) } \end{array}$ , and let $n \in \mathbb N$ be such that $z \in K _ { n }$ and let $k _ { 1 } \in \mathbb { N }$ be large enough that 

$$
2 ^ {n} \leq \varepsilon k _ {1}.\tag{4.42}
$$

By (4.39) there exist $g _ { j _ { 1 } } ^ { ( k _ { 1 } ) }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { 0 < r _ { j _ { 1 } } ^ { ( k _ { 1 } ) } \le \frac { 1 } { k _ { 1 } } } \end{array}$ such that $g \in B \left( g _ { j _ { 1 } } ^ { ( k _ { 1 } ) } , r _ { j _ { 1 } } ^ { ( k _ { 1 } ) } \right)$ In particular, 

$$
\frac {1}{2 ^ {n}} \frac {\left\| g - g _ {j _ {1}} ^ {(k _ {1})} \right\| _ {C (K _ {n})}}{1 + \left\| g - g _ {j _ {1}} ^ {(k _ {1})} \right\| _ {C (K _ {n})}} \leq r _ {j _ {1}} ^ {(k _ {1})}.
$$

Hence 

$$
\left| g (z) - g _ {j _ {1}} ^ {(k _ {1})} (z) \right| \leq \left\| g - g _ {j _ {1}} ^ {(k _ {1})} \right\| _ {C (K _ {n})} \leq \frac {2 ^ {n} r _ {j _ {1}} ^ {(k _ {1})}}{1 - 2 ^ {n} r _ {j _ {1}} ^ {(k _ {1})}} <   2 \varepsilon ,
$$

where we have used (4.42). By (4.41) and the fact that $\begin{array} { r } { 0 < \varepsilon < \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left( g \left( z \right) - t \right) } \end{array}$ we deduce that 

$$
t <   g (z) - 2 \varepsilon \leq g _ {j _ {1}} ^ {(k _ {1})} (z) \leq \sup _ {j, k \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{g _ {j} ^ {(k)} \right\} (z),
$$

and given the arbitrariness of $t < f \left( z \right)$ we obtain (4.40). 

Proof (Proposition 4.77). By Proposition 4.75(ii), 

$$
f (z) = \sup \left\{g (z): g \text {   affine   continuous }, g \leq f \right\}
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , and (4.36) follows from Proposition 4.78. To prove (4.37) fix $w \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ and let $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Then for every $i \in \mathbb N$ and by Theorem 4.70, 

$$
f ^ {\infty} (z) = \lim _ {t \rightarrow \infty} \frac {f (w + t z) - f (w)}{t} \geq \lim _ {t \rightarrow \infty} \frac {a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot (w + t z) - f (w)}{t} = b _ {i} \cdot z.
$$

Therefore 

$$
f ^ {\infty} (z) \geq \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{b _ {i} \cdot z \right\}
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Conversely, for $t > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\frac {f (w + t z) - f (w)}{t} = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \frac {a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot (w + t z) - f (w)}{t}} \\ & {\qquad \leq \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} b _ {i} \cdot z + \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \frac {a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot w - f (w)}{t} = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} b _ {i} \cdot z,} \end{array}
$$

and this concludes the proof of (4.37). 

In the case that f is real-valued it is possible to give an explicit characterization of the coeficients $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { i }$ in the previous proposition. 

Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  \mathbb { R }$ be a convex function and let $\varphi \in C _ { c } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ be any function with $\varphi \geq 0$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { m } } \varphi \left( z \right) d z = 1 } \end{array}$ . Define 

$$
\begin{array}{l} a _ {\varphi} := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (z) ((m + 1) \varphi (z) + \nabla \varphi (z) \cdot z) d z, \\ b _ {\varphi} := - \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (z) \nabla \varphi (z) d z. \end{array}
$$

When necessary we will also write $a _ { \varphi } \left( f \right)$ and $b _ { \varphi } \left( f \right)$ to highlight the dependence on $f .$ 

Theorem 4.79 (De Giorgi). Let f and $\varphi$ be as above. Then 

(i) $f \left( z \right) \geq a _ { \varphi } + b _ { \varphi } \cdot z \ \mathrm { f o r \ a l l } \ z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ;$ 

(ii) $\begin{array} { r } { f \left( z \right) = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { k \in \mathbb { N } , q \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { m } } \left\{ a _ { \varphi _ { k , q } } + b _ { \varphi _ { k , q } } \cdot z \right\} } \end{array}$ for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , where 

$$
\varphi_ {k, q} (z) := k ^ {m} \varphi (k (q - z)), \quad z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}.\tag{4.43}
$$

Proof. (i) Assume first that $f \in C ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Then by Theorem 4.61, for any $z ,$ $\xi \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ we have 

$$
f (z) \geq f (\xi) + \nabla f (\xi) \cdot (z - \xi).
$$

Multiply the previous inequality by $\varphi \left( \xi \right)$ and integrate in $\xi$ over $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ to obtain 

$$
f (z) \geq \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} (f (\xi) - \nabla f (\xi) \cdot \xi) \varphi (\xi) d \xi + z \cdot \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \nabla f (\xi) \varphi (\xi) d \xi .
$$

Integrating by parts now yields 

$$
f (z) \geq \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (\xi) ((m + 1) \varphi (\xi) + \nabla \varphi (\xi) \cdot \xi) d \xi - z \cdot \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (\xi) \nabla \varphi (\xi) d \xi .
$$

This proves (i) when $f \in C ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . In the general case, let $\psi _ { \varepsilon }$ be a standard mollifier. Applying the previous inequality to the smooth convex function $f _ { \varepsilon } : = \psi _ { \varepsilon } *$ f gives 

$$
f _ {\varepsilon} (z) \geq \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f _ {\varepsilon} (\xi) ((m + 1) \varphi (\xi) + \nabla \varphi (\xi) \cdot \xi) d \xi - z \cdot \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f _ {\varepsilon} (\xi) \nabla \varphi (\xi) d \xi .
$$

Since $\varphi$ has compact support, by Theorem 2.75 we may now let $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ 

(ii) Let $k \in \mathbb { N } , q \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ . By replacing the function $\varphi$ with $\varphi _ { k , q }$ in (i) we obtain 

$$
f (z) \geq a _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} + b _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} \cdot z \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}
$$

and hence $f \geq g$ , where 

$$
g \left(z\right) := \sup _ {k \in \mathbb {N}, q \in \mathbb {Q} ^ {m}} \left\{a _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} + b _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} \cdot z \right\}.
$$

Since $g$ is everywhere finite and convex, it is continuous, and so is $f$ (see Corollary 4.38). Hence, to prove (ii) it sufices to show that 

$$
f (q) = g (q) \text {   for   all   } q \in \mathbb {Q} ^ {m},
$$

since $\mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ is dense in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

For $k \in \mathbb { N } , q \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} a _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} + b _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} \cdot z \\ = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f \left(\xi\right) (m + 1)   k ^ {m} \varphi \left(k \left(q - \xi\right)\right) - k ^ {m + 1} \nabla \varphi \left(k \left(q - \xi\right)\right) \cdot (\xi - z) d \xi \\ = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f \left(q - \frac {w}{k}\right) \left((m + 1)   \varphi \left(w\right) - \nabla \varphi \left(w\right) \cdot (k \left(q - z\right) - w)\right) d w, \end{array}
$$

where we have made the change of variables $w = k \left( q - \xi \right)$ . Taking $z = q$ we obtain 

$$
a _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} + b _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} \cdot q = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f \left(q - \frac {w}{k}\right) ((m + 1) \varphi (w) + \nabla \varphi (w) \cdot w) d w.
$$

Since the integrand is continuous and with compact support, we may let $k \to \infty$ to get 

$$
\lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} a _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} + b _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} \cdot q = f (q) \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} ((m + 1) \varphi (w) + \nabla \varphi (w) \cdot w) d w = f (q),
$$

where we have used the facts that 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi (w) d w = 1, \quad \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \nabla \varphi (w) \cdot w d w = - m \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi (w) d w = - m.
$$

Since 

$$
f (q) = \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} a _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} + b _ {\varphi_ {k, q}} \cdot q \leq g (q),
$$

(ii) follows. 

A simple use of the approximation result given in Proposition 4.75 gives an extension of Jensen’s inequality for real-valued functions to functions that may take the value ∞. We begin with the real-valued case. 

Theorem 4.80 (Jensen’s inequality). Let V be a Banach space and let $f : V \to \mathbb { R }$ be bounded from above in a neighborhood of a point. Then f is convex if and only if given any probability measure µ on a measurable space (X, M), where X has at least two distinct elements, and any function $g \in$ ${ \cal L } ^ { 1 } \left( \left( X , \mathfrak { M } , \mu \right) ; V \right)$ , then 

$$
f \left(\int_ {X} g d \mu\right) \leq \int_ {X} f \circ g d \mu .\tag{4.44}
$$

Proof. Assume that Jensen’s inequality (4.44) holds, and let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ be as in the statement. Fix $z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } \in V$ and $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ . Set 

$$
\mu := \theta \delta_ {x _ {1}} + (1 - \theta) \delta_ {x _ {2}},
$$

where $x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } \in X , x _ { 1 } \neq x _ { 2 }$ . Define 

$$
g \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} z _ {1} \text {   if   } x = x _ {1}, \\ z _ {2} \text {   otherwise }. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then 

$$
f \left(\int_ {X} g d \mu\right) \leq \int_ {X} f \circ g d \mu
$$

becomes 

$$
f \left(\theta g \left(x _ {1}\right) + (1 - \theta) g \left(x _ {2}\right)\right) \leq \theta \left(f \circ g\right) \left(x _ {1}\right) + (1 - \theta) \left(f \circ g\right) \left(x _ {2}\right),
$$

that is, 

$$
f \left(\theta z _ {1} + (1 - \theta) z _ {2}\right) \leq \theta f \left(z _ {1}\right) + (1 - \theta) f \left(z _ {2}\right),
$$

and so $f$ is convex. 

Conversely, assume that f is convex. Then by Proposition 4.42 and The orem 4.51, for every $v _ { 0 } \in V$ there exists $v ^ { \prime } \in V ^ { \prime }$ such that 

$$
f (v) \geq f (v _ {0}) + \langle v ^ {\prime}, v - v _ {0} \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \quad \text { for   all } v \in V.
$$

Let $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ and g be as in the statement and set 

$$
v _ {0} := \int_ {X} g d \mu .
$$

Then 

$$
f (g (w)) \geq f \left(\int_ {X} g d \mu\right) + \left\langle v ^ {\prime}, g (w) - \int_ {X} g d \mu \right\rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} \quad \text { for   all } w \in X.
$$

Integrating with respect to $\mu$ yields 

$$
\int_ {X} f (g (w)) d \mu (w) \geq f (\int_ {X} g d \mu),
$$

which is the desired inequality. 

We now extend Jensen’s inequality to the case that f may take the value ∞. 

Corollary 4.81. Let V be a Banach space and let $f : V  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a convex, lower semicontinuous function. Given any probability measure $\mu$ on a measurable space (X, M) and any function $g \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) ; V \right)$ , then 

$$
f \left(\int_ {X} g d \mu\right) \leq \int_ {X} f \circ g d \mu .\tag{4.45}
$$

Proof. By Proposition 4.75, 

$$
f (v) = \sup \left\{h (v): h \text {   affine   continuous }, h \leq f \right\}.
$$

Let h be any afine function such that $f \geq h$ . If X has only one element, then (4.45) holds as equality. Otherwise, applying Jensen’s inequality to h we have 

$$
\int_ {X} f \circ g d \mu \geq \int_ {X} h \circ g d \mu \geq h \left(\int_ {X} g d \mu\right),
$$

and taking the supremum over all afine functions h below f yields 

$$
\int_ {X} f \circ g d \mu \geq f \left(\int_ {X} g d \mu\right).
$$

This concludes the proof. 

Exercise 4.82. Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a lower semicontinuous function and let $Q \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be the unit cube. Prove that f is convex if and only if 

$$
f (z) \leq \int_ {Q} f (z + v (x)) d x
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and all Q-periodic functions $v \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ <sub>, with</sub> 

$$
\int_ {Q} v (x) d x = 0,
$$

for which the right-hand side of the previous inequality is well-defined. 

## 4.8 Convex Envelopes

As we will see in relaxation problems, in the case of nonconvex integrands f one is interested in “convexifying” f. This brings us to various notions of convex envelopes. 

Definition 4.83. Let V be a vector space and let $f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ . The convex envelope $\mathcal { C } f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ of f is defined by 

$$
\mathcal {C} f (v) := \sup \left\{g (v): g: V \rightarrow [ - \infty , \infty ] \text {   convex,   } g \leq f \right\}.
$$

The following result relates the convex envelope of a function with the convex hull of its epigraph. 

Theorem 4.84. Let V be a vector space and let $f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ . Then 

$$
\mathrm{dom} _ {e} \mathcal {C} f = \mathrm{co} (\mathrm{dom} _ {e} f)
$$

and 

$$
\mathcal {C} f (v) = \inf \left\{t \in \mathbb {R}: (v, t) \in \operatorname{co} (\operatorname{epi} f) \right\}, \quad v \in V.
$$

Proof. If $v \in \mathop { \mathrm { c o } } \left( \mathop { \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } } f \right)$ , then by Proposition 4.2, v can be written as a convex combination of elements of $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ , that is, 

$$
v = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \theta_ {i} v _ {i}
$$

for some $n \in \mathbb { N } , \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \theta _ { i } = 1 , \theta _ { i } \geq 0 , v _ { i } \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f .$ . Since $\mathcal { C } f \leq f .$ , it follows that $v _ { i } \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } \mathcal { C } f .$ Since dom $. . e ^ { \textstyle \mathcal { C } f }$ is a convex set, we have that $v \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } \mathcal { C } f$ and so $\mathrm { c o } \left( \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f \right) \subset \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } \mathcal { C } f$ . To prove the converse inclusion, note that the function 

$$
g \left(v\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} - \infty \text {   if   } v \in \operatorname{co} \left(\operatorname{dom} _ {e} f\right), \\ \infty \quad \text { otherwise }, \end{array} \right.

is convex and below f, and so $g \leq \mathcal { C } f$ , which implies that

\operatorname{co} \left(\operatorname{dom} _ {e} f\right) = \operatorname{dom} _ {e} g \supset \operatorname{dom} _ {e} \mathcal {C} f.

To prove the second part of the theorem define 

$$
h (v) := \inf \left\{t \in \mathbb {R}: (v, t) \in \operatorname{co} (\operatorname{epi} f) \right\}, \quad v \in V.
$$

Since co (epi f) is a convex set, by Proposition 4.22 it follows that h is convex. Moreover, if $v \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f ,$ , then $( v , f ( v ) ) \in \mathrm { e p i } f \subset \mathrm { c o } ( \mathrm { e p i } f )$ , and so $h \left( v \right) \leq$ $f \left( v \right)$ . Hence by the definition of convex envelope we have that 

$$

$$

To prove the reverse inequality let $g : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be any convex function, with $g \leq f$ . Then epi $f \subset \operatorname { e p i } g$ , and since epi g is a convex set by Proposition 4.22, we have that

\operatorname{co} \left(\operatorname{epi} f\right) \subset \operatorname{epi} g.

Hence for every $v \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} g \left(v\right) = \inf \left\{t \in \mathbb {R}: \left(v, t\right) \in \operatorname{epi} g \right\} \\ \leq \inf \left\{t \in \mathbb {R}: \left(v, t\right) \in \operatorname{co} \left(\operatorname{epi} f\right) \right\} = h \left(v\right). \end{array}\tag{4.46}
$$

On the other hand, if $v \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } h$ , then there exists $t \in \mathbb R$ such that $( v , t ) \in$ co $) ( \mathrm { e p i } f )$ . In particular, we may write

$$

for some $n \in \mathbb { N } , \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \theta _ { i } = 1 , \theta _ { i } \geq 0 , v _ { i } \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ . Hence $v \in \mathrm { c o } ( \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f ) =$ $\operatorname { d o m } _ { e } \mathcal { C } f$ by the first part of the proof. Since $g \left( v \right) \leq \mathcal { C } f \left( v \right) < \infty$ , it follows that $v \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g ,$ . Thus $\mathrm { d o m } _ { e } h \subset \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } g$ , which implies that the inequality (4.46) holds everywhere. Another type of convex envelope is obtained by restricting the class of admissible functions below f to afine continuous functions. 

Definition 4.86. Given a dual pair (V, W) and a function $f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ , the polar or conjugate function $f ^ { * } : W \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ of f is defined by 

$$
f ^ {*} (w) := \sup _ {v \in V} \left\{\langle v, w \rangle_ {V, W} - f (v) \right\}, \quad w \in W,
$$

and the bipolar or biconjugate function $f ^ { * * } : V \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ of f is defined by 

$$
f ^ {* *} (v) := \sup _ {w \in W} \left\{\langle v, w \rangle_ {V, W} - f ^ {*} (w) \right\}, \quad v \in V.
$$

The spaces $V , W$ are endowed with the topologies $\sigma \left( V , W \right)$ and $\sigma \left( W , V \right)$ respectively. Since $f ^ { * }$ is the supremum of a family of continuous and convex functions, $f ^ { * }$ is convex and lower semicontinuous. The same holds true for $f ^ { * * }$ , and $f ^ { * * } \leq f$ . Even when $f$ is convex and lower semicontinuous it may happen that $f ^ { * * } \neq f$ . Indeed, if $f$ takes the value $- \infty$ at some point and $f \not \equiv - \infty$ (see Proposition 4.26), then $f ^ { * } \equiv \infty$ , and in turn, $f ^ { * * } \equiv - \infty$ 

Remark 4.87. If V is a topological vector space and $f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ , then we may take $W$ to be the topological dual of V, so that 

$$
f ^ {*} \left(v ^ {\prime}\right) = \sup _ {v \in V} \left\{\langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} - f (v) \right\}, \quad v ^ {\prime} \in V ^ {\prime},
$$

and 

$$
f ^ {* *} (v) = \sup _ {v ^ {\prime} \in V ^ {\prime}} \left\{\langle v ^ {\prime}, v \rangle_ {V ^ {\prime}, V} - f ^ {*} (v ^ {\prime}) \right\}, \quad v \in V.
$$

In what follows, whenever the space $W$ is not specified, it is understood that $W : = V ^ { \prime }$ 

Proposition 4.88. Let $( V , W )$ be a dual pair and $f : V  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ . Then 

$$
f ^ {*} = f ^ {* * *}.
$$

Proof. From the definition of $f ^ { * * }$ we have that 

$$
f ^ {* *} (v) \geq \langle v, w \rangle_ {V, W} - f ^ {*} (w)
$$

for all $v \in V$ and $w \in W$ . Therefore 

$$
f ^ {*} (w) \geq f ^ {* * *} (w) = \sup _ {v \in V} \left\{\langle v, w \rangle_ {V, W} - f ^ {* *} (v) \right\}.
$$

Conversely, 

$$
f ^ {* * *} (w) \geq \langle v, w \rangle_ {V, W} - f ^ {* *} (v) \geq \langle v, w \rangle_ {V, W} - f (v)
$$

for all $v \in V$ and $w \in W$ , where we have used the fact that $f ^ { * * } \leq f$ . Taking the supremum over all $v \in V$ , we conclude that 

$$
f ^ {* * *} (w) \geq f ^ {*} (w)
$$

for all $w \in W$ , and this completes the proof.

Theorem 4.91. Let V be a topological vector space, let $f : V  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a convex function not identically equal to $\infty _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , and let $( v , v ^ { \prime } ) \in V \times V ^ { \prime }$ . Then $v ^ { \prime } \in \partial f \left( v \right)$ if and only if

The second part of the theorem is a consequence of Theorems 4.96 and Theorem 4.40.

Remark 4.99. (i) Note that under the assumptions of the previous theorem,

Moreover, $\gamma ^ { * * }$ is continuous since $\gamma$ is real-valued and nonnegative. Here we recall Remark 2.30.
