As a consequence of the previous theorem we have the following proposition: 

Proposition 4.100. Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be bounded from below by an afine function. Let $\{ \varphi _ { j } \}$ be a decreasing sequence of upper semicontinuous functions $\varphi _ { j } : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {j \to \infty} \varphi_ {j} (z) = 0
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and 

$$
\lim _ {| z | \to \infty} \frac {\varphi_ {j} (z)}{| z |} = \infty .\tag{4.59}
$$

Then 

$$
\mathcal {C} \left(\operatorname{lsc} f\right) = \inf _ {j \in \mathbb {N}} \left(f + \varphi_ {j}\right) ^ {* *}.
$$

Proof. By hypothesis there exist $( \alpha , \beta ) \in \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
f (z) \geq \alpha + \beta \cdot z\tag{4.60}
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Fix $j \in \mathbb N$ . By (4.59), (4.60) it follows that 

$$
\lim _ {| z | \to \infty} \frac {(f + \varphi_ {j}) (z)}{| z |} = \infty .
$$

By (4.59) we may find $M > 0$ such that $\varphi _ { j } \left( z \right) \geq \left| \beta \right| \left| z \right|$ whenever $| z | \geq M$ , which, together with (4.60), entails 

$$
(f + \varphi_ {j}) \geq \alpha - | \beta | M.
$$

By Theorem 4.98 and Remark 4.99(iii) we have 

$$
\left(f + \varphi_ {j}\right) ^ {* *} = \mathcal {C} \left(\operatorname{lsc} \left(f + \varphi_ {j}\right)\right)
$$

and thus 

$$
\mathcal {C} \left(\operatorname{lsc} f\right) \leq \inf _ {j \in \mathbb {N}} \left(f + \varphi_ {j}\right) ^ {* *}.\tag{4.61}
$$

To prove the reverse inequality, note first that since $\varphi _ { j }$ is upper semicontinuous, then lsc $( f + \varphi _ { j } ) - \varphi _ { j }$ is lower semicontinuous and below $f .$ . Therefore lsc $\left( f + \varphi _ { j } \right) - \varphi _ { j } \leq$ lsc f, or equivalently, 

$$
\operatorname{lsc} \left(f + \varphi_ {j}\right) \leq \operatorname{lsc} f + \varphi_ {j} \quad \text { for   each } j \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Hence for every $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and by the fact that the bipolar is lower semicontin uous, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \inf _ {j \in \mathbb {N}} (f + \varphi_ {j}) ^ {* *} (z) = \lim _ {j \to \infty} (f + \varphi_ {j}) ^ {* *} (z) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \lim _ {j \to \infty} \operatorname{lsc} (f + \varphi_ {j}) (z) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \operatorname{lsc} f (z) + \lim _ {j \to \infty} \varphi_ {j} (z) = \operatorname{lsc} f (z). \end{array}\tag{4.62}
$$

Here we have used the fact that since the sequence $\{ \varphi _ { j } \}$ is decreasing, then so are the sequences $\left\{ { \left( { f + \varphi _ { j } } \right) ^ { * * } } \right\}$ and {lsc $( f + \varphi _ { j } ) \}$ . In particular, 

$$
\inf _ {j \in \mathbb {N}} (f + \varphi_ {j}) ^ {* *} = \lim _ {j \to \infty} (f + \varphi_ {j}) ^ {* *}
$$

is a convex function, and thus from (4.62) we deduce that 

$$
\inf _ {j \in \mathbb {N}} (f + \varphi_ {j}) ^ {* *} \leq \mathcal {C} (\operatorname{lsc} f).
$$

This, together with (4.61), gives the result. 

Remark 4.101. When condition (4.59) is violated one can conclude only that 

$$
f ^ {* *} \leq \inf _ {j \in \mathbb {N}} (f + \varphi_ {j}) ^ {* *} \leq \mathcal {C} (\operatorname{lsc} f).

However, if $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  \mathbb { R }$ satisfies (4.60), then in view of Remark 4.93 we have that

$$

A result in the same spirit of the previous proposition is the following. 

Proposition 4.102. Let {f } $\{ f _ { j } \}$ be an increasing sequence of lower semicontinuous functions $f _ { j } : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that

## 4.9 Star-Shaped Sets

Given a vector space $V ,$ a set $E \subset V$ is said to be star-shaped with respect to a set $F \subset E$ if E is star-shaped with respect to each point of $F , { \mathrm { i . e . } }$ , if $\theta v + ( 1 - \theta ) w \in E$ for all $v \in F , w \in E$ , and $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ 

If $V = \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is star-shaped with respect to a point $z _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , the function $\varphi : S ^ { m - 1 }  [ 0 , \infty ]$ , defined by 

$$
\varphi (z) := \sup \left\{s \geq 0: z _ {0} + s z \in E \right\} \quad z \in S ^ {m - 1},
$$

is called the radial function of the set E. In the next theorem, we assume, without loss of generality, that $z _ { 0 } = 0$ and for any $z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } \in S ^ { m - 1 }$ we define d $( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } )$ to be the measure of the angle formed by the vectors $z _ { 1 }$ and $z _ { 2 }$ . 

Exercise 4.106. Consider the ball $B \left( 0 , r \right) \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , let w $\notin B \left( 0 , r \right)$ , and define 

$$
C := \operatorname{co} (B (0, r) \cup \{w \}).
$$

Let $\varphi$ be the radial function of C. Prove that 

$$
\varphi \left(z\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} r & \text {   if   } z \in S ^ {m - 1} \\ & \text {   and   } d \left(z _ {1}, z\right) \geq \arccos \frac {r}{| w |}, \\ \frac {r}{\cos \left(\arccos \frac {r}{| w |} - d \left(z _ {1} , z\right)\right)} & \text {   if   } z \in S ^ {m - 1} \\ & \text {   and   } d \left(z _ {1}, z\right) <   \arccos \frac {r}{| w |}. \end{array} \right.
$$

Theorem 4.107. Assume that $C \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is a bounded closed set, star-shaped with respect to a ball $B \left( 0 , \varepsilon \right) \subset C$ , and let $B \left( 0 , R \right) \supset C$ . Then for all $z _ { 1 }$ , $z _ { 2 } \in S ^ { m - 1 }$ , 

$$
\left| \varphi \left(z _ {1}\right) - \varphi \left(z _ {2}\right) \right| \leq \left(R \sqrt {\left(\frac {R}{\varepsilon}\right) ^ {2} - 1}\right) d \left(z _ {1}, z _ {2}\right).\tag{4.74}
$$

We begin with a preliminary result that is of independent interest. Given an arbitrary nonempty set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , a convex component of E is a maximal (in the sense of inclusion) convex subset of E. The kernel of $E .$ , denoted by ker $E _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ , is the set 

ker $E : = \{ z \in E : \theta z + ( 1 - \theta ) w \in E$ for all $w \in E$ and $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 ) \}$ 

Lemma 4.108. Given an arbitrary nonempty set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , the kernel of E is the intersection of all convex components of E. 

Proof. Let $\{ C _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ be the family of all convex components of E. Define 

$$
C _ {0} := \bigcap_ {\alpha \in I} C _ {\alpha}
$$

and let $z \in C _ { 0 }$ . Since 

$$
E = \bigcup_ {\alpha \in I} C _ {\alpha},
$$

for all $w \in E$ there exists $\alpha \in I$ such that $w \in C _ { \alpha }$ , and so 

$$
\theta z + (1 - \theta) w \in C _ {\alpha} \subset E
$$

for all $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , which implies that $z \in$ ker $E$ and, in turn, that $C _ { 0 } \subset$ ker $E .$ . 

Conversely, let $z \in$ ker E and let $C _ { \alpha }$ be an arbitrary convex component of E. Let 

$$
K _ {\alpha} := \left\{\theta z + (1 - \theta) w: \theta \in [ 0, 1 ], w \in C _ {\alpha} \right\}.
$$

Then $C _ { \alpha } \subset K _ { \alpha }$ and, since $z \in$ ker E, $K _ { \alpha } \subset E$ . Also, $K _ { \alpha }$ is convex, since for any $w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 } \in C _ { \alpha }$ and $\theta , \theta _ { 1 } , \theta _ { 2 } \in ( 0 , 1 )$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \theta (\theta_ {1} z + (1 - \theta_ {1}) w _ {1}) + (1 - \theta) (\theta_ {2} z + (1 - \theta_ {2}) w _ {2}) \\ = [ \theta \theta_ {1} + (1 - \theta) \theta_ {2} ] z + (1 - [ \theta \theta_ {1} + (1 - \theta) \theta_ {2} ]) \\ \times \left[ \frac {\theta (1 - \theta_ {1})}{1 - [ \theta \theta_ {1} + (1 - \theta) \theta_ {2} ]} w _ {1} + \frac {(1 - \theta) (1 - \theta_ {2})}{1 - [ \theta \theta_ {1} + (1 - \theta) \theta_ {2} ]} w _ {2} \right], \end{array}
$$

which is still in $K _ { \alpha }$ since $C _ { \alpha }$ is convex. By the maximality of $C _ { \alpha }$ it follows that $C _ { \alpha } = K _ { \alpha }$ , and so $z \in C _ { \alpha }$ . Given the arbitrariness of $C _ { \alpha }$ we have that $z \in C _ { 0 }$ , which shows that ker $E \subset C _ { 0 }$ , and this completes the proof. 

We are now ready to prove Theorem 4.107. 

Proof (Theorem $\it 4 . 1 0 7 )$ . Step 1: Assume first that C is convex. Let $z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } \in$ $S ^ { m - \overset { \cdot } { 1 } }$ and assume that $\varphi \left( z _ { 2 } \right) \leq \varphi \left( z _ { 1 } \right) : = s _ { 1 }$ . The point $w _ { 1 } : = s _ { 1 } z _ { 1 }$ is in $C ,$ and so the set 

$$
C _ {w _ {1}} := \operatorname{co} (B (0, \varepsilon) \cup \{w _ {1} \})
$$

is contained in C. Hence, $\mathrm { i f } \varphi _ { w _ { 1 } }$ denotes the radial function of $C _ { w _ { 1 } }$ , then $\varphi _ { w _ { 1 } } \leq$ $\varphi$ and $\varphi _ { w _ { 1 } } \left( z _ { 1 } \right) = \varphi \left( z _ { 1 } \right)$ . Moreover, by Exercise 4.106, for any $z \in S ^ { m - 1 }$ 

$$
\varphi_ {w _ {1}} (z) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \varepsilon & \text {if} \theta (z) \geq \theta_ {0}, \\ \frac {\varepsilon}{\cos (\theta_ {0} - \theta (z))} & \text {if} \theta (z) <   \theta_ {0}, \end{array} \right.
$$

where 

$$
\theta (z) := d (z _ {1}, z), \quad \theta_ {0} := \arccos \frac {\varepsilon}{s _ {1}}.
$$

If d $( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } ) ~ > ~ \theta _ { 0 }$ let $z _ { 3 } ~ \in ~ S ^ { m - 1 }$ be a point between $z _ { 1 }$ and $z _ { 2 }$ such that $d \left( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 3 } \right) = \theta _ { 0 }$ , while if d $( z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } ) \le \theta _ { 0 }$ let $z _ { 3 } : = z _ { 2 }$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} g \left(z _ {3}\right) := \frac {\varphi_ {w _ {1}} \left(z _ {1}\right) - \varphi_ {w _ {1}} \left(z _ {3}\right)}{d \left(z _ {1} , z _ {3}\right)} = \frac {s _ {1} - \frac {\varepsilon}{\cos (\theta_ {0} - \theta (z _ {3}))}}{\theta \left(z _ {3}\right)} \\ = \frac {s _ {1} \cos \left(\theta_ {0} - \theta \left(z _ {3}\right)\right) - \varepsilon}{\theta \left(z _ {3}\right) \cos \left(\theta_ {0} - \theta \left(z _ {3}\right)\right)}. \end{array}
$$

Note that $g \left( z _ { 3 } \right)$ increases as $z _ { 3 }$ tends to $z _ { 1 }$ . Moreover, by Taylor’s formula, if $\theta \left( z _ { 3 } \right)$ is small, then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & g (z _ {3}) = \frac {\varepsilon \cos \theta (z _ {3}) + s _ {1} \sqrt {1 - \left(\frac {\varepsilon}{s _ {1}}\right) ^ {2}} \sin \theta (z _ {3}) - \varepsilon}{\theta (z _ {3}) \left[ \frac {\varepsilon}{s _ {1}} \cos \theta (z _ {3}) - \sqrt {1 - \left(\frac {\varepsilon}{s _ {1}}\right) ^ {2}} \sin \theta (z _ {3}) \right]} \\ & \qquad = \frac {s _ {1} \sqrt {1 - \left(\frac {\varepsilon}{s _ {1}}\right) ^ {2}} (1 + o (1))}{\frac {\varepsilon}{s _ {1}} (1 + o (1))} \\ & \qquad = s _ {1} \sqrt {\left(\frac {s _ {1}}{\varepsilon}\right) ^ {2} - 1} (1 + o (1)). \end{array}
$$

Hence 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\varphi (z _ {1}) - \varphi (z _ {2})}{d (z _ {1} , z _ {2})} \leq \frac {\varphi_ {w _ {1}} (z _ {1}) - \varphi_ {w _ {1}} (z _ {2})}{d (z _ {1} , z _ {2})} \\ \quad \leq \frac {\varphi_ {w _ {1}} (z _ {1}) - \varphi_ {w _ {1}} (z _ {3})}{d (z _ {1} , z _ {3})} = g (z _ {3}) \\ \quad \leq R \sqrt {\left(\frac {R}{\varepsilon}\right) ^ {2} - 1}. \end{array}
$$

Step 2: Assume now that $C \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is as in the statement of the problem and let $\{ C _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ be the family of all convex components of C. Since C is starshaped with respect to a ball $B \left( 0 , \varepsilon \right)$ , we have that $B \left( 0 , \varepsilon \right) \subset$ ker C, and so in view of the previous lemma, we may apply the previous step to each convex component $C _ { \alpha }$ of $C .$ . 

We claim that 

$$
\varphi (z) = \max _ {\alpha \in I} \varphi_ {\alpha} (z),\tag{4.75}
$$

where $\varphi _ { \alpha }$ is the radial function of $C _ { \alpha }$ . Indeed, since $C _ { \alpha } \subset C$ for all $\alpha \in I .$ , we have that $\varphi _ { \alpha } \leq \varphi$ . Conversely, if $\varphi \left( z \right) = s$ , then $w : = s z \in C$ , and so we may find $\alpha \in I$ such that $s z \in C _ { \alpha }$ . Thus $\varphi _ { \alpha } \left( z \right) \geq s$ , which, together with the fact that $\varphi \geq \varphi _ { \alpha }$ , shows that $\varphi \left( z \right) = \varphi _ { \alpha } \left( z \right)$ , so that (4.75) holds. 

We are now ready to conclude the proof. For any $z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } \in S ^ { m - 1 }$ assume that $\varphi \left( z _ { 2 } \right) \leq \varphi \left( z _ { 1 } \right)$ and let $\alpha \in I$ be such that $\varphi _ { \alpha } \left( z _ { 1 } \right) = \varphi \left( z _ { 1 } \right)$ . Then by (4.75), 

$$
\frac {\varphi (z _ {1}) - \varphi (z _ {2})}{d (z _ {1} , z _ {2})} = \frac {\varphi_ {\alpha} (z _ {1}) - \varphi (z _ {2})}{d (z _ {1} , z _ {2})} \leq \frac {\varphi_ {\alpha} (z _ {1}) - \varphi_ {\alpha} (z _ {2})}{d (z _ {1} , z _ {2})} \leq R \sqrt {\left(\frac {R}{\varepsilon}\right) ^ {2} - 1}.
$$

This completes the proof. 

Exercise 4.109. Let C be as in Exercise 4.106 and let $R : = | w |$ . Prove that for this set, the constant $R { \sqrt { \left( { \frac { R } { \varepsilon } } \right) ^ { 2 } - 1 } }$ in (4.74) is sharp. 

Functionals Defined on $L ^ { p }$ 

Integrands $f = f \left( z \right)$ 

Mathematics is the science which draws necessary conclusions. 

Benjamin Peirce (1809–1880) 

We study necessary and suficient conditions for the sequential lower semicontinuity of functionals of the form 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x,
$$

where $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ and 

$$
f: \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \to [ - \infty , \infty ].
$$

We assume throughout this chapter that E is a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ . In view of Proposition 1.68 note that without loss of generality we may always assume that the domain of integration E is a Borel set. 

We are interested in the following types of convergence: 

• strong convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ for $1 \leq p \leq \infty ;$ 

• weak convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ for $1 \leq p < \infty$ 

• weak star convergence in $L ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ ); 

• weak star convergence in the sense of measures in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

The reason why the last type of convergence is of interest is that for $1 < p \leq \infty$ , bounded sequences in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ admit weakly convergent subsequences (respectively weakly star if $p = \infty )$ , but when $p = 1$ , due to lack of reflexivity of the space $L ^ { 1 } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ one can conclude only that an energybounded sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ with 

$$
\sup _ {n} \left\| v _ {n} \right\| _ {L ^ {1}} <   \infty
$$

admits a subsequence (not relabeled) such that $v _ { n } { \mathcal { L } } ^ { N } | E \stackrel { * } {  } \lambda$ in $\mathcal { M } \left( \boldsymbol { E } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , i.e., if for all $u \in C _ { 0 } \left( E \right)$ , 

5 Integrands $f = f \left( z \right)$ 

$$
\int_ {E} u v _ {n} d x \rightarrow \int_ {E} u d \lambda
$$

(see Remark 2.51). In particular, we will provide conditions under which the lower semicontinuity property 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f \left(v _ {n}\right) d x \geq \int_ {E} f \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x
$$

holds whenever $v _ { n } { \mathcal { L } } ^ { N } \mid E \ { \stackrel { * } {  } } \ \lambda$ in $\mathcal { M } \left( \boldsymbol { E } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and λ admits the Radon– Nikodym decomposition 

$$
\lambda = \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \lfloor E + \lambda_ {s},
$$

with $\lambda _ { s }$ and $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } | ~ E$ mutually singular. 

The proofs in the next sections use heavily the fact that the Lebesgue measure is nonatomic (see Remark 1.161). 

## 5.1 Well-Posedness

As mentioned in Section 1.1.1, measurability of functions with values in the Euclidean space $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ or in the extended real line $\overline { { \mathbb { R } } } : = [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is understood when these target spaces are endowed with the Borel σ-algebras associated to the respective usual topologies. Therefore if $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m } $ $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ , then measurability of $f \circ v : E  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is ensured provided f is a Borel function. 

Theorem 5.1. Let E be a Borel subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with finite measure, let $1 \leq$ $p \leq \infty$ , and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a Borel function. Then 

$$
\int_ {E} \left(f (v (x))\right) ^ {-} d x <   \infty\tag{5.1}
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ if and only if there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that 

$$
f (z) \geq - C (1 + | z | ^ {p}) f o r a l l z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} i f 1 \leq p <   \infty ,\tag{5.2}
$$

$$
f \text {   is   locally   bounded   from   below   if   } p = \infty .\tag{5.3}
$$

The proof uses the following lemma. 

Lemma 5.2. Let $L > 0$ and let $a _ { n } \to \infty$ . Then there exists $b _ { n } \geq 0$ such that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} b _ {n} \leq L \quad a n d \quad \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} a _ {n} b _ {n} = \infty .
$$

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that $L = 1$ . For every $k \in \mathbb N$ define 

$$
M _ {k} := \min \left\{n: a _ {l} \geq 2 ^ {k} \text {   for   all   } l \geq n \right\}.
$$

Let $\left\{ { M } _ { k _ { j } } \right\}$ be a strictly increasing subsequence of $\{ M _ { k } \}$ , with $k _ { j } \ \geq j$ , and define 

$$
b _ {n} := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0 & \text {if n <   M_{k_{1}}}, \\ \frac {1}{2 ^ {k _ {j}}} \frac {1}{M _ {k _ {j + 1}} - M _ {k _ {j}}} & \text {if M_{k_{j}} \leq n <   M_{k_{j+ 1}}}. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} b _ {n} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {n = M _ {k _ {j}}} ^ {M _ {k _ {j + 1}} - 1} \frac {1}{2 ^ {k _ {j}}} \frac {1}{M _ {k _ {j + 1}} - M _ {k _ {j}}} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {k _ {j}}} \leq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {j}} = 1
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} a _ {n} b _ {n} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {n = M _ {k _ {j}}} ^ {M _ {k _ {j + 1}} - 1} \frac {1}{2 ^ {k _ {j}}} \frac {a _ {n}}{M _ {k _ {j + 1}} - M _ {k _ {j}}} \\ \geq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {n = M _ {k _ {j}}} ^ {M _ {k _ {j + 1}} - 1} \frac {1}{M _ {k _ {j + 1}} - M _ {k _ {j}}} = \infty . \end{array}
$$

This completes the proof. 

We are now ready to prove Theorem 5.1. 

Proof (Theorem 5.1). Note that (5.2) and (5.3) imply (5.1) for $1 \leq p < \infty$ and $p = \infty$ , respectively. 

Conversely, assume that (5.1) is satisfied. By considering constant functions, it follows that f cannot take the value $- \infty$ 

Step 1: Suppose first that $1 \leq p < \infty$ . Assume by contradiction that (5.2) does not hold. Then we can find a sequence $\{ z _ { n } \} \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {f (z _ {n})}{1 + | z _ {n} | ^ {p}} = - \infty .
$$

By the previous lemma with $L : = | E |$ and 

$$
a _ {n} := - \frac {f (z _ {n})}{1 + | z _ {n} | ^ {p}},
$$

we can find $b _ { n } \geq 0$ such that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} b _ {n} \leq | E | \quad \text { and } \quad \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {f (z _ {n})}{1 + | z _ {n} | ^ {p}} b _ {n} = - \infty .\tag{5.4}
$$

By Corollary 1.21 we may construct a countable family $\{ E _ { n } \}$ of mutually disjoint measurable subsets of $E _ { : }$ , with 

$$
| E _ {n} | = \frac {b _ {n}}{1 + | z _ {n} | ^ {p}}.
$$

Setting 

$$
v := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} z _ {n} \chi_ {E _ {n}},
$$

it now follows from (5.4) that 

$$
\int_ {E} | v | ^ {p} d x = \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} | z _ {n} | ^ {p} | E _ {n} | \leq \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} b _ {n} \leq | E | <   \infty ,
$$

while 

$$
\int_ {E} (f (v)) ^ {-} d x \geq - \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} f (z _ {n}) | E _ {n} | = - \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {f (z _ {n})}{1 + | z _ {n} | ^ {p}} b _ {n} = - \infty .
$$

Step 2: If $p = \infty$ , assume by contradiction that (5.3) does not hold. Then we can find a bounded sequence $\{ z _ { n } \} \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} f (z _ {n}) = - \infty .
$$

By the previous lemma with $L : = | E |$ and $a _ { n } : = - f \left( z _ { n } \right)$ , we can find $b _ { n } \geq 0$ such that 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} b _ {n} \leq | E | \quad \text { and } \quad \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} f (z _ {n}) b _ {n} = - \infty .\tag{5.5}
$$

By Corollary 1.21 we may construct a countable family $\{ E _ { n } \}$ of mutually disjoint measurable subsets of $E$ , with $| E _ { n } | = b _ { n }$ . Setting 

$$
v := \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} z _ {n} \chi_ {E _ {n}},
$$

it now follows from (5.5) and the fact that $\left\{ z _ { n } \right\}$ is bounded that $v \in$ $L ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and 

$$
\int_ {E} (f (v)) ^ {-} d x \geq - \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} f (z _ {n}) | E _ {n} | = - \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} f (z _ {n}) b _ {n} = - \infty .
$$

This concludes the proof. 

Remark 5.3. Applying the previous proposition to f and $- f .$ , it follows that if $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is a Borel function, then $f \circ v \in L ^ { 1 } ( E )$ for every $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ if and only if f does not take the values −∞ and ∞ and, moreover, there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that 

$$
\left| f (z) \right| \leq C \left(1 + | z | ^ {p}\right) \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \text {   if   } 1 \leq p <   \infty ,
$$

f is locally bounded if $p = \infty$ 

Exercise 5.4. Prove that the previous proposition still holds if $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ is replaced by the space $L ^ { p } \left( \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , where $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ is a measure space with $\mu$ finite and nonatomic. What can you conclude if the measure $\mu$ has atoms (recall Proposition 1.22)? 

Exercise 5.5. Let E be a Borel subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with finite measure, let $1 \le p \le$ ∞, and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a Borel function. Prove that the integral $\textstyle \int _ { E } f \left( v \left( x \right) \right)$ dx is well-defined for every $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ (that is, the integrals $\textstyle \int _ { E } { \bigl ( } f \left( v \left( x \right) \right) { \bigr ) } ^ { - }$ dx and $\textstyle \int _ { E } { ( f ( v ( x ) ) ) ^ { + } }$ dx are not both infinite) if and only if $f$ $\mathrm { o } \overline { { \mathrm { r } } } - f \ \mathrm { ( o r \ b o t h ) }$ satisfies condition (5.2) if $1 \leq p < \infty$ and (5.3) if $p = \infty$ 

Next we address the case that E has infinite measure. 

Theorem 5.6. Let E be a Borel subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with infinite measure, let $1 \leq$ $p \leq \infty$ , and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a Borel function. Then 

$$
\int_ {E} \left(f (v (x))\right) ^ {-} d x <   \infty\tag{5.6}
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ if and only if there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that 

$$
f (z) \geq - C | z | ^ {p} \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \text {   if   } 1 \leq p <   \infty ,\tag{5.7}
$$

$$
f (z) \geq 0 \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \text {   if   } p = \infty .\tag{5.8}
$$

Proof. Note that (5.7) and (5.8) imply (5.6) for $1 \leq p < \infty$ and $p = \infty$ respectively. 

Conversely, assume that (5.6) is satisfied. For $p = \infty$ and taking constant functions, we have that f cannot take negative values. 

Consider now the case $1 \leq p < \infty$ . First note that $f > - \infty$ . Indeed, if $f \left( z _ { 0 } \right) = - \infty$ for some $z _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , using the fact that the Lebesgue measure is nonatomic, choose a measurable subset $E _ { 1 } \subset E$ , with $0 < | E _ { 1 } | < \infty$ , and define 

$$
v \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} z _ {0} \text {   if   } x \in E _ {1}, \\ 0 \text {   otherwise }. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and still 

$$
\int_ {E} (f (v)) ^ {-} d x \geq (f (z _ {0})) ^ {-} | E _ {1} | = \infty ,
$$

which violates (5.6). 

Assume by contradiction that (5.7) does not hold. Then we can find a sequence $\{ z _ { n } \} \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {f (z _ {n})}{| z _ {n} | ^ {p}} = - \infty ,
$$

and thus 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {| z _ {n} | ^ {p}}{f (z _ {n})} = 0.
$$

Extract a subsequence $\{ z _ { n _ { k } } \}$ such that 

$$
\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {| z _ {n _ {k}} | ^ {p}}{- f (z _ {n _ {k}})} <   \infty .
$$

By Proposition 1.20 we may construct a countable family $\{ E _ { k } \}$ of mutually disjoint measurable subsets of $E _ { : }$ , with 

$$
| E _ {k} | = - \frac {1}{f (z _ {n _ {k}})}.
$$

Defining 

$$
v := \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} z _ {n _ {k}} \chi_ {E _ {k}},
$$

it now follows that 

$$
\int_ {E} | v | ^ {p} d x = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {| z _ {n _ {k}} | ^ {p}}{- f (z _ {n _ {k}})} <   \infty ,
$$

while 

$$
\int_ {E} \left(f (v)\right) ^ {-} d x \geq - \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} f \left(z _ {n _ {k}}\right) | E _ {k} | = \infty .
$$

Hence we have reached a contradiction, and so (5.7) holds. 

Exercise 5.7. Prove that the previous proposition still holds if $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ is replaced by the space $L ^ { p } \left( \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , where $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ is a measure space with $\mu$ nonatomic. What can you conclude if the measure $\mu$ has atoms (recall Proposition 1.22)? 

Exercise 5.8. Let $E$ be a Borel subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with infinite measure, let $1 \leq$ $p \leq \infty ,$ , and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a Borel function. Prove that the integral $\textstyle \int _ { E } f \left( v \left( x \right) \right)$ dx is well-defined for every $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ (that is, the integrals $\textstyle \int _ { E } { \bigl ( } f \left( v \left( x \right) \right) { \bigr ) } ^ { - }$ dx and $\textstyle \int _ { E } { ( f ( v ( x ) ) ) ^ { + } }$ dx are not both infinite) if and only if $f$ or −f (or both) satisfies condition (5.7) if $1 \leq p < \infty$ and (5.8) if $p = \infty$ 

## 5.2 Sequential Lower Semicontinuity

This section is dedicated to finding necessary and suficient conditions for sequential lower semicontinuity with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { p } , 1 \leq$ $p \leq \infty$ , weak convergence in $L ^ { p } , 1 \leq p < \infty$ , weak star convergence in $L ^ { \infty }$ and weak star convergence in the sense of measures. 

## 5.2.1 Strong Convergence in L<sup>p</sup>

From now on we will assume that the integrand f satisfies the appropriate growth conditions from below that are necessary and suficient to guarantee that $( f \circ v ) ^ { - } \in L ^ { 1 } ( E )$ for all $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , so that the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x
$$

is well-defined (see Theorems 5.1 and 5.6). 

Theorem 5.9. Let E be a Borel subset $o f \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with finite measure, let $1 \leq$ $p \leq \infty .$ , and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a Borel function. Assume that there exists $C > 0$ such that 

$$
f (z) \geq - C (1 + | z | ^ {p}) \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \text {   if   } 1 \leq p <   \infty ,\tag{5.9}
$$

$$
f \text {is locally bounded from below if} p = \infty .\tag{5.10}
$$

Then the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x
$$

is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ if and only if f is lower semicontinuous. 

Proof. Assume that 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (v) d x
$$

is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Let $\{ z _ { n } \} \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be such that $z _ { n }  z$ , and set $v _ { n } \left( x \right) : = z _ { n }$ $v \left( x \right) : = z$ . Then $v _ { n } \to v$ in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , and so 

$$
f \left(z\right) = \frac {1}{\left| E \right|} \int_ {E} f \left(v\right) d x \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \frac {1}{\left| E \right|} \int_ {E} f \left(v _ {n}\right) d x = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \rightarrow \infty} f \left(z _ {n}\right),
$$

i.e., f is lower semicontinuous. 

Conversely, suppose that f is lower semicontinuous and let $\ v _ { n } \ \to \ v$ in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Consider first the case $1 \leq p < \infty$ 

Without loss of generality we may assume that 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x,
$$

and, by extracting a further subsequence if necessary (see Theorem 2.20), that $v _ { n } \to v$ pointwise $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. in E. By (5.9) we can apply Fatou’s lemma to conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x + \int_ {E} [ C + C | v | ^ {p} ] d x \\ \qquad = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} [ f (v _ {n}) + C + C | v _ {n} | ^ {p} ] d x \\ \qquad \geq \int_ {E} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} [ f (v _ {n}) + C + C | v _ {n} | ^ {p} ] d x \\ \qquad \geq \int_ {E} f (v) d x + \int_ {E} [ C + C | v | ^ {p} ] d x, \end{array}
$$

and thus, since E has finite measure, 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f \left(v _ {n}\right) d x \geq \int_ {E} f \left(v\right) d x.\tag{5.11}
$$

The case $p = \infty$ is similar. Let 

$$
M := \sup _ {n} \| v _ {n} \| _ {L ^ {\infty}} <   \infty .
$$

By (5.10) there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that 

$$
f (z) \geq - C \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \text {   with   } | z | \leq M.
$$

Hence, again by Fatou’s lemma, we have that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x + C | E | = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} [ f (v _ {n}) + C ] d x \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \int_ {E} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} [ f (v _ {n}) + C ] d x \geq \int_ {E} f (v) d x + C | E |, \end{array}
$$

and so (5.11) holds. 

Remark 5.10. Applying the previous proposition to f and −f it follows that if $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  \mathbb { R }$ is a Borel function satisfying (5.9) and (5.10), then the functiona 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x
$$

is continuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ if and only if f is continuous. 

Exercise 5.11. Prove that the previous proposition still holds if $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ is replaced by the space $L ^ { p } \left( \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , where $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ is a measure space with $\mu$ finite. 

Next we consider the case that E has infinite measure. 

Theorem 5.12. Let E be a Borel subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with infinite measure, let $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a Borel function. Assume that there exists $C > 0$ such that 

$$
f (z) \geq - C | z | ^ {p} \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \text {   if   } 1 \leq p <   \infty ,
$$

$$
f (z) \geq 0 \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \text {   if   } p = \infty .
$$

Then the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x
$$

is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ if and only if f is lower semicontinuous. 

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that there exists $v _ { 0 } ~ \in$ $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ such that 

$$
\int_ {E} f \left(v _ {0} (x)\right) d x <   \infty .\tag{5.12}
$$

The proof of the suficiency follows an argument entirely similar to that of the previous theorem. As for the necessity, consider a Borel subset $E _ { 1 } \subset E$ with finite measure, and let $z _ { n } \longrightarrow z$ in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Define 

$$
v _ {n} \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} z _ {n} & \text { if } x \in E _ {1}, \\ v _ {0} \left(x\right) & \text { if } x \in E \setminus E _ {1}. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then $v _ { n } \to v$ in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , where 

$$
v \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} z & \text { if } x \in E _ {1}, \\ v _ {0} \left(x\right) & \text { if } x \in E \setminus E _ {1}. \end{array} \right.
$$

Hence 

$$
\begin{array}{c} | E _ {1} |   f (z) + \int_ {E \setminus E _ {1}} f (v _ {0}) d x = \int_ {E} f (v) d x \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x \\ = | E _ {1} | \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} f (z _ {n}) + \int_ {E \setminus E _ {1}} f (v _ {0}) d x, \end{array}
$$

and by (5.12) we conclude that 

$$
f \left(z\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} f \left(z _ {n}\right).
$$

Thus the proof is complete. 

Exercise 5.13. Prove that the previous proposition still holds if $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ is replaced by $L ^ { p } \left( \left( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu \right) ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , where $( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \mu )$ is a measure space that admits at least one measurable set of positive finite measure. What happens if $\mu : { \mathfrak { M } } \to \{ 0 , \infty \} ?$ 

## 5.2.2 Weak Convergence and Weak Star Convergence in ${ \pmb { L } } ^ { p }$

Since functionals that are sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak (respectively weak star when $p = \infty )$ convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ are sequentially lower semicontinuous also with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , without loss of generality we may assume in what follows that the integrand f satisfies all the necessary conditions for strong convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

Theorem 5.14. Let E be a Borel subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with finite measure, let $1 \leq$ $p \leq \infty$ , and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a lower semicontinuous function. Assume that there exists $C > 0$ such that 

f (z) ≥ −C (1 + |z|<sup>p</sup>) for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ if $1 \leq p < \infty$ , 

f is locally bounded from below if $p = \infty$ 

Then the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x
$$

is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ (weak star if $p = \infty )$ if and only if f is convex. 

Proof (Suficiency). We consider only the case $1 \leq p < \infty$ , since the case $p = \infty$ can be treated in an entirely similar way. The proof of the suficiency part is based on the the blowup method. Assume that f is convex. 

Step 1: Suppose first that f is nonnegative. Let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ be a sequence weakly converging to some $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Without loss of generality we may assume that 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x <   \infty .
$$

By Remark 2.51, passing to a subsequence if necessary, there exists a (positive) Radon measure $\mu$ such that 

$$
f (v _ {n} (\cdot)) \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left\lfloor E \stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} \mu \quad \text { in } \mathcal {M} (E; \mathbb {R}) \right.\tag{5.13}
$$

as $n \to \infty$ . We claim that 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) \geq f (v (x _ {0})) \quad \text { for } \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text { a.e. } x _ {0} \in E.\tag{5.14}
$$

If (5.14) holds, then the conclusion of the theorem follows. Indeed, since by the Radon–Nikodym and Lebesgue decomposition theorems 

$$
\mu = \frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \lfloor E + \mu_ {s},
$$

where $\mu _ { s } \geq 0$ , by Proposition 1.203(i) with $X = E$ we have 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x \geq \mu (E) \geq \int_ {E} \frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} d x \geq \int_ {E} f (v) d x.
$$

Thus, to conclude the proof of the theorem, it sufices to prove (5.14) for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ $\mathrm { a . e . ~ } x _ { 0 } \in E$ 

Take $x _ { 0 } \in E$ a point of Lebesgue density one for E such that, in view of Besicovitch’s derivation theorem and Corollary 1.159, 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) = \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\mu (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon) \cap E)}{\varepsilon^ {N}} <   \infty ,\tag{5.15}
$$

$$
\lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\varepsilon^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon) \cap E} | v (x) - v (x _ {0}) | d x = 0.\tag{5.16}
$$

Since $f$ is convex and lower semicontinuous, by Proposition 4.77 we may write 

$$
f (z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot z \right\},\tag{5.17}
$$

for some $a _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } , b _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . By Proposition 1.15 we may choose $\varepsilon _ { k } \ \searrow \ 0$ such that $\mu ( \partial Q ( x _ { 0 } , \varepsilon _ { k } ) \cap E ) = 0$ . Using Proposition 1.203(iii), with $X : = E$ and the (relatively) open set $A : = Q ( x _ { 0 } , \varepsilon _ { k } ) \cap E$ , by (5.15) for any fixed $i \in \mathbb N$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \frac {\mu (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E)}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} f (v _ {n}) d x \\ \geq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} (a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot v _ {n}) d x \\ = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} (a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot v) d x, \end{array} \tag {5.1}\tag{5.18}
$$

where we have used the fact that $v _ { n }  v$ in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Since $x _ { 0 }$ is a point of density one for E, we have 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} a _ {i} d x = a _ {i},
$$

and by (5.16) we obtain 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} b _ {i} \cdot (v (x) - v (x _ {0})) d x = 0.
$$

Hence from (5.18) it follows that 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) \geq a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot v (x _ {0}),
$$

and taking the supremum over all i and using (5.17) we conclude (5.14). 

Step 2: Since $f \left( z \right) \geq a _ { 1 } + b _ { 1 } \cdot z$ for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ (see (5.17)), we have that the function $f \left( z \right) - \left( a _ { 1 } + b _ { 1 } \cdot z \right)$ is convex, nonnegative, and lower semicontinuous. By Step 1, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x - a _ {1} | E | - \int_ {E} b _ {1} \cdot v d x \\ = \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {E} (f (v _ {n}) - (a _ {1} + b _ {1} \cdot v _ {n})) d x \\ \geq \int_ {E} f (v) d x - a _ {1} | E | - \int_ {E} b _ {1} \cdot v d x. \end{array}
$$

Since $E$ has finite measure and $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , the result follows. 

Proof (Necessity). Let $z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m } , y \in S ^ { N - 1 } , \theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , and for $n \in \mathbb N$ and $x \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ define 

$$
v _ {n} (x) := z _ {2} + \chi (n x \cdot y) (z _ {1} - z _ {2}),
$$

where $\chi$ is the characteristic function of the interval [0, θ] in [0, 1] extended periodically to R with period one. In view of Example 2.86 we have that $v _ { n } \stackrel { * } {  } z _ { 2 } + \theta ( z _ { 1 } - z _ { 2 } )$ in $L ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , hence weakly in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Thus 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f \left(z _ {2} + \theta \left(z _ {1} - z _ {2}\right)\right) = \frac {1}{| E |} \int_ {E} f \left(z _ {2} + \theta \left(z _ {1} - z _ {2}\right)\right) d x \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{| E |} \int_ {E} f \left(z _ {2} + \chi \left(n x \cdot y\right) \left(z _ {1} - z _ {2}\right)\right) d x \\ = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{| E |} \int_ {E} \chi \left(n x \cdot y\right) f \left(z _ {1}\right) + \left(1 - \chi \left(n x \cdot y\right)\right) f \left(z _ {2}\right) d x \\ = \theta f \left(z _ {1}\right) + (1 - \theta) f \left(z _ {2}\right). \end{array}
$$

Therefore $f$ is convex. 

Exercise 5.15. Show that the suficiency part of the previous proof still holds with the Lebesgue measure replaced by a (positive) finite Radon measure<sup>1</sup>. Prove also that the necessity part of the theorem continues to hold for $L ^ { p } \left( ( X , { \mathfrak { M } } , \nu ) ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , where (X, M, ν) is a measure space with $\mu$ finite and nonatomic (recall Proposition 2.87). 

In order to prove the analogous result for the case in which E has infinite measure we present first an auxiliary result. 

Proposition 5.16. Let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a convex, lower semicontinuous function such that 

$$
f (z) \geq - \frac {1}{p} | z | ^ {p} \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \text {   and   for   some   } 1 \leq p <   \infty .
$$

Then there exist a constant $a \geq 0$ and a vector $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
f (z) \geq a + b \cdot z \geq - \frac {1}{p} | z | ^ {p} \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}.\tag{5.19}
$$

Moreover, $| b | \leq 1$ for $p = 1$ , while for $p > 1$ 2 

$$
| b | ^ {p ^ {\prime}} \leq \left[ \frac {1}{(p ^ {\prime}) ^ {1 / p}} + \frac {1}{p ^ {1 / p} (p - 1) ^ {1 / p ^ {\prime}}} \right] ^ {p ^ {\prime}} a.\tag{5.20}
$$

Proof. It sufices to consider the case that f is not identically ∞. The existence of some $a \in \mathbb { R }$ and a vector $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ satisfying (5.19) follows from Theorem 4.19 applied to the convex sets epi f and 

$$
A := \left\{(z, t) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R}: t <   - \frac {1}{p} | z | ^ {p} \right\}.
$$

To see this, let $( \beta , \gamma ) \in ( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \times \mathbb { R } ) \setminus \{ ( 0 , 0 ) \}$ and $s \in \mathbb { R }$ be such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \beta \cdot z + \gamma t \geq s \text {   for   every   } (z, t) \in \operatorname{epi} f, \\ \beta \cdot z + \gamma t \leq s \text {   for   every   } (z, t) \in A. \end{array}
$$

We claim that $\gamma > 0 . \mathrm { I f } \ z \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } \ f$ , then letting $t \to \infty$ in the first inequality we obtain that $\gamma \geq 0$ . Assume by contradiction that $\gamma = 0$ . Then $\beta \neq 0$ , and so, taking $z _ { n } : = n \beta$ and $\begin{array} { r } { t _ { n } < - \frac { 1 } { p } | z _ { n } | ^ { p } , n \in \mathbb { N } } \end{array}$ , we have that $( z _ { n } , t _ { n } ) \in A$ . It follows that 

$$
n \left| \beta \right| ^ {2} \leq s
$$

for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , which is a contradiction. Hence $\gamma > 0$ , and so 

$$
\frac {\beta}{\gamma} \cdot z + f (z) \geq \frac {s}{\gamma} \quad \text { for   all } z \in \mathrm{dom} _ {e} f,
$$

$$
\frac {s}{\gamma} \geq \frac {\beta}{\gamma} \cdot z - \frac {1}{p} | z | ^ {p} \quad \mathrm{forall} z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$

and in turn, 

$$
f (z) \geq \frac {s}{\gamma} - \frac {\beta}{\gamma} \cdot z \geq - \frac {1}{p} | z | ^ {p}
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . It sufices to define $\begin{array} { r } { a : = \frac { s } { \gamma } , b : = - \frac { \beta } { \gamma } } \end{array}$ to obtain (5.19). 

Taking $z = 0$ in (5.19) we obtain that $a \geq 0$ . Assume that $b \neq 0$ and in (5.19) set 

5 Integrands $f = f \left( z \right)$ 

$$
z := - \mu \frac {b}{| b |}
$$

with $\mu > 0$ . We get 

$$
a - \mu | b | \geq - \frac {\mu^ {p}}{p}
$$

for all $\mu > 0$ , or, equivalently, 

$$
| b | \leq \inf _ {\mu > 0} \left(\frac {a}{\mu} + \frac {\mu^ {p - 1}}{p}\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text {if p = 1 ,} \\ a ^ {1 / p ^ {\prime}} \left[ \frac {1}{(p ^ {\prime}) ^ {1 / p}} + \frac {1}{p ^ {1 / p} (p - 1) ^ {1 / p ^ {\prime}}} \right] & \text {if p > 1 .} \end{array} \right.
$$

This concludes the proof. 

We are now ready to treat the case that E has infinite measure. 

Theorem 5.17. Let E be a Borel subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with infinite measure, let $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a lower semicontinuous function. Assume that there exists $C > 0$ such that 

$$
f (z) \geq - C | z | ^ {p} \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \text {   if   } 1 \leq p <   \infty ,\tag{5.21}
$$

$$
f (z) \geq 0 \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \text {   if   } p = \infty .\tag{5.22}
$$

Suppose that there exists $v _ { 0 } \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ such that 

$$
\int_ {E} f \left(v _ {0} (x)\right) d x <   \infty .
$$

Then the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x
$$

is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ (weak star if $p = \infty )$ if and only if 

(i) f is convex; 

(ii) $f \geq 0 \ i f \ 1 < p \leq \infty ,$ 

(iii) $f \left( 0 \right) = 0 \ i f \ 1 \leq p < \infty ;$ 

(iv) min $f = 0 \ i f p = \infty .$ 

Proof. We begin by proving the necessity part. Using an argument similar to that of Theorem 5.12 it can be shown that sequential lower semicontinuity of the functional with respect to weak convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ (weak star if $p = \infty )$ yields sequential lower semicontinuity in $L ^ { p } \left( E _ { 1 } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ for any Borel subset $E _ { 1 } \subset E$ with finite measure. Therefore, by the previous theorem we conclude that $f$ is convex. 

In view of (5.22), we need to prove (ii) only for $1 < p < \infty$ . By Proposition 5.16 there exist a constant $a \geq 0$ and a vector $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
f (z) \geq a + b \cdot z \geq - C | z | ^ {p} \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}.
$$

If $a = 0$ , then by (5.20), $b = 0 ;$ hence $f \geq 0$ . If $a > 0$ , let $\varepsilon > 0$ be such that $a - \varepsilon \left| b \right| > 0$ . Since 

$$
| \{x \in E: | v _ {0} (x) | > \varepsilon \} | \leq \frac {1}{\varepsilon^ {p}} \int_ {E} | v _ {0} (x) | ^ {p} d x <   \infty ,
$$

the set 

$$
E _ {\varepsilon} := \{x \in E: | v _ {0} (x) | \leq \varepsilon \}
$$

has infinite measure. Therefore 

$$
\infty > \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon}} f (v _ {0}) d x \geq \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon}} (a + b \cdot v _ {0}) d x \geq (a - \varepsilon | b |) | E _ {\varepsilon} | = \infty ,
$$

and we have reached a contradiction. 

We now prove (iii), i.e., that $f \left( 0 \right) = 0$ for all $1 \leq p < \infty$ . By Proposition $4 . 7 7$ we may write 

$$
f (z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot z \right\}
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . If $a _ { i } > 0$ for some $i \in \mathbb N$ , then reasoning as above but now with $a _ { i } - \varepsilon \left| b _ { i } \right| > 0$ , we obtain that 

$$
\infty > \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon}} (f (v _ {0})) ^ {+} d x \geq \int_ {E _ {\varepsilon}} (a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot v _ {0}) ^ {+} d x \geq (a _ {i} - \varepsilon | b _ {i} |) | E _ {\varepsilon} | = \infty ,
$$

which is a contradiction. Hence $a _ { i } ~ \leq ~ 0$ for all $\textit { i } \in  { \mathbb { N } } ,$ , and so $f \left( 0 \right) =$ $\mathrm { s u p } _ { i \in \mathbb { N } } \left\{ a _ { i } \right\} \leq 0$ , which, together with either (5.21) or (5.22), yields $f \left( 0 \right) = 0$ 

Finally we prove (iv). Let $R : = \| v _ { 0 } \| _ { L ^ { \infty } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ) }$ . Since f is lower semicontinuous, by the Weierstrass theorem there exists $z _ { 0 } \in \overline { { B \left( 0 , R \right) } }$ such that 

$$
\min _ {\overline {{B (0 , R)}}} f = f \left(z _ {0}\right) \geq 0.
$$

If $f \left( z _ { 0 } \right) > 0$ , then 

$$
\infty > \int_ {E} f (v _ {0}) d x \geq f (z _ {0}) | E | = \infty ,
$$

which is a contradiction. Hence $f \left( z _ { 0 } \right) = 0$ , and since f is nonnegative, it follows that 

$$
\min _ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f = f \left(z _ {0}\right) = 0.
$$

This concludes the proof of the necessity part of the theorem. 

Conversely, in the cases in which $1 < p \leq \infty$ we have $f \geq 0$ , and so the same argument as in the proof of the previous theorem yields sequential lower semicontinuity. If $p = 1$ and if $f \geq 0$ , then similar reasoning will assert sequential lower semicontinuity. If $p = 1$ and if f takes negative values, then using once more Proposition 5.16, and since $a \geq 0$ , we have that $g \left( z \right) =$ $f \left( z \right) - b \cdot z$ is a nonnegative, convex, lower semicontinuous function. Hence if $v _ { n } \to v$ in $L ^ { 1 }$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x - \int_ {E} b \cdot v d x \\ = \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {E} g (v _ {n}) d x \geq \int_ {E} g (v) d x \\ = \int_ {E} f (v) d x - \int_ {E} b \cdot v d x, \end{array}
$$

and thus 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f \left(v _ {n}\right) d x \geq \int_ {E} f \left(v\right) d x,
$$

which gives the desired result. 

Exercise 5.18. For which measures does the necessity part of the theorem continue to hold? For which measures does the suficiency part of the theorem continue to hold? 

## 5.2.3 Weak Star Convergence in the Sense of Measures

As we remarked in the beginning of this chapter, due to lack of reflexivity of the space $L ^ { 1 } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ , if $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ is such that 

$$
\sup _ {n} \left\| v _ {n} \right\| _ {L ^ {1}} <   \infty ,
$$

one can conclude only that $\{ v _ { n } \}$ admits a subsequence (not relabeled) such that $v _ { n } { \mathcal { L } } ^ { N } | E \stackrel { * } {  } \lambda$ in $\mathcal { M } \left( \boldsymbol { E } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Thus we will also study sequential lower semicontinuity under this natural notion of convergence. In particular, we will address necessary and suficient conditions under which the lower semicontinuity property 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f \left(v _ {n}\right) d x \geq \int_ {E} f \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x
$$

holds, whenever $v _ { n } { \mathcal { L } } ^ { N } \mid E \ { \overset { * } {  } } \lambda$ in $\mathcal { M } \left( \boldsymbol { E } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and λ admits the Radon– Nikodym decomposition 

$$
\lambda = \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}   \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \lfloor E + \lambda_ {s},
$$

with $\lambda _ { s }$ and $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } | ~ E$ mutually singular. 

Since functionals that are sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak star convergence in the sense of measures are in particular sequentially lower semicontinuous also with respect to weak convergence in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , without loss of generality we may assume in what follows that the integrand f satisfies all the necessary conditions for weak convergence in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

We will study the following cases: 

• The Borel set E has finite measure. We divide this case into two subcases: There exists a compact set $K \subset E$ such that 

$$
| E \setminus K | = 0.\tag{5.23}
$$

– For all compact sets $K \subset E$ 

$$
| E \setminus K | > 0.\tag{5.24}
$$

• The Borel set E has infinite measure. 

Note that (5.24) is satisfied if, $\mathrm { e . g . , } E$ is open. 

When (5.23) holds, then for every $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we have that 

$$
\int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x = \int_ {K} f (v (x)) d x,
$$

and thus there is no loss of generality in considering the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {1} (K; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {K} f (v (x)) d x.
$$

This case will be treated in the next theorem. 

Theorem 5.19. Let E be a compact subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a convex, lower semicontinuous function. Then the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {1} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x
$$

is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak star convergence in the sense of measures. 

More generally, for any sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ such that 

$$
v _ {n} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left\lfloor E \stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} \lambda \quad i n \mathcal {M} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \right.
$$

we have 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f \left(v _ {n}\right) d x \geq \int_ {E} f \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x + \int_ {E} f ^ {\infty} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \left\| \lambda_ {s} \right\|}\right) d \left\| \lambda_ {s} \right\|,
$$

where $f ^ { \infty }$ is the recession function of $f$ . 

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that f is not identically $\infty$ , since otherwise there is nothing to prove. 

Step 1: Assume that f is nonnegative. Let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ be such that $v _ { n } { \mathcal { L } } ^ { N } | ~ E \stackrel { * } {  } \lambda$ in $\mathcal { M } \left( \boldsymbol { E } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

As in the suficiency proof of Theorem 5.14, we use the blowup method. Let the Radon measure $\mu$ be as in (5.13). In view of Proposition A.57 we have that 

$$
\sup _ {n} \int_ {E} | v _ {n} | d x <   \infty ,
$$

and so by extracting a further subsequence if necessary, we may assume that 

$$
\left| v _ {n} \right| \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left\lfloor E \stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} \nu \quad \text { in } \mathcal {M} (E; \mathbb {R}) \right.
$$

for some (positive) Radon measure ν (see Remark 2.51). 

We claim that for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x _ { 0 } \in E$ , 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) \geq f \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0})\right),\tag{5.25}
$$

and for $\| \lambda _ { s } \|$ a.e. $x _ { 0 } \in E$ 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}) \geq f ^ {\infty} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0})\right).\tag{5.26}
$$

If (5.25) and (5.26) hold, then the conclusion of the theorem follows. Indeed, since by Corollary 1.116, 

$$
\mu = \frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left\lfloor E + \frac {d \mu}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} \| \lambda_ {s} \| + \mu_ {s}, \right.
$$

where $\mu _ { s }$ is a (positive) Radon measure singular with respect to $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \lfloor E + \rfloor \lvert \lambda _ { s } \rvert \rvert$ , by Proposition 1.203(i) with $X = E$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n})   d x \geq \mu   (E) \geq \int_ {E} \frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}   d x + \int_ {E} \frac {d \mu}{d   \| \lambda_ {s} \|}   d   \| \lambda_ {s} \| \\ \geq \int_ {E} f \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right)   d x + \int_ {E} f ^ {\infty} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d   \| \lambda_ {s} \|}\right)   d   \| \lambda_ {s} \|. \end{array}
$$

Step 2: We prove (5.25). Take $x _ { 0 } \in E$ a point of Lebesgue density one of E with respect to $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ such that 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) = \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\mu (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon) \cap E)}{\varepsilon^ {N}} <   \infty ,\tag{5.27}
$$

$$
\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) = \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\lambda (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon) \cap E)}{\varepsilon^ {N}},\tag{5.28}
$$

where we have used Theorem 1.155. 

Since f is convex and lower semicontinuous, by Proposition 4.77 we may write 

$$
f (z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot z \right\}.\tag{5.29}
$$

By Proposition 1.15 we may choose $\varepsilon _ { k } \searrow 0$ such that $\mu ( \partial Q ( x _ { 0 } , \varepsilon _ { k } ) \cap E ) = 0$ and $\nu ( \partial Q ( x _ { 0 } , \varepsilon _ { k } ) \cap E ) = 0$ . Invoking Corollary 1.204 with $X : = E$ and the (relatively) open set $A : = Q ( x _ { 0 } , \varepsilon _ { k } ) \cap E$ , for all i, $k \in \mathbb N$ we have 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} b _ {i} \cdot v _ {n} d x = \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} b _ {i} \cdot d \lambda ,\tag{5.30}
$$

while by Proposition 1.203, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \frac {\mu (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E)}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} f (v _ {n}) d x \\ \geq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} (a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot v _ {n}) d x \\ = a _ {i} + \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} b _ {i} \cdot d \lambda , \end{array} \tag {5.3}\tag{5.31}
$$

where in the last identity we used the fact that $x _ { 0 } \in E$ is a point of density one of E. Using (5.28) we have that 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} b _ {i} \cdot d \lambda = b _ {i} \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} \left(x _ {0}\right),
$$

which, together with (5.31), yields 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) \geq a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}).
$$

The inequality (5.25) now follows from (5.29). 

Step 3: We prove (5.26). Take $x _ { 0 } \in E$ such that (see Theorem 1.155) 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}) = \lim _ {\varepsilon \rightarrow 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\mu (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon) \cap E)}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon) \cap E)} <   \infty ,\tag{5.32}
$$

$$
\frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}) = \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\lambda (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon) \cap E)}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon) \cap E)},\tag{5.33}
$$

$$
\lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\mathcal {L} ^ {N} (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon) \cap E)}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon) \cap E)} = 0.\tag{5.34}
$$

Choosing $\varepsilon _ { k } \searrow 0$ such that $\mu ( \partial Q ( x _ { 0 } , \varepsilon _ { k } ) \cap E ) = 0$ and $\nu ( \partial Q ( x _ { 0 } , \varepsilon _ { k } ) \cap E ) = 0$ and reasoning as in the previous step we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d \mu}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}) = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \frac {\mu (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E)}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E)} \\ = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E)} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} f (v _ {n}) d x \\ \geq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E)} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} (a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot v _ {n}) \\ = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} \frac {1}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E)} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} b _ {i} \cdot d \lambda , \end{array} \tag {5}\tag{5.35}
$$

where in the last equality we have used (5.34) and (5.30). By (5.33) we have that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {k \to \infty} {\liminf} \frac {1}{\| \lambda_ {s} \|   (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E)} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E} b _ {i} \cdot d \lambda   (x) \\ = b _ {i} \cdot \underset {k \to \infty} {\lim} \frac {\lambda (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E)}{\| \lambda_ {s} \|   (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}) \cap E)} = b _ {i} \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d   \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}), \end{array}\tag{5.36}
$$

which, together with (5.35), yields 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}) \geq b _ {i} \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}).
$$

Taking the supremum over all i, it follows from (5.29) and Proposition 4.77 that 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}) \geq f ^ {\infty} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0})\right).
$$

Step 4: Here we remove the additional assumption that $f \geq 0$ . By Proposition 4.75 there exist $a \in \mathbb { R }$ and $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that $f \left( z \right) \geq a + b \cdot z \ \left( \mathrm { s e e } \ ( 5 . 1 7 ) \right)$ ; we have that the function $g \left( z \right) : = f \left( z \right) - \left( a + b \cdot z \right)$ is convex, nonnegative, and lower semicontinuous. Using (for the first time) the fact that E is compact we have that $\mathcal { M } \left( E \right)$ is the dual of $C _ { 0 } \left( E \right) = C _ { b } \left( E \right)$ , and so 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} b \cdot v _ {n} d x = \int_ {E} b \cdot d \lambda .
$$

Hence, by Steps 1–3 applied to $g _ { ; }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x - a | E | - \int_ {E} b \cdot d \lambda = \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {E} g (v _ {n}) d x \\ \qquad \geq \int_ {E} g \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x + \int_ {E} g ^ {\infty} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|}\right) \\ \qquad = \int_ {E} f \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x - a | E | - \int_ {E} b \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} d x \\ \qquad + \int_ {E} f ^ {\infty} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|}\right) d \| \lambda_ {s} \| - \int_ {E} b \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} d \| \lambda_ {s} \| \\ \qquad = \int_ {E} f \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x + \int_ {E} f ^ {\infty} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|}\right) d \| \lambda_ {s} \| - a | E | - \int_ {E} b \cdot d \lambda , \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that by Theorem 4.70, for every $w \in \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} g ^ {\infty} (z) = \lim _ {t \to \infty} \frac {g (w + t z) - g (w)}{t} \\ = \lim _ {t \to \infty} \frac {f (w + t z) - b \cdot (t z) - f (w)}{t} = f ^ {\infty} (z) - b \cdot z. \end{array}
$$

Since $E$ has finite measure and $\int _ { E } \boldsymbol { b } \cdot d \boldsymbol { \lambda }$ is well-defined and finite, the result follows. 

Exercise 5.20. Show that the previous theorem still holds if the Lebesgue measure is replaced by a (positive) nonatomic finite Radon measure. 

We now turn to the case in which (5.24) holds. 

Theorem 5.21. Let E be a Borel subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with finite measure for which there is no compact set $K \subset E$ such that $\dot { \mathcal { L } } ^ { N } \left( E \setminus K \right) = 0$ , and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m } $ $( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a convex, lower semicontinuous function. Then the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {1} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x
$$

is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak star convergence in the sense of measures $i f$ and only if 

$$
\liminf _ {| z | \to \infty} \frac {f (z)}{| z |} \geq 0.\tag{5.37}
$$

More generally, if $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ is a convex, lower semicontinuous function satisfying (5.37), then for any sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ such that 

$$
v _ {n} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left\lfloor E \stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} \lambda \quad i n \mathcal {M} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \right.,
$$

we have 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f \left(v _ {n}\right) d x \geq \int_ {E} f \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x + \int_ {E} f ^ {\infty} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \left\| \lambda_ {s} \right\|}\right) d \left\| \lambda_ {s} \right\|.
$$

Remark 5.22. We note that in view of Theorem 4.73, condition (5.37) is equivalent to $f ^ { \infty } \geq 0$ 

Proof (Suficiency). Without loss of generality we may assume that $f$ is not identically $\infty .$ , since otherwise there is nothing to prove. By condition (5.37) for $\varepsilon > 0$ , then there exists $M > 0$ such that 

$$
\frac {f (z)}{| z |} \geq - \varepsilon
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ with $| z | > M$ . Since $f$ is lower semicontinuous, by the Weierstrass theorem $f \left( \cdot \right) + \varepsilon \left| \cdot \right|$ is bounded from below in ${ \overline { { B \left( 0 , M \right) } } }$ , and so there exists $a _ { \varepsilon } \in \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
g _ {\varepsilon} (z) := f (z) + \varepsilon | z | + a _ {\varepsilon} \geq 0
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ be such that $v _ { n } { \mathcal { L } } ^ { N } | E \ { \stackrel { * } { \to } } \ \lambda$ in $\mathcal { M } \left( \boldsymbol { E } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . By Proposition A.57 we have 

$$
\sup _ {n} \left\| v _ {n} \right\| _ {L ^ {1}} =: C <   \infty .
$$

As we already remarked in the proof of the previous theorem, the hypothesis that E is compact is not needed for nonnegative integrands. Hence we may apply Steps 1–3 of the previous theorem to $g _ { \varepsilon }$ to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x + \varepsilon C + a _ {\varepsilon} | E | \geq \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {E} g _ {\varepsilon} (v _ {n}) d x \\ \quad \geq \int_ {E} g _ {\varepsilon} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x + \int_ {E} g _ {\varepsilon} ^ {\infty} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|}\right) \\ = \int_ {E} f \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x + \varepsilon \int_ {E} \left| \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} \right| d x + a _ {\varepsilon} | E | \\ + \int_ {E} f ^ {\infty} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|}\right) d \| \lambda_ {s} \| + \varepsilon \int_ {E} \left| \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} \right| d \| \lambda_ {s} \|, \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that by Theorem 4.70, for every $w \in \operatorname { d o m } _ { e } f$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & g ^ {\infty} (z) = \lim _ {t \to \infty} \frac {g (w + t z) - g (w)}{t} \\ & \qquad = \lim _ {t \to \infty} \frac {f (w + t z) + \varepsilon | w + t z | - f (w) - \varepsilon | w |}{t} = f ^ {\infty} (z) + \varepsilon | z |. \end{array}
$$

Hence 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (v _ {n}) d x + \varepsilon C \geq \int_ {E} f \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x + \varepsilon \int_ {E} \left| \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} \right| d x \\ \quad + \int_ {E} f ^ {\infty} \left(\frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|}\right) d \| \lambda_ {s} \| + \varepsilon \int_ {E} \left| \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} \right| d \| \lambda_ {s} \|, \end{array}
$$

and the result now follows by letting $\varepsilon \to 0$ 

Proof (Necessity). Step 1: We claim that there exists a sequence $\{ K _ { j } \} \subset E$ of pairwise disjoint compact sets with positive Lebesgue measure such that for any compact $K \subset E$ we have that $K _ { j } \subset E \setminus K$ for all $j$ suficiently large. 

Indeed, assume first that $E$ is unbounded in the measure-theoretic sense, that is 

$$
\left| E \setminus \overline {{B (0 , r)}} \right| > 0 \text {   for   all   } r > 0.\tag{5.38}
$$

By the inner regularity of the Lebesgue measure there exists a compact set $K _ { 1 } \subset E$ with $| K _ { 1 } | > 0$ . Let $r _ { 1 } \geq 1$ be so large that $K _ { 1 } \subset \overline { { B \left( 0 , r _ { 1 } \right) } }$ . Since $\left| E \setminus \overline { { B \left( 0 , r _ { 1 } \right) } } \right| > 0$ , again by the inner regularity of the Lebesgue measure we may find a compact set $K _ { 2 } \subset E \setminus \overline { { B \left( 0 , r _ { 1 } \right) } }$ with $| K _ { 2 } | > 0$ . Find $r _ { 2 } > r _ { 1 } + 1$ such that $K _ { 2 } \subset \overline { { B \left( 0 , r _ { 2 } \right) } }$ . Inductively we can construct a sequence of pairwise disjoint compact sets $\{ K _ { j } \}$ and a sequence of radii $\{ r _ { j } \}$ such that $| K _ { j } | > 0$ , $K _ { j } \subset E \backslash \overline { { B \left( 0 , r _ { j - 1 } \right) } }$ , and $r _ { j } > r _ { j - 1 } + 1$ . The sequence $\{ K _ { j } \}$ satisfies the claim. Next assume that (5.38) fails, so that there exists $R ~ > ~ 0$ such that $\left| E \setminus \overline { { B \left( 0 , R \right) } } \right| = 0$ . Define 

$$
C := \left\{x \in \overline {{E}}: \left| E \cap \overline {{B (x , r)}} \right| > 0 \text {   for   all   } r > 0 \right\} \cap \overline {{B (0 , R)}}.
$$

We show that C is compact. Since C is bounded it sufices to prove that C is closed. Thus, let $\{ x _ { l } \} \subset C$ be such that $x _ { l } \to x$ . Then $x \in \overline { { E } } \cap \overline { { B \left( 0 , R \right) } }$ Fix $r > 0$ and let l be so large that $\begin{array} { r } { | x _ { l } - x | < \frac { r } { 2 } } \end{array}$ . Since $x _ { l } \in C$ we have that $\left| E \cap { \overline { { B \left( x _ { l } , { \frac { r } { 2 } } \right) } } } \right| > 0$ , and so 

$$
\left| E \cap \overline {{B (x , r)}} \right| \geq \left| E \cap \overline {{B \left(x _ {l} , \frac {r}{2}\right)}} \right| > 0,
$$

where we have used the fact that $\overline { { B \left( x , r \right) } } \supset \overline { { B \left( x _ { l } , \frac { r } { 2 } \right) } }$ . Hence $x \in C$ 

Next we prove that $| E \setminus C | = 0$ . Indeed, 

$$
E \setminus C \subset E _ {1} \cup \left(E \setminus \overline {{B (0 , R)}}\right),
$$

where 

$$
E _ {1} := \left\{x \in E \cap \overline {{B (0 , R)}}: \left| E \cap \overline {{B (x , r)}} \right| = 0 \text {   for   some   } r > 0 \right\},
$$

and since $\left| { \cal E } \backslash \overline { { { \cal B } \left( 0 , R \right) } } \right| = 0$ , it sufices to show that $| E _ { 1 } | = 0$ . This follows from the Vitali–Besicovitch covering theorem, since the family of closed balls 

$$
\left\{\overline {{B (x , r)}}: x \in E _ {1}, \left| E \cap \overline {{B (x , r)}} \right| = 0 \right\}
$$

is a fine Morse cover for $E _ { 1 }$ . Hence we have shown that $| E \setminus C | = 0$ . In view of the hypothesis on $E$ we cannot have that $E \supset C ,$ , and so there exists a point $x _ { 1 } \in C \setminus E$ . By the definition of the set C we have that $\left| E \cap { \overline { { B \left( x _ { 1 } , r \right) } } } \right| > 0$ for all $r > 0$ 

We are now ready to construct the sequence $\{ K _ { j } \}$ even in this case. By the inner regularity of the Lebesgue measure, there exists a compact set $K _ { 1 } \subset E$ with $| K _ { 1 } | > 0$ . Since $x _ { 1 } \in \overline { { E } } \setminus E$ we have that dist $( x _ { 1 } , K _ { 1 } ) > 0$ . Let $r _ { 1 } ~ <$ 1 be so small that $K _ { 1 } \subset E \setminus \overline { { B \left( x _ { 1 } , r _ { 1 } \right) } }$ . Since $\left| E \cap { \overline { { B \left( x _ { 1 } , r _ { 1 } \right) } } } \right| \ > \ 0$ , again by the inner regularity of the Lebesgue measure, there exists a compact set $K _ { 2 } \subset E \cap \overline { { B \left( x _ { 1 } , r _ { 1 } \right) } }$ with $| K _ { 2 } | > 0$ . Find $0 < r _ { 2 } <$ min $\left\{ r _ { 1 } , { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \right\}$ such that $K _ { 2 } \subset E \setminus \overline { { B \left( x _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } \right) } }$ . Inductively we can construct a sequence of pairwise disjoint compact sets $\{ K _ { j } \} \subset E$ and a sequence of radii $\{ r _ { j } \}$ such that $| K _ { j } | >$ $0 , \ K _ { j } \ \subset \ { \overline { { B \left( x _ { 1 } , r _ { j - 1 } \right) } } } \setminus { \overline { { B \left( x _ { 1 } , r _ { j } \right) } } }$ , and $r _ { j } < \operatorname* { m i n } \left\{ r _ { j - 1 } , { \frac { 1 } { j } } \right\}$ . Moreover, since $x _ { 1 } \in \overline { { E } } \setminus E$ , for any compact $K \subset E$ we have that dist $( x _ { 1 } , K ) > 0$ , and so there is $j _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { N }$ such that $K _ { j } \subset E \backslash K$ for all $j \geq j _ { 0 }$ . Hence the claim is satisfied also in this case. 

Step 2: We prove that (5.37) holds. Suppose, without loss of generality, that f is not identically $\infty$ and let $z _ { 0 } \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f$ . Replacing f with the integrands 

$$
g (z) := f (z - z _ {0}) - f (z _ {0}), \quad z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$

and using the fact that E has finite measure, we have that the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {1} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} g (v (x)) d x
$$

is still sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak star convergence in the sense of measures. Moreover, (5.37) holds for $g$ if and only if it holds for $f .$ . Thus, without loss of generality, we may assume that $f \left( 0 \right) = 0$ . Assume by contradiction that 

$$
\liminf _ {| z | \to \infty} \frac {f (z)}{| z |} <   0.
$$

Then we may find a sequence $\{ z _ { n } \} \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that $| z _ { n } | >$ ∞ and 

$$
f \left(z _ {n}\right) \leq - c \left| z _ {n} \right| \text {   for   all   } n \in \mathbb {N},\tag{5.39}
$$

for some constant $c > 0$ . Let $\{ K _ { i } \} \subset E$ be the sequence constructed in Step 1 and select a subsequence $\left\{ z _ { n _ { j } } \right\}$ such that 

$$
| K _ {j} | > \frac {1}{\left| z _ {n _ {j}} \right|}.
$$

By Proposition 1.20 find a Borel set $E _ { j } \subset K _ { j }$ such that 

$$
| E _ {j} | = \frac {1}{| z _ {n _ {j}} |}.
$$

Define 

$$
v _ {j} := z _ {n _ {j}} \chi_ {E _ {j}}.
$$

We claim that $v _ { j } \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \big | \ E \stackrel { * } {  } \ 0$ in $\mathcal { M } \left( \boldsymbol { E } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Indeed, fix $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } \left( E \right)$ . Given $\varepsilon > 0$ find a compact set $K \subset E$ such that 

$$
| \varphi (x) | \leq \varepsilon \quad \text { if } x \in E \setminus K.\tag{5.40}
$$

If $j$ is suficiently large, then $E _ { j } \subset E \setminus K$ , and so 

$$
\left| \int_ {E} \varphi v _ {j} d x \right| = \left| z _ {n _ {j}} \right| \left| \int_ {E _ {j}} \varphi d x \right| \leq \varepsilon \left| z _ {n _ {j}} \right| | E _ {j} | = \varepsilon .\tag{5.41}
$$

On the other hand, by (5.39) we have 

$$
\int_ {E} f (v _ {j}) d x = f (z _ {n _ {j}}) \frac {1}{| z _ {n _ {j}} |} \leq - c.
$$

Hence 

$$
\liminf _ {j \to \infty} \int_ {E} f \left(v _ {j}\right) d x \leq - c <   \int_ {E} f \left(0\right) d x = 0,
$$

which is a contradiction and proves the theorem. 

Remark 5.23. Note that if f is lower semicontinuous, then condition (5.37) is stronger than (5.2) with $p = 1$ , although it still does not guarantee that f is bounded from below, as confirmed by the function $f : \mathbb { R } \longrightarrow ( - \infty , \infty ]$ defined by 

$$
f \left(z\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} - \log z \text {   if   } z > 0, \\ \infty \qquad \text {   if   } z \leq 0. \end{array} \right.
$$

Exercise 5.24. Show that the suficiency part of the previous theorem still holds with the Lebesgue measure replaced by a (positive) finite Radon measure, while the necessity part requires in addition the measure to be nonatomic. What happens in the case of measures with atoms? 

We consider next the case that E has infinite measure. In view of Theorems 5.6 and 5.17, it sufices to consider the case that $f \left( 0 \right) = 0$ and $f \left( z \right) \geq - C \left| z \right|$ for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Theorem 5.25. Let E be a Borel subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with infinite measure, and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a convex, lower semicontinuous function such that $f \left( 0 \right) = 0$ . Assume that there exists $C > 0$ such that 

$$
f (z) \geq - C | z | f o r a l l z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}.
$$

Then the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {1} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x
$$

is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak star convergence in the sense of measures if and only $i f f \geq 0$ 

More generally, if $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a convex, lower semicontinuous function such that $f \left( 0 \right) = 0$ , then for any sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ such that $v _ { n } { \mathcal { L } } ^ { N } | E \stackrel { * } {  } \lambda$ in $\mathcal { M } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we have 

$$
