Theorem 6.17 (Michael continuous selection theorem). Let X be a metric space and let Y be a Banach space. If the multifunction 

$$
\Gamma : X \to \{C \subset Y: C \text {   convex,   nonempty,   closed } \}
$$

is lower semicontinuous, then for every $x _ { 0 } \in X$ and every y<sub>0</sub> $\in \ b { T } \left( \ b { x } _ { 0 } \right)$ there exists a continuous function $u : X \to Y$ such that u $( x _ { 0 } ) = y _ { 0 }$ and u $( x ) \in$ $T \left( x \right)$ for every $x \in X$ 

In order to prove the previous theorem we need some auxiliary results that are of interest in themselves. We begin by showing that given any cover in an open space there exists a locally finite partition of unity subordinated to it. 

Theorem 6.18 (Partition of unity). Let X be a metric space and let $\{ U _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ be an open cover of X. Then there exists a locally finite partition of unity subordinated to it. 

Proof. Step 1: We assume first that I is finite, say $I = \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ . For each $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ define the continuous function 

$$
u _ {i} (x) := \operatorname{dist} (x, X \setminus U _ {i}), \quad x \in X,
$$

and set $\textstyle u : = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } u _ { i }$ . Note that $u > 0$ , since $U _ { 1 } , \ldots , U _ { n }$ is a cover of X and $u _ { i } > 0$ in $U _ { i } , i = 1 , \dotsc , n$ . Next, for each $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ we define the continuous function 

$$
v _ {i} (x) := \max \left\{u _ {i} (x) - \frac {1}{n + 1} u (x), 0 \right\}, \quad x \in X.
$$

We claim that supp $v _ { i } \subset U _ { i }$ for each $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ . Indeed, 

$$
\operatorname{supp} v _ {i} = \overline {{\left\{x \in X : u _ {i} (x) > \frac {1}{n + 1} u (x) \right\}}} \subset \left\{x \in X: u _ {i} (x) \geq \frac {1}{n + 1} u (x) \right\}.
$$

Since $u > 0 ,$ , the closed set $\begin{array} { r } { \left. x \in X : u _ { i } \left( x \right) \geq \frac { 1 } { n + 1 } u \left( x \right) \right. } \end{array}$ is contained in $U _ { i } =$ $\{ x \in X : u _ { i } \left( x \right) > 0 \}$ 

Next we show that $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } v _ { i } > 0$ . For all $x \in X$ we have 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} v _ {i} (x) \geq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left(u _ {i} (x) - \frac {1}{n + 1} u (x)\right) = u (x) - \frac {n}{n + 1} u (x) = \frac {1}{n + 1} u (x) > 0.
$$

It now sufices to define for each $i = 1 , \ldots , n ,$ , 

$$
\varphi_ {i} \left(x\right) := \frac {v _ {i} \left(x\right)}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} v _ {j} \left(x\right)}, \quad x \in X.
$$

Step 2: Assume next that $I \ = \ \mathbb { N } .$ . For each $i \in \mathbb N$ define the continuous function $u _ { i } : X \to \left[ 0 , { \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { i } } } \right]$ by 

$$
u _ {i} \left(x\right) := \min \left\{\operatorname{dist} \left(x, X \setminus U _ {i}\right), \frac {1}{2 ^ {i}} \right\}, \quad x \in X.
$$

Then $u _ { i } ~ > ~ 0$ in $U _ { i } , \ u _ { i } \ = \ 0$ outside $U _ { i }$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { u _ { i } \ \le \ \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { i } } } \end{array}$ . Hence the function $\begin{array} { r } { u : = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty } \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { i - 1 } } u _ { i } } \end{array}$ is continuous and $u > 0$ since $\{ U _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { N } }$ is a cover of X. Next, for i ∈ N we define the continuous function $v _ { i } : X \to \left[ 0 , 1 \right]$ by 

$$
v _ {i} (x) := \max \left\{u _ {i} (x) - \frac {1}{3} u (x), 0 \right\}, \quad x \in X.
$$

As in the previous step we have that supp $v _ { i } \subset U _ { i }$ . We claim that $\{ v _ { i } \} _ { i \in \mathbb { N } }$ is locally finite. For any fixed $x \in X$ , since u is positive and continuous there exist $\varepsilon , r > 0$ such that u $( y ) > \varepsilon$ for all $y \in B \left( x , r \right)$ . Let $i _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { N }$ be so large that $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { i _ { 0 } } } } < { \frac { \varepsilon } { 3 } }$ . From the definition of $v _ { i }$ and the fact that $\begin{array} { r } { u _ { i } \le \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { i } } } \end{array}$ it follows that $v _ { i } \left( y \right) = 0$ for all $y \in B \left( x , r \right)$ and $i \geq i _ { 0 }$ 

Next we show that $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { \infty } v _ { i } \ > \ 0$ . Fix $x \in X$ . Since $u _ { i } \left( x \right) > 0$ for some $i \in \mathbb N$ and $\begin{array} { r } { u _ { n } \leq \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { n } } < \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { i } } } \end{array}$ for all $n \geq i$ , it follows that there exists $i _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { N }$ such that 

$$
u _ {i _ {0}} (x) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} u _ {i} (x),
$$

and so 

$$
u (x) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {i - 1}} u _ {i} (x) \leq u _ {i _ {0}} (x) \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{2 ^ {i - 1}} = 2 u _ {i _ {0}} (x).
$$

Hence 

$$
v _ {i _ {0}} (x) \geq u _ {i _ {0}} (x) - \frac {1}{3} u (x) \geq u _ {i _ {0}} (x) - \frac {2}{3} u _ {i _ {0}} (x) = \frac {1}{3} u _ {i _ {0}} (x) > 0.
$$

It now sufices to define for each $i \in \mathbb N$ V. 

$$
\varphi_ {i} (x) := \frac {v _ {i} (x)}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} v _ {j} (x)}, \quad x \in X.
$$

Step 3: Finally, if $\{ U _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ is an arbitrary open cover of $X ,$ , note that for any $x \in X$ 

$$
X = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \overline {{B (x , n)}}.
$$

Since each closed ball $\overline { { B \left( x , n \right) } }$ is compact it may be covered by a finite number of open sets in the cover. Thus we may select a countable subcover of X and then apply Step 2 (defining $\varphi _ { \alpha } \equiv 0$ if $U _ { \alpha }$ does not belong to the countable subcover). 

Remark 6.19. (i) Note that as a consequence of Step 3 in the above proof, all but at most a countable number of $\varphi _ { \alpha }$ are identically zero. 

(ii) Given $x _ { 0 } \in X$ it is possible to construct the locally finite partition of unity such that $\varphi _ { \alpha } \left( x _ { 0 } \right) = 1$ for some α and thus $\varphi _ { \beta } \left( x _ { 0 } \right) = 0$ for all $\beta \neq \alpha$ . To see this, choose $\alpha \in I$ such that $x _ { 0 } \in U _ { \alpha }$ and let $r > 0$ be such that $\overline { { B \left( x _ { 0 } , r \right) } } \subset U _ { \alpha }$ . It sufices to apply the previous theorem to the open cover $\left\{ \hat { U } _ { \beta } \right\} _ { \beta \in I }$ of X, where 

$$
\hat {U} _ {\beta} := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} U _ {\beta} \setminus \overline {{B (x _ {0} , r)}} & \text { if } \beta \neq \alpha , \\ U _ {\alpha} & \text { if } \beta = \alpha . \end{array} \right.
$$

As a consequence of the previous result we have the following. 

Lemma 6.20. Let X be a metric space, let Y be a locally convex topological vector space, and let 

$$
\Gamma : X \to \{C \subset Y: C \text {   convex,   nonempty } \}
$$

be a lower semicontinuous multifunction. If $x _ { 0 } \in X , y _ { 0 } \in T ( x _ { 0 } )$ , and if $A \subset Y$ is a convex, balanced neighborhood of the origin, then there exists a continuous function u : $X  Y$ such that u $( x _ { 0 } ) = y _ { 0 }$ and u $( x ) \in ( T \left( x \right) + A )$ for all $x \in X$ 

Proof. For every $x \in X$ choose $y _ { x } \in T \left( x \right)$ , with $y _ { x _ { 0 } } : = y _ { 0 }$ . Since Γ is lower semicontinuous it follows that ${ \cal { T } } ^ { - } ( y _ { x } + A )$ is open in X and thus the family $\{ T ^ { - } ( y _ { x } + A ) \} _ { x \in X }$ is an open cover of X. By Remark 6.19 there exists a locally finite partition of unity $\{ \varphi _ { x } \} _ { x \in X }$ subordinated to $\{ T ^ { - } ( y _ { x } + A ) \} _ { x \in X }$ such that $\varphi _ { x _ { 0 } } \left( x _ { 0 } \right) = 1$ and $\varphi _ { x } \left( x _ { 0 } \right) = 0$ for all $x \neq x _ { 0 }$ . Note that if $\varphi _ { x } \left( z \right) > 0$ , then $z \in T ^ { - } ( y _ { x } + A )$ , and so $y _ { x } \in T \left( z \right) + A$ , where we have used the fact that A is balanced. Since $T \left( z \right)$ and A are convex sets, so is their sum $\boldsymbol { { \cal T } } \left( z \right) + \boldsymbol { { \cal A } }$ , and since $\{ \varphi _ { x } \} _ { x \in X }$ is locally finite, the convex combination 

$$
u (z) := \sum_ {x \in X} \varphi_ {x} (z) y _ {x}
$$

belongs to $T \left( z \right) + A$ . The function u is continuous and 

$$
u \left(x _ {0}\right) = \sum_ {x \in X} \varphi_ {x} \left(x _ {0}\right) y _ {x} = \varphi_ {x _ {0}} \left(x _ {0}\right) y _ {x _ {0}} = y _ {0}.
$$

This completes the proof. 

Lemma 6.21. Let X be a metric space, let Y be a topological vector space, and let 

$$
\Gamma : X \to \mathcal {P} (Y) \setminus \{\emptyset \}
$$

be a lower semicontinuous multifunction. Let $A \subset Y$ be a neighborhood of the origin and let $u : X \to Y$ be a continuous function such that 

$$
\Gamma (x) \cap (u (x) + A) \neq \emptyset
$$

for all $x \in X$ . Then the multifunction $\Gamma ^ { \prime } : X  \mathcal { P } ( Y ) \backslash \{ \emptyset \}$ , defined by 

$$
\Gamma^ {\prime} (x) := \Gamma (x) \cap (u (x) + A), \quad x \in X,
$$

is lower semicontinuous. 

Proof. Fix an open set $W \subset Y$ . To prove that $\varGamma ^ { \prime }$ is lower semicontinuous we need to show that the set $\left( T ^ { \prime } \right) ^ { - } \left( W \right)$ is open in $X$ . Let $x _ { 0 } \in \left( T ^ { \prime } \right) ^ { - } \left( W \right)$ . If $y _ { 0 } \in T ^ { \prime } \left( x _ { 0 } \right) \cap W$ , then in particular, by the definition of $\varGamma ^ { \prime }$ , y belongs to the open set $( u \left( x _ { 0 } \right) + A ) \cap W$ , and thus we may find a balanced neighborhood $D \subset Y$ of the origin such that 

$$
y _ {0} + D + D \subset (u (x _ {0}) + A) \cap W,\tag{6.16}
$$

where we have used the continuity of addition. Since u is continuous, the set $U : = u ^ { - 1 } \left( u \left( x _ { 0 } \right) + D \right)$ is a neighborhood of $x _ { 0 }$ in X. Also, since $y _ { 0 } \in$ $\Gamma \left( x _ { 0 } \right) \cap \left( y _ { 0 } + D \right)$ , we have that $x _ { 0 }$ belongs to the set $T ^ { - } ( y _ { 0 } + D )$ , which is open since Γ is lower semicontinuous. 

We claim that the neighborhood $U _ { 0 } : = U \cap T ^ { - } ( y _ { 0 } + D )$ of $x _ { 0 }$ is contained in $\left( T ^ { \prime } \right) ^ { - } \left( W \right)$ . Given the arbitrariness of $x _ { 0 } \in \left( T ^ { \prime } \right) ^ { - } \left( W \right)$ this will prove that $\left( T ^ { \prime } \right) ^ { - } \left( W \right)$ is an open set in $X$ , and in turn that $\varGamma ^ { \prime }$ is lower semicontinuous. 

To prove the claim we begin by showing that 

$$
y _ {0} + D \subset u (x) + A\tag{6.17}
$$

for all $x \in U$ . To see this, let $x \in U$ and $y \in D$ . By the definition of $U$ and the fact that D is balanced we have that $( u \left( x _ { 0 } \right) - u \left( x \right) ) \in D$ , while by (6.16) we may find $z \in A$ such that $u \left( x _ { 0 } \right) + z \in W$ and 

$$
y _ {0} + (u (x _ {0}) - u (x)) + y = u (x _ {0}) + z.
$$

Hence 

$$
y _ {0} + y = u (x) + z \in u (x) + A
$$

and so (6.17) holds. 

If $x \in U _ { 0 } = U \cap T ^ { - } ( y _ { 0 } + D )$ , then there exists $y \in T \left( x \right) \cap \left( y _ { 0 } + D \right)$ , and so by (6.16) we have that $y = y + 0 \in y _ { 0 } + D + D \subset W$ . On the other hand, by (6.17), 

$$
\Gamma^ {\prime} (x) \cap W = \Gamma (x) \cap (u (x) + A) \cap W \supset \Gamma (x) \cap (y _ {0} + D) \cap W \neq \emptyset ,
$$

since $y \in T \left( x \right) \cap \left( y _ { 0 } + D \right) \cap W$ . Hence $T ^ { \prime } \left( x \right) \cap W \neq \emptyset$ for all $x \in U _ { 0 }$ , which shows that $U _ { 0 } \subset ( { \Gamma } ^ { \prime } ) ^ { - } ( W )$ 

We now turn to the proof of Michael’s continuous selection theorem. 

Proof (Michael’s continuous selection theorem). By Lemma 6.20 there exists a continuous function $u _ { 1 } : X \to Y$ such that $u _ { 1 } \left( x _ { 0 } \right) = y _ { 0 }$ and 

$$
u _ {1} (x) \in \left(\Gamma (x) + B \left(0, \frac {1}{2}\right)\right)
$$

for all $x \in X$ . Inductively, assume that continuous functions $u _ { 1 } , \ldots , u _ { \ell } : X \to$ $Y$ have been constructed such that $u _ { n } \left( x _ { 0 } \right) = y _ { 0 }$ , 

$$
u _ {n} (x) \in \left(\Gamma (x) + B \left(0, \frac {1}{2 ^ {n}}\right)\right), \quad u _ {n} (x) \in \left(u _ {n - 1} (x) + B \left(0, \frac {1}{2 ^ {n - 2}}\right)\right)\tag{6.18}
$$

for all $x \in X$ and all $n = 2 , \ldots , \ell .$ . Define the multifunction 

$$
\Gamma_ {\ell} (x) := \Gamma (x) \cap \left(u _ {\ell} (x) + B \left(0, \frac {1}{2 ^ {\ell}}\right)\right).\tag{6.19}
$$

Note that for all $x \in X$ the set $T _ { \ell } \left( x \right)$ is nonempty by (6.18) and convex, since it is the intersection of two convex sets. By Lemma 6.21, $\varGamma _ { \ell }$ is lower semicontinuous, and so we may apply Lemma 6.20 to $\varGamma _ { \ell }$ to find a continuous function $u _ { \ell + 1 } : X \to Y$ such that for all $x \in X$ , 

$$
u _ {\ell + 1} (x) \in \left(\Gamma_ {\ell} (x) + B \left(0, \frac {1}{2 ^ {\ell + 1}}\right)\right).
$$

Then, by (6.19), $\begin{array} { r } { u _ { \ell + 1 } \left( x \right) \in \left( { \Gamma \left( x \right) + B \left( 0 , \frac { 1 } { 2 ^ { \ell + 1 } } \right) } \right) } \end{array}$ , while 

$$
u _ {\ell + 1} (x) \in \left(u _ {\ell} (x) + B \left(0, \frac {1}{2 ^ {\ell}}\right) + B \left(0, \frac {1}{2 ^ {\ell + 1}}\right)\right) \subset u _ {\ell} (x) + B \left(0, \frac {1}{2 ^ {\ell - 1}}\right)
$$

for all $x \in X$ 

Hence we have constructed a sequence $\{ u _ { n } \}$ of continuous functions satisfying (6.18) for all positive integers $n \geq 2$ . In particular, by (6.18) , 

$$
\left\| u _ {n + \ell} (x) - u _ {n} (x) \right\| _ {Y} \leq \frac {1}{2 ^ {n - 2}}
$$

for all $x \in X$ and for all $n \geq 2$ and $\ell \in \mathbb { N }$ . Since Y is a Banach space it follows that $C \left( X ; Y \right)$ is also a Banach space and thus $\{ u _ { n } \}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $C \left( X ; Y \right)$ . Thus $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges uniformly to a continuous function u : $X  Y$ such that u $( x _ { 0 } ) = y _ { 0 }$ . Since $T \left( x \right)$ is a closed set, it follows from $( 6 . 1 8 ) _ { 1 }$ that $u \left( x \right) \in T \left( x \right)$ for all $x \in X$ 

Remark 6.22. Note that the fact that X is a metric space has been used in Lemma 6.20 only to guarantee the existence of a locally finite partition of unity subordinated to an arbitrary cover of X. Thus Michael’s continuous selection theorem continues to hold when X is a topological vector space for which a locally finite partition of unity subordinated to an arbitrary cover of X exists, namely for paracompact spaces. We refer to [Mi56] and [W04] for more details. 

As a corollary of the previous theorem we have the following result (see also Example 6.16 above). 

Corollary 6.23. Let X, Y be Banach spaces and let $L : Y \to X$ be linear, continuous, and onto. Then there exists a continuous function $u : X \to Y$ such that u $( x ) \in L ^ { - 1 } \left( \{ x \} \right)$ for all $x \in X$ 

Proof. Define 

$$
\Gamma : X \to \mathcal {P} (Y) \setminus \{\emptyset \}
$$

as 

$$
\Gamma (x) := L ^ {- 1} (\{x \}), \quad x \in X.
$$

By the open mapping theorem the function L sends open sets into open sets and thus (see Example 6.16 above) Γ is lower semicontinuous. Since L is linear, continuous, and onto, the set $T \left( x \right)$ is convex, closed, and nonempty for all $x \in X$ . Hence we may apply the previous theorem to obtain a continuous selection $u : X \to Y$ 

## 6.2 Integrands

In the remainder of this chapter, $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is a Lebesgue measurable set, and as usual, $B \left( E \right)$ is the class of Borel subsets of $E$ 

## 6.2.1 Equivalent Integrands

Consider a function 

$$
f: E \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \to [ - \infty , \infty ].
$$

We say that $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable if it is measurable with respect to the σ-algebra generated by products of Lebesgue measurable subsets of E and Borel subsets of $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Then for every measurable function $v : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ the function $f \left( \cdot , v \left( \cdot \right) \right)$ is Lebesgue measurable. 

Proposition 6.24. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set and let $f , g :$ $E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable functions. Assume that for every $M > 0$ there exists a nonnegative function $\gamma _ { M } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ such that 

$$
f (x, z), g (x, z) \geq - \gamma_ {M} (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { \ } a . e . \ x \ \in \ E$ and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ with $| z | \leq M$ . Then the following two conditions are equivalent: 

(i) for every $v \in L ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and every Lebesgue measurable set $G \subset E$ 

$$
\int_ {G} f (x, v (x)) d x \leq \int_ {G} g (x, v (x)) d x;
$$

(ii) $f \left( x , z \right) \leq g \left( x , z \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Proof. Obviously (ii) implies (i). The proof of the converse implication is established in two steps. 

Step 1: Assume that E has finite measure. For $k \in \mathbb N$ define $f _ { k } : = \operatorname* { i n f } \left. f , k \right.$ $g _ { k } : = \operatorname* { i n f } \left\{ g , k \right\}$ . It is enough to show that 

f<sub>k</sub> (x, z) ≤ g<sub>k</sub> (x, z) for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. x ∈ E and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ with $| z | \leq k$ 

For $n \in \mathbb { N }$ define 

$$
\begin{array}{c} S _ {n, k} := \left\{(x, z) \in E \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: | z | \leq k, f _ {k} (x, z) > g _ {k} (x, z) + \frac {1}{n} \right\}, \\ S _ {n, k} (x) := \left\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: (x, z) \in S _ {n, k} \right\}, \\ \Pi_ {n, k} := \left\{x \in E: S _ {n, k} (x) \neq \emptyset \right\}. \end{array}
$$

Since the set $S _ { n , k }$ is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable, we have that $\varPi _ { n , k }$ is Lebesgue measurable by the projection theorem. We claim that $| \varPi _ { n , k } | = 0$ . Indeed, assume by contradiction that $| \varPi _ { n , k } | > 0$ . Then by Aumann’s selection theorem we may find measurable functions $v _ { n , k } : I I _ { n , k } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that $v _ { n , k } \left( x \right) \in$ $S _ { n , k } \left( x \right)$ for every $x \in \varPi _ { n , k }$ . Hence $| v _ { n , k } \left( x \right) | \leq k$ . Extend $v _ { n , k }$ to be zero on $E \setminus \varPi _ { n , k }$ . Then $v _ { n , k } \in L ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , and so by hypothesis, 

$$
\int_ {\Pi_ {n, k}} f (x, v _ {n, k} (x)) d x \leq \int_ {\Pi_ {n, k}} g (x, v _ {n, k} (x)) d x.\tag{6.20}
$$

By definition of $S _ { n , k }$ and $f _ { k }$ , 

$$
k \geq f _ {k} (x, v _ {n, k} (x)) > g _ {k} (x, v _ {n, k} (x)) + \frac {1}{n}\tag{6.21}
$$

for all $x \in \varPi _ { n , k }$ , and so, since $k > g _ { k } \left( x , v _ { n , k } \left( x \right) \right) = \operatorname* { i n f } \left\{ g \left( x , v _ { n , k } \left( x \right) \right) , k \right\}$ , we have that 

$$
g \left(x, v _ {n, k} (x)\right) + \frac {1}{n} = g _ {k} \left(x, v _ {n, k} (x)\right) + \frac {1}{n} <   f _ {k} \left(x, v _ {n, k} (x)\right) \leq f \left(x, v _ {n, k} (x)\right),
$$

and upon integration over $\varPi _ { n , k }$ 2 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {\Pi_ {n, k}} g (x, v _ {n, k} (x)) d x + \frac {1}{n} | \Pi_ {n, k} | \leq \int_ {\Pi_ {n, k}} f (x, v _ {n, k} (x)) d x \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \int_ {\Pi_ {n, k}} g (x, v _ {n, k} (x)) d x \end{array}
$$

by (6.20). Since E is bounded, it follows by (6.21) that the right-hand side of the previous inequality is finite, and thus $| \varPi _ { n , k } | = 0$ . Define 

$$
N _ {k} := \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \Pi_ {n, k}.
$$

Then $| N _ { k } | = 0$ and hence 

$f _ { k } \left( x , z \right) \leq g _ { k } \left( x , z \right)$ for all $x \in E \setminus N _ { k }$ and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ with $| z | \leq k .$ 

Step 2: In the case that E has infinite measure it sufices to apply Step 1 to $E _ { j } : = E \cap B \left( 0 , j \right)$ 

Remark 6.25. Since every Lebesgue measurable set $G \subset E$ may be written as the union of a Borel set and a set of Lebesgue measure zero, property (i) may be equivalently stated for Borel sets $G \subset E$ 

Similarly, we can prove the following result. 

Proposition 6.26. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set and let $f , g :$ $E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable functions such that 

$$
f (x, v (x)) = g (x, v (x)) \text {for} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {a.e.} x \in E
$$

for every $v \in C _ { b } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Then 

$$
f (x, z) = g (x, z) \text {   for   } \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {   a.e.   } x \in E \text {   and   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}.
$$

Proof. Let 

$$
\begin{array}{c} S := \{(x, z) \in E \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: f (x, z) \neq g (x, z) \}, \\ S (x) := \{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: (x, z) \in S \}, \\ \Pi := \{x \in E: S (x) \neq \emptyset \}. \end{array}
$$

Since the set S is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable, by the projection theorem we have that Π is a Lebesgue measurable set, and so by Aumann’s selection theorem we may find measurable functions $w : \pi \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that $w \left( x \right) \in S \left( x \right)$ for every $x \in \pi$ . Assume by contradiction that $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( \varPi \right) > 0$ . Then by Lusin’s theorem there exists a compact set $K \subset \pi$ such that $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( K \right) > 0$ and w is continuous on K. By the Tietze extension theorem we may extend w outside K as a function $v \in C _ { b } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Hence $( x , v ( x ) ) \in S$ for all $x \in K$ , but this contradicts the hypothesis. 

Motivated by the previous proposition, in what follows we say that two functions $f , g : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ are equivalent integrands (in the $L ^ { p }$ sense) if for every $v \in C _ { b } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we have 

$$
g \left(x, v (x)\right) = f (x, v (x)) \text {for} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {a.e.} x \in E.
$$

Note that for equivalent integrands, 

$$
\int_ {E} f (x, v (x)) d x = \int_ {E} g (x, v (x)) d x
$$

whenever the integrals are defined. Since Lebesgue integration does not distinguish $g$ from $f ,$ , for simplicity, and in analogy with Lebesgue spaces, we identify equivalent integrands. 

## 6.2.2 Normal and Carath´eodory Integrands

In this subsection we introduce the notion of normal and Carath´eodory inte grands. 

Definition 6.27. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set and let $B \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be a Borel set. A function $f : E \times B \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is said to be a normal integrand if: 

(i) for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ the function $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous on $B ;$ ; 

(ii) there exists a Borel function $g : E \times B \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
f (x, \cdot) = g (x, \cdot)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ 

The next result can be regarded as a “uniform” Lusin theorem. 

Theorem 6.28. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set, let $B \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be a Borel set, and let $f : E \times B \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be such that for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ the function $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous. Then the following conditions are equivalent: 

(i) f is a normal integrand. 

(ii) For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a closed set $C _ { \varepsilon } \subset E$ , with $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( E \setminus C _ { \varepsilon } \right) \leq \varepsilon$ , such that the restriction of f to $C _ { \varepsilon } \times B$ is lower semicontinuous. 

Proof. Step 1: We prove that (i) implies (ii). By eventually modifying f on a subset of E of Lebesgue measure zero, we may assume that $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous on $B$ for all $x \in E$ and that $f$ is a Borel function on $E \times B$ Moreover, after composing f with an isomorphism from $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ to [0, 1], we may assume that $f : E \times B  [ 0 , 1 ]$ . Let $\mathcal { A }$ be the countable family obtained by taking all finite unions of open balls with rational radii centered at $z \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ and 

$$
\mathcal {F} := \left\{r \chi_ {A}: r \in \mathbb {Q} \cap [ 0, 1 ], A \in \mathcal {A} \right\}.
$$

Then $\mathcal { F }$ is a countable family of lower semicontinuous functions. For any lower semicontinuous $g : B  [ 0 , 1 ]$ we have 

$$
g (z) = \sup \left\{\psi (z): \psi \in \mathcal {F} \text { and } \psi \leq g \right\}\tag{6.22}
$$

for all $z \in B$ . Indeed, the inequality $\geq$ is immediate. To prove the reverse inequality fix $z _ { 0 } ~ \in ~ B$ . If $g \left( z _ { 0 } \right) = 0 .$ , then there is nothing to prove. Thus assume that $g \left( z _ { 0 } \right) > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb { Q }$ be such that 

$$
g \left(z _ {0}\right) > r > 0.
$$

Since $g$ is lower semicontinuous, there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that 

$$
g (z) > r
$$

for all $z \in B \left( z _ { 0 } , \varepsilon \right)$ . Consider a ball $B \left( z _ { 1 } , \varepsilon _ { 1 } \right) \in \mathcal { A }$ such that 

$$
z _ {0} \in B (z _ {1}, \varepsilon_ {1}) \subset B (z _ {0}, \varepsilon).
$$

Then 

$$
\sup \left\{\psi \left(z _ {0}\right): \psi \in \mathcal {F} \text { and } \psi \leq g \right\} \geq r \chi_ {B (z _ {1}, \varepsilon_ {1})} \left(z _ {0}\right) = r.
$$

It sufices to let $r \nearrow g \left( z _ { 0 } \right)$ to obtain (6.22). 

Since $\mathcal { F }$ is countable, we may write $\mathcal { F } = \{ r _ { n } \chi _ { A _ { n } } \}$ , and set 

$$
\begin{array}{l} G _ {n} := \left\{x \in E: f (x, \cdot) \geq r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (\cdot) \right\}, \\ F _ {n} := \left\{(x, z) \in E \times B: f (x, z) <   r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (z) \right\}. \end{array}
$$

Using the facts that $f$ is a Borel function and $r _ { n } \chi A _ { n }$ is a lower semicontinuous function, we have that the set $F _ { n }$ is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable. The set $G _ { n }$ is the complement of the projection of $F _ { n }$ and thus it is Lebesgue measurable by the projection theorem. 

Since $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous on B, for every $x \in E$ in view of (6.22) we may write 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {n} \chi_ {G _ {n}} (x) r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (z)\tag{6.23}
$$

for all $( x , z ) \in E \times B$ . By Remark 1.95 applied to each function $\chi _ { G _ { n } }$ , for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ we may find a closed set $C _ { n } \subset E$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left(E \setminus C _ {n}\right) \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n + 1}}
$$

and the restriction of $\chi _ { G _ { n } }$ to $C _ { n }$ is continuous. Let 

$$
C _ {\varepsilon} := \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} C _ {n}.
$$

Then $C _ { \varepsilon }$ is closed and $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( E \setminus C _ { \varepsilon } \right) \leq \varepsilon . } \end{array}$ 

Since each function $\chi _ { G _ { n } } \left( x \right) r _ { n } \chi _ { A _ { n } } \left( z \right)$ restricted to $C _ { \varepsilon } \times B$ is lower semicontinuous, it follows that $f$ , which is their pointwise supremum, is also lower semicontinuous on $C _ { \varepsilon } \times B$ by Proposition 3.5. 

Step 2: We prove that (ii) implies (i). Taking $\textstyle \varepsilon : = { \frac { 1 } { k } } , k \in \mathbb { N }$ , let $C _ { k } \subset E$ be the closed set given in (ii) and let 

$$
F := \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} C _ {k}.
$$

Then $F$ is a Borel set, with $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( E \setminus F \right) = 0$ , and $f : F \times B \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is a Borel function. Setting 

$$
g \left(x, z\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} f \left(x, z\right) & \text { if } x \in F, \\ \infty & \text { if } x \notin F, \end{array} \right.
$$

we have that g is a Borel function such that $f \left( x , \cdot \right) = g \left( x , \cdot \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ . Hence f is a normal integrand. 

Remark 6.29. (i) Theorem 6.28 still holds if the Lebesgue measure $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ is replaced by a (positive) Radon measure on a measurable set E. 

(ii) It follows from the previous theorem that if f is a normal integrand, then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every compact set $K \subset E$ there exists a compact set $K _ { \varepsilon } \subset K$ such that $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( K \backslash \overline { { K _ { \varepsilon } } } \right) \leq \varepsilon$ for which the restriction of $f$ to $K _ { \varepsilon } \times B$ is lower semicontinuous. To see this, it sufices to apply Theorem 6.28 to f restricted to $K \times B$ 

In the special case that f is nonnegative we obtain a stronger result. 

Corollary 6.30. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set, let $B \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be a Borel set, and let $f : E \times B  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a normal integrand. Then there exists a sequence $\{ ( E _ { n } , \varphi _ { n } ) \}$ , where $E _ { n } \subset E$ has finite Lebesgue measure and $\varphi _ { n } \in C _ { c } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , such that 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {n} \chi_ {E _ {n}} (x) \varphi_ {n} (z)
$$

for every $( x , z ) \in E \times B$ 

Proof. We proceed as in the previous theorem, with the exception that $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ need not be replaced by [0, 1] via an isomorphism because f is bounded from below. Accordingly, the family $\mathcal { F }$ now is 

$$
\mathcal {F} := \left\{r \chi_ {A}: r \in \mathbb {Q} \cap [ 0, \infty), A \in \mathcal {A} \right\}.
$$

Then, as before, (6.23) holds, that is, 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {n} \chi_ {G _ {n}} (x) r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (z)\tag{6.24}
$$

for every $( x , z ) \in E \times B$ . Since $A _ { n } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is open, for each $k \in \mathbb N$ the function 

$$
\psi_ {n, k} \left(z\right) := \inf \left\{1, k \text { dist } \left(z, \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \setminus A _ {n}\right) \right\}
$$

is continuous and 

$$
\chi_ {A _ {n}} (z) = \sup _ {k} \psi_ {n, k} (z).
$$

Thus for every $( x , z ) \in E \times B$ 2 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {n, k} \chi_ {G _ {n}} (x) r _ {n} \psi_ {n, k} (z).
$$

Let $\{ F _ { j } \}$ be an increasing sequence of Lebesgue sets with finite measure such that 

$$
\bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} F _ {j} = E,
$$

and let $\{ \psi _ { j } \} \subset C _ { c } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ be an increasing sequence of nonnegative functions such that for every $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , 

$$
\sup _ {j} \psi_ {j} (z) = 1.
$$

Then for every $( x , z ) \in E \times B$ 2 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {n, k, j} \chi_ {G _ {n} \cap F _ {j}} (x) r _ {n} \psi_ {n, k} (z) \psi_ {j} (z).
$$

This completes the proof. 

In the next result we present conditions that are equivalent to normality and may be easier to verify in applications. 

We will also give an alternative proof to Theorem 6.28. For simplicity we consider only the case $B : = \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Proposition 6.31. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set and let $f$ : $E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be such that for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \ \in \ E$ the function $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous. Then the following conditions are equivalent: 

(i) f is a normal integrand; 

(ii) f is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable; 

(iii) the set 

$E _ { \infty } : = \{ x \in E : f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous and $\neq \infty \}$ 

is Lebesgue measurable and the multifunction 

$$
\Gamma : E _ {\infty} \to \left\{C \subset \mathbb {R} ^ {m + 1}: C \text {   nonempty,   closed } \right\}
$$

defined as 

$$
\Gamma (x) := \operatorname{epi} f (x, \cdot) = \{(z, t) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R}: f (x, z) \leq t \}, \quad x \in E _ {\infty},
$$

is measurable. 

The proof is hinged on the following result, which is of interest in itself. 

Lemma 6.32. Let $G \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Borel set endowed with the σ-algebra of Lebesgue measurable sets and let 

$$
\Gamma : G \to \{C \subset \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: C \text {   nonempty,   closed } \}
$$

be a multifunction. Then the following conditions are equivalent: 

(i) Γ is measurable; 

(ii) there exists a multifunction 

$$
\Gamma^ {\prime}: G \to \{C \subset \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: C \text {   nonempty,   closed } \}
$$

such that $\mathrm { G r } T ^ { \prime }$ is a Borel set of $G \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , and ${ \cal { T } } \left( x \right) = { \cal { T } } ^ { \prime } \left( x \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e .$ $x \in G ;$ 

(iii) for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a closed set $C _ { \varepsilon } \subset G$ , with $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( G \backslash C _ { \varepsilon } \right) \leq \varepsilon } \end{array}$ , such that the graph of Γ restricted to $C _ { \varepsilon }$ , that is, 

$$
\left\{(x, z) \in C _ {\varepsilon} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \in \Gamma (x) \right\},
$$

is closed. 

Proof. Step 1: We first prove that (i) implies (iii) under the additional assumption that $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( G \right) < \infty$ . Let $\left\{ C _ { n } \right\}$ be the countable family of all closed subsets of $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that are complementary to open balls with center in $\mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ and positive rational radius. Write $\mathbb { R } ^ { m } \setminus C _ { n } = B _ { m } \left( z _ { n } , r _ { n } \right)$ . We claim that for al $x \in G$ , 

$$
\Gamma (x) = \bigcap_ {n: C _ {n} \supset \Gamma (x)} C _ {n}.
$$

Indeed, if $x \in G$ , then the set $\mathbb { R } ^ { m } \setminus { \cal { T } } \left( x \right)$ is open, and so it can be written as the union of all open balls with center in $\mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ and positive rational radius that are contained in it. De Morgan’s law now establishes the claim. Let $G _ { n } : = \Gamma ^ { - } \left( B _ { m } \left( z _ { n } , r _ { n } \right) \right)$ and set 

$$
F _ {n} := G \setminus G _ {n} = \left\{x \in G: \Gamma (x) \subset C _ {n} \right\}.
$$

Then $G _ { n }$ and $F _ { n }$ are Lebesgue measurable by Proposition 6.3 and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{Gr} \varGamma = \{(x, z) \in G \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \in \varGamma (x) \} \\ = \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} [ (G _ {n} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \cup (F _ {n} \times C _ {n}) ]. \end{array}\tag{6.25}
$$

To see the latter, fix $( x , z ) \in \operatorname { G r } { \cal { T } }$ and $n \in \mathbb N$ . If $T \left( x \right) \subset C _ { n }$ , then $x \in F _ { n }$ and so $( x , z ) \in F _ { n } \times C _ { n }$ , while if $\varGamma \left( x \right)$ is not contained in $C _ { n }$ , then $x \in G _ { n }$ and so 

$$
\operatorname{Gr} \Gamma \subset \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left[ \left(G _ {n} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right) \cup \left(F _ {n} \times C _ {n}\right) \right].
$$

Conversely, let $\begin{array} { r } { ( x , z ) \in \bigcap _ { n = 1 } ^ { \infty } \left[ \left( G _ { n } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \cup \left( F _ { n } \times C _ { n } \right) \right] } \end{array}$ and assume by contradiction that $z \not \in T ( x )$ . Since ${ \cal { T } } \left( x \right)$ is closed we have that dist $( z , T \left( x \right) ) > 0$ , and so by the density of the rationals in the reals we may find n ∈ N such that $z \in B _ { m } \left( z _ { n } , r _ { n } \right)$ and $B _ { m } \left( z _ { n } , r _ { n } \right) \cap { \cal { T } } \left( x \right) = \emptyset$ . This last condition implies that $x \notin G _ { n } ;$ therefore $( x , z ) \in ( F _ { n } \times C _ { n } )$ , which is a contradiction since $z \in B _ { m } \left( z _ { n } , r _ { n } \right)$ . Thus (6.25) holds. 

For every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $n \in \mathbb N$ we may find compact sets $K _ { n } ~ \subset ~ G _ { n }$ and $K _ { n } ^ { \prime } \subset F _ { n }$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left(G \setminus (K _ {n} \cup K _ {n} ^ {\prime})\right) \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {n}}.
$$

Define 

$$
K _ {\varepsilon} := \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} K _ {n} \cup K _ {n} ^ {\prime}.
$$

Then $K _ { \varepsilon }$ is compact, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left(G \setminus K _ {\varepsilon}\right) = \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left(G \setminus \left(\bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} K _ {n} \cup K _ {n} ^ {\prime}\right)\right) \\ = \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left(G \setminus (K _ {n} \cup K _ {n} ^ {\prime})\right)\right) \leq \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

and, by (6.25), 

$$
\left\{(x, z) \in K _ {\varepsilon} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \in \Gamma (x) \right\} = \bigcap_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \left[ \left(K _ {n} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right) \cup \left(K _ {n} ^ {\prime} \times C _ {n}\right) \right],
$$

which is a closed set. 

Step 2: To prove that (i) implies (iii) in the general case, we write 

$$
G = \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} G ^ {(k)}, \quad G ^ {(k)} := \{x \in G: k - 1 \leq | x | <   k \},
$$

and apply the previous step to $\varGamma$ restricted to each $G ^ { ( k ) }$ to find compact sets $K ^ { ( k ) } \subset \joinrel \subset { \vec { G } } ^ { ( k ) }$ , with 

$$
\mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left(G ^ {(k)} \setminus K ^ {(k)}\right) \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2 ^ {k}},
$$

such that the set 

$$
\left\{(x, z) \in K ^ {(k)} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \in \Gamma (x) \right\}
$$

is closed. Let 

$$
C _ {\varepsilon} := \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} K ^ {(k)}.
$$

Then only finitely many $K ^ { ( k ) }$ intersect any bounded region, and so $C _ { \varepsilon }$ is closed. We claim that the set 

$$
\{(x, z) \in C _ {\varepsilon} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \in \Gamma (x) \}
$$

is closed. Indeed, let $\{ ( x _ { j } , z _ { j } ) \} \subset C _ { \varepsilon } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be such that $z _ { j } \in T \left( x _ { j } \right)$ for all $j \in \mathbb N$ and $( x _ { j } , z _ { j } ) \to ( x , z )$ as $j \to \infty$ , for some $( x , z ) \in C _ { \varepsilon } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Then the sequence $\{ x _ { j } \}$ must be bounded by some positive integer , and so 

$$
(x _ {j}, z _ {j}) \in \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\ell} \left\{(x, z) \in K ^ {(k)} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \in \Gamma (x) \right\}
$$

for all $j \in \mathbb N$ . Since it is a finite union of closed sets, this set is closed, and thus it must contain $( x , z )$ , that is, $z \in T \left( x \right)$ . Thus the claim holds. 

Step 3: Next we show that (iii) implies (ii). Taking $\begin{array} { r } { \varepsilon : = \frac { 1 } { k } , k \in \mathbb { N } } \end{array}$ , let $C _ { k } \subset G$ be the closed set given in (iii) and let 

$$
F := \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} C _ {k}.
$$

Then F is a Borel set and $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( G \backslash F \right) = 0$ . Moreover, the set 

$$
\{(x, z) \in F \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \in \Gamma (x) \} = \bigcup_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \left\{(x, z) \in C _ {k} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \in \Gamma (x) \right\}
$$

is a Borel set since it is the union of closed sets. Define 

$$
\Gamma^ {\prime}: G \to \{C \subset \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: C \text {   nonempty,   closed } \}
$$

as 

$$
\Gamma^ {\prime} \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \Gamma \left(x\right) & \text { if } x \in F, \\ \mathbb {R} ^ {m} & \text { if } x \in G \setminus F. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then ${ \cal { T } } \left( x \right) = { \cal { T } } ^ { \prime } \left( x \right)$ for all $x \in F$ and 

$$
\operatorname{Gr} \Gamma^ {\prime} = \left\{(x, z) \in F \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: z \in \Gamma (x) \right\} \cup \left(\left(G \setminus F\right) \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right),
$$

which is a Borel set. 

Step 4: Finally, we prove that (ii) implies (i). The equivalence of the fact that Gr $\varGamma ^ { \prime }$ is a Borel set with the weak measurability of the multifunction $\varGamma ^ { \prime }$ is a consequence of Remark 6.11 together with the completeness of the Lebesgue measure on the σ-algebra of Lebesgue measurable subsets. In turn, by Remark 6.4, $\varGamma ^ { \prime }$ is measurable. Let $C \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be any closed set. Then $\left( T ^ { \prime } \right) ^ { - } \left( C \right)$ is Lebesgue measurable. Since ${ \cal { T } } \left( x \right) = { \cal { T } } ^ { \prime } \left( x \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { a . e . } x \in G$ , we deduce that $T ^ { - } \left( C \right)$ difers from $\left( T ^ { \prime } \right) ^ { - } \left( C \right)$ by at most a set of Lebesgue measure zero, and so, again by the completeness of the Lebesgue measure, it is Lebesgue measurable. 

We now turn to the proof of Proposition 6.31 

Proof (Proposition 6.31). Let $E _ { 1 } \subset E$ be the set of points $x \in E$ such that the function $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous. By hypothesis $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( E \setminus E _ { 1 } \right) = 0$ 

Step 1: We prove that (ii) implies (iii). Since f is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable, then so is the function 

$$
h: E _ {1} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R} \to [ - \infty , \infty ]
$$

defined by 

$$
h (x, z, t) := f (x, z) - t.
$$

In turn, the set 

$$
F := \{(x, z, t) \in E _ {1} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R}: h (x, z, t) \leq 0 \}
$$

is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \mathcal { B } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \times \mathbb { R } \right)$ measurable. By the projection theorem, the projection of $F$ onto R<sup>N</sup> is Lebesgue measurable. Since $\pi _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { N } } \left( F \right) = E _ { \infty }$ , we have proved that the set $E _ { \infty }$ is Lebesgue measurable. It remains to show that $\varGamma$ is measurable. Note that if $x \in E _ { \infty }$ , then the function $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous, and so the set epi $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is closed in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m } \times \mathbb { R }$ by Proposition 3.4. Thus $\varGamma$ is welldefined. Moreover, 

$$
\operatorname{Gr} \Gamma = \{(x, z, t) \in E _ {\infty} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R}: (z, t) \in \Gamma (x) \} = F,
$$

and so it is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times B \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \times \mathbb { R } \right)$ measurable. Thus, by Remark 6.11 and the completeness of the Lebesgue measure, $\varGamma$ is weakly measurable, and actually measurable by Remark 6.4. Thus (iii) holds. 

Step 2: We show that (iii) implies (i). By Proposition 1.68 we may find a Borel set $G \subset E _ { \infty }$ such that $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } ( E _ { \infty } ) \backslash G ) = 0$ . Since the restriction of $\varGamma$ to $G$ is still measurable, by Lemma 6.32, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a closed set $C _ { \varepsilon } \subset G$ , with $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( G \setminus C _ { \varepsilon } \right) \leq \varepsilon$ , such that the graph of $\varGamma$ restricted to $C _ { \varepsilon }$ that is, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\big \{(x, z, t) \in C _ {\varepsilon} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R}: (z, t) \in \varGamma (x) \big \}} \\ & {\qquad = \big \{(x, z, t) \in C _ {\varepsilon} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \times \mathbb {R}: f (x, z) \leq t \big \} = \mathrm{epi} f | _ {C _ {\varepsilon} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}},} \end{array}
$$

is closed. It follows by Proposition 3.4 that the function 

$$
f: C _ {\varepsilon} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \to [ - \infty , \infty ]
$$

is lower semicontinuous. On the other hand, if $x \in E _ { 1 } \backslash E _ { \infty }$ , then $f \left( x , z \right) = \infty$ for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . By the inner regularity of the Lebesgue measure we may find a closed set $C _ { \varepsilon } ^ { \prime } \subset E _ { 1 } \setminus E _ { \infty }$ such that $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( ( E _ { 1 } \setminus E _ { \infty } ) \setminus C _ { \varepsilon } ^ { \prime } \right) \leq \varepsilon$ . Since $C _ { \varepsilon } ^ { \prime }$ is closed, the function 

$$
f: (C _ {\varepsilon} \cup C _ {\varepsilon} ^ {\prime}) \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \to [ - \infty , \infty ]
$$

is still lower semicontinuous and $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( E \setminus \left( C _ { \varepsilon } \cup C _ { \varepsilon } ^ { \prime } \right) \right) \leq 2 \varepsilon$ . It now follows from Theorem 6.28 that f is a normal integrand. 

Step 3: Finally, we prove that (i) implies (ii). Assume that f is a normal integrand. Then there exist a measurable set $E _ { 2 } \subset E$ , with $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( E \setminus E _ { 2 } \right) = 0$ , and a Borel function $g : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
f (x, \cdot) = g (x, \cdot)
$$

for all $x \in E _ { 2 }$ . This implies that $f : E _ { 2 } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \mathcal { B }$ measurable. Since $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( E \setminus E _ { 2 } \right) = 0$ , by the completeness of the Lebesgue measure it follows that $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable. 

Next we introduce the notion of Carath´eodory function. 

Definition 6.33. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set and let $B \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be a Borel set. A function $f : E \times B \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is said to be a Carath´eodory function if 

(i) for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ the function $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is continuous on $B ;$ ; (ii) for $a l l z \in B$ the function $f \left( \cdot , z \right)$ is measurable on E. 

The relation between normal integrands and Carath´eodory functions is the subject of the next theorem. 

Theorem 6.34. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set, let $B \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be a Borel set, and let $f \ : E \times B \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a Carath´eodory function. Then f is a normal integrand. 

Proof. By eventually modifying f on a subset of E of Lebesgue measure zero, we may assume that $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is continuous on B for all $x \in E$ and that for all $z \in B$ the function $f \left( \cdot , z \right)$ is measurable on $E$ . Moreover, after composing f with an isomorphism from $[ - \infty , \infty ]$ to [0, 1], we may assume that $f : E \times B \to$ [0, 1]. Let A and $\mathcal { F } = \{ r _ { n } \chi _ { A _ { n } } \}$ be as in Theorem 6.28 and let $\left\{ z _ { k } \right\}$ be dense in B. For each k, $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , define 

$$
G _ {k, n} := \left\{x \in E: f (x, z _ {k}) \geq r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (z _ {k}) \right\}.
$$

Since $f \left( \cdot , z _ { k } \right)$ is measurable on E it follows that the set $G _ { k , n }$ is Lebesgue measurable. In turn, the set 

$$
G _ {n} := \bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} G _ {k, n} = \{x \in E: f (x, z _ {k}) \geq r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (z _ {k}) \text {   for   all   } k \in \mathbb {N} \}
$$

is Lebesgue measurable. We claim that 

$$
G _ {n} = \left\{x \in E: f (x, z) \geq r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (z) \text {   for   all   } z \in B \right\}.
$$

Indeed, if $x \in G _ { n }$ and $z \in B$ , since $\left\{ z _ { k } \right\}$ is dense in B we may find a subsequence $\left\{ z _ { k _ { j } } \right\}$ of $\left\{ z _ { k } \right\}$ that converges to z. Since $f \left( x , z _ { k _ { j } } \right) \geq r _ { n } \chi _ { A _ { n } } \left( z _ { k _ { j } } \right)$ for all $j \in \mathbb N$ , using the continuity of $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ and the lower semicontinuity of $r _ { n } \chi A _ { \ i }$ we conclude that $f \left( x , z \right) \geq r _ { n } \chi _ { A _ { n } } \left( z \right)$ , and so the claim holds. 

Since $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is continuous on B for every $x \in E$ , in view of (6.22) we may write 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {n} \chi_ {G _ {n}} (x) r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (z)
$$

for all $( x , z ) \in E \times B$ . By Proposition 1.68, for all $n \in \mathbb N$ we may find Borel sets $H _ { n } \subset G _ { n }$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( H _ { n } \right) = \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( G _ { n } \right) } \end{array}$ . Define the function 

$$
g (x, z) = \sup _ {n} \chi_ {H _ {n}} (x) r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (z)
$$

$x \in E , z \in B$ . The function g is a Borel function since it is the supremum of Borel functions. Moreover, 

$$
f (x, \cdot) = g (x, \cdot)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ . Since $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is continuous on B for every $x \in E$ it follows that f is a normal integrand. 

The analogous statement of Theorem 6.28 for Carath´eodory functions is Scorza-Dragoni’s theorem below. 

Theorem 6.35 (Scorza-Dragoni). Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set, let $B \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ be a Borel set, and let $f : E \times B \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be a Carathéodory function. Then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a closed set $C _ { \varepsilon } \subset E$ , with $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \left( E \setminus C _ { \varepsilon } \right) \leq \varepsilon$ , such that the restriction of f to $C _ { \varepsilon } \times B$ is continuous. 

Proof. Since f and −f are normal integrands in view of the previous theorem, the result follows by applying Theorem 6.28 to both f and $- f$ 

## 6.2.3 Convex Integrands

In this subsection we extend the results of Section 4.7 to functions f that depend also on x. We begin with the case that f is real-valued. 

Theorem 6.36. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set and let $f : E \times$ $\mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to \mathbb { R }$ be an $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable function such that $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is convex in R<sup>m</sup> $f o r \ \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ u . e . \ x \in E$ . Then there exist measurable functions $a _ { i } : E \to \mathbb { R }$ and $b _ { i } : E  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Moreover, if f is nonnegative, then the functions $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { i }$ may be taken to be bounded. 

Proof. By De Giorgi’s theorem, for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ we may write 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\},
$$

where 

$$
a _ {i} (x) := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) ((m + 1) \varphi_ {i} (z) + \nabla \varphi_ {i} (z) \cdot z) d z,\tag{6.26}
$$

$$
b _ {i} (x) := - \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) \nabla \varphi_ {i} (z) d z,
$$

and the functions $\varphi _ { i }$ are of the form 

$$
\varphi_ {i} (z) := k _ {i} ^ {m} \varphi (k _ {i} (q _ {i} - z)), \quad z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$

for $\boldsymbol { k } _ { i } \in \mathbb { N } , q _ { i } \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ , and some $\varphi \in C _ { c } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ (see (4.43)). 

The measurability of $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { i }$ follows from Exercise 6.38 below. 

To prove the second part of the theorem, assume that $f \geq 0$ . By the first part of the theorem, and since $f$ is nonnegative, we may write 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\} ^ {+}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . For $k \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ define $\sigma _ { 0 } : \equiv 0$ and 

$$
\sigma_ {k} \left(s\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & s \leq k - 1, \\ - s + k & k - 1 <   s <   k, \\ 0 & s > k, \end{array} \right.
$$

and let 

$$
\phi_ {i, k} (x) := \sigma_ {k} \left(\left| a _ {i} (x) \right| + \left| b _ {i} (x) \right|\right).
$$

Since $0 \leq \phi _ { i , k } \leq 1$ , it follows that 

$$
\left(a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot z\right) ^ {+} = \sup _ {k \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{\phi_ {i, k} (x) a _ {i} (x) + \phi_ {i, k} (x) b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\},
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ and for all $z ~ \in ~ \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Note that $\phi _ { i , k } a _ { i } \ \in \ L ^ { \infty } \left( E \right)$ and $\phi _ { i , k } b _ { i } \in L ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

Remark 6.37. Note that if f is continuous in the x variable, then it follows from formulas (6.26) that the functions $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { i }$ are continuous, and, in turn, so are the functions $\phi _ { i , k }$ 

Exercise 6.38. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.36, prove that the functions $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { i }$ defined in (6.26) are measurable. 

Next we show that the statement of the previous theorem continues to hold when $f$ takes the value $\infty .$ , although there is no explicit representation of the approximating functions. 

Theorem 6.39. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set and let $f : E \times$ $\mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to \left( - \infty , \infty \right]$ be a normal integrand such that $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is convex in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \ \in \ E$ . Then there exist measurable functions $a _ { i } : E \to \mathbb { R }$ and $b _ { i } : E  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Moreover, if f is nonnegative, then the functions $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { i }$ may be taken to be bounded. 

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is convex and lower semicontinuous in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for all $x \in E$ 

Consider the multifunction 

$$
\Gamma : E \to \{C \subset \mathbb {R} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}, C \text { closed,   nonempty } \}
$$

defined by 

$$
\Gamma (x) := \{(a, b) \in \mathbb {R} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: a + b \cdot z \leq f (x, z) \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \}
$$

for $x \in E$ . Note that $T \left( x \right) \neq \emptyset$ for all for $x \in E$ by Proposition 4.75, and next we prove that the graph of Γ belongs to M $( E ) \otimes B ( \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ , where M (E) is the σ-algebra of Lebesgue measurable subsets of E. Let A be the countable family of all finite unions of open balls of $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ with rational radii centered at $z \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ . For $A \in { \mathcal { A } } , x \in E$ , and $( a , b ) \in \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ set 

$$
f _ {A} (x) := \inf _ {z \in A} f (x, z), g _ {A} (a, b) := \inf _ {z \in A} (a + b \cdot z).
$$

Then $g _ { A } : \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to \mathbb { R }$ is upper semicontinuous and $f _ { A }$ is measurable. To check the latter statement we observe that the set 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f _ {A} ^ {- 1} \left((- \infty , t)\right) = \left\{x \in E: \inf _ {z \in A} f (x, z) <   t \right\} \\ = \left\{x \in E: f (x, z) <   t \text {   for   some   } z \in A \right\} \end{array}
$$

is the projection onto E of the set 

$$
f ^ {- 1} \left((- \infty , t)\right) \cap (E \times A) = \{(x, z) \in E \times A: f (x, z) <   t \},
$$

so the measurability of the set $f _ { A } ^ { - 1 } \left( \left( - \infty , t \right) \right)$ follows from the projection the orem. 

In particular, we have that the function 

$$
(x, a, b) \in E \times \mathbb {R} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \mapsto f _ {A} (x) - g _ {A} (a, b)\tag{6.27}
$$

is M $( E ) \otimes B \left( \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ measurable. We claim that the graph of $\varGamma$ coincides with 

6 Integrands $f = f \left( x , z \right)$ 

$$
G := \bigcap_ {A \in \mathcal {A}} \left\{\left(x, a, b\right) \in E \times \mathbb {R} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: f _ {A} (x) \geq g _ {A} (a, b) \right\}.
$$

Indeed, if $( a , b ) \in T \left( { \boldsymbol { x } } \right)$ and if $A \in A$ , then for any $w \in A$ , 

$$
\inf _ {z \in A} (a + b \cdot z) \leq a + b \cdot w \leq f (x, w).
$$

Therefore, taking the infimum over all such $w ,$ we conclude that $g _ { A } \left( a , b \right) \leq$ $f _ { A } \left( x \right)$ . Conversely, if $( x , a , b ) \in G$ and if there exists $z _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
a + b \cdot z _ {0} > f (x, z _ {0}),
$$

then choose $\varepsilon > 0$ so small that 

$$
a + b \cdot z _ {0} > f (x, z _ {0}) + \varepsilon .
$$

Let $A \in { \mathcal { A } }$ be a neighborhood of $z _ { \mathrm { 0 } }$ for which 

$$
\inf _ {z \in A} (a + b \cdot z) \geq a + b \cdot z _ {0} - \varepsilon .
$$

Then 

$$
g _ {A} (a, b) = \inf _ {z \in A} (a + b \cdot z) > f (x, z _ {0}) \geq \inf _ {z \in A} f (x, z) = f _ {A} (x),
$$

and this contradicts the fact that $( x , a , b ) \in G$ 

The claim together with (6.27) ensures that the graph of Γ belongs to M $( E ) \otimes B \left( \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

By Aumann’s measurable selection theorem there exists a sequence of measurable functions $a _ { i } : E \to \mathbb { R }$ and $b _ { i } : E  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
\left(a _ {i} (x), b _ {i} (x)\right) \in \Gamma (x)
$$

for every $x \in E$ and $\{ ( a _ { i } ( x ) , b _ { i } ( x ) ) \}$ is dense in $\varGamma ( x )$ . We claim that for all $x \in E$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\}.\tag{6.28}
$$

By the definition of $\varGamma$ we have that 

$$
f (x, z) \geq \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\}.
$$

To prove the reverse inequality, fix $( x , z ) \in E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and let 

$$
f (x, z) > t.
$$

By Proposition 4.75 (ii) we may find $( a , b ) \in T ( x )$ such that 

$$
a + b \cdot z > t.
$$

Since $\{ ( a _ { i } \left( x \right) , b _ { i } \left( x \right) ) \} _ { i \in \mathbb { N } }$ is dense in $\varGamma ( x )$ , for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $i \in \mathbb N$ such that 

$$
\left| a - a _ {i} (x) \right| + \left| b - b _ {i} (x) \right| \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{1 + | z |}.
$$

Hence we deduce that 

$$
\sup _ {j \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {j} (x) + b _ {j} (x) \cdot z \right\} \geq a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot z > t - 2 \varepsilon ,
$$

and by letting first $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ and then $t \nearrow f \left( x , z \right)$ , we obtain (6.28). 

This concludes the first part of the proof. The second part follows exactly as in the previous theorem. We omit the details. 

Next we consider the case in which the function f is lower semicontinuous in x uniformly with respect to z. 

Proposition 6.40. Let $\varOmega \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be an open set and let $f : \varOmega \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be such that $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is convex and lower semicontinuous in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for all $x \in E$ Assume that for every $x _ { 0 } \in \varOmega$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
f (x, z) \geq (1 - \varepsilon) f (x _ {0}, z)\tag{6.29}
$$

for all $x \in \varOmega$ , with $| x - x _ { 0 } | \leq \delta$ , and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Then 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{\varphi_ {i} (x) \left(a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot z\right) ^ {+} \right\}
$$

for all $( x , z ) \in \varOmega \times \mathbb R ^ { m }$ , where $\varphi _ { i } \in C _ { c } ^ { \infty } ( \varOmega ) , \varphi _ { i } \geq 0 , a _ { i } \in \mathbb R$ , and $b _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ $i \in \mathbb N$ 

Proof. Let G be the class of all functions $g : \varOmega \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ of the form 

$$
g (x, z) = \varphi (x) (a + b \cdot z) ^ {+}, (x, z) \in \Omega \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$

where $\varphi \in C _ { c } ^ { \infty } ( \varOmega ) , \varphi \geq 0 , a \in \mathbb { R }$ , and $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , and such that $g ( x , z ) \leq f ( x , z )$ for all $( x , z ) \in \varOmega \times \mathbb R ^ { m }$ . Note that $\mathcal { G } \neq \emptyset$ because $0 \in \mathcal G$ 

We claim that 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {g \in \mathcal {G}} g (x, z) \quad \text { for   all } (x, z) \in \Omega \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}.\tag{6.30}
$$

By definition of $\mathcal { G }$ , it follows that 

$$
f \geq \sup _ {g \in \mathcal {G}} g.
$$

Conversely, fix $x _ { 0 } \ \in \ \varOmega , \ \varepsilon \ > \ 0$ , and let $\delta$ be such that (6.29) is satisfied. Consider a cutof function $\varphi \in C _ { c } ^ { \infty } ( \varOmega )$ , with $0 \leq \varphi \leq 1 , \varphi \equiv 1$ on $B ( x _ { 0 } , \delta / 2 )$ , $\varphi \equiv 0$ outside $B ( x _ { 0 } , \delta )$ . Using Proposition 4.77 we can write 

6 Integrands $f = f \left( x , z \right)$ 

$$
f (x _ {0}, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} (a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot z) ^ {+},
$$

for some $a _ { i } \in \mathbb { R }$ and $b _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Consider 

$$
f _ {i} ^ {\varepsilon} (x, z) := (1 - \varepsilon) \varphi (x) \left(a _ {i} + b _ {i} \cdot z\right) ^ {+}.
$$

By (6.29) it follows that $f _ { i } ^ { \varepsilon } \in \mathcal G$ , and we get 

$$
(1 - \varepsilon) f (x _ {0}, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} f _ {i} ^ {\varepsilon} (x _ {0}, z) \leq \sup _ {g \in \mathcal {G}} g (x _ {0}, z);
$$

hence the claim (6.30) follows by letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ 

By Proposition 4.78 and (6.30) there exists a sequence $f _ { i }$ in $\mathcal { G }$ such that $f ( x , z ) = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { i \in \mathbb { N } } f _ { i } ( x , z )$ for all $( x , z )$ in $\varOmega \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Remark $6 . 4 1$ . (i) By further specializing the class $\mathcal { G }$ , we may also assume the functions $\varphi _ { j }$ to have the form 

$$
\varphi_ {j} (x) = \varphi_ {j} ^ {1} (x _ {1}) \varphi_ {j} ^ {2} (x _ {2}) \dots \varphi_ {j} ^ {N} (x _ {N}),
$$

where $\varphi _ { j } ^ { i } \in C _ { c } ^ { \infty } ( \varOmega ) , \varphi _ { j } ^ { i } \geq 0 , i = 1 , \dots , N , j \in \mathbb { N } .$ 

(ii) In the case in which Ω is replaced by a measurable set $E ,$ the statement of the proposition still holds, provided the functions $\varphi _ { i }$ are required only to be continuous and bounded, and the proof is similar with obvious adaptations. 

We are now ready to prove the general case. 

Proposition 6.42. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set and let $f$ : $E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a lower semicontinuous function such that $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is convex in R<sup>m</sup> for all $x \in E$ . Assume that one of the following two conditions is satisfied: 

(i) there exists a continuous function $v _ { 0 } : E  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ with 

$$
(f (\cdot , v _ {0} (\cdot))) ^ {+} \in L ^ {\infty} (E);\tag{6.31}
$$

(ii) the set E is closed and there exists a function $\gamma : [ 0 , \infty )  [ 0 , \infty )$ , with 

$$
\lim _ {s \to \infty} \frac {\gamma (s)}{s} = \infty
$$

such that 

$$
f (x, z) \geq \gamma (| z |)
$$

for all $x \in E$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Then there exist two sequences of continuous functions 

$$
a _ {i}: E \to \mathbb {R}, \qquad b _ {i}: E \to \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$

such that 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\}
$$

for all $x \in E$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Moreover, if f is nonnegative, then the functions $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { i }$ may be taken to be bounded and condition (i) may be weakened to 

$$
(f (\cdot , v _ {0} (\cdot))) ^ {+} \in L _ {\mathrm{loc}} ^ {\infty} (E).\tag{6.32}
$$

Proof. Step 1: Assume first that condition (i) is satisfied and define 

$$
g (x, z) := f (x, z + v _ {0} (x)) - C _ {0},
$$

where $C _ { 0 } : = \Big \| ( f ( \cdot , v _ { 0 } ( \cdot ) ) ) ^ { + } \Big \| _ { L ^ { \infty } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ) }$ . Then g satisfies the same hypotheses of f and 

$$
- \infty <   g (x, 0) = f (x, v _ {0} (x)) - C _ {0} \leq 0.\tag{6.33}
$$

Consider the multifunction 

$$
\Gamma : E \to \{C \subset \mathbb {R} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: C \neq \emptyset , \text { convex,   closed } \}
$$

defined by 

$$
\Gamma (x) := \left\{(a, b) \in \mathbb {R} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: g (x, z) \geq a + b \cdot z \text {for all} z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \right\}.
$$

By Proposition 4.75 we have that $T ( x )$ is well-defined. We claim that Γ is lower semicontinuous. Fix an open set $A \subset \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . We need to show that 

$$
\Gamma^ {-} (A) := \{x \in E: \Gamma (x) \cap A \neq \emptyset \}
$$

is relatively open in E. Assume that $T ^ { - } ( A ) \neq \emptyset$ and fix $x _ { 0 } \in T ^ { - } ( A ) , ( a _ { 0 } , b _ { 0 } ) \in$ $A ,$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that 

$$
g (x _ {0}, z) \geq a _ {0} + b _ {0} \cdot z \quad \text { for   all } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m},\tag{6.34}
$$

$$
\{(a, b) \in \mathbb {R} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: | a - a _ {0} | + | b - b _ {0} | <   4 \varepsilon \} \subset A.\tag{6.35}
$$

We claim that there exists an open ball B in $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ containing $x _ { 0 }$ such that 

$$
g (x, z) \geq a _ {0} + b _ {0} \cdot z - \varepsilon (1 + | z |) \quad \text { for   all } x \in B \cap E \text { and } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}.\tag{6.36}
$$

Assume that (6.36) is false. Then there exist a sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} \subset E$ converging to $x _ { 0 }$ and a sequence $\{ z _ { n } \} \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
g (x _ {n}, z _ {n}) <   a _ {0} + b _ {0} \cdot z _ {n} - \varepsilon (1 + | z _ {n} |) \quad \text { for   all } n \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{6.37}
$$

If $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } | z _ { n } | < \infty$ , then we can assume that $z _ { n }$ converges to some $z _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , and due to the lower semicontinuity of $g _ { \mathrm { : } }$ letting $n \to \infty$ in (6.37) we get 

$$
g (x _ {0}, z _ {0}) \leq a _ {0} + b _ {0} \cdot z _ {0} - \varepsilon (1 + | z _ {0} |),
$$

which contradicts (6.34). Therefore sup $\ d u _ { n } \left. z _ { n } \right. = \infty$ , and without loss of generality we can assume that $| z _ { n } | \to \infty$ , with 

$$
w _ {n} := \frac {z _ {n}}{| z _ {n} |} \to w _ {0}
$$

The convex envelope of an $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable integrand is normal. This property follows from the proposition below. 

Proposition 6.43. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set and let $f$ : $E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable. Then $f ^ { * }$ , and therefore also $f ^ { * * }$ is a normal integrand.

$$

$$

In turn, the set 

$$

$$

$$

it follows that Gr Γ is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times B \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \times \mathbb { R } \right)$ measurable, and so by Aumann’s measurable selection theorem there exists a sequence of Lebesgue measurable functions $\{ ( v _ { n } , \psi _ { n } ) \} , v _ { n } : E _ { \infty } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m } , \psi _ { n } : E _ { \infty } \to \mathbb { R } , n \in \mathbb { N } .$ , such that for each $x \in E _ { \infty }$ the set $\left\{ \left( v _ { n } \left( x \right) , \psi _ { n } \left( x \right) \right) \right\} _ { n \in \mathbb { N } }$ is dense in epi $\overline { { f \left( x , \cdot \right) } }$ 

We claim that for all $( x , w ) \in \bar { E _ { \infty } } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , 

$$
f ^ {*} \left(x, w\right) = \sup _ {(z, t) \in \operatorname{epi} f (x, \cdot)} \left\{z \cdot w - t \right\}.
$$

Indeed, if $( x , w ) \in E _ { \infty } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , then $f \left( x , \cdot \right) \not \equiv \infty$ , and so epi $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is nonempty. Let $\left( z ^ { \prime } , t \right) \in \mathrm { e p i } f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ . Then 

$$

$$

and so 

$$
f ^ {*} \left(x, w\right) \geq \sup _ {\left(z, t\right) \in \mathrm{epi} f (x, \cdot)} \left\{z \cdot w - t \right\}.
$$

The reverse inequality follows from the facts that 

$$

$$

and that $\left( z , f \left( x , z \right) \right) \in \mathrm { e p i } f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ for all $z \in \mathrm { d o m } _ { e } f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ 

Thus the claim holds, and so, since for each $x \in E _ { \infty } .$ , the set

h (x, v (x)) \geq s (x, v (x)) \geq r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (v (x)) = \chi_ {B _ {n}} (x) r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (v (x)),
$$

and thus $x \in F _ { n }$ . This proves (6.46). In particular, by (6.44), 

$$
\mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left(B _ {n} \setminus F _ {n}\right) = 0,
$$

and so 

$$
h (x, v (x)) \geq \chi_ {B _ {n}} (x) r _ {n} \chi_ {A _ {n}} (v (x))
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Consequently, by (6.45), 

$$
h (x, v (x)) \geq g (x, v (x))
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ , and so 

$$
\int_ {G} h (x, v (x)) d x \geq \int_ {G} g (x, v (x)) d x
$$

for every Lebesgue measurable set $G \subset E$ and for all Lebesgue measurable functions $v : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . By Proposition 6.24 we obtain (ii). 

Now we prove (iii). Fix $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and a Borel set $G \subset E$ . Setting $\psi _ { 1 } \left( x \right) : = g \left( x , v \left( x \right) \right)$ , it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {G} g (x, v (x)) d x = \int_ {G} \psi_ {1} (x) d x \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \inf \Big \{\int_ {G} \psi (x) d x \colon \psi : G \to [ 0, \infty ] \text {measurable}, \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \psi (x) \geq s (x, v (x)) \text {for} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {a.e.} x \in G \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Conversely, if $\psi$ is admissible for the right-hand side of the above inequality, then an argument similar to that used to establish (ii), where now $\psi \left( x \right)$ replaces $h \left( x , v \left( x \right) \right)$ , yields 

$$
\psi (x) \geq g (x, v (x))
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in G .$ 

Finally, assume that $m = d + l$ with d, $l \in \mathbb N$ , and that for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ , and for all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ the function $s \left( x , u , \cdot \right)$ is convex in $\mathbb { R } ^ { l }$ . For every Borel set $G \subset E$ and for every Lebesgue measurable function $u : G \to \mathbb { R } ^ { d } , v : G \to \mathbb { R } ^ { l }$ define 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {G} ^ {*} s (x, u (x), v (x)) d x := \inf \Big \{\int_ {G} \psi (x) d x \colon \psi : G \to [ 0, \infty ] \text {measurable}, \\ \psi (x) \geq s (x, u (x), v (x)) \text {for} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {a.e.} x \in G \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Note that the map 

$$
v \mapsto \int_ {G} ^ {*} s (x, u (x), v (x)) d x
$$

is convex, and by (iii) so is 

$$
v \mapsto \int_ {G} g (x, u (x), v (x)) d x.
$$

Hence for any fixed $\theta \in [ 0 , 1 ] \cap \mathbb { Q }$ and v, $w \in L ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { l } \right)$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {G} g (x, u (x), (1 - \theta) v (x) + \theta w (x)) d x \\ \qquad \leq (1 - \theta) \int_ {G} g (x, u (x), v (x)) d x + \theta \int_ {G} g (x, u (x), w (x)) d x. \end{array}
$$

Since this is true for all $G \in \mathcal { B } ( E ) , u \in L ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , and v, $w \in L ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { l } \right)$ it follows from Proposition 6.24 that there exists a set $N _ { \theta } \subset E$ , with $| \dot { N } _ { \theta } | = \dot { 0 }$ , such that 

$$
g (x, u, (1 - \theta) \zeta + \theta w) \leq (1 - \theta) g (x, u, \zeta) + \theta g (x, u, w)\tag{6.47}
$$

for all $x \in E \setminus N _ { \theta } , u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , and $\zeta , w \in \mathbb { R } ^ { l }$ . Let 

$$
N _ {0} := \bigcup_ {\theta \in [ 0, 1 ] \cap \mathbb {Q}} N _ {\theta}.
$$

Then $| N _ { 0 } | = 0$ and (6.47) holds for all $\theta \in [ 0 , 1 ] \cap \mathbb { Q } , x \in E \setminus N _ { 0 } , u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , and all $\zeta , w \in \mathbb { R } ^ { l }$ . Now fix $\theta \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ and let $\theta _ { n } \in [ 0 , 1 ] \cap \mathbb { Q }$ be such that $\theta _ { n } \to \theta$ By (6.47), 

$$
g (x, u, (1 - \theta_ {n}) \zeta + \theta_ {n} w) \leq (1 - \theta_ {n}) g (x, u, \zeta) + \theta_ {n} g (x, u, w)
$$

for all $n \in \mathbb { N } , x \in E \setminus N _ { 0 } , u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , and all $\zeta , w \in \mathbb { R } ^ { l }$ . By letting $n \to \infty$ and using the fact that $g \left( x , u , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous in $\mathbb { R } ^ { l }$ for $\bar { \mathcal { L } ^ { N } } \mathrm { a . e . } x \in E$ , we establish that fo $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ the function $g \left( x , u , \cdot \right)$ is convex. This concludes the proof. 

## 6.3 Well-Posedness

Throughout this section we assume that the set E has finite measure. Let $f$ : $E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be an $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable function. For every measurable function $v : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ consider the superposition operator 

$$
v \mapsto f (\cdot , v (\cdot)).
$$

In this section we study necessary and suficient conditions for the superposition operator to map $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ into $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ . We begin with the case $1 \leq p < \infty$ 

## 6.3.1 Well-Posedness, $1 \leq p < \infty$

In this subsection we characterize the class of $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable integrands $f$ for which 

$$
\int_ {E} \left(f (x, v (x))\right) ^ {-} d x <   \infty
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . The main result of this subsection is given by the following theorem. Note that although its proof its somewhat involved, the main novelty with respect to similar results available in the literature (see, $\mathrm { e . g . , [ B u 8 9 ] , [ K r 7 6 ] ) }$ is that no regularity assumptions (e.g., continuity or lower semicontinuity) are made on $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ 

Theorem 6.45. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, let $1 \leq p < \infty$ , and let $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable. Then 

$$
\int_ {E} \left(f (x, v (x))\right) ^ {-} d x <   \infty\tag{6.48}
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ if and only if there exist a nonnegative function $\gamma \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and a constant $C > 0$ such that 

$$
f (x, z) \geq - C | z | ^ {p} - \gamma (x) \text {for} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {a.e.} x \in E \text {and for all} z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}.\tag{6.49}
$$

Proof. If (6.49) holds, then 

$$
(f (x, z)) ^ {-} \leq C | z | ^ {p} + \gamma (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , and therefore (6.48) is satisfied. 

To prove the converse implication, we observe that replacing f by $- f ^ { - }$ , we may assume without loss of generality that $f \leq 0$ 

Step 1: Fix a Borel function $g : E  [ 1 , \infty ]$ and for every $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ define the function $g _ { v } : E \to [ - \infty , 0 ]$ as 

$$
g _ {v} \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} f \left(x, v \left(x\right)\right) & \text { if } | v \left(x\right) | \leq g \left(x\right), \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }. \end{array} \right.\tag{6.50}
$$

Let $J ( g ) : E  [ - \infty , 0 ]$ be the essential infimum of the family 

$$
\left\{g _ {v}: v \in L ^ {p} \left(E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right) \right\}.
$$

By Remark 1.107(i) it follows that if $g _ { 1 } , g _ { 2 } : E \to [ 1 , \infty ]$ are two measurable functions such that $g _ { 1 } = g _ { 2 } \ \mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. in some Borel set $B \in B \left( E \right)$ , then 

$$
J \left(g _ {1}\right) = J \left(g _ {2}\right) \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text { a.e. in } B.\tag{6.51}
$$

Step 2: For each $x \in E$ and $n \in \mathbb { N }$ define 

$$
h (x, n) := J (n) (x).
$$

We claim that there exist a function $\gamma \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and a constant $C > 0$ such that 

$$
h (x, n) \geq - C n ^ {p} - \gamma (x) \text {   for   } \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {   a.e.   } x \in E \text {   and   for   all   } n \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{6.52}
$$

Assuming that the claim holds, in the remainder of this step we prove that (6.49) is satisfied. For any $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ construct a function $g \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { N } \right)$ such that 

$$
| v (x) | \leq g (x) \leq | v (x) | + 1\tag{6.53}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ 

We show that 

$$
h (x, g (x)) = J (g) (x)\tag{6.54}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ . Indeed, since g is integer-valued, for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ let 

$$
E _ {n} := \left\{x \in E: g (x) = n \right\}.
$$

By the locality property (6.51), for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E _ { n }$ we have 

$$
h (x, g (x)) = h (x, n) = J (n) (x) = J (g) (x),
$$

which proves (6.54). 

In turn, also by (6.50), (6.53), and (6.54), for every Borel set B and for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in B$ we have 

$$
f (x, v (x)) = g _ {v} (x) \geq J (g) (x) = h (x, g (x)),
$$

and so by (6.52) and (6.53),
