and so letting $\varepsilon \to 0$ and using the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem we obtain 

$$
I ^ {*} (\psi) \geq \int_ {K} f ^ {*} (x, \psi) d x \geq t
$$

by (6.122), and thus (6.121) follows. 

Step 2: By (6.114) and Step 1 we have that for every $v \in L ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ 

$$
I (v) = \sup _ {\psi \in C _ {0} (\Omega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m})} \int_ {\Omega} \psi (x) \cdot v (x) - f ^ {*} (x, \psi (x)) d x.
$$

Fix $v \in L ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and for $x \in \varOmega$ and $\xi \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ define 

$$
g _ {v} (x, \xi) := \xi \cdot v (x) - f ^ {*} (x, \xi).
$$

Note that for $\psi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we have that $g _ { v } \left( \cdot , \psi \left( \cdot \right) \right) \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ if and only if $\psi \in \mathcal { X }$ . Hence we invoke Remark 6.61 to deduce that 

$$
I (v) = \sup _ {\psi \in \mathcal {X}} \int_ {\Omega} g _ {v} (x, \psi (x)) d x = \int_ {\Omega} \bar {h} _ {v} (x) d x,
$$

where 

$$
\bar {h} _ {v} (x) := \sup _ {\xi \in \Gamma (x)} [ \xi \cdot v (x) - f ^ {*} (x, \xi) ] = \tilde {f} (x, v (x)).
$$

Thus we have shown that 

$$
\int_ {\Omega} f (x, v (x)) d x = \int_ {\Omega} \tilde {f} (x, v (x)) d x\tag{6.125}
$$

for all $v \in L ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ . Since $f \geq { \tilde { f } }$ this implies in particular that $f \left( x , v \left( x \right) \right) =$ $\tilde { f } \left( x , v \left( x \right) \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathcal { \Omega }$ , whenever $f \left( \cdot , v \left( \cdot \right) \right) \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ 

Fix $w \in L ^ { \infty } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and $B \in B \left( \varOmega \right)$ bounded, and define 

$$
v \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} w \left(x\right) \text { if } x \in B, \\ v _ {0} \left(x\right) \text { if } x \in \varOmega \setminus B. \end{array} \right.
$$

By (6.125), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {B} f (x, w (x)) d x + \int_ {\Omega \setminus B} f (x, v _ {0} (x)) d x \\ = \int_ {B} \tilde {f} (x, v (x)) d x + \int_ {\Omega \setminus B} \tilde {f} (x, v _ {0} (x)) d x. \end{array}
$$

Since $f \left( \cdot , v _ { 0 } \left( \cdot \right) \right) \in L ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ it follows 

$$
\int_ {\Omega \setminus B} f (x, v _ {0} (x)) d x = \int_ {\Omega \setminus B} \tilde {f} (x, v _ {0} (x)) d x <   \infty ,
$$

and so 

$$
\int_ {B} f (x, w (x)) d x = \int_ {B} \tilde {f} (x, v (x)) d x
$$

for all $w \in L ^ { \infty } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and $B \in B \left( { \varOmega } \right)$ bounded. We may now apply Theorem 6.24 to conclude that 

$$
f (x, z) = \tilde {f} (x, z)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \varOmega$ and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Proof (Suficiency of Theorem 6.57). Let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ be such that $v _ { n } \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mid \varOmega \stackrel { * } {  } \lambda$ in $\mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and set $\nu : = \mathcal { L } ^ { N } | \mathcal { Q } + | \lambda _ { s } |$ . Let $\varGamma _ { \nu }$ be the essential supremum of the family of multifunctions $\mathcal { F } : = \{ \varGamma _ { \psi } : \psi \in \mathcal { X } \}$ with respect to $\nu .$ 

Step 1: We claim that 

$$
f _ {s} (x, z) = \sup \left\{\xi \cdot z: \xi \in \Gamma_ {\nu} (x) \right\}\tag{6.126}
$$

for $\nu \ \mathrm { a . e . } \ x \in \varOmega$ and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . By Remark 6.14(ii) there exists a sequence $\{ b _ { i } \} \subset { \mathcal { X } }$ such that 

$$
\Gamma_ {\nu} (x) = \overline {{\{b _ {i} (x) \}}}\tag{6.127}
$$

for ν a.e. $x \in \varOmega$ . Let $\left\{ \varphi _ { n } \right\}$ be a countable dense subset of X. Then 

$$
\Gamma_ {\nu} (x) = \overline {{\{b _ {i} (x) \} \cup \{\psi_ {n} (x) \}}}
$$

for $\nu \ \mathrm { a . e . } \ x \ \in \ \varOmega$ . Therefore, without loss of generality, in (6.127) we may assume that sequence $\{ b _ { i } \}$ is dense in $\mathcal { X }$ , and thus for every $x \in \varOmega$ and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ ， 

$$
f _ {s} (x, z) = \sup \left\{\psi (x) \cdot z: \psi \in \mathcal {X} \right\} = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\},
$$

and the claim (6.126) follows from (6.127). 

Step 2: We claim that 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{b _ {i} (x) \cdot z - f ^ {*} (x, b _ {i} (x)) \right\}\tag{6.128}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \varOmega$ and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

The equality (6.128) follows from (6.96), the fact that 

$$
\Gamma_ {\nu} (x) = \Gamma (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \varOmega$ (see Remark 6.14(iii)), and (6.112). 

Step 3: The remainder of the proof follows closely that of Theorem 5.19. We indicate only the main changes. Define 

$$
a _ {i} (x) := - f ^ {*} (x, b _ {i} (x)).
$$

By replacing $f \left( x , z \right)$ with $f \left( x , z \right) - a \left( x \right)$ we can assume, without loss of generality, that $f \geq 0$ 

We choose a point $x _ { 0 } \in \varOmega$ that satisfies (6.128), (5.27)–(5.28), 

$$
\lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {\| \lambda \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon))}{\varepsilon^ {N}} <   \infty ,\tag{6.129}
$$

and is a Lebesgue point for all functions $a _ { i } , i \in \mathbb { N }$ . Choosing $\varepsilon _ { k } \searrow 0$ such that $\mu ( \partial Q ( x _ { 0 } , \varepsilon _ { k } ) ) = 0$ and $\| \lambda \| \left( \partial Q ( x _ { 0 } , \varepsilon _ { k } ) \right) = 0$ , in place of (5.31) we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} f (x, v _ {n} (x))   d x \\ \qquad \geq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} [ a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot v _ {n} (x) ]   d x \\ \qquad = a _ {i} (x _ {0}) + \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} b _ {i} (x) \cdot d \lambda (x), \end{array}
$$

where we have used Proposition 1.203(iii) and the fact that $x _ { 0 }$ is a Lebesgue point for $a _ { i }$ . Write 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} b _ {i} (x) \cdot d \lambda (x) = \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} (b _ {i} (x) - b _ {i} (x _ {0})) \cdot d \lambda (x) \\ + b _ {i} (x _ {0}) \cdot \frac {\lambda (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \end{array}
$$

and use the continuity of $b _ { i }$ and (6.129) to conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {k \to \infty} \frac {1}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} b _ {i} (x) \cdot d \lambda (x) = b _ {i} (x _ {0}) \cdot \lim _ {k \to \infty} \frac {\lambda (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))}{\varepsilon_ {k} ^ {N}} \\ = b _ {i} (x _ {0}) \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) \end{array}
$$

by (5.28). Hence 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) \geq a _ {i} (x _ {0}) + b _ {i} (x _ {0}) \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}),

and taking the supremum over all $i \in \mathbb N$ , by (6.128) we get

\frac {d \mu}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0}) \geq f \left(x _ {0}, \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x _ {0})\right).
$$

It remains to show that for $\| \lambda _ { s } \| \mathrm { a . e . } x _ { 0 } \in E$ 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}) \geq f _ {s} \left(x _ {0}, \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0})\right).

Take $x _ { 0 } \in \varOmega$ that satisfies (6.126), (5.32)–(5.34), and 

$$
\lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0 ^ {+}} \frac {1}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon))} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon)} | a _ {i} | d x = 0,\tag{6.130}
$$

for all $i \in \mathbb N$ 

Choosing $\varepsilon _ { k } \ \searrow \ 0$ such that $\mu ( \partial Q ( x _ { 0 } , \varepsilon _ { k } ) ) = 0 { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } \| \lambda \| \left( \partial Q ( x _ { 0 } , \varepsilon _ { k } ) \right) = 0$ then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d \mu}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}) \\ = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \frac {\mu (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))} \\ = \lim _ {k \to \infty} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} f (x, v _ {n} (x)) d x \\ \geq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {1}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} [ a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot v _ {n} (x) ] d x \\ = \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} \frac {1}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} b _ {i} (x) \cdot d \lambda (x), \end{array} \tag {6.131}
$$

where in the last equality we have used (6.130). Write 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} b _ {i} (x) \cdot d \lambda (x) \\ = \frac {1}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} (b _ {i} (x) - b _ {i} (x _ {0})) \cdot d \lambda (x) \\ + b _ {i} (x _ {0}) \cdot \frac {\lambda (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))}{\| \lambda_ {s} \| (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))} \end{array}
$$

and use the continuity of $b _ { i }$ and (5.33) to conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {k \to \infty} \frac {1}{\| \lambda_ {s} \|   (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))} \int_ {Q (x _ {0}, \varepsilon_ {k})} b _ {i}   (x) \cdot d \lambda   (x) \\ = b _ {i}   (x _ {0}) \cdot \lim _ {k \to \infty} \frac {\lambda   (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))}{\| \lambda_ {s} \|   (Q (x _ {0} , \varepsilon_ {k}))} = b _ {i}   (x _ {0}) \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d   \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}). \end{array}

Hence by (6.131) we obtain 

$$
\frac {d \mu}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}) \geq b _ {i} (x _ {0}) \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x _ {0}),

and taking the supremum over all i it follows by (6.126) that

Remark 6.63. Condition (6.95) has been used only in the necessity part of the proof to conclude that the sequentially lower semicontinuous functional I is actually lower semicontinuous with respect to weak star convergence. In the suficiency part of the proof we need only a much weaker condition, namely that there exist functions $a \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ and $b \in C _ { 0 } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ such that 

$$
f (x, z) \geq a (x) + b (x) \cdot z
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathcal { \Omega }$ and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Indeed, since $b \in C _ { 0 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ , it sufices to replace $f \left( x , z \right)$ with $f \left( x , z \right) - \left( a \left( x \right) + b \left( x \right) \cdot z \right)$ in Step 3 of the suficiency proof. 

Note that under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.57, since $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is convex and lower semicontinuous in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { a . e . } x \in \varOmega$ and (6.95) holds, by Theorem 4.92(iii) we have that $f \left( x , \cdot \right) = f ^ { \ast \ast } \left( x , \cdot \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathcal { \Omega }$ . Hence by (6.97) and the definition of $f ^ { * * } \left( x , \cdot \right)$ the inequality 

$$
f (x, \cdot) = f ^ {* *} (x, \cdot) \geq \tilde {f} (x, \cdot)
$$

is satisfied for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathcal { \Omega }$ . To our knowledge, it is still an open problem to characterize the class of integrands f for which the opposite inequality holds. By the suficiency and the necessity parts and by (6.128), sequentia lower semicontinuity holds if and only if f can be written (up to equivalent integrands) as 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\}, \quad (x, z) \in \Omega \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m},\tag{6.132}
$$

for some $a _ { i } \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ and $b _ { i } \in C \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ (with at least one $a _ { i } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ and $b _ { i } \in C _ { 0 } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ) )$ . In particular, if $f \geq 0$ , then we can set $a _ { 1 } : \equiv 0$ and $b _ { 1 } : \equiv 0$ Note that by Proposition 4.77, if (6.132) holds, then 

$$
f ^ {\infty} (x, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\}, \quad (x, z) \in \Omega \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$

and so the recession function $f ^ { \infty }$ must be lower semicontinuous in $( x , z )$ (up to equivalent integrands). Next we present two easily verifiable conditions under which (6.132) holds. 

Corollary 6.64. Let $f : \varOmega \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ be Borel measurable. Assume that $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is convex and lower semicontinuous in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in \varOmega$ . Then (6.96) holds if either of the two following conditions is satisfied: 

(i) f is lower semicontinuous in $\varOmega \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and there exists a continuous function $v _ { 0 } : \varOmega \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ with $f ( \cdot , v _ { 0 } ( \cdot ) ) \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { \infty } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } )$ ; 

(ii) $f : \varOmega \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ is locally bounded, and $\nabla _ { z } f$ exists for all $x \in \varOmega$ and for $\mathcal { L } ^ { m } \ a . e . \ z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , with $\nabla _ { z } f \left( \cdot , z \right)$ continuous. 

Proof. By Proposition 6.42 it follows that condition (i) implies (6.132), while if (ii) is satisfied, then by De Giorgi’s theorem 6.36, for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } \dot { x } \in \mathcal { \Omega }$ and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ we may write 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x) + b _ {i} (x) \cdot z \right\},
$$

where 

6 Integrands $f = f \left( x , z \right)$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} a _ {i} \left(x\right) := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f \left(x, z\right) \left(\left(m + 1\right) \varphi_ {i} \left(z\right) + \nabla \varphi_ {i} \left(z\right) \cdot z\right) d z, \\ b _ {i} \left(x\right) := - \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f \left(x, z\right) \nabla \varphi_ {i} \left(z\right) d z, \end{array}
$$

and $\varphi _ { i } \in C _ { c } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ are nonnegative and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { m } } \varphi _ { i } \left( z \right) d z = 1 } \end{array}$ . Since f is locally bounded, $a _ { i } \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ . Integrating by parts, we have that 

$$
b _ {i} (x) := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \nabla_ {z} f (x, z) \varphi_ {i} (z) d z,
$$

and so the continuity of $b _ { i }$ follows by the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem using also Theorem 4.36. 

## 6.5 Integral Representation in ${ \pmb L } ^ { p }$

Throughout this section we assume that $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is a Lebesgue measurable set, and we find suficient conditions for a functional 

$$
\mathcal {E}: L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \to (- \infty , \infty ]
$$

to have an integral representation of the type 

$$
\mathcal {E} (v) = \int_ {E} h (x, v (x)) d x
$$

for all $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and for some integrand h. We start with the case that $1 \leq p < \infty$ 

Theorem 6.65. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set, let $1 \leq p < \infty$ , and let 

$$
I: L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \times \mathcal {B} (E) \to (- \infty , \infty ]
$$

satisfy the following properties: 

$\left( I _ { 1 } \right) I ( v ; \cdot )$ is additive, that is, 

$$
I (v; B _ {1} \cup B _ {2}) = I (v; B _ {1}) + I (v; B _ {2})
$$

for all $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and all $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } \in B ( E )$ such that $B _ { 1 } \cap B _ { 2 } = \varnothing$ ; $\left( I _ { 2 } \right) I ( \cdot ; B )$ is local, that is, for all $B \in B ( E )$ 

$$
I (v; B) = I (w; B)
$$

for all v, $w \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ such that $v = w ~ \mathcal { L } ^ { N } ~ a . e .$ . on $B \in B ( E )$ 

For every $B \in B ( E )$ let τ be either the weak or the strong topology in $L ^ { p } \left( B ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and let $\mathcal { E } _ { p } \left( \cdot ; B \right)$ be the greatest functional below $I \left( \cdot , B \right)$ that is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to τ. Assume that 

$( I _ { 3 } ) \ : \mathcal { E } _ { p }$ is proper, that is, $\mathcal { E } _ { p } > - \infty$ , and there exists $v _ { 0 } \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v _ {0}; B) \in \mathbb {R}
$$

for every $B \in B ( E )$ 

Then there exists a normal integrand h : $E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ that satisfies the condition 

$$
h (x, z) \geq - C | z | ^ {p} - a (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \ \in \ E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , for some nonnegative function $a \in$ $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and some constant $C > 0$ , and such that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) = \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v _ {0}; B) + \int_ {B} h (x, v (x)) d x
$$

for all $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and $B \in B ( E )$ 

Proof. Step 1: As in Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 5.29 we can show that $\mathcal { E } _ { p }$ satisfies conditions $\left( I _ { 1 } \right)$ and $\left( I _ { 2 } \right)$ . Note that here we use heavily the fact that, by $\left( I _ { 3 } \right)$ , the functional $\mathcal { E } _ { p }$ and, in view of (5.50), all the functionals $\mathcal { H } _ { \beta }$ defined in Step 1 of Theorem 5.29 never take the value $- \infty$ , so that $\mathcal { H } _ { \beta } ( v ; B _ { 1 } ) + \mathcal { H } _ { \beta } ( v ; B _ { 2 } )$ and $\mathcal { E } _ { p } ( v ; B _ { 1 } ) + \mathcal { E } _ { p } ( v ; B _ { 2 } )$ are always well-defined. 

Step 2: By replacing the functional $\mathcal { E } _ { p } \left( \cdot ; B \right)$ with $\mathcal { E } _ { p } ( \cdot + v _ { 0 } ; B ) - \mathcal { E } _ { p } ( v _ { 0 } ; B )$ , where $v _ { 0 }$ is the function given in $\left( I _ { 3 } \right)$ , in the remainder of the proof we assume that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (0; B) = 0 \text {   for   each   } B \in \mathcal {B} (E).\tag{6.133}
$$

We claim that for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta = \delta \left( \varepsilon \right) > 0$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) + \frac {\varepsilon}{\delta} \int_ {B} | v | ^ {p} d x \geq - \varepsilon\tag{6.134}
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and $B \in B ( E )$ . Since $\mathcal { E } _ { p } \left( \cdot ; E \right)$ is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , by (6.133) this implies that for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta = \delta \left( \varepsilon \right) > 0$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; E) > - \varepsilon \text {   for   all   } v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \text {   with   } \int_ {E} | v | ^ {p} d x \leq \delta .\tag{6.135}
$$

For $B \in B \left( E \right)$ and $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we may find $k \in \mathbb N$ and $\eta \in [ 0 , 1 )$ such that 

$$
\int_ {B} | v | ^ {p} d x = (k + \eta) \delta\tag{6.136}
$$

and, by Propositions 1.89 and 1.20, $k + 1$ pairwise disjoint subsets of B such that 

$$
B = \bigcup_ {i = i} ^ {k + 1} B _ {i}, \quad \int_ {B _ {i}} | v | ^ {p} d x \leq \delta \text { for   all } i = 1, \dots , k + 1.
$$

Indeed, let $B _ { 1 } \subset B , B _ { 1 } \in B ( E )$ , be such that 

$$
\int_ {B _ {1}} | v | ^ {p} d x = \frac {k + \eta}{k + 1} \delta .
$$

Recursively, having found disjoint Borel sets $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { i } \subset B$ with $i \leq k$ and 

$$
\int_ {B _ {i}} | v | ^ {p} d x = \frac {k + \eta}{k + 1} \delta ,
$$

and since 

$$
\int_ {B \setminus \bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {i} B _ {j}} | v | ^ {p} d x = (k + \eta) \delta - \frac {k + \eta}{k + 1} \delta i \geq \frac {k + \eta}{k + 1} \delta (k + 1 - i),
$$

we may find $B _ { i + 1 } \subset B \setminus \bigcup _ { j = 1 } ^ { i } B _ { j } , B _ { i + 1 } \in B ( E )$ , such that 

$$
\int_ {B _ {i + 1}} | v | ^ {p} d x = \frac {k + \eta}{k + 1} \delta .
$$

By Step 1, (6.133), and (6.135) we have 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B _ {i}) = \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v \chi_ {B _ {i}}; E) > - \varepsilon \text {   for   all   } i = 1, \dots , k + 1,
$$

which implies that, again by Step 1, 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) = \sum_ {i = i} ^ {k + 1} \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B _ {i}) \geq - (k + 1) \varepsilon .
$$

In turn, by (6.136) this yields 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) + \frac {\varepsilon}{\delta} \int_ {B} | v | ^ {p} d x \geq - (k + 1) \varepsilon + (k + \eta) \varepsilon \geq - \varepsilon
$$

for all $\varepsilon > 0 , B \in { \cal B } \left( E \right)$ , and $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , and the claim is proved. 

Next we show that $\mathcal { E } _ { p } ( v ; \cdot )$ is a measure, absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. By Proposition 1.168 and $\left( I _ { 1 } \right)$ , to prove that $\mathcal { E } _ { p } ( v ; \cdot )$ is a signed measure it is enough to verify that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B _ {n}) \rightarrow \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) \text { whenever } B _ {n} \nearrow B, B _ {n}, B \in \mathcal {B} (E).
$$

By $( I _ { 1 } ) , ( I _ { 2 } )$ , and (6.133), 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) = \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v \chi_ {B}; E) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v \chi_ {B _ {n}}; E) = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B _ {n}).
$$

To obtain the opposite inequality, by (6.134) for every $\varepsilon > 0$ we have that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) + \frac {\varepsilon}{\delta} \int_ {B} | v | ^ {p} d x = \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B _ {n}) + \frac {\varepsilon}{\delta} \int_ {B _ {n}} | v | ^ {p} d x} \\ & {\qquad + \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B \setminus B _ {n}) + \frac {\varepsilon}{\delta} \int_ {B \setminus B _ {n}} | v | ^ {p} d x} \\ & {\qquad \geq \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B _ {n}) + \frac {\varepsilon}{\delta} \int_ {B _ {n}} | v | ^ {p} d x - \varepsilon .} \end{array}
$$

Hence 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) + \frac {\varepsilon}{\delta} \int_ {B} | v | ^ {p} d x \geq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \mathcal {E} (v; B _ {n}) + \frac {\varepsilon}{\delta} \int_ {B} | v | ^ {p} d x - \varepsilon ,
$$

or, equivalently, 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) \geq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B _ {n}) - \varepsilon ,
$$

and we may now let $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ 

Thus $\mathcal { E } _ { p } ( v ; \cdot )$ is a measure, and by $\left( I _ { 2 } \right)$ and (6.133) it is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. 

Step 3: For every $\varepsilon > 0 , B \in { \mathcal { B } } \left( E \right)$ , and $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we define 

$$
\varPhi_ {\varepsilon} (v; B) := - \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) - \frac {\varepsilon}{\delta} \int_ {B} | v | ^ {p} d x,
$$

where $\delta = \delta \left( \varepsilon \right) > 0$ is the constant given in the previous step. For every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $B \in B \left( E \right)$ we also set 

$$
\mu_ {\varepsilon} (B) := \sup \left\{\Phi_ {\varepsilon} (v; B ^ {\prime}): B ^ {\prime} \in \mathcal {B} (E), B ^ {\prime} \subset B, v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \right\}.
$$

We claim that $\mu _ { \varepsilon }$ is a (positive) Borel measure. Note that $\mu _ { \varepsilon } \geq 0$ by (6.133), while $\mu _ { \varepsilon } \leq \varepsilon \mathrm { ~ b y ~ } ( 6 . 1 3 4 )$ 

If $B _ { 1 } , \ B _ { 2 } \ \in \ B ( E )$ , with $B _ { 1 } ~ \subset ~ B _ { 2 }$ , then every Borel subset of $B _ { 1 }$ is a Borel subset of $B _ { 2 }$ , and so $\mu _ { \varepsilon } \left( B _ { 1 } \right) \leq \mu _ { \varepsilon } \left( B _ { 2 } \right)$ , that is, $\mu _ { \varepsilon }$ is an increasing set function. 

If $B _ { 1 } , \ B _ { 2 } \ \in \ B ( E )$ , with $B _ { 1 } \cap B _ { 2 } = \emptyset$ , then for any $B ^ { \prime } \in B ( E )$ , with $B ^ { \prime } \subset B _ { 1 } \cup B _ { 2 }$ , and any $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \varPhi_ {\varepsilon} \left(v; B ^ {\prime}\right) = \varPhi_ {\varepsilon} \left(v; B ^ {\prime} \cap B _ {1}\right) + \varPhi_ {\varepsilon} \left(v; B ^ {\prime} \cap B _ {2}\right) \\ \leq \mu_ {\varepsilon} \left(B _ {1}\right) + \mu_ {\varepsilon} \left(B _ {2}\right), \end{array}
$$

where we have used the fact that $\varPhi _ { \varepsilon } \left( v ; \cdot \right)$ is a signed measure. Taking the supremum over all admissible $B ^ { \prime }$ and v gives 

$$
\mu_ {\varepsilon} \left(B _ {1} \cup B _ {2}\right) \leq \mu_ {\varepsilon} \left(B _ {1}\right) + \mu_ {\varepsilon} \left(B _ {2}\right).\tag{6.137}
$$

To prove the reverse inequality fix real numbers $t _ { i } < \mu _ { \varepsilon } ( B _ { i } ) , i = 1$ , 2, and find $B _ { i } ^ { \prime } \in B ( E ) , B _ { i } ^ { \prime } \subset B _ { i }$ , and $v _ { i } \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ such that 

$$
t _ {i} <   \varPhi_ {\varepsilon} (v _ {i}; B _ {i} ^ {\prime}),
$$

i = 1, 2. Define 

$$
v \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} v _ {1} \left(x\right) \text {   if   } x \in B _ {1}, \\ v _ {2} \left(x\right) \text {   if   } x \in E \setminus B _ {2}. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , and so 

$$
\begin{array}{c} t _ {1} + t _ {2} <   \Phi_ {\varepsilon} (v _ {1}; B _ {1} ^ {\prime}) + \Phi_ {\varepsilon} (v _ {2}; B _ {2} ^ {\prime}) = \Phi_ {\varepsilon} (v; B _ {1} ^ {\prime}) + \Phi_ {\varepsilon} (v; B _ {2} ^ {\prime}) \\ = \Phi_ {\varepsilon} (v; B _ {1} ^ {\prime} \cup B _ {2} ^ {\prime}) \leq \mu_ {\varepsilon} (B _ {1} \cup B _ {2}), \end{array}
$$

where we have used the locality of $\begin{array} { r } { \varPhi _ { \varepsilon } ( \cdot ; B _ { i } ^ { \prime } ) , i = 1 , 2 } \end{array}$ , and again the fact that $\varPhi _ { \varepsilon } \left( v ; \cdot \right)$ is a signed measure. Letting $t _ { i } \nearrow \mu _ { \varepsilon } ( B _ { i } ) , i = 1$ , 2, gives, also by (6.137), 

$$
\mu_ {\varepsilon} \left(B _ {1} \cup B _ {2}\right) = \mu_ {\varepsilon} \left(B _ {1}\right) + \mu_ {\varepsilon} \left(B _ {2}\right).
$$

Since $\mu _ { \varepsilon } \left( \varnothing \right) = 0$ it follows that $\mu _ { \varepsilon }$ is a finitely additive measure. Hence by Proposition 1.9, to prove that $\mu _ { \varepsilon }$ is a measure it is enough to verify that 

$$
\mu_ {\varepsilon} (B _ {n}) \rightarrow \mu_ {\varepsilon} (B) \text { whenever } B _ {n} \nearrow B, B _ {n}, B \in \mathcal {B} (E).
$$

Using the fact that $\mu _ { \varepsilon }$ is an increasing set function, we have that 

$$
\sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \mu_ {\varepsilon} (B _ {n}) \leq \mu_ {\varepsilon} (B).
$$

To prove the reverse inequality fix a real number $t < \mu _ { \varepsilon } \left( B \right)$ and find $B ^ { \prime } \in$ $B \left( E \right)$ , with $B ^ { \prime } \subset B _ { i }$ , and $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ such that 

$$
t <   \varPhi_ {\varepsilon} (v; B ^ {\prime}).
$$

Since $\varPhi _ { \varepsilon } \left( v ; \cdot \right)$ is a signed measure, we have that 

$$
t <   \Phi_ {\varepsilon} (v; B ^ {\prime}) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \Phi_ {\varepsilon} (v; B ^ {\prime} \cap B _ {n}) \leq \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \mu_ {\varepsilon} (B _ {n}),
$$

and so letting $t \nearrow \mu _ { \varepsilon } \left( B \right)$ we obtain 

$$
\mu_ {\varepsilon} (B) \leq \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} \mu_ {\varepsilon} (B _ {n}).
$$

Hence $\mu _ { \varepsilon }$ is a (positive) finite Borel measure. Moreover, if $B \in B \left( E \right)$ has Lebesgue measure zero, then $\mu _ { \varepsilon } \left( B \right) = 0 \mathrm { ~ b y ~ } ( 6 . 1 3 3 )$ . Hence $\mu _ { \varepsilon }$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure and thus by the Radon– Nikodym theorem there exists a function $a _ { \varepsilon } \in L ^ { 1 } ( E )$ such that 

$$
\mu_ {\varepsilon} (B) = \int_ {B} a _ {\varepsilon} (x) d x
$$

for all $B \in B \left( E \right)$ . By the definition of $\mu _ { \varepsilon }$ and $\varPhi _ { \varepsilon } \left( v ; B \right)$ and by (6.134) we obtain that 

$$
\varPhi_ {\varepsilon} (v; B) = - \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) - \frac {\varepsilon}{\delta} \int_ {B} | v | ^ {p} d x \leq \mu_ {\varepsilon} (B) = \int_ {B} a _ {\varepsilon} (x) d x
$$

for all $B \in B \left( E \right)$ and $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , or equivalently, 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) \geq - \int_ {B} \left(a _ {\varepsilon} (x) + \frac {\varepsilon}{\delta} | v | ^ {p}\right) d x
$$

for all $B \in B \left( E \right)$ and $v ~ \in ~ L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Take $\varepsilon = 1$ and let $a : = a _ { 1 }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { C : = \frac { 1 } { \delta ( 1 ) } } \end{array}$ . Then 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) \geq - \int_ {B} (a (x) + C | v | ^ {p}) d x
$$

for all $B \in B \left( E \right)$ and $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

As in the proof of Theorem 5.29, since $\mathcal { E } _ { p } ( v ; \cdot )$ may not be a Radon measure, next we consider the Yosida transforms. In what follows we replace the functional $\mathcal { E } _ { p } \left( v ; B \right)$ with 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) + \int_ {B} (a (x) + C | v | ^ {p}) d x
$$

and thus the new functional, still denoted by $\mathcal { E } _ { p }$ , is nonnegative and 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (0; B) = \int_ {B} a (x) d x
$$

for all $B \in B ( E )$ 

Step 4: For every $k \in \mathbb { N } , B \in { \cal B } ( E )$ , and $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ define 

$$
\mathcal {Y} ^ {k} (v; B) := \inf \left\{\mathcal {E} _ {p} (u; B) + k \int_ {B} | w (x) - v (x) | ^ {p} d x: w \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \right\}.
$$

Exactly as in Substep 3a of the proof of Theorem 5.29, for $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ we have that $y ^ { k } ( v ; \cdot )$ is a (positive) finite Radon measure absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) = \sup _ {k} \mathcal {Y} ^ {k} (v; B)\tag{6.138}
$$

for every $B \in B ( E )$ , that 

$$
\mathcal {Y} ^ {k} (v; B) \leq \mathcal {E} _ {p} (0; B) + k \int_ {B} | v | ^ {p} d x = \int_ {B} (a + k | v | ^ {p}) d x\tag{6.139}
$$

for all $k \in \mathbb { N } , B \in { \mathcal { B } } ( E )$ , and that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | \mathcal {Y} ^ {k} (v; B) - \mathcal {Y} ^ {k} (u; B) | \\ \leq C k \left(\int_ {B} (a + | u | ^ {p} + | v | ^ {p}) d x\right) ^ {1 / p ^ {\prime}} \left(\int_ {B} | v - u | ^ {p} d x\right) ^ {1 / p} \end{array}\tag{6.140}
$$

for all $k \in \mathbb { N } , B \in { \mathcal { B } } ( E )$ , and $u \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ 

Let 

$$
\mathfrak {M} := \left\{B \in \mathcal {B} (E): | B | <   \infty \right\}.
$$

By (6.139), for every $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ the set function 

$$
B \in \mathfrak {M} \mapsto \mathcal {Y} ^ {k} (z; B)
$$

is nonnegative, countably additive, and bounded from above by a measure that is finite on M and absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. By Corollary 1.38 we may extend $y ^ { k } ( z ; \cdot )$ to a measure $\mu _ { k , z }$ defined on $B ( E )$ . Since $\mu _ { k , z } \left( B \right) = \mathcal { V } ^ { k } ( z ; B )$ for all $B \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ , it follows that $\mu _ { k , z }$ is still absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure and it is $\sigma { \mathrm { - f i n i t e } }$ Thus by the Radon–Nikodym theorem we may find a nonnegative measurable function $f _ { k , z } : E \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\mu_ {k, z} (B) = \int_ {B} f _ {k, z} (x) d x
$$

for all $B \in B ( E )$ , and so 

$$
\mathcal {Y} ^ {k} (z; B) = \int_ {B} f _ {k, z} (x) d x\tag{6.141}
$$

for all $B \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

In particular, if $j \in \mathbb N$ and $z , w \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ are such that $| z | , | w | \leq j$ , then by (6.140) and Young inequality, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | \mathcal {Y} ^ {k} (z; B) - \mathcal {Y} ^ {k} (w; B) | \leq C k \left(\int_ {B} (a + 2 j ^ {p}) d x\right) ^ {1 / p ^ {\prime}} | B | ^ {1 / p} | z - w | \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq C k \left[ \int_ {B} (a + 2 j ^ {p}) d x + | B | \right] | z - w | \end{array}
$$

for all $B \in { \mathfrak { M } }$ 

Thus, also by (6.139), (6.141), and Proposition 1.87 there exists a measurable set $N _ { 1 } \subset E$ , with $| N _ { 1 } | = 0$ , such that 

$$
0 \leq f _ {k, z} (x) \leq a (x) + k | z | ^ {p}\tag{6.142}
$$

for every $x \in E \setminus N _ { 1 }$ and every $z \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ , and 

$$
\left| f _ {k, z} (x) - f _ {k, w} (x) \right| \leq C k (a (x) + 2 j ^ {p} + 1) | z - w |\tag{6.143}
$$

for every $x \in E \setminus N _ { 1 } , j \in \mathbb { N }$ , and every $z , w \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ , with $| z | , | w | \leq j$ 

Fix $x \in E \setminus N _ { 1 }$ . Since the function $z \mapsto f _ { k , z } \left( x \right)$ is locally Lipschitz continuous on $\mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ , using the density of $\mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ we may uniquely extend it to a locally Lipschitz continuous function on $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that still satisfies (6.142) and (6.143). For every $x \in E$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ define 

$$
f _ {k} \left(x, z\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} f _ {k, z} \left(x\right) & x \in E \setminus N _ {1}, \\ 0 & x \in N _ {1}. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then by (6.142) and (6.143) the function $f _ { k } \left( x , z \right)$ is a Carath´eodory function and 

$$
0 \leq f _ {k} (x, z) \leq a (x) + k | z | ^ {p}
$$

for every $x \in E$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Since $y ^ { k } ( v ; \cdot )$ is a measure, it follows from (6.141) that 

$$
\mathcal {Y} ^ {k} (s; B) = \int_ {B} f _ {k} (x, s (x)) d x
$$

for all $B \in B ( E )$ and for every simple function s that takes values on $\mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ and such that 

$$
| \{x \in E: s (x) \neq 0 \} | <   \infty .
$$

Using the continuity with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ of both sides of the previous identity (see (6.140), (6.142), (6.143), and Corollary 6.51) we conclude that for every $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ 

$$
\mathcal {Y} ^ {k} (v; B) = \int_ {B} f _ {k} (x, v (x)) d x.
$$

Since for $k \leq n$ we have $\mathcal { V } ^ { k } ( v ; B ) \le \mathcal { V } ^ { n } ( v ; B )$ , we may find a set $N _ { 2 }$ with $| N _ { 2 } | = 0$ such that 

$$
f _ {k} (x, z) \leq f _ {n} (x, z)
$$

for all $x \in E \setminus N _ { 2 }$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Define 

$$
h \left(x, z\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \sup _ {k \in \mathbb {N}} f _ {k} \left(x, z\right) & x \in E \setminus N _ {2}, \\ 0 & x \in N _ {2}. \end{array} \right.
$$

By Theorem 6.34, each $f _ { k }$ is a normal integrand, and thus $h ,$ being the supremum of an increasing sequence of normal integrands, is still normal. Hence by (6.138) and the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem we have 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) = \int_ {B} h (x, v (x)) d x
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and $B \in B ( E )$ 

Exercise 6.66. Let $\varOmega = ( 0 , 1 )$ , let $m = 1$ , and for every $v \in L ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ and $x \in \varOmega$ let 

$$
T \left(v\right) \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1 \text {   if   } | \{y \in \Omega : v \left(y\right) = v \left(x\right) \} | = 0, \\ 0 \text {   otherwise.   } \end{array} \right.
$$

For every $v \in L ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ and $B \in B ( { \mathcal { \Omega } } )$ define 

$$
I (v; B) := \int_ {B} T (v) (x) d x.
$$

(i) For every $v \in L ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ and $B \in B ( { \mathcal { \Omega } } )$ define 

$$
N (v; B) := \{t \in \mathbb {R}: | \{y \in \Omega : v (x) = t \} | \neq 0 \}
$$

and prove that $N \left( v ; B \right)$ is at most countable and that if $w \in L ^ { p } ( \varOmega )$ is such that $v = w \ C ^ { 1 } \ { \mathrm { a . e } } .$ . on B, then $N \left( v ; B \right) = N \left( w ; B \right)$ 

(ii) For every $v \in L ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega ) , B \in B ( \varOmega )$ , and $x \in \varOmega$ let 

$$
T ^ {B} \left(v\right) (x) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1 \text {   if   } v \left(x\right) \notin N \left(v; B\right), \\ 0 \text {   otherwise. } \end{array} \right.
$$

Prove that $T \left( v \right) \left( x \right) = T ^ { B } \left( v \right) \left( x \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { 1 }$ a.e. $x \in B$ 

(iii) Prove that the functional I satisfies conditions $( I _ { 1 } ) , ( I _ { 2 } )$ , and $\left( I _ { 3 } \right)$ 

(iv) Prove that for every $B \in B ( { \mathcal { \Omega } } )$ and $c \in \mathbb { R }$ , 

$$
I \left(v _ {c}; B\right) = | B |,
$$

where $v _ { c } \left( x \right) : = x + c$ for $x \in \varOmega$ 

(v) Prove that there is no integrand $h : \varOmega \times \mathbb { R } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
I (v; B) = \int_ {B} h (x, v (x)) d x
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega )$ and $B \in B ( { \mathcal { \Omega } } )$ 

Next we address the case that $p = \infty$ 

Theorem 6.67. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set and let 

$$
I: L ^ {\infty} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \times \mathcal {B} (E) \to (- \infty , \infty ]
$$

satisfy properties $( I _ { 1 } ) \ – ( I _ { 2 } )$ of the previous theorem. For every $B \in B ( E )$ let $\tau$ be either the weak star or the Mackey topology in $L ^ { \infty } \left( B ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and let $\mathcal { E } _ { \infty } \left( \cdot ; B \right)$ be the greatest functional below $I \left( \cdot , B \right)$ that is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to τ. Assume that $\mathcal { E } _ { \infty }$ satisfies assumption $\left( I _ { 3 } \right)$ of the previous theorem. Then there exists a normal integrand $h : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to \left( - \infty , \infty \right] ( d e -$ pending on $\tau )$ that satisfies condition (6.70) such that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {\infty} (v; B) = \mathcal {E} _ {\infty} (v _ {0}; B) + \int_ {B} h (x, v (x)) d x
$$

for all $v \in L ^ { \infty } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and $B \in B ( E )$ 

If, in addition, I satisfies the growth condition 

${ \left( { I _ { 5 } } \right) } ^ { \prime }$ for every $M > 0$ there exists $\gamma _ { M } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ such that for all $B \in B ( E )$ 

$$
| I (v; B) | \leq \int_ {B} \gamma_ {M} (x) d x
$$

for all $v \in L ^ { \infty } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ with $| v \left( x \right) | \leq M$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in B$ 

then τ can also be taken as the strong topology in $L ^ { \infty } ( B ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ 

Proof. The proof is almost identical to that of Theorem 5.31. The only slight diference concerns the case in which $\tau$ is the strong topology. Note that in this case, by ${ \left( { I _ { 5 } } \right) } ^ { \prime }$ the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {1} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \mathcal {T} _ {M} (v; B) + \int_ {B} \gamma_ {M} d x
$$

is nonnegative, and so applying to this functional the reasoning in (5.66), once again we deduce that $\mathcal { T } _ { M }$ is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { 1 }$ 

## 6.6 Relaxation in L<sup>p</sup>

In this section we treat relaxation properties of functionals of the form 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto I (v) := \int_ {E} f (x, v) d x,
$$

where E is a Borel subset of R $^ N , 1 \le p \le \infty$ , and $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ is an $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable function. 

As in Section 5.4 we consider the relaxed energy 

$$
\mathcal {E}: L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \to [ - \infty , \infty ]
$$

of I, that is, the greatest functional E below I that is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to the topology τ. We will address the following types of convergence: 

• weak convergence in $L ^ { { p } } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } } 1 \leq { \boldsymbol { p } } < \infty ;$ 

• weak star convergence in $L ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ ; 

weak star convergence in the sense of measures $L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

By Propositions 3.16 and 3.18, when I satisfies a suitable coercivity con dition we have that $\mathcal { E } \left( v \right)$ coincides with 

$$
\mathcal {I} \left(v\right) := \inf \left\{\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}; E\right): \left\{v _ {n} \right\} \subset L ^ {p} \left(E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right), v _ {n} \stackrel {\tau} {\rightarrow} v \right\}
$$

for all $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

## 6.6.1 Weak Convergence and Weak Star Convergence in ${ \pmb { L } } ^ { p }$ , $1 \leq p \leq \infty$

In this subsection we characterize the relaxed energy 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p}: L ^ {p} \left(E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right) \to [ - \infty , \infty ]
$$

of I with respect to weak convergence in $L ^ { p } , 1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , that is, the functional $\mathcal { E } _ { p }$ is the greatest functional below I that is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak (respectively weak star if $p = \infty )$ convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

For every $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ define 

$$
\begin{array}{c}\mathcal {I} _ {p} (v) := \inf \left\{\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right): \{v _ {n} \} \subset L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}), \right.\\v _ {n} \rightharpoonup v (\stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} \text {   if   } p = \infty) \text {   in   } L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \Bigg \}.\end{array}
$$

Since $\mathcal { E } _ { p } \leq I$ , for every $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ we have 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v) \leq \mathcal {I} _ {p} (v).\tag{6.144}
$$

Note that the functional $\mathcal { T } _ { p }$ may fail to be sequentially lower semicontinuous, and thus in general we may have strict inequality in (6.144). Indeed, we have the following theorem. 

Theorem 6.68. Let E be a Borel subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , let $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , and let $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be an $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable function satisfying 

$$
f (x, z) \geq a (x) + b (x) \cdot z\tag{6.145}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \ \in \ E$ and for a $l l \ z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , where $a \in L ^ { 1 } ( E ) , b \in L ^ { p ^ { \prime } } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and $C > 0$ . Then for every $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ we have 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v) = \int_ {E} f ^ {* *} (x, v (x)) d x,
$$

where for every fixed $x \in E$ the function $f ^ { * * } ( x , \cdot )$ is the bipolar of $f ( x , \cdot )$ . In addition, for every $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ for which $\mathcal { T } _ { p } ( v ) < \infty$ we have 

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {p} (v) = \int_ {E} \mathcal {C} (\operatorname{lsc} f) (x, v (x)) d x,
$$

where for every fixed $x \in E$ the function $\mathcal { C } \left( \mathrm { l s c } f \right) \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is the convex envelope of the lower semicontinuous envelope of $f ( x , \cdot )$ 

Remark 6.69. (i) We recall that by Propositions 3.16, 3.18, we have 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v) = \mathcal {I} _ {p} (v) = \int_ {E} f ^ {* *} (x, v) d x
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ provided the function f in Theorem 6.68 satisfies the additional coercivity condition 

$$
f (x, z) \geq C \gamma (| z |) - \psi (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , where $C > 0 , \psi \in L ^ { 1 } ( E )$ , and where for $t \geq 0$ , 

$$
\gamma (t) := t ^ {p} \quad \text { if } 1 <   p <   \infty ,
$$

$$
\gamma \left(t\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0 & \text { if } 0 \leq t <   R, \\ \infty & \text { if } t \geq R, \end{array} \right. \quad \text { if } p = \infty ,
$$

for some $R > 0$ , and $\gamma : [ 0 , \infty )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ is an increasing function with 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \frac {\gamma (t)}{t} = \infty
$$

if $p = 1$ 

(ii) In view of Remark 4.93, if the function f in Theorem 6.68 is real-valued, that is, $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \longrightarrow \mathbb { R }$ , then for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E .$ , 

$$
f ^ {* *} (x, \cdot) = \operatorname{lsc} (\mathcal {C} f) (x, \cdot) = \mathcal {C} (\operatorname{lsc} f) (x, \cdot) = \mathcal {C} f (x, \cdot),
$$

and so by the previous theorem, for every $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ for which $\mathcal { T } _ { p } ( v ) <$ ∞ we have 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v) = \mathcal {I} _ {p} (v) = \int_ {E} f ^ {* *} (x, v) d x.
$$

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that there exists $v _ { 0 } ~ \in$ $L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ such that 

$$
\int_ {E} f (x, v _ {0} (x)) d x <   \infty .\tag{6.146}
$$

Since the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} (a (x) + b (x) \cdot v (x)) d x
$$

is continuous with respect to weak (respectively weak star if $p = \infty )$ convergence, replacing $f \left( x , z \right)$ by $f \left( x , z \right) - \left( a \left( x \right) + b \left( x \right) \cdot z \right)$ , we may assume without loss of generality that $f \geq 0$ . For every Borel set $B \in B ( E )$ we define the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto I (v; B) := \int_ {B} f (x, v) d x.
$$

Since I satisfies the hypotheses $( I _ { 1 } ) – ( I _ { 2 } )$ in Theorems 6.65, 6.67 and $\mathcal { E } _ { p }$ satisfies hypothesis $\left( I _ { 3 } \right)$ , using these results we deduce the existence of a normal function $h : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) = \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v _ {0}; B) + \int_ {B} h (x, v) d x\tag{6.147}
$$

for every $B \in B ( E )$ and $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ 

We claim that $\mathcal { E } _ { p } ( v _ { 0 } ; \cdot )$ is a Radon measure. By Step 1 of Theorem 6.65 and by (6.146), $\mathcal { E } _ { p } ( v _ { 0 } ; \cdot )$ is nonnegative, finite, and finitely additive, and so in view of Propositions 1.60 and 1.9 it sufices to prove that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} \left(v _ {0}; \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v _ {0}; E _ {n})
$$

for every increasing sequence $\{ E _ { n } \}$ of Lebesgue measurable sets $E _ { n } ~ \subset ~ E$ Consider one such sequence $\{ E _ { n } \}$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {E} _ {p} \left(v _ {0}; \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \mathcal {E} _ {p} \left(v _ {0}; E _ {k}\right) + \mathcal {E} _ {p} \left(v _ {0}; \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \setminus E _ {k}\right) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \mathcal {E} _ {p} \left(v _ {0}; E _ {k}\right). \end{array}
$$

Therefore 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} \left(v _ {0}; \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \geq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v _ {0}; E _ {k}).
$$

Conversely, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {E} _ {p} \left(v _ {0}; \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) = \mathcal {E} _ {p} \left(v _ {0}; E _ {k}\right) + \mathcal {E} _ {p} \left(v _ {0}; \left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \setminus E _ {k}\right) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \mathcal {E} _ {p} \left(v _ {0}; E _ {k}\right) + \int_ {\left(\bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \setminus E _ {k}} f \left(x, v _ {0} \left(x\right)\right) d x. \end{array}
$$

By (6.146) we have 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} \left(v _ {0}; \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} E _ {n}\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v _ {0}; E _ {k}).
$$

Having concluded that $\mathcal { E } _ { p } ( v _ { 0 } ; \cdot )$ is a Radon measure, we observe that since 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v _ {0}; B) \leq \int_ {B} f (x, v _ {0} (x)) d x
$$

for every Borel set $B \subset E$ , by the Radon–Nikodym theorem there exists a function $\psi \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v _ {0}; B) = \int_ {B} \psi (x) d x
$$

for every Borel set $B \subset E$ 

Hence (6.147) reduces to 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v; B) = \int_ {B} (\psi (x) + h (x, v)) d x
$$

for every $B \in B ( E )$ and $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ . Observe that the function $\tilde { h } : E \times$ $\mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ defined by 

$$
\tilde {h} (x, z) := \psi (x) + h (x, z)
$$

for $x \in E$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is a normal integrand, and that the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} \tilde {h} (x, v) d x
$$

satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 6.54. Therefore $\tilde { h } \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is convex in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ 

Moreover, in view of Proposition 6.43, $f ^ { * * }$ is a nonnegative normal integrand. By Theorems 6.54 and 6.56, for every $B \in B ( E )$ the functional 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {B} f ^ {* *} (x, v) d x
$$

is sequentially weakly (respectively weakly star if $p = \infty )$ lower semicontinu ous in $L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ , and since $f ^ { * * } \leq f$ , we deduce that for every $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ , 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (v, B) = \int_ {B} \tilde {h} (x, v) d x \geq \int_ {B} f ^ {* *} (x, v) d x.
$$

Hence for every Borel subset $B \subset E$ and for every $v \in L ^ { \infty } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ 

$$
\int_ {B} f ^ {* *} (x, v) d x \leq \int_ {B} \tilde {h} (x, v) d x \leq \int_ {B} f (x, v) d x,
$$

and thus by Proposition 6.24, 

$$
f ^ {* *} (x, z) \leq \tilde {h} (x, z) \leq f (x, z)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Since $\tilde { h } \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is convex in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ ${ \mathrm { a . e . ~ } } x \in E$ , it follows that 

$$
f ^ {* *} (x, z) = \tilde {h} (x, z)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

The last statement in the theorem can be proved following an argument entirely identical to that used in the proof of Theorem 5.32 starting from (5.72). We observe that $\mathcal { C } \left( \mathrm { l s c } f \right)$ is a Borel function, since it can be written as 

$$
\mathcal {C} \left(\operatorname{lsc} f\right) (x, z) = \inf _ {k \in \mathbb {N}} \left(f _ {k}\right) ^ {* *} (x, z)
$$

and the functions $\left( f _ { k } \right) ^ { * * }$ are normal integrands by Proposition 6.43. 

## 6.6.2 Weak Star Convergence in the Sense of Measures in $L ^ { 1 }$

In this subsection we consider only the case in which the domain of integration is an open set $\varOmega \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ . We study the relaxation of functionals of the type 

$$
v \in L ^ {1} (\Omega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto I (v) := \int_ {\Omega} f (x, v (x)) d x,\tag{6.148}
$$

where 

$$
f: \Omega \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \to (- \infty , \infty ],
$$

with respect to weak star convergence in the sense of measures. 

For any $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we define the functional 

$$
H \left(\lambda\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} I \left(v\right) \text {   if   } \lambda = v \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \big \lfloor \Omega \text {   for   some   } v \in L ^ {1} \left(\varOmega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right), \\ \infty \quad \text {   otherwise,   } \end{array} \right.
$$

and we characterize the relaxed energy 

$$
\mathcal {H}: \mathcal {M} (\Omega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \to [ - \infty , \infty ]
$$

of H with respect to weak star convergence in $\mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , that is, the functional H is the greatest functional below H that is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak star convergence in $\mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

For every $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ define 

$$
\begin{array}{r l}\mathcal {I} (\lambda) :=&\inf \Big \{\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right): \{v _ {n} \} \subset L ^ {1} (\varOmega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}),\\&v _ {n}   \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \big \lfloor   \varOmega \stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} \lambda   \text { in }   \mathcal {M} \left(\varOmega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right) \Big \}.\end{array}\tag{6.149}
$$

Since $\mathcal { H } \leq H$ , for every $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we have 

$$
\mathcal {H} (\lambda) \leq \mathcal {I} (\lambda).
$$

Theorem 6.70. Let $\varOmega \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be an open set and let $f : \varOmega \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be Borel measurable. Assume that there exist a function $a \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ and a constant $C > 0$ such that 

$$
f (x, z) \geq a (x) + C | z |\tag{6.150}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in \varOmega$ and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Then for every $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

$$
\mathcal {H} (\lambda) = \mathcal {I} (\lambda) = \int_ {\Omega} \tilde {f} \left(x, \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x + \int_ {\Omega} f _ {s} \left(x, \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|}\right) d \| \lambda_ {s} \|,
$$

where for $x \in \varOmega$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \tilde {f} (x, z) := \sup \left\{\xi \cdot z - f ^ {*} (x, \xi): \xi \in \Gamma (x) \right\}, \\ f _ {s} (x, z) := \sup \left\{\psi (x) \cdot z: \psi \in \mathcal {X} \right\}, \end{array}\tag{6.151}
$$

$\varGamma$ is the essential supremum of the family of multifunctions $\{ \boldsymbol { T } _ { \psi } : \psi \in \mathcal { X } \}$ , with 

$$
\mathcal {X} := \left\{\psi \in C _ {0} (\Omega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}): f ^ {*} (\cdot , \psi (\cdot)) \in L ^ {1} (\Omega) \right\},
$$

and for every fixed $x \in \varOmega$ the function $f ^ { * } \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is the polar function of $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ 

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that there exists $v _ { 0 } ~ \in$ $L ^ { 1 } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ such that 

$$
\int_ {\Omega} f (x, v _ {0} (x)) d x <   \infty .
$$

Step 1: We show that, without loss of generality, we may assume that $f \left( x , \cdot \right) = f ^ { * * } \left( x , \cdot \right)$ , and hence in what follows $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is convex and lower semicontinuous. Applying Proposition 6.43 we deduce that $f ^ { * * }$ is a normal integrand. 

For any $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we define the functional 

$$
J \left(\lambda\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \int_ {\Omega} f ^ {* *} \left(x, v \left(x\right)\right)   d x \text { if } \lambda = v   \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \big \lfloor   \Omega \text { for some} v \in L ^ {1} \left(\Omega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right), \\ \infty \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \text { otherwise }, \end{array} \right.
$$

and let $\mathcal { I }$ be the greatest functional below J that is sequentially lower semi continuous with respect to weak star convergence in $\mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

Since $\mathcal { T } \leq H$ , we have 

$$
\mathcal {J} \leq \mathcal {H}.
$$

Moreover, if $\mathcal { E } _ { 1 }$ is the greatest functional below I that is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak convergence in $L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , then by Theorem 6.68, 

$$
\mathcal {H} \left(v \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \lfloor \Omega\right) \leq \mathcal {E} _ {1} (v) = \int_ {\Omega} f ^ {* *} (x, v (x)) d x
$$

for every $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Therefore 

$$
\mathcal {H} (\lambda) \leq J (\lambda)
$$

for all $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , and by relaxing with respect to weak star convergence in $\mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , we conclude that 

$$
\mathcal {H} (\lambda) \leq \mathcal {J} (\lambda).
$$

Thus we have proved that $\mathcal { I } = \mathcal { H }$ . In turn, the integrand $f$ may be replaced by the normal integrand $f ^ { * * }$ , and with an abuse of notation, in the sequel we write $f$ in place of $f ^ { * * }$ . Therefore below, when we write $f ^ { * }$ this should be read as $f ^ { * * * }$ , but in view of Proposition 4.88, $f ^ { * }$ and $f ^ { * * * }$ coincide; hence there is no ambiguity. 

Step 2: We claim that the functional I defined in (6.149) is convex. Let $\lambda _ { 1 } , \ \lambda _ { 2 } \ \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and let $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ . It sufices to consider the case in which $\mathcal { T } \left( \lambda _ { 1 } \right)$ and $\mathcal { T } \left( \lambda _ { 2 } \right)$ are both finite. Hence for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ we may find $\{ v _ { n } \} , \{ w _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ such that $v _ { n } \ L ^ { N } { \big | } \ \varOmega \ { \stackrel { * } {  } } \ \lambda _ { 1 } , w _ { n } \ L ^ { N } { \big | } \ \varOmega \ { \stackrel { * } {  } } \ \lambda _ { 2 }$ in $\mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ L , and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {\Omega} f (x, v _ {n} (x)) d x \leq \mathcal {I} (\lambda_ {1}) + \varepsilon , \\ \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {\Omega} f (x, w _ {n} (x)) d x \leq \mathcal {I} (\lambda_ {2}) + \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Let $\left\{ h _ { k } \right\}$ be a sequence of functions in $L ^ { \infty } \left( \varOmega ; \{ 0 , 1 \} \right)$ such that $h _ { k } \stackrel { * } {  } \theta$ in $L ^ { \infty } \left( \varOmega \right)$ (see Example 2.86). For $x \in \varOmega$ define 

$$
u _ {n, k} (x) := \left(1 - h _ {k} (x)\right) v _ {n} (x) + h _ {k} (x) w _ {n} (x).
$$

Since 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \lim _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {\Omega} f (x, u _ {n, k}) d x \\ \qquad = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \lim _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {\Omega} (1 - h _ {k}) f (x, v _ {n}) + h _ {k} f (x, w _ {n}) d x \\ \qquad = (1 - \theta) \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {\Omega} f (x, v _ {n}) d x + \theta \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {\Omega} f (x, w _ {n}) d x \\ \qquad \leq (1 - \theta) \mathcal {I} (\lambda_ {1}) + \theta \mathcal {I} (\lambda_ {2}) + \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

and since 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \lim _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {\Omega} u _ {n, k} \psi d x = \langle (1 - \theta) \lambda_ {1} + \theta \lambda_ {2}, \psi \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}}
$$

for a countable dense family of functions $\psi$ in $C _ { 0 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ , using a diagonalization argument we may find an increasing sequence $\left\{ k _ { n } \right\}$ of positive integers such that 

$$
u _ {n, k _ {n}} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \left\lfloor \Omega \stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} (1 - \theta) \lambda_ {1} + \theta \lambda_ {2} \right.
$$

and 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \int_ {\Omega} f (x, u _ {n, k _ {n}}) d x \leq (1 - \theta) \mathcal {I} (\lambda_ {1}) + \theta \mathcal {I} (\lambda_ {2}) + \varepsilon .
$$

We deduce that 

$$
\mathcal {I} \left((1 - \theta) \lambda_ {1} + \theta \lambda_ {2}\right) \leq (1 - \theta) \mathcal {I} (\lambda_ {1}) + \theta \mathcal {I} (\lambda_ {2}) + \varepsilon ,
$$

and the convexity of I follows by letting $\varepsilon \to 0$ 

Step 3: In view of (6.150), for every $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

$$
H (\lambda) \geq \int_ {\Omega} a d x + C \| \lambda \|,
$$

which shows that H is coercive. By Proposition 3.16 we conclude that $\mathcal { H } = \mathcal { T }$ and that H is lower semicontinuous with respect to weak star convergence in $\mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

Consider now the duality pair $\left( \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) , C _ { 0 } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \right)$ under the duality 

$$
\langle u, \phi \rangle_ {\mathcal {M} (\varOmega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}), C _ {0} (\varOmega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m})} := \int_ {\varOmega} \phi \cdot d \lambda
$$

for $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and $C _ { 0 } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Then the functional $\mathcal { H }$ is convex and lower semicontinuous with respect to the topology $\sigma \left( \mathcal { M } , C _ { 0 } \right)$ . It follows from Proposition 4.92, taking as V the topological vector space 

$$
\left(\mathcal {M} \left(\varOmega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right), \sigma \left(L ^ {1}, C _ {0}\right)\right),
$$

that 

$$
\mathcal {H} = \mathcal {H} ^ {* *} \leq H ^ {* *}.
$$

Conversely, by Theorem 4.92, $H ^ { * * }$ is sequentially lower semicontinuous and below $H .$ , and therefore $\mathcal { H } ^ { * * } \geq H ^ { * * }$ . Since by Theorem A.72 the topological dual of $\left( \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) , \sigma \left( L ^ { 1 } , C _ { 0 } \right) \right)$ is $C _ { 0 } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , for each $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {H} (\lambda) = H ^ {* *} (\lambda) \\ \qquad = \sup _ {\psi \in C _ {0} (\Omega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m})} \left[ \int_ {\Omega} \psi (x) \cdot d \lambda (x) - H ^ {*} (\psi) \right] \\ \qquad = \sup _ {\psi \in C _ {0} (\Omega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m})} \left[ \int_ {\Omega} \psi (x) \cdot d \lambda (x) - \int_ {\Omega} f ^ {*} (x, \psi (x)) d x \right], \end{array}\tag{6.152}
$$

where in the last identity we have used Step 1 of the necessity part of the proof of Theorem 6.57. 

Fix $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and let $E \subset \varOmega$ be a Borel set such that 

$$
\mathcal {L} ^ {N} (E) = 0 = \left\| \lambda_ {s} \right\| (\Omega \setminus E).\tag{6.153}
$$

Set $\boldsymbol { \nu } : = \mathcal { L } ^ { N } \vert \textit { \Omega } + \vert \vert \lambda _ { s } \vert \vert$ . Then $\lambda \ll \nu$ and 

$$
\frac {d \lambda}{d \nu} (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x) & \text {if} x \in \Omega \setminus E, \\ \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x) & \text {if} x \in E, \end{array} \right.
$$

with $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { d \lambda } { d \nu } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega , \nu \right) } \end{array}$ . Define 

$$
h \left(x, z\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} f ^ {*} \left(x, z\right) & \text { if } x \in \varOmega \setminus E, \\ 0 & \text { if } x \in E. \end{array} \right.\tag{6.154}
$$

Then for $\psi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {\Omega} \psi (x) \cdot d \lambda (x) - \int_ {\Omega} f ^ {*} (x, \psi (x)) d x \\ = \int_ {\Omega} \left[ \psi (x) \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \nu} (x) - h (x, \psi (x)) \right] d \nu . \end{array}
$$

Hence by (6.152), 

$$
\mathcal {H} (\lambda) = \sup _ {\psi \in C _ {0} (\Omega ; \mathbb {R} ^ {m})} \int_ {\Omega} \left[ \psi (x) \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \nu} (x) - h (x, \psi (x)) \right] d \nu .
$$

We show that 

$$
\mathcal {H} (\lambda) = \sup _ {\psi \in \mathcal {X}} \int_ {\Omega} \left[ \psi (x) \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \nu} (x) - h (x, \psi (x)) \right] d \nu .
$$

Indeed, if $\psi \not \in { \mathcal { X } }$ , then since by (6.117), 

$$
\int_ {\Omega} f ^ {*} (x, \psi (x)) d x > - \infty ,
$$

we have 

$$
\int_ {\Omega} h (x, \psi (x)) d \nu = \int_ {\Omega} f ^ {*} (x, \psi (x)) d x = \infty ,
$$

and thus 

$$
\int_ {\Omega} \left[ \psi (x) \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \nu} (x) - h (x, \psi (x)) \right] d \nu = - \infty .
$$

Define 

$$
g (x, \xi) := \xi \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \nu} (x) - h (x, \xi),
$$

and note that by (6.153) and (6.154), if $\psi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , then 

$$
\int_ {\Omega} g (x, \psi (x)) d \nu = - \int_ {\Omega} f ^ {*} (x, \psi (x)) d x + \int_ {\Omega} \psi (x) \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \nu} (x) d \nu ,
$$

and so $g \left( \cdot , \psi \left( \cdot \right) \right) \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega , \nu \right)$ if and only if $\psi ~ \in ~ { \mathcal { X } }$ . Hence we may apply Remark 6.61 to deduce that 

$$
\mathcal {H} (\lambda) = \int_ {\Omega} \check {g} (x) d \nu ,
$$

where 

$$
\check {g} (x) := \sup _ {\xi \in \Gamma_ {\nu} (x)} \left(\xi \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \nu} (x) - h (x, \xi)\right),
$$

where $\varGamma _ { \nu }$ is the essential supremum of the family of multifunctions $\mathcal { F } : =$ $\{ T _ { \psi } : \psi \in \mathcal { X } \}$ with respect to $\nu .$ 

Since $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { L } ^ { N } | \mathcal { Q } \ll \nu , } \end{array}$ , by Remark 6.14(iii), 

$$
\Gamma_ {\nu} (x) = \Gamma (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in \varOmega$ , and so for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in \varOmega \setminus E$ we have 

$$
\check {g} (x) = \sup _ {\xi \in \Gamma (x)} \left(\xi \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x) - f ^ {*} (x, \xi)\right) = \tilde {f} \left(x, \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}} (x)\right).
$$

On the other hand, by Step 1 of the suficiency proof of Theorem 6.57, for $\| \lambda _ { s } \| \mathrm { a . e . } x \in E$ , 

$$
\check {g} (x) = \sup _ {\xi \in \Gamma_ {\nu} (x)} \left(\xi \cdot \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x)\right) = f _ {s} \left(x, \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|} (x)\right).
$$

This concludes the proof. 

Remark 6.71. (i) Without the growth condition (6.150) for nonnegative integrands f it is possible to prove that 

$$
\mathcal {H} (\lambda) = \int_ {\Omega} h \left(x, \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x + \int_ {\Omega} h ^ {\infty} \left(x, \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|}\right) d \| \lambda_ {s} \|
$$

for each $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , where $h : \varOmega \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ 0 , \infty ]$ is a normal integrand, with $h ( x , \cdot )$ convex and $h ^ { \infty }$ lower semicontinuous in $\varOmega \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . We refer to [AmBu88] for the precise statement, which holds without any measurability hypotheses on $f$ (provided the integral in (6.148) is replaced by the Lebesgue upper integral). However, in this case we are not aware of any explicit formula relating h to $f .$ 

(ii) If in place of the growth condition (6.150) we assume that there exist functions $a \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ and $b \in C _ { 0 } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ such that 

$$
f (x, z) \geq a (x) + b (x) \cdot z
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathcal { \Omega }$ and all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , then the previous theorem can be applied to show that for every $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

$$
\mathcal {E} (\lambda) = \int_ {\Omega} \tilde {f} \left(x, \frac {d \lambda}{d \mathcal {L} ^ {N}}\right) d x + \int_ {\Omega} f _ {s} \left(x, \frac {d \lambda}{d \| \lambda_ {s} \|}\right) d \| \lambda_ {s} \|,
$$

where $\mathcal { E }$ is the greatest functional below H that is lower semicontinuous with respect to weak star convergence in $\mathcal { M } \left( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ (we refer to [BouVa88] for more details). Note that in general we can conclude only that $\mathcal { E } \leq \mathcal { H }$
