Integrands $f = f \left( x , u , z \right)$ 

But just as much as it is easy to find the diferential of a given quantity, so it is dificult to find the integral of a given diferential. Moreover, sometimes we cannot say with certainty whether the integral of a given quantity can be found or not. 

Johann Bernoulli 

In this chapter we consider functionals of the type 

$$
(u, v) \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \times L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto I (u, v) := \int_ {E} f (x, u (x), v (x)) d x,\tag{7.1}
$$

where $1 \leq p , q \leq \infty$ , E is a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ , and $f :$ $E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ is an $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \mathcal { B }$ measurable function that is measurable with respect to the σ-algebra generated by products of Lebesgue measurable subsets of E and Borel subsets of $\mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

In what follows, normal and Carath´eodory integrands should be understood in the sense of Definitions 6.27, 6.33 with respect to the variables $\left( x , \left( u , z \right) \right)$ . 

## 7.1 Convex Integrands

In this section we prove approximation results for normal integrands under some convexity assumptions. We begin with the case that f is real-valued. 

Theorem 7.1. Let E be a Lebesgue measurable subset $o f \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and let $f : E \times$ $\mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \xrightarrow { } \mathbb { R }$ be a Carath´eodory function such that $f \left( x , \cdot , \cdot \right) \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and $f \left( x , u , \cdot \right)$ is convex in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ . Then there exist two sequences of Carath´eodory functions 

$$
a _ {i}: E \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \to \mathbb {R}, b _ {i}: E \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \to \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$

such that 

$$
f (x, u, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x, u) + b _ {i} (x, u) \cdot z \right\}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Moreover, if f is nonnegative, then the functions $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { i }$ may be taken to be bounded. 

Proof. By De Giorgi’s theorem (Theorem 4.79) for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ we may write 

$$
f (x, u, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x, u) + b _ {i} (x, u) \cdot z \right\},
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} a _ {i} \left(x, u\right) := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f \left(x, u, z\right) \left(\left(m + 1\right) \varphi_ {i} \left(z\right) + \nabla \varphi_ {i} \left(z\right) \cdot z\right) d z, \\ b _ {i} \left(x, u\right) := - \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f \left(x, u, z\right) \nabla \varphi_ {i} \left(z\right) d z, \end{array}
$$

and the functions $\varphi _ { i }$ are of the form 

$$
\varphi_ {i} (z) := k _ {i} ^ {m} \varphi (k _ {i} (q _ {i} - z)), \quad z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$

for $\boldsymbol { k } _ { i } \in \mathbb { N } , q _ { i } \in \mathbb { Q } ^ { m }$ , and some $\varphi \in C _ { c } ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \left( \sec \left( 4 . 4 3 \right) \right)$ 

Since $f \left( x , \cdot , \cdot \right) \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ , it follows by the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem that the functions $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { i }$ are Carath´eodory. 

If, in addition, $f$ is nonnegative, then for $k \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ define $\sigma _ { 0 } : \equiv 0$ and 

$$
\sigma_ {k} \left(s\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & 0 \leq s \leq k - 1, \\ - s + k & k - 1 <   s <   k, \\ 0 & s > k, \end{array} \right.
$$

if $k \geq 1$ . We claim that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} (a _ {i} (x, u) + b _ {i} (x, u) \cdot z) ^ {+} \\ = \sup _ {k \in \mathbb {N} _ {0}} \sigma_ {k} (| a _ {i} (x, u) | + | b _ {i} (x, u) |) (a _ {i} (x, u) + b _ {i} (x, u) \cdot z) \end{array}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ and all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Indeed, if $a _ { i } \left( x , u \right) + b _ { i } \left( x , u \right) \cdot z \leq$ $0 ,$ then since $\sigma _ { k } \geq 0$ , the supremum on the right-hand side is reached for $k = 0$ If $a _ { i } \left( x , u \right) + b _ { i } \left( x , u \right) \cdot z > 0$ , then since $0 \leq \sigma _ { k } \leq 1$ for all $k \geq 0$ , it follows that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & a _ {i} (x, u) + b _ {i} (x, u) \cdot z \\ & \qquad \geq \sigma_ {k} (| a _ {i} (x, u) | + | b _ {i} (x, u) |) (a _ {i} (x, u) + b _ {i} (x, u) \cdot z). \end{array}
$$

It sufices to take $k \in \mathbb N$ so large that $\left| a _ { i } \left( x , u \right) \right| + \left| b _ { i } \left( x , u \right) \right| \leq k - 1$ , so that 

$$
\sigma_ {k} \left(\left| a _ {i} (x, u) \right| + \left| b _ {i} (x, u) \right|\right) = 1.
$$

Then the functions 

$$
\begin{array}{l} a _ {i, k} \left(x, u\right) := \sigma_ {k} \left(\left| a _ {i} \left(x, u\right) \right| + \left| b _ {i} \left(x, u\right) \right|\right) a _ {i} \left(x, u\right), \\ b _ {i, k} \left(x, u\right) := \sigma_ {k} \left(\left| a _ {i} \left(x, u\right) \right| + \left| b _ {i} \left(x, u\right) \right|\right) b _ {i} \left(x, u\right), \end{array}
$$

where $x \in E$ and $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , are bounded Carath´eodory functions. 

A similar result holds if f is allowed to take the value $\infty$ , but in this case there is no explicit formula for the functions $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { i }$ . 

Theorem 7.2. Let E be a Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ and let $f :$ $E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a normal integrand such that $f \left( x , u , \cdot \right)$ is convex in R<sup>m</sup> for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ and all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ . Assume also that f satisfies one of the following two conditions: 

(i) there exists a continuous function $v _ { 0 } : \mathbb { R } ^ { d }  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ such that 

$$
(f (x, \cdot , v _ {0} (\cdot))) ^ {+} \in L ^ {\infty} (\mathbb {R} ^ {d})
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ 

(ii) there exists a function $\gamma : [ 0 , \infty ) \to [ 0 , \infty )$ , with 

$$
\lim _ {s \to \infty} \frac {\gamma (s)}{s} = \infty ,
$$

such that 

$$
f (x, u, z) \geq \gamma (| z |)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ and for all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Then there exist two sequences of Carath´eodory functions 

$$
a _ {i}: E \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \to \mathbb {R}, b _ {i}: E \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \to \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$

such that 

$$
f (x, u, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i} (x, u) + b _ {i} (x, u) \cdot z \right\}\tag{7.2}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Moreover, if f is nonnegative, then the functions $a _ { i }$ and $b _ { i }$ may be taken to be bounded. 

Proof. Assume first that (i) holds. Then for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ 

$$
\operatorname{esssup} \left(f (x, \cdot , v _ {0} (\cdot))\right) ^ {+} <   \infty ,
$$

and due to the lower semicontinuity of the function 

$$
u \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \mapsto (f (x, u, v _ {0} (u))) ^ {+},\tag{7.3}
$$

we conclude that for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ , 

$$
\sup _ {u \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}} (f (x, u, v _ {0} (u))) ^ {+} <   \infty .\tag{7.4}
$$

Define $g : E  [ 0 , \infty ]$ as 

$$
g (x) := \sup _ {u \in \mathbb {Q} ^ {d}} \left(f (x, u, v _ {0} (u))\right) ^ {+}, \quad x \in E.
$$

Then $g$ is measurable and by $( 7 . 4 )$ real-valued for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ . By applying Lusin’s theorem to $g$ and Theorem 6.28 to the normal integrand $f _ { ; }$ , we may find a sequence of increasing compact sets $\{ K _ { n } \} \subset E$ , with 

$$
\left| E \setminus \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} K _ {n} \right| = 0,\tag{7.5}
$$

such that $g : K _ { n } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ is continuous and $f : K _ { n } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to ( - \infty , \infty ]$ is lower semicontinuous for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Hence for each fixed $n \in \mathbb { N }$ the function $g$ is bounded on $K _ { n }$ by some constant $M _ { n } > 0$ . Using once again the lower semicontinuity of the function (7.3) we obtain 

$$
0 \leq (f (x, u, v _ {0} (u))) ^ {+} \leq M _ {n}
$$

for all $( x , u ) \in K _ { n } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ . Thus we may apply Theorem 6.42(i) (where the role of x in that theorem is now played by the variables $( x , u )$ , and E there is $K _ { n } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ here) to write 

$$
f (x, u, z) = \sup _ {i \in \mathbb {N}} \left\{a _ {i, n} (x, u) + b _ {i, n} (x, u) \cdot z \right\}\tag{7.6}
$$

for all $x \in K _ { n } , u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , where $a _ { i } \in C \left( K _ { n } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ and $b _ { i } \in$ $C \left( K _ { n } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

Moreover, since $K _ { n } \subset K _ { n + 1 }$ , by replacing $a _ { i , n }$ and $b _ { i , n }$ with $a _ { i , n + 1 } \big | _ { K _ { n } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } }$ and $b _ { i , n + 1 } \big | _ { K _ { n } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } } .$ , respectively, we can assume that 

$$
a _ {i, n} (x, u) = a _ {i, n + 1} (x, u), \quad b _ {i, n} (x, u) = b _ {i, n + 1} (x, u)
$$

for all $x \in K _ { n }$ and $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ . Hence the functions 

$$
a _ {i}: \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} K _ {n} \to \mathbb {R}, b _ {i}: \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} K _ {n} \to \mathbb {R} ^ {m}
$$

defined by 

$$
a _ {i} (x, u) := a _ {i, n} (x, u) \text {if} x \in K _ {n} \text {and} u \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d},
$$

$$
b _ {i} (x, u) := b _ {i, n} (x, u) \text {if} x \in K _ {n} \text {and} u \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d},
$$

are Carath´eodory and, in view of (7.5), satisfy (7.2). 

When condition (ii) is satisfied, then one can proceed as in the first part of the theorem to find an increasing sequence of compact sets $\{ K _ { n } \} \subset E$ such that (7.5) holds and $f : K _ { n } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to ( - \infty , \infty ]$ is lower semicontinuous for each $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Thus we may apply Theorem 6.42(ii) (where the role of x in that theorem is now played by the variables $( x , u )$ , and the closed set E there is $K _ { n } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ here) and then continue as in (7.6). 

The second part of the proof follows as in the proof of the previous theorem. We omit the details. 

## 7.2 Well-Posedness

In this section we characterize the class of $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable integrands f for which 

$$
\int_ {E} \left(f (x, u (x), v (x))\right) ^ {-} d x <   \infty
$$

for every $u \in L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ and $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

Theorem 7.3. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, $1 \leq p , q \leq \infty$ , and let $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ be $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable. Then 

$$
\int_ {E} \left(f (x, u (x), v (x))\right) ^ {-} d x <   \infty\tag{7.7}
$$

for every $u \in L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ and $v \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ if and only if 

(i) when $1 \leq p , q < \infty$ , there exist a nonnegative function $\omega \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and a constant $C > 0$ such that 

$$
f (x, u, z) \geq - C \left(| u | ^ {q} + | z | ^ {p}\right) - \omega (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ ; 

(ii) when $p = q = \infty$ , for every $M > 0$ there exists a nonnegative function $\omega _ { M } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ such that 

$$
f (x, u, z) \geq - \omega_ {M} (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ with $| u | , | z | \leq M$ ; 

(iii) when $1 \leq p < \infty$ and $q = \infty$ , for every $M > 0$ there exist a nonnegative function $\omega _ { M } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and a constant $C _ { M } > 0$ such that 

$$
f (x, u, z) \geq - C _ {M} | z | ^ {p} - \omega_ {M} (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \ w i t h \ | u | \le M$ ; 

(iv) when $p = \infty$ and $1 \leq q < \infty$ , for every $M > 0$ there exist a nonnegative function $\omega _ { M } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and a constant $C _ { M } > 0$ such that 

$$
f (x, u, z) \geq - C _ {M} | u | ^ {q} - \omega_ {M} (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ with $| z | \leq M$ 

Proof. Step 1: We prove (i). Without loss of generality, we may assume that $p \geq q$ . Define the integrand 

$$
g (x, w, z) := f \left(x, w | w | ^ {\frac {p}{q} - 1}, z\right).
$$

Note that if $w \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , then $w \left| w \right| ^ { \frac { p } { q } - 1 } \in L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , and hence by (7.7) we have that 

$$
\int_ {E} \left(g (x, w (x), v (x))\right) ^ {-} d x <   \infty
$$

for every $( w , v ) \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d + m } \right)$ . By Theorem 6.45, this implies that there exist a nonnegative function $\omega \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and a constant $C > 0$ such that 

$$
f \left(x, w | w | ^ {\frac {p}{q} - 1}, z\right) \geq - C \left(| w | ^ {p} + | z | ^ {p}\right) - \omega (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $( w , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , or, equivalently, 

$$
f (x, u, z) \geq - C \left(| u | ^ {q} + | z | ^ {p}\right) - \omega (x)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Step 2: Case (ii) follows from Theorem 6.47, where the variable z there is now replaced by the pair $( u , z )$ 

Step 3: We treat only the case (iii), since the case (iv) may be obtained from (iii) by interchanging u and z. 

As in the proof of Theorem 6.47, fix $M > 0$ and define the functions 

$$
\tau_ {M} \left(u\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} u & \text { if } | u | \leq M, \\ \frac {u}{| u |} M & \text { if } | u | > M, \end{array} \right.
$$

and 

$$
f _ {M} (x, u, z) := f (x, \tau_ {M} (u), z).
$$

Note that if $u \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , then $\tau _ { M } \left( u \right) \in L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ . Since the functional 

$$
(u, v) \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d + m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f _ {M} (x, u (x), v (x)) d x
$$

is well-defined and does not take the value −∞, by Theorem 6.45 there exist a function $a _ { M } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and a constant $C _ { M } > 0$ such that if $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } , | u | \leq M$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f \left(x, u, z\right) = f _ {M} \left(x, u, z\right) \geq - C _ {M} \left(| u | ^ {p} + | z | ^ {p}\right) - a _ {M} \left(x\right) \\ \geq - C _ {M} \left| z \right| ^ {p} - (C _ {M} M ^ {p} + a _ {M} \left(x\right)) \end{array}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

## 7.3 Sequential Lower Semicontinuity

In this section we study necessary and suficient conditions for the sequential lower semicontinuity of functionals of the form 

$$
(u, v) \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \times L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (x, u (x), v (x)) d x,
$$

where $1 \leq p , q \leq \infty$ and 

$$
f: E \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \to [ - \infty , \infty ]
$$

is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable. 

We are interested in the following types of convergence: 

• strong convergence in $L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right) \times L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } } 1 \leq p , q \leq \infty ;$ 

• strong–weak convergence in $L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right) \times L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) { \mathrm { ~ f o r ~ } } 1 \leq p , q < \infty .$ 

From now on we will assume that the integrand f satisfies the appropriate growth conditions from below that are necessary and suficient to guarantee that $\left( f \circ ( u , v ) \right) ^ { - } \in L ^ { 1 } ( E )$ for all $\left( u , v \right) \in L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right) \times L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , so that the functional 

$$
(u, v) \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \times L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (x, u (x), v (x)) d x
$$

is well-defined (see Theorem 7.3). 

## 7.3.1 Strong–Strong Convergence

In this subsection we study necessary and suficient conditions for the sequential lower semicontinuity of the functional (6.74) with respect to strong convergence $L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right) \times L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ for $1 \leq p , q \leq \infty$ . The next theorem follows from Theorem 7.4. 

Theorem 7.4. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, $1 \leq p , q \leq \infty$ , and let $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be an $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable function that satisfies conditions $( i ) - ( i v )$ of Theorem 7.3. Then the functional 

$$
(u, v) \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \times L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (x, u (x), v (x)) d x\tag{7.8}
$$

is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right) \times L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ if and only if (up to equivalent integrands) $f \left( x , \cdot , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous in $\mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ 

Proof. Suppose first that the functional (7.8) is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right) \times L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Without loss of generality we may assume that $q \geq p .$ . Since E has finite measure, we have that $L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ is continuously embedded in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , and so by hypothesis it follows that the functional 

$$
(u, v) \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d + m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (x, u (x), v (x)) d x
$$

is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { q } \left( \bar { E } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d + m } \right)$ . The result now follows from Theorems 6.49 and 6.52. 

The converse follows by applying Fatou’s lemma to the modified integrand obtained by adding to f the lower bound provided by (i)–(iv). 

## 7.3.2 Strong–Weak Convergence $1 \leq p , q < \infty$

We study necessary and suficient conditions for sequential lower semicontinuity of the functional (7.8) with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { q } , 1 \leq q < \infty$ 2 and weak convergence in $L ^ { p } , 1 \leq p < \infty$ . Since functionals that are sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to this kind of convergence are also sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to strong convergence, with out loss of generality, in what follows we may assume that the integrand f satisfies all the necessary conditions for strong convergence obtained in the previous subsections. 

Theorem 7.5. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, $1 \leq p , q < \infty$ , and let $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be an $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable function such that 

$$
f (x, u, z) \geq - C \left(| u | ^ {q} + | z | ^ {p}\right) - \omega (x)\tag{7.9}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \ \in \ E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , for some $\omega \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and $C > 0$ . Assume that $f \left( x , \cdot , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous in $\mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e .$ $x \in E$ . Then the functional 

$$
(u, v) \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \times L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} f (x, u (x), v (x)) d x
$$

Lemma 7.7. Let $g : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a proper convex, lower semicontinuous function such that

$$
\int_ {E _ {n k}} | \xi_ {n} (x) | ^ {p} d x \leq 1 \text {   for   all   } n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

These last two relations are analogous to (7.38) and thus lead to a contradic tion as in Case 1. 

Case 3: Finally, if 

$$
\begin{array}{r l r} & & {\underset {k \to \infty} {\liminf} \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \left[ \int_ {B _ {n k} ^ {-}} | \xi_ {n} (x) | ^ {p} d x + k \int_ {B _ {n k} ^ {+}} | \beta (x, u _ {n} (x)) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d x \right] = \infty ,} \\ & & {\underset {k \to \infty} {\liminf} \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {B _ {n k} ^ {+}} | \beta (x, u _ {n} (x)) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d x =: T \in (0, \infty)} \end{array}
$$

(note that the sequence $\left\{ \left| \beta \left( \cdot , u _ { n } \left( \cdot \right) \right) \right| ^ { p ^ { \prime } } \right\}$ is bounded in $L ^ { 1 } ( E ) )$ , then fix $k \in \mathbb N$ so large that 

$$
\frac {T}{2} \frac {1}{p} k ^ {1 / p} > 1 + 2 L
$$

and 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {B _ {n k} ^ {+}} | \beta \left(x, u _ {n} \left(x\right)\right) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d x > \frac {T}{2}.
$$

Select $n _ { 0 } = n _ { 0 } \left( k \right) \in \mathbb { N }$ so large that for all $n \geq n _ { 0 }$ ， 

$$
\int_ {B _ {n k} ^ {+}} | \beta (x, u _ {n} (x)) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d x > \frac {T}{2},
$$

and so 

$$
\frac {1}{p} k ^ {1 / p} \int_ {B _ {n k} ^ {+}} | \beta (x, u _ {n} (x)) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d x > \frac {T}{2} \frac {1}{p} k ^ {1 / p} > 1 + 2 L
$$

for all $n \geq n _ { 0 }$ . By Proposition 1.20 we may find $E _ { n k } \subset B _ { n k } ^ { + }$ measurable such that 

$$
\frac {1}{p} k ^ {1 / p} \int_ {E _ {n k}} | \beta (x, u _ {n} (x)) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d x = 1 + 2 L \text {   for   all   } n \in \mathbb {N} \text {   large. }\tag{7.39}
$$

Without loss of generality we may assume that $\beta \left( x , u _ { n } \right) \neq 0$ on $E _ { n k }$ . Construct measurable functions $\alpha _ { n } : E _ { n k } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ such that 

$$
| \alpha_ {n} (x) \xi_ {n} (x) | ^ {p} = k | \beta (x, u _ {n} (x)) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}}.\tag{7.40}
$$

Note that in view of $( 7 . 3 7 ) , 0 \leq \alpha _ { n } \left( x \right) \leq 1$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E _ { n k }$ and for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ large. For $x \in E$ and for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ large define 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & U _ {n} := (1 - \chi_ {E _ {n k}}) u + \chi_ {E _ {n k}} u _ {n}, \\ & V _ {n} := (1 - \chi_ {E _ {n k}}) v + \chi_ {E _ {n k}} (\alpha_ {n} \xi_ {n} + (1 - \alpha_ {n}) v _ {n}). \end{array}
$$

By (7.39) and (7.40), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {E} | V _ {n} | ^ {p}   d x \leq C \left(\int_ {E} (| v | ^ {p} + | v _ {n} | ^ {p})   d x + \int_ {E _ {n k}} | \alpha_ {n}   \xi_ {n} | ^ {p}   d x\right) \\ \qquad = C \left(\int_ {E} (| v | ^ {p} + | v _ {n} | ^ {p})   d x + \int_ {E _ {n k}} k   | \beta   (x, u _ {n}   (x)) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}}   d x\right) \\ \qquad \leq C \left(\int_ {E} (| v | ^ {p} + | v _ {n} | ^ {p})   d x + \frac {1}{p}   k ^ {1 - 1 / p}\right), \end{array}
$$

and this shows that the sequence $\{ V _ { n } \}$ is bounded in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ (recall that k has been fixed). On the other hand, by H¨older’s inequality, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {E} | V _ {n} - v | d x \leq \int_ {E _ {n k}} | v | d x + \int_ {E _ {n k}} | \alpha_ {n} \xi_ {n} + (1 - \alpha_ {n}) v _ {n} | d x \\ \leq \int_ {E _ {n k}} | v | d x + C | E _ {n k} | ^ {1 / p ^ {\prime}}. \end{array}
$$

Since $| E _ { n k } | \to 0$ as $n  \infty$ , it follows that $\{ V _ { n } \}$ converges weakly to v in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Moreover, by the convexity of $g \left( x , u , \cdot \right)$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {E} g (x, U _ {n}, V _ {n}) d x - \int_ {E} g (x, u, v) d x \\ = \int_ {E _ {n k}} g (x, u _ {n}, \alpha_ {n} \xi_ {n} + (1 - \alpha_ {n}) v _ {n}) d x - \int_ {E _ {n k}} g (x, u, v) d x \\ \leq \int_ {E _ {n k}} \alpha_ {n} g (x, u _ {n}, \xi_ {n}) d x + \int_ {E _ {n k}} (1 - \alpha_ {n}) g (x, u _ {n}, v _ {n}) d x \\ - \int_ {E _ {n k}} g (x, u, v) d x \\ \leq - \frac {1}{p} \int_ {E _ {n k}} | \beta (x, u _ {n}) | | \alpha_ {n} \xi_ {n} | d x + 2 L \\ = - \frac {1}{p} k ^ {1 / p} \int_ {E _ {n k}} | \beta (x, u _ {n}) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d x + 2 L = - 1, \end{array}
$$

where in the last inequality we used (7.36), (7.32), and (7.33), and the latter two equalities used (7.40) and (7.39) in this order. 

This contradicts the sequential lower semicontinuity of the functional. 

The proof of part (iii) in the previous theorem can be significantly simplified under an additional, mildly restrictive assumption. 

Corollary 7.8. Assume that in addition to the hypotheses of the previous theorem 

$$
\int_ {E} f (x, u (x), v _ {0} (x)) d x <   \infty\tag{7.41}
$$

for some $v _ { 0 } \in L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and all $u \in L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ . Then condition (iii) can be replaced by the condition that 

$$
| \beta (x, u) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}} \leq C _ {1} | u | ^ {q} + b _ {1} (x)\tag{7.42}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { \ } _ { a . e . \mathrm { ~ } x } \in E$ and all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , for some constant $C _ { 1 } > 0$ , and some function $b _ { 1 } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ 

Proof. In the sufficiency part of the previous proof all that was required from $\beta$ was that $\left\{ \left| \beta \left( \cdot , u _ { n } \left( \cdot \right) \right) \right| ^ { p ^ { \prime } } \right\}$ be equi-integrable whenever $\{ u _ { n } \}$ converges strongly in $L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ <sub>, which here is satisfied in view of (7.42).</sub> 

Conversely, in the necessity part of the proof, by (7.34) and (7.41), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {E} | \beta (x, u (x)) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d x \\ \qquad \leq C (p) C _ {1} (p) \int_ {E} (g (x, u (x), v _ {0} (x)) + | v _ {0} (x) | ^ {p}) d x <   \infty \end{array}
$$

for all $u \in L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ . The conclusion now follows from Corollary 6.46. 

As corollaries of Theorem 7.5 we have the following: 

Corollary 7.9. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure and let $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be an $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable function. Assume that for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ } a . e . \mathrm { ~ } x \in E \mathrm { ~ } t h e$ function $f \left( x , \cdot , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous in $\mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } ~ a . e .$ . x ∈ E and for $a l l u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ the function $f \left( x , u , \cdot \right)$ is convex. Then for any sequence $\{ u _ { n } \}$ of measurable functions such that $u _ { n } \to u$ in measure for some function u, and for any sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ such that $v _ { n } \stackrel { b } {  } v$ (in the biting sense) for some function $v \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we have 

$$
\int_ {E} f \left(x, u \left(x\right), v \left(x\right)\right) d x \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \int_ {E} f \left(x, u _ {n} \left(x\right), v _ {n} \left(x\right)\right) d x.
$$

Proof. Since $v _ { n } \stackrel { b } {  } v$ there exists a decreasing sequence $\{ E _ { k } \} \subset E$ of measurable sets, with $| E _ { k } | \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$ , such that 

$$
v _ {n} \rightharpoonup v \text {   weakly   in   } L ^ {1} (E \setminus E _ {k}; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \text {   for   every   } k.
$$

Applying Theorem 7.5 and Remark 7.6 to the function $\chi _ { E \backslash E _ { k } } \left( x \right) f \left( x , u , z \right)$ we conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {E \setminus E _ {k}} f (x, u, v) d x \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E \setminus E _ {k}} f (x, u _ {n}, v _ {n}) d x \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (x, u _ {n}, v _ {n}) d x. \end{array}
$$

The result now follows by Lebesgue’s monotone convergence theorem. 

From the previous corollary we may obtain the following result. 

Corollary 7.10. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, let $\{ u _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of nonnegative, measurable functions such that $u _ { n } \ \to \ u$ in measure for some function u, and let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { 1 } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ be a sequence of nonnegative functions bounded in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and such that 

$$
\int_ {F} v   d x \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {F} v _ {n}   d x
$$

for every measurable set $F ~ \subset ~ E$ and for some nonnegative function $v \in$ $L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Then 

$$
\int_ {E} u v d x \leq \liminf _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} u _ {n} v _ {n} d x.\tag{7.43}
$$

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} u _ {n} v _ {n} d x = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} u _ {n} v _ {n} d x <   \infty
$$

and that $v _ { n } \stackrel { b } {  } w$ for some function $w \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Let $\{ E _ { k } \} \subset E$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets, with $| E _ { k } |  0$ as $k \to \infty$ , such that 

v  w weakly in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \setminus E _ { k } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ for every k. 

Then by hypothesis, 

$$
\int_ {F \setminus E _ {k}} v   d x \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {F \setminus E _ {k}} v _ {n}   d x = \int_ {F \setminus E _ {k}} w   d x
$$

for every measurable set $F \subset E$ , and so letting $k \to \infty$ we deduce that 

$$
\int_ {F} v d x \leq \int_ {F} w d x.
$$

By Proposition 1.87 we conclude that $v \left( x \right) \leq w \left( x \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ . Setting $f \left( x , u , z \right) : = \left( u z \right) ^ { + }$ by Corollary 7.9 we have 

$$
\int_ {E} u v   d x \leq \int_ {E} u w   d x \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} u _ {n} v _ {n}   d x.
$$

This concludes the proof.

## 7.4 Relaxation

Consider the relaxed energy 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {q, p}: L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \times L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \to [ - \infty , \infty ]
$$

of the functional I defined in (7.1), that is, the functional $\mathcal { E } _ { \boldsymbol { q } , \boldsymbol { p } }$ is the greatest functional that is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ and weak convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and less than or equal to I. 

Theorem 7.13. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, let $1 \leq p , q < \infty$ , and let $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be an $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable function such that 

$$
f (x, u, z) \geq \alpha (x, u) + \beta (x, u) \cdot z
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , where 

$$
\alpha : E \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \to \mathbb {R}, \quad \beta : E \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \to \mathbb {R} ^ {m}
$$

are Carath´eodory functions, with 

$$
| \alpha (x, u) | \leq a (x) + C | u | ^ {q}, \quad | \beta (x, u) | \leq b (x) + C | u | ^ {\frac {q}{p ^ {\prime}}}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and for all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , and for some $a \in L ^ { 1 } ( E ) , b \in L ^ { p ^ { \prime } } ( E )$ and $C > 0$ . Then 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {q, p} ((u, v); B) = \int_ {B} \mathrm{S} f (x, u (x), v (x)) d x,
$$

where for every fixed $x \in E$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \text {S} f (x, u, z) := \sup \{g \left(u, z\right): g \left(\cdot , \cdot\right) \leq f \left(x, \cdot , \cdot\right), \\ g \text {is lower semicontinuous}, \\ g \left(w, \cdot\right) \text {is convex in} \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \text {for all} w \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \} \end{array}
$$

for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Proof. Without loss of generality we may assume that there exists $( u _ { 0 } , v _ { 0 } ) \in$ $L ^ { q } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ) \times L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ such that 

$$
\int_ {B} f (x, u _ {0} (x), v _ {0} (x)) d x <   \infty .
$$

We claim that the functional 

$$
(u, v) \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \times L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {E} (\alpha (x, u) + \beta (x, u) \cdot v) d x
$$

is continuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ and weak con vergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ 

By Corollary 6.51 the functional 

$$
u \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \mapsto \int_ {E} \alpha (x, u) d x
$$

is continuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , and so, in view of (2.47), it remains to establish the continuity of 

$$
u \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \mapsto \beta (x, u) \in L ^ {p ^ {\prime}} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}).\tag{7.44}
$$

By Corollary 6.51 the functional 

$$
u \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \mapsto \int_ {E} | \beta (x, u) | ^ {p ^ {\prime}} d x
$$

is continuous with respect to strong convergence in $L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , and so the continuity of (7.44) follows from the Vitali convergence theorem. 

Since 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathrm{S} (f (x, u, z) - \alpha (x, u) - \beta (x, u) \cdot z)} \\ & {\qquad = \mathrm{S} (f (x, u, z)) - \alpha (x, u) - \beta (x, u) \cdot z,} \end{array}
$$

replacing $f \left( x , u , z \right)$ by $f \left( x , u , z \right) - \left( \alpha \left( x , u \right) + \beta \left( x , u \right) \cdot z \right)$ , we may assume without loss of generality that $f \geq 0$ 

Let $\varOmega$ be an open subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ with finite measure that contains $E _ { i }$ and for every Borel set $B \in B ( { \mathcal { \Omega } } )$ we define the functional 

$$
(u, v) \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \times L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto I (u, v; B) := \int_ {B} f (x, u, v) d x,
$$

where we have extended $f$ to $( \varOmega \setminus E ) \times \mathbb R ^ { d } \times \mathbb R ^ { m }$ and $u _ { 0 } , v _ { 0 }$ to $( \varOmega \backslash E )$ by zero. 

As in the proof of Theorem 6.65, it can be shown that $\mathcal { E } _ { \boldsymbol { q } , \boldsymbol { p } }$ satisfies $( I _ { 1 } ) -$ $\left( I _ { 3 } \right)$ (where here $\tau$ is the strong–weak topology in $L ^ { q } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ) ^ { - } \times L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ) )$ ). Hence we deduce the existence of a normal function 

$$
h: \Omega \times \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \to (- \infty , \infty ]
$$

such that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {q, p} (u, v; B) = \mathcal {E} _ {q, p} (u _ {0}, v _ {0}; B) + \int_ {B} h (x, u, v) d x\tag{7.45}
$$

for every $B \in B ( \varOmega ) , u \in L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , and $v \in L ^ { p } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ 

As in the proof of Theorem 6.68 we can show that $\mathcal { E } _ { q , p } ( u _ { 0 } , v _ { 0 } ; \cdot )$ is a Radon measure and that there exists a function $\psi \in L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {q, p} (u _ {0}, v _ {0}; B) = \int_ {B} \psi (x) d x
$$

for every Borel set $B \subset \varOmega$ 

Hence (7.45) reduces to 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {q, p} (u, v; B) = \int_ {B} \left(\psi (x) + h (x, u, v)\right) d x
$$

for every $B \in B ( \varOmega ) , u \in L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , and $v \in L ^ { p } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ . Observe that the function $\tilde { h } : \varOmega \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ 0 , \infty ]$ defined by 

$$
\tilde {h} (x, u, z) := \psi (x) + h (x, u, z)
$$

for $x \in \varOmega , u \in \mathbb R ^ { d }$ , and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is a normal integrand, and that the functional 

$$
(u, v) \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \times L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {\Omega} \tilde {h} (x, u, v) d x
$$

satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 7.5. Therefore $\tilde { h } \left( x , u , \cdot \right)$ is convex in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \varOmega$ and for all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ . Moreover, since 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {q, p} (u, v; B) = \int_ {B} \tilde {h} (x, u, v) d x \leq \int_ {B} f (x, u, v) d x
$$

for every $B \in B ( \varOmega ) , u \in L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , and $v \in L ^ { p } ( \varOmega ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ , by Proposition 6.24, 

$$
\tilde {h} (x, u, z) \leq f (x, u, z)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \varOmega$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

In particular, for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in \varOmega$ the function $\tilde { h } \left( x , \cdot , \cdot \right)$ is admissible in the definition of $\operatorname { S } f \left( x , \cdot , \cdot \right)$ , and so 

$$
\tilde {h} (x, u, z) \leq \mathrm{S} f (x, u, z)\tag{7.46}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \varOmega$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

To prove the reverse inequality, we apply Proposition 6.44 with $\textrm { S } f$ in place of s to find a normal integrand $g : \Omega \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ 0 , \infty ]$ satisfying properties (i)–(iii) and such that for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathcal { \Omega }$ and for all $u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , the function $g \left( x , u , \cdot \right)$ is convex in $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Since S $f \leq f$ and f is $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable, by (ii) (with $h : = f )$ we deduce that $g \left( x , u , z \right) \leq f \left( x , u , z \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in$ $E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . It follows from the definition of $\textrm { S } f$ that $g \left( x , u , z \right) \leq \mathrm { S } f \left( x , u , z \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , which together with (i), yields $g \left( x , u , z \right) = \mathrm { S } f \left( x , u , z \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Thus S f satisfies all the hypotheses of Theorem 7.5, and so for every $B \in B ( { \mathcal { \Omega } } )$ the functional 

$$
(u, v) \in L ^ {q} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {d}) \times L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto \int_ {B} \mathrm{S} f (x, u, v) d x
$$

is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous, and since $\mathrm { ~ S ~ } f \le f$ we deduce that for every $\left( u , v \right) \in L ^ { q } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right) \times L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ ， 

$$
\mathcal {E} _ {p} (u, v, B) = \int_ {B} \tilde {h} (x, u, v) d x \geq \int_ {B} \mathrm{S} f (x, u, v) d x.
$$

Using once more Proposition 6.24, we conclude that 

$$
\mathrm{S} f (x, u, v) \leq \tilde {h} (x, u, z)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in \mathcal { \Omega }$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . This, together with (7.46), completes the proof. 

We observe that by Theorem 4.92(iii), 

$$
\mathrm{S} f (x, u, z) \leq f ^ {* *} (x, u, z),\tag{7.47}
$$

where $f ^ { * * } \left( x , u , z \right)$ is the polar of $f \left( x , u , \cdot \right)$ evaluated at $z ,$ , and the strict in equality is possible. 

Exercise 7.14. Let $d = m = 1$ and consider the function $f : \mathbb { R } \times \mathbb { R } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ defined by 

$$
f (u, z) := (| z | + 1) ^ {| u |}
$$

for $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R }$ . Prove that for $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R }$ ,

f ^ {* *} (u, z) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} (| z | + 1) ^ {| u |} & \text { if } | u | \geq 1, \\ 1 & \text { if } | u | <   1, \end{array} \right.

while

\operatorname{S} f (u, z) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} (| z | + 1) ^ {| u |} & \text { if } | u | > 1, \\ 1 & \text { if } | u | \leq 1. \end{array} \right.
$$

Prove also that $f ^ { * * }$ and $\textrm { S } f$ are not equivalent integrands. 

However, under some relatively mild coercivity hypotheses on the integrand f it can be shown that $f ^ { * * } = \mathrm { S } f$ 

Proposition 7.15. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, and let $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be an $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \times \boldsymbol { B }$ measurable function such that 

$$
f (x, u, z) \geq \gamma (| z |)\tag{7.48}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \ \in \ E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , where $\gamma : [ 0 , \infty )  [ 0 , \infty )$ satisfies 

$$
\lim _ {s \to \infty} \frac {\gamma (s)}{s} = \infty .
$$

Assume that $f \left( x , \cdot , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous in $\mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ Then 

$$
f ^ {* *} (x, u, z) = \mathrm{S} f (x, u, z)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and for all $( u , z ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ 

Proof. In view of (7.47) it remains to show that $f ^ { * * } \leq \mathrm { S } f$ . By the definition of $\textrm { S } f$ this will be a consequence of the lower semicontinuity of $f ^ { * * } ( x , \cdot , \cdot )$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ , which will be established next. The proof follows closely that of Proposition 6.42. 

Fix $x \in E$ for which (7.48) holds and $f \left( x , \cdot , \cdot \right)$ is lower semicontinuous. We define the Yosida transforms 

$$
f _ {n} (x, u, z) := \inf \left\{f (x, y, z) + n | u - y |: y \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d} \right\}
$$

u $\in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } , z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . As in (6.41), (6.42), and (6.43), we can show that for all $u ,$ $u _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d } , z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , 

$$
f \left(x, u, z\right) = \sup _ {n \in \mathbb {N}} f _ {n} \left(x, u, z\right), \quad f ^ {* *} (x, u, z) = \sup _ {n} f _ {n} ^ {* *} (x, u, z),
$$

and 

$$
f _ {n} ^ {* *} (x, u, z) + n \left| u - u _ {0} \right| \geq f _ {n} ^ {* *} (x, u _ {0}, z).\tag{7.49}
$$

Therefore, to prove the lower semicontinuity of $f ^ { * * } ( x , \cdot , \cdot )$ it sufices to prove it for each $f _ { n } ^ { * * }$ . Hence fix $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and let $\left( u _ { k } , z _ { k } \right) \longrightarrow \left( u _ { 0 } , z _ { 0 } \right)$ as $k \to \infty$ . Using the lower semicontinuity of $f _ { n } ^ { * * } ( x , u _ { 0 } , \cdot )$ together with (7.49), we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & f _ {n} ^ {* *} (x, u _ {0}, z _ {0}) \leq \liminf _ {k \to \infty} f _ {n} ^ {* *} (x, u _ {0}, z _ {k}) \\ & \quad \leq \liminf _ {k \to \infty} (n | u _ {k} - u _ {0} | + f _ {n} ^ {* *} (x, u _ {k}, z _ {k})) \\ & \quad = \liminf _ {k \to \infty} f _ {n} ^ {* *} (x, u _ {k}, z _ {k}), \end{array}
$$

and this concludes the proof.

Young Measures 

Nature laughs at the dificulties of integration. 

Pierre-Simon de Laplace (1749–1827) 

Often in applications we deal with energies of the type 

$$
v \mapsto \int_ {E} f (x, v (x)) d x,\tag{8.1}
$$

where $f \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is nonconvex. The study of equilibria leads to the search for minimizers of the energy, possibly subject to constraints, and the nonconvexity of the energy density may prevent the existence of solutions. One way to “resolve” this issue is to relax the energy and, under appropriate hypotheses, use the direct method to obtain a minimizer for 

$$
v \mapsto \int_ {E} f ^ {* *} (x, v (x)) d x.
$$

A major setback in this approach has to do with the fact that the relaxed energy density $f ^ { * * }$ may be far below $f ,$ and in this way, qualitative properties of the equilibrium energy may be lost. 

A compromise between the nonexistence of the minimizers of the original problem and working with the convexified energy can be reached using the notion of Young measures. Here minimizers are obtained for an energy with energy density the original $f$ and where the class of admissible fields is en larged to include certain probabili $\mathrm { t y }$ measures that are intrinsically related to minimizing sequences for (8.1). 

## 8.1 The Fundamental Theorem for Young Measures

Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure. By the Riesz representation theorem in $L ^ { p }$ and in $C _ { 0 }$ (see Theorems 2.112 and 1.200), the dual of the space $L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \right)$ is $L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ . We recall that a function $\lambda : E \to { \mathcal { M } } \left( { \mathbb { R } } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ belongs to $L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ ) if and only if for all $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ the map 

$$
x \in E \mapsto \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi (v) d \lambda_ {x} (v) \text { is   measurable }
$$

and 

$$
\| \lambda \| _ {L _ {w} ^ {\infty} (E; \mathcal {M} (\mathbb {R} ^ {m}; \mathbb {R}))} := \operatorname * {e s s s u p} _ {x \in E} \| \lambda_ {x} \| \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right) <   \infty ,
$$

where for simplicity we write $\lambda _ { x }$ in place of $\lambda \left( x \right)$ and $\| \lambda _ { x } \| \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ is the total variation of the signed Radon measure $\lambda _ { x }$ 

In what follows, $\operatorname* { P r } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ is the family of all (positive) Radon measures that are also probability measures, that is, the family of all (positive) Radon measures with measure one. 

Definition 8.1. A Young measure $\nu : E \to \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ is an element of the space $L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ such that $\nu _ { x } \in \operatorname { P r } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ 

Theorem 8.2. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure and let $\{ v _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of measurable functions, with $v _ { n } : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m } . \ T h e n$ there exist a subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ v _ { n } \}$ and a map $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ such that 

(i) $\nu _ { x } \geq 0 , \nu _ { x } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \leq 1$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E .$ ; 

$\begin{array} { r } { ( i i ) \varphi ( v _ { n _ { k } } ) \stackrel { * } {  } \langle \nu _ { x } , \varphi \rangle _ { \mathcal { M } , C _ { 0 } } = \int _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { m } } \varphi ( z ) d \nu _ { x } ( z ) } \end{array}$ in $L ^ { \infty } \left( E \right)$ for all $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ ; (iii) for any normal integrand $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  ( - \infty , \infty ]$ bounded from below, 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (x, v _ {n _ {k}} (x))   d x \geq \int_ {E} \overline {{f}} (x)   d x,
$$

where for $x \in E$ 2 

$$
\overline {{f}} (x) := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) d \nu_ {x} (z).
$$

Moreover, the map $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ is a Young measure if and only $i f$ the subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ satisfies 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n _ {k}} (x) | > t \} | = 0.\tag{8.2}
$$

Proof. Define $\nu _ { n } : E \to \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ as $\nu _ { n } \left( x \right) : = \delta _ { v _ { n } \left( x \right) }$ for $x \in E$ . Then 

$$
\left\| \nu_ {n} (x) \right\| (\mathbb {R} ^ {m}) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} d \delta_ {v _ {n} (x)} = 1,
$$

and for any $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ the map 

$$
x \in E \mapsto \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi (z) d \delta_ {v _ {n} (x)} (z) = \varphi (v _ {n} (x))
$$

is measurable. Thus $\nu _ { n } \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ and 

$$
\left\| \nu_ {n} \right\| _ {L _ {w} ^ {\infty} (E; \mathcal {M} (\mathbb {R} ^ {m}; \mathbb {R}))} = 1
$$

for all n. Since $L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ is the dual of $L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \right)$ ), by Corollary A.55 there exists a subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ v _ { n } \}$ and a map $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } ( E ; \mathcal { M } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } ) )$ such that 

$$
\nu_ {n _ {k}} \stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} \nu \text {in} L _ {w} ^ {\infty} (E; \mathcal {M} (\mathbb {R} ^ {m}; \mathbb {R})),
$$

i.e., for all $\psi \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \right)$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\int_ {E} \psi (x, v _ {n _ {k}} (x)) d x = \int_ {E} \langle \nu_ {n _ {k}} (x), \psi (x, \cdot) \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} d x \rightarrow \int_ {E} \langle \nu_ {x}, \psi (x, \cdot) \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} d x\\= \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \psi (x, z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x.\end{array}\tag {8.3}
$$

In particular, if $h \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , then the function 

$$
\psi (x, z) := h (x) \varphi (z),
$$

where $x \in E$ and $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , belongs to $L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \right)$ by Theorem 2.108, since the function $| h \left( \cdot \right) | \ \| \varphi \| _ { \infty }$ is in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ , and thus 

$$
\int_ {E} h (x) \varphi (v _ {n _ {k}} (x)) d x \rightarrow \int_ {E} h (x) \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi (z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x.\tag{8.4}
$$

This proves (ii). Moreover, taking $h , \varphi \geq 0$ we obtain that $\nu _ { x } \geq 0$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ , and the lower semicontinuity of the norm implies that 

$$
\left\| \nu \right\| _ {L _ {w} ^ {\infty} (E; \mathcal {M} (\mathbb {R} ^ {m}; \mathbb {R}))} \leq 1,
$$

so that (i) holds. 

To prove (iii) note first that since $| E | < \infty$ , without loss of generality we may assume that $f \geq 0$ . We use Corollary 6.30 to find a sequence $\{ ( E _ { j } , \varphi _ { j } ) \}$ , where $E _ { j } \subset E$ has finite Lebesgue measure and $\varphi _ { j } \in C _ { c } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , such that 

$$
f (x, z) = \sup _ {j} \chi_ {E _ {j}} (x) \varphi_ {j} (z)
$$

for every $( x , z ) \in E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . For each $j \in \mathbb N$ let 

$$
f _ {j} (x, z) = \sup _ {i \leq j} \chi_ {E _ {i}} (x) \varphi_ {i} (z)
$$

for every $( x , z ) \in E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . We claim that $f _ { j } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \right)$ . Indeed, this follows from Theorem 2.108 and the facts that for fixed $x \in E$ the function $f _ { j } \left( x , \cdot \right)$ is in $C _ { c } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ and 

$$
\left| f _ {j} (x, z) \right| \leq \chi_ {F _ {j}} (x) \max _ {i \leq j} \| \varphi_ {i} \| _ {\infty} \in L ^ {1} (E)
$$

for every $( x , z ) \in E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , where 

$$
F _ {j} = \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {j} E _ {i}.
$$

By (8.3) for each fixed $j \in \mathbb N$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\underset {k \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {E} f (x, v _ {n _ {k}} (x))   d x \geq \underset {k \to \infty} {\lim} \int_ {E} f _ {j} (x, v _ {n _ {k}} (x))   d x} \\ & {\qquad = \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f _ {j} (x, z)   d \nu_ {x} (z)   d x.} \end{array}
$$

By the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem, and using the fact that $f \geq 0$ , letting $j \to \infty$ in the previous inequality yields 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (x, v _ {n _ {k}} (x))   d x \geq \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z)   d \nu_ {x} (z)   d x.
$$

To prove the last part of the statement of the theorem, assume that (8.2) holds. Then for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $t > 0$ such that 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n _ {k}} (x) | \geq t \} | <   \varepsilon .\tag{8.5}
$$

Let $\varphi _ { t } : [ 0 , \infty ) \to [ 0 , 1 ]$ be defined by 

$$
\varphi_ {t} \left(s\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text { if } s \leq t, \\ 1 - s + t & \text { if } t <   s <   t + 1, \\ 0 & \text { if } s \leq t + 1. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then the function 

$$
\psi (x, z) := \chi_ {E} (x) \varphi_ {t} (| z |), \quad (x, z) \in E \times \mathbb {R} ^ {m},
$$

belongs to $L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \right)$ , and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | E | = | \{x \in E: | v _ {n _ {k}} (x) | \leq t \} | + | \{x \in E: | v _ {n _ {k}} (x) | > t \} | \\ \qquad \leq \int_ {E} \varphi_ {t} (| v _ {n _ {k}} (x) |) d x + | \{x \in E: | v _ {n _ {k}} (x) | > t \} |. \end{array}
$$

Taking the limit superior in the previous inequality and using (8.3) and (8.5) we obtain 

$$
| E | \leq \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {t} (| z |) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x + \varepsilon \leq \int_ {E} \nu_ {x} (\mathbb {R} ^ {m}) d x + \varepsilon \leq | E | + \varepsilon ,
$$

where we have used the facts that $\varphi _ { t } \leq 1 , \nu _ { x } \geq 0$ , and $\nu _ { x } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \leq 1$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ . Letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ we obtain that 

$$
\int_ {E} \nu_ {x} (\mathbb {R} ^ {m}) d x = | E |,
$$

which, recalling again that $\nu _ { x } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \leq 1$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ , implies that $\nu _ { x } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) = 1$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { \tilde { N } }$ a.e. $x \in E$ , and we conclude that ν is a Young measure. Conversely, assume that ν is a Young measure. Then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} | E | - | \{x \in E: | v _ {n _ {k}} | > t + 1 \} | = | \{x \in E: | v _ {n _ {k}} | \leq t + 1 \} | \\ \geq \int_ {E} \varphi_ {t} \left(| v _ {n _ {k}} (x) |\right) d x. \end{array}
$$

Taking the limit inferior in the previous inequality and using (8.3) we obtain 

$$
| E | - \limsup _ {k \to \infty} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n _ {k}} | > t + 1 \} | \geq \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {t} (| z |)   d \nu_ {x} (z)   d x.
$$

Since $0 \leq \varphi _ { t } \leq 1$ and $\varphi _ { t } ~ \nearrow ~ 1$ , letting $t \to \infty$ in the previous inequality and using the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem, we obtain 

$$
| E | - \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {t \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n _ {k}} | > t + 1 \} | \geq \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} d \nu_ {x} (z)   d x = | E |  ,
$$

where we have used the fact that $\nu _ { x } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) = 1$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ . Hence 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n _ {k}} | > t \} | = 0.
$$

This concludes the proof. 

In view of (8.2) and (8.4) we now introduce the concept of Young measure ν generated by a sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ 

Definition 8.3. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure. A sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ of measurable functions $v _ { n } : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ satisfying 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n} | > t \} | = 0\tag{8.6}
$$

is said to generate a Young measure $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } ( E ; \mathcal { M } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } ) )$ if for every $h \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we have 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} h (x) \varphi (v _ {n} (x)) d x = \int_ {E} h (x) \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi (z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x.
$$

The next proposition is similar to de la Vall´ee Poussin’s theorem. 

Proposition 8.4. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure and let $\{ v _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of measurable functions $v _ { n } : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . Then condition $\left( 8 . 6 \right)$ is satisfied if and only if there exists a continuous, nondecreasing function $g : [ 0 , \infty )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that g $( t ) \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty$ and 

$$
\limsup _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} g (| v _ {n} (x) |)   d x <   \infty .\tag{8.7}
$$

Proof. Suppose that (8.7) holds. Since g is nondecreasing, for any $t > 0$ we have 

$$
g (t) | \{x \in E: | v _ {n} (x) | > t \} | \leq \int_ {E} g (| v _ {n} (x) |) d x,
$$

and so 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} g \left(t\right) \left| \left\{x \in E: \left| v _ {n} \left(x\right) \right| > t \right\} \right| \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} g (\left| v _ {n} (x) \right|) d x <   \infty .
$$

Since $g ( t )  \infty$ as $t \to \infty$ we obtain (8.6). 

Conversely, assume that (8.6) holds. Then we may choose $0 < t _ { j } < t _ { j + 1 }$ ， $j \in \mathbb N$ , with $t _ { j } \to \infty$ as $j \to \infty$ , such that 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n} (x) | > t _ {j} \} | \leq \frac {1}{j ^ {3}}.
$$

Define 

$$
h \left(t\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0 \text {   if   } t \in \left[ 0, t _ {1}\right), \\ j \text {   if   } t \in \left[ t _ {j}, t _ {j + 1}\right), j \in \mathbb {N}. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then 

$$
\int_ {E} h (| v _ {n} (x) |) d x = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} j \left| \{x \in E: t _ {j} \leq | v _ {n} (x) | <   t _ {j + 1} \} \right|,
$$

and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} h (| v _ {n} (x) |)   d x \leq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} j \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {k \to \infty} | \{x \in E: t _ {j} \leq | v _ {n} (x) | <   t _ {j + 1} \} | \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j ^ {2}} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

It now sufices to replace the function h with a continuous, nondecreasing function, $0 \leq g \leq h$ , such that $g ( t )  \infty$ as $t \to \infty$ 

Remark 8.5. In applications we will be particularly interested in the cases in which $g \left( t \right) : = t ^ { p } , 1 \leq p < \infty$ , and for $p = \infty$ , 

$$
g \left(t\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {t}{\alpha - t} & 0 \leq t <   \alpha , \\ \infty & t \geq \alpha , \end{array} \right.
$$

corresponding to Young measures generated by sequences bounded in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) , 1 \le p \le \infty$ , with 

$$
\sup _ {n} \left\| v _ {n} \right\| _ {L ^ {\infty}} <   \alpha
$$

if $p = \infty$ . Precisely, in view of Theorem 8.2 and Proposition 8.4, any bounded sequence in $L ^ { \boldsymbol { p } } \left( \boldsymbol { E } ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) , 1 \le \boldsymbol { p } \le \infty ,$ , admits a subsequence that generates a Young measure $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ ) such that 

$$
\int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} g (| z |) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x <   \infty .
$$

We are now ready to prove the first main result of this chapter. 

Theorem 8.6 (Fundamental theorem for Young measures). Let $E \subset$ $\mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure and consider a sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ of measurable functions $v _ { n } : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that generates a Young measure $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ . Then 

(i) for any normal integrand $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  [ - \infty , \infty ]$ such that $\{ f ^ { - } ( \cdot , v _ { n } ( \cdot ) ) \}$ is equi-integrable, 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (x, v _ {n} (x))   d x \geq \int_ {E} \overline {{f}} (x)   d x;
$$

(ii) for any Carath´eodory function $f ~ : ~ \boldsymbol { E } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ such that $\{ f ( \cdot , v _ { n } ( \cdot ) ) \} \subset L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ one has 

$$
f (\cdot , v _ {n} (\cdot)) \rightharpoonup \overline {{f}} i n L ^ {1} (E)
$$

if and only if $\{ f ( \cdot , v _ { n } ( \cdot ) ) \}$ is equi-integrable; 

(iii) if $K \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is a compact set, then 

$$
\operatorname{supp} \nu_ {x} \subset K f o r \mathcal {L} ^ {N} a. e. x \in E
$$

if and only if dist $( v _ { n } , K ) \to 0$ in measure. 

Proof. (i) Since $\{ f ^ { - } ( \cdot , v _ { n } ( \cdot ) ) \}$ is equi-integrable, by Theorem 2.29, for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ we may find a constant $M > 0$ such that 

$$
\int_ {\{f ^ {-} (x, v _ {n}) \geq M \}} f ^ {-} (x, v _ {n}) d x \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Let $f _ { M } : = \operatorname* { m a x } \left. f , - M \right.$ , which is a normal integrand bounded from below. By Theorem 8.2(iii), 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {E} f (x, v _ {n}) d x} \\ & {\qquad = \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \left[ \int_ {\{f (x, v _ {n}) > - M \}} f _ {M} (x, v _ {n}) d x - \int_ {\{f ^ {-} (x, v _ {n}) \geq M \}} f ^ {-} (x, v _ {n}) d x \right]} \\ & {\qquad \geq \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \int_ {E} f _ {M} (x, v _ {n} (x)) d x - \varepsilon} \\ & {\qquad \geq \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f _ {M} (x, z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x - \varepsilon} \\ & {\qquad \geq \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x - \varepsilon ,} \end{array}
$$

where in the last inequality we used the fact that $f _ { M } \geq f$ , and we may now let $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ 

(ii) Assume that $\{ f ( \cdot , v _ { n } ( \cdot ) ) \}$ is equi-integrable and fix $h \in L ^ { \infty } \left( E \right)$ . Then the function $\pm h \left( x \right) f ( x , z )$ is a normal integrand, $\{ \pm h ( \cdot ) ~ f ( \cdot , v _ { n } ( \cdot ) ) \}$ is equiintegrable, and so by (i) we get 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \left(\pm \int_ {E} h \left(x\right) f (x, v _ {n} (x)) d x\right) \geq \pm \int_ {E} h \left(x\right) \overline {{f}} (x) d x,
$$

that is, 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} h (x) f (x, v _ {n} (x)) d x = \int_ {E} h (x) \overline {{f}} (x) d x.
$$

Conversely, if $f ( \cdot , v _ { n } ( \cdot ) )  \overline { { f } }$ in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ , then $\{ f ( \cdot , v _ { n } ( \cdot ) ) \}$ is equi-integrable by the Dunford–Pettis theorem. 

(iii) Assume that dist $( v _ { n } , K ) \to 0$ in measure and let $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \backslash K )$ . Then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a compact set $K _ { 1 } \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \setminus K$ such that 

$$
| \varphi (z) | <   \varepsilon \text {   for   all   } z \notin K _ {1}.\tag{8.8}
$$

Thus we may find a constant $C _ { \varepsilon } > 0$ such that 

$$
| \varphi (z) | \leq \varepsilon + C _ {\varepsilon} \operatorname{dist} (z, K) \text {   for   all   } z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \setminus K.
$$

Indeed, if not, there exists a sequence $\{ z _ { j } \} \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \setminus K$ such that 

$$
\left| \varphi \left(z _ {j}\right) \right| \geq \varepsilon + j \operatorname{dist} \left(z _ {j}, K\right).\tag{8.9}
$$

By (8.8) it follows that $z _ { j } \in K _ { 1 }$ and up to the extraction of a subsequence if necessary, $z _ { j }  z \in K _ { 1 }$ . In particular, dist $( z , K ) > 0$ , and so letting $j \to \infty$ in (8.9) we reach a contradiction. 

Hence $( | \varphi ( v _ { n } ) | - \varepsilon ) ^ { + }  0$ in measure, and since $\varphi$ is bounded we apply (ii) to conclude that 

$$
\langle \nu_ {x}, (| \varphi (\cdot) | - \varepsilon) ^ {+} \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} = 0 \text {for} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {a.e.} x \in E.
$$

Letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ we have that 

$$
\langle \nu_ {x}, \varphi \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} = 0 \text {   for   all   } \varphi \in C _ {0} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {m} \setminus K\right).
$$

Hence supp $\nu _ { x } \subset K$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ 

Conversely, assume that supp $\nu _ { x } \subset K$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ . Let 

$$
f (x, z) := \chi_ {E} (x) \min \left\{\operatorname{dist} (z, K), 1 \right\}.
$$

Then $f$ is a bounded Carath´eodory function and thus $\{ f ( \cdot , v _ { n } ( \cdot ) ) \}$ is equiintegrable. By part (ii) we obtain that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} \min \left\{\mathrm{dist} (v _ {n} (x), K), 1 \right\} d x \\ = \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \min \left\{\mathrm{dist} (z, K), 1 \right\} d \nu_ {x} (z) d x = 0, \end{array}
$$

since supp $\nu _ { x } \subset K$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ . By Vitali’s convergence theorem we conclude that dist $( v _ { n } , K ) \to 0$ in measure. 

We now present several important applications of the fundamental theorem for Young measures. 

Corollary 8.7. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure and let $\{ v _ { n } \} , \ \{ w _ { n } \}$ be two sequences of measurable functions, $v _ { n } , w _ { n } : E \to$ $\mathbb { R } ^ { m } . ~ I f \left\{ v _ { n } \right\}$ generates a Young measure ν and $\{ w _ { n } \}$ converges in measure to a measurable function $w : E  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , then $\left\{ v _ { n } + w _ { n } \right\}$ generates the translated Young measure $T _ { w } \left( \nu \right)$ , where $\langle \Gamma _ { a } \nu , \varphi \rangle _ { \mathcal { M } , C _ { 0 } } : = \langle \nu , \varphi ( \cdot + a ) \rangle _ { \mathcal { M } , C _ { 0 } } ~ f o r ~ a \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . In particular, $i f w _ { n } \to 0$ in measure, then $\left\{ v _ { n } + w _ { n } \right\}$ generates the Young measure ν. 

Proof. In view of Definition 8.3, we first prove that $\left\{ v _ { n } + w _ { n } \right\}$ satisfies (8.6). Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and, in view of (8.6) for $\{ v _ { n } \}$ , choose $t > 0$ large enough such that 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \left| \left\{x \in E: | v _ {n} (x) | > \frac {t}{3} \right\} \right| <   \frac {\varepsilon}{2}, \quad \left| \left\{x \in E: | w (x) | > \frac {t}{3} \right\} \right| <   \frac {\varepsilon}{2},
$$

where for the latter inequality we used the fact that 

$$
\bigcap_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \left\{x \in E: | w (x) | > k \right\} = \emptyset .\tag{8.10}
$$

Since 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \left|\left\{x \in E: | w _ {n} (x) - w (x) | > \frac {t}{3} \right\}\right| = 0,
$$

we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n} (x) + w _ {n} (x) | > t \} | \\ \quad \leq \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} \left| \left\{x \in E: | v _ {n} (x) | > \frac {t}{3} \right\} \right| + \left| \left\{x \in E: | w (x) | > \frac {t}{3} \right\} \right| \\ \quad + \underset {n \to \infty} {\lim} \left| \left\{x \in E: | w _ {n} (x) - w (x) | > \frac {t}{3} \right\} \right| \\ <   \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Thus $\left\{ v _ { n } + w _ { n } \right\}$ satisfies (8.6). 

Now let $h \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ . Since $\varphi$ is uniformly continuous there exists $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
| \varphi (z) - \varphi (z ^ {\prime}) | \leq \varepsilon
$$

for all $z , z ^ { \prime } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ with $| z - z ^ { \prime } | < \delta$ . We have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \int_ {E} h (x) \varphi (v _ {n} (x) + w _ {n} (x)) d x - \int_ {E} h (x) \varphi (v _ {n} (x) + w (x)) d x \right| \\ \leq 2 \| \varphi \| _ {\infty} \int_ {E \cap \{| w _ {n} - w | \geq \delta \}} | h (x) | d x + \varepsilon \int_ {E \cap \{| w _ {n} - w | <   \delta \}} | h (x) | d x, \end{array}
$$

and thus 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \left| \int_ {E} h (x)   \varphi (v _ {n} (x) + w _ {n} (x)) d x - \int_ {E} h (x)   \varphi (v _ {n} (x) + w (x)) d x \right| \\ \leq \varepsilon \int_ {E} | h (x) | d x. \end{array}
$$

Given the arbitrariness of $\varepsilon ,$ , we deduce that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} h (x) \varphi (v _ {n} (x) + w _ {n} (x)) d x = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} h (x) \varphi (v _ {n} (x) + w (x)) d x \\ = \int_ {E} h (x) \left\langle \nu_ {x}, \varphi (\cdot + w (x)) \right\rangle d x = \int_ {E} h (x) \left\langle \Gamma_ {w (x)} \nu_ {x}, \varphi \right\rangle d x, \end{array}
$$

where we applied Theorem 8.6 to the Carath´eodory function 

$$
(x, y) \mapsto h (x) \varphi (y + w (x)).
$$

This concludes the proof. 

The next result shows that if a sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ generates a Young measure $\nu ,$ then there exists a sequence $\{ w _ { n } \}$ that still generates ν but has better integrability properties. 

Corollary 8.8. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure and let $\{ v _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of measurable functions $v _ { n } : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that generates a Young measure ν and such that 

$$
\limsup _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} g (| v _ {n} (x) |) d x <   \infty ,
$$

for some continuous nondecreasing function $g : [ 0 , \infty )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ with $g ( t ) $ ∞ as $t \to \infty$ . Then there exists a sequence $\{ w _ { n } \}$ of measurable functions $w _ { n }$ : $E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that generates the same Young measure ν and such that $\{ g ( | w _ { n } ( \cdot ) | ) \}$ is equi-integrable. Moreover, 

$$
\int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} g (| z |) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x <   \infty .
$$

Proof. By Theorem 8.6(i) we have 

$$
\int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} g (| z |) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x <   \infty .
$$

By extracting a subsequence if necessary, we may assume that 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} g (| v _ {n} (x) |)   d x = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} g (| v _ {n} (x) |)   d x.
$$

By the decomposition lemma there exists a subsequence of $\{ v _ { n } \}$ (not relabeled) and an increasing sequence of numbers $r _ { n }  \infty$ such that $\{ \tau _ { r _ { n } } \circ g$ $\left( | v _ { n } ( \cdot ) | \right) \}$ is equi-integrable and 

$$
| \{x \in E: g (| v _ {n} (x) |) \neq \tau_ {r _ {n}} \circ g (| v _ {n} (x) |) \} | \to 0,\tag{8.11}
$$

where for $r > 0$ the truncation $\tau _ { r } : \mathbb { R } \to \mathbb { R }$ is defined by 

$$
\tau_ {r} (s) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} s & \quad \text { if } \quad | s | \leq r, \\ \frac {s}{| s |} r & \quad \text { if } \quad | s | > r. \end{array} \right.
$$

Define 

$$
w _ {n} \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} v _ {n} (x) & \text { if } g \left(\left| v _ {n} (x) \right|\right) \leq r _ {n}, \\ z _ {0} & \text { if } g \left(\left| v _ {n} (x) \right|\right) > r _ {n}, \end{array} \right.
$$

where $z _ { 0 } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is such that $g ( | z _ { 0 } | ) \in \mathbb { R }$ . By (8.11), 

$$
| \{x \in E: v _ {n} (x) \neq w _ {n} (x) \} | \rightarrow 0,
$$

and so by Corollary $8 . 7 , \{ w _ { n } \}$ generates the same Young measure ν. Observe that 

$$
g \left(\left| w _ {n} (x) \right|\right) \leq \tau_ {r _ {n}} \circ g \left(\left| v _ {n} (x) \right|\right) + g \left(\left| z _ {0} \right|\right),
$$

and equi-integrability follows. 

The following corollary is particularly useful in applications (see, e.g., [FoTa89]). 

Corollary 8.9. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure and let $\{ v _ { n } \} , v _ { n } : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , be a sequence of measurable functions that generates a Young measure ν. Then $\{ v _ { n } \}$ converges in measure to a function $v : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ if and only if $\nu _ { x } = \delta _ { v ( x ) }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ 

Proof. Assume first that $\{ v _ { n } \}$ converges to v in measure. Let $w _ { n } : = v$ for all $n .$ . Then by Corollary $8 . 7 , \{ v _ { n } \}$ and $\{ w _ { n } \}$ generate the same Young measure. Since $\{ w _ { n } \}$ generates the Young measure $\delta _ { v } .$ , it follows that $\nu _ { x } = \delta _ { v ( x ) }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ ${ \mathrm { a . e . ~ } } x \in E$ 

Conversely, assume that $\nu _ { x } ~ = ~ \delta _ { v ( x ) }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { a . e . } x \in E$ . Since $\nu \in$ $L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \right)$ , the function v is measurable. Fix ε, $\eta > 0$ . By Lusin’s theorem choose $K \subset E$ compact such that $| E \setminus K | \leq \eta$ and $v : K  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is uniformly continuous. Find $\rho > 0$ such that 

$$
| v (x) - v (x ^ {\prime}) | \leq \frac {\varepsilon}{2}\tag{8.12}
$$

for all $x , x ^ { \prime } \in K$ , with $| x - x ^ { \prime } | \leq \rho .$ . Since $K$ is compact there exist $x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { \ell } \in$ $K , \ell \in \mathbb { N }$ , such that 

$$
K \subset \bigcup_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} B (x _ {i}, \rho).
$$

Let $E _ { i } : = B ^ { * } \left( x _ { i } , \rho \right) \cap K$ , where 

$$
B ^ {*} \left(x _ {i}, \rho\right) := B \left(x _ {i}, \rho\right) \setminus \bigcup_ {j = 1} ^ {i - i} B \left(x _ {j}, \rho\right),
$$

and define 

$$
w (x) := \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} v \left(x _ {i}\right) \chi_ {E _ {i}} (x).
$$

Note that by (8.12), 

$$
\left| \left\{x \in E: | v (x) - w (x) | > \frac {\varepsilon}{2} \right\} \right| \leq \eta .\tag{8.13}
$$

Let 

$$
f (x, z) := \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} \chi_ {E _ {i}} (x) \varphi (| z - v (x _ {i}) |),
$$

where $\varphi : [ 0 , \infty )  [ 0 , 1 ]$ is a continuous function such that $\varphi = 0$ on $[ 0 , \textstyle { \frac { \varepsilon } { 2 } } ]$ and $\varphi = 1$ on $\lbrack \varepsilon , \infty )$ . Then $f$ is a bounded Carath´eodory function, and thus $\{ f ( \cdot , v _ { n } ( \cdot ) ) \}$ is equi-integrable. Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n} - w | > \varepsilon \} | \leq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} | \{x \in E _ {i}: | v _ {n} - v (x _ {i}) | > \varepsilon \} | + \eta \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} \int_ {E _ {i}} \varphi (| v _ {n} (x) - v (x _ {i}) |) d x + \eta \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad = \int_ {E} f (x, v _ {n} (x)) d x + \eta , \end{array}
$$

and so by Theorem 8.6(ii) we obtain that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n} - w | > \varepsilon \} | \leq \underset {n \to \infty} {\lim} \int_ {E} f (x, v _ {n} (x)) d x + \eta \\ = \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) d \delta_ {v (x)} (z) d x + \eta = \int_ {E} f (x, v (x)) d x + \eta \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\ell} \int_ {E _ {i}} \varphi (| v (x) - v (x _ {i}) |) d x + \eta \\ \leq \left| \left\{x \in K: | v - w | > \frac {\varepsilon}{2} \right\} \right| + \eta \leq 2 \eta , \end{array}
$$

where we have used (8.13) and the fact that $\varphi \leq 1$ . Hence 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n} - v | > 2 \varepsilon \} | \\ \quad \leq \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} | \{x \in E: | v _ {n} - w | > \varepsilon \} | + | \{x \in E: | v - w | > \varepsilon \} | \\ \quad \leq 2 \eta . \end{array}
$$

It now sufices to let $\eta  0 ^ { + }$
