The next result deals with pairs of sequences. 

Corollary 8.10. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure and let $\left\{ u _ { n } \right\} , ~ \left\{ v _ { n } \right\}$ be two sequences of measurable functions, with $u _ { n } \ : \ E \ \to \ \mathbb { R } ^ { d } a n d v _ { n } \ : \ E \ \to \ \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ . If $\{ v _ { n } \}$ generates the Young measure $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ and $u _ { n }$ converges pointwise $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. in E to a function $u : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , then the sequence $\left\{ \left( u _ { n } , v _ { n } \right) \right\}$ generates the Young measure 

$$
x \mapsto \delta_ {u (x)} \otimes \nu_ {x}.
$$

Proof. In view of Definition 8.3, we first prove that $\left\{ \left( u _ { n } , v _ { n } \right) \right\}$ satisfies (8.6). For $t > 0$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | \{x \in E: | (u _ {n}, v _ {n}) (x) | > t \} | \\ \leq \left| \left\{x \in E: | u _ {n} (x) | > \frac {t}{\sqrt {2}} \right\} \right| + \left| \left\{x \in E: | v _ {n} (x) | > \frac {t}{\sqrt {2}} \right\} \right| \\ \leq \left| \left\{x \in E: | u _ {n} (x) - u (x) | > \frac {t}{2 \sqrt {2}} \right\} \right| + \left| \left\{x \in E: | u (x) | > \frac {t}{2 \sqrt {2}} \right\} \right| \\ + \left| \left\{x \in E: | v _ {n} (x) | > \frac {t}{\sqrt {2}} \right\} \right|. \end{array}
$$

Due to property (8.6) for $\{ v _ { n } \}$ , using an argument analogous to that of (8.10), and since $u _ { n }$ converges pointwise, and hence in measure, to u we deduce that (8.6) is satisfied by $\left\{ \left( u _ { n } , v _ { n } \right) \right\}$ 

Let $h \in L ^ { 1 } ( E ) , \psi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \right)$ , and $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Then 

$$
\left| h (x) \psi \left(u _ {n}\right) \right| \leq \left\| \psi \right\| _ {\infty} \left| h (x) \right|,
$$

and so by the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem, $h \psi ( u _ { n } )  h \psi ( u )$ strongly in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ . Since $\{ v _ { n } \}$ generates the Young measure $\nu ,$ we have that $\varphi ( v _ { n } ) \stackrel { * } {  } \overline { { \varphi } }$ in $L ^ { \infty } \left( E \right)$ , and so 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \int_ {E} h (x) \psi (u _ {n}) \varphi (v _ {n}) d x = \int_ {E} h (x) \psi (u) \left(\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi (z) d \nu_ {x} (z)\right) d x,
$$

that is, 

$$
\left(\psi \otimes \varphi\right)\left(u _ {n}, v _ {n}\right) \stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} \left\langle \delta_ {u (\cdot)} \otimes \nu ., \psi \otimes \varphi \right\rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} \text {   in   } L ^ {\infty} (E).
$$

Since tensors of the form $\psi \otimes \varphi$ are dense in $C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , the proof is complete. 

Next we study the relation between biting convergence and Young measures. 

Theorem 8.11. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure and let $\{ v _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of measurable functions $\boldsymbol { v } _ { n } \ : \ E \ \to \ \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that generates a Young measure $\nu$ . Then for any Carath´eodory function $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to [ - \infty , \infty ]$ such that $\{ f ( \cdot , v _ { n } ( \cdot ) ) \}$ is bounded in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ , there exists a subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ v _ { n } \}$ such that 

$$
f (\cdot , v _ {n _ {k}} (\cdot)) \stackrel {{b}} {{\rightharpoonup}} \overline {{f}} i n L ^ {1} (E).
$$

Proof. By the biting lemma there exist a function $g \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ , a subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ v _ { n } \}$ , and a decreasing sequence of Lebesgue measurable sets $\{ E _ { j } \} \subset$ $E$ , with $| E _ { j } | \to 0$ , such that 

$$
f (\cdot , v _ {n _ {k}} (\cdot)) \rightharpoonup g \text {   in   } L ^ {1} (E \setminus E _ {j}) \text {   for   every   } j \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

By Theorem 8.6(ii) we have that $g = { \overline { { f } } }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E \backslash E _ { j }$ for every $j \in \mathbb N$ Since $| E _ { j } |  0$ it follows that $g = { \overline { { f } } }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ 

Remark 8.12. As a consequence of the previous theorem, if $\{ v _ { n } \}$ is bounded in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , then by taking as f a projection, that is, $f \left( z \right) : = z _ { i } , i = 1 , \ldots , m$ where $z = ( z _ { 1 } , \ldots , z _ { m } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , we obtain that there exists a subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ v _ { n } \}$ such that 

$$
v _ {n _ {k}} (\cdot)) \stackrel {{b}} {{\rightharpoonup}} v \text {in} L ^ {1} (E),
$$

where for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ 

$$
v (x) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} z d \nu_ {x} (z).
$$

Using the techniques developed in this chapter we next give a proof of the decomposition lemma stated and proved in Chapter 2, where here the domain of integration is a Lebesgue measurable set of $\bar { \mathbb R } ^ { N }$ with finite measure. 

Lemma 8.13 (Decomposition lemma, II). Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure and let $\{ u _ { n } \}$ be a sequence of functions uniformly bounded in $L ^ { p } \left( E \right) , 1 \leq p < \infty$ . For $r > 0$ consider the truncation $\tau _ { r } : \mathbb { R } \to \mathbb { R }$ defined $b y$ 

$$
\tau_ {r} (z) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} z & \text {   if   } | z | \leq r, \\ \frac {z}{| z |} r & \text {   if   } | z | > r. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then there exists a subsequence of $\{ u _ { n } \}$ (not relabeled) and an increasing sequence of numbers $r _ { n } \to \infty$ such that the truncated sequence $\{ \tau _ { r _ { n } } \circ u _ { n } \}$ is p-equi-integrable, and 

$$
\left|\left\{x \in E: u _ {n} (x) \neq \left(\tau_ {r _ {n}} \circ u _ {n}\right) (x) \right\}\right|\rightarrow 0.\tag{8.14}
$$

Proof. Without loss of generality, by Theorem 8.2 we may assume that the sequence $\{ u _ { n } \}$ generates a Young measure $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ ) and by Theorem 8.6 (i), 

$$
\int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} | z | ^ {p} d \nu_ {x} (z) d x <   \infty .\tag{8.15}
$$

Using Theorem 8.6(ii) we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {r \to \infty} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} | \tau_ {r} \circ u _ {n} | ^ {p} d x = \lim _ {r \to \infty} \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} | \tau_ {r} (z) | ^ {p} d \nu_ {x} (z) d x \\ = \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} | z | ^ {p} d \nu_ {x} (z) d x, \end{array}
$$

where the last equality has been obtained via the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem. Therefore we may find an increasing sequence of numbers $r _ { n } \to \infty$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} | \tau_ {r _ {n}} \circ u _ {n} | ^ {p} d x = \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R}} | z | ^ {p} d \nu_ {x} (z) d x.\tag{8.16}
$$

Property (8.14) follows directly from the boundedness of the sequence $\{ u _ { n } \}$ in L<sup>p</sup>. By Corollary 8.7 the sequence $\{ \tau _ { r _ { n } } \circ u _ { n } \}$ generates the same Young measure $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ , and in view of (8.15), (8.16), and Theorem 8.6(ii) the sequence $\{ \tau _ { r _ { n } } \circ u _ { n } \}$ is p-equi-integrable. 

## 8.2 Characterization of Young Measures

In this section we prove that every Young measure is generated by a sequence of measurable functions. 

Theorem 8.14. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure and let $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } ( E ; \mathcal { M } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } ) )$ be a Young measure. Then there exists a continuous, nondecreasing function $g : [ 0 , \infty )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ such that $g ( t )  \infty$ as $t \to \infty$ and 

$$
\int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} g (| z |) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x <   \infty .\tag{8.17}
$$

Proof. We claim that 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \int_ {E} \int_ {\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: | z | > t \}} d \nu_ {x} (z)   d x = 0.\tag{8.18}
$$

Indeed, since $\nu _ { x } \in \operatorname { P r } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ , by Proposition $\mathrm { 1 . 7 ( i i ) }$ we have that 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \int_ {\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: | z | > t \}} d \nu_ {x} (z) = 0,
$$

and since 

$$
0 \leq \int_ {\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: | z | > t \}} d \nu_ {x} (z) d x \leq \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} d \nu_ {x} (z) = 1,
$$

(8.18) follows by the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem. We can now proceed as in the proof of Proposition 8.4 to show that (8.18) implies (8.17). Precisely, choose $0 < t _ { j } < t _ { j + 1 } , j \in \mathbb { N }$ , with $t _ { j } \to \infty$ as $j \to \infty$ , such that 

$$
\int_ {E} \int_ {\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: | z | > t _ {j} \}} d \nu_ {x} (z) d x \leq \frac {1}{j ^ {3}},
$$

and define 

$$
h \left(t\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0 \text {   if   } t \in \left[ 0, t _ {1}\right), \\ j \text {   if   } t \in \left[ t _ {j}, t _ {j + 1}\right), j \in \mathbb {N}. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {E} \int_ {\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: | z | \leq t _ {k} \}} h (| z |)   d \nu_ {x} (z)   d x \\ \qquad = \int_ {E} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k - 1} \int_ {\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: t _ {j} \leq | z | <   t _ {j + 1} \}} h (| z |)   d \nu_ {x} (z)   d x \\ \qquad = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k - 1} j \int_ {E} \int_ {\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: t _ {j} \leq | z | <   t _ {j + 1} \}} d \nu_ {x} (z)   d x \\ \qquad \leq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k} \frac {1}{j ^ {2}} \leq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j ^ {2}} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

By the Lebesgue monotone convergence theorem, letting $k \to \infty$ we obtain 

$$
\int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} h (| z |) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x \leq \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{j ^ {2}} <   \infty .
$$

It now sufices to replace the function h with a continuous, nondecreasing function $0 \leq g \leq h$ 

Next we show that the condition (8.17) is equivalent to the existence of a sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ of measurable functions $v _ { n } : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that generates ν and such that $\{ g ( | v _ { n } ( \cdot ) | ) \}$ is equi-integrable. We begin with the case of a homogeneous Young measure. 

Definition 8.15. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure. A Young measure $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ is said to be homogeneous $i f$ there exists a probability measure $\mu \in \operatorname { P r } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ such that $\nu _ { x } = \mu$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ 

Exercise 8.16. Let a, $b \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ and $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , and consider the function 

$$
v \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} a \text {   if   } x \in (0, \theta), \\ b \text {   if   } x \in (\theta , 1). \end{array} \right.
$$

Extend v periodically to all of R with period 1 and let $v _ { n } \left( x \right) : = v \left( n x \right)$ . Prove that the sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ generates the homogeneous Young measure 

$$
\nu_ {x} = \theta \delta_ {a} + (1 - \theta) \delta_ {b}.
$$

## 8.2.1 The Homogeneous Case

Theorem 8.17. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, let $\nu \in \mathcal P \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , and let $g : [ 0 , \infty )  [ 0 , \infty ]$ be a continuous, nondecreasing function such that $g ( t )  \infty \ a s t  \infty$ . Then the following two conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\int _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { m } } g ( | z | ) d \nu ( z ) < \infty ;$ 

(ii) there exists a sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ of measurable functions $v _ { n } : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that generates ν and such that $\{ g ( | v _ { n } ( \cdot ) | ) \}$ is equi-integrable. 

Proof. That (ii) implies (i) follows from Theorem 8.6(ii). In the remainder of the proof we show that (i) implies (ii). 

Step 1: Fix $R > 0$ and define $D _ { R } : = \overline { { B _ { m } \left( 0 , R \right) } }$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathbb {H} _ {R} := \Big \{\mu \in \operatorname * {P r} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right): \operatorname{supp} \mu \subset D _ {R},   \mu \text { is generated by a sequence }   \{v _ {n} \} \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \text { with } \| v _ {n} \| _ {L ^ {\infty} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m})} \leq R \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

We claim that $\mathbb { H } _ { R }$ is convex. Indeed, fix $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { H } _ { R }$ and $\theta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ . Let $\{ v _ { n } \} , \{ w _ { n } \}$ be two sequences of measurable functions $v _ { n } , w _ { n } : E \to D _ { R }$ that generate $\mu _ { 1 }$ and $\mu _ { 2 }$ , respectively. By Proposition 2.87 there exists a sequence $\{ E _ { k } \}$ of Lebesgue measurable sets, with $E _ { k } ~ \subset ~ E$ , such that $\chi _ { E _ { k } } \ \stackrel { * } { \ } \ \theta$ in $L ^ { \infty } \left( E \right)$ . For $n , k \in \mathbb { N }$ define 

$$
w _ {n, k} (x) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l} v _ {n} (x) \text { if } x \in E _ {k}, \\ w _ {n} (x) \text { if } x \in E \setminus E _ {k}. \end{array} \right.
$$

Let $h \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\int_ {E} h (x) \varphi (w _ {n, k} (x)) d x\\= \int_ {E} \chi_ {E _ {k}} (x) h (x) \varphi (v _ {n} (x)) d x + \int_ {E} (1 - \chi_ {E _ {k}} (x)) h (x) \varphi (w _ {n} (x)) d x\\\rightarrow \theta \int_ {E} h (x) \varphi (v _ {n} (x)) d x + (1 - \theta) \int_ {E} h (x) \varphi (w _ {n} (x)) d x\end{array}
$$

as $k \to \infty$ , and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \lim _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {E} h (x) \varphi (w _ {n, k} (x)) d x \\ = \int_ {E} h (x) d x (\theta \langle \mu_ {1}, \varphi \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} + (1 - \theta) \langle \mu_ {2}, \varphi \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}}), \end{array}
$$

where we have used Theorem 8.6(ii). Since $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and $C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ are separable, we may extract a diagonal sequence $\{ w _ { n , k _ { n } } \}$ for which the previous limit exists for each $h$ and $\varphi$ in a dense set of $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and $C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , respectively (and hence by density for all $h \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ) )$ . Since the sequence $\{ w _ { n , k _ { n } } \}$ generates the Young measure $\theta \mu _ { 1 } + \left( 1 - \theta \right) \mu _ { 2 }$ , we have that $\theta \mu _ { 1 } + \left( 1 - \theta \right) \mu _ { 2 } \in$ $\mathbb { H } _ { R }$ and the claim is proved. 

Step 2: We claim that $\mathbb { H } _ { R }$ is relatively closed in $\operatorname* { P r } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ with respect to the weak star topology $\sigma \left( \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) , C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right) \right) \left( \sigma \left( \mathcal { M } , C _ { 0 } \right) \right.$ for simplicity), i.e., 

$$
\overline {{\mathbb {H} _ {R}}} ^ {\sigma (\mathcal {M}, C _ {0})} \cap \operatorname * {P r} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right) = \mathbb {H} _ {R}.
$$

Indeed, let $\mu \in \overline { { \mathbb { H } _ { R } } } ^ { \sigma ( \mathcal { M } , C _ { 0 } ) } \cap \mathrm { P r } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and let $\{ h _ { j } \}$ and $\{ \varphi _ { j } \}$ be dense in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and $C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , respectively. By the definition of weak star topology in $\mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ , for every $n \in \mathbb { N }$ there exists $\mu _ { n } \in \mathbb { H } _ { R }$ such that 

$$
\left| \langle \mu - \mu_ {n}, \varphi_ {j} \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} \right| <   \frac {1}{2 n \max _ {0 \leq i \leq n} \left(1 + \| h _ {i} \| _ {L ^ {1} (E)}\right)}, \quad j = 1, \ldots , n.\tag{8.19}
$$

By the definition of $\mathbb { H } _ { R } .$ , the homogeneous Young measure $\mu _ { n }$ is generated by a sequence $\left\{ v _ { n } ^ { ( k ) } \right\} _ { k \in \mathbb { N } }$ with 

$$
\sup _ {k \in \mathbb {N}} \left\| v _ {n} ^ {(k)} \right\| _ {L ^ {\infty} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m})} \leq R.\tag{8.20}
$$

Choose $k = k \left( n \right) \in \mathbb { N }$ suficiently large that with $v _ { n } : = v _ { n } ^ { ( k ( n ) ) }$ we have 

$$
\left| \langle \mu_ {n}, \varphi_ {j} \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} \int_ {E} h _ {i} d x - \int_ {E} h _ {i} \varphi_ {j} (v _ {n}) d x \right| <   \frac {1}{2 n}, i, j = 1, \dots , n,
$$

so that by (8.19), 

$$
\left| \langle \mu , \varphi_ {j} \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} \int_ {E} h _ {i} d x - \int_ {E} h _ {i} \varphi_ {j} (v _ {n}) d x \right| <   \frac {1}{n}, \quad i, j = 1, \dots , n.\tag{8.21}
$$

By (8.20), Proposition 8.4, and Theorem 8.6(iii), a subsequence $\{ v _ { n _ { k } } \}$ of $\{ v _ { n } \}$ generates a Young measure ν with supp $\mu \subset D _ { R }$ . From (8.21) and the density properties of $\{ h _ { j } \}$ and $\{ \varphi _ { j } \}$ it follows that $\mu = \nu$ . Hence $\mu \in \mathbb { H } _ { R }$ 

Step 3: Let 

$$
\mathbb {M} _ {R} := \left\{\mu \in \operatorname * {P r} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right): \operatorname{supp} \mu \subset D _ {R} \right\}.
$$

Note that $\mathbb { H } _ { R } \subset \mathbb { M } _ { R }$ . We claim that $\mathbb { H } _ { R } \supset \mathbb { M } _ { R }$ . Assume by contradiction that there exists $\mu \in \mathbb { M } _ { R }$ such that $\mu \notin \mathbb { H } _ { R }$ . By Steps 1 and 2, 

$$
\mu \notin \overline {{\mathbb {H} _ {R}}} ^ {\sigma (\mathcal {M}, C _ {0})} = \overline {{\mathrm{co} \mathbb {H} _ {R}}} ^ {\sigma (\mathcal {M}, C _ {0})},
$$

and therefore by the Hahn–Banach theorem there exist a linear functional $L :$ $\mathcal { M } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } )  \mathbb { R }$ , continuous with respect to the weak star topology $\sigma \left( \mathcal { M } , C _ { 0 } \right)$ , and $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
L (\nu) \geq \alpha \text {   for   all   } \nu \in \mathbb {H} _ {R}, \quad \alpha > L (\mu).
$$

By Theorem A.72 there exists $\varphi \in C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ such that 

$$
L (\nu) = \langle \nu , \varphi \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi d \nu
$$

for all $\nu \in \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ , and so 

$$
\langle \nu , \varphi \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} \geq \alpha \text {   for   all   } \nu \in \mathbb {H} _ {R}, \quad \alpha > \langle \mu , \varphi \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}}.\tag{8.22}
$$

Define 

$$
\varphi_ {R} (z) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \varphi (z) \text {   if   } | z | \leq R, \\ \infty \quad \text {   otherwise.   } \end{array} \right.
$$

Since supp $\mu \subset D _ { R }$ we have that 

$$
\alpha > \langle \mu , \varphi \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {R} (z) d \mu (z) \geq \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {R} ^ {* *} (z) d \mu (z) \geq \varphi_ {R} ^ {* *} (a),\tag{8.23}
$$

by Jensen’s inequality and where $\begin{array} { r } { a : = \int _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { m } } z d \mu ( z ) } \end{array}$ . Note that $| a | \le R$ . Since $\varphi _ { R }$ is lower semicontinuous, it follows by Theorem 4.98 that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \varphi_ {R} ^ {* *} (a) = \inf \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m + 1} \theta_ {i} \varphi_ {R} (z _ {i}): \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m + 1} \theta_ {i} = 1, \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m + 1} \theta_ {i} z _ {i} = a, \theta_ {i} \geq 0, z _ {i} \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m} \right\} \\ = \inf \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m + 1} \theta_ {i} \varphi (z _ {i}): \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m + 1} \theta_ {i} = 1, \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m + 1} \theta_ {i} z _ {i} = a, \theta_ {i} \geq 0, z _ {i} \in D _ {R} \right\}. \end{array}
$$

Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and write 

$$
\varphi_ {R} ^ {* *} (a) + \varepsilon \geq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m + 1} \theta_ {i} \varphi (z _ {i}),
$$

where $\theta _ { i } \geq 0 , z _ { i } \in D _ { R } , i = 1 , \ldots , m + 1$ , 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m + 1} \theta_ {i} = 1, \quad \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m + 1} \theta_ {i} z _ {i} = a.
$$

Observe that since $\delta _ { z _ { i } } \in \mathbb { H } _ { R }$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , m + 1$ , and $\mathbb { H } _ { R }$ is convex (see Step 1), we have 

$$
\nu := \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m + 1} \theta_ {i} \delta_ {z _ {i}} \in \mathbb {H} _ {R}.
$$

Therefore by (8.22) and (8.23), 

$$
\varphi_ {R} ^ {* *} (a) + \varepsilon \geq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m + 1} \theta_ {i} \varphi (z _ {i}) = \langle \nu , \varphi \rangle_ {\mathcal {M}, C _ {0}} \geq \alpha > \varphi_ {R} ^ {* *} (a),
$$

and letting $\varepsilon \to 0 ^ { + }$ we obtain a contradiction. 

Step 4: We are now ready to prove the general case. Since the set E has finite measure, by rescaling, we may assume that $| E | = 1$ . Let $\nu \in \operatorname { P r } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ be such that (i) holds. Since $\nu \in \operatorname { P r } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , by Proposition 1.7(ii) we have that 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \nu \left(\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: | z | > t \}\right) = 0.
$$

Hence for all $k \in \mathbb N$ suficiently large, say $k \geq k _ { 0 }$ , we have that 

$$
\nu \left(\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: | z | \leq k \}\right) > 0.
$$

For $k \geq k _ { 0 }$ consider the probability measure $\nu _ { k }$ , defined by 

$$
\nu_ {k} (F) := c _ {k} \nu (F \cap D _ {k}) F \in \mathcal {B} (\mathbb {R} ^ {m}),
$$

where 

$$
c _ {k} := \frac {1}{\nu (D _ {k})}, \quad D _ {k} := \overline {{B _ {m} (0 , k)}}.
$$

Note that $\nu _ { k } \in \mathbb { M } _ { k }$ , where 

$$
\mathbb {M} _ {k} := \left\{\mu \in \operatorname * {P r} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {m}\right): \operatorname{supp} \mu \subset D _ {k} \right\}.
$$

By Step 3, for each fixed $k \geq k _ { 0 }$ there exists a sequence $\{ v _ { n , k } \}$ of measurable functions $v _ { n , k } : E \to D _ { k }$ that generates $\nu _ { k }$ . Let $\{ h _ { j } \}$ and $\{ \varphi _ { j } \}$ be dense in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ and $C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , respectively. Since $\{ v _ { n , k } \}$ generates $\nu _ { k }$ and $v _ { n , k } : E \to$ $D _ { k }$ , by Theorem 8.6(ii) for all $i , j \in \mathbb N$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) \varphi_ {j} (v _ {n, k} (x)) d x = \int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) d x \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {j} (z) d \nu_ {k} (z) \\ = c _ {k} \int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) d x \int_ {D _ {k}} \varphi_ {j} (z) d \nu (z), \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} g \left(| v _ {n, k} (x) |\right) d x = | E | \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} g (| z |) d \nu_ {k} (z) \\ = c _ {k} \int_ {D _ {k}} g (| z |) d \nu (z), \end{array}
$$

where we have used the facts that $| E | = 1$ and that for each fixed $k \in \mathbb N$ the sequences $\{ \varphi _ { j } \left( v _ { n , k } \left( \cdot \right) \right) \}$ and $\{ g \left( \left. v _ { n , k } \left( \cdot \right) \right. \right) \}$ are equi-integrable, since $\| v _ { n , k } \| _ { L ^ { \infty } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ) } \leq k$ . By virtue of the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem, we obtain that 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) \varphi_ {j} (v _ {n, k} (x)) d x = \int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) d x \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {j} (z) d \nu (z)
$$

and 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} g \left(| v _ {n, k} (x) |\right) d x = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} g (| z |) d \nu (z).
$$

Extract a diagonal sequence $\{ v _ { \ell } \}$ of $\{ v _ { n , k } \}$ such that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lim _ {\ell \to \infty} \int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) \varphi_ {j} (v _ {\ell} (x)) d x = \int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) d x \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {j} (z) d \nu (z), \\ \lim _ {\ell \to \infty} \int_ {E} g (| v _ {\ell} (x) |) d x = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} g (| z |) d \nu (z), \end{array}
$$

for all i, $j \in \mathbb N$ . By the density properties of $\{ h _ { j } \}$ and $\{ \varphi _ { j } \}$ and Theorem $8 . 6 ( \mathrm { i i } )$ , it follows that $\{ v _ { \ell } \}$ generates ν and $\{ g ( | \dot { v _ { \ell } } ( \cdot ) | ) \}$ is equi-integrable in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ 

Exercise 8.18. Prove that if the measurable set $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is bounded, then in Step 1 it is possible to use the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma and thus avoid Proposition 2.87. 

## 8.2.2 The Inhomogeneous Case

We are now ready to consider the inhomogeneous case. 

Theorem 8.19. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, let $\nu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( E ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ be a Young measure, and let $g : [ 0 , \infty ) $ $[ 0 , \infty ]$ be a continuous, nondecreasing function such that $g ( t )  \infty \ a s t  \infty$ Then the following two conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { E } \int _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { m } } g ( | z | ) d \nu _ { x } ( z ) d x < \infty ; } \end{array}$ 

(ii) there exists a sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ of measurable functions $v _ { n } : E \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that generates ν and such that $\{ g ( | v _ { n } ( \cdot ) | ) \}$ is equi-integrable in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ 

Proof. That (ii) implies (i) follows from Theorem 8.6(ii). 

Step 1: To prove that (i) implies (ii) we first claim that, without loss of generality, we may consider the case that the set $E$ is an open set with finite measure. Indeed, condition (i) implies that 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} g (| z |) d \nu_ {x} (z) <   \infty
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ . Select any $x _ { 0 } \in E$ for which the previous integral is finite and $\nu _ { x _ { 0 } } \in \operatorname { P r } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ . Fix an open set $\varOmega \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ of finite measure that contains $E$ and define 

$$
\mu_ {x} := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \nu_ {x} & \text { if } x \in E, \\ \nu_ {x _ {0}} & \text { if } x \in \varOmega \setminus E. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then $\mu \in L _ { w } ^ { \infty } \left( \varOmega ; \mathcal { M } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } ; \mathbb { R } \right) \right)$ is a Young measure and (i) is satisfied. Thus if we show that there exists a sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ of measurable functions $\begin{array} { r l } { \boldsymbol { v } _ { n } } & { { } : } \end{array}$ $\varOmega  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that generates $\mu$ and such that $\{ g ( | v _ { n } ( \cdot ) | ) \}$ is equi-integrable in $L ^ { 1 } \left( \varOmega \right)$ , then the sequence $\{ v _ { n } \}$ restricted to E generates ν. Also, without loss of generality we may assume that 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} g (| z |) d \nu_ {x} (z) <   \infty\tag{8.24}
$$

for all $x \in E$ 

Step 2: In view of the previous step we may assume that $E$ is an open set with finite measure. Let $\{ h _ { j } \} _ { j \in \mathbb { N } } \subset C _ { c } \left( E \right)$ and $\{ \varphi _ { \mathcal { I } } \} _ { \mathcal { I } \in \mathbb { N } }$ be dense in $L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ 

and $C _ { 0 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ , respectively. Set $h _ { 0 } = 1$ and $\varphi _ { 0 } = g$ . For $j \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ and $x \in E$ define 

$$
\psi_ {j} (x) := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {j} (z) d \nu_ {x} (z)\tag{8.25}
$$

and let 

$$
F := \bigcap_ {j \in \mathbb {N} _ {0}} \left\{x \in E: x \text {   Lebesgue   point   for   } \psi_ {j} \right\},
$$

where we used the fact that in view of (8.24), $\psi _ { j } \in L ^ { 1 } \left( E \right)$ for all $j \in \mathbb { N } _ { 0 }$ Then $| E \setminus F | = 0$ . For each $k \in \mathbb N$ set 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {G} _ {k} := \Big \{Q (x, \varepsilon) \subset E: x \in F, 0 <   \varepsilon \leq \frac {1}{k}, \\ \qquad \frac {1}{\varepsilon^ {N}} \int_ {Q (x, \varepsilon)} | \psi_ {j} (y) - \psi_ {j} (x) |   d y <   \frac {1}{k}, j = 0, \ldots , k \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

By Vitali’s covering theorem and Lebesgue’s diferentiation theorem we may write 

$$
E = \bigcup_ {\ell} Q (x _ {k \ell}, \varepsilon_ {k \ell}) \cup N _ {k}, | N _ {k} | = 0,
$$

for some mutually disjoint cubes $Q \left( x _ { k \ell } , \varepsilon _ { k \ell } \right) \in \mathcal { G } _ { k }$ . For each i, $j \in \mathbb { N } _ { 0 }$ let $k > j$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Big | \int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) \psi_ {j} (x) d x - \sum_ {\ell} \psi_ {j} (x _ {k \ell}) \int_ {Q (x _ {k \ell}, \varepsilon_ {k \ell})} h _ {i} (x) d x \Big | \\ \qquad \leq \sum_ {\ell} \int_ {Q (x _ {k \ell}, \varepsilon_ {k \ell})} | h _ {i} (x) (\psi_ {j} (x) - \psi_ {j} (x _ {k \ell})) | d x \\ \qquad \leq \| h _ {i} \| _ {\infty} \sum_ {\ell} \int_ {Q (x _ {k \ell}, \varepsilon_ {k \ell})} | \psi_ {j} (x) - \psi_ {j} (x _ {k \ell}) | d x \\ \qquad \leq \| h _ {i} \| _ {\infty} \frac {1}{k} \sum_ {\ell} | Q (x _ {k \ell}, \varepsilon_ {k \ell}) | = \| h _ {i} \| _ {\infty} \frac {1}{k} | E |. \end{array}
$$

Hence 

$$
\int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) \psi_ {j} (x) d x = \lim _ {k \rightarrow \infty} \sum_ {\ell} \psi_ {j} (x _ {k \ell}) \int_ {Q (x _ {k \ell}, \varepsilon_ {k \ell})} h _ {i} (x) d x\tag{8.26}
$$

for every $i , j \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ 

By the previous theorem and (8.24), for each fixed $k , \ell \in \mathbb { N }$ there exists a sequence $\{ v _ { n k \ell } \}$ of measurable functions $v _ { n k \ell } : Q \left( x _ { k \ell } , \varepsilon _ { k \ell } \right) \ \longrightarrow \ \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that generates $\nu _ { x _ { k \ell } }$ and such that $\{ g ( | v _ { n k \ell } ( \cdot ) | ) \}$ is equi-integrable in $Q \left( \boldsymbol { x } _ { k \ell } , \varepsilon _ { k \ell } \right)$ 

Fix $k , \ell \in \mathbb { N }$ . Since $\left\{ v _ { n k \ell } \right\} _ { n }$ generates $\nu _ { x _ { k \ell } }$ , we may choose $n _ { k \ell }$ such that 

$$
\left| \int_ {Q (x _ {k \ell}, \varepsilon_ {k \ell})} h _ {i} (x) \varphi_ {j} \left(v _ {n _ {k \ell} k \ell} (x)\right) d x - \psi_ {j} (x _ {k \ell}) \int_ {Q (x _ {k \ell}, \varepsilon_ {k \ell})} h _ {i} (x) d x \right| \leq \frac {1}{2 ^ {\ell} k}\tag{8.27}
$$

for all $i , j = 0 , \ldots , k$ . Set 

$$
v _ {k} \left(x\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} v _ {n _ {k \ell} k \ell} \left(x\right) & \text { if } x \in Q \left(x _ {k \ell}, \varepsilon_ {k \ell}\right) \text { for   some } \ell , \\ 0 & \text { if } x \in N _ {k}. \end{array} \right.
$$

We claim that $\{ v _ { k } \}$ generates ν. Indeed, fix $i , j \in  { \mathbb { N } } _ { 0 }$ and let $k >$ max $\{ i , j \}$ By (8.26), (8.27), and the fact that $| N _ { k } | = 0$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\underset {k \to \infty} {\lim} \int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) \varphi_ {j} (v _ {k} (x)) d x = \underset {k \to \infty} {\lim} \sum_ {\ell} \int_ {Q (x _ {k \ell}, \varepsilon_ {k \ell})} h _ {i} (x) \varphi_ {j} (v _ {n _ {k \ell} k \ell} (x)) d x} \\ & {\qquad = \underset {k \to \infty} {\lim} \sum_ {\ell} \psi_ {j} (x _ {k \ell}) \int_ {Q (x _ {k \ell}, \varepsilon_ {k \ell})} h _ {i} (x) d x} \\ & {\qquad = \int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) \psi_ {j} (x) d x} \\ & {\qquad = \int_ {E} h _ {i} (x) \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \varphi_ {j} (z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x,} \end{array}
$$

where in the last identity we have used (8.25). In particular, taking $i = j = 0$ , we get 

$$
\lim _ {k \to \infty} \int_ {E} g (v _ {k}) d x = \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} g (z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x,
$$

and so by Theorem 8.6(ii) we conclude that $\{ g ( | v _ { k } ( \cdot ) | ) \}$ is equi-integrable. This concludes the proof. 

## 8.3 Relaxation

In this section we consider functionals of the form 

$$
v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \mapsto I (v) := \int_ {E} f (x, v) d x,
$$

where $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ is a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , and $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to ( - \infty , \infty ]$ is a normal integrand. We recall that $\mathcal { E } _ { p }$ is the greatest functional below I that is sequentially lower semicontinuous with respect to weak (respectively weak star if $p = \infty )$ convergence in $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ ， and it coincides with $\mathcal { T } _ { p } .$ , where 

$$
\begin{array}{c}\mathcal {I} _ {p} (v) := \inf \Big \{\liminf _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right): \{v _ {n} \} \subset L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}),\\v _ {n} \rightharpoonup v (\stackrel {*} {\rightharpoonup} \text {if} p = \infty) \text {in} L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}) \Big \},\end{array}
$$

provided $f$ satisfies suitable coercivity conditions (see Remark 6.69(i)). 

Theorem 8.20. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, $1 < p < \infty$ , and let $f : E \times \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \to ( - \infty , \infty ]$ be a normal integrand satisfying 

$$
f (x, z) \geq \frac {1}{C} | z | ^ {p} - C\tag{8.28}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , and for some $C > 0$ . Then for every $v \in L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {E} _ {p} (v) = \mathcal {I} _ {p} (v) = \int_ {E} f ^ {* *} (x, v (x)) d x \\ \qquad = \inf _ {\nu \in \mathcal {Y} _ {v}} \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x, \end{array}\tag{8.29}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {Y} _ {v} := \Big \{\nu \in L _ {w} ^ {\infty} \left(E; \mathcal {M} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {m}; \mathbb {R}\right)\right),   \nu \text {is a Young measure}, \\ \qquad \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} | z | ^ {p} d \nu_ {x} (z) d x <   \infty , \\ \qquad v \left(x\right) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} z d \nu_ {x} (z) f o r \mathcal {L} ^ {N} a. e. x \in E \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Moreover, if 

$$
\int_ {E} f ^ {* *} (x, v (x)) d x <   \infty\tag{8.30}
$$

then the infimum is realized by some Young measure $\nu ^ { 0 } \in \mathcal { V } _ { v }$ such that 

$$
f ^ {* *} (x, v (x)) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \ a . e . \ x \in E$ 

Proof. We observe that the first two equalities in (8.29) follow by Remark 6.69(i). 

Let $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ be such that $v _ { n }  v$ in $L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and, without loss of generality, and in view of Remark 8.5, assume that 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} I \left(v _ {n}\right)
$$

and $\{ v _ { n } \}$ generates a Young measure ν. By Remarks 8.12 and 8.5 it follows that $\nu \in \mathcal { V } _ { v }$ . By the fundamental theorem for Young measures (i) we have that 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (x, v _ {n} (x)) d x \geq \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x,
$$

and given the arbitrariness of $\{ v _ { n } \}$ we deduce that 

$$
\mathcal {I} _ {p} (v) \geq \inf _ {\nu \in \mathcal {Y} _ {v}} \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x.
$$

To prove the reverse inequality fix any $\nu \in \mathcal { V } _ { v }$ . By Jensen’s inequality, 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) d \nu_ {x} (z) \geq \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f ^ {* *} (x, z) d \nu_ {x} (z) \geq f ^ {* *} (x, v (x))\tag{8.31}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ , where we have used the fact that $\begin{array} { r } { v \left( x \right) = \int _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { m } } z d \nu _ { x } ( z ) } \end{array}$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ . Integrating over E and then taking the infimum over all $\nu \in \mathcal { V } _ { v }$ , we conclude that 

$$
\inf _ {\nu \in \mathcal {Y} _ {v}} \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x \geq \int_ {E} f ^ {* *} (x, v (x)) d x.\tag{8.32}
$$

By Theorem 6.68, (8.29) follows. 

To prove the second part of the theorem, in view of (8.28), by replacing f with $f + C$ we can assume, without loss of generality, that $f \geq 0$ . Due to the coercivity condition (8.28) it is possible to find a sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ converging weakly to v in $L ^ { p } ( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ and such that 

$$
\int_ {E} f ^ {* *} (x, v (x)) d x = \mathcal {I} _ {p} (v) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (x, v _ {n} (x)) d x <   \infty .
$$

By Remark 8.12, up to a subsequence (not relabeled), $\{ v _ { n } \}$ generates a Young measure $\nu ^ { 0 }$ and by the fundamental theorem for Young measures and the first part of the theorem we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \inf _ {\nu \in \mathcal {Y} _ {v}} \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z)   d \nu_ {x} (z)   d x = \mathcal {I} _ {p} (v) = \lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {E} f (x, v _ {n} (x))   d x \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z)   d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z)   d x, \end{array}
$$

which shows that the infimum is attained. Hence by (8.30) and (8.29), 

$$
\int_ {E} \left[ \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z) - f ^ {* *} (x, v (x)) \right] d x = 0.
$$

Since by (8.31) the expression in square brackets is nonnegative, it follows that 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (x, z) d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z) = f ^ {* *} (x, v (x))
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ . This concludes the proof. 

Exercise 8.21. Prove that the previous theorem continues to hold in the cases $p = 1$ and $p = \infty$ provided 

(a) the coercivity condition (8.28) is replaced by 

$$
f (x, z) \geq \frac {1}{C} g (| z |) - C
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ and for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , for some $C > 0$ , and where $g : [ 0 , \infty ) \to [ 0 , \infty )$ is a continuous, nondecreasing function such that 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \frac {g (t)}{t} = \infty
$$

for $p = 1$ , and 

$$
g \left(t\right) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {t}{\alpha - t} & 0 \leq t <   \alpha , \\ \infty & t \geq \alpha , \end{array} \right.
$$

for some $\alpha > 0$ , for $p = \infty$ ; 

(b) ${ \mathcal { V } } _ { v }$ is given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {Y} _ {v} := \Big \{\nu \in L _ {w} ^ {\infty} \left(E; \mathcal {M} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {m}; \mathbb {R}\right)\right),   \nu \text {is a Young measure}, \\ \qquad \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} g (| z |)   d \nu_ {x} (z)   d x <   \infty , \\ \qquad v \left(x\right) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} z   d \nu_ {x} (z) \text {for} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {a.e.} x \in E \Big \} \end{array}
$$

for $p = 1$ , and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {Y} _ {v} := \Big \{\nu \in L _ {w} ^ {\infty} \left(E; \mathcal {M} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {m}; \mathbb {R}\right)\right),   \nu \text {is a Young measure}, \\ \qquad \operatorname{supp} \nu_ {x} \subset K \text {for} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {a.e.} x \in E \text {and for some compact} \\ \qquad \operatorname{set} K \subset \mathbb {R} ^ {m},   v (x) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} z   d \nu_ {x} (z) \text {for} \mathcal {L} ^ {N} \text {a.e.} x \in E \Big \} \end{array}
$$

for $p = \infty$ 

Recalling the observation made at the beginning of this chapter, the next result illustrates a situation in which the minimum of a certain constraint energy functional does not exist as an $L ^ { p }$ function but may be attained at a “generalized” function, namely the Young measure generated by a minimizing sequence. 

Theorem 8.22. Let $E \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { N }$ be a Lebesgue measurable set with finite measure, let $1 \leq p \leq \infty$ , and let $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { m }  \mathbb { R }$ be a continuous function bounded from below by an afine function. If $\alpha \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \inf \left\{\int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x: v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}), \frac {1}{| E |} \int_ {E} v (x) d x = \alpha \right\} \\ = \inf \left\{\int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x: \nu \in \mathcal {Y} ^ {\alpha} \right\} = f ^ {* *} (\alpha) | E |, \end{array}\tag{8.33}
$$

where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {Y} ^ {\alpha} := \Big \{\nu \in L _ {w} ^ {\infty} \left(E; \mathcal {M} \left(\mathbb {R} ^ {m}; \mathbb {R}\right)\right),   \nu \text {is a Young measure}, \\ \qquad \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} | z | ^ {p} d \nu_ {x} (z) d x <   \infty , \frac {1}{| E |} \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} z d \nu_ {x} (z) d x = \alpha \Big \}, \end{array}
$$

and the infimum is attained in any of the first two expressions if and only if $\alpha \in \mathrm { c o } M _ { \alpha }$ , where 

$$
M _ {\alpha} := \left\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: f (z) = f ^ {* *} (\alpha) + \beta \cdot (z - \alpha) \text {for all} \beta \in \partial f ^ {* *} (\alpha) \right\}.
$$

Moreover, if f satisfies the growth condition 

$$
\lim _ {| z | \to \infty} \frac {f (z)}{| z |} = \infty ,\tag{8.34}
$$

then any minimizing sequence $\{ v _ { n } \} \subset L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ admits a subsequence generating a Young measure $\nu \in \mathcal { V } ^ { \alpha }$ such that supp $\nu _ { x } \subset M _ { \alpha }$ for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \inf \left\{\int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x: v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}), \frac {1}{| E |} \int_ {E} v (x) d x = \alpha \right\} \\ = \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x = f ^ {* *} (\alpha) | E |. \end{array}
$$

Proof. In view of Theorem 5.38, to prove (8.33) it sufices to show that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \inf \left\{\int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x: v \in L ^ {p} (E; \mathbb {R} ^ {m}), \frac {1}{| E |} \int_ {E} v (x) d x = \alpha \right\} \\ \qquad \geq \inf \left\{\int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x: \nu \in \mathcal {Y} ^ {\alpha} \right\} \geq f ^ {* *} (\alpha) | E |. \end{array}
$$

The latter inequality follows from Jensen’s inequality as in (8.31) and (8.32), while to prove the first it sufices to observe that to each function $v \in$ $L ^ { p } \left( E ; \mathbb { R } ^ { m } \right)$ we can associate the Young measure $\nu \in \mathcal { V } ^ { \alpha }$ defined by 

$$
\nu_ {x} := \delta_ {v (x)} \text {   for   } x \in E.
$$

Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {E} f (v (x)) d x = \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \inf \left\{\int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (z) d \tilde {\nu} _ {x} (z) d x: \tilde {\nu} \in \mathcal {Y} ^ {\alpha} \right\}. \end{array}
$$

Hence (8.33) holds. 

Next we show that the infimum is attained in (8.33) if and only if $\alpha \in$ co $M _ { \alpha }$ . Again by Theorem 5.38 it sufices to show that the infimum 

$$
\inf \left\{\int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (z) d \nu_ {x} (z) d x: \nu \in \mathcal {Y} ^ {\alpha} \right\} = f ^ {* *} (\alpha) | E |\tag{8.35}
$$

is attained if and only if $\alpha \in \mathrm { c o } M _ { \alpha }$ . Suppose now that the infimum is attained at some Young measure $\nu ^ { 0 } \in \mathcal { V } ^ { \alpha }$ . Given any $\beta \in \partial f ^ { * * } \left( \alpha \right)$ (recall Theorem 4.53) it follows that 

$$
f (z) \geq f ^ {* *} (z) \geq f ^ {* *} (\alpha) + \beta \cdot (z - \alpha),\tag{8.36}
$$

for all $z \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (z) d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z) d x \geq \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f ^ {* *} (z) d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z) d x \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} [ f ^ {* *} (\alpha) + \beta \cdot (z - \alpha) ] d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z) d x \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad = f ^ {* *} (\alpha) | E |, \end{array}
$$

where in the last identity we have used the fact that 

$$
\frac {1}{| E |} \int_ {E} \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} z d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z) d x = \alpha .\tag{8.37}
$$

It now follows from (8.35) that all the inequalities must be identities. From (8.36) we deduce that 

$$
\int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f (z) d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} f ^ {* *} (z) d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z) = \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} [ f ^ {* *} (\alpha) + \beta \cdot (z - \alpha) ] d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z)
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ and, in turn, 

$$
\operatorname{supp} \nu_ {x} ^ {0} \subset \left\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: f (z) = f ^ {* *} (z) = f ^ {* *} (\alpha) + \beta \cdot (z - \alpha) \right\}\tag{8.38}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N }$ a.e. $x \in E$ . Define 

$$
v (x) := \int_ {\mathbb {R} ^ {m}} z d \nu_ {x} ^ {0} (z), \quad x \in E.
$$

Since for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ the measure $\nu _ { x } ^ { 0 }$ is a probability measure, it follows from Lemma 5.39 and (8.38) that 

$$
v (x) \in \operatorname{co} \left\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: f (z) = f ^ {* *} (z) = f ^ {* *} (\alpha) + \beta \cdot (z - \alpha) \right\}
$$

for $\mathcal { L } ^ { N } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } x \in E$ , which, together with (8.37), yields 

$$
\alpha \in \operatorname{co} \left\{z \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}: f (z) = f ^ {* *} (z) = f ^ {* *} (\alpha) + \beta \cdot (z - \alpha) \right\}.
$$

The final part of the theorem follows exactly as in the proof of the previous theorem using Remark 8.21. 

Remark 8.23. As a consequence of the previous theorem, it follows in particular that condition (8.34) implies $\alpha \in \mathrm { c o } M _ { \alpha }$ . We are not aware of a direct proof of this fact. 

Appendix 

# Functional Analysis and Set Theory

One should always generalize. 

(Man muss immer generalisieren) 

Carl Jacobi 

In order to keep this book as self-contained as possible, in this appendix we collect without proofs several results from functional analysis that have been used throughout the book. This part is intended mostly for graduate students. Most proofs will be omitted. Basic references are [AliBo99], [Bre83], [DuSc88], [Ru91], [Yo95]. The reader should be warned that in [DuSc88] and [Ru91] the definitions of normal spaces and topological vector spaces are diferent from the standard ones. 

## A.1 Some Results from Functional Analysis

## A.1.1 Topological Spaces

Definition A.1. Let X be a nonempty set. A collection $\tau \subseteq { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ is a topology if 

(i) $\emptyset , X \in \tau ;$ 

(ii) if $U _ { i } \in \tau$ for $i = 1 , \dots , M$ , then $U _ { 1 } \cap \ldots \cap U _ { M } \in \tau ,$ 

(iii) if $\{ U _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ is an arbitrary collection of elements of τ then $\textstyle \bigcup _ { \alpha \in I } U _ { \alpha } \in \tau$ 

Example A.2. Given a nonempty set X, the smallest topology consists of $\{ \emptyset , X \}$ , while the largest topology contains all subsets as open sets, and is called the discrete topology. 

The pair $( X , \tau )$ is called topological space and the elements of τ open sets. For simplicity, we often apply the term topological space only to X. A set $C \subset X$ is closed if its complement $X \backslash C$ is open. The closure E of a set 

$E \subset X$ is the smallest closed set that contains E. The interior $\overset { \circ } { \boldsymbol { E } }$ of a set $E \subset X$ is the union of all its open subsets. 

A subset E of a topological space X is said to be dense if its closure is the entire space, i.e., ${ \overline { { E } } } = X$ . We say that a topological space is separable if it contains a countable dense subset. 

Given a point $x \in X$ , a neighborhood<sup>1</sup> of x is any open set $U \in \tau$ that contains x. Given a set $E \subset X$ , a neighborhood of $E$ is any open set $U \in \tau$ that contains E. A topological space is a Hausdorf space if for any x, $y \in X$ with $x \neq y$ we may find two disjoint neighborhoods of x and $y .$ 

Given a topological space X and a sequence $\{ x _ { n } \}$ , we say that $\{ x _ { n } \}$ converges to a point $x \in X$ if for every neighborhood U of x we have that $x _ { n } \in U$ for all n suficiently large. Note that unless the space is Hausdorf, the limit may not be unique. 

A topological space is a normal space if for every pair of disjoint closed sets $C _ { 1 } , C _ { 2 } \subset X$ we may find two disjoint neighborhoods of $C _ { 1 }$ and $C _ { 2 }$ 

Definition A.3. Let X, Y be two topological spaces and let $f : X \to Y$ be a function from X into Y. We say that f is continuous if $f ^ { - 1 } \left( U \right)$ is open for every open set $U \subset Y$ 

The space of all continuous functions $f : X \to Y$ is denoted by $C \left( X ; Y \right)$ The next two theorems give important characterizations of normal spaces. 

Theorem A.4 (Urysohn). A topological space X is normal if and only if for any two disjoint closed sets $C _ { 1 } , C _ { 2 } \subset X$ there exists a continuous function $f : X \to [ 0 , 1 ]$ such that $f \equiv 1$ in $C _ { 1 }$ and $f \equiv 0$ in $C _ { 2 }$ 

Theorem A.5 (Tietze extension). A topological space X is normal if and only for any closed set $C \subset X$ and any continuous function $f : C \to \mathbb { R }$ there exists a continuous function $F : X  \mathbb { R }$ such that F $( x ) = f \left( x \right)$ for all $x \in C .$ Moreover, if $f \left( C \right) \subset \left[ a , b \right]$ then F may be constructed so that 

$$
F (C) \subset [ a, b ].
$$

We now introduce the notion of a base for a topology. Let $( X , \tau )$ be a topological space. A family $\beta$ of open sets of X is a base for the topology τ if every open set $U \in \tau$ may be written as union of elements of $\beta .$ . Given a point $x \in X$ , a family $\beta _ { x }$ of neighborhoods of x is a local base at x if every neighborhood of x contains an element of $\beta _ { x }$ 

Proposition A.6. Let X be a nonempty set and let ${ \beta \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right) }$ be a family of sets such that 

(i) for every $x \in X$ there exists $B \in \beta$ such that $x \in B$ ; 

(ii) for every $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } \in \beta$ , with $B _ { 1 } \cap B _ { 2 } \neq \varnothing$ , and for every $x \in B _ { 1 } \cap B _ { 2 }$ there exists $B _ { 3 } \in \beta$ such that $x \in B _ { 3 }$ and $B _ { 3 } \subset B _ { 1 } \cap B _ { 2 }$ 

Then the collection $\tau \subset { \mathcal { P } } \left( X \right)$ of arbitrary unions of members of $\beta$ is a topology for which $\beta$ is a base. 

As we will see later on, the metrizability and the normability of a given topology depend on the properties of a base (see Theorems A.17 and A.40 below). 

Definition A.7. Let $( X , \tau )$ be a topological space. 

(i) The space X satisfies the first axiom of countability if every $x \in X$ admits a countable base of open sets. 

(ii) The space X satisfies the second axiom of countability if it has a countable base. 

The following result is used in Chapter 4. 

Theorem A.8 (Lindel¨of). Let $( X , \tau )$ be a topological space satisfying the second axiom $o f$ countability. Then every family $\mathcal { F } \subset \tau$ contains a countable subfamily $\{ U _ { n } \} \subset { \mathcal { F } }$ such that 

$$
\bigcup_ {U \in \mathcal {F}} U = \bigcup_ {n} U _ {n}.
$$

In the text we use several notions of compactness. 

## Definition A.9. Let X be a topological space.

(i) A set $K \subset X$ is compact if given any open cover of K, i.e., any collection $\{ U _ { \alpha } \}$ of elements of τ such that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { \alpha } U _ { \alpha } \supset K$ , then we may find a finite subcover (i.e., a finite subcollection $o f \left\{ U _ { \alpha } \right\}$ whose union still contains K); 

(ii) a set $E \subset X$ is relatively compact (or precompact) if its closure E is compact; 

(iii) a set $E \subset X$ is σ-compact if it can be written as a countable union of compact sets; 

(iv) the topological space X is locally compact if every point $x \in X$ has a neighborhood whose closure is compact. 

Remark A.10. A closed subset of a compact topological space is compact. On the other hand, a compact set of a Hausdorf space is closed. 

Note that if the topology is not Hausdorf then compact sets may not be closed. 

Example A.11. Given a nonempty set X endowed with the smallest topology, any nonempty set strictly contained in X is compact but not closed. 

The next theorem is used to construct cutof functions and partitions of unity. These two notions will play a central role in [FoLe10]. 

Theorem A.12. If X is a locally compact Hausdorf space and $K \subset U \subset X$ with K compact and U open, then there exists W open such that W is compact and $K \subset W \subset { \overline { { W } } } \subset U$ 

Corollary A.13. If X is a locally compact Hausdorf space and $K \subset U \subset X$ with K compact and U open, then there exists a function $\varphi \in C _ { c } ( X )$ such that $0 \leq \varphi \leq 1 , \varphi \equiv 1$ on K, and $\varphi \equiv 0$ on $X \setminus U$ 

The function $\varphi$ is usually referred to as a cutof function. To introduce partitions of unity we need the notion of a locally finite family. 

Definition A.14. Let X be a topological space and let $\mathcal { F }$ be a collection of subsets of X. Then 

(i) $\mathcal { F }$ is locally finite if every $x \in X$ has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many $U \in { \mathcal { F } }$ 

(ii) $\mathcal { F }$ is σ-locally finite $i f$ 

$$
\mathcal {F} = \bigcup_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} \mathcal {F} _ {n},
$$

where each ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ is a locally finite collection in $X$ 

We are now ready to introduce partitions of unity. Their existence is proved in Theorems 2.77 and 6.18. 

Definition A.15. If X is a topological space, a partition of unity on X is a family $\{ \varphi _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ of continuous functions $\varphi _ { \alpha } : X \to [ 0 , 1 ]$ such that 

$$
\sum_ {\alpha \in I} \varphi_ {\alpha} (x) = 1
$$

for all $x \in X$ . A partition of unity is locally finite if for every $x \in X$ there exists a neighborhood U of x such that the set $\{ \alpha \in I : U$ ∩ supp $\varphi _ { \alpha } \neq \varnothing \}$ is finite. If $\{ U _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ is an open cover of X, a partition of unity subordinated to the cover $\{ U _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ is a partition of unity $\{ \varphi _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ such that supp $\varphi _ { \alpha } \subset U _ { \alpha }$ for each $\alpha \in I$ 

## A.1.2 Metric Spaces

Definition A.16. A metric on a set X is a map d : $X \times X \to [ 0 , \infty )$ such that 

(i) d $\left( x , y \right) \leq d \left( x , z \right) + d \left( z , y \right)$ for all $x , y , z \in X$ ; 

(ii) $d \left( x , y \right) = d \left( y , x \right)$ for all $x , y \in X$ 

(iii) $d ( x , y ) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$ 

A metric space $( X , d )$ is a set X endowed with a metric d. When there is no possibility of confusion we abbreviate by saying that X is a metric space. If $r > 0$ , the (open) ball of center $x _ { 0 } \in X$ and radius r is the set 

$$
B \left(x _ {0}, r\right) := \left\{x \in X: d \left(x _ {0}, x\right) <   r \right\}.
$$

If $x \in X$ and $E \subset X$ , the distance of x from the set E is defined by 

$$
\operatorname{dist} (x, E) := \inf \left\{d (x, y): y \in E \right\},
$$

while the distance between two sets $E _ { 1 } , E _ { 2 } \subset X$ is defined by 

$$
\operatorname{dist} \left(E _ {1}, E _ {2}\right) := \inf \left\{d (x, y): x \in E _ {1}, y \in E _ {2} \right\}.
$$

A metric space $( X , d )$ can always be rendered into a topological space $( X , \tau )$ by taking as a base for the topology $\tau$ the family of all open balls. We then say that $\tau$ is determined by d. Note that $( X , \tau )$ is a Hausdorf normal space. Indeed, if $x \neq y$ then $\begin{array} { r } { B \left( x , \frac { d \left( x , y \right) } { 2 } \right) } \end{array}$ and $B \left( y , { \frac { d ( x , y ) } { 2 } } \right)$ are disjoint neigh borhoods of x and $y ,$ respectively, while if $C _ { 1 } , C _ { 2 } \subset X$ are disjoint and closed, then the open sets 

$$
U _ {1} := \left\{x \in X: \operatorname{dist} \left(x, C _ {1}\right) <   \operatorname{dist} \left(x, C _ {2}\right) \right\},
$$

$$
U _ {2} := \left\{x \in X: \operatorname{dist} \left(x, C _ {1}\right) > \operatorname{dist} \left(x, C _ {2}\right) \right\},
$$

are two disjoint neighborhoods of $C _ { 1 }$ and $C _ { 2 }$ , respectively. 

A topological space X is metrizable if its topology can be determined by a metric. 

## Theorem A.17. A topological space is metrizable if and only if

(i) singletons are closed; 

(ii) for any closed set $C \subset X$ and for any $x \notin C$ there exist disjoint open neighborhoods of C and x; 

(iii) it has a σ-locally finite base. 

A sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} \subset X$ converges (strongly) to $x \in X$ if 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} d \left(x _ {n}, x _ {0}\right) = 0.
$$

A Cauchy sequence in a metric space is a sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} \subset X$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {n, m \to \infty} d \left(x _ {n}, x _ {m}\right) = 0.
$$

A metric space X is said to be complete if every Cauchy sequence is convergent. 

Theorem A.18 (Baire category theorem). Let $( X , d )$ be a complete metric space. Then the intersection of a countable family of open dense sets in X is still dense in X. 

## A.1.3 Topological Vector Spaces

Let X be a vector space over R and let $E \subset X$ . The set E is said to be balanced if $t x \in E$ for all $x \in E$ and $t \in [ - 1 , 1 ]$ . We say that $E \subset X$ is absorbing if for every $x \in X$ there exists $t > 0$ such that $s x \in E$ for all $0 \leq s \leq t$ 

Definition A.19. Given a vector space X over R endowed with a topology τ, the $p a i r \left( X , \tau \right)$ is called a topological vector space if the functions 

$$
\begin{array}{l} X \times X \to X, \\ (x, y) \mapsto x + y, \end{array} \quad a n d \quad \begin{array}{l} \mathbb {R} \times X \to X, \\ (t, x) \mapsto t x, \end{array}
$$

are continuous with respect to $\tau$ 

Remark A.20. (i) In a topological vector space a set U is open if and only if $x + U$ is open for all $x \in X$ . Hence to give a base it is enough to give a local base at the origin. 

(ii) Using the continuity of addition and scalar multiplication it is possible to show that each neighborhood U of the origin is absorbing and it contains a neighborhood of zero W such that $W + W \subset U$ and $\bar { \overline { { W } } } \subset U$ , as well as a balanced neighborhood of zero. 

As a corollary of Theorem A.17 we have the following: 

Corollary A.21. A topological vector space is metrizable if and only if 

(i) singletons are closed; 

(ii) it has a countable base. 

Definition A.22. Let X be a topological vector space. A set $E \subset X$ is said to be topologically bounded if for each neighborhood U of 0 there exists $t > 0$ such that $E \subset t U$ 

Note that when the topology τ is generated by a metric $d ,$ sets bounded in the topological sense and in the metric sense may be diferent. To see this, it sufices to observe that the metric $\textstyle d _ { 1 } : = { \frac { d } { d + 1 } }$ generates the same topology as $d ,$ but since $d _ { 1 } \leq 1$ , every set in X is bounded with respect to $d _ { 1 }$ 

We now define Cauchy sequences in a topological vector space. 

Definition A.23. Let X be a topological vector space. A sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} \subset X$ is called a Cauchy sequence if for every neighborhood U of the origin there exists an integer $\overline { { n } } \in \mathbb { N }$ such that 

$$
x _ {n} - x _ {k} \in U
$$

for all k, $n \geq \overline { { n } }$ . The space X is complete if every Cauchy sequence is convergent. 

Note that Cauchy (and hence convergent) sequences are bounded in the topological sense. 

Proposition A.24. Let X be a topological vector space and let $\{ x _ { n } \} \subset X$ be a Cauchy sequence. Then the set $\{ x _ { n } : n \in \mathbb { N } \}$ is topologically bounded. 

Proof. Let U be a neighborhood of the origin. Using the continuity of addition, construct a balanced neighborhood of the origin W such that $W + W \subset U$ Since $\{ x _ { n } \} \subset X$ is a Cauchy sequence there exists $\overline { { n } } \in \mathbb { N }$ such that $x _ { n } { - } x _ { k } \in W$ for all $k , n \geq \pi$ . In particular, $x _ { n } \in x _ { \overline { { n } } } + W$ for all $n \geq \overline { { n } }$ . Since W is absorbing we may find $t > 1$ so large that $x _ { k } \in t W \subset t U$ for all $k = 1 , \ldots , \overline { { n } }$ . Moreover, for $n \geq \overline { { n } }$ 2 

$$
x _ {n} \in x _ {\overline {{n}}} + W \subset t W + W \subset t W + t W \subset t U,
$$

which shows that $x _ { n } \in t U$ for all $n \in \mathbb { N } .$ 

Topologically bounded sets play an important role in the normability of locally convex topological vector spaces (see Theorem A.40 below): 

Definition A.25. A topological vector space X is locally convex if every point $x \in X$ has a neighborhood that is convex. 

Proposition A.26. A locally convex topological vector space admits a local base at the origin consisting of balanced convex neighborhoods of zero. 

Let X be a vector space over R and let $E \subset X$ . The function $p _ { E } : X \to$ R defined by 

$$
p _ {E} (x) := \inf \left\{t > 0: x \in t E \right\}, \quad x \in X,
$$

is called the gauge or Minkowski functional of E. 

Definition A.27. Let X be a vector space over R. A function $p : X  \mathbb { R }$ is called a seminorm if 

$$
p (x + y) \leq p (x) + p (y)
$$

for all x, $y \in X$ and $p \left( t x \right) = \left| t \right| p \left( x \right)$ for all $x \in X$ and $t \in \mathbb { R }$ 

Remark A.28. Let X be a vector space over R and let $E \subset X$ . The gauge p of set E is a seminorm if and only if E is balanced, absorbing, and convex. 

Theorem A.29. If F is a balanced, convex local base of 0 for a locally convex topological vector space X, then the family $\{ p _ { U } : U \in { \mathcal { F } } \}$ is a family of continuous seminorms. Conversely, given a family P of seminorms on a vector space X, the collection of all finite intersections of sets of the form 

$$
V (p, n) := \left\{x \in X: p (x) <   \frac {1}{n} \right\}, \quad p \in \mathcal {P}, n \in \mathbb {N},
$$

is a balanced, convex local base of 0 for a topology τ that turns X into a locally convex topological vector space such that each p is continuous with respect to τ . 

We now $\mathrm { g i v e }$ some necessary and suficient conditions for the topology τ given in the previous theorem to be Hausdorf and for a set to be topologically bounded. 

Corollary A.30. Let P be a family of seminorms on a vector space X and let τ be the locally convex topology generated by P. Then 

$( i ) \tau$ is Hausdorf if and only if $p \left( x \right) = 0$ for all $p \in \mathcal P$ implies that $x = 0$ ; 

$( i i )$ a set $E \subset X$ is topologically bounded if and only if the set $p \left( E \right)$ is bounded in R for all $p \in \mathcal P$ 

We now introduce the notion of dual space. 

Definition A.31. Let X and Y be two vector spaces. A map $L : X \to Y$ is called a linear operator if 

(i) $L \left( x + y \right) = L \left( x \right) + L \left( y \right)$ for all x, $y \in X$ ; 

(ii) $L \left( t x \right) = t L \left( x \right)$ for all $x \in X$ and $t \in \mathbb { R }$ 

If X and Y are topological vector spaces, then the vector space of all continuous linear operators from X to Y is denoted by $\mathcal { L } \left( X ; Y \right)$ . In the special case $Y = \mathbb { R }$ , the space ${ \mathcal { L } } \left( X ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ is called the dual space of X and it is denoted by $X ^ { \prime }$ . The elements of $X ^ { \prime }$ are also called continuous linear functionals. 

The bilinear (i.e., linear in each variable) mapping 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle_ {X ^ {\prime}, X}: X ^ {\prime} \times X \to \mathbb {R}, \\ (L, x) \mapsto L (x), \end{array}\tag{A.1}
$$

is called the duality pairing. 

The dual space $\mathcal { L } \left( X ^ { \prime } ; \mathbb { R } \right)$ of $X ^ { \prime }$ is called bidual space of X and it is denoted by $X ^ { \prime \prime }$ 

Definition A.32. Let X, Y be topological vector spaces. An operator $L : X \to$ Y is bounded if it sends bounded sets of X into bounded sets of Y. 

Theorem A.33. Let X, Y be topological vector spaces and let $L : X \to Y$ be linear and continuous. Then L is bounded. 

Proof. Let $E \subset X$ be a bounded set and let $W \subset Y$ be a neighborhood of zero. Since L is continuous and $L \left( 0 \right) = 0$ , there exists a neighborhood $U \subset X$ of zero such that $L \left( U \right) \subset W$ . By the boundedness of E there exists $t > 0$ such that $E \subset t U$ . Hence 

$$
L (E) \subset L (t U) = t L (U) \subset t W.
$$

This shows that $L \left( E \right)$ is bounded in $Y$ . 

Exercise A.34. On the vector space $C \left( \left[ 0 , 1 \right] \right)$ consider two topologies, the first, τ, given by the metric 

$$
d (f, g) = \int_ {0} ^ {1} \frac {| f (x) - g (x) |}{1 + | f (x) - g (x) |} d x, \quad f, g \in C ([ 0, 1 ]),
$$

and the second, $\tau _ { p }$ , given by the family of seminorms $\left\{ p _ { x } \right\} _ { x \in [ 0 , 1 ] }$ , where 

$$
p _ {x} (f) := | f (x) |, \quad f \in C ([ 0, 1 ]).
$$

Prove that 

1. the identity $I : \left( C \left( \left[ 0 , 1 \right] \right) , \tau _ { p } \right) \ \longrightarrow \ \left( C \left[ 0 , 1 \right] , \tau \right)$ maps bounded sets into bounded sets; 

2. the identity $I : ( C ( [ 0 , 1 ] ) , \tau _ { p } )  ( C [ 0 , 1 ] , \tau )$ is sequentially continuous but not continuous. 

3. Deduce that the topology $\tau _ { p }$ is not compatible with any metric. 

We now present several versions of the Hahn–Banach theorem. These are heavily used in the second part of the text, starting from Chapter 4. 

Theorem A.35 (Hahn–Banach, analytic form). Let X be a vector space, let Y be a subspace of X, and let $p : X  \mathbb { R }$ be a convex function. Then for any linear functional $L : Y  \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
L (x) \leq p (x) \quad f o r a l l x \in Y
$$

there exists a linear functional $L _ { 1 } : X \to \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
L _ {1} (x) = L (x) \quad f o r a l l x \in Y
$$

and 

$$
L (x) \leq p (x) \quad f o r a l l x \in X.
$$

The finite-dimensional version of the next theorem may be found in Chapter 4. 

Theorem A.36 (Hahn–Banach, first geometric form). Let X be a topological vector space, and let $E , ~ F ~ \subset ~ X$ be nonempty disjoint convex sets. Assume that E has an interior point. Then there exist a continuous linear functional $L : X \to \mathbb { R } , L \neq 0$ , and a number $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ such that 

$$
L (x) \geq \alpha \quad f o r a l l x \in E a n d L (x) \leq \alpha \quad f o r a l l x \in F.
$$

As a corollary of Hahn–Banach theorem one can prove the following result (see also Exercise 2.43). 

Corollary A.37. Let X be a topological vector space. Then the dual $X ^ { \prime }$ of X is not the null space if and only if X has a convex neighborhood of the origin strictly contained in X. 

In view of the previous corollary it is natural to restrict attention to locally convex topological vector spaces. 

Theorem A.38 (Hahn–Banach, second geometric form). Let X be a locally convex topological vector space, and let C, $K \subset X$ be nonempty disjoint convex sets, with C closed and K compact. Then there exist a continuous linear functional $L : X \to \mathbb { R }$ and two numbers $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that 

$L \left( x \right) \leq \alpha - \varepsilon$ for all $x \in C$ and $L \left( x \right) \geq \alpha + \varepsilon$ for all $x \in K$ 

## A.1.4 Normed Spaces

Definition A.39. A norm on a vector space X is a map 

$$
\| \cdot \|: X \to [ 0, \infty)
$$

such that 

(i) $\left\| x + y \right\| \leq \left\| x \right\| + \left\| y \right\| { \mathrm { ~ } } f o r { \mathrm { ~ } } a l l { \mathrm { ~ } } x , y \in X ,$ 

(ii) tx = |t| x for all x ∈ X and $t \in \mathbb { R }$ ; 

(iii) $\| x \| = 0$ implies $x = 0$ 

A normed space $( X , \| \cdot \| )$ is a vector space X endowed with a norm ·. For simplicity, we often say that X is a normed space. 

If for every x, $y \in X$ we define 

$$
d \left(x, y\right) := \left\| x - y \right\|,
$$

then $( X , d )$ is a metric space. We say that a normed space X is a Banach space if it is complete as a metric space. 

A topological vector space is normable if its topology can be determined by a norm. 

Theorem A.40. A topological vector space X is normable if and only if it is locally convex and it has a topologically bounded neighborhood of 0. 

Two norms $\left\| \cdot \right\| _ { 1 }$ and $\lVert \cdot \rVert _ { 2 }$ are equivalent if there exists a positive constant $C > 0$ such that 

$$
\frac {1}{C} \| x \| _ {1} \leq \| x \| _ {2} \leq C \| x \| _ {1} \quad \text { for   all } x \in X.
$$

Equivalent norms induce the same topology on $X ,$ . 

Proposition A.41. Let X and Y be normed spaces with norms $\left\| \cdot \right\| _ { X }$ and $\lVert \cdot \rVert _ { Y }$ , respectively. 

(i) A linear operator $L : X \to Y$ is continuous if and only if 

$$
\| L \| _ {\mathcal {L} (X; Y)} := \sup _ {x \in X \setminus \{0 \}} \frac {\| L (x) \| _ {Y}}{\| x \| _ {X}} <   \infty ;
$$

(ii) the mapping $L \in { \mathcal { L } } \left( X ; Y \right) \mapsto \| L \| _ { \mathcal { L } ( X ; Y ) }$ is a norm; 

(iii) if Y is a Banach space then so is $\mathcal { L } \left( X ; Y \right)$ ; conversely, if $X \neq \{ 0 \}$ and $\mathcal { L } \left( X ; Y \right)$ is a Banach space then so is Y. 

As a corollary of the Hahn–Banach theorem one has the following result. 

Corollary A.42. Let X be a normed space. Then for all $x \in X$ 

$$
\| x \| _ {X} = \max _ {L \in X ^ {\prime}, \| L \| _ {X ^ {\prime}} \leq 1} \frac {| L (x) |}{\| x \| _ {X}}.
$$

Remark A.43. This corollary is especially useful for $L ^ { p }$ spaces. 

Theorem A.44 (Banach–Steinhaus). Let X, Y be Banach spaces and let $\{ L _ { \alpha } \} _ { \alpha \in I }$ be a family of linear continuous operators $L _ { \alpha } : X \to Y$ such that 

$$
\sup _ {\alpha \in I} \| L _ {\alpha} (x) \| _ {Y} <   \infty
$$

for every $x \in X$ . Then 

$$
\sup _ {\alpha \in I} \| L _ {\alpha} \| _ {\mathcal {L} (X; Y)} <   \infty .
$$

Definition A.45. Let X and Y be normed spaces with norms $\left\| \cdot \right\| _ { X }$ and $\lVert \cdot \rVert _ { Y }$ A continuous linear operator $L \in \mathcal { L } \left( X ; Y \right)$ is said to be compact if it maps every bounded subset of X onto a relatively compact subset of Y. 

In particular, if L is compact then from every bounded sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} \subset X$ we may extract a subsequence $\{ x _ { n _ { k } } \}$ such that $\{ L \left( x _ { n _ { k } } \right) \}$ converges in Y. 

Definition A.46. We say that the normed space X is embedded in the normed space Y and we write 

$$
X \hookrightarrow Y
$$

if X is a vector subspace of Y and the immersion 

$$
\begin{array}{c} i: X \to Y, \\ x \mapsto x, \end{array}
$$

is continuous. 

Note that since the immersion is linear, in view of Proposition A.41 the continuity of i is equivalent to requiring the existence of a constant $M > 0$ such that 

$$
\left\| x \right\| _ {Y} \leq M \left\| x \right\| _ {X} \quad \text { for   all } x \in X.
$$

We say that X is compactly embedded in Y if the immersion i is a compact operator. Compact embeddings will play an important role in the study of Sobolev spaces in [FoLe10]. 

## A.1.5 Weak Topologies

Given a locally convex topological vector space X, for each $L \in X ^ { \prime }$ the function $p _ { L } : X \to [ 0 , \infty )$ defined by 

$$
p _ {L} (x) := | L (x) |, \quad x \in X,\tag{A.2}
$$

is a seminorm. In view of Theorem A.29, the family of seminorms $\{ p _ { L } \} _ { L \in X ^ { \prime } }$ generates a locally convex topology $\sigma \left( X , X ^ { \prime } \right)$ on the space X, called the weak topology, such that each $p _ { L }$ is continuous with respect to $\sigma \left( X , X ^ { \prime } \right)$ . In turn, this implies that every $L \in X ^ { \prime }$ is $\sigma \left( X , X ^ { \prime } \right)$ continuous. 

Theorem A.47. Let X be a locally convex topological vector space and let $E \subset X$ . Then 

(i) E is bounded with respect to the (strong) topology if and only if it weakly bounded; 

(ii) if E is convex then E is closed if and only if it weakly closed. 

Definition A.48. Given a locally convex topological vector space X, a sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} \subset X$ converges weakly to $x \in X$ if it converges to x with respect to the weak topology $\sigma \left( X , X ^ { \prime } \right)$ 

We write $x _ { n } \to x$ . In view of Theorem A.29 and (A.2), we have the following result. 

Proposition A.49. Let X be a locally convex topological vector space. A sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} \subset X$ converges weakly to $x \in X$ if and only if 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} L (x _ {n}) = L (x)
$$

for every $L \in X ^ { \prime }$ 

Similarly, given a locally convex topological vector space X, for each $x \in X$ the function $p _ { x } : X ^ { \prime } \to [ 0 , \infty )$ defined by 

$$
p _ {x} (L) := | L (x) |, \quad L \in X ^ {\prime},\tag{A.3}
$$

is a seminorm. In view of Theorem A.29, the family of seminorms $\{ p _ { x } \} _ { x \in X }$ generates a locally convex topology $\sigma \left( X ^ { \prime } , X \right)$ on the space $X ^ { \prime }$ , called the weak star topology, such that each $p _ { x }$ is continuous with respect to $\sigma \left( X ^ { \prime } , X \right)$ 

Definition A.50. Let X be a locally convex topological vector space. A sequence $\{ L _ { n } \} \subset X ^ { \prime }$ is weakly star convergent to L in $X ^ { \prime }$ if it converges to L with respect to the weak star topology $\sigma \left( X ^ { \prime } , X \right)$ 

We write $L _ { n } \stackrel { * } { \to } L$ . In view of Theorem A.29 and (A.3), we have the following result. 

Proposition A.51. Let X be a locally convex topological vector space. A sequence $\{ L _ { n } \} \subset X ^ { \prime }$ converges weakly star to $L \in X ^ { \prime }$ if and only if 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} L _ {n} (x) = L (x)
$$

for every $x \in X$ 

Theorem A.52 (Banach–Alaoglu). If U is a neighborhood of 0 in a locally convex topological vector space $X$ , then 

$$
K := \{L \in X ^ {\prime}: | L (x) | \leq 1 \text {   for   every   } x \in U \}
$$

is weak star compact. 

Corollary A.53. If X is a normed space then the closed unit ball of $X ^ { \prime }$ , 

$$
\left\{L \in X ^ {\prime}: \| L \| _ {X ^ {\prime}} \leq 1 \right\},
$$

is weak star compact. 

If X is separable, it actually turns out that weak star compact sets are metrizable, and thus one can work with the friendlier notion of sequentia compactness. 

Theorem A.54. Let X be a separable, locally convex topological vector space and let $K \subset X ^ { \prime }$ be weak star compact. Then $( K , \sigma \left( { X } ^ { \prime } , X \right) )$ is metrizable. 

Hence, also in view of the Banach–Alaoglu theorem, we have the following: 

Corollary A.55. Let U be a neighborhood of 0 in a separable locally convex topological vector space X and let $\{ L _ { n } \} \subset X ^ { \prime }$ be such that 

$| L _ { n } \left( x \right) | \leq 1$ for every $x \in U$ and for all $n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

Then there exists a subsequence $\left\{ L _ { n _ { k } } \right\}$ that is weakly star convergent. In particular, if X is a separable Banach space and $\{ L _ { n } \} \subset X ^ { \prime }$ is any bounded sequence in $X ^ { \prime }$ , then there exists a subsequence that is weakly star convergent. 

For Banach spaces the converse of Theorem A.54 holds: 

Theorem A.56. Let X be a Banach space. Then the unit ball $B \left( 0 ; 1 \right)$ in $X ^ { \prime }$ endowed with the weak star topology is metrizable if and only if X is separable. 

Proposition A.57. Let X be a Banach space. If a sequence $\{ L _ { n } \} \subset X ^ { \prime }$ converges weakly star to $L \in X ^ { \prime }$ , then it is bounded and 

$$
\| L \| _ {X ^ {\prime}} \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \| L _ {n} \| _ {X ^ {\prime}}  .
$$

Proposition A.58. Let X be a Banach space. If $X ^ { \prime }$ is separable then so is X. 

The converse is false in general (take, for example, the separable space $L ^ { 1 } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { N } \right)$ and its dual $L ^ { \infty } \left( \mathbb { R } ^ { \bar { N } } \right) )$ ). 

We now study analogous results for the weak topology. An infinitedimensional Banach space when endowed with the weak topology is never metrizable. However, we have the following: 

Theorem A.59. Let X be a Banach space whose dual $X ^ { \prime }$ is separable. Then the unit ball $B \left( 0 ; 1 \right)$ endowed with the weak topology is metrizable. 

Definition A.60. Let X be a locally convex topological vector space. A set $K \subset X$ is called sequentially weakly compact if every sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} \subset K$ has a subsequence converging weakly to a point in K. 

Theorem A.61. Let X be a Banach space. If $K \subset X$ is weakly compact then it is weakly sequentially compact. 

Using Banach–Alaoglu’s theorem one can prove the following theorem: 

Theorem A.62 (Eberlein–Smulian).<sup>ˇ</sup> Let E be a subset of a Banach space X. Then the weak closure of E is weakly compact if and only if for any sequence $\{ x _ { n } \} \subset E$ there exists a subsequence weakly convergent to some element of X. 

As an immediate application of the Hahn–Banach theorem we have the following: 

Proposition A.63. Let X be a normed space and consider the linear operator mapping $J : X  X ^ { \prime \prime }$ defined by 

$$
J (x) (L) := L (x), \quad L \in X ^ {\prime}.
$$

Then $\| J \left( x \right) \| _ { X ^ { \prime \prime } } = \| x \| _ { X }$ for all $x \in X$ . In particular, J is injective and continuous.
